Airbnb has teased its plans to build its own AI travel agent before, but on Thursday the company announced that the new AI feature will launch in the first half of 2027. In the company’s Q3 shareholder letter on Thursday , Airbnb also provided more detail about how the agent will work, what it will actually do, and how it’s different from a typical AI chatbot.

In prior interviews, CEO Brian Chesky sketched out the travel company’s approach to AI, describing a plan to build an AI agent that has a richer interface than a conventional chatbot. He also expressed his opinions about how chatbots aren’t the right interface for travel, noting that people take pleasure in the planning process and in anticipating a trip. Any agent that it built, then, shouldn’t take away from the inspiration and the browsing, he told TechCrunch in an interview last month.

Chesky today reiterated that belief, telling analysts on the earnings call that people won’t use one AI agent for everything.

“Today’s AI agents like Muse and Instinct are good at simple routine tasks like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment. But planning a trip is different,” he said. “Travel is aspirational. Discovering where to go and where to stay is part of the experience. In fact, 80% of travelers say they enjoy spending time researching trips. People want to look at photos. They want to compare homes. They want to make decisions with people they’re traveling with,” he continued. “And I don’t think the general-purpose agents are the best to do that. So that is why we are building our own AI agent,” Chesky said.

Airbnb described its agent as having a personalized interface that’s designed specifically for travel, where it will “build an interface” around a user’s question instead of simply responding as a chatbot would.

“What we are doing is developing a custom-designed AI-native experience that responds to what guests are looking for,” Chesky said. “So instead of relying on traditional chat alone, which is very text-heavy—which, again, is definitely not the way you should plan travel, our agent draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface components—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what they’re looking for.”

The exec said the agent will feel “a little bit like generative UI” as it’s designed to offer up “the right interface at the right time” for someone’s specific travel needs.

In its shareholder letter, the company touted that its nearly 20 years of experience in bringing hosts and guests together is informing how the agent is built, as it incorporates insights about how people both book and host on its platform. The agent will also be able to help travelers beyond the booking itself.

“Our agent will be able to help guests throughout their trip—from changing a reservation or resolving a payment issue to getting help with refunds, rebooking, or 24-hour safety support. These are things an outside agent can’t easily do on its own,” the company wrote.

Over time, Airbnb expects the agent will be able to help travelers with other aspects of their trip, including not only homes and hotels, but also services and experiences. Services and experiences are two areas that have become a bigger focus for the company following its redesign last year.

While the company previously said to expect its AI agent sometime in the next year, it’s now more specifically committing to roll out the new technology to consumers in the first half of 2027.

The news of the agent’s release was delivered alongside strong third-quarter earnings, with revenue growing 19% to $4.87 billion, topping Wall Street estimates. It also raised its 2026 revenue growth forecast, which it now predicts will be in the high teens, instead of the mid-teens.

“Airbnb is back in growth mode,” Chesky told analysts on the Q3 earnings call on Thursday. “It’s rare for a marketplace of our size to reaccelerate growth, but that’s exactly what we’re doing. Q3 was our fastest revenue growth in more than three years,” he added.

scraped.description: Nasdaq’s slide into correction territory puts its history of recoveries in focus. Here's what history shows.
scraped.author: Deena Zaidi,Nick Wells
scraped.h1: Nasdaq drops into correction territory — here’s what typically happens next
scraped.body_text:
In this article

The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later.

The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market.

Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022.

Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months.

The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later.

The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development.

Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade.

Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well.

The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974.

"The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said.

Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said.

Chip stocks tumbled Thursday, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) falling 12% and for its worst day since the Covid-19 breakout of March 2020.

— CNBC's Fred Imbert contributed to the report

articles.title: Oigan, políticos: está bien hablar sobre el cambio climático
articles.summary: Los votantes latinos están preocupados por el cambio climático y se encuentran entre los más confiados en su capacidad para generar cambios políticos.
articles.ai_summary: Latino voters express significant concern about climate change and confidence in their ability to influence political change.

scraped.title: Oigan, políticos: está bien hablar sobre el cambio climático » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Los votantes latinos están preocupados por el cambio climático y se encuentran entre los más confiados en su capacidad para generar cambios políticos.
scraped.author: Pearl Marvell
scraped.h1: Oigan, políticos: está bien hablar sobre el cambio climático
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Mientras se asienta el polvo tras las elecciones de mitad de mandato, una cosa resulta evidente: los latinos están furiosos con Trump.

The New York Times estima que los demócratas obtuvieron el 69% del voto hispano, un cambio de 29 puntos respecto de 2024. Probablemente sea una respuesta a las redadas del ICE, que han deportado e incluso matado a seres queridos, y al aumento del costo de la vida cotidiana. Pero muchos latinos también viven en zonas afectadas de manera desproporcionada por impactos climáticos como el calor extremo y las inundaciones, lugares conocidos como comunidades de primera línea.

Para conocer mejor lo ocurrido en las elecciones de mitad de mandato, Yale Climate Connections conversó con Jennifer Carman, directora de estrategia de encuestas del Programa de Yale sobre Comunicación del Cambio Climático y autora principal de un reciente estudio revisado por pares sobre las actitudes frente al clima en comunidades de primera línea. (El YPCCC es la organización editora de Yale Climate Connections).

Esta entrevista ha sido editada y condensada.

Yale Climate Connections: ¿Cómo se siente ante lo que acabamos de presenciar?

Jennifer Carman: Muchos de los lugares de Estados Unidos donde están las comunidades de primera línea son también los más preocupados por el cambio climático : los latinos, las personas del suroeste y quienes viven en las zonas fronterizas. Cuando se profundiza en esas comunidades, se observa que experimentan muchos cambios en su forma de votar.

Valoramos mucho tus perspectivas, por lo tanto, queremos que nos mandes tus preguntas sobre el cambio climático y sus efectos.

Las considero un grupo electoralmente muy disputado. Pero lo que estamos viendo es cuán increíblemente poderosas y eficaces pueden ser como bloque electoral. También lo vimos en 2024, porque experimentaron algunos de los mayores giros hacia Trump en 2024, y esa fue entonces la gran historia.

Lo que vemos este año es que realmente han dado marcha atrás. Y en algunos lugares, especialmente si se observan los condados fronterizos de Texas, algunos de esos giros hacia los demócratas son incluso mayores que los que ocurrieron en 2024.

Mi advertencia para los demócratas es que tampoco deberían considerar esto como un realineamiento permanente. Creo que, según lo que hagan los demócratas con el poder que tienen, se definirá si continúan contando con el apoyo de los latinos en las zonas fronterizas durante el próximo ciclo electoral.

YCC: ¿Qué sabemos sobre lo que piensan los latinos acerca del cambio climático?

Carman: A los latinos les preocupa más el cambio climático que a otros grupos raciales y étnicos de Estados Unidos.

También el cambio climático les afecta de maneras particulares. Las comunidades latinas enfrentan muchos impactos climáticos según el lugar donde viven; muchos latinos trabajan al aire libre y en las regiones más calurosas del país. Por eso tantas de nuestras comunidades de primera línea son desproporcionadamente latinas.

¡No podemos hacer este trabajo sin ti! Aproximadamente el 83 % de cada dólar que donas se destina directamente a pagar a nuestro equipo de reporteros, editores, meteorólogos y productores de radio. El otro 17 % cubre este sitio web, computadoras portátiles, un sistema de nómina y otros gastos similares necesarios para nuestro trabajo.

Desde mi perspectiva, lo importante que hay que tener presente es involucrar a las comunidades de primera línea y a las comunidades latinas, no solo en este ciclo electoral, sino en todos los ciclos electorales. Pero creo que este ciclo demuestra que, si se produce esa participación, es posible ganar, y ganar por márgenes sorprendentemente grandes; incluso lograr cambios en estados que los demócratas no creían que podían ganar.

YCC: ¿Necesitan los comunicadores sobre cambio climático hacer más para destacar la intersección entre estos temas y el cambio climático?

Carman: Creo que necesitamos tener más conversaciones sobre el cambio climático como un tema muy práctico, como algo que afecta la vida de las personas y que incide en los asuntos de los que ya estamos hablando: el hecho de que la gente está sufriendo más daños por el calor y facturas más altas. Sabemos que, si se experimentan temperaturas más altas, hay que usar el aire acondicionado con más frecuencia, y eso es costoso; o, si no se tiene aire acondicionado, se sufre. Hay partes del país donde hace un calor extremo y las personas no pueden permitirse tener aire acondicionado o no pueden permitirse usarlo.

YCC: O no tienen derecho a instalarlo si alquilan la vivienda.

El clima está cambiando y nuestros periodistas están aquí para ayudarte a comprender lo que está pasando. ¡Suscríbete a nuestro boletín informativo y nunca te pierdas una historia!

Carman: Sí, exactamente. Hay estudios que han concluido que los apartamentos [sin aire acondicionado] pueden superar los 100 grados Fahrenheit en verano, y eso tiene efectos económicos y sobre la salud. Muchos de estos problemas relacionados con el costo de la vida se ven agravados por el cambio climático.

Cuando se trata de hablar sobre el cambio climático, es realmente importante hacerlo no solo como un problema amplio y abstracto que nos afecta a todos, sino también como algo que nos afecta personalmente. También nos afecta individualmente a todos. Por ejemplo, hoy en mi oficina hacen 80 grados Fahrenheit en noviembre.

Hablar sobre el cambio climático puede ser realmente intimidante. Creo que esa es parte de la razón por la que ocurre este silenciamiento climático. Suena como algo enorme, y uno no quiere tener una conversación sobre sistemas gigantescos, corrientes oceánicas y todas estas diversas cosas interconectadas. El cambio climático sí tiene esos efectos, pero también tiene consecuencias muy personales y directas. Y hay cosas que la gente puede hacer al respecto. Por ejemplo, votar.

Ponerle un nombre a lo que las personas están experimentando es muy poderoso. Está haciendo más calor, y el hecho de que haga mucho más calor es peligroso. Y el hecho de que haya más inundaciones, de que estemos teniendo estas lluvias torrenciales inusuales en el suroeste y en Florida, incendios forestales en Hawái y olas de calor en Alaska: es realmente importante ponerle un nombre a eso, y tenemos un nombre para ello. Ese nombre es cambio climático.

YCC: ¿De dónde proviene el silenciamiento climático?

Carman: Creo que proviene de varias cosas. Una de ellas es qué voces se amplifican. El grupo de los Desestimadores [del cambio climático] representa alrededor del 11% [del público estadounidense], mientras que los Alarmados constituyen aproximadamente el 25% de la población. Es decir, hay dos veces y media más Alarmados que Desestimadores, pero siempre sorprende a la gente cuando se le dice eso, porque los Desestimadores son muy ruidosos y reciben mucha exposición en las plataformas. Hay canales de noticias enteros que usan principalmente el tiempo y el espacio de que disponen para amplificar las voces de los Desestimadores, como nuestro presidente.

Leer: Las Seis Américas del calentamiento global

Cuando esas son las voces que se escuchan, eso es lo que uno cree que piensa todo el mundo. También puede resultar intimidante cuestionarlas.

Sigue nuestro canal de WhatsApp y suscríbete a nuestro canal de Youtube .

Los políticos tienen mucho más permiso para hablar del cambio climático de lo que creen. Al entrar en este próximo Congreso, lo que realmente espero que ocurra es que los miembros del Congreso puedan verlo. Muchas políticas destinadas a reducir los impactos del cambio climático y a proteger a las personas de sus efectos son muy populares.

El noventa y dos por ciento de los votantes registrados apoya proteger a los trabajadores de niveles peligrosos de calor, y es una de esas políticas que parecen de sentido común. Sin embargo, Florida y Texas han prohibido las leyes de protección contra el calor.

Las comunidades de primera línea son fundamentales para construir coaliciones porque desempeñan un papel importante no solo al conectar el clima con estos otros temas, sino también con todos ellos. Todas estas cuestiones de asequibilidad: las comunidades de primera línea las han estado experimentando durante décadas.

YCC: Y los latinos son el grupo demográfico que más cree en su capacidad de generar cambios colectivos a nivel gubernamental.

Carman: Creo que es importante reconocer que las comunidades de primera línea no están indefensas. Debido al abandono histórico, las personas han tenido que asumir muchas responsabilidades por sí mismas, pero el potencial de acción política es realmente alto.

Ya están haciendo mucho para protegerse. Hay mucho desarrollo de capacidades y poder comunitario en las comunidades de primera línea, y creo que las personas dentro de esas comunidades lo saben. Pueden servir como ejemplos poderosos, ejercer un liderazgo sólido y representar un gran potencial de poder político. Creo que es importante que el movimiento climático y los políticos en general tengan esto presente, especialmente a medida que avance el nuevo Congreso.

scraped.body_text:

By Gabrielle Becerra Mellet

ABC South West WA

Topic: Oceans

The whale carcass washed ashore at Peppermint Grove beach in Capel. ( ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

A 12.5-metre whale carcass in WA's South West is at least the fourth dead whale to wash up on WA beaches in recent weeks.

Debate continues over how best to remove the remains and who should pay.

Peppermint Grove Beach will remain closed into next week, as shark patrols and site testing continue.

A run of whale carcasses washing up on West Australian beaches has sparked debate on the best method to remove remains and who should foot the bill.

Whale researchers say centralised responsibility and offshore disposal are the preferable approaches, but concede both carry complications.

Peppermint Grove Beach, around 200km south of Perth in the Shire of Capel, was the latest to deal with the problem, with the rotting 12.5-metre humpback washing ashore on Tuesday.

The 14-tonne carcass was removed with a crane on Wednesday and trucked to a disposal site.

It is at least the fourth whale carcass to have washed up on a WA beach in recent weeks.

The whale was removed by crane and buried on shore. ( ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

The state government insists the responsibility for removals rests with the land manager, which in most cases is the local government.

The policy left one Perth council saddled with a bill of almost $180,000 to remove a carcass from its beach.

While the Shire of Capel has not revealed the cost of the removal, it noted the process was "entirely necessary" in the interests of public safety.

Shire president John Fergusson said a formal agreement between councils and state government was needed to manage whale disposal.

The Shire of Capel says the beach will be closed for at least a week for testing and patrols. ( ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

"I think there probably should be some cooperative or mutual model available for this type of procedure," he said.

Griffith University marine scientist Olaf Meynecke said dealing with dead whales was complex and costly, and most local councils lacked the appropriate resources.

"They do not have the knowledge, the management plans in place," Dr Meynecke said.

"It's a big burden; the issue of carcass removal should be centralised, and it should come from at least the state."

Olaf Meynecke says removing whale carcasses is complex and costly. ( ABC: Glenn Mullane )

A Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions spokesperson said it had been in contact with the Shire of Capel regarding the removal.

"DBCA will provide technical advice on carcass handling and removal, access to specialist equipment and experienced staff to assist with the operation if required," they said.

Transporting to landfill remains the most common method of carcass disposal.

Some researchers say towing a whale back out to sea, where possible, is preferred. ( ABC South West WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet )

But Macquarie University marine scientist Vanessa Pirotta said towing the remains back out to sea was preferable.

"[It] means the animal can go back into the environment and have the animal contribute back to the natural ecosystem that it was a part of," Dr Pirotta said.

But she acknowledged complications with this method, including the risk of the carcass washing back on shore.

Vanessa Pirotta says taking whale remains back out to sea is preferable, but carries risks. ( ABC News )

"Authorities and decision makers will need to ensure that the whale is disposed of correctly to ensure that there's not a risk of an animal stranding again due to currents or weather," she said.

Dr Meynecke said towing a whale offshore was ethical and environmentally friendly, with satellite tracking and search-and-rescue software a potential resource.

"The idea is that the modelling allows us to predict where the whale might end up when we place it in a certain area out at sea," he said.

Crowds gather at a whale carcass that washed up at City Beach in Perth. ( ABC News: Andrew O'Connor )

"If we're tracking it live with a satellite tracker, we know exactly where it's going, and if it does happen to move back to shore, it can be intercepted again with the same contractor."

Mr Fergusson said he understood calls for the remains to be towed out to sea, but the risks were high.

"If you're towing it offshore and it's shedding, then it's providing attraction for sharks," he said.

"If you do tow it offshore, unless you tow it a long, long way, there's a very real risk it will just wash back up on shore."

scraped.h1: Sony revives the original Walkman headphones, adds USB-C
scraped.body_text:
Orange ear cushions included.

Color us nostalgic.

Sony has brought back the MDR-3-series headphones that debuted in 1979 alongside the Walkman TPS-L2 cassette player.

Originally called the “MDR-3L2,” the first Walkman headphones were known for their sleek, adjustable gray plastic headband, which extended via metal sliders and ended in signature orange, circular ear cushions. The lightweight, on-ear headphones are a contrast to the bulky headsets that are popular these days, which use wide, cushioned headbands for long-term comfort and large earcups that can support big drivers and are often heavily padded for noise isolation.

The new MDR-3R (note the slightly different name) headphones look just like the originals and come with orange and blue ear cushions.

New headphones are often wireless these days, but the MDR-3R continues the wired tradition of the MDR-3, with an essential twist: a USB-C connector.

“The MDR-3R has been redesigned for modern use while preserving the experience value of freely taking music out into the world, which the original MDR-3 helped popularize,” Sony’s announcement says.

For better or worse, the new headphones also use “the same 23 mm driver units as the MDR-3 to reproduce sound quality close to the original,” per Sony. Audiophiles will prefer something more advanced, perhaps with additional acoustic features. A review of the new headphones from Gizmodo says that the MDR-3R headphones “hold their own,” have “bright and clear” mids and highs, and good stereo separation. However, we don’t expect strong bass.

Unlike their predecessor, the MDR-3R has an in-line remote control and an integrated microphone. Without noise-canceling, though, the microphone isn’t ideal for calls in noisy environments.

But nostalgic gear isn’t about having top-of-the-line capabilities; it’s about showing off your love of old-school tech while enjoying familiar technologies that have reliably served their functions for years.

The MDR-3R may also capitalize on surging renewed interest in wired headphones and even physical media and Walkmans. Today’s Walkmans aren’t cassette players, of course, but are Android-powered , touchscreen media players.

The headphones are available for $60.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

scraped.h1: Generation Z and diversity redefine US politics in groundbreaking election
scraped.body_text:
Melat Kiros becomes the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress, embodying a new era of political representation.

Save

Share

The outcome of the 2026 US midterm elections has marked a historic shift in American politics, as a new generation of younger and more diverse leaders won key positions across the country.

Out of 117 Generation Z candidates who ran for Congress this year, 24 made it onto the general election ballot. Among them was Melat Kiros, a 29-year-old Ethiopian-born democratic socialist from Colorado, who became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. She joins Representative Maxwell Frost of Florida, who became the first Gen Z member of the House in 2022.

The election brought several historic breakthroughs for marginalized and underrepresented groups:

First Muslim American Senator: Dr. Abdul El-Sayed won his race in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the US Senate.

First Native American Woman Senator: Peggy Flanagan was elected to the Senate, following Deb Haaland’s victory as governor of New Mexico.

Historic Senate Representation: Illinois became the first state represented in the Senate by two women of color (Juliana Stratton and Tammy Duckworth).

Additionally, three Black women will serve in the Senate at the same time for the first time in U.S. history.

State governor races saw record-breaking diversity across the country:

Black Leadership: Keisha Lance Bottoms (Georgia) became the first Black woman elected governor in US history. Alongside new governors Byron Donalds (Florida), David Crowley (Wisconsin), Aaron Ford (Nevada), and re-elected Wes Moore (Maryland), a record five Black governors will serve together in 2027.

Latino Leadership: Gina Hinojosa became Texas’s first Latina governor after defeating incumbent Greg Abbott, while Xavier Becerra became California’s first Latino governor since 1875.

Amy Acton (Ohio), Amy Klobuchar (Minnesota), and Marsha Blackburn (Tennessee) all became the first female governors of their respective states. In total, at least 17 women will serve as governors in 2027, breaking the previous record of 14.

Women also set new records in the House of Representatives:

Democratic women won at least 100 House seats, setting a new record for the party.

Overall female representation in the House is projected to reach at least 139 seats in the upcoming 120th Congress.

scraped.title: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
scraped.description: The new Michigan senator will face an uphill battle to transform the U.S. relationship with Israel. But he has options — and public pressure.
scraped.author: Jonah Valdez
scraped.h1: Abdul El-Sayed Won His Senate Seat With a Mandate on Palestine. Can He Deliver?
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

The new senator from Michigan will face an uphill battle if he wants to transform the U.S. relationship with Israel. But he has options — and public pressure.

One senator out of the 100 who will fill the upper chamber of the 120th Congress was elected to his seat on a loud campaign promise to end U.S. complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

Abdul El-Sayed will walk into a newfound Democratic majority after animating his base with pro-Palestine pledges seldom heard from a U.S. Senate contender. As a first-term senator, he’ll lack seniority on the committees to which he’s assigned. And although his critiques of the U.S. relationship with Israel have proven overwhelmingly popular in public opinion surveys and among voters at the polls, the same can’t be said for most of his soon-to-be colleagues.

“It’s going to be a fight,” said Beth Miller, political advocacy director for Jewish Voice for Peace Action, which supported El-Sayed’s campaign. “The Democratic establishment, when it’s in control, has not taken measures in support of Palestine in the past. And so this is about making sure that now they finally start listening to what the overwhelming majority of their bases say.”

El-Sayed’s run marked the first time the Jewish-led, anti-Zionist group backed a Senate campaign . Pro-Palestine lobbying groups like JVP Action have been pushing for legislation to block weapons transfers to Israel for years , aligning themselves with a small but growing number of left-leaning House members. The group helped author the Block the Bombs Act, introduced by Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., which netted 82 co-sponsors and became a pro-Palestine litmus test in some Democratic primary campaigns.

Building consensus around a single bill in the Senate is harder, but the upper chamber offers stronger levers to pull. Senators can force votes called Joint Resolutions of Disapproval that would block foreign security assistance, such as weapons sales to Israel. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has exercised this option repeatedly throughout the genocide in Gaza to try and block the sale of certain bombs, firearms, and other military equipment to Israel. While his resolutions failed in the Republican-controlled Senate , the most recent ones drew support from wide majorities of Democrats — soon to be the party in power.

Yet with the looming threat that Democrats might actually be able to pass legislation, El-Sayed would find himself under pressure from the likely Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, who has long maintained the support of the pro-Israel lobby , to fall in line with party priorities.

“The question is, ‘Who does he want to be?’ Does he want to be someone like Bernie, who is willing to sometimes stand up to leadership?” said Hamid Bendaas, communications director for the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which also backed El-Sayed’s run. “It’s hard to do that as a freshman and someone who’s just getting in there.”

Bendaas expressed confidence that the Michigan senator would be a champion of pro-Palestine legislation, but he noted that El-Sayed would have to balance his priorities, especially after running a campaign focused on economic populism and providing universal healthcare through Medicare for All.

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

There is a tension revealed by the dilemma facing Sen.-elect El-Sayed: While a growing share of Americans — and an overwhelming majority of Democrats — disapprove of the U.S. spending billions of dollars on aid to Israel, voters’ clear No. 1 concern in the 2026 election cycle was the cost of living and their own economic precarity.

Some pundits have encouraged pro-Palestine candidates like El-Sayed to put their anti-genocide principles aside, arguing that more moderate Democrats performed better on Tuesday night. They compare El-Sayed’s 7-percentage-point defeat of Mike Rogers to James Talarico’s 12-point win over Ken Paxton in Texas — and some have already asked Talarico to defy his new colleague.

But on the campaign trail, El-Sayed often connected the issues of a high cost of living and outsized U.S. spending on aid to Israel. “We ought to be spending our money here, to build schools and provide healthcare and child care here, rather than sending our money abroad to a foreign government that’s done terrible things with our money,” he said in a September interview with Bloomberg TV. El-Sayed’s approach made him the target of nearly $40 million in outside spending from the super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee , which supported widespread anti-Arab and Islamophobic attacks and accusations of antisemitism in an attempt to keep a vocal critic of Israel out of the Senate.

“None of it mattered,” said Yousef Munayyer , a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. who likened the gravity of El-Sayed’s win to that of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. “And this is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”

“This is not the Commie Corridor. This is a swing state. A lot of taboos here have been shattered, and people are going to learn from this and be emboldened now.”

In addition to bringing joint resolutions to block future weapons transfers — like the Trump administration’s planned sale of $2.8 billion in 2,000-pound bombs to Israel — El-Sayed could introduce resolutions citing the Foreign Assistance Act; Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., used one to demand a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank. He would also be able to introduce amendments to the Pentagon’s annual spending bill that carves out billions of dollars in joint U.S.–Israel weapons research. (The Senate is currently sitting on this year’s $1.15 trillion National Defense Authorization Act, which would even more deeply enmesh Israeli technology within the Pentagon’s programs and supply chain.)

Munayyer, the former head of the U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights, said that despite the uncertainty over whether moderate Democrats will be willing to link arms with progressives next session, El-Sayed’s win creates an environment ripe for accountability over Israel.

“You have a climate now where there’s going to be a lot less intimidation felt by people who had previously been hesitant to speak out on these issues because they thought it was political suicide,” he said.

Even Republicans are beginning to feel the shifting winds. On the morning of Election Day, President Donald Trump made a surprise announcement on Fox News that the U.S. would halt the annual $4 billion in military aid to Israel. The move would only cut off one path for Israel to get weapons from the U.S. — still allowing direct weapons sales to Israel from U.S. companies and weapons development and sharing with the Pentagon — and Trump said it was made in agreement with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who had been previewing it for months . Tactically, Trump said the goal was to take a “talking point” away from Democrats. He cited El-Sayed by name.

While ballots were still being counted on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance, an expected 2028 presidential contender, posted on X an early post-mortem of the massive GOP losses across the country. He wrote that the party could bring back “voters who had abandoned us” if they “End the war” in Iran and “Change our relationship to Israel.”

Such recognition from the Trump White House is new territory for U.S. politics, Munayyer said.

“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics,” Munayyer said. “A robust debate in the presidential primary campaigns in both parties, where the question of the U.S.-Israel relationship is going to come up time and again. That’s never happened before, and it’s gonna be seismic.”

“We are about to witness, in my view, something we have never seen before in American politics.”

The question is whether Democrats will stay on top of the wave. If Schumer, a staunch supporter of Israel, remains in charge of the Senate majority, he’ll have power over appointments to key committees — giving him the opportunity to curb the influence of a figure like El-Sayed.

“I don’t think that Democrats want to have a messy fight about this stuff when the base is largely in agreement on it,” Munayyer said. But while Senate Democrats have evolved on the issue of Israel and Palestine — even Sanders expressed far weaker critiques of the Israeli state a few years ago — it’s one thing to be the dissenting party when you’re in the minority. It’s another to wield serious power.

El-Sayed is perhaps the most vocal supporter of Palestinian rights of any U.S. senator elected since James Abourezk of South Dakota, who in the late 1970s became the first Arab American to serve in the Senate. Abourezk frequently advocated for a Palestinian state and was an early critic of the pro-Israel lobby . After his time in Congress, he founded the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee.

El-Sayed, now the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, frequently referred to Israel on the campaign trail as an “ethnostate” and said he opposes any nation that organizes its government by ethnicity and religion. In an appearance on ABC News, El-Sayed argued Israel was not a U.S. ally. Two days before the election, he spent a large portion of his sit-down with “ 60 Minutes ” calling for Palestinians’ right of self-determination and repudiated the question of whether Israel had a right to exist. In his victory speech, he criticized attempts by pro-Israel critics to conflate advocacy for Palestinians rights as “hate.”

Even so, in the lead-up to the general election, El-Sayed started being subjected to pressure from some on the pro-Palestine left . Critics chastised his decision to stump with former Vice President Kamala Harris over her complicity in the Biden administration’s support for the genocide in Gaza. The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Fairplay, the nation’s leading nonprofit fighting to protect kids from the dangers of Big Tech and AI, released the following statement today in response to the Emma v. Google lawsuit .

Fairplay Associate General Counsel for AI and Privacy Brendan Bouffard said: “The idea of an untested AI chatbot helping a 13-year-old girl plan her own suicide should terrify all of us, but this is the sick new reality Google has created by forcing its AI products onto school-issued devices. Google claims its Chromebooks are there to help students learn, but in reality, the company was experimenting on kids like Emma by pushing them to use Gemini, a product the company knew was dangerous but rushed out anyway.

“We commend Emma’s parents and the EdTech Law Center for filing this urgent lawsuit. We also call on Congress and state legislatures to pass the People-First Chatbot Bill , model legislation we helped draft that will protect kids from AI harms.

“Let this be a reminder that ‘Google’ is not a verb. It’s the name of a surveillance and advertising company whose presence in schools has nothing to do with learning and everything to do with turning our kids into lifelong loyal customers.”

Fairplay, formerly known as Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood, educates the public about commercialism's impact on kids' wellbeing and advocates for the end of child-targeted marketing. Fairplay organizes parents to hold corporations accountable for their marketing practices, advocates for policies to protect kids, and works with parents and professionals to reduce children's screen time.

scraped.title: Energy and Water Issues Propel Democrats to Victory in Arizona - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: For the first time in 60 years, Democrats will have a trifecta in Arizona, opening the door for reform of the state’s groundwater laws and climate policies.
scraped.author: By Wyatt Myskow
scraped.h1: Energy and Water Issues Propel Democrats to Victory in Arizona
scraped.body_text:
PHOENIX—Two years after President Donald Trump won Arizona with 52 percent of the vote, Democrats are poised to win a trifecta in the state House, Senate and governor’s office, and could potentially win every statewide elected position. The battleground state’s blue wave could fundamentally alter how it responds to increasingly deadly heat and persistent drought brought on by climate change.

Central to the Democrats’ wins, party members and candidates said, was their focus on addressing the state’s growing energy demand and declining water resources, which are increasingly top issues for Arizonans.

Attorney General Kris Mayes, who has made protecting the state’s water resources and fighting rising energy costs her top two priorities, won her bid for reelection. Democrats Clara Pratte and Jonathon Hill took two seats on the state’s currently all-Republican commission that regulates utilities. And, for the first time since 1966, Democrats are almost guaranteed to have a trifecta with incumbent Gov. Katie Hobbs winning her reelection bid against Republican-candidate Rep. Andy Biggs. Even the party’s candidate for state mine inspector, Brian Matlock , leads in the polls, with his potential win marking the first time that seat has gone to a Democrat since 1976.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Taken together, the Democrats’ wins present an opportunity for major changes to how the state approaches climate change and energy policy , potentially paving the way for new renewable energy development and groundwater regulations. The latter has proven to be one of the state’s stickiest policy debates over the last decade, and an issue where Hobbs has attempted to make strides but been stopped from enacting reform by the Republican-controlled legislature.

“What we’ve seen is data centers have brought [energy and water] issues to the forefront,” Priya Sundareshan, Democratic leader in the state Senate, told Inside Climate News at the Arizona Democrats watch party Tuesday night. “The bipartisan response to data centers that we know voters have is around their energy use and their water use, and those are fundamentally questions that we have failed to address at the state level, and we continue to fail to address because of Republican control of the legislature.”

Arizona knows extreme weather well, she said, from record-hot summers to flooding that left communities evacuated over the last week to dwindling water supplies .

“All of that is directly tied to the changing climate, and that’s something where we can tie that picture together and be able to show voters that we can see the big picture,” Sundareshan said. “We can work toward a future that makes sure that we can all live here.”

In an interview with Inside Climate News, Mayes, the attorney general, said focusing her office and campaign on energy and water issues “were pivotal” to her victory. During her first four years, Mayes sued Fondomonte Arizona, a subsidiary of a Saudi Arabian company, which was pumping an unlimited amount of water from a groundwater basin on state trust land to irrigate alfalfa that was eventually fed to cattle in Saudi Arabia. She also challenged the Arizona Corporation Commission—of which she was once an elected member—over its decisions to roll back renewable energy and energy efficiency programs. And she has called for a statewide moratorium on new data center development until a plan for them can be developed.

“I did 70 town halls all over Arizona, many of them about water and data centers,” she said. “I think that resonated with Arizonans. People are worried about our water supplies, and they didn’t think that they had politicians working hard enough on those issues, and they saw in me somebody that was willing to stick my neck out against powerful entities and I will continue to do that.”

Many of the state’s races are far from a done deal, with only a fraction of the votes counted so far. But Democrats hold overwhelming leads for many seats that put them out of reach for Republicans. The final count for the state Senate and House remain undecided, though it is clear Democrats will have a majority in both.

Democrats flipped Scottsdale’s Congressional District 1 in one of the country’s most contested races, with Dr. Amish Shah winning the seat he failed to take in 2024. They also beat incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani in southern Arizona’s Congressional District 6, with Democrat JoAnna Mendoza flipping the seat.

But it’s too early to call some of the state’s other races for the U.S. House of Representatives. Democrats are maintaining close races in three other Republican-held districts. Only one Arizona Republican, Paul Gosar, has won his reelection for his House seat so far.

Polling has consistently shown energy and water issues were top of mind for voters. The Center for the Future of Arizona found 69 percent of voters don’t have confidence that the state will have enough water in the long-term, and that water was the top issue for its voters. Recent polling from The Nature Conservancy in Arizona and the Arizona PIRG Education Fund found about 80 percent of Arizonans said their electricity bills rose in the last two years. More than 60 percent said their summer power bills are difficult to afford.

“The people of Arizona deserve leaders who are looking out for us and ensuring that we can afford to fill our gas tank and keep our lights on, and that’s why they re-elected Governor Hobbs,” said Climate Power’s Arizona State Director Diali Avila in a statement. “Andy Biggs and his fellow Republicans rubber-stamped Trump’s agenda at every turn, and now they’re paying the price. Arizonans need relief from skyrocketing costs, and Governor Hobbs will work to bring down costs for Arizonans—not enrich oil and gas billionaires.”

Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.

That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.

Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Donations from readers like you fund every aspect of what we do. If you don’t already, will you support our ongoing work, our reporting on the biggest crisis facing our planet, and help us reach even more readers in more places?

Please take a moment to make a tax-deductible donation. Every one of them makes a difference.

Thank you,

David Sassoon Founder and Publisher

Vernon Loeb Executive Editor

Wyatt has lived in the Southwest since birth and graduated from Arizona State University with his bachelor’s degree in journalism.

Daily news & progressive opinion—funded by the people, not the corporations—delivered straight to your inbox.

A project of Common Dreams

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced today that he was moving to commute all death sentences in California, marking a historic step towards ending the death penalty in California and across the country.

The American Civil Liberties Union, ACLU of Southern California, ACLU of Northern California, ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties, and ACLU California Action joined the hundreds of organizations and individuals urging the Gov. Newsom to take this necessary step to address the persistent and systemic flaws with the death penalty in California.

Anthony D. Romero, executive director of the American Civil Liberties Union, issued the following statement:

“Today, Gov. Newsom made history by announcing his intention to commute every death sentence in California and clear the largest death row in the nation. In doing so, he honored his commitment to end a system that conflicts with human dignity, fairness, and the values enshrined in our Constitution.

“These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long. By taking this step, Gov. Newsom has affirmed that the death penalty has no place in California and he showed real courage by confronting racialized injustice head-on.

“The evidence against the death penalty has been overwhelming for decades. As the ACLU and allies have documented in courts across the country, a person’s risk of execution is predictable, but for all the wrong reasons: race, geography, and politics. Such profound, systemic injustice demands a systemic response. Today, California comes closer to closing the chapter on a cruel and morally and legally corrupt practice and sets a powerful example for others to follow.”

Gov. Newsom’s announcement comes amid ongoing legal challenges to California’s death penalty system. In April 2024, the ACLU, alongside the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and the Office of the State Public Defender, brought a lawsuit challenging the state’s death penalty statute as racially discriminatory and unconstitutional under the Equal Protection guarantees of the California Constitution.

The evidence presented in that lawsuit revealed pervasive racial bias in California’s implementation of the death penalty. Black people are up to eight times more likely to be sentenced to death when compared to similarly situated non-Black defendants, while Latino people are at least six times more likely to be sentenced to death.

Under California law, the governor has the unilateral authority to commute death sentences in cases without additional felony convictions. For cases involving additional felony convictions, the governor’s commutation request now goes to the California Supreme Court for review and approval.

Additional statements below are from ACLU affiliates in California:

Abdi Soltani, executive director of the ACLU of Northern California:

“The death penalty has no place in California – or any society that values justice, fairness, and human rights . Our organization has fought for decades against this antiquated, inhumane system, and we applaud the governor for taking bold action to end it.”

Chandra Bhatnagar, executive director of the ACLU of Southern California:

“From its inception, California has imposed the death penalty in a racially discriminatory manner, creating a two-tiered system of justice. With this historic act of clemency, the state can turn the page — rejecting a broken, biased system and embracing a more just and equitable future for all.”

Norma Chávez-Peterson, executive director of the ACLU of San Diego & Imperial Counties:

“Systemic injustices call for systemic solutions. By granting universal clemency to all people with death sentences in California, Governor Newsom has joined a chorus of leaders nationwide who have rejected the death penalty and recognized it as a failed and unjust experiment. This isn’t about individual cases, it is about addressing a system that is racist, fundamentally flawed, ineffective, and unfixable.”

The American Civil Liberties Union was founded in 1920 and is our nation's guardian of liberty. The ACLU works in the courts, legislatures and communities to defend and preserve the individual rights and liberties guaranteed to all people in this country by the Constitution and laws of the United States.

The think tank and polling firm's " 2026 Post-Election Report: How Democrats Rode Economic Populism to Landslide Victory " lays out "where the election was won," how Democratic candidates attracted voters as "the GOP playbook flopped," the issues that defined this cycle, and what the 2028 contests may look like. It highlights various pieces of polling.

As Google faces allegations that its Gemini chatbot helped a 13-year-old girl plan how to kill herself, the company, plus Meta and TikTok, sued to block a California law meant to safeguard minors from social media addiction.

The parents of a 13-year-old girl who allegedly used Google's Gemini artificial intelligence chatbot to plan her suicide sued the tech titan Wednesday on the child's behalf, a move that came as Google, Meta, and TikTok filed lawsuits to block California from enforcing a new law designed to protect children from the addictive features of social media platforms.

Parents of a girl identified as "Emma" in a lawsuit filed in Santa Clara County Superior Court in California alleged that Google effectively turned a school-issued Chromebook laptop computer into a tool allowing a dangerous psychological relationship between their daughter and Gemini.

"The death penalty is a flawed, expensive, and error-filled practice that fails us all," said Equal Justice Initiative's Bryan Stevenson, urging other elected officials to follow the California governor's lead.

Opponents of capital punishment applauded on Thursday after Gov. Gavin Newsom moved to commute all of California's death sentences, sparing up to 548 lives as the term-limited Democrat prepares to leave office with eyes on the White House .

The New York Times had reported last month that Newsom was mulling the move, which he addressed in a Thursday letter initially obtained by The Sacramento Bee: "After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish. I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."

“Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings,” said one protester in the streets of Asuncíon. “We are fed up with 70 years of plunder.”

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña, a close ally of US President Donald Trump , on Thursday announced his resignation after a major digital bank with close ties to his government collapsed, freezing millions of customers' savings, sparking mass protests , and spurring the lower house of the South American country's Congress to unanimously impeach him.

“I have made the decision to submit my resignation as president of the republic,” Peña declared in a video posted on social media . “I do so thinking of the stability of our country, social peace, and the need to preserve our democratic institutions.”

scraped.title: Democrats' state wins open the door for major clean energy progress
scraped.description: Victories in governor races and statehouses mean Democrats in many states could now push utilities and data centers to adopt cleaner energy and curb costs.
scraped.h1: Democrats’ state wins open the door for major clean energy progress
scraped.body_text:

Next Upcoming

By Canary Media

Canary Media

5 November 2026

Democrats’ historic wins in Tuesday’s midterm elections will give them control of Congress and a chance to combat the Trump administration’s anti-climate agenda, but the president’s veto power will limit their options.

At the state level, however, Democrats’ victories offer immediate opportunities to advance clean energy as well as energy affordability.

Democrats flipped governor’s seats in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio, and Texas — and likely Alaska. They won control of both houses of state legislatures in five states where they did not previously have it — Michigan, Minnesota, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin — and their chances are looking good in Arizona as well. Come January, Democrats will have trifectas — hold the governor’s office and both houses of the legislature — in 21 or more states, up from 16 , adding at least Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. Democrats also broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas.

States hold significant power over key facets of energy policy, including what kinds of power plants utilities can build or must shut down, how energy-efficient buildings must be, and how much pollution industries can emit.

“ Almost every policy you can think of to decarbonize our economy, except maybe border adjustment taxes, can be done at a state level,” Jay Inslee, former governor of Washington state, said at a Wednesday press conference. His state has instituted some of the country’s most aggressive climate policies , including a carbon cap-and-invest regime, a 100 % clean electricity standard, incentives for electric vehicles and EV chargers, and ​ “ the nation’s leading building code standards,” he said — all of which ​ “ could not be stopped by Donald Trump.”

Washington is one of about two dozen states with some form of policy calling for electricity to be 100 % renewable, carbon-free, or carbon-neutral in the coming years. Almost all these policies were enacted because Democrats held sufficient political power to overcome Republican opposition.

When Democrats are in power at the state level, ​ “ we don’t even have to wait for Congress,” Inslee said.

BloombergNEF highlighted this dynamic in a postelection memo, noting that newly empowered Democratic trifectas ​ “ should lead to policies boosting clean-tech sectors like renewables, energy storage, heat pumps and EVs.” Democratic state governments could also push through policies requiring data centers to use clean energy and curb costs for residents in Michigan , Minnesota , Pennsylvania , and Wisconsin , and measures that would boost solar and battery development in Arizona and Nevada .

Some states that have already passed clean energy mandates are eyeing opportunities to go further. In Michigan, Democratic leaders are considering new climate and energy measures after fighting back efforts from House Republicans earlier this year to repeal the state’s 2040 target for 100 % clean energy .

In Minnesota, two years of partisan deadlock in the state House held back efforts to expand virtual power plants and legalize plug-in solar , according to advocates promoting those policies. Now, bills will have a better chance to move forward.

Trish Demeter, managing director at clean energy trade group Advanced Energy United, highlighted other opportunities in a Thursday press conference, including in states where anger over data centers and rising utility bills has galvanized voters.

She pointed to Pennsylvania, where clean energy boosters are pushing a reform package meant to streamline the state’s ​ “ complicated and burdensome siting and permitting regime for building new large-scale wind, solar, and batteries.” Similar reforms have been gaining traction in other states that are struggling to build clean energy to meet growing demand for power, although those efforts face pushback from local communities.

Pennsylvania environmental groups are also tracking a dozen environmental or clean energy bills that have been blocked by Republicans in the state Senate. Among them are a legislative package backed by Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro that aims to impose pollution, clean-energy, and affordability requirements on data centers, and another that would expand access to distributed solar and other energy resources.

In Wisconsin, where Democrats have regained their first trifecta in 16 years , climate advocates are pushing for policies that will constrain utility spending on fossil-fueled power plants to serve data centers and promote solar, wind, and batteries instead. To this end, Advanced Energy United is lobbying Wisconsin Democrats to impose more-stringent utility planning regimes .

The breaking of Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas could also ​ “ constrain those states’ support for fossil fuels and restrictions on clean power,” BloombergNEF wrote. Republicans in the Texas legislature have pushed a variety of pro–fossil fuel and anti–clean energy policies in recent years, though sometimes unsuccessfully .

And in Georgia, Democratic candidates for the state’s Public Service Commission, which regulates utilities, won a 3 – 2 majority after two decades of Republican control. That could position the PSC to work with Democratic Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms to push utility Georgia Power to expand consumer access to rooftop solar and energy efficiency and to prioritize clean energy and batteries instead of fossil gas–fired power plants to serve uncertain data center demand.

Governors and state lawmakers are most directly responsible for dealing with public outrage over high and rising electricity costs.

Last year, Democrats won governorships in New Jersey and Virginia in large part by committing to lowering utility bills, which they’ve sought to carry out in conjunction with aggressive climate programs. This year’s Democratic gubernatorial victors — including Bottoms of Georgia , Amy Acton of Ohio , and Gina Hinojosa of Texas — ran on promises to promote clean energy, bring down utility bills, and curb unchecked growth of power-hungry data centers.

These issues have risen to the top of voters’ concerns, said Caroline Spears, executive director of Climate Cabinet , a group that supports state and local pro-climate candidates. Of the 120 candidates her group backed this year, 86 had won election, nine had lost, and 24 were too close to call as of Wednesday morning.

“ This was the affordability election,” she said during a press briefing her organization held. ​ “ Talking to voters across the country, utility bills, electricity prices, gas prices, affordability came up over and over and over.”

She added, ​ “ The good news is that climate solutions and clean energy solutions and affordability are the same.” Solar, wind, and batteries are cheaper and can be built faster than gas-fired power plants, and have made up more than 90 % of new additions to the grid in the past several years.

The Trump administration has put its thumb on the scale for fossil fuels, weakening pollution restrictions on coal plants , forcing aging power plants to stay running , and directing massive investments to support new gas power plants, pipelines, and export terminals . But states regulate utilities that deliver electricity and gas to customers, and hold varying degrees of power to direct the mix of fossil-fueled and carbon-free resources those utilities rely on.

State regulators ​ “ have a lot more control over the incentives to bring cheaper, cleaner sources on the grid than we do at the federal level,” U.S. Rep. Sean Casten, an Illinois Democrat and outspoken climate champion, said at a press conference on Wednesday. ​ “ They’re the ones who set the interconnection rules. They’re in many cases the ones who are directly facilitating with the ISOs and RTOs,” the entities that oversee wholesale energy markets and regional grid operations for about two-thirds of the country. ​ “ They’re the ones who are making sure that you can actually monetize the value you create.”

Most of the country’s utilities have been backsliding on their carbon-cutting commitments over the past two years, primarily by delaying the closure of coal plants and dramatically expanding plans to build new gas-fired power plants. That shift in utility priorities has been largely driven by the seemingly insatiable demand for electricity from AI data centers.

But opposition to data centers was a decisive factor in races up and down the ballot.

“ Basically every sitting Dem governor or governor-elect embraced clean energy as a key guardrail against data center pollution,” Lori Lodes, president of Climate Power , a clean energy and climate advocacy group, said at a press event. She cited examples from the platforms of Nevada Governor-elect Aaron Ford and Wisconsin Governor-elect David Crowley, as well as Acton, Bottoms, and Hinojosa.

“ This is an issue that really defined affordability for folks, and governors, senators, House elect members, all saw it as a huge opportunity,” she said.

scraped.title: Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives
scraped.description: For years, Missouri Republicans worked to undo or restrict voter-approved laws and amendments. In passing Amendment 6, voters have not only protected the ballot initiative process but also dramatically strengthened their power over the legislature.
scraped.author: Jeremy Kohler
scraped.h1: Missouri Voters Just Made It Much Harder for Lawmakers to Overturn Citizen-Led Initiatives
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

Across the country on Tuesday, voters delivered a wave of Democratic victories, flipping seats in Congress as well as state legislatures, and weakening a number of Republican majorities.

Missouri was no exception. Democrats made significant gains in the state House, picking up 16 seats, though Republicans still hold every statewide office and maintain control of the legislature.

Nonetheless, the election was more than just a rebuke of President Donald Trump. It reflected a long-simmering frustration with Missouri politicians who, time and again, have sought to override the will of voters — a practice that has intensified under years of Republican control. What’s more, voters went beyond weakening the Republican majority. They approved a constitutional amendment that curtailed the powers of the legislature and shifted more authority directly to the people.

Amendment 6, approved by a decisive margin, sharply limits the legislature’s ability to overturn laws and constitutional amendments enacted through citizen initiatives, and its ability to revive laws voters rejected through referendums.

Missouri Republicans have only themselves to blame, according to political observers who have watched the conflict between lawmakers and voters intensify. They resisted a voter-approved Medicaid expansion, repealed paid sick leave protections and sought to reverse abortion rights. They sometimes packaged their efforts with unrelated culture-war provisions, like limiting healthcare for transgender minors, that were intended to appeal to conservative voters.

Then they tried to persuade voters this summer to surrender some of their own power by changing the constitution to make it harder to pass initiatives in the first place. Voters rejected that proposal by more than a 4-to-1 margin .

“I think the people of Missouri are trying to wrest control back from our legislature because our legislature at this point does not seem to really be representing the majority view in the state,” said Jayne Woods, a professor at the University of Missouri law school who has written about the tension between direct democracy and legislative power.

Benjamin Singer is the co-founder and executive director of the Respect Missouri Voters campaign, which helped organize the push for Amendment 6. He said the frustration stretched back decades, including periods when Democrats controlled the legislature. He said when the campaign began organizing in late 2024, many volunteers were still angry about lawmakers’ decision in 2011 to weaken restrictions on puppy mills that voters had approved just a year earlier.

The campaign, he said, had already built a substantial volunteer operation before Republican lawmakers moved in 2025 to undo voter-approved measures that were intended to mandate paid sick leave and protect abortion rights. Respect Missouri Voters ultimately gathered enough signatures to put Amendment 6 on the ballot, seeking not only to protect the initiative process but to strengthen the electorate’s power over the legislature.

With the passage of that amendment, lawmakers now must get 80% support in both the House and Senate before they can propose changing or repealing measures enacted through citizen initiatives, or move to revive laws voters rejected through referendums. Even then, voters must approve any change in a statewide election. The restriction applies to measures voters have approved since 2010, including the constitutional amendment protecting abortion rights that voters approved in 2024.

Republican lawmakers put a measure on Tuesday’s ballot to restore abortion restrictions , but voters rejected that, too . With the passage of Amendment 6, abortion opponents don’t have a clear path to try again.

Amendment 6 also strengthens the referendum process. In addition to restricting lawmakers’ ability to reenact laws similar to those voters have rejected, the amendment explicitly protects the right of citizens to enact laws and constitutional amendments with a simple statewide majority, rejecting the higher threshold Republican lawmakers had sought to impose earlier this year. And it safeguards the power of Missouri’s courts to rewrite misleading ballot language, a power that Republican officials have repeatedly tried to strip away.

The result, political observers said, could make the legislature less consequential than it once was. Republicans still have the votes to pass most laws, but when voters reject those laws at the ballot box or enact their own measures or constitutional amendments through citizen initiatives, lawmakers will now face significant obstacles to overriding them.

Denny Hoskins, the secretary of state and one of Amendment 6’s most prominent Republican opponents, acknowledged how profoundly it would change the balance of power. Before the election, he told the Missouri Independent that if the amendment passed, “it will basically cut our legislature off at the knees as far as being able to pass laws to reduce crime and cut taxes.”

In text messages on Wednesday, Hoskins said that Amendment 6 weakens the legislature and governor “regardless of party” and predicted that it would be challenged in court. He said that “giving power back to the people” might be a great slogan but that the amendment’s sponsors “have no idea what this actually will do.”

Hoskins himself had tried to keep Amendment 6 off the ballot. In August, he refused to certify the initiative petition, arguing that it violated constitutional restrictions on ballot measures. He also rejected a separate petition seeking a statewide referendum on a newly gerrymandered congressional map that Republican lawmakers, working at Trump’s behest, had approved to give their party another seat in Congress.

The Missouri Supreme Court overruled him in both cases, ordering that the measures appear on the ballot. The court found Hoskins in contempt when he sought to use the map in spite of its ruling. Hoskins backed down and the justices did not have him arrested.

On Tuesday, voters rejected the map too. With Amendment 6 now in place — and Democrats significantly bolstering their numbers in the House — Republican lawmakers aren’t likely to gather enough support to override the voters’ rejection of their map.

Travis Crum, a law professor at Washington University in St. Louis and an expert on voting rights and election law, said he knew of no other state with a restriction quite like Missouri’s 80% threshold. But he said the amendment was understandable given the legislature’s repeated attempts to reverse voter-approved policies and its unsuccessful effort this summer to make citizen initiatives harder to pass.

“I think that there’s just been this boiling frustration with how the legislature has ignored the initiative process and then sort of tried to rewrite it to its own ends,” he said.

John Hancock, a former Missouri Republican Party chair and longtime GOP consultant, acknowledged that Republican lawmakers had brought some of the backlash on themselves. But he warned that Amendment 6 could make Missouri a magnet for well-financed out-of-state interest groups seeking to enact laws through ballot initiatives — possibly on taxation or gun policy.

That concern about wealthy outside interests was also central to the Republican-backed proposal to restrict citizen initiatives that voters rejected in August. Gov. Mike Kehoe had spent months warning voters about out-of-state special interests trying to rewrite the state constitution, even while a campaign supporting his proposal to phase out the state income tax benefited from funding from a Delaware nonprofit with undisclosed donors.

Woods said the defeat suggested voters weren’t persuaded by that argument. Regardless of who finances an initiative campaign, she noted, Missourians are the ones organizing, gathering support and ultimately deciding whether to approve the measures.

“I think that the people of the state pretty resoundingly said, ‘No, we don’t believe that that’s true,’” Woods said. “‘We believe this is our citizens who are doing this. This is what we want as citizens.’”

I am a St. Louis-based reporter covering Missouri and the Midwest.

I’m interested in tips about abuses of power, political influence, harmful policing and court practices, reproductive rights, public spending, and illegal or unethical business practices in Missouri and the Midwest.

articles.ai_summary: Documents reveal that the Trump administration engaged in discussions about deporting Iranians during wartime, despite the rarity of such actions.

scraped.h1: Trump administration held deportation talks with Iran during war: documents
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Δ

WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump’s administration held secret talks with Iran on deporting Iranians even as the war there dragged on, court documents obtained by The Associated Press show.

The court documents unsealed Thursday show the Republican administration as recently as mid-October said it had plans to deport the Iranians through an unnamed third country, although it was unclear when it intended to do so. The judge in the case ordered the government to give the court 24-hour notice of any finalized plans to deport Iranians to Iran or to any other country and five days’ written notice before any such deportation is carried out.

The documents show that the administration maintained contacts with Iranian officials during the war over the removals, specifically for submitting travel documents and figuring out “possible avenues for removal.”

“We are at war with a country where the President of the United States has said, as recently as two or three days ago, if not yesterday, that it is essentially lawless … A country that is an enemy of the United States, according to the current president. A country that, according to our president, murdered tens of thousands of protestors,” Judge Ana Reyes said according to the Oct. 15 transcript.

“And what you’re telling me is that the United States of America is going to send individuals back to that region, facing what you and I and everyone who would ever look at this would know would be, at a minimum, a serious threat of certain death.”

“Yes, your honor,” Justice Department attorney Dimitar Georgiev-Remmel said. “The government is executing lawful orders of removal.”

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The development emerged from an ongoing lawsuit that alleges the Trump administration’s immigration agencies have been sharing confidential information about Iranian asylum seekers with the Iranian government, violating national immigration regulations and endangering countless Iranians, court filings argue.

The new court documents show the coordination continued during the war.

The lawsuit depicts a coordinated campaign between the U.S. and Iranian governments to identify Iranians in Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody and pressure them to return to Iran — a marked departure from decades of diplomatic hostility between the two governments and an ongoing war. DHS has denied that it is sharing asylum application records with the Iranian government.

Hundreds of emails exchanged between U.S. immigration officials exposed how the two countries worked together to arrange for more than 100 Iranians to be flown back to Iran on three immigration flights in September and December 2025 and January 2026.

Deportations of Iranians back to their home country are historically rare, owing to the lack of diplomatic relations between the U.S. and Iran and the possible persecution they could face if they were sent to Iran.

But under the Trump administration, ICE has aggressively pushed to deport people even from countries that have typically been reluctant to take people back or with whom the U.S. has had icy or no diplomatic relations.

Sometimes that has meant sending people back to their home country but it has also meant deporting people to other countries that they have no connection with.

The Trump administration has deported people, including Iranians, to countries other than their own in an attempt to circumvent diplomatic hurdles with governments that won’t take their people back. During Trump’s second term, countries including El Salvador, Costa Rica and Panama have accepted noncitizens from the U.S.

In June, an Iranian woman was among the two dozen migrants the U.S. deported to the Central African Republic.

Activists abroad have expressed concern about deportees returning to Iran, whose theocracy has been cracking down on intellectuals and where the government vociferously cracks down on any dissent.
