articles.ai_summary: Russell Brand has been found guilty of rape and sexual assault, with expectations of a significant prison sentence and additional allegations pending.

scraped.title: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
scraped.description: Brand is told to expect a prison sentence "of some length" and faces more rape allegations, it can now be reported.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Russell Brand found guilty of rape and sexual assault
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Brand found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

Russell Brand has been convicted of rape and sexual assault, and is now expected to face a substantial prison sentence.

A jury found the entertainer guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court in London.

He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape, and one count of attempted indecent assault. The jury deliberated for eight-and-a-half hours.

Brand was taken into custody after the verdicts were delivered, and was refused bail. He is due to be sentenced on Monday.

It can now be reported that Brand is also facing further rape allegations made by two women and the 51-year-old has already been questioned by officers in relation to the complaints. The Metropolitan Police said its investigation "remains ongoing".

During the trial, Brand faced allegations from six women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009, when he rose to fame as one of Britain's most high-profile entertainers.

The women came to court to reveal how Brand used his immense fame to force them into sexual activity.

Brand, who told his wife Laura Brand "I love you" after entering the dock, displayed no emotion as the jury delivered its verdicts.

Afterwards he mouthed "I'm good, I'm good" to his defence counsel as he left the dock. His walk was steadily paced, and he continued to show little emotion.

The judge, Mr Justice Bennathan, told Brand to expect "a significant custodial term" after the verdicts were delivered.

Brand was denied bail and taken into custody after the verdicts, with sentencing due on Monday

The jury found Brand guilty of raping a fan after meeting her at a 2009 stand-up show at the Hammersmith Apollo.

Brand was found guilty of groping an MTV worker during a party at a Soho bar in 2004, but not guilty of going on to rape her in a toilet.

He was convicted of kissing and groping a Choice FM worker after encountering her in a corridor at the Capital Radio building in 2004 or 2005.

Brand was also convicted by the jury of sexually assaulting a Channel 4 worker in 2009 when she had been forced to give him a massage.

Brand was found not guilty by the jury of raping a woman he met at a cabaret show on the fringes of the 1999 Labour Party conference in Bournemouth.

He was also cleared of trying to drag an MTV worker in to a toilet to indecently assault her in 2001.

Brand was pictured arriving at court on Thursday with his wife Laura Brand before the verdicts were delivered

Brand was taken into custody following the verdicts and Laura Brand left court shortly afterwards

Brand had claimed to be the victim of a media conspiracy to paint him as a sexual predator and insisted in court that consent was "more important than sex itself".

But he faced the compelling evidence of six women who accused him of crimes over the course of a decade.

Brand was also confronted with his own words from his 2007 book in which he claimed sex was a "birthright" and friends who revealed his relentless pursuit of sleeping with 5,000 women.

Mr Justice Bennathan ruled that Brand must be remanded into custody until sentencing on Monday, when he is expected to receive a lengthy prison sentence.

The judge said "I regret the hardship caused to the children, of course" after being told that Brand would like bail over the weekend to explain the convictions to his children.

But he said Brand "has considerable resources", adding: "Whatever the good intentions of the family and the defendant today, I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence."

This video can not be played

Brand faced further questioning from officers in July 2025

Russell Brand on Trial

Get the latest news and analysis on BBC podcast Russell Brand on Trial - available on BBC Sounds, YouTube, iPlayer, or wherever you get your BBC podcasts

After the verdict, Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy paid tribute to the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination of the women who came forward and reported what happened to them".

"Despite intense media and public scrutiny, they relived deeply personal and traumatic experiences and placed their trust in us. Without their bravery, this outcome would not have been possible," he said.

"Brand used his influence, status and fame to exploit and sexually offend against women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement."

He added: "I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

David Roberts, senior crown prosecutor in the London rape and serious sexual assault unit, described Brand as "predatory".

"He was a manipulator with an insatiable desire to get what he wanted regardless of whether consent was given or not," he said.

"As his career took off, he seized opportunities to assault the women around him. Although his tactics varied, at the centre of every assault was an abuse of power and sexual greed, with a complete disregard for the impact of his actions.

Ron Brand, Russell's father told the BBC he was "bemused and shocked" by the verdicts, adding: "I just didn't expect this - it's wrong... it's devastating."

In his evidence, Brand admitted using his fame to "facilitate sexual access" and being "obsessed" with sex and "extremely promiscuous" in the past.

He said he had "dedicated a lot of my life to what seems now beyond reckless, philandering, and idiocy".

But he insisted the sex was always consensual, and he denied all the charges.

His barrister told jurors that Brand "had an immense amount of sex", but that "none of it was unlawful".

Court sketches portrayed Laura Brand looking on as her husband was sentenced

Allegations about Brand's behaviour first emerged in the media in September 2023.

The Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches programme jointly reported that four women had accused him of rape, sexual assault and emotional abuse - claims he strongly denied.

The investigation into other reports against Brand began soon after the story broke.

Brand first rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music.

He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. He was married to pop star Katy Perry from 2010 to 2012.

In recent years he has reinvented himself as an online social, political and religious commentator.

Channel 4, The Times and Sunday Times and the BBC all paid tribute to the women involved in the case, highlighting their "courage".

Channel 4, which aired Big Brother and its spin-off programmes at the time Brand was a presenter, said it recognised the "profound impact of these crimes".

The Times and The Sunday Times also paid tribute to women who took part in their investigation with Channel 4 but who did not have their cases brought before a court, saying their contributions had been "vital".

A BBC spokesperson said there could be "no place for the abuse of power" and added: "Across the industry we must work together to ensure that anyone who suffers at someone else's hand feels able to report it, that their concerns are taken seriously and that they are listened to."

The corporation restated its apology to staff who felt they could not speak up with concerns about Brand's behaviour when he worked at the BBC between 2006 and 2008, because he was seen as "too influential".

scraped.title: The Trump Administration’s Border Wall Strategy: Waive the Laws it Doesn’t Like.
scraped.description: In just a year and a half, the Department of Homeland Security has issued an unprecedented number of waivers of federal laws for border wall construction, threatening the southern border’s fragile ecosystem and the communities that depend on it.
scraped.author: Bala Sivaraman
scraped.h1: The Trump Administration’s Border Wall Strategy: Waive the Laws it Doesn’t Like.
scraped.body_text:
Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

In just a year and a half, the Department of Homeland Security has issued an unprecedented number of waivers of federal laws for border wall construction, threatening the southern border’s fragile ecosystem and the communities that depend on it.

By Bala Sivaraman

The U.S.-Mexico border spans a vast, interconnected region of exceptional ecological, cultural, and economic value. Its deserts, rivers, grasslands, mountains, and coastal habitats support remarkable biodiversity, wildlife migration, and clean water.

Just as important, countless communities on opposite sides of the border are linked by generations of family ties, cultural traditions stretching back millennia, and economic activity critical to the entire U.S. economy. The border is a remarkable place.

But construction of the Trump administration’s border wall is putting that all in jeopardy. The administration intends to use billions of taxpayer dollars to construct its system of land and water barriers across nearly the entire border. That includes many hundreds of miles of double wall or wall paired alongside water barriers.

These plans threaten the communities and biodiversity along the entirety of the U.S.-Mexico border. And in order to advance them, the administration is not just breaking the law, it is waiving the law entirely.

But Earthjustice is fighting back — and winning. In October, a court issued an order immediately halting border wall construction throughout Big Bend National Park in Texas.

Read on to learn more about the Trump administration’s plans and our legal fight to stop them.

A view of the Rio Grande River in Big Bend National Park. (Deb Snelson / Getty Images)

While development of a wall along the southern border was a cornerstone commitment of Trump’s first term, its actual construction was stalled in many places because of a lack of significant funding appropriated by Congress and lawsuits against the administration’s efforts to unlawfully use funds that were set aside for other purposes.

That all changed last year when Congress appropriated $46.5 billion to U.S. Customs and Border Patrol (CBP) for the “construction, installation, or improvement of new or replacement primary, waterborne, and secondary barriers” through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Armed with more than twice the amount of funding than all previous spending on border barrier construction combined, the Trump administration has since doubled down on an obscure authority to speed construction: issuing waivers that allow CBP to blatantly disregard federal and local laws.

Under the 2005 REAL ID Act, the Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS) is authorized to waive any legal requirements it deems necessary to “ensure expeditious construction of the barriers and roads” along the southern border.

Similar waivers were issued throughout Trump’s first term as well. But the rate at which the second Trump administration has doled out waivers is unprecedented. In the past year and a half, DHS has invoked over 30 waivers , accounting for roughly half the total number the agency has issued in its more than two-decade history.

This push to sideline legal oversight is central to the administration’s goal to build as much wall as quickly as it can.

Bedrock environmental and public health regulations, like the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act, and Endangered Species Act, are the most frequent targets of these exemptions. But other laws have also been waived, including those related to Native American religious freedom, procurement and contracting, and transparency.

By waiving these laws, DHS is giving itself a free pass to ignore the significant, often irreparable consequences of its operations and hide its decisions from the public. Already, wall construction has destroyed habitat for threatened wildlife, desecrated sacred sites, and heightened extreme flooding risks in border towns from Texas to California.

“The reality is that this wall will make our communities less safe and less resilient, and will put people’s lives in danger,” says Martin Castro, watershed science director at the Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) in Laredo, Texas.

In October 2025, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem waived a wide swath of procurement and contracting laws for every single CBP sector, including Laredo. Noem then issued another waiver for the Laredo sector in December that allows CBP to bypass nearly every major environmental law to build border wall in the sector.

Castro warns that the administration’s plan to remove vegetation along the Rio Grande’s banks and install hundreds of miles of buoys and barriers will destroy a unique riparian corridor, home to an abundance of rare native species and drought-tolerant vegetation endemic to the region.

“Removing this vegetation increases soil erosion, sedimentation, and saltation of the river,” Castro stresses, noting that doing so threatens the health of aquatic species and compromises the quality of drinking water for millions of residents along both sides of the border.

But the harms of the wall extend far beyond the environmental impact. The buildout of this network of land and water barriers poses an “inevitable threat to human life, property, and critical bridge infrastructure,” according to a recent report commissioned by RGISC.

The analysis, by geomorphologist Mark Tomkins, PhD, underscores the dangers of erecting such massive infrastructure within a floodplain. It warns that both the wall and buoy system will drastically exacerbate the impacts of floods, causing water levels to rise higher and faster, and sweeping heavy equipment, cars, boats and other hazardous debris downstream. This debris will accumulate under bridges, eroding their support columns and potentially inciting collapse.

Had the government not waived laws like the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act for the Laredo sector, it would have had to account for those impacts, consider alternatives that would be less harmful, and respond to public input. Because of the waiver authority, it did not have to conduct any analysis before beginning to implement its plan.

These dangers aren’t hypothetical — they’re already happening . Two bridges along the U.S.-Mexico border had to shut down this summer due to buoys drifting into the river after major flooding.

Big Bend National Park in Texas. (National Park Service)

The federal government’s waiver authority to build border wall infrastructure was first applied in southern California, where it has caused devastating ecological and cultural damage. Two 30-foot-high prison-style walls now cut directly through Friendship Park, marring the binational landmark shared by San Diego and Tijuana that was established in 1971 as a symbol of solidarity and good will between the United States and Mexico.

The development of border barriers in the park has turned this vision of international kinship on its head.

“They’ve already destroyed the park”, says Dan Watman of Friends of International Friendship Park, an organization working to restore the site’s original mission and to protect Yogurt Canyon, which surrounds it.

Watman pointed to the first Trump administration’s use of a waiver to disregard the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, among other laws, to build wall barriers that destroyed habitat for the vulnerable burrowing owl.

“Today, there are no more burrowing owls left there,” he says.

Watman is deeply concerned that additional border wall construction in the park will continue to damage the canyon’s wildlife habitat and disrupt water flows.

He is also weary that the destruction of Friendship Park is just a preview of what the entire southern border will look like if the Trump administration continues down this path.

Dan Watman, with Friends of Friendship Park, speaks during a demonstration in front of the U.S. Customs and Border Protection – San Diego Border Patrol Sector Headquarters in 2022 in Chula Vista, California. (Nelvin C. Cepeda / The San Diego Union-Tribune via Getty Images)

For years, Earthjustice has worked successfully to protect border communities, wildlife, and public lands from the Trump administration’s reckless wall construction agenda.

When the first Trump administration declared a national emergency to justify building more miles of border wall in Texas, a move that would have destroyed a historic chapel and cemetery, we sued on behalf of the families whose loved ones were buried on the threatened site, successfully delaying the construction. The Biden administration ultimately withdrew the emergency declaration, saving the site.

We are now supporting a lawsuit filed by the Center for Biological Diversity to stop the Trump administration from using waivers to sidestep federal laws in its relentless push to construct border wall infrastructure in and around Big Bend National Park in Texas.

Disregarding vital environmental and public health regulations to build roads and other barriers here would have far-reaching, irreparable impacts on the park’s ecosystem and the local communities that have long relied on the economic and cultural benefits it provides.

In October, the district court took emergency action and blocked wall construction throughout the entire Big Bend region while the legal case continues.

This is a major victory, but our work is not over: The Trump administration has now asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

Earthjustice will not rest in this fight to protect one of the world’s most biologically rich and diverse ecosystems.

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“Take a deep breath — but not too deep if you live near a coal ash dumpsite.”

Stay informed on how we hold accountable those who break our environmental laws.

scraped.title: How the midterms could unleash a new era for clean energy in these 3 states
scraped.description: Democrats achieved long-sought “trifectas” in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. They have big plans for climate action.
scraped.author: Jake Bittle
scraped.h1: How the midterms could unleash a new era for clean energy in these 3 states
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

When Trump was elected both in 2016 and 2024, promising to make the federal government hostile to climate action, many climate advocates insisted that state and local governments would take up the mantle of pushing for clean energy. That’s the thesis of the “ America Is All In ” coalition, which brings together cities and states that have vowed to uphold America’s “climate commitments … [i]n the absence of federal leadership.” The unspoken caveat in these claims is that the states leading the way on climate policy are concentrated in a few liberal parts of the country, like New England and the West Coast.

The Democratic Party’s historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could change that. Democrats have secured control of both state legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion — also known as a “trifecta” — in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, three states that have spent years or decades under Republican or divided control. The three states have also lagged on support for clean energy. Democrats also restored trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan, and Nevada this week, but those are states where they last had unified control earlier this decade.

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy. He said that the six states where Democrats have secured trifectas would be one of the world’s largest emitters if they made up their own country, rivaling Canada and Saudi Arabia. “This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.”

Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, and Arizona.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Compared to its neighbors in the Upper Midwest, Wisconsin has been far less ambitious when it comes to ditching fossil fuels in its power sector. While Michigan and Minnesota have both passed laws that mandate that the states get all their power from clean sources by 2040, Wisconsin set a measly 10 percent renewable electricity standard more than two decades ago. It blew past that goal but never set a new target. Unlike most other states, it doesn’t even require utilities to plan for what kinds of power plants they want to build. The state gets a larger share of its electricity from coal than its immediate neighbors.

Renewable energy advocates in the Badger State believe they can make some short-term gains with Democrats’ first trifecta since 2010. Erik Kanter, the policy director for the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said he believes that the new legislature can agree on the “low-hanging fruit” of making utilities plan for the future, which he said will nudge more of them to build renewables rather than extending the lifespans of gas and coal plants. The Wisconsin legislature failed this year to pass a law that would require data centers to source their power from clean sources, and Kanter expects such a measure to pass once Democrats take control. The legislature will also likely renew programs like Knowles-Nelson, a longstanding fund for parks and ecosystem preservation, which once enjoyed bipartisan approval but has lost support from Republicans in recent years.

Weiskopf, of Climate Cabinet, believes that even more ambitious moves are in the offing. He expects Wisconsin’s new class of legislators to pursue a 100 percent clean electricity standard, filling what he calls a “Wisconsin-sized hole” in the Upper Midwest. Not only would that help to phase out coal in the state, it would also make it easier for neighboring states to meet their climate goals, since the whole region shares the same interconnected power grid.

The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die. Even though the party managed to flip the lower house of the legislature a few years ago, Republican leaders in the upper chamber often refused to bring climate bills to a vote . The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“You don’t want to let yourself fully imagine what it can be, because you’ve been let down in the past,” said Lindsey Williams, a state senator who represents a swath of the Pittsburgh metro area. “Now we’re in that moment of, wow, there’s so many things that we can accomplish.”

Every year since 2019, Williams has introduced a bill that would establish mandatory energy and water efficiency standards for appliances like ovens and showerheads, a measure she said could save consumers millions of dollars a year. The legislation has never moved forward — but she thinks it will in next year’s session.

She hopes Democrats will use their first trifecta since 1993 to advance a full-scope climate agenda. In addition to passing laws that would allow community solar and warehouse rooftop solar , Democratic lawmakers also want to pass a funding package for struggling mass transit systems like Philadelphia’s. The $1.5 billion infusion would help prevent the transit “death spiral” for those systems and would reduce reliance on gasoline-powered cars.

The state’s reelected centrist governor, Josh Shapiro, appears to be on board with at least some of these proposals. Although he withdrew the state from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative , a Northeast-wide carbon pricing system , he has promised to create a similar cap-and-trade system for Pennsylvania itself if he can get legislative support. He has also named funding for mass transit as a leading item on his agenda for the new legislative session next year. But Democrats will have to be careful: While they will now control both chambers, they’ll have slim majorities in each, and may have just a narrow two-year window to pass climate policy before one flips back.

“We need to be brave and lead,” said Williams. “Yes, what are the low-hanging fruits, but what are the big ambitious things that we can get done this session?”

The last time Democrats had a trifecta in the Grand Canyon State was in 1966, decades before the general public was even aware of global warming. The state has ample sunshine and wind, so its renewable energy industry has grown quickly over recent years , and its grid is cleaner than in regions like the Midwest. Furthermore, the many new-built suburbs of the Phoenix metroplex tend to be heated with electricity rather than natural gas . Yet Republicans in the state legislature have all but banned climate and environmental policy, prohibiting the state government from regulating greenhouse gas emissions or energy usage, and numerous climate and water bills have failed in recent years.

Lauren Kuby, a longtime Democratic legislator who represents the Phoenix suburb of Tempe, says she and her colleagues have a long wish list that spans several issues. Their first order of business is to reform the Arizona Corporation Commission , the state’s utility regulator, which Kuby says has been slow to embrace new technologies like solar and wind even as developers seek to build more of them. Legislators want to pass a law that would direct the commission to make utilities invest in solar, batteries, and “virtual power plants,” or networks of homes and businesses that coordinate their energy usage. As part of the reform, they might even change the commission’s name, taking out the “corporation” and replacing it with “public utilities.” The two Democrats who appear set to win seats on the commission will make these reforms easier to push through.

The legislature could also break long-standing logjams on the crucial issue of water — a scarce resource in a desert state where climate change is worsening droughts. Kuby and other senators have been trying for years to pass a bill that would regulate groundwater pumping in the state’s rural areas. These areas are home to massive dairies and alfalfa farms like Riverview and the Saudi-backed Fondomonte , which have been blamed for sinking land and dried-up residential wells. The bill has failed in several legislative sessions , but Kuby believes that some form of regulation can pass in the coming year, bringing an end to the water free-for-all in the desert areas outside Phoenix.

“That has been languishing and has not been heard in the legislature, even though we have agreement from a lot of Republicans on water and environmental protection,” said Kuby. Of the trifecta, she said, “It’s a game-changer.”

articles.ai_summary: Georgia made history by electing its first Black woman governor and the first Black woman commissioner of agriculture on Election Day.

scraped.title: Black Democrats Made History, So Did a Black Farmer
scraped.description: In a major upset, Katherine Juhan-Arnold defeated a Republican incumbent to lead Georgia’s agriculture department, the oldest in the nation.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright
scraped.h1: Black Democrats Made History, So Did a Black Farmer
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

On Election Day, Black women in Georgia broke barriers in more ways than one.

Voters there not only elected the first Black woman governor in U.S. history, but also chose Katherine Juhan-Arnold as the state’s first woman and Black commissioner of agriculture.

“Georgia, we did it! I am overwhelmed with gratitude,” Juhan-Arnold wrote in a Facebook statement. “The campaign may be over, but our work is just beginning.”

In her first run for office, the farmer defeated incumbent and seventh-generation farmer Tyler J. Harper. Harper, 40, has been the state’s agriculture commissioner since 2023, and previously served as a state senator from 2013 to 2022. Juhan-Arnold, 37, founded Baby Katie’s Pharm & Kitchen, a nonprofit focused on bringing fresh foods and gardening to low-income communities.

She’ll represent 67,000 farmers, nearly 3,000 of whom are Black. Capital B reached out to Juhan-Arnold but did not hear back.

The win is no small feat for this often overlooked, but powerful role. Every state has a commissioner or secretary of agriculture who shapes farming and environmental policy.

The official oversees and enforces policies and regulations for agriculture, livestock, food safety, forestry, and pest control. The department can conduct gas and oil inspections, administer the National School Lunch Program, inspect grocery stores, or oversee benefits for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) and the federal supplemental nutrition program for women, infants, and children known as WIC.

However, only 12 states — mostly in the Southeast — allow voters to elect their commissioners. The rest of the states give that power to the governor, board or commission that appoints their agriculture leader. Historically, white Republican men have held these offices more than other statewide officials combined, according to an analysis by InvestigateMidwest.

This isn’t surprising to John Boyd Jr., president and founder of the National Black Farmers Association. For decades, Black farms have declined, and producers have been pushed out of the industry. They continue to remain underrepresented in positions of power — from the federal Department of Agriculture to state directors and even local-level county committees.

With voters electing Juhan-Arnold, it is vindication for Black farmers, especially women who have been degraded by President Donald Trump and his administration, Boyd added.

“It’s a real leg up for us,” Boyd said. “Having a person who looks like you and can relate to the struggles a Black family farm goes through is a real breakthrough.”

This year, only seven states held elections. Juhan-Arnold wasn’t the only Black person hoping to make history as a state’s top agricultural official. Yet, the three Black men who ran in other states lost those races.

In South Carolina, fourth-generation farmer and Democrat DeShawn Blanding saw an opening to fill the seat, which hadn’t had someone new in office for the past 20 years. With only 45% of the vote, he lost to Republican Cody Simpson, a seventh-generation white farmer. United Citizens Party candidate Chris Nelums, a Black pastor in South Carolina, also faced defeat in the race, receiving less than 1% of the votes.

In Florida, Kyle “KC” Gibson, an AME pastor, ran for agriculture commissioner this year, after unsuccessful bids for governor in 2022, 2018, and 2014, and lieutenant governor in 2022. While he hopes to fulfill his childhood dream of becoming governor one day, the 56-year-old also loves agriculture.

Unlike other agencies, the Florida Department of Agriculture & Consumer Services does more than food, water, and agriculture. It issues licenses for private investigators, concealed weapons permits, and conducts inspections for rides at the county fair. As a firearm instructor, former firefighter, and beekeeper hobbyist, Gibson felt this role would be a good fit. His love for agriculture grew through his grandfather, who was a farmer.

He had only three months to campaign, and as a result secured less than 1% of the vote. He lost to incumbent Republican Wilton Simpson. On the campaign trail, he said, many Black voters were not aware of the race, didn’t understand the role of commissioner, or were dismissive of farming.

“Most people are saying, ‘Well, Black people don’t do that.’ I say, ‘Well, how many Black people do you know that are farmers? If you go back two generations, you had some agriculture, and that’s how you survived,” Gibson recalled, as he approached voters.

He added: “It’s very vital, but it’s an under-watched and an underrepresented position. There are still a lot of African Americans that live in rural areas that depend on that department.”

However, he isn’t deterred. He’s already filed paperwork to run again in 2030.

Capital B reached out to Blanding and Nelums, but they didn’t respond by the time of publication.

ALABAMA: Commissioner of Alabama Department of Agriculture and Industries

Candidates: Democrat Ron Sparks ran against Republican Corey Hill.

Sparks, 74, previously served two terms as the state’s agriculture commissioner from 2003 to 2011. He was one of the youngest elected officials in Alabama when he became a county commissioner for DeKalb County. Hill, 56, is a cattle and poultry farmer who owns a local grocery store. He is currently the mayor of Douglas.

Salary: $100,833

Results : Hill won with 54% of the vote. Sparks garnered 45%.

GEORGIA: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Democrat Katherine Juhan-Arnold ran against incumbent Republican Tyler J. Harper.

Salary: $125,987

Results: Newcomer Juhan-Arnold defeated Harper 53% to 46%, respectively.

FLORIDA: Commissioner of Agriculture and Consumer Services

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Wilton Simpson ran against Democrat Joey Mendoza Atkins and Kyle “KC” Gibson, who has no party affiliation

Simpson, 60, is a lifelong egg farmer who was backed by Trump and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. He was a state senator for a decade. Mendoza, 41, is a trial attorney who has provided legal aid to farm workers. Gibson, 56, is a pastor and ran for governor several times.

Salary: $139,987

Results: Simpson won his reelection bid, garnering 51% of the vote to Atkins’ 48%. Gibson had less than 1%.

IOWA: Secretary of Agriculture

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Mike Naig ran against Democrat Chris Jones.

Naig, 48, grew up on a family farm and has been the state’s secretary of agriculture for two terms. Jones, 65, is an environmental scientist and researcher. His expertise is in water quality and sustainable agriculture practices.

Salary: $103,212

Results: Naig defeated Jones 52% to 47%.

NORTH DAKOTA: Agriculture Commissioner

Candidates: Incumbent Republican Doug Goehring ran against Democrat Vern Thompson.

Goehring, 61, is a farmer and rancher and seeking re-election. He’s been agriculture commissioner since 2009. Thompson is a former farmer and now trucker. He is the mayor of Minnewaukan and previously served in both the state legislature and other local councils.

Salary: $145,003

Results: Goehring will keep his seat. He secured 62.7% of the vote whereas Thompson pulled only 37%.

SOUTH CAROLINA: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Republican Cody Simpson ran against Democrat DeShawn Blanding, Libertarian Michael Sullens and United Citizens Party nominee Chis Nelums.

Simpson, 35, is a fifth-generation farmer and state executive director for the USDA’s Farm Service Agency. Blanding, 29, is a fourth-generation farmer and agriculture researcher and policy advocate. He’s worked as a policy analyst for the U.S. Senate Committee on Agriculture and aide for USDA’s National Resources Conservation Services. Sullens is a restaurant operator, and Nelums is an entrepreneur.

Salary: $162,000

Results: Simpson beat his challengers with 51% of the vote; Blanding received 45%, Nelums 0.79%, and Sullens 1.9%.

TEXAS: Commissioner of Agriculture

Candidates: Republican Nate Sheets ran against Democrat Clayton Tucker and Libertarian Austin Kelly.

Sheets, 55, is a rancher and served in the U.S. Navy Reserves. He received an endorsement from Gov. Greg Abott. Tucker, 35, is a rancher, former kindergarten teacher, and agriculture researcher for the National Science Foundation. He was backed by several congressional leaders, including Reps. Jamie Raskin and Lloyd Doggett. Kelly is an agriculture scientist and a student pursuing his doctorate at Texas A&M University.

Salary: $140,937

Results: Tucker won with 51% of the votes, becoming the state’s first Democratic agriculture commissioner in four decades.

scraped.body_text:
For You

City Council member Nithya Raman has defeated incumbent Karen Bass in the Los Angeles mayoral race, NBC News projects, capping off a rapid political ascent for a progressive challenger who railed against the “broken status quo” in the country’s second-largest metropolis.

Raman, 45, who is part of the Democratic Socialists of America, unseated Bass, a former six-term congresswoman and a fixture of California’s political scene for decades. The result means three major cities will be led by democratic socialists, with Raman joining New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Janeese Lewis George , who won the mayor’s race in Washington, D.C., this week.

Bass faced intense scrutiny over her response to a January 2025 wildfire in the Pacific Palisades neighborhood, the most destructive in Los Angeles history. The blaze erupted while she was in the West African nation of Ghana attending a presidential inauguration. It went on to destroy thousands of homes and kill 12 people.

Follow live updates on the midterm elections.

Raman, a former urban planner and activist, accused Bass of mismanaging the city’s homelessness problem and rising housing prices. She blasted City Hall for what she characterized as “a reluctance to move forward with the transformative policy change that this city needs right now.”

Bass, for her part, argued Raman was “not ready for primetime” after six years on the City Council.

The two Democrats also differed sharply on Israel’s war in Gaza, highlighting a generational split in the party. Speaking at a September forum co-hosted by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles, Raman said she agreed with left-wing influencer Hasan Piker that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians; Bass rejected that label.

Raman’s candidacy drew comparisons to that of Mamdani, whose campaign rallied New York City voters dissatisfied with the political old guard. Raman touted her progressive bona fides while stressing her “independence” from the Democratic Socialists of America.

The incoming mayor’s agenda will be defined in part by the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles, a complex undertaking that will test the city’s physical infrastructure, public transportation services and security systems.

Raman endorsed Bass at the beginning of the year before she launched a last-minute bid of her own. Bass and Raman took the top two spots in a June 2 primary contest, advancing to a runoff over populist insurgent Spencer Pratt, a former reality television star who blasted the city’s political establishment with provocative social media videos.

On the City Council, Raman represents a district that ranges from the San Fernando Valley to the Santa Monica Mountains. She was born in India and moved to the U.S. with her family as a child, later attending Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Daniel Arkin is a senior reporter at NBC News.

scraped.h1: Super Bowl champion Rod Woodson says the KKK tried to burn his family's home down when he was 11 years old
scraped.body_text:
Rod Woodson recalls a terrifying story to Craig Carton, explaining how the KKK tried to destroy his house.

Super Bowl champion Rod Woodson said the Ku Klux Klan tried to burn down his house when he was a kid.

Woodson, whose father was Black and mother was White, said he was 11 years old when he woke up in the middle of the night to flames emanating from the back of his house.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

"I woke up, it was like 2:00 in the morning. I look up and we only had a two-bedroom house. So my mom and dad bedroom was right here. Our bed, all three boys stayed in the other side of the other bedroom. I wake up, I look and I see this flickering, these lights outside of the back of our our window and I'm like, ‘What the heck?’" Woodson said during an appearance on OutKick’s "The Craig Carton Show."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Rod Woodson speaks onstage at the 22nd annual Harold and Carole Pump Foundation Gala at The Beverly Hilton in Beverly Hills, Calif., on Aug. 19, 2022. (Getty Images for Harold & Carole Pump Foundation)

"And I looked and our house is on fire, like right below our window."

The Pro Football Hall of Famer said he ran to get his dad and notify him that the house was on fire. The family got out of the house, and the fire department conducted an investigation.

"We get a letter a week later from the KKK saying, ‘If you guys don't get your mixed race butts out of this area, it's going to happen again.’ And so, it was the KKK," Woodson said.

The 61-year-old, who grew up in Fort Wayne, Indiana, said the Ku Klux Klan doused the house in gasoline, but dogs began barking, causing the attackers to flee before returning. The gasoline had partially dried by the time they returned, preventing the house from immediately going up in flames.

RAVENS ANNOUNCER & NFL LEGEND ROD WOODSON TELLS CRAIG HIS SHOCKING KKK STORY - LISTEN NOW

Pittsburgh Steelers cornerback Rod Woodson (26) looks on before a preseason game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Three Rivers Stadium on Aug. 24, 1995 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (George Gojkovich/Getty Images)

Woodson said they were "very blessed" that the gasoline had dried a little bit.

"We stayed in the same house, you know, for all my childhood until I got to high school and then we moved out a little bit further out," Woodson said.

The 11-time Pro Bowler said that the Black Panthers also gave his family issues because they were half-White, saying there were letters and calls to the house.

"My dad used to just say, ‘You are who you are. You're your best of both worlds. Everybody's gonna ask you to choose, What are you? You black? Why? What are you? What are you?’" Woodson said.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Baltimore Ravens safety Rod Woodson stands on the sidelines against the Oakland Raiders at Oakland Alameda Coliseum during the 2000-01 AFC Championship game on Jan. 14, 2001. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"And they still ask that question. What are you? What? I'm like, listen, I am who I am."

Woodson played in the NFL for 18 seasons, spending 10 seasons with the Pittsburgh Steelers, one with the San Francisco 49ers, four with the Baltimore Ravens and two with the then-Oakland Raiders.

In his illustrious career, Woodson played in 238 games, recording 1,158 tackles, 13.5 sacks and 71 interceptions. He returned 12 of those interceptions for touchdowns, an NFL record. He won the Super Bowl with the Ravens following the 2000 season.

scraped.description: The selloff came a day after the Dow soared more than 1,500 points.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Dow plunges 1,800 points, wiping out gains from midterm results rally
scraped.body_text:
The Nasdaq fell 5.5%, putting the tech-heavy index into correction territory.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down more than 1,800 points on Thursday, wiping out all of the rally from a day earlier when midterm election results propelled the index to its best trading session in more than a year.

The S & P 500 finished trading down 4.3%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq fell 5.5%, putting the index into correction territory, meaning it has fallen more than 10% from a previous peak last month.

The Dow closed down 1,833 points, or about 3.4%.

The selloff hammered many artificial intelligence firms as investors appeared to digest risk for the sector posed by newly empowered Democrats, many of whom ran campaigns critical of artificial intelligence data centers.

Nvidia, the chipmaking giant behind many of the semiconductors used in AI products, closed down 9% on Thursday. Rival chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices saw shares fell 17%. SanDisk, another AI hardware firm, plummeted more than 22% in value by market close.

The slide also hit some other major tech firms behind AI development.

Microsoft, which holds a large stake in OpenAI, saw its stock price close down more than 3%. Amazon, which has spent hundreds of billions on its build-out of AI infrastructure, also dropped more than 2%.

The downturn in markets largely reversed blockbuster gains from the previous session.

On Wednesday, the Dow jumped 1,570 points, or 3%, recording its best one-day performance since April 9, 2025, when President Donald Trump announced the suspension of a far-reaching set of reciprocal tariffs.

Even as stocks climbed on Wednesday, Yorkville analyst Dan Ives warned ABC News of potential midterm fallout for the tech sector.

"The Democratic blue tidal wave across the Senate and House was a seismic shift that will have a negative impact on the pace of the AI Revolution buildout in the US over the next few years," Ives told ABC News in a statement.

Tuesday's midterm elections catapulted Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidates to statewide victories in Republican strongholds like Ohio and Texas, both of which play host to a number of AI data centers.

A strong performance in House contests, meanwhile, appeared to set Democrats on a path toward a comfortable majority in the lower chamber.

OpenAI unveiled a new set of data center policies Thursday for that it called "responsible AI infrastructure" in the aftermath of the election.

The ChatGPT maker said it would abide by fresh commitments, including a vow to pay for all electricity and infrastructure used at its facilities. It also will create a "water plan" for each location as part of an effort to "protect local resources," and will "create opportunities for local workers and businesses" for employment, the AI company said in a blog post .

articles.summary: California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."
articles.ai_summary: California Governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of over 500 inmates to life in prison, citing moral and legal concerns about state-sanctioned killing.

scraped.title: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he'll commute all death row sentences to life in prison | CBC News
scraped.description: California governor Gavin Newsom is commuting the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."
scraped.h1: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he'll commute all death row sentences to life in prison
scraped.body_text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom says he will commute the death sentences of more than 500 inmates to life in prison with no possibility of parole, saying he believes state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with the values of California, undermines the foundations of the legal system and "diminishes each of us."

In an open letter , Newsom says his decision comes after three decades of openly opposing state-sanctioned executions. He issued a moratorium on all inmate executions in the state in 2019, but said it wasn't enough as their death sentences remained intact.

There are currently 548 people on death row in California, which Newsom describes as "the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere."

California last put a ⁠prisoner to death in ⁠2006, when Republican Arnold Schwarzenegger was ‌governor.

Newsom's decision, which he calls the most difficult of his career, comes just months before the end of his eight-year term as governor, and amid speculation he will launch a bid to run as the Democratic candidate for president in 2028.

Newsom speaks with incarcerated men at San Quentin State Prison in San Quentin, Calif., in March 2023. (Eric Risberg/The Associated Press)

The state constitution requires the California Supreme Court's approval to grant clemency to anyone convicted of a felony more than once, which means the court would have to approve 382 of those commutations, or roughly 70 per cent, according to numbers provided by Newsom's office.

California voters rejected a ballot measure in 2016 that would have repealed the death penalty in the state.

"I recognize the limits of this clemency action," Newsom wrote, "which does not repeal the death penalty and is limited to commuting California's current death sentences."

Repealing the law rests with the legislature and voters, but he says that, as governor, he has clemency authority "for moments when law as applied cannot be squared with justice."

"For me," he said, "this is that moment."

Last month, the California District Attorneys Association sent a letter to Newsom expressing "grave concerns" about the possibility he would commute the sentences, warning that such a sweeping action would inflict additional anguish on victims' families.

"Every death sentence in California represents an individual case in which a jury heard the evidence, considered the circumstances and determined that the most serious punishment under our law was warranted," association President Jeannine M. Pacioni said.

"To simply erase all those judgments with the stroke of a pen, without considering the facts of each case or the families affected, would be a profound disservice to the administration of justice."

Newsom said he is aware his decision will surface painful memories for the families of victims of crime.

"As Governor, I alone bear responsibility for this decision and its impact, just as I alone would bear responsibility for each execution," Newsom wrote.

Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, seen here in December 2007, survived two state-sanctioned execution attempts in September. (J. Miles Cary/ Knoxville News Sentinel/USA Today Network/Reuters)

The debate over capital punishment in the U.S. intensified recently after Tennessee's failed execution of condemned killer Christa Pike, ‌who survived two attempts to inject her with lethal drugs on Sept. 30.

Pike was hospitalized afterward and was sent back to prison on Oct. 10.

The death penalty received further scrutiny after U.S. War Secretary Pete Hegseth announced plans to ​livestream the firing-squad execution of Nidal Hasan, who was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding more ⁠than 30 others in a shooting at the Fort Hood military base in ⁠Texas on Nov. 5, 2009.

U.S. President Donald Trump later ruled out a livestream ⁠of ⁠the execution, but Hasan is still ​scheduled to be executed by firing squad on Dec. 3.

The American Civil Liberties Union, which has said the implementation of the death penalty reflects racial bias, applauded Newsom's announcement.

"These commutations reflect what justice demands: an end to a racist, error-prone, and inhumane punishment that has burdened California for far too long," executive director Anthony Romero said in a statement.

The ACLU is involved in an ongoing legal challenge to California's death penalty statute, alleging it is racially discriminatory and unconstitutional.

Newsom has said in the past that it is wrong for the government to kill its citizens and that capital punishment in practice has discriminated against mentally ill people and people of color.

In 2023, Newsom announced plans to transform San Quentin prison , a facility in the San Francisco Bay Area known for maintaining the largest number of prisoners on death row in the country, into a place where inmates could be rehabilitated and receive job training before returning to society.

That work was completed earlier this year.

Digital Producer

Stephanie Hogan is a digital producer with CBC News, based in Toronto. She writes on a variety of subjects, with an interest in politics, health and the arts. She was previously political editor for The National and worked in various roles in TV and radio news.

articles.title: Texas rejects the Republican establishment in historic midterm election: What comes next?
articles.summary: While Texas has “turned blue," the question remains if we can build a movement powerful enough to demand something fundamentally different.
articles.ai_summary: Texas has shifted politically, raising questions about the future of the Republican establishment in the state.

scraped.title: Texas rejects the Republican establishment in historic midterm...
scraped.description: Texas has long been upheld as a crown jewel of Republican, even far-right political dominance. For decades, the state has been treated as virtually un
scraped.author: PSL Webmaster
scraped.h1: Texas rejects the Republican establishment in historic midterm election: What comes next?
scraped.body_text:
Texas has long been upheld as a crown jewel of Republican, even far-right political dominance. For decades, the state has been treated as virtually unwinnable territory for Democrats, with Republicans controlling statewide offices and presenting their rule as an inevitable reflection of Texas politics. This midterm election season has flipped that claim on its head. Millions of Texans delivered a resounding rejection of the Republican establishment, producing a historic Democratic sweep that will reverberate far beyond the state’s borders.

Democrat Gina Hinojosa defeated incumbent Republican Greg Abbott by approximately seven percentage points, ending more than three decades of Republican control of the Texas governor’s office. Abbott, who had won his previous three elections by at least 10 percentage points, was seeking a fourth consecutive term – which would’ve made him the state’s longest-serving governor.

James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton by approximately 12 percentage points, making him the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Texas since 1988. Democrats also won the other major statewide elections, including the lieutenant governor’s race against incumbent Dan Patrick.

These Democratic victories in Texas are historic – and reflect a growing rejection of the political establishment, the billionaire class and the increasingly repressive policies that have defined the Trump era and been willingly carried out within the Texas political realm. And further, they expose the fact that the Republican Party’s supposed stronghold in Texas is not fixed – in fact, even in seemingly the most conservative places, a light for a different future exists when the people will it into existence.

The question now is not simply whether Texas has “turned blue.” It is whether the millions of people who mobilized against the Republican agenda can build a movement powerful enough to demand something fundamentally different.

The midterm results in Texas cannot be divorced from the broader political climate across the country. Working people are confronting rising grocery prices, housing costs, stagnant wages and an increasingly precarious economic future. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has doubled down on policies that scapegoat immigrants, attack LGBTQ people, undermine public education, seek to strip us of our civil liberties and funnel enormous resources toward war, militarization and repression.

Republicans across the board have offered few solutions to these worsening crises, and instead have relied on culture-war politics, racist scapegoating and gerrymandering and increasingly authoritarian measures in desperate attempts to consolidate their own power.

Abbott and Paxton embodied this agenda. Abbott’s administration has spent years attacking reproductive rights, restricting public education and expanding the state’s repressive apparatus. Paxton has become synonymous with corruption allegations and the interests of the wealthy political establishment. Both figures have been central in an administration that has prioritized attacking working people rather than addressing the conditions making their lives increasingly difficult. And in Texas, that rejection also extends to the enormous influence of billionaires like Elon Musk, whose growing political and economic footprint in the state has become a dangerous symbol of the power wealthy individuals wield over public life and safety.

Texas is one of the wealthiest states in the country. It is also a place, like many across the country, where millions of people who produce that wealth struggle to afford housing, healthcare, groceries and other basic necessities – not to mention mounting Texas property taxes. The contradiction is impossible to ignore, and the election results are an expression of growing frustration with that reality.

The results have also been fueled by the escalating assault on immigrant communities. Texas sits at the center of the country’s deportation apparatus. It leads the nation in ICE arrests, with 1 in 4, or 25%, taking place in Texas (the next closest is Florida, at around 11%). Harris County and the greater Houston area, specifically, lead the nation in ICE arrests and active detainments. And despite the administration’s continued claims that ICE is targeting “criminals,” a rising share of those being detained and deported have no criminal record.

ICE raids in Texas have affected far more than only the families of those taken into custody – they create a culture of fear that extends into all of our communities. The March 2025 ICE killing of 23-year old Ruben Ray Martinez in South Padre Island, the July 2026 ICE murder of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston and the October 2026 ICE shooting of Wilber Rafael Garces Perez in Austin have mobilized immigrant and non-immigrant communities alike with anger.

The Trump administration has attempted to use immigration enforcement to divide working people, blaming immigrants for economic insecurity while corporations and billionaires actually profiting from exploitation and rising costs continue to accumulate wealth. But the growing opposition to ICE demonstrates the limits of that strategy. More and more people recognize the culprit as not immigrants, but the very political establishment seeking to blame immigrants while failing to provide us with basic human needs.

Perhaps one of the most extraordinary developments in this election was the level of voter participation. More than 7.7 million Texans voted early, surpassing the previous midterm record set in 2018. More than 40% of registered voters cast ballots before Election Day. Particularly significant was the increase in Black and Latino voter participation. Early voting surged in the heavily-Latino Hidalgo and Cameron counties, while Black turnout saw a substantial increase, especially in the Houston area.

This mobilization is especially important given the state’s long history of voter suppression and efforts to undermine the political power of communities of color. It also comes amid aggressive Republican redistricting efforts designed to consolidate political power and weaken the electoral influence of communities that have historically challenged the status quo.

Black people have played a central, detonator role in driving political change in this country. From Reconstruction to the Civil Rights Revolution, Black political mobilization has forced the political establishment to capitulate to demands it would’ve otherwise ignored. The increased participation we saw in Texas should be understood within this historical context – as it represents a refusal to accept that the political direction of the state is predetermined and that working class communities have no meaningful power to change it.

The significance of these results extends well beyond Texas. Democrats made major gains across the South and other traditionally-Republican strongholds, including historic victories in Georgia, Iowa, Ohio and South Carolina.

Together, these results demonstrate that the political landscape in this country is not fixed. States that have been written off as permanently conservative can, in fact, become centers of political upheaval. The idea of an immutable “Trump country” obscures the millions of people living in these places who are struggling with the same economic and political conditions as working class people everywhere else.

Texas has always had a rich history of working class struggle, labor organizing, and anti-racist resistance. The notion that the state is inherently conservative has often served to discourage people from imagining a different political future. This election challenges that assumption. But we should be careful not to confuse a rejection of Republican rule with an automatic mandate for the Democratic Party’s entire agenda. That distinction is critical to understanding what comes next.

The Democratic Party will undoubtedly present the results as proof that its electoral strategy is working. But what happens now that voters have gone home?

History offers us plenty of reasons to be skeptical of the “blue wave.” Democrats have repeatedly campaigned on opposing deeply unpopular Republican policies, mobilized people around promises of change, then retreated to the same status quo politics once in office. They’ve absorbed the energy of mass movements, channeled it into electoral campaigns and ultimately failed to deliver the fundamental changes people were demanding.

Take immigration enforcement as an example – which is bipartisan in both its development and continued expansion. Talarico has compared ICE to a “secret police force,” reflecting the deep-seated anger that has developed around its increasingly violent operations. Yet, he’s stopped short of supporting the agency’s abolition – where the mood of the majority of people is really at. If ICE is functioning as a repressive force, why should the movement settle for reforms that leave the institution intact, and simply change the party that manages it?

The same issue applies to the broader political landscape in Texas. A Democratic victory in the governor’s office doesn’t automatically undo the laws and policies that have been implemented over years of Republican rule. Many of them are embedded in state legislation, and require a square confrontation with the Republican-controlled legislative infrastructure that has built and maintained them. Can we count on Hinojosa to do that on her own, without mass pressure from below?

Consider just a few examples:

If Democrats are serious about representing the people who mobilized to defeat the Republican establishment, they should be held accountable for repealing these measures, ending state-mandated collaboration with ICE, restoring local democratic authority, protecting workers’ rights, expanding reproductive rights, and directing public resources towards housing, healthcare, education and other essential services.

The Democratic victories in Texas are significant, but they should not be mistaken for a solution to the problems that brought millions of people to the polls. The Democratic Party has a long record of campaigning against Republican attacks, mobilizing working class communities and promising change, only to retreat once in power and preserve the same systems that produced the crisis in the first place.

The question is whether we allow our energy to dissipate after Election Day, or whether we use it as a foundation for building a sustained movement capable of winning real material change. None of this will happen simply because Democrats won an election – history shows quite the opposite. It will take organization and pressure from below: from workers, students, immigrants, Black communities, women, LGBTQ people and everyone else whose interests are so clearly at odds with the billionaire class and the political establishment that serves it.

The Texas election has demonstrated that millions of people are willing to mobilize against the status quo. The task now is to build something that can carry that struggle forward, well beyond the ballot box – an independent, multiracial, working class movement that does not limit its political horizon to the Democrats or Republicans.

The Republican political establishment has been dealt a historic blow in Texas. What comes next depends on whether people who made that defeat possible keep up the pressure.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

scraped.body_text:
The centrepiece of every UN climate summit is for countries to negotiate the wording of a large number of legal agreements – and COP31 in the Turkish city of Antalya is no different.

These texts are hashed out behind closed doors in the “ blue zone ” at the COP, where diplomats from nearly 200 nations – not including the US – will be haggling over each individual verb .

Over the course of the two-week summit, negotiators will be trying to reach consensus on more than 100 separate agreements – but, first, they must agree which issues are on the agenda.

The complexity of this process can make it challenging to keep track of what countries are fighting about and how negotiations are progressing.

Carbon Brief’s real-time text tracker, below, offers a helping hand by decoding the agenda and keeping a searchable record of every document for each part of the negotiations.

The first column of the interactive tracker lists the topic of each agenda item, with further columns including dates, page counts and links to the original PDFs.

The table is searchable via the interactive text box and can be sorted using the arrow icons.

This year’s talks come with a twist: Turkey holds the presidency and is hosting COP31, but Australia is jointly running the show as “ president of negotiations ”.

The pair have already announced their intention to produce a “cover text” – an overarching political document summarising key negotiated outcomes, along with issues not on the official agenda.

This could include a recognition that warming is set to “ overshoot ” the 1.5C limit and the impacts this is already causing . It may also include potential solutions, such as the Turkish presidency’s “ electrification ” target, for 35% of global final energy to come from electricity by 2035.

While the summit is not seen as a banner year for the negotiations, falling half-way between two “ global stocktakes ” of progress, there are still plenty of major topics up for discussion.

These include efforts to finalise the “ global goal on adaptation ” and whether to continue a contested process on how to cut emissions, known as the “ mitigation work programme ”.

Negotiators will also be trying to agree on the details of a new “ just transition mechanism ”, also referred to as the “Belém-Antalya mechanism for global just transitions” (BAM).

While most of the items on the agenda are agreed in advance, parties can suggest late additions. These must be signed off before negotiations can begin, often resulting in an “ agenda fight ”.

COP30 agreed to put two new items on the agenda for future summits.

These are the provision of climate finance by developed countries, under Article 9.1 of the Paris Agreement , and making global “ finance flows ” consistent with the treaty, under Article 2.1c .

Ahead of COP31, the African group of nations filed a request to add climate-related trade tariffs to the agenda. COP30 had agreed to annual “ dialogues ” on this matter at the Bonn climate talks .

The African group also wants further items added, on tripling adaptation finance and on funding for the Green Climate Fund , a flagship UN body designed to support climate action.

Ahead of the opening of the summit, Carbon Brief’s text tracker counts 104 substantive items on the agenda, not including procedural matters, such as the election of COP officials.

The figure below illustrates the status of the COP31 negotiations overall, in a traffic-light format. Each agenda item is colour-coded according to its current status.

For topics shown in red, negotiators have not yet managed to put anything down on paper, perhaps because parties have fundamentally different views on how they should proceed.

For items in orange, negotiators are working on an “informal text”, which is an early draft setting out the views of different parties, but not yet expressed in formal legal language.

Once a draft legal agreement becomes available, topics will be colour-coded yellow. At this point, areas of remaining disagreement will be denoted in the text with [square brackets] and “options”.

As such, texts with many square brackets or options tend to be an indicator of a high level of disagreement between parties. For this reason, the tracker table above counts and displays the number of outstanding brackets and options in each document.

During the course of the summit, negotiators may work through many iterations of texts on each agenda item. These documents may include “bridging text”, designed to resolve differences of opinion and to find a “landing zone” that all groups can agree on.

Agreement is reached on a given topic once all brackets and options have been resolved, at which point the item will be coloured green in Carbon Brief’s traffic-light chart.

Where agreement cannot be reached, discussions may be subject to “ rule 16 ”, meaning negotiations are postponed until the next session. These topics are colour-coded grey.

The figure below gives an at-a-glance overview of the status of the main topics up for negotiation.

As parties narrow down the options and brackets towards the end of each summit, they start to generate “clean” texts, which contain no areas of disagreement and can be converted into “draft decisions” that are ready for formal adoption at the closing plenary of the meeting.

Finally, at the closing plenary, each draft decision must be gavelled through by the COP president, signifying its formal adoption as a legal agreement and outcome of the summit.

This last step is usually a formality, but dramatic exceptions are possible.

During the closing plenary at COP29 , the president of the meeting failed to adopt a deal relating to the “ global stocktake ” from 2023, which had called for “transitioning away” from fossil fuels.

Carbon Brief also ran text trackers for COP28 , COP29 and COP30 .

Words by Simon Evans. Tracker maintained by Ho Woo Nam.
