articles.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
articles.summary: Paraguayan lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after his resignation, as the collapse of a digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings. Paraguayan lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after his resignation, as the collapse of a digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings.(Image credit: Jorge Saenz)
articles.ai_summary: Paraguayan lawmakers impeached President Santiago Peña just minutes after his resignation following the collapse of a digital bank linked to his administration.

scraped.title: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
scraped.description: Paraguayan lawmakers voted to impeach President Santiago Peña minutes after his resignation, as the collapse of a digital bank tied to his government froze millions of people's savings.
scraped.h1: Paraguay's president is impeached minutes after resigning following a bank collapse
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

A demonstrator holds a mock U.S. dollar bill depicting Paraguayan President Santiago Peña during a protest against the government and Ueno Bank, which Paraguay's central bank seized amid a solvency crisis, in Asunción, Paraguay, Wednesday. Jorge Saenz/AP hide caption

ASUNCIÓN, Paraguay — Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced his resignation Thursday after the collapse of a major digital bank tied to his government triggered widespread protests, froze millions of people's savings and cost him the support of his own party.

The crisis at Ueno Bank turned Peña's long-ruling Colorado Party against him, a stunning reversal for the former International Monetary Fund economist who had enjoyed the backing of the country's most powerful politicians and was welcomed in Washington just weeks ago as a key ally of the Trump administration.

Minutes after Peña's announcement, the lower house voted 78-0 to impeach him, sending the charges to the Senate. Congressional leaders were expected to accept his resignation later Thursday, clearing the way for Vice President Pedro Alliana to be sworn in without waiting for a Senate trial.

Opposition senators were still demanding a trial, arguing that allowing Peña to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life, with legal protections that could prevent his prosecution.

Paraguay President Santiago Peña speaks to the media at United Nations headquarters, Sept. 19, 2023. Ted Shaffrey/AP hide caption

As lawmakers debated his impeachment, Peña said in a video posted to X that he was stepping down in the interest of "the stability of our country, social peace and the need to preserve our democratic institutions."

Even Peña's mentor, Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, backed impeachment, saying the party would not side with "the plundering of public and private funds and pensioners' money." The United States Treasury sanctioned Cartes in 2023 over bribery allegations that the Trump administration lifted last year.

Peña, who until last year held a stake in a company linked to Ueno, expressed contrition. But he stopped short of accepting responsibility for the turmoil, which has left millions of depositors, retirees and workers scrambling to recoup their frozen savings and unpaid wages.

"I want to apologize to the people if I have failed them at any point," he said. "It was never my intention to betray the trust they placed in me."

The turmoil has hit Paraguay's currency. The guaraní fell nearly 4% against the U.S. dollar Thursday, bringing its losses this week to nearly 7%, according to central bank exchange-rate data.

Ueno Bank, which exploded from an obscure finance company to a household name in less than five years, claimed more than 60% of Paraguay's adults as customers. Many Paraguayans are left asking how a bank linked to the president could grow so rapidly in size and importance despite repeated warnings about its lending practices.

The answer lies in the uncomfortable proximity of Peña's Colorado Party to the country's regulators and business elite, a weakness that has endured even as steady economic management and rapid growth recently earned Paraguay coveted investment-grade credit ratings.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress on Wednesday. "We are fed up with 70 years of plunder."

Soon after winning its banking license in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere in Paraguay. The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries, grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

Government money poured into Ueno's coffers under Peña. He also appointed Carlos Carvallo, president of Financiera Ueno, the predecessor to Ueno Bank, to run the central bank, the agency charged with supervising the digital lender.

As of last month, Ueno reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, about a quarter of its total, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydroelectric dams.

Even as retirees' savings and other public money piled up at Ueno, worries were escalating inside the central bank. In June, its inspectors found a pattern of risky lending to insiders, reported ABC Color, a leading Paraguayan newspaper. Ueno had extended large sums to companies tied to its owners, beyond what the law allows and without enough collateral to cover the debts if they went bad.

As recently as last month, Peña defended Ueno and the central bank's oversight, dismissing the concerns as a smear campaign that was spooking the public.

But on Monday, it all came crashing down. Regulators investigating Ueno's loans to companies linked to its owners found poorly documented lending, the central bank said, as well as expenses the bank had wrongly counted as assets.

Once the books were corrected, Ueno's capital, the cushion banks must keep to absorb losses, fell to less than half the legal minimum. The central bank announced the lender's seizure Tuesday, beginning a process to transfer deposits and recoverable assets to other banks before liquidating what remained.

Ueno's app, cards and transfers went dark and its branches locked their doors, leaving desperate depositors lined up outside. On Wednesday, a rush to open new accounts elsewhere crashed other banks' mobile apps, fueling public panic.

Officials have appealed for calm. Under a law rushed through Congress on Wednesday, a state guarantee fund must repay stranded depositors within five business days, starting Thursday with small accounts of up to about $1,600 held by customers with no debts to Ueno. The fund insures up to about $36,000 per customer, which the central bank says will cover the full balances of an estimated 97% of clients.

On Thursday, a judge ordered six Ueno executives, including founder Miguel Vázquez and bank President Juan Manuel Gustale, jailed pending trial and two others placed under house arrest. Prosecutors have charged 27 bank officials and associates with breach of trust and attempted fraud, alleging that Ueno made large loans to related companies without adequate guarantees and diverted some of the money to other group businesses.

Gustale's lawyer pushed back on the charges, arguing that senior executives had relied on staff for lending decisions. "The president or board is not responsible for deciding who receives a particular loan," José Fernández Zacur told local media.

Still in their Ueno uniforms, young employees burned their credit cards and cursed Peña outside the Labor Ministry on Thursday, demanding severance and unpaid wages. Peña's resignation did little to calm them. Many vowed to keep protesting until lawmakers finished impeaching him, saying his departure alone would neither bring accountability nor return their money.

"Let the impeachment process take place and let him lose his immunity," said Adolfo Villalba, one of the protesters on Thursday.

The Labor Ministry estimates the collapse has affected about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs at the bank and its related businesses.

Many saw Ueno's collapse not just as reckless banking but as a case study in official corruption. Only Venezuela ranks worse in South America on Transparency International's latest index of perceived corruption.

"This is yet another assault on honest, hard-working citizens, people whose small savings are the fruit of years of labor," said Belarmino Balbuena, one of thousands who marched on Congress in the capital, Asunción, on Wednesday.

The crowds shouted, "We want your head, Peña!" Their signs branded him "the enemy of savers" and pleaded, "Give us back our money." Riot police fired pepper spray and rubber bullets to push them back.

At the national stadium that once bore Ueno's name, the bank's logo had already been scrubbed away. Across the capital, fresh graffiti called politicians thieves.

About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in Oc...
articles.ai_summary: A strike at a Micron Technology plant in Taiwan highlights labor unrest and demands for better profit sharing amid the global AI industry's growth.

scraped.title: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
scraped.description: Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry show growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.
scraped.h1: A rare strike in Taiwan exposes labor unrest beneath the global AI rush
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

Labor disputes and unionization in Taiwan’s semiconductor industry highlight growing worker discontent over the unequal distribution of profits from the AI boom.

About a dozen workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taoyuan in Taiwan went on strike in October, the first in the island’s semiconductor industry, after their union and the chipmaker failed to reach an agreement on salaries and bonuses. Their one-day action, while largely symbolic, is a reflection of the growing discontent among laborers in the artificial intelligence industry over how profits are distributed.

The leading American memory chipmaker has posted record profits this year on the back of surging demand for AI chips. Unions representing workers at Micron’s facilities in Taoyuan and Taichung have been negotiating with the company for months for a profit-sharing agreement similar to those reached by employees at rivals Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix in South Korea.

“Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit instead of this unequal distribution between high-level executives and the rank and file,” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union, told Rest of World .

Making a profit is perfectly fine, but the rank and file should get a share of the profit.” Jerry Lin, president of Micron’s Taoyuan union

The global tech industry is heavily reliant on Taiwan’s semiconductor industry. Idaho-based Micron, the world’s third-biggest memory chipmaker, employs more than 15,000 workers in Taiwan. They produce over 60% of the company’s dynamic random access memory chips, used in AI servers. A prolonged workers’ strike could severely disrupt already strained supplies of memory chips worldwide.

Micron on October 22 said it had reached an agreement with the Taichung union for higher salaries and quarterly bonuses, and bigger contributions to the pension accounts of all workers at its Taiwan operations. But many union members rejected the deal, which they said was made in secret, while the majority of members of the Taoyuan union said they were dissatisfied with the terms of the agreement.

“We do not accept the deal. None of our demands were fulfilled,” a Taoyuan union member, who asked not to be named because he is not authorized to speak to the media, told Rest of World . “We are surprised that the Taichung union representatives signed the deal.”

The Taoyuan union, which is registered as a separate entity with more than 2,300 members, can still go on strike.

Micron respects the workers’ “lawful rights and the applicable legal process,” a spokesperson for the company told Rest of World. “We are committed to constructive engagement with the Taoyuan and Taichung unions to reach a solution that works for all parties.”

Labor disputes and strikes in Taiwan have historically been associated with traditional industries. The actions by the Micron workers’ unions signal a broader shift as semiconductor workers increasingly organize to demand greater transparency and a fairer share of the value they help create, Wu Yu-ren, a labor relations professor at National Chung Cheng University, told Rest of World .

Over the past few months, membership in Micron’s two worker unions has surged from around 440 to more than 13,000. Earlier this year, employees of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. — which makes about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors and 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models — also discussed unionizing and striking over pay.

Taiwan’s high-tech companies have traditionally used generous benefits and bonuses to discourage workers from forming unions. White-collar tech workers have tended to change jobs instead of seeking collective action.

Now, “ soaring demand for high-end memory has driven up share prices and corporate profits, making workers question how those gains are distributed,” Wu said. “The labor actions of Samsung and SK Hynix have also influenced the unionization of Taiwan tech workers.”

Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common.” Pan Shih-wei, former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor.

Across the world, policymakers, economists, and civil society groups are grappling with the widening gap between those who are benefiting from the AI boom and those who are being left behind. U.S. startups alone have created 19 billionaires worth a combined $59 billion over the past year, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index .

The Micron workers’ actions come as American frontier AI company Anthropic prepares to launch what could be the world’s biggest initial public offering, valuing the company at nearly $2 trillion. Its founders, investors, and some employees stand to become very wealthy.

In Taiwan, negotiations between Micron’s Taoyuan union and the company are continuing. In the event of another strike, the impact of a brief stop in production would likely be limited if backup personnel are available for equipment maintenance, process monitoring, and troubleshooting, Ellie Wang, an analyst at consulting firm TrendForce, told Rest of World .

“The main consequence would be heightened customer concern over delivery reliability,” she said.

But if worker discontent spreads to other facilities or if there are prolonged strikes, it could disrupt supplies to downstream AI hardware makers such as Nvidia, and drive up prices. It would also hurt Taiwan’s wider economy, with the semiconductor sector making up more than a fifth of gross domestic product.

The stakes are high. Taiwan’s president, Lai Ching-te, attended Micron’s opening ceremony for its new plant in Taichung last month, and urged the company and its workers to reach an agreement. “Corporations and employees should help each other like fish and water,” he said.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Labor said it would provide assistance and facilitate further dialogue between Micron and the Taoyuan union. “We hope that both parties will be willing to negotiate, reach a consensus as soon as possible and bring the dispute to an end,” it said in a statement .

Building a constructive labor-management relationship before disputes escalate will be a challenge for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry, Pan Shih-wei, a former labor minister and adjunct labor relations professor, told Rest of World . “Taiwan has traditionally relied on government intervention for labor disputes, and companies lack established channels for dialogue with workers.”

The Micron dispute could lead to a wider labor movement as younger workers become more conscious of their rights, Pan said.

“High-tech companies really need to take a closer look at how they manage labor relations,” he said. “Discussions about strikes and the distribution of profits will become increasingly common. … Ultimately, determining the profit-sharing ratio requires negotiations and engagement between the parties.”

A growing number of startups are editing powerful Chinese open-weight models for Western businesses that are concerned about censorship and security.

Some languages require far more tokens for AI models to process, raising costs and reducing context for the people who use them.

Africa must develop AI systems with local control to protect critical infrastructure such as mobile money networks from growing AI-powered cyberthreats.

scraped.title: Police welcome 10-year sentence for activist Joshua Wong amid int'l outcry
scraped.description: The National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force has welcomed the 10-year prison sentence handed to Joshua Wong, saying that it was a "proper sentence" to reflect the offence committed.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: ‘Truly reflective of his offence’: Police welcome 10-year prison sentence for activist Joshua Wong amid int’l outcry
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

The National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force has welcomed the 10-year prison sentence handed to Joshua Wong , saying that it was a “proper sentence” to reflect the offence committed.

Steve Li, chief superintendent of the National Security Department of the Hong Kong Police Force, told reporters on Thursday outside the High Court that he hoped the activist would gain a proper understanding of China and become a law-abiding person after serving his sentence.

Wong, who has been behind bars since late 2020, was sentenced to another 10 years in jail on Thursday after he pleaded guilty in September to conspiring to collude with foreign forces.

Wong was accused of conspiring with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and other unnamed individuals in 2020 to request that foreign countries impose sanctions and blockades against the governments of Hong Kong and mainland China.

Judge William Tam said on Thursday that the case was of a “grave nature” under the Beijing-imposed national security law, which warrants at least 10 years’ imprisonment and a maximum of life imprisonment.

When asked by HKFP whether authorities would appeal to seek a heavier sentence, Li said: “[The sentence] is truly reflective of his offence committed during the period, of the grave nature of the offence. Of course, I have to discuss with DOJ [Department of Justice] colleagues whether we will [appeal], but personally I think it is a proper sentence to him.”

In a statement sent by Wong from prison and obtained by HKFP, Wong said a national security police officer told him that they were “enemies.” When asked whether authorities considered Wong an enemy, Li said that was not his perspective.

“I personally won’t regard him as an enemy. He is an offender. And as police officers, we need to do the things to rectify the situation and to reinforce the law,” Li said.

In a statement on Thursday, Chief Executive John Lee described Wong, Law and their affiliates as “among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability.”

Wong is currently serving a four-year, eight-month jail term for conspiracy to subvert state power in the landmark “Hong Kong 47” case , in which 45 prominent pro-democracy campaigners were convicted and sentenced to up to 10 years in jail in 2024.

Judge Tam ordered that the new 10-year prison term run concurrently with the remaining two months and two days of his existing sentence.

The 30-year-old activist is due to be released in November 2036, when he will be 40.

In a statement released on Thursday, Amnesty International said that the Hong Kong authorities had made a young man who spoke truth to power a criminal.

Sarah Brooks, deputy regional director of the human rights organisation, said that the sentence “cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction.”

“Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security… Amnesty International reiterates its call on the Hong Kong authorities to overturn Joshua Wong’s national security convictions and to repeal all legislation that violates Hong Kong’s international human rights obligations,” the statement reads.

Having first emerged in the public eye as an opponent of a government-proposed national education scheme, Wong formed the student activist group Scholarism in 2011. He quickly rose to prominence as a youth activist, later becoming a key student leader during the 2014 Umbrella Movement.

In 2016, Wong co-founded the political party Demosisto with Nathan Law, who ran in the legislative election representing the party and was elected as the city’s youngest lawmaker.

Li said on Thursday that Law, who now resides in the United Kingdom, should hand himself in to the Hong Kong police as soon as possible.

The national security police chief also said that Wong had committed various offences since he began participating in social movements.

“He started taking part in the social movement whilst he was a youngster, and has committed various offences since his adulthood, including his offence under the national security laws, and the organising and inciting unlawful assembly, and also the contempt of law in various occasions.”

“I sincerely hope that for the rest of his time in the prison, apart from reflecting on the wrongdoings he has done to the country and to the HKSAR, he must seize opportunities, to learn how to respect the law and to properly understand his own country.”

articles.title: Well Done, America

scraped.body_text:

Newly-elected Georgia governor Keisha Lance Bottoms

Well that was a night. The glad spectacle of a newly sentient America tottering back to its capacious ideals was dubbed Orange Crush, Bluenami, a political earthquake , a wily tweak to Hegseth's coveted public execution and "one of the great acts of defiance in American history." It was both landslide too big to rig or stop and "extinction-level" rout. Above all, it was a thunderous rejection of fear, greed, lies, cruelty, war-mongering, authoritarianism . Tell your kids, urged Abdul El-Sayed, "The bad guys lost."

Who knew, pundits marveled: Turns out if you keep lying, stealing, abusing children , terrorizing, kidnapping, assaulting neighbors, shooting people in the street, making it impossible to get food, gas, health care or education while gloating about it and lining your fat pockets, everyone hates you. So it was that a " Trump Reckoning " and GOP "Armageddon" beyond even their worst doomsday scenarios arrived wherein Democrats swept "nearly every race that matters” as Americans en masse embraced all the shithole, lunatic, transgender, anti-Semitic, dog-eating, Medicare-wanting Muslim Brotherhood communists they'd been so helpfully warned about, alas, in vain.

This, of course, despite MAGA's best/worst efforts to re-draw districts, shutter polling places, strong-arm election officials, browbeat brown and black voters, pre-litigate election results they couldn't buy, and launch 1,000 DOJ "polling monitors" into all 50 states in hopes of targeting vulnerable minority districts. And yet, noted Garrett Graff, nothing untoward happened. Instead, voters "gave America another chance." Millions stood up, showed up, voted early, refused to bend the knee or be silenced. Graff said a friend wrote from deep-red Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom still had a stunning, razor-thin lead. "My flabbers are gasted,” she wrote. “Be on the lookout for pigs in the sky."

"So much history was made last night," Graff added, much of it shaped by both the 250 years and then Trump's dark reign of white supremacist politics. The startling result: The most diverse set of newly elected lawmakers the country has ever seen, with one historian writing Dems are winning races "they haven’t won since they were the white supremacist party.” An Atlanta Journal-Constitution story begins, "In 1860, an enslaved man named Sheppard Peek was listed among the possessions of William Peek, a white man in Crawfordville"; Sheppard's value was placed at $1,400. In Georgia on Tuesday, his great-great-granddaughter, Keisha Lance Bottoms, was elected the first Black female governor in the country.

Bottoms is just one of many historic firsts . Xavier Becerra , the son of Mexican immigrants, became California's first elected Latino governor. Deb Haaland became New Mexico’s first Native governor. Wisconsin and Nevada elected their first Black governors. There are three other first women governors. New Hampshire's Chris Pappas will become the first out gay man in the Senate. A trans woman won a House seat in...Alabama. Colorado elected its first Gen Z woman; she will be one of a record 100 women to serve simultaneously in the House. Democrats gained full control of a record six state governments, Southern voters swung 20 points to Dems, Jon Ossoff was easily re-elected on a platform, essentially, of "I don't like Nazis." Virginia ended Jim Crow after 124 years, and enshrined abortion in its constitution. Nancy LaCore, a former Navy admiral fired by Hegseth, flipped Nancy Mace's seat in South Carolina. The GOP lost all four of its gerrymandered districts in Florida. Egyptian-born Adam Hamaway, 57, will be the first Muslim elected to the House from New Jersey. A Rutgers-educated doctor, he served 8 years as a combat surgeon in the US Army before starting private practice in Princeton; he also volunteered in Gaza , Syria , Lebanon , Sudan , Jordan.

Beating back a grotesquely Islamophobic campaign, Michigan's Dr. Abdul El-Sayed will become the first Muslim in the Senate.In his victory speech, he thanked "everyone who sent a dollar, made a call, posted a story and most importantly gave us your stake in democracy . You took a chance on the unlikeliest of candidates." Summoning "all the kids who watched and the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocked someone for their name or how they pray, let them (know) the bad guys lost...We deserve an America big enough for all our kids - let's go build it." He also cited the "delicious irony" that JD, whose "view of America is small, like him," is constitutionally obligated to swear him in come January.

In another sweet spot and longtime pipe dream, Talarico took back Texas from the scandal-smeared Paxton in "not just a tsunami, but a bloodbath." Adding to the schadenfreude was the upset win by Gina Hinojosa, the state's first Latina governor-elect, over monstrous Greg Abbott . In a stunning twist, Dems also won every statewide office down to railroad commissioner, along with four Supreme Court seats; the wins prompted an explosion of noisy joy in Austin that "sounded like an Eastern European city that just overthrew a dictator.” The cherry on top: Texas' new Dem Attorney General, who campaigned on investigating Elon Musk after he moved his business there to escape California woke, can now prosecute him for state level crimes without any DOJ interference.

Musk, who spent half a billion dollars nationwide and lost every race he tried to buy, is among MAGA fat cats, tech bros and grifters who'll likely be targeted by California's (easily reelected) Robert Garcia, set to chair the House Oversight Committee. His blunt message : "Lawyer up." Many others also feel "the only way we want Dems to reach across the aisle is with a subpoena." With an " accountability bill " ready, Dean Blundell argues, "A LOT of people need to go to jail" - Hegseth, the Trump family crypto empire, the DOJ hacks who covered up Epstein crimes, the Rapist-In-Chief, the sadists of ICE once it's been "torn down to the studs." Scores of voters also demanded justice for their victims Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Salgado Araujo by putting "I Voted" stickers on their memorials: "They were on the ballot."

Over at the presumably ketchup-encrusted White House , Trump remains in his own daft fantasy world, the "lamest of lame ducks." He burbles he "looks forward to working with" the trans jihadists he says are destroying America, but he'll veto everything. He's awash in his "magnificent" ballroom. He insists if he was on the ballot "we'd have won IN A LANDSLIDE," but of course he was and CNN 's John King is happy to name all the places he told voters to pretend he was: "They did. They'd had enough." Even his cultists - and ex-cultists - blame him: "The reason isn't them, it's you. You fucked us. We chose Hitler with Down Syndrome, and we lost." Online, meanwhile, the White House posted a desperate "PSA: Trump Is Still Your President." Like we could forget.

Still, the seismic shift tentatively feels like a new dawn, a path toward redemption, a sliver of hope, the long-ago thing with feathers we can barely remember. Candidates, volunteers, organizers, lawyers stepped up, and vast numbers of Americans showed up to support them. The mood was buoyant. Some said they wished Mitch McConnell was alive to see the Senate results. The Borowitz Report said Mike Johnson begged God to "rapture him up" immediately; tearfully, he said that as a loyal Republican he couldn't bear to be in a "minority" because he hates 'em all. Another report said a bitter Elon Musk put Ken Paxton on eBay; no buyers yet. Also, tragically, two sources say cracks and peeling have again emerged in the Reflecting Pool, but MAGA is on it. Said an Interior spokesperson, "The Reflecting Pool has never looked this beautiful, and it's all thanks to President Donald J. Trump."

Update : Can you say learned nothing, knows nothing, never will, truly astoundingly losing it? On Thursday, our lame-duck loser displayed his stellar grasp on political priorities - what election? - by signing an entirely meaningless order proclaiming nobody can de-Cheesecake Factory his tacky abomination of a golden whorehouse of an Oval Office, 'cause then he'd be some pissed and don't forget we won World War One. Beyond the surreal looking-glass,

scraped.title: Voters Demanded Change – on the Environment, and Democracy
scraped.description: Affordable clean energy, data center guardrails, and government accountability played out in midterm contests across the country.
scraped.author: Abigail Dillen
scraped.h1: Voters Demanded Change – on the Environment, and Democracy
scraped.body_text:
Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Earthjustice serves hundreds of public-interest clients, providing top-tier legal representation free of charge — and we win. Because the earth needs a good lawyer.

Our Stories

Affordable clean energy, data center guardrails, and government accountability played out in midterm contests across the country.

By Abigail Dillen

On Tuesday, Americans voted for a change in direction – including on the environment.

Data centers were one major issue on the ballot. On Tuesday, data center bans or restrictions passed in at least 38 jurisdictions and counting across the country. In the states where the buildout is happening fastest, including Georgia, Ohio, and Texas, governors’ races turned on voter recognition of the need for stronger guardrails and robust community protections.

With rising power demand for data centers and rising energy costs, this election was also about the future of energy. Voters angry about growing energy bills focused attention on races for seats on the Georgia Public Service Commission, the body that regulates utilities in that state. Similar dynamics were seen in races for two seats on the Arizona Corporation Commission, another utility regulator, and one seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, which regulates the oil and gas industry.

These are small agencies with tremendous power. With these seats, there is an opportunity to usher in clean energy for people who are struggling with soaring energy costs. These were the opposite of sleepy races: Voters are understanding the connection between data centers, utility rates, and regulatory bodies.

And, in the midst of a rush to drill more oil and gas and entrench our fossil fuel dependence, voters rejected a ballot measure to establish a constitutional “right to gas” in Colorado, a major oil-and-gas-producing state. The oil and gas industry presented voters with a false choice between prosperity and policies aimed at reducing greenhouse gas emissions. Voters know better.

Among the most important debates in the country is how to build the infrastructure we need faster without running over people and wrecking the things we can’t afford to lose. For example, clean water and clean air. This “abundance” debate has its origins in the California housing crisis, and it has come to stand for the proposition that deregulation is the answer to our country’s problems. As data centers show what speed without guardrails looks like, the debate came full circle in California, with voters rejecting Prop 45, a sloppy effort to kill environmental review in the permitting process for even the most consequential projects.

This election is a thrilling reminder and a profound challenge: We can move forward together in this country if we are willing to throw in together, believe in our ambition for real change, and act on it.

Over the last two years, too many people have underestimated American voters and their ability to care about all the things that matter at once. This election was about the cost of living and an economy that must work infinitely better for everyone. It was also about our health, our health care, and the health of the communities where we live and work. It was about justice and the rights that Americans are not going to give up, no matter how much money is spent and how much power is abused to create division and drive despair.

People across this country did the real work to organize and vote. A whole bunch of courageous, good people stepped up to lead this work. The hope that millions of Americans felt on election night is a call to the most ambitious action. Let’s get to work!

We’ve received your feedback — thank you!

“People have a right to see the view from the mountaintop — the Clean Air Act says so.”

Stay informed on how we hold accountable those who break our environmental laws.

articles.title: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
articles.summary: Tens of millions voted to punish Trump over inequality, war and ICE terror. The new Congress will deliver nothing on those issues unless it is forced to.
articles.ai_summary: A statement from the PSL emphasizes the need for continued activism to address issues highlighted by voters in the recent elections.

scraped.title: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
scraped.description: Voters handed Donald Trump and the Republican Party a crushing defeat on Nov. 3. Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kans
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: PSL Statement: The Democratic wave and the fight ahead
scraped.body_text:
Voters handed Donald Trump and the Republican Party a crushing defeat on Nov. 3. Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. Alaska and Mississippi may be called for the Democrats too. It was the same story in the House, where Democrats won in districts Trump had carried by 15 points in 2024 (like Kentucky’s 6th) and even newly gerrymandered districts in North Carolina and Alabama. The national popular vote in the House is projected to show a Democratic margin of about 13 points, the largest margin for either party in 50 years.

The election was a referendum not just on Trump as an individual but on the reactionary MAGA agenda to shred democratic rights and put the whole country on the platter for the billionaires. The country voted against not just the price of groceries and fuel, but against an unprovoked war on Iran. In the NBC News exit poll, 62% of voters said Trump made the wrong decision in starting the war, and about three-quarters called it a crucial or major factor in their vote. Even the “cost of living” issue has to be placed in class terms to be properly understood. The issue is not just economic hardship in the abstract, but that this pain comes at a time when billionaires’ wealth has surged upwards by 32% in just the last year . The S&P 500 is up 28% since Trump’s election. While the recession is already here for huge sections of the working class, the country’s 977 billionaires are doing better than ever before. Everyone can see that the mass introduction of AI will only deepen these trends.

Trump and Fox News have tried to spin this loss, deflecting blame onto individual Republican candidates. But the electoral map provides an indisputable single picture. According to a Washington Post analysis, voters moved at least 15 points toward the Democrats in every kind of county: whether rural, suburban or urban, racially diverse or majority-white. MAGA’s supposed inroads among Black, Latino and Gen-Z voters — which many exaggerated to begin with — proved to be a short-lived and passing phenomenon. The shifts were stark in areas that have been wrongly called “Trump Country” for the last decade; now that term can be retired. Democrats won Senate seats in South Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and Texas, and may even win Mississippi; Trump carried every one of those states by 13 to 23 points in 2024. This means they swung between 17 and 26 points toward the Democrats in just two years time — a stunning reversal.

The vote in rural states and regions requires special attention. Farm bankruptcies have jumped 85 percent over the last two years, largely due to Trump’s tariffs, combined with the bungling and chaotic response to other nations’ retaliatory tariffs. Then the Iran war choked off shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, so diesel prices soared by nearly 70 percent and fertilizer and farm equipment, the other key input costs, followed. “Compared to last year, our fuel bill is $50,000 higher,” Kansas farmer Vance Ehmke told the Hastings Tribune. When grocery prices became a political problem for consumers, Trump quadrupled the quota for low-tariff Argentine beef, hitting cattle producers a second time.

The more detailed election results will allow for more in-depth local analysis but already these swings disprove the caricature of all Trump voters as some sort of solid fascist bloc. In 2020, millions of working people voted for Joe Biden in hopes he would make life more bearable. Instead, the COVID-era social support programs expired, consumer prices soared anyway, and in 2024 many of the same voters gave Trump a chance to deliver on his promises to improve their lives. Now he’s failed them too.

The limits of Congress and the Democratic Party

Anyone disgusted by Elon Musk’s attempt to buy the elections will delight in his failure. Anyone who has suffered under this administration, or has been outraged by MAGA’s extreme racism, will no doubt enjoy watching Gina Hinojosa unseat Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, and watching South Carolina’s Black working class turn out in droves to remove Darline Graham, appointed to the seat after the death of her brother Lindsey Graham. That Mississippi may end up with its first Black Senator since 1881 is historic, and itself a searing indictment of white supremacy. It cannot be disconnected from the recent upsurges in response to the police killing of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley and the apparent cover-up in the Nolan Wells case.

But the feeling of satisfaction of seeing MAGA defeated must not turn into illusions about the role of Congress or the Democratic Party that now holds it. Put simply, there is no indication that the Democrats have either the will or the program to fight on the issues that drove mass turnout: ending the war, bringing down prices, ejecting the billionaire class from power, defending civil rights, or stopping ICE terror.

This isn’t just about Democratic politicians “selling out.” The obstacles are built into the capitalist political system. Only a third of the Senate faces voters in each election cycle exactly so that these defenders of the capitalist system can’t be dislodged by any voter “wave.” The filibuster survives as an internal procedural rule (not in the Constitution), and the lifetime-appointed Supreme Court sits above it all, for the same reason. In addition, nearly $12 billion was spent on these midterms — that’s not just to win the race, but to purchase influence with whoever comes into office. The 50 largest donors contributed almost $2.8 billion of it, and OpenSecrets found that 1 percent of donors supplied 98 percent of the money given to outside groups. Small donors contributed less than 10 percent of the overall midterm funds raised. Big Money sets the stage for Election Day, and then kicks right back into motion the very next day.

Three times in two decades a wave election has handed the Democrats control of Congress: after the 2006 midterms, then in 2008, giving them 59 Senate seats in Barack Obama’s first term, and then again the White House and both chambers in 2021. Each time they promised universal health care, immigration reform, climate action, a $15 minimum wage, a law protecting abortion rights, not to mention universal childcare, a permanent child tax credit, student debt relief, the protection of voting rights, and so on. Each time a section of the party exercised a veto on behalf of corporate America.

The political system is riddled with such “veto points” precisely to frustrate the popular sentiment for transformative change, and the Democratic Party, as a ruling-class party, always produces the figures ready to use these vetoes. This cycle of failure and frustration is what opened the road for Trump.

The longer historical record tells the same story. For the 48 years from 1933 until 1981, Democrats controlled both houses of Congress the entire time , except for brief windows from 1947 to 1949 and again from 1953 to 1955. Yes, those majorities passed the Wagner Act and Social Security in 1935, in the wake of the 1934 general strikes in Toledo, Minneapolis and San Francisco. But the same majorities let Southern Democrats filibuster an anti-lynching bill to death in 1938 and kept Jim Crow intact for another generation, until the civil rights movement forced the issue. What Congress delivered in terms of progressive reforms always depended on the forces built outside it, and it’s a body that has not delivered anything substantial in favor of the working class in half a century.

The midterm vote was a gauge of mass consciousness and it measured the anger of the masses. But it did not magically transform this undemocratic political system into something new. On all the issues, super-majorities want the Iran war to end, want to stop AI-induced job destruction, want to win Medicare for all, and oppose ICE’s campaign of terror. In a democratic system, the mass turnout yesterday would translate into immediate policy change. But that’s not going to happen. Not one ICE detainee will be released because of this result. Trump can still order strikes on Iran at any second. The billionaires still control all the board rooms that set prices, wages and the introduction of job-destroying technology. What appears as a “democracy” is in fact the dictatorship of capital, and that is as true today as it was before the midterms.

That makes it all the more necessary for people who voted for change to immediately start demanding it from the incoming Congress. The new Democratic majority has real powers if it chooses to use them. It could pass Medicare for All and legalization for the undocumented, and could make Trump veto them in public. Even if he does, this would create real legislative momentum that the next president couldn’t ignore. Congress controls the power of the purse, and could hold up budgets until it claws back the money Republicans pushed through by reconciliation in June, which funds ICE through the end of Trump’s term. It could use its investigative power, as the Church Committee did with COINTELPRO in 1975, to expose this administration’s surveillance of activists and deportation of people for their political views. This is just scratching the surface of what can be demanded. People voted for real change, not to have one thousand meaningless committee hearings full of theatrical speeches made for social media and fundraising videos.

On the appeal of socialism

Notably, Trump’s anti-communist ads did not stop candidates who call themselves socialists, nor did it scare away Democratic voters. This attack line has become less and less potent, and voters are tired of it. A 2025 Cato Institute/YouGov poll found 62 percent of Americans aged 18 to 29 view socialism favorably, and when you look across all ages, the total number of people who hold such a view now numbers 100 million. The fog of anti-communism has lifted in a big way, even if the definition and understanding of socialism remains quite weak — in part because of the incorrect definitions given by many who proclaim themselves “socialist.”

Nor did the issue of Palestine scare away voters. Quite the contrary. What last year was waved away as “exceptional” New York City, when Mamdani was elected, was repeated elsewhere. Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in Michigan to become the first Muslim elected to the Senate, and he carried real movement energy against the Gaza genocide and ICE, while speaking to working-class concerns. On Election Day, Trump himself announced the end of U.S. military aid to Israel in the coming period. This is just an accounting trick, planned with Netanyahu himself, meant to hide full support for the apartheid state, but it does reflect the real change in consciousness that has taken place across the entire electorate, largely due to the work of the Palestine solidarity movement. That movement’s nonstop organizing and advocacy, its constant presence in the streets and on social media, has created such a powerful argument that it now impacts even the Republican base.

While the progressive and democratic socialist wing of the Democratic Party scored important victories, the strategy of changing the Democratic Party from within is nothing new. Throughout history the party has changed its insurgents far more easily than they have changed it. Elected without an independent base, they must observe a discipline set by party leaders and donors, starting with votes for Hakeem Jeffries as Democratic leader. On November 1, the New York Times reported that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is urging fellow democratic socialists toward a “culture of welcoming” over the “purity-minded litmus tests” of the Gaza movement. This is ridiculous. Every political trend, from right to left, must draw lines. The question is whether backing the party leaders who armed a genocide falls inside them.

Operating inside a party that by design does not hold members to its platform is what allowed Manchin, Sinema and now John Fetterman and Haley Stevens to do as they please. We must also recognize the Democratic Party, as an imperialist party, is wholly devoted to the idea of the encirclement of China and Russia, US domination over trade routes and energy supplies in the Middle East, the exploitation of Africa for its natural resources, and the management of Latin America as its “backyard.” It was the Democrats in power that led the country into the Korean War, the Vietnam War, and, more recently, the US/NATO-instigated war between Russia and Ukraine, and the genocide in Gaza. This isn’t an incidental aspect of the Democratic Party, and for progressives to advance anything domestically, they’ll be first asked to go along with the needs of the Empire. That’s where AOC’s “litmus test” comment is really headed.

Independent campaigns and the road ahead

PSL candidates ran against that machinery, and made significant inroads in the working-class with mass grassroots canvassing gaining new levels of visibility for the socialist program. Greg Levy, the PSL member who ran for Senate in Ohio, has about 94,500 votes, 2 percent of the total, despite exclusion from every debate and a smear campaign built on a Republican-funded PAC that promoted him without his consent. Joe Tache in Massachusetts faced the same debate exclusion, even while polling over 10 percent and meeting all the fundraising thresholds. He still built a campaign with the feel of a social movement, and brought around 55,000-60,000 votes after closing his campaign with a 700-person rally in Boston. Andre Easton, running for a House seat in the Bronx, is nearing a 9 percent total — which is the highest percentage of any House candidate representing a socialist or communist party since the early 1940s. Meanwhile, Frank Lara won his election for the school board of South San Francisco, campaigning on an anti-billionaires platform to put the needs of public school students and teachers first. The Peace and Freedom Party’s Alexander Kraft, who was endorsed by the PSL, brought in a strong 39% running for mayor of El Cajon, in San Diego County, against a Republican incumbent.

PSL candidates are distinguished from those running in the Democratic Party because they are beholden to the platform and perspective of the Party; it is not something they can cast to the side for short-term convenience.

Each of these campaigns was run vigorously, and will produce many lessons that now must be studied and expounded further, which we will do in the coming days.

Across the board, tens of millions went to the polls to politically punish Trump, and they succeeded. But they were also dreaming of peace, justice and good jobs — a dream that the capitalist system will not deliver.

Rebuilding a socialist movement in the historic heartland of anti-communism is no simple task. But the gap between what the majority wants and what this system will allow is exactly where the socialist movement can grow. That is what the PSL will keep doing, 365 days a year.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

Democrats took both houses of Congress, flipping Senate seats in Kansas, Iowa, Ohio, Maine, North Carolina, South Carolina and Texas, where James Talarico became the first Democrat elected to the Senate since 1988. Alaska and Mississippi may be called for the Democrats too. scraped.title: Henry Nowak and the return of clan justice
scraped.author: Samuel Rubinstein
scraped.h1: Henry Nowak and the return of clan justice Politicians can’t ignore public concern
scraped.body_text:
A protest in Southampton. (Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty)

A protest in Southampton. (Justin Tallis/AFP/Getty)

On 1 June 2026, shortly after the sentencing of Henry Nowak’s murderer, the man who is touted to be our next prime minister put out a statement : “Today’s revelations will further damage people’s confidence in our political system.” It will, I predict, come to be regarded as shocking that Andy Burnham could speak of “today’s revelations” and mean, and assume that everyone else would understand, not the horror of Nowak’s murder, but another round of Mandelson rigmarole. Nothing could better demonstrate what Tony Blair, in his recent essay , called a “politics bubble” — a blinkered, superficial clique of which Burnham, for all his anti-Westminster posturing, is very much a part.

But soon enough it became obvious, even within the bubble, that Nowak was not just a murdered teenager but a moment , a moment demanding a response. After days of trying to quell the situation, Sir Keir Starmer has hosted the Nowak family at Downing Street. Yet the response so far has generally been half-baked. There are vague references to avoiding “division”, indistinguishable from what came in the wake of Manchester and Southport. There seems to be no effort whatsoever to grapple with the — admittedly difficult — facts of the case. Nigel Farage has been met with incoherent screeching. It is seriously suggested that his call for “pure, cold rage” somehow “incited” yobs to hurl bins at discombobulated bobbies. “Eleven police officers were injured during unrest in Southampton last night”, said James O’Brien: “is that cold enough for you?” One wonders what he thinks “cold” means. Starmer called Farage’s “appeal for rage… unforgivable”, but he feels angry all the time. The Mandelson rigmarole made him “absolutely furious”. Does the murder of Nowak make him furious? Does it not fill him with pure, cold rage?

The bubble’s response is awash with deflection and denial. Their Hail Mary is that we all have goldfish memories, or that we will have the good graces to forget the events of the past six years. “Beware those cunningly politicising people’s pain,” said Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi MP. In 2020 he wrote that “we cannot allow #GeorgeFloyd to become merely another statistic, but need structural change to ensure a better society for all”. Not only do calls for “structural change” now fall on deaf ears: you are guilty of “sowing division” or “politicising pain” if you dare to make them.

The government’s effort to cast “two-tier policing” as a crankish conspiracy theory also rests on some forlorn hope of collective amnesia. In 2020, it was unilaterally decreed that the police should junk color-blindness as an ideal. They were foolhardy enough to put this in writing : “Our commitment to racial equity… does not mean treating everyone ‘the same’ or being ‘color blind’.” Shabana Mahmood recently had to intervene to ensure that the sentencing guidelines would not grant special leniency to ethnic minorities. Now they have the temerity to say that the very notion of two-tier justice is a far-Right fantasy, that the only reason anybody in Britain believes it is Elon Musk . I have always disliked that voguish and overused term, “gaslighting”: gaslighting is simply lying, and usually bad lying at that. The “politics bubble” response to Nowak’s murder, their flat-out denial of two-tier policing, isn’t making us question our own sanity. We are only questioning theirs.

“The bubble’s response is awash with deflection and denial.”

It has become the standard position of the “politics bubble” that now is not a good time to speak about the Nowak murder. This is the gist of Starmer’s response to Farage, and of the calls from various quarters against “politicizing” something that is, apparently, otherwise non-political. It is deemed improper or uncivil to try to draw any lessons from it at all. Instead we are told that the tragedy should not be “politicized” because this would be disrespecting the wishes of a grieving family. What kind of sick person would do that? Only “scum”, wrote Dan Hodges — a rather divisive word. Drawing a leaf from this book, Robert Peston asked Farage: “Why does the family of Henry Nowak mean nothing to you?” The strategy has ascended now to the highest level, to be limply deployed by the prime minister at PMQs. Rage, Starmer declared: that is Farage’s “response to a father who’s lost his son and asked for that not to happen”.

The strategy is selective. We have heard much in recent days about “exploiting” and “weaponizing”: the bubble is exploiting and weaponizing people’s compassion. They are demanding that total deference be paid to the wishes — or, rather, what they purport to be the wishes — of a family that has been through unspeakable anguish. But no such deference has ever been paid to the family of Rhiannon Whyte , stabbed to death with a screwdriver by an asylum seeker in 2024. Her grieving mother has said that Starmer has “blood on his hands”; her message, that we should stop the boats, remains unheeded. Sir David Amess MP was murdered by an Islamist extremist in 2021. His daughter has been repeatedly appealing to Downing Street for a public inquiry. Starmer still has not commissioned one: Katie Amess says he has “just ignored us”.

If the wishes of grieving families risk posing any challenge to the status quo, then they are ignored; if they fit the agenda, then they can be indulged. Recent years have seen a spate of “[victim’s name] Laws”, kneejerk responses to heart-wrenching tragedies, usually ill-conceived . Martyn’s Law , named after a victim of the Manchester arena bombing, is costing businesses billions, and does nothing to address the actual cause of the attack. It is not hard to see why these laws sail through parliament; who would dare set themselves against a dead child? These quick fixes duck thorny questions about immigration, integration, and crime, and bring governments back into their comfort zone: burdening businesses with statutory obligations and red tape. These laws, like the mawkish appeals now to the wishes of Nowak’s family, are examples of what Madeleine Grant calls “ tweeslop ”, a “mobilization of the British people’s worst instincts for sentimentality and self-congratulation”. It is, we might say, the British vice.

The bubble repeats ad nauseam a single sentence from the statement given outside the court by Nowak’s father. It is the only part of his remarks which has garnered attention: “We do not want his death to be used to create further division, hatred or tension.” The statement as a whole, however, makes perfectly clear that the Nowak family does think the murder has a political dimension. In fact it strays quite close, in places, to talk of two-tier policing, dwelling on the difference between the police’s treatment of Digwa and of Nowak. In calling for “stronger action” on the “ownership and carrying of all knives”, it seems to suggest removing the legal exemptions given to religious Sikhs. The family urges a “common sense approach to law and order”: “ common sense ” always was, in ordinary parlance, the antithesis to “woke”.

By Samuel Rubinstein

But let us suppose for a moment that the Nowak family really did want the murder to be kept out of “politics” altogether. Of course we must feel sympathy for a grieving family; but sympathy cannot be our only feeling. Victims’ families do not have a monopoly on our response to a crime. It is wrong to suggest that a grieving family ought to dictate the parameters of public conversation. To grant them such a thing would be to dissolve a foundational premise of our criminal law. Crimes are not just crimes against a person or a person’s family: they are crimes against the crown, breaches of the king’s peace, attacks on the very fabric of society, attacks against us all. There is a good reason that the case which convicted Nowak’s murderer is R . v. Digwa, rather than The Nowak Family v. Digwa.

These appeals to the supposed wishes of the Nowak family rest on the old logic of the clan. Someone from Family X kills someone from Family Y; then Family Y determines how to respond. The patriarch of Family Y, in the Nowak case, has issued (what is held to be) his definitive response; now the rest of us ought to quiet down and move on. This seems to be the government’s position. But, to put it bluntly, that is not how we do things. It is not how we have done things since the very early Middle Ages. Our systems of criminal justice moved past the feud a long time ago. We moved past it when the family or the clan forfeited its traditional monopoly; when it came to accept, in other words, that any crime is inherently political, that everyone else in society has an interest in punishing and preventing it.

We know, of course, that not all cultures work this way. The logic of the clan and the feud predominate in many parts of the world. It is especially important to reject the clan logic in this instance, because that very logic was at play in the murder of Nowak. The family of Vickrum Digwa embodies the alternative theory of justice which England overcame long ago. Crime, for the Digwa family, really was non-political. Finding their son committing a murder — catching him red-handed — they felt no higher obligation to the state, to the crown, to the king’s peace, to British society. The mother hid the weapon. The brother spun a cover story. Even after Digwa’s conviction, they shouted at Nowak’s family in court. They resented that the case had ever got to court. Perhaps they thought the murder ought to have remained a private, family matter.

These appeals to the wishes of families are appeals to clan logic; and if clan logic is now infiltrating wider British society, it makes sense that it should do so via emotional manipulation, to which Britain is so susceptible. The appeals are designed to banish avoidable events from the realm of the political: that is the plain meaning of “politicize” as a verb of disapproval. They turn human tragedies into acts of God, about which nothing can be done save a sigh and a sob. The British mainstream has always liked to tut at those Right-wing Americans who traffic in “thoughts and prayers” after every school shooting. But the “politics bubble” could hardly be clearer: there is to be no talk of radically overhauling the police, of abolishing “two-tier” justice, of restoring an older, liberal ideal of treating people as individuals rather than members of groups, of defining anti-racism in terms of color-blindness. There is, in the “politics bubble”, supposed to be no political talk at all. “Thoughts and prayers” are reassuringly inert and inoffensive. “Thoughts and prayers” are what they’re after. But “thoughts and prayers” do not meet the moment. And they will not spare other families from the devastation that has torn through Henry Nowak’s.

scraped.title: Why Gen Z is obsessed with horror
scraped.author: Kathleen Stock
scraped.h1: Why Gen Z is obsessed with horror Modern life is terrifying
scraped.body_text:
Nikki, played by Inde Navarette, pulls off an astonishing feat as the obsessed young woman. (Youtube)

Nikki, played by Inde Navarette, pulls off an astonishing feat as the obsessed young woman. (Youtube)

It’s often observed that horror films are a good barometer of pressing cultural anxieties. If so, the weather doesn’t look very good for social interaction right now. Backrooms has just been released, exploiting the spooky Covidian aesthetics of deserted buildings, and taking $118 million in its first weekend. Meanwhile, another low-budget shocker has been crushing the box office for three weeks straight: Obsession , by 26-year-old wunderkind director Curry Barker. To watch this film is to experience unaccountable dread and terror, as you enter the mind of a Gen Z man trying and failing to get a date.

The young man in question is called Bear. Never was a name so ironically bestowed for this Bear is anxious, tentative, and terrified of overstepping. He’s in love with a co-worker at the local music store, a girl called Nikki, but cannot steel himself to declare his affections to her. In a hippy shop selling crystals and dreamcatchers, he buys a “One Wish Willow” — marketed as a “collectible toy from the Eighties”. He breaks it in half as instructed, and wishes “that Nikki Freeman loved me more than anyone else in the world”. He immediately gets his heart’s desire, and all hell breaks loose.

To boomers, this may sound like a familiar tale of the terrifyingly unhinged power of the female libido, with shades of Fatal Attraction or Single White Female . But this film is no nostalgic reprise of that late-Eighties theme. The obsession of the title belongs as much to the male as to the female; and if anything, the latter is to be thoroughly pitied. Thanks to the fulfillment of Bear’s wish, Nikki is subject to an all-consuming romantic possession that drives her towards abject self-debasement and social humiliation against her better nature. During a rare moment of lucidity, she begs for death as a release, and who would blame her? We’ve all been there, Nikki love.

By Kathleen Stock

Actress Inde Navarrette pulls off an astonishing feat as the obsessed young woman, alternating insane aggression with comic pathos. Her devotion is child-like in its intensity, completely untrammeled by attempts to play it cool. Most of the time she is all id, no ego, openly begging Bear for more affection, ferociously guarding him against imagined rivals, and covering the front door with tape to stop him leaving for work. When that fails, she becomes literally rooted to the spot until he returns, with devastating consequences for the carpet.

But for all of Nikki’s spellbound antics, the more interesting character is Bear — sensitively played by another relative unknown, Michael Johnstone. His story makes a compelling contrast to the original “monkey paw” trope, created by author W.W. Jacobs in 1902. Jacobs’ short story depicted a cozy working-class domestic scene, interrupted by the arrival of an acquaintance fresh from the colonies, carrying with him a mysterious shriveled object that will grant three wishes. Ignoring the visitor’s dire warnings and his own misgivings — “it seems to me that I’ve got all that I want” — the family patriarch, Mr White, wishes for two hundred pounds. Next morning White receives this exact sum as compensation for his son’s death, “caught in the machinery” at work. The old man’s second wish is to bring his horribly mangled son back. His third wish is to cancel out the second, finding himself too afraid to answer the ominous knock at the door.

As befits a child of his time, director Barker says he first came across The Monkey’s Paw via an episode of The Simpsons , but one hopes he has read Jacobs’ story too. Along with all the timely social anxieties it expressed about the costs to the working classes of industrial progress, and the threat from the exotic foreigner (Mr White, anyone?), there was a simpler message there too. The Indian fakir who originally put the spell on the monkey’s paw, Jacobs wrote, “wanted to show that fate ruled people’s lives, and that those who interfered with it did so to their sorrow”. White’s mistake was to fail to accept his lot in life, trying in Promethean fashion to alter destiny instead. As such, he firmly belongs in the pantheon of classic Gothic overreachers, along with Victor Frankenstein and Dorian Gray.

But Bear’s tragic flaw is precisely the opposite. He is a chronic underreacher who uses his modernized monkey’s paw as a lazy proxy for a deliberate, intentional choice. Romantically he is paralyzed, terrified of being seen to “take advantage” of a girl — even though that’s precisely what he eventually does. And even after it seems clear Nikki has fallen under his spell, still he can’t bring himself to publicly own his feelings. When she asks him if he likes her, his guarded response is: “Why, do you like me?”.

Crazy as she is, Nikki can tell what Bear’s real problem is. At one point she gives him a “Tiger’s Eye” stone as a love gift, to bring him “confidence and will-power”. But it doesn’t work, reappearing during the film’s finale to no avail. It’s not hard to conclude that through this character, Barker has neatly encapsulated the predicament of a generation: unable to ask a pretty girl for a light, let alone steal fire from the gods.

According to some recent estimates, nearly 50% of men between 18-25 have never asked a woman out on a date. Possible reasons are legion, but include the fact that there are simply fewer chance encounters with strangers as social life has moved online. There is an attendant awareness in the young of social media’s potential for making private humiliations public. And there’s the surrounding progressive culture, placing huge emphasis on the potential for men to get sexual approaches wrong. Unfortunately, the threat of heavy social censure only seems to produce confusion and fear in conscientious types, while leaving habitual sex pests perfectly unperturbed.

By Poppy Sowerby

In a sense, then, Obsession acts as a permission structure to examine this inadvertent mess, drawing to the surface of consciousness a widespread ambivalence, but without telling viewers how to feel about it. Such story-telling neutrality makes a nice contrast with the socially conscious horror that was popular about a decade ago, following the success of Jordan Peele’s Get Out . Made at a moment of peak didacticism, Peele’s film — though otherwise pretty good — was widely interpreted as saying black people should be afraid of white people, and that white people should feel bad about this. For a while afterwards, we got a spate of clunky lectures disguised as horror films, addressed primarily to viewer’s consciences and only secondarily to their viscera.

But Obsession prefers showing not telling, and is all the better for it. When I eventually staggered out of the cinema, senses bruised by spectacle and noise, the world looked temporarily different. Strangers’ smiles seemed uncanny, the birdsong eerily pronounced. I felt peculiarly in touch with the numinous, and that doesn’t often happen to me in Horsham. It was as if I’d had a tiny holiday from reality, or a restorative miniature psychotic break.

You don’t get much of this uncanny afterglow from streaming films at home, which is another reason why the phenomenal success of Obsession and Backrooms is so cheering. It is striking that both Barker and Kane Parsons — the 20-year-old director of Backrooms — began experimenting with their craft on much smaller screens , bypassing turgid studio systems by taking their output straight to YouTube, and building massive fanbases there. But still the silver screen retained its old power to bewitch. As a result, now these directors are luring the kids out of their bedrooms to watch with other people — a fact that may do wonders for the birth rate, if nothing else.

Presumably these newcomers are encountering the thrill of mental surrender to a huge cinematic experience at close quarters, with no pause or mute button available, in a place where it is frowned upon to have a rival screen out at the same time. And who knows? Perhaps they are also learning of that time-honored way to make an easy move on your love object, something that also used to be big in the Eighties: reaching for a trembling hand in the scary dark.
