articles.summary: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House Former senior White House advisor Calley Means says he had full White House approval for a federal look at how much sugar American children eat - until Trump's former Chief-of-Staff Susie Wiles killed it. White House chief of staff Susie Wiles listens as President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after signing an executive order reclassifying marijuana as a less dangerous drug in the Oval Office of the White House, D...
articles.ai_summary: Former senior White House advisor Calley Means claims that a federal investigation into children's sugar consumption was halted by Trump's Chief-of-Staff.

scraped.title: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Ex-MAHA Insider Tells Rogan What Trump Didn't Know About His Own White House
scraped.body_text:
Former senior White House advisor Calley Means says he had full White House approval for a federal look at how much sugar American children eat - until Trump's former Chief-of-Staff Susie Wiles killed it.

"And that's where Susie told me, we can't do that. I need the sugar industry money. I need the money for the midterms," Means told Joe Rogan in an episode published Friday. In fact, according to Means, Wiles was up to all sorts of bad stuff.

Means, who quit on Oct. 22 without giving a reason and says he connected Robert F. Kennedy Jr. with Donald Trump in 2024, spent more than two hours naming the people he says stood between MAHA voters and what they voted for. He said a Wiles aide put an executive order on his desk declaring glyphosate, the weed killer in Bayer's Roundup, a national security issue, told him it was "final," and said Kennedy "should not be calling the president or calling anyone." Trump, he said, didn't know his own Justice Department then pushed the Supreme Court to take the case Bayer went on to win.

" There is a very concentrated group of people in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for and are frankly, I think it's very clear, doing things for other reasons, particularly in many cases to enrich their families," Means said near the top of the episode.

The episode went up the same day Trump announced that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff on Monday, with Wiles moving to the Trump political operation after Republicans' midterm wipeout . Means taped it before the shakeup, and Wiles is who he spent most of the first hour on. He marked the news on X:

Susie Wiles is out as chief of staff.

— Calley Means (@calleymeans) November 6, 2026

"Susie Wiles is the most powerful chief of staff in modern American history. And she has taken a stranglehold on any policy decision," Means said, adding that cabinet secretaries spend meetings "constantly worrying about how to get on Susie's good side."

He then walked Rogan through the people around her. Wiles, he said, was one of the country's top lobbyists before the White House , and "her career has been taking money from the industries and foreign governments who would pay her the most money" - including, in his account, as a top consultant to Benjamin Netanyahu and to the pharmaceutical and pesticide industries. James Blair, the head of political operations and "her friend from Florida," he said "has taken a lot of money from industries like the sugar industry."

Tony Fabrizio, Trump's chief pollster, is the one every policy "goes through," Means said, because his polling tells the team what is politically worth doing, while he takes money from "almost every single industry we're fighting against right now to this day." Later in the episode the show pulled up what Means said was the client list on Fabrizio's website: Pfizer, PhRMA, Philip Morris, Procter & Gamble, R.J. Reynolds and Dow Chemical among them. On school lunch reform, Means said, Fabrizio was "getting paid by Pepsi and giving political analysis that the juice isn't worth the squeeze."

When Means pitched healthier school meals to Fabrizio, citing Rogan's listeners, the pollster brushed it off, he said: "[MAHA] is not really a big part of our strategy." The strategy, by Means' account, was gerrymandering ("they were obsessed with redistricting") and campaign gimmicks like no tax on tips, all justified by the need for campaign cash.

Richard Walters, who joined the White House from FGS Global, came from a firm that "lobbied for pesticides, lobbied for pharma" and was paid by the pesticide trade group CropLife right before he left, Means said. While Wiles was "out getting cancer treatment," he added, "Richard was effectively chief of staff." Trump disclosed Wiles' breast cancer diagnosis in March, saying she would keep working through treatment.

Then the family business. Wiles' daughter Katie is a lobbyist at Continental Strategy , and Means said that was an open channel. "If a company hired Susie's daughter, then that was getting a high priority," he said, calling it "an open discussion in the White House." By his account the firm had "almost zero in revenue" before Trump's return and shot up to "30-ish million dollars a year in revenue." Florida filings already put Continental's lobbying pay near $5 million in 2023.

Ballard Partners, where Wiles worked before the campaign, was the other route. "If you hire Ballard, you get a meeting with Susie and you can get things done," Means said, calling the firm's reported $98 million "the down payment." Later in the episode he laid out the whole menu:

"If any special interest is watching, and you're trying to rig the system, unless it changes, pay Ballard, pay Continental, Susie's daughter, pay Checkmate, Chris [LaCivita's] son. That's another one that shot up. And, you know, pound Susie with donations and calls. Everyone knows this playbook. It's an open secret in DC."

Chris LaCivita ran Trump's 2024 campaign with Wiles. His son, Chris LaCivita Jr., joined Checkmate Government Relations after the election and registered to lobby for more than 40 clients in 2025.

Means stressed it isn't a Trump problem alone. "This is how DC works," he said, and he said he doesn't think Trump "knows about most of this."

Means' most detailed account was glyphosate, the herbicide in Bayer's Roundup. He said getting the word into the first MAHA report was "the biggest policy battle I had seen up to that time," and that as Bayer's push for legal immunity stalled in the states and in Congress, he warned Wiles' team and USDA leadership that the administration should stay out of it.

Then, he said, a Wiles aide called him into a room and put an executive order on the desk. "And it was the glyphosate EO that says it's a national security issue," Means said. "And he said, this is final. It's national security. It's coming out tomorrow." The aide told him to "please inform Bobby" and that Kennedy "should not be calling the president or calling anyone," Means said. Wiles then called Kennedy's office, and the order came out the next day.

That was February's "Promoting the National Defense by Ensuring an Adequate Supply of Elemental Phosphorus and Glyphosate-Based Herbicides," published in the Federal Register on Feb. 23, which Kennedy publicly defended at the time. "I will tell you, the Secretary of War, the major generals, they don't see our lack of glyphosate on US farms as a national security issue," Means said. He said the order was driven by Courtney Knupp, then a National Security Council staffer - "she, with Susie, drove the E.O." - who has since been named CEO of the United Soybean Board.

The Supreme Court came next. Means said Heidi Overton, then a White House aide and now Trump's pick for FDA commissioner, worked with the Justice Department, without consulting Kennedy, on the argument for the Court to take up the Roundup case, and that the solicitor general's office brought in Sarah Harris, who he said came from Bayer's main law firm. The solicitor general urged the justices to take the case, and the Court ruled for Bayer's Monsanto in June.

Trump himself didn't know his Justice Department had pushed for it, Means said. When a regenerative farmer raised the ruling at a meeting with Trump and Kennedy, he said, the president called it "a terrible idea." "And the people around him, I think treat him horribly. They treat him like they talk about him like a baby," Means said.

The single most prioritized health issue for Blair, Means said, was "to get a better pathway for fruit flavored vapes" - ahead of Medicare, health access or food. Blair argued that approving vapes "was a core midterm issue," aimed at young men, Means said.

Then-FDA Commissioner Marty Makary was pressed on it "meeting after meeting" in the West Wing and held his ground, Means said. Makary was pushed out in May. Overton then "wrote up a policy to relax standards" on fruit-flavored vapes, Means said, and public health groups sued over the FDA's flavored e-cigarette policy in July.

When Means pushed the other way on food, he said, Blair told him "the food industry, we don't want to beat up on them too much."

Asked by Rogan what was stopping Trump, Means pointed at the bureaucracy. Kennedy, "my hero," runs a 90,000-person department, and "he's surrounded by demons who want him out and want him just destroyed," Means said. "They were sending around a memo, a CIA manual, about how to be a bad bureaucrat and subvert an institution from within. That's like sent around by all the career officials."

Means appeared to be describing the Simple Sabotage Field Manual, a 1944 guide from the CIA's wartime predecessor, the OSS, which the CIA publishes on its website. It tells saboteurs inside an organization to insist on going through channels, refer everything to committees and haggle over the wording of communications.

Means also pointed to Moderna's mRNA flu shot, which the FDA refused to review in February. He said the trial compared it against an outdated flu vaccine and showed "a 0.8% absolute risk reduction." Asked about side effects, he said, "it can't be definitively said, but there were deaths," in the trial group.

Overton, a Makary protege from Johns Hopkins, told the two of them the corporate pressure had grown too much, Means said. "And I'm like, okay, this place turns you into demons," he said. The shot was approved in August after what Means called a "sham advisory committee." After Makary's exit, he added, the FDA told Pfizer it no longer has to run the new COVID vaccine study that had been a condition of the shot's reapproval.

Kratom's concentrated opioid compound 7-OH, which Means called "gas station heroin," followed the same path. He said regulators set a strict 0.05% limit early in the term, then, after "unrelenting lobbying," raised the allowed concentration 20-fold. "Again, I don't think Trump even knows about this," he said.

The line Means said he heard most from Wiles was about the midterms. "Susie said to me many times, we need money for the midterms, [Calley]. We need money for the midterms," he said.

The sharpest example came when David Kessler, the 1990s FDA commissioner who took on Big Tobacco, petitioned the FDA to examine sugar and refined carbohydrates in children's diets. Means said the initiative had a 60 Minutes segment behind it, full White House approval and a pass through the interagency process before Wiles told him she needed the sugar industry money. Earlier in the episode he gave it as a "direct quote": "I need the money from the sugar people to win the midterms."

"Okay. The midterms are over. Now what?" Rogan asked. Whatever the strategy was, he added, "they got destroyed." Means pinned the loss on "the strategy of James Blair and Tony Fabrizio and Susie," and said the point now is "why the hell aren't we doing these now?"

Rogan didn't let Trump off the hook. "Don't you think he takes some responsibility?" he asked, pointing to the Iran war and "the cryptocurrency thing." "Of course he's the ultimate responsibility," Means said, while arguing that senior staffers are now working to throw the president under the bus for the loss.

What finally pushed him out, Means said, was a federal definition of ultra-processed food that was "simply a definition, not even tied to regulation." He said he had Harvard, Tufts, the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Medical Association lined up behind it. A Mondelez lobbyist told him "we don't want it done. This will hurt our business," and said he would call Wiles. "He talked about these people at the White House like they were extensions of him," Means said.

In a meeting with Means and Kennedy, Wiles said they were "doing great" and that she didn't know "about any special interest concerns," Means said, adding that she "lied to us to our face." Afterward, he said, he heard her saying "we need to do something about [MAHA]."

School meals were the other casualty. Means spent six months on an interagency rule to end donuts and sugary pastries at school breakfast, the most common breakfast for American schoolchildren in his telling, and to add a protein requirement. "There was dozens of meetings and calls saying that taking junk food out of school lunches would hurt the companies," he said. "And when I left, the day I left, the stocks of the major junk food companies went up 8 percent."

The market data back up the size of the move. General Mills closed up 8.0% on Oct. 22, the day Means resigned, and Kraft Heinz gained 6.8%, though it was a strong day for consumer staples broadly, with the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF up 3.3%.

When he left, Means said, Wiles texted him "saying how much she admired me" and asked him "not to speak negatively of her." Asked what he would tell Trump now, he said, "I would recommend that he clears house," and that the president should "go to war with Congress" and stop "trying to make friends with John [Thune] anymore, who's a demon."

The fight moved to X on Saturday. Means posted what he called "a formal request" for Wiles and Blair to stop "harassing" him with texts and calls, and offered to "vigorously correct and apologize" for any factual error sent to him in writing:

This is a formal request for Susie Wiles and James Blair to stop harassing me with texts and calls. If there is a factual inaccuracy in what I said, send it to me in writing and I will vigorously correct and apologize for any misstatements. I will note that everything I said is...

— Calley Means (@calleymeans) November 7, 2026

Blair answered 42 minutes later, saying he had called Means the night before and told him he would consider suing if Means defamed him. "Calley, your poor me act is tiring and embarrassing for a grown man who launched a smear campaign," Blair wrote. "I've been called worse things by better people than you. And I haven't even gotten started."

scraped.title: The Incoming Democrat Governor Of Texas Is Already Going After Elon Musk
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: The Incoming Democrat Governor Of Texas Is Already Going After Elon Musk
scraped.body_text:
Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D-TX) has asked the state's parks department to hold off on a proposed sale of state land to SpaceX until she takes office, contacting the department's executive director before she is sworn in this January. The move puts part of Elon Musk's expansion plans in South Texas on hold.

Hinojosa won the governorship this week as Democrats swept the statewide races in Texas , a result that put the state's relationship with Musk and his companies in question . Musk relocated several of his businesses to Texas in recent years, and he has close ties to President Donald Trump and outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott (R-TX).

Investors reacted the morning after the vote. Tesla and SpaceX each fell nearly 6% in premarket trading on Wednesday. Musk had spent heavily to prevent that outcome. The billionaire, one of the Republican Party's largest donors, had given more than $445 million to Republican candidates and causes this cycle and urged his followers on X to vote against Democrats. About $190 million of it went into Ken Paxton's (R-TX) race for the U.S. Senate, most of it through the Senate Leadership Fund, the super PAC aligned with Senate Republican leaders.

The sale under discussion covers about 1,300 acres of public land in Cameron County, including Boca Chica State Park , which covers about 1,055 acres and sits next to SpaceX's Starbase rocket facility. Acquiring the land would allow SpaceX to expand its operations at the site, which serves as the company's main launch and production hub for its Starship program.

A draft agenda for the Texas Parks and Wildlife Commission's Thursday meeting included the sale, according to the Texas Tribune . The item came off the agenda at Hinojosa's request, she said , though the department had already said in October that the commission was not considering the sale at its November meeting. Hinojosa did not say whether the department agreed to wait until she takes office, and the commission did not announce a new date for the discussion. Texas Monthly first reported the proposed deal last month, and environmental groups opposed it after the news became public.

Hinojosa tied her intervention to her personal connection to the area. The park lies in the Rio Grande Valley, where she grew up.

"It's such an important resource," Hinojosa said of the park. "The Valley is so important to me as the place I am from, and I will never forget it."

The Boca Chica pause is the first concrete action Hinojosa has taken against Musk, one of Texas's largest employers, and it arrives before she holds any formal authority over state agencies. Abbott remains governor until January, and the Parks and Wildlife Commission's members serve under his appointments.

Musk's companies came to Texas largely on the strength of the state's business climate. He moved the headquarters of Tesla, SpaceX, X, and The Boring Company to the state, citing in part his opposition to Democratic policies in California. Tesla relocated its headquarters to Austin in 2021, and Musk announced in 2024 that SpaceX and X would follow after California enacted a law he publicly opposed. Starbase incorporated as its own city in 2025.

Hinojosa's election also raises questions beyond Musk's holdings. During the campaign, she promised a temporary moratorium on data centers in Texas , a pledge that bears on the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout the Trump administration has promoted as part of its push to reindustrialize the American economy. Texas has become one of the country's leading destinations for large-scale data center construction.

CNN's Jake Tapper pressed Hinojosa on that issue in an interview on Thursday.

"Your victory, in particular, is one that we're told AI investors are worried about, given your promises of a temporary data center moratorium ," Tapper said.

Hinojosa said she intends to change the terms on which Texas deals with major companies.

"We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans ," she said.

Tapper also asked about Boca Chica, and whether Musk might move his companies out of Texas. "Selling our beach to Elon Musk is just something that is almost unimaginable. It's unacceptable," Hinojosa said. "Our beaches are enshrined in our Texas Constitution as being free and open to the people of Texas."

Hinojosa claims she remains open to working with Musk , though she placed conditions on that relationship.

"We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms ," Hinojosa told Tapper. "It cannot be just running over the people of Texas, and that's what changes now that I will be governor."

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa: "We can have a strong working relationship with Elon Musk and his companies, but it has to be on our terms" Jake Tapper asked her about blocking the sale of a Texas state park to SpaceX, and whether Musk might leave the state over it. Her... https://t.co/owsQCmw5iW pic.twitter.com/Zzl8At5X2J

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 6, 2026

Hinojosa did not say in the interview what terms she would require of Musk's companies. On data centers, she said Texas needs to "stop what we are doing with data centers until we have those protections," new state laws she did not spell out.

Hinojosa takes office in January, and the fate of the Boca Chica land sale, and the working relationship between Musk's companies and the state of Texas, now rests with her administration.

scraped.title: 'We can't let the party off the hook': Black voters demand results after Democrats' midterm wins
scraped.description: After delivering major midterm victories for Democrats, Black voters are demanding affordability, economic opportunity, and voting rights.
scraped.author: Gerren Keith Gaynor
scraped.h1: ‘We can’t let the party off the hook’: Black voters demand results after Democrats’ midterm wins
scraped.body_text:
Political strategists say the Black-lash is shifting from electoral victories to demands for action on affordability, economic opportunity and voting rights.

Black voters are again rightfully getting their flowers for delivering what has been described as a “ Blue Tsunami ” in last week’s midterm election. Exit polls show Black voters, who had near-historically high turnout rates in key states, overwhelmingly backed Democrats over Republicans, 90% to 9%.

But as Democrats celebrate the consequential and historic wins on Nov. 3 that gave them huge majorities in the U.S. Congress and governorships, the “Black-lash” isn’t over simply because Black voters delivered at the ballot box. Now, Democrats must do what Black voters expect of them.

“The Black-lash was never about electing Democrats, and so the Black-lash does not end just because Democrats won,” Terrance Woodbury, a Democratic pollster and founding partner of HIT Strategies who coined the term, told theGrio. “The Black-lash is going to force Democrats to deliver.”

Woodbury’s warning reflects a broader sentiment among Black political strategists and organizers who say the next Congress must turn electoral victories into tangible results for Black communities, particularly in economic opportunity, affordability, and the protection of voting rights.

The pollster told theGrio that while Democrats won 90% of Black votes on election night, less than half said they believe that Democrats will make their lives better. It reflects a reality that the so-called backbone of the Democratic Party isn’t guaranteed to show up at the polls for them in future elections.

Democratic leaders also recognize the marching orders from Black voters.

“This election wasn’t some mandate for Democrats. It was an opportunity,” said Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear , who chairs the Democratic Governors Association and is a potential 2028 presidential candidate. Beshear told theGrio, “Now we’ve got to seize that opportunity and make sure we don’t squander it.”

Melanie Campbell, president and CEO of the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation, said Black voters expect action from the newly elected Congress, even as Democrats face the challenges of governing with President Donald Trump in the White House.

“I’m looking for y’all to get some stuff done, and also make sure that if you can’t get it done, you better be caught trying,” Campbell told theGrio.

Exit poll data from the National Coalition for Black Civic Participation showed that a little more than 71% of Black voters said they backed Democrats who they believed would protect voting rights and combat racism and hate.

Campbell is among several Black-led organizations already developing policy agendas and plans for the first 100 days of the new Congress, focusing on voting rights, economic opportunity, and other priorities affecting Black communities. The State of the People, for example, is releasing a comprehensive policy book called “ The Black Papers .”

Maryland Governor Wes Moore , who was overwhelmingly re-elected on Tuesday for a second term and is also rumored to run for president in 2028, told theGrio that he believes Congress should act even more urgently.

“I think we need to be aggressive and fast. I don’t think we need a 100-day plan. I think we need a 100-hour plan,” said Moore.

The Maryland governor and former Rhodes Scholar called on Congress to take immediate action to end Trump’s war in Iran and reverse his tariffs and federal cuts to health care. However, he also called for more specific policies to boost economic opportunity for Black communities, such as expanding access to government contracts for Black-owned businesses and expanding trade and apprenticeship programs for Black young adults.

Democratic strategist Ashley Etienne, who previously served as communications director for Vice President Kamala Harris , said the midterm elections demonstrated the political leverage Black voters now possess and the importance of using it to demand meaningful policy changes.

“We now are in a power position. We now have leverage,” Etienne told theGrio. “My advice to them would be become very clear-eyed about what the expectation is for those votes, and the expectation is that you legislate, lead in a way that has demonstrable impact on our lives.”

Etienne also challenged the notion that addressing the specific economic challenges facing Black Americans amounts to “identity politics,” arguing that Democrats must develop policies that reflect the needs of the communities that helped elect them.

“If you’ve got an economic agenda, you should have an agenda that is reflective of the unique challenges of all of these communities,” she said.

The political leverage of Black voters in the midterm elections wasn’t built overnight.

Campbell said much of that groundwork was laid long before the midterms, with Black women helping to organize not only themselves but also their families and communities.

The organizing was particularly visible among HBCU students, Black churches, and grassroots organizations that mobilized voters in states like Georgia, Mississippi, and North Carolina.

“That’s our culture,” said Campbell.

Woodbury of HIT Strategies said the midterm results showed renewed support for Democrats among Black men, some of whom shifted toward Trump during the 2024 presidential election. But he cautioned against interpreting that shift as a permanent return to the Democratic Party.

“My warning to Democrats is just to not wave a mission accomplished flag,” Woodbury told theGrio. “They didn’t just come home; they remain swing voters.”

The pollster said Democrats must recognize that Black voters were motivated not simply by party loyalty but by a desire to protect their rights, improve their communities and prevent further harm.

For Etienne, the message is that Black voters must continue organizing around their demands, rather than relying on electoral victories alone to produce change.

“We can’t let the party off the hook,” she said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog gave opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government on Sunday evening.

After the formal announcement, Eisenkot, who ran as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s main rival, now has to launch complicated negotiations with potential coalition partners. He has six weeks to form a government.

At the ceremony in Jerusalem, Eisenkot said he wanted a leadership that people can trust, that will act in the interests of the public and that represents all parts of society.

The Oct. 27 election gave neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor Eisenkot a clear majority in parliament. Among the kingmakers — and most politically fraught potential allies — are the Arab-led parties. They made historic gains in the election and have been a target of Netanyahu and his allies.

Eisenkot said Sunday that the conditions for parties joining his governing coalition are support for Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, for its declaration of independence, for military or national service, and recognizing the Hamas militant group as a terrorist organization.

While the announcement doesn’t guarantee that Eisenkot will be the next prime minister, Herzog’s decision is another blow to Netanyahu, who lost his parliamentary majority in the election.

Here’s a closer look at what lies ahead:

In Israel, people vote for parties, which form alliances. A coalition needs to have a majority of at least 61 seats in the 120-member assembly, known as the Knesset, to form a government.

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot secured a majority in the election. Netanyahu’s coalition plunged from a peak of 68 seats to just 53. The opposition bloc, led by Eisenkot, won 48 seats, and Arab-led parties secured the other 19.

Eisenkot has three options: a power-sharing agreement with Netanyahu, support from Arab-led parties — something several members of his bloc do not support — or an agreement with the ultra-Orthodox parties, which demand military exemptions for their community.

Eisenkot, a former army chief, and his partners made equal military service a central part of their campaign. Specifically, they are seeking an end to the long-standing draft exemptions enjoyed by the ultra-Orthodox.

After Herzog announced Saturday that he would tap Eisenkot, the candidate vowed to form a government as quickly as possible.

But doing so will almost certainly require compromises or broken promises.

Netanyahu has repeatedly claimed the election was “stolen” by Arab parties, which rallied their supporters to vote in large numbers. But he has offered little evidence to support the claims.

Netanyahu is expected to continue his pressure tactics against Eisenkot, saying any alliance with the Arab parties would be an act of betrayal.

Israel’s Shin Bet security agency has launched an investigation into possible foreign interference in the vote, but the country’s Central Elections Commission — and Herzog — say the vote was valid and even if wrongdoing is found, it did not have a significant impact on the result.

Netanyahu called for a “national unity” government with Eisenkot on Saturday night. But it remains unclear whether the two rivals could agree on a power-sharing agreement, and these coalitions are fragile and often collapse.

Eisenkot has the option of forming a coalition with the support of the two Arab-led parties, which won an unprecedented 19 seats in the highest Arab election turnout. Only one Arab party, Ra’am, has ever joined a governing coalition, in 2021. Ra’am has said it will support Eisenkot, but the party does not have enough seats on its own to push Eisenkot into the majority.

Breaking with decades of precedent, the second Arab-led party, the Joint List, said it will support Eisenkot from outside the coalition to end Netanyahu’s grip on power.

That cooperation is fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israel’s wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Eisenkot and other opposition parties, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel’s policies but reject its identity as a Jewish state.

One of Eisenkot’s partners, the more conservative Yisrael Beytenu party, already has said it will not join a coalition with Arab-led parties.

Eisenkot also says that any party that joins him must support mandatory military service or civil service. It remains unclear whether the ultra-Orthodox religious parties are prepared to compromise.

These religious parties, which were part of Netanyahu’s outgoing coalition, want to preserve their military exemptions, which they say are needed to preserve their devout lifestyle. But the exemptions have grown especially controversial among the broader public during the past three years of war.

Anticipating its position as a swing vote, the ultra-Orthodox party United Torah Judaism has left the door open to cooperating with Eisenkot.

Eisenkot has 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible two-week extension from the president. If he is unable to form a government, Netanyahu could then be given a chance put together a coalition. If Netanyahu is also unable to do so, the country will return to elections early next spring.

Israel’s new members of Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday evening. Netanyahu and his Cabinet will remain in office in a caretaker capacity, with limited powers, until a coalition is formed.

— Lidman reported from Tel Aviv, Israel.

scraped.title: Democrats’ midterm victory puts Supreme Court’s conservative majority under new pressure
scraped.description: Democratic midterm victories have renewed questions about Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito retiring and the future of the Supreme Court's
scraped.author: Bolarinwa Oladeji
scraped.h1: Democrats’ midterm victory puts Supreme Court’s conservative majority under new pressure
scraped.body_text:
Democratic midterm victories have renewed questions about Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito retiring and the future of the Supreme Court's conservative majority.

The political consequences of the 2026 midterm elections may reach beyond Congress and into the Supreme Court , where the future of its conservative majority is becoming a renewed concern for Republicans.

Democrats’ victories have changed the calculations surrounding two of the court’s most senior conservative members, Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito.

At 78 and 76 respectively, both are approaching an age at which retirement decisions carry significant political implications, particularly because Supreme Court appointments can influence American law for decades.

The Associated Press has called Democratic control of both the House and Senate , with the new Congress expected to take office in January 2027. That leaves Republicans with a narrow window to confirm another Supreme Court nominee before the Senate changes hands.

The situation has prompted discussion of what some legal commentators describe as a possible “reverse Ginsburg” scenario. The comparison refers to the decision by the late Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg to remain on the bench during Barack Obama’s presidency. After her death in September 2020, President Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett , whose confirmation strengthened the court’s conservative majority.

An opinion piece published by The Hill on November 7 explores the possibility that Thomas and Alito could face a similar legacy question from the opposite ideological direction. If either justice leaves the court during a future Democratic administration, a Democratic president could have the opportunity to appoint a liberal successor, potentially changing the court’s current 6-3 conservative balance.

The timing is central to the argument. Trump remains president until January 2029, but Democrats will control the Senate from the start of the next Congress. That could make confirmation of conservative nominees considerably more difficult if a vacancy occurs before the next presidential election.

The Washington Post reported November 5 that Alito had said he had no plans to retire during the current lame-duck session. He also indicated that he intended to remain on the court through its current term. Thomas, meanwhile, has previously indicated that he has no plans to step down.

There are competing considerations. Supreme Court justices hold lifetime appointments and are not obligated to retire according to party advantage. Pressuring judges to leave simply to preserve an ideological majority could also deepen concerns about political influence over the judiciary.

The possibility of a shift is therefore not an immediate outcome of the election. It would depend on vacancies arising, the presidency and Senate being controlled by Democrats, and the confirmation of replacement justices.

Still, the midterm results have made succession at the Supreme Court a more urgent political question. The conservative majority built through years of Republican appointments could ultimately depend not only on the justices’ judicial records, but also on when they choose to leave the bench.

scraped.title: How Democrats will try to end Trump's tariffs
scraped.description: Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is likely the next House speaker, has made clear that ending President Trump's tariffs is one of Democrats' top priorities.
scraped.author: Kevin Breuninger
scraped.h1: How Democrats will try to end Trump's tariffs
scraped.body_text:
The battle for Congress is over. The war over President Donald Trump 's tariffs is about to heat up.

The knotted web of tariffs that Trump spent the last two years weaving could soon face its biggest threat, as Democrats prepare to unload their new legislative firepower against the Republican president's signature policy.

Democrats have made no secret of their plans to bombard Trump and his associates with investigations as soon as the next Congress is sworn in. They are also preparing a first-100-hours legislative blitz, putting forward a series of bills that would unwind much of Trump's agenda.

Both prongs of attack will take aim at Trump's unprecedented use of tariffs , which Democrats have quickly identified as a main target following their landslide victory in Tuesday's midterm elections .

Ending Trump's tariff regime, and especially his trade war against Canada, is something Democrats "absolutely have to do immediately," Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., told MS NOW's "Morning Joe" Thursday.

Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic minority leader who could be elected House speaker in the next Congress, has made clear that ending Trump's tariffs is a top priority.

"We should restore congressional authority as it relates to tariffs, because the Trump tariffs are making life more expensive for the American people," he said at a press conference in late August.

If picked as speaker, Jeffries would speed legislation to the House floor that reasserts congressional authority over trade.

Democrats are also laying the groundwork for investigations into Trump's tariffs, which the party folded into its winning campaign message linking high costs with alleged Trumpworld corruption.

Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, on Oct. 28 asked Trump to hand over records related to tariff exemptions. Trump, Raskin alleges, has wielded the exemption power to cut " sweetheart deals " for industries whose leaders have plied the president with gifts .

The plans are likely to ratchet up the pressure, both legally and politically, that Trump's tariffs were already facing.

The administration is already embroiled in multiple lawsuits challenging different parts of the government's tariff policy.

The most recent suit, filed Oct. 20, targets Trump's use of a Great Depression-era law to impose 50% tariffs on a range of Canadian goods.

Another court case accuses Trump of trying to recreate the near-global "liberation day" tariffs that the Supreme Court struck down as illegal in late February. The administration has since been ordered to refund $166 billion in tariff revenue it had collected under the scrapped policy.

Congress, not the president, holds the power to levy taxes under the U.S. Constitution. Over decades, the legislative branch has ceded some of those powers to the executive. But Trump has asserted virtually unchecked tariff powers – which Democrats say they are intent on clawing back.

"Every day Trump insists on his indiscriminate taxes on so many of the products Americans need, he digs a deeper hole for Republicans enabling his tariff spree," said Sen. Ron Wyden of Oregon, who is poised to lead the Senate Finance Committee when Democrats take it over.

"If Democrats somehow had a veto-proof majority, or if voters shame Republicans into doing the right thing, there would be no shortage of trade policies to address," Wyden said in a statement to CNBC before Election Day.

"One of the most obvious priorities would be repealing Trump's tariffs on Canada, which are raising prices and harming communities on both sides of the border," he said. "I'll also continue to work to ensure Congress has the final say on tariffs, so future presidents can't reenact Trump's economically disastrous trade taxes."

The Wall Street Journal, citing Wyden, reported Thursday that Democrats are eyeing the Canada trade war as the "first target" in their efforts against his tariff agenda.

As Wyden's statement suggested, the Senate's rules will hamper Democrats' anti-tariff efforts.

Despite their blowout victory Tuesday night, the party will still lack a 60-vote filibuster-proof majority in the Senate, giving Republicans a crucial tool to block legislation even in their diminished state.

Trump is also poised to lean heavily on his veto pen in the next Congress, presenting a major obstacle for Democrats' legislative priorities.

Overriding a presidential veto requires two-thirds majorities in both the House and Senate, meaning that even with their historic electoral gains, Democrats would need significant Republican help to force a bill into law over Trump's objection.

Democrats may consider it worthwhile to pass legislation even if Trump vetoes it, as doing so could help them build political narratives in the 2028 election cycle. But they may have other options available.

"Absent the brute force of a veto-proof coalition, Congress might consider other political solutions, such as adding riders on 'must-pass' bills or negotiation with the administration," Kit Johnson, a senior tax manager for BDO's customs and international trade group, told CNBC in an email.

Trump has said he plans to use the veto power to force Democrats to the negotiating table. But when it comes to tariffs, it's hard to imagine what deal Trump might accept.

Trump has tried to reshape U.S. trade, foreign and economic policy around his asserted power to slap steep duties on imported goods. He describes tariffs as a win-win, praising them as both a powerful negotiating tool and a major revenue generator.

After Tuesday's election, Trump seemed to suggest tariffs were non-negotiable.

"If I took tariffs off — we have 3,000 plants under construction right now. Every single plant would stop building," Trump told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a phone call Wednesday .

Since taking office in January 2025, Trump has hiked tariffs on nearly every country on the planet, leading to multiple protracted trade wars, most notably against Canada and China. He insists Americans do not share the burden of the duties, even though tariffs by definition are taxes on foreign goods paid by those importing them. The nonprofit Tax Foundation estimates Trump's tariffs have raised the average U.S. household's tax burden by $820 in 2026.

Trump has also consistently overstated the amount of revenue the government has amassed through his tariffs. He claimed before Election Day that tariffs enabled him to offer every U.S. adult $5,000 "dividend" checks if Republicans were to win both chambers of Congress – a plan that would cost roughly $1.2 trillion. But the duties – which are collected from U.S. importers – have only brought in around $300 billion in total between January 2025 and July 2026, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model .

What's more, about $138 billion of that total has been refunded since the Supreme Court ruling in February. Nearly $20 billion in tariff collections are still set to be refunded.

Most voters do not share Trump's rosy view of tariffs. Sixty-five percent of respondents to the CNBC Voter Poll on Nov. 3 said the duties have hurt the U.S. economy, while just 22% say they helped.

What remains to be seen is how hard Republicans in Congress will push back on Democrats' efforts.

A number of GOP lawmakers came out against the duties during the campaign, as their opponents gained ground blaming inflation on Trump's tariffs and the Iran war.

As they try to regroup and look forward to the 2028 election cycle, some Republicans – who largely supported free trade prior to Trump's political rise – may be less willing to continue aligning themselves with Trump's aggressive protectionism.

scraped.title: Don’t be fooled by Bernie Sanders — tech won the midterms | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Its power is irresistible. Its importance is irreversible.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: Don’t be fooled by Bernie Sanders — tech won the midterms
scraped.body_text:
Its power is irresistible. Its importance is irreversible.

Thanks to the loud noises of a few boldface names on the left, Americans are getting the impression that the Democrats of 2026 are the anti-technology party. With the blue team surging into Congress this election cycle, the logical inference is that the tech industry lost big — a huge deal for the many voters who had just about resigned themselves to the idea that technology is the one thing that can’t be stopped in America.

Drawing this conclusion would be a colossal misread of reality, no matter how sensationalist the headlines about draconian tech crackdown plans coming from Bernie Sanders and company.

The left elites do not want to de-technologize our economy, our government, or anything else. They simply want to control the technology — the better to control everything downstream of it.

At the tactical level, Democrats did not win because they ran against tech. At the strategic level, the domestic and international left is more convinced than ever that the only way it can end the Trump era and re-establish itself as the ruling elite is by wielding technology with renewed force.

First, the ground truth. As observed by Adam Kovacevich, the tech-optimist Democrat who founded the Chamber of Progress and came from Google’s public policy shop, AI and data centers ranked a distant 19th among issues in a New York Times/Siena survey. Democrats in gubernatorial contests who didn’t support data center bans performed better than those who did. And almost all Democrats Kovacevich defines as “pro-innovation” have won their races. (So far.)

The exit polls tell the same story. Almost 40% cited the economy as their top concern; nearly a third cited the “state of democracy.” The rest prioritized immigration, health care, foreign policy, and crime.

Now, one could argue that all these priorities have to do with tech in some sense. Tech has largely eaten the economy. Tech is reworking our form of government. Tech is what’s behind the intense push to fill out well-paying jobs with skilled immigrants. Health care is rapidly being technologized. Foreign policy is already dominated by the race to technologically transform the global battlefield — a dynamic that has focused unprecedented controversy around Israel, a country that has rapidly vaulted to cyber-superpower status. Crime? Seen any headlines about cyberattacks lately …?

Yes, in a very real sense, as Donald Trump so memorably put it, everything is computer now.

RELATED: America’s ‘AI czar’ could revolutionize our form of government

Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

But the left elite has no qualms about the force of these transformative technological changes. It only opposes the vector, which has arrowed in a nominally rightward direction ever since the most influential faction of Silicon Valley decided they could only remain masters of their own destiny if they threw in with Trump.

The left elites do not want to de-technologize our economy, our government, our immigration policy, our health care industry, our foreign policy, or anything else. They simply want to control the technology — the better to control everything downstream of it.

Right-wingers may look at that fact and see within it a darkly pulsating evil. Because they share little religious unity, many on the right insist on seeing that menace in ideological, not religious terms — not demonic but communist, socialist, or third-worldist.

Yet whatever kernels of insight may lurk therein, the truth is that the right is even more desperate to control the tech than the left is, and that tortured desire defines the political battle space far more than any of the hoary modern “isms” that Americans keep being told to conform our transformed postmodern reality to. It’s not going to work.

Everyone — left, right, center, white, brown, or purple — fears erasure, defeat, and destruction at the hands of adversaries who have aced them out for control of godlike tech.

RELATED: Sorry, Bill Gates. We’re sitting out this apocalypse.

BAY ISMOYO/AFP/Getty Images

That’s why the midterms weren’t a referendum on the breakneck advancement of technology to an even greater position of dominance over our country and our way of life. And yet despite real defeats for data centers in local elections, tech’s commanding position remains intact. Those setbacks may turn out to be Tootsie Roll-sized speed bumps. (Think stopping data centers stops AI? Think again. )

Tech elites who embraced Trump — Elon Musk first among them — may worry about reprisals from Democrats looking to throw bloody beefsteaks to the slavering mob. But at a time when almost nothing but tech has consequential energy behind it, it is technology that was the victor on Tuesday and technology that will define the fateful choices America’s elites will make — with or without public support — about just what our country and our people are to become.

James Poulos

BlazeTV Host

Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.

The attack, which Poland’s defense minister described as an “act of terror,” happened on Saturday in Main Square, in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. It is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

By Saturday evening, mourners had left candles in memory of the victims. The square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as authorities continued their investigation.

St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight in tribute to the victims. It was the first time the call had been missed since World War II.

Authorities also found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers (93 miles) northeast of Krakow. They likely died from gunshot wounds.

Marie-Ange Collaer wrote on Facebook that she and her family survived the shooting during a trip to Krakow from Brussels.

“We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around,” she wrote. “Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere.”

U.K. resident Neil Thaxton and his wife also lived through the attack.

“We had just walked through the main square and heard the gunshots,” Thaxton wrote on Facebook. “We thought it was fireworks then people started running, we went into a gift shop and the staff took us in the back of the shop and locked the doors and turned the lights off.”

Alexandros Maronitis, a tourist from Greece, told The Associated Press that he couldn’t get back to his lodgings for five hours after the tragedy.

“We saw the shooter when they picked him up with the ambulance,” Maronitis said. “So, we’re a bit afraid. It’s our first time in Poland. We heard it’s a safe country.”

American tourist Marylin Green mourned the losses in the “beautiful city” during her first trip to Poland that also included the capital.

“I’m Polish, my parents were from here,” she said. “I loved Warsaw. So I was really looking forward to coming here, too.”

Witness Andy Hill told the BBC that he’d felt like he was in a movie scene.

“It doesn’t feel real,” the British tourist said. “And the trouble is, you have such an instantaneous moment to make a decision: Run. Stand still. There’s an element of shock. But I just thought the easiest thing to do is dive through a doorway and just take refuge behind the windows.”

Prosecutors said Sunday they opened an investigation into the murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act “constituting a terrorist offense.”

Four women and two men were killed in the Main Square shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from an unidentified foreign country were also among the dead.

A video posted on social media showed a police officer repeatedly shooting the attacker, who was lying on the street. The officer later slowly collapsed to the ground.

The two police officers who stopped the gunman, in actions authorities hailed as heroic, remain in the hospital. They were both conscious by Sunday afternoon.

“If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher,” Klęczar said.

Michał Pędziwiatr and Mateusz Wierdak, two local surgeons who were having a bite to eat nearby, also stepped in.

Wierdak “took care of the officer who subdued the attacker because he truly needed urgent help,” Pędziwiatr told Polish news website onet. “Without protection, without gloves, he simply focused on the officer, stopping the bleeding in his chest. This probably saved his life.”

Five foreigners are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The suspect is also in critical condition after undergoing multiple surgeries. There was confusion on Saturday about his age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the suspect holds “very radical” and “ultranationalistic” views.

“Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies,” Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found on the suspect or in his car in Krakow. Both father and son had gun permits, they said.

Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising.

The Swit shooting club in Starachowice, where the suspect is believed to have trained, issued a statement on Sunday saying it offered only “static shooting,” which involves firing from a fixed position at a stationary target. The club added that the suspect “was never trained in our club in the areas of dynamic, tactical or combat shooting.”

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects. Officials blamed the school attacks on online “glorification of violence,” and said that some of the attackers were active in the far-right environment.

The Krakow shooter’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other “extreme right lone actors” committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.

“We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland,” he said.

– Ciobanu reported from Warsaw, Poland. Associated Press writer Stefanie Dazio in Berlin contributed to this report.

scraped.body_text:

Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he hopes Democrats prioritize healthcare and food assistance when they take control of Congress in January, though he urged them not to forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I hope one of the first things that the Congress does is to stop these Medicaid cuts, stop the SNAP cuts, roll back the cuts, the effective cuts in the Affordable Care Act,” Shapiro said in an interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that aired Sunday.

Shapiro noted that in Pennsylvania alone, 510,000 people are losing healthcare and 143,000 more are losing SNAP or food assistance due to cuts approved during President Donald Trump’s second term.

“In general, though, I think Democrats need to have an aggressive agenda that cuts costs, that ends the war, that gets put on the president’s desk,” he said. “Hopefully, he will sign it because it’ll be common-sense stuff that makes people’s lives better.”

Trump has said that he intends to work with Democrats when Congress begins its new term, though he has also touted a new “VETO”-branded hat since Republicans lost the majority in the midterm elections.

Shapiro said that if Trump chooses to veto Democrats’ legislation, “it’s yet another signal to the American people the president actually doesn’t care about their well-being.”

While the governor stressed the importance of revitalizing Medicaid and SNAP programs, he also said Democrats shouldn’t forget to hold the Trump administration accountable.

“I think the Congress needs to be responsive to where voters are on corruption, and there has to be real accountability for this administration,” Shapiro said, adding that Democrats need to “walk and chew gum at the same time” to pass effective legislation and also “have real accountability for the corruption that exists in Washington.”

“It can’t be either/or,” he said. “It has to be both/and.”

Shapiro added that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., who is poised to become the next speaker of the House, “has made very clear that both are going to be on the agenda for the first 100 days and for these next two years.”

The governor said that he doesn’t think Democrats should be thinking about the 2028 elections yet. Instead, “we should be thinking about how to make people’s lives better in 2027,” he said.

“It’s incumbent upon the Congress to now do that, and it’s incumbent upon governors now to continue to lead the way in our states,” Shapiro said.

Shapiro, who has been floated as a potential 2028 presidential contender, did not commit to running.

Asked whether he is more likely to run than not, Shapiro answered that his focus was on “figuring how we advance policies like raising the minimum wage and many other things that have been blocked by Republicans,” as Pennsylvania Democrats won a majority in the state legislature Tuesday.

He also did not directly answer whether he was committed to serving his full four-year term.

“Well, I committed to run for governor, and that’s the work I’m focused on doing,” Shapiro said. “And if I’ve got something to say about my future, I’d love to come back on your show and talk about it.”

Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

scraped.title: As the Colorado River shrinks, calls to drain Lake Powell grow
scraped.description: Groups are pushing to drain the lake entirely to reveal its long-submerged rock arches and spires and allow wildlife along the Colorado River to recover.
scraped.author: Jim Robbins, Yale Environment 360
scraped.h1: As the Colorado River shrinks, calls to drain Lake Powell grow
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

The 27-year-long drought in the Southwestern U.S. — the longest dry period in the last 1,200 years — is taking a serious toll on the flow of the Colorado River. Climate change is shrinking the snowpack in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, the source of roughly 80 percent of the river’s annual flow, and higher temperatures are melting the snowpack earlier in the year, which saps runoff in late summer and fall. Warmer weather is also increasing evaporation from the river’s 40 reservoirs, including its two largest — lakes Powell and Mead.

Last month, Lake Powell, on the Utah-Arizona border, reached a record low, at less than 150 feet above dead pool, the point at which water can no longer flow through the Glen Canyon Dam’s bypass tubes to reach Lake Mead, behind Hoover Dam, 300 miles downstream. The low water levels reduced the generation of hydropower from both reservoirs, complicated how riverine ecosystems are managed, and slashed deliveries of water to the Lower Basin states of Arizona, California, and Nevada.

Farmers are fallowing fields. Developers in some areas have paused housing construction for lack of guaranteed water supplies. And the Bureau of Reclamation has curtailed its “environmental flows” — releases of cold water from Powell — which is threatening protected fish and preventing the buildup of sandbars that provide habitat for wildlife in the Grand Canyon. No matter how the river is managed going forward, observers say, ecosystems both downstream and up will see significant changes.

Faced with the prospect of even lower Colorado River levels, the federal and state governments have been scrambling to come up with ways to meet the competing demands of disparate interests that rely on its flow, from topping off Lake Powell with water diverted from upstream reservoirs, to slashing downstream water deliveries by 40 percent, to paying farmers to keep their allocations of water in the river. The crisis is even causing some to consider a fix once deemed unthinkable: draining Lake Powell entirely.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

When the Glen Canyon Dam was built in the 1960s, proponents hyped its benefits: cheap hydropower, subsidized water for cotton and alfalfa growers, real estate on the new lakeshore, and a playground for boaters. But detractors bemoaned the drowning of Glen Canyon itself, a red rock labyrinth of gorges, spires, cliffs, and grottoes that conservationists described as even more beautiful than the Grand Canyon.

Over the decades, some environmental advocates have argued for removing the Glen Canyon Dam and restoring the canyon, but the idea was always dismissed as too expensive and, because it would wipe out power generation, wildly impractical.

Now, a more tempered approach is gaining support, with groups like the Glen Canyon Institute arguing not to remove the dam but to drain Lake Powell through new diversion tunnels that would be drilled below the existing bypass tubes, close to the riverbed. The upsides, say advocates, would be manifold. The water would boost hydropower production in Lake Mead. The stunning formations of Glen Canyon and sites sacred to Indigenous people would reemerge. Wildlife would return, and riparian habitat above and below the dam site would eventually be restored. The plan is called Fill Mead First.

For more than four decades, the Glen Canyon Dam was considered a huge asset to the river basin, said Eric Balken, executive director of the Glen Canyon Institute. But it’s now “becoming a liability because it might actually prevent water from flowing downstream. All of the core assumptions around the dam have been turned on their head.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

That’s because of the dam’s structural limitations. If the lake drops below minimum power pool, its penstocks — the large pipes that send water to the dam’s eight turbines — will be left stranded, high and dry. Lake water will instead be released through bypass tubes, which sit below the penstocks but have less than half their capacity to discharge water.

These tubes were not built for sustained long-term use, and sending high volumes of water through them could cause vibrations, scouring, and other effects that could cause irreparable damage to the dam. While the Bureau of Reclamation has long warned about relying solely on the bypass tubes to release water, after inspecting and relining them in 2025 it said they might work if needed. But another challenge will remain: Relying on the narrow tubes will make it harder for Upper Basin states (Colorado, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) to meet their delivery obligations to Lower Basin states and, by international agreement, Mexico.

Allowing more water to flow through the Glen Canyon Dam — by draining the lake through the existing bypass tubes and newly drilled diversion tunnels near the riverbed — is no longer dismissed out of hand. “That conversation has evolved,” said Kathryn Sorensen, director of research at the Kyl Center for Water Policy at Arizona State University.

Lower release structures, said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University, are “an utterly reasonable idea” and should be part of the discussion. As for Powell’s potential loss of hydropower, proponents of dam removal say those megawatts could be replaced with solar power. The new Gemini solar plant near Las Vegas has a capacity of 690 megawatts; the Glen Canyon Dam currently has a capacity of around 730 megawatts.

The Lower Basin states, which primarily take their water from Lake Mead and are seeing their allotments held back to prop up Lake Powell, have urged the federal government to consider modifying the dam with lower outlets rather than cutting back on deliveries, as the Biden administration ordered in 2024.

“Addressing the infrastructure limitations may be the one long-term measure that would best achieve operation and management improvements to the Glen Canyon Dam,” representatives of the Lower Basin states wrote to Interior Secretary Doug Burgum last year.

Draining Lake Powell completely “could [annually] reduce evaporative losses by a couple hundred thousand acre-feet,” said Sorensen: Experts say 11 percent of the water in the reservoir is lost to evaporation each year. “On a river that is much smaller than anyone expected, that water really matters,” she said. But while the Glen Canyon Institute plan is gaining some traction, she added, “it faces a lot of obstacles.”

One of those obstacles is the federal government, which did not even consider the possibility of draining Lake Powell as an option in its recent environmental impact statement — finalized in August — which addressed ways to manage the Colorado over the next 10 years.

Officials in Page, Arizona, which has a thriving water-based recreation industry, have also opposed draining the lake. The BlueRibbon Coalition, which represents off-road and motorized outdoor recreation, leads the opposition. It has put forward a model bill called the Colorado River Abundance Act, which would supply treated water to Lower Basin states, allowing more water to be retained in Lake Powell. The treated water would come from nuclear-powered desalination of seawater and briny water and through “advanced water reuse,” in which wastewater is cleaned with filter technologies, at an estimated cost of $40 billion.

Another obstacle is time: New diversion tunnels would likely take a decade to study, design, and build. And the price tag could be in the billions.

The Colorado’s reduced flows are, meanwhile, taking a toll on riverine ecosystems, which scientists call “novel” because they have been radically altered by 70 years of human activity — most significantly by the elimination of seasonal flooding. For a number of reasons, including low lake levels, the Bureau of Reclamation has canceled many environmental flows from the Glen Canyon Dam in recent years, depriving the Colorado of a large pulse of sediment, which is a part of the river’s natural ecology. The flows rebuild sandbars and beaches used by boaters in the Grand Canyon, and they create shallow-water habitat for threatened and endangered native fish.

The bureau also occasionally releases cold water from the dam to lower the river’s temperature and keep invasive, warm-water-loving bass from taking up residence in the Grand Canyon stretch and displacing native fish. But because of the drought, which is already reducing hydroelectric production, those releases have also been curtailed.

Draining the lake completely would allow Glen Canyon to recover as the river flushes out built-up sediment, experts say. Native cottonwoods and willows would take root and help push out invasives, like tamarisk. River otters, beavers, birds, and amphibians would return to the canyon. And the drowned red rock arches, natural bridges, amphitheaters, and waterfalls would gradually emerge from the muck, along with thousands of sites sacred to Native Americans.

A shift in the hydrological regime would also have profound effects on hundreds of miles of river ecosystems below Glen Canyon Dam, including in the Grand Canyon. “It would change in ways that are only partially predictable,” said Schmidt. “Suddenly the river would have great fluctuations. The river would have much more sediment. The river would be much more turbid.” A refugium of native fish, the Grand Canyon would suddenly be swamped with non-native fish, many of which were introduced into Lake Powell for sport fishing. “It just keeps getting more complicated,” Schmidt acknowledges. “It’s all a trade-off in this screwy manmade world.”

For now, Fill Mead First remains a pipe dream, one that’s getting a lot more attention as river levels continue to drop and global temperatures rise. The federal government will ultimately decide the Glen Canyon Dam’s future, but Eric Balken, for one, thinks a new regime is long overdue. Propping up Lake Powell is “kicking the can down the road,” he said. “But they are running out of road.”

scraped.body_text:

The King led the Royal Family and political leaders in the Remembrance Service in London

King Charles III led the nation in a solemn two-minute silence on Remembrance Sunday in London to honour veterans who had died in conflict.

On a stone-grey autumn morning, he laid a wreath at the Cenotaph in Whitehall before a march-past by 10,000 armed forces veterans.

That included a shrinking number of World War Two veterans, with 12 taking part this year, including 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who described it as a "very emotional day".

Meanwhile, the number of former prime ministers reached a record high, with nine lined up to lay wreaths, while Andy Burnham attended for the first time as the current occupant of No 10 Downing Street.

And for the first time, the leader of Reform UK, Nigel Farage, had enough MPs in Parliament to qualify to lay a wreath alongside other major party leaders.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham laid a wreath at the Cenotaph

Queen Camilla and Catherine, Princess of Wales, watched the event from the balcony of the Foreign and Commonwealth Office

The Prince of Wales and the Princess Royal were among royals in attendance, along with military chiefs, senior politicians, diplomats and faith leaders, watched by big crowds squeezed behind railings along Whitehall.

Queen Camilla and the Princess of Wales watched from a balcony above the Cenotaph in the Foreign Office.

Among the flags on the roof of that Whitehall building was the Ukrainian blue and yellow. It went up when Russia invaded and four years later it is now visibly frayed - a reminder of the length of that war and of current threats.

At 11:00 GMT, as the first strike of Big Ben echoed from the nearby Houses of Parliament, the big two-minute silence filled the usually frenetic streets, before the playing of the Last Post.

The King had his eyes closed, the crowds in Whitehall stopped for their own thoughts, in a rare moment of calm in the capital.

Veterans arrived at Whitehall ahead of the service

The poignant parade past the Cenotaph included representatives of about 340 different military and civilian groups, from the Royal Naval Association and the Royal Marines Association to Transport for London and the Royal National Lifeboat Institute.

Alongside those marching were flotillas of disability scooters and families helping veterans in wheelchairs.

Those who took part in WW2 are now increasingly frail - and there were 12 participants in the march-past compared to 20 last year. The oldest participant this year was aged 105.

"In everlasting remembrance" the King wrote on the wreath he laid at the Cenotaph

Annie Duplock had joined the Land Army at the age of 16

Taking part for the first time was 103-year-old Annie Duplock, who had been part of the Land Army that had helped to feed the country at war.

She had joined the Land Army in 1940 as a 16-year-old, having lied about her age, and worked on a farm in Leicestershire.

"I feel very honoured to be taking part in the parade and to represent the Land Girls. I'm very excited, although a little apprehensive as I don't quite know what to expect," she said.

"I think it will be a very emotional day, bringing back memories of all those who didn't return home. It will be lovely to be there and remember them."

(Top left to bottom right) former Prime Ministers Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss, Boris Johnson, Theresa May, Lord Cameron, Gordon Brown, Sir Tony Blair and Sir John Major

Archbishop of Canterbury Dame Sarah Mullally led those gathered at the Cenotaph in prayer

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the annual event was a time to "reflect on the selflessness and courage it takes to commit your life to protecting others".

He earlier announced that he wanted to tackle the problem of homelessness among ex-service personnel to "ensure that any veteran sleeping rough is offered appropriate accommodation before Christmas".

Mark Atkinson, the director general of the Royal British Legion, said: "As we come together on Remembrance Sunday, we pay tribute to all those who have served and sacrificed, from generations past to those still serving today."

Remembrance events took place across the country as thousands gathered to pay their respects to those who died in past conflicts.

First Minister of Scotland John Swinney placed a wreath at the Stone of Remembrance outside the City Chambers during an event in Edinburgh.

Veterans, military personnel and cadets also marched through the centres of British cities such as Manchester, Birmingham and Leeds.

A silent poppy drop was held as part of the Festival of Remembrance at Durham Cathedral while wreaths were laid at Canterbury Cathedral.

For more than a century, this national Remembrance event has been held around the Cenotaph.

The monument was built as a focal point for honouring those who had fought and died in World War One, including those who had no grave, and as a place to mourn for those families who might not be able to visit war cemeteries overseas.

The word "cenotaph" means "empty tomb" in Greek and it was designed by the architect Sir Edwin Lutyens in a simple, austere style, with no sense of triumphalism and with almost no decoration.

The monument had been originally built in 1919 as a temporary, plaster and wood structure. But it proved so popular with the public that it was replaced in 1920 with a permanent version, in the same design but in stone.

It was opened at 11:00 on 11 November 1920 by King George V. His great-grandson, Charles, was there again, on an overcast morning 106 years later, to continue paying respect.
