scraped.description: The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.
scraped.h1: Transcript: Sen. Elizabeth Warren on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan," Nov. 8, 2026
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 8, 2026 / 1:12 PM EST / CBS News

The following is the transcript of the interview with Sen. Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, that aired on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Nov. 8, 2026.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We go now to Massachusetts Democrat Elizabeth Warren, the expected incoming Senate Banking Committee Chair, and she joins us from Cambridge. Good morning to you, Senator.

SEN. ELIZABETH WARREN: Good morning.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So you have written an outline here, an op-ed about what it's going to look like with Democrats in the majority. You said Democrats won by being populist economic fighters who are unafraid to call out corrupt politicians and corporate interests who have rigged the system at the expense of everyone else. That has echoes of President Trump's populist economic message. Not what he said there, of course, but certainly what he has said to voters again and again. What specific policies do you think you can work with him on?

SEN. WARREN: Look, President Trump himself said that he wants to reduce interest rates on credit cards to 10%. I got the bill, I'm ready to go. President Trump says he wants to do more on housing. We're ready. We have the bills ready to go. And besides that, we got a whole bunch more that the American people have told us that they want on price gouging, on protecting our rural hospitals, on making sure that people have access to health care. We have a lot of work lined out that we can do. In fact, one of the best parts of this election was how many Democrats stood up and didn't just say, "I'm for the middle class." They said, "Here, I understand what is broken. Here are my specific plans to fix it, and I am committed to doing that." So you end up with this situation where, in Michigan and Texas, you've got the candidates saying the same thing, break up big medicine. You end up with a situation where in Kansas and in South Carolina, you've got the Democratic candidates saying, "We love that road to housing bill, but we want to go bolder, bigger, more housing." Situation where in North Carolina and Alaska, we've got candidates saying, "Hey, we need to break up the grocery monopolies--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--and stop price gouging." Iowa and Maine, where- where the Senate candidates there said "We're going to shore up Social Security and make billionaires pay their fair share," and you know, Margaret, those may sound like lots of different pieces.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SEN. WARREN: They're not. They're all about economic power--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: --and people have told us that's what they want, and we've got the team to deliver now.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, I mean, I don't have to tell you it's different to campaign than it is to actually legislate. But President Trump has said he does want to work with Democrats on a few things here: immigration, tax cuts- or cuts, or quote "maybe certain things having to do with taxes to make it more convenient, a lot of economic development initiatives." Does that track with your expectations of how this White House will be able to work with you, run by Stephen Miller and of course President Trump?

SEN. WARREN: Look, let's- let's be clear. The American people are the ones who've really set the agenda here. They're the ones who have told us what they wanted. They didn't just tell Democrats. They delivered a message to the Republicans--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN:--pretty loud and clear. And I just follow through on what happened in the- just this last summer. We put together a bipartisan housing bill that is going to expand the supply of housing and help bring down the cost of housing, and for the first time ever in American history--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: --going to ban private equity. Donald Trump didn't even sign the damn thing, and yet it is now law. We got a lot of ways to deliver for the American people, whether Donald Trump wants to be part of it or not.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because you got a veto-proof majority on that particular bill, that's going to be perhaps more challenging. You have said you want to bring big tech CEOs, Wall Street executives, and giant corporations who may have broken the law to face consequences. To be clear, is your focus going to be legislation or is it going to be investigation?

SEN. WARREN: Look, we- we have to do both. But I do want to be clear: if you've been making your profits by cheating American families and scamming your investors, you better get ready for some investigations, serious ones.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Who do you have in mind there when you say that?

SEN. WARREN: Anyone who's been cheating. That's what investigations are all about.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay, so you don't have a list of people you plan to subpoena yet. You- even though you're going to be in this chair?

SEN. WARREN: We- I- it is important that we go through the steps--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Okay.

SEN. WARREN: --for investigation because look, the American people are just damn sick of this.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: They are sick of a White House that wouldn't enforce the laws even when they got cheated. They are sick of a White House that dropped investigations that said, "Oh, if you make a nice contribution to Donald Trump's ballroom--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: --then there won't be any enforcement of the law when you've cheated millions of American customers."

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well--

SEN. WARREN: That has to end.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Under- and we saw that in the polling, a concern about corruption. Senator Chris Coons, who is slated to take over Senate Foreign Relations in the new Congress, has said he wants questions answered about- it appears to be Nvidia, the chip maker, and its CEO Jensen Huang--

SEN. WARREN: Yes.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The New York Times says he may have had a close relationship with a spy from China. Is there anything you can tell us about that? Is AI going to be a focus for you, and specifically this tech- this chip maker?

SEN. WARREN: Well, on the chip maker specifically, you know, this is an issue where we have actually substantial bipartisan support in the Banking Committee. We've got- we've got Republicans and Democrats. I'm on bipartisan bills in order to- to put more restraints on the ability to export our chips to China.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yeah.

SEN. WARREN: In fact, we have worked on a bipartisan basis to try to stop Donald Trump from encouraging Nvidia, permitting Nvidia to send these chips to China, and now we're seeing some of the consequences of that. So, we've got a lot of places where work needs to be done and a lot of different avenues to do it, but the central part is going to be lowering costs for families and rooting out the corruption. It's- it's not a long agenda.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, one of the things Democrats promised was to end the war with Iran. There are a few more weeks left in this Republican--

SEN. WARREN: Yeah.

MARGARET BRENNAN: --majority. You sit on the Armed Services Committee. There are senators like Senators Bennet and Senator Mark Kelly who have said something to the effect of Democrats should cut off funding for White House operations in order to pressure President Trump to end the war. There are people in the House making noise like that. I mean, what does this look like? Are we looking at cutting off all government funding? Are we looking at a government shutdown in the next few weeks?

SEN. WARREN: Look, the pressure is building to end this war. People have told us they want us to stop the war, a war that is illegal, that is halfway around the world, that to this day, the Trump administration can't explain what their goals are, and what their exit ramp looks like. They want us to stop it. They want us not to spend money over there. They want to be able to buy gasoline and heating oil fuel because they want this economy to work again. The way I think of this is the wind is at our backs to end this war, we got a lot of different tools on the table to get this done--

MARGARET BRENNAN: Leverage, you mean?

SEN. WARREN: This is a democracy, and- yes, and the American people have spoken, and it is time to listen to the American people. Democrats are ready to fight for that, and we invite the Republicans to join us.

MARGARET BRENNAN: We will watch for what that looks like. Senator Elizabeth Warren, thank you for joining us today. Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us.

scraped.title: Philip Rivers finalizing agreement to return to NC State as Wolfpack’s new head coach in remarkable move
scraped.description: Philip Rivers appears poised to take the NC State football head coaching job at his alma mater. NIL fundraising and transfer portal resources were key parts of negotiations.
scraped.author: Trey Wallace
scraped.h1: Philip Rivers finalizing agreement to return to NC State as Wolfpack’s new head coach in remarkable move
scraped.body_text:
"There are no dominant teams in college football. There's no juggernaut out there. Like this time a year ago, you really could tell Indiana was legitimate, that they were a powerhouse."

After N.C. State officials made the trek to Fairhope, Alabama earlier this week to formally meet with Philip Rivers , the former Wolfpack and NFL quarterback appears to be set to take the head coaching position at his alma mater.

The two sides are finalizing an agreement that is expected to be hammered out over the next 24 hours, sources told OutKick. The board of trustees at N.C. State have a meeting this coming week to approve the contract.

Conversations about Rivers taking the job in Raleigh had picked up after the school announced that Dave Doeren had been fired nearly two weeks ago.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Following a series of informal discussions with major donors about what it would take to make N.C. State competitive in the current era of college athletics, several Wolfpack boosters put a plan in motion to provide Rivers with the resources needed to hit the ground running.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

By the end of the week, all that was needed was pen to paper for the NC State alum.

But first, Rivers was going to finish his job as head coach of St. Michael Catholic in the Alabama high school football playoffs. His season came to an end on Friday night in Fairhope, as they lost in the opening round.

Phillip Rivers of the North Carolina State Wolfpack throws a pass against the Maryland Terrapins at Byrd Stadium in College Park, Md., on Nov. 9, 2002. (Getty Images)

According to multiple sources, Rivers had already begun putting together a coaching and front office staff for when he formally accepted the job offer and signed a contract.

On Friday night, Rivers was coaching St. Michael Catholic in their Alabama high school playoff game, where his son Gunner also plays. In addition to the intrigue of coaching for the first time in college, Gunner is also committed to NC State and will enroll in January to start his own collegiate career.

One of the biggest points of emphasis for Rivers taking the job in Raleigh was that he would be given enough money to work with for a veteran coaching staff, given that this will be his first college job.

Sources tell OutKick that one of his contract asks was that he be given a big enough pool of money to attract assistant coaches with college experience that would be open to making a move to Raleigh.

Former NC State quarterback Philip Rivers attends the game between the North Carolina Tar Heels and the NC State Wolfpack at Carter-Finley Stadium in Raleigh, N.C., on Nov. 29, 2025. (Getty Images)

Also, having the NIL resources outside of the revenue-sharing that schools participate in was a key part of negotiations for NC State athletic director Boo Corrigan landing the former NFL quarterback.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL’S JERRY JONES? TEXAS TECH BOOSTER CODY CAMPBELL DEMANDS RETURN ON INVESTMENT

From a fan perspective, it's obvious that the Wolfpack would be making a hire that would excite the base, and more importantly help sell tickets and also lead to an influx of donations needed to help fund rosters in the future.

This is seen as a win-win for both sides, given that this would obviously be an interesting splash around college football, especially in recruiting players who are familiar with the new head coach.

But there is also the obvious fact that players are going to go where the money leads them, though that's clearly not the case for every player.

Still, putting together a formidable roster that can compete in the ACC and subsequently for a spot in the upcoming expanded College Football Playoff is key to making sure this hire doesn’t turn into a dud over the next few years.

NICK SABAN SPEAKS TRUTH ON CFP EXPANSION: ‘THERE’S NOT 24 TEAMS’ THAT CAN WIN A NATIONAL TITLE, BUT MONEY WINS

We have seen countless coordinators in the college ranks receive their first shot at a head coaching job and watch it turn into chaos; just look at what is taking place with Tosh Lupoi at Cal this season, where general manager Ron Rivera is already sounding the alarms.

But, for a high school coach to be given an opportunity to start their collegiate career at the top, and especially at a school like NC State, goes to show you how much Wolfpack officials think about Rivers.

Philip Rivers No. 17 of the Indianapolis Colts walks off the field at halftime against the San Francisco 49ers at Lucas Oil Stadium on Dec. 22, 2025, in Indianapolis, Ind. (Getty Images)

Now, the donors who have promised Rivers with the funds needed to compete will be tasked with making sure he can attack the transfer portal to add players to this NC State roster so that he can hit the ground running for the 2027 season.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

This will be an interesting situation to watch unfold over the next few months, with NC State fans expecting this team to once again start competing for ACC titles on a yearly basis.

Welcome to college football, Philip Rivers.

Trey Wallace is the Sr. College Sports Reporter for OutKick.

scraped.description: The U.S. did not say whether any military action would be involved in preventing weapons technology or sanctioned items from entering Iran.
scraped.h1: Live Updates: Iran downplays new U.S. task force aimed at disrupting ground transport routes
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 8, 2026 / 1:01 PM EST / CBS News

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that it's "time for the White House to make its own [choice]" about how to proceed as negotiations to end the war stretch on into a fifth week.

"American voters have made their choice. Time for the White House to make its own," Araghchi said in a social media post.

"Our 2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results," the post continued. "Or choose war, and see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell."

Araghchi previously said that, during mediated, indirect talks with the U.S., Iran had presented a proposal that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the U.S. agreed to certain conditions.

Yemen's Houthis on Sunday claimed responsibility for an attack on the financial district of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, which witnesses said caused damage to a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Aramco. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis had said earlier Sunday that its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions.

In a statement, Houthi military spokesperson Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the Iran-backed group carried out four military operations using ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones. Saree said the Riyadh airport was targeted in addition to the financial center, Aramco oil storage tanks, and the eastern Saudi city of Abqaiq.

He said the Houthis were responding to attacks in recent days on a village near Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and at a market in southwestern Yemen, which he said left dozens dead or wounded and blamed on Saudi Arabia.

Aramco facilities and infrastructure have been repeatedly struck by the Houthis in recent months, with tankers, refineries, storage areas and the company headquarters all targeted by the group.

"Aramco tower in KAFD has been targeted, that's the sure thing," one witness told AFP, referring to the King Abdullah Financial District. Two other witnesses confirmed seeing damage to the building.

One witness in the area of the Aramco skyscraper told AFP they saw a projectile strike the building but they were unsure what type of projectile it was.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said there were no casualties at the Aramco facility.

AP/AFP

Israel's defense minister hinted at a resuming attacks on Iran on Sunday, saying the "mission is not complete."

"With regard to Iran, the mission is still not complete. Iran is trying to renew its efforts to obtain nuclear weapons -- alongside other grave efforts that place the State of Israel in real danger," Israel Katz said.

He also warned the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon to not join Tehran in retaliating against Israel.

"We will not withdraw from the security zones in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and if the terrorist organisation Hezbollah chooses to join Iran in an attack on Israel, it will suffer extremely severe blows," Katz said.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose political bloc failed to reach a majority in the country's elections, has previously suggested he wants to resume attacks on Iran.

However, on the eve of the midterm elections President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper he had no plans to strike Iran.

CBS/AFP

Witnesses in the Saudi capital of Riyadh said they heard a loud explosion Sunday morning and described damage across multiple floors of an Aramco building in the King Abdullah Financial District Some floors appeared to be heavily damaged.

The witnesses spoke on condition of anonymity because of security concerns.

The Saudi-led coalition said its air defenses intercepted two ballistic missiles and two cruise missiles targeting Riyadh and other regions early Sunday, accusing the Houthis of launching the weapons.

The Saudi Energy Ministry said the attempted attack resulted in "falling shrapnel that caused minor damage to the building." It added that there were no casualties.

CBS/AP

Iran's military has dismissed the U.S.'s new task force which aims to disrupt Iranian ground shipping routes as "wordplay."

In a statement to Iran's semi-official Fars news agency, a Revolutionary Guard Corps spokesman said Tehran had made preparations and communicates closely with neighbours.

"The Iron Gate plan is merely a wordplay, the Americans cannot achieve their objectives of imposing ‌severe economic pressure ‌to cause economic ⁠collapse in Iran ‌through ⁠this approach," Mohebbi told the semi-official Fars news agency.

CBS/AFP

Houthi authorities said Sunday that Saudi strikes killed 33 people, many of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's revived civil war.

The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country.

The death toll from the Saudi-led coalition's strikes on Al-Shariya village located east of Yemen's capital Sanaa has risen to 33, with 39 people wounded, Houthi health ministry spokesman Anees Alasbahi said in a post on X.

The Houthis' Saba news agency said on Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."

"According to the near-final figures, the dead include 12 men, 8 women and 13 children, while the injured include 16 men, 10 women and 13 children," Alasbahi said.

Saudi Arabia, fighting in Yemen in support of the internationally-recognized government, has not commented on the report. The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched towards Riyadh province.

The Iran-backed Houthis, meanwhile, said they had launched multiple missile and drone attacks against Saudi troops and infrastructure both in the Gulf kingdom and Yemen.

Yemen slipped back into war between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed government in July after years of relative calm, opening a new front in the conflict in the Middle East.

Since then, Saudi Arabia has regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has expanded its attacks against the oil-rich kingdom.

U.S. forces disabled a commercial vessel in the Gulf of Oman on Saturday after the ship's civilian crew ignored repeated warnings and attempted to violate the naval blockade against Iran multiple times, U.S. Central Command said.

A U.S. military aircraft fired precision munitions at the stern of St.Kitts-flagged M/V Huda, which disabled the ship after the crew was directed to abandon targeted spaces. The cargo vessel tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port, CENTCOM said.

"All mariners transiting near Iranian coastal areas or surrounding waters are advised to heed blockade warnings from U.S. forces," CENTCOM said.

Earlier Saturday, CENTCOM said "strict enforcement" of the U.S. blockade on Iranian ports in the Strait of Hormuz continues.

Iran established a chokehold on the strait, a vital strategic waterway in global trade, at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October.

-CBS/AP

In what the U.S. military is calling an expansion of the naval blockade, U.S. Central Command announced a new task force Saturday aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items like military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

The U.S. said the task force will be made up of about 20 civilian and military personnel, based in Florida, and will be tasked with the goal of "preventing the movement of advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue streams across Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea."

The announcement made no mention of how the task force would be carrying out its goal, including whether any military operations will be involved.

China, Iran's largest trade partner, has taken to conducting commerce over land, especially by train across central Asia due to the blockade on Iranian ports. The U.S. said the blockade has prevented some $25 billion in Iranian crude oil from being sold, much of it in Asia.

In addition to China, Iran has conducted large amounts of trade over land and via the Caspian Sea with Russia. The landlocked Caspian Sea has proven especially advantageous with a direct route between southwest Russia and northern Iran. Tehran is located just 80 miles south of the Caspian Sea.

Whether any U.S. ships could take to the Caspian Sea was again unclear. CBS News has reached out to the White House for more details.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-proclaimed limit of 1,200 miles on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets amid fears of renewed all-out war.

The comments by the spokesman of Iran's paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country's supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini, warned "any kind and level of threat" from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.

Asked at a Tehran press conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, "That restriction has been lifted for us."

He did not say whether Iran had missiles capable of exceeding the limit, saying only Iran would "demonstrate these capabilities in practice" rather than make statements.

Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 1,200-mile limit — a range that puts parts of Greece and the Balkans, the entire Arabian Peninsula, the Levant and most of Egypt within reach. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran's space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.

The Iranian military, meanwhile, said a tanker east of the Strait of Hormuz had hit a naval mine and caught fire. It did not identify the nationality or destination of the tanker, which it said had turned off its navigational beacon and was sailing in a "prohibited area."

Saudi strikes killed 22 people, most of them women and children, in Yemen's Sanaa province, as deaths mount in the country's civil war, Houthi media said on Saturday.

More than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed in the impoverished country, according to the U.N.

"The number of victims of the Saudi enemy warplane massacre in the Al-Shariyah area ... has risen to 22 citizens, most of them children and women, while the number of wounded has risen to 30," the Houthis' Saba news agency said.

The Iran-backed group's Al-Masirah TV provided the same toll.

Saba said earlier Saturday that operations to recover victims from the rubble were ongoing and that "aircraft targeted paramedics with two strikes."

The Saudi-led coalition in a statement on Saturday said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi missile launched toward Riyadh province.

On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province killed 30 people. The Houthis said Saudi airstrikes were to blame, while Yemen's government forces accused the Iran-backed group of having fired a ballistic missile at the site.

AFP/CBS

Iran's military is "stronger" and more motivated than it was when the United States and Israel started the war in February, Iranian state media reported on Saturday, citing an army spokesman.

"Today, the Islamic Republic's armed forces... having gained experience from direct confrontation with the United States and the Israeli regime, are on higher alert and are stronger than they were at the beginning of the war," spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said, according to the state news agency IRNA.

"They now possess greater motivation, commitment, and self-confidence."

CBS/AFP

President Trump confirmed on Friday the U.S. carried out "minor strikes" in Iran, after local state media reported missiles striking Qeshm Island on the Strait of Hormuz.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Mr. Trump was asked whether the U.S. carried out more strikes on the island.

"I don't want to talk about it," the president said. "We do minor strikes. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe 5."

On Saturday, Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that two missiles had struck Qeshm island, added that there was no official information on the damage. Iranian state television also reported two explosions on the island.

The Trump administration is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear program, the U.S. military's Central Command announced Friday.

The reward , which is being administered through the State Department's Rewards for Justice national security program, also comes with "possible relocation" for the tipster.

The State Department said it is calling for "information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel, such as those in the scientific community, or the movement of any of the above."

Since the U.S. launched its war with Iran in February, President Trump has repeatedly reiterated that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon.

In its reward form, the State Department noted that according to the United Nations' International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran's uranium stockpile is believed to include uranium that has been enriched to 60% purity – "a level that is a short technical step from" the 90% level required to produce nuclear weapons.

"Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level," the State Department said in its Rewards for Justice post. "Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons."

Iran suspended IAEA inspections following the June 2025 strikes on Iranian nuclear facilities by the U.S. and Israel.

"The regime's lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like centrifuges," the State Department said Friday.

The Treasury Department on Friday targeted several firms exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for allegedly helping Tehran evade sanctions and fund its proxies.

Some of the providers dealt with Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges already sanctioned by Washington.

The latest targets were coordinated with the Canadian government as several of the individuals and entities named are based in Vancouver and Toronto.

"Anyone, anywhere in the world, who helps Tehran evade sanctions risks being held accountable," State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott said in a statement .

Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to embark on his first post-midterm foreign trip to attend a Group of Seven foreign ministers meeting in France next week.

He'll likely face questions about the Trump administration's policies, namely in Iran, after huge Republican losses in elections that gave Democrats control of Congress.

The State Department said Friday that Rubio would travel to Paris to meet his counterparts from Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy and Japan on Monday and Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that a Saudi strike on a market in southwestern Yemen had killed or wounded 30 people.

The Houthis' Saba news agency said the "horrific massacre" had "resulted in the martyrdom and injury of more than 30 citizens."

The Houthis' political bureau said in a statement carried by Saba: "It is regrettable that these documented Saudi crimes have become like a forgotten file in the drawers of the United Nations and the so-called international community."

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels said Friday that the Saudi-led coalition fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognized government had targeted a market in the southwest of the country, killing and wounding "dozens of civilians."

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a post on X that Saudi aircraft struck the Al-Hadara market in the Taiz governorate on Friday "with three airstrikes, leaving dozens of civilians dead and wounded."

"These brutal crimes will not go unanswered and unpunished," he added.

The Saudi-led coalition said Friday , meanwhile, that air defense systems had intercepted two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed Friday to have destroyed another U.S. drone over Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.

In a statement carried by the state TV network IRIB, the IRGC said a U.S. MQ-1 drone was "intercepted and destroyed over Qeshm Island by the IRGC's new advanced air defense system."

The IRGC claimed this was the 16th American MQ-1 drone it had intercepted during the war, and the second in two days . Iranian forces have also claimed to have shot down other U.S. drones, including more than two dozen of the more advanced, and more expensive MQ-9 Reapers .

A seafarer was killed in an explosion caused by a suspected missile attack on an oil tanker Thursday in the Persian Gulf, a Greek company that manages the vessel said Friday.

The MT Velos Sapphire, a Marshall Islands-flagged tanker, which was not carrying cargo, was hit Thursday as it sailed toward Bahrain, management firm Velos Tankers said in a statement, according to Reuters.

"The company is greatly saddened to report the death of one of its seafarers, who was found fatally injured on board after having initially been reported missing in the aftermath of the explosion," the statement said.

Velos said, according to Reuters, that no crew members were injured and they managed to extinguish a fire on the ship caused by the blast.

The vessel was brought to Khalifa Bin Salman Port in Bahrain, and the damage to its hull was still being assessed, Reuters said.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis said Friday that it had intercepted a drone in the region of Mecca, Islam's holiest city, following repeated attacks on Saudi Arabia by the Yemeni rebels.

"Interception and destruction of a drone in the Mecca region," Turki al-Malki, the coalition's spokesman, wrote on X , without elaborating.

Since the breakdown of a truce in July, Saudi Arabia has traded blows with the Houthis, who have retaliated with strikes on Saudi airports, energy infrastructure and military sites that killed at least 20 people in October.

The Houthis have repeatedly denied targeting the holy cities of Mecca or Medina in Saudi Arabia and said they would not do so.

On Thursday, the Saudi coalition said it intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis at the Medina region, a claim rejected by the Iranian proxy group as a "blatant and grave falsehood."

CBS/AFP

The Iranian supreme leader's adviser on international affairs, Aliakbar Velayati, said Friday that Iran was now "one of the main architects" of security in the Middle East.

Referring to how the U.S.-Iran war has changed the region in a series of posts on X , Velayati said that a "tsunami of geopolitical changes in West Asia swept up the Israeli and U.S. elections," and that "Iran is now one of the main architects of the regional order, a reality that cannot be erased or replaced."

Iran is a "bridge between the Persian Gulf, Central Asia, the Caucasus, and the Sea of Oman," he added, saying that "any energy or transit corridor seeking to bypass us will either be costly or unstable."

"The domino effect of crises, from Gaza to the Red Sea and from Lebanon to Iraq, has shown that regional security is indivisible," Velayati said. "Either collective security is achieved, or everyone will experience collective insecurity."

Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has not been seen in public since being wounded in the strikes that killed his father on Feb. 28.

A tanker was hit by an explosion Thursday in the Strait of Hormuz, a British navy agency said Friday.

The master of a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz near Oman's coast reported "an explosion at the waterline" of the vessel, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations center said, adding that the crew were all safe and the ship was "still under its own power and is continuing on its voyage."

Iran's state media reported Thursday that five oil tankers and a tugboat had caught on fire in or near the strait after hitting sea mines. It was unclear if the UKMTO report was in relation to one of those incidents claimed by Iran.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Friday, in a statement carried by state media, that two more oil tankers had hit mines and caught on fire in or near the strait.

President Trump has accused Iran of lying about such incidents in an effort to drive up energy prices.

President Trump called Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani to discuss efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war, a U.S. official confirmed to CBS News Friday, amid a diplomatic push to avoid a new round of major hostilities.

Their discussion, which the White House had not provided any information about by Friday morning, came as Iran's top diplomat made his own calls Thursday to counterparts across the Persian Gulf aimed at maintaining "stability in the region" amid concerns in many Gulf capitals that Mr. Trump will order major new U.S. strikes.

Al Thani received a call from Mr. Trump, according to a statement from the emir's office , during which the pair discussed "the latest regional developments, particularly diplomatic efforts aimed at de-escalating tensions in the region."

The emir "emphasized the importance of continuing dialogue and relying on diplomatic means to settle disputes and prevent further escalation," the statement said.

Motorists could soon see U.S. gas prices drop below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to energy experts.

Patrick De Haan, a petroleum analyst at price-tracking firm GasBuddy, told CBS News he expected the national average for gas, which the price-tracking firm put at $4.06 a gallon on Thursday and early Friday morning, to dip below the $4 threshold by next week. He also predicted diesel could fall below $6 a gallon by Thanksgiving.

Gas and diesel prices have both dropped over the last week, thanks largely to market expectations that the U.S. midterm election results would underscore public dissatisfaction with the Iran war and pile pressure on the Trump administration to make a deal to end the conflict, De Haan said.

"Oil prices have been falling in the run-up to the election," he said. "My read is because there was optimism that after the midterms these problems would be addressed."

Read more here.

The Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's government said Friday that air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels at Najran, a major city in southwest Saudi Arabia.

"Debris fell as a result of the interception, and damage assessment is underway," the statement said.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in a statement carried by state media Friday that two oil tankers hit mines and caught fire in or near the Strait of Hormuz, a day after Tehran claimed five other tankers had met similar fates.

"Two violating oil tankers — one east of the Strait of Hormuz and the other within the Strait itself — that attempted to transit via an unauthorized route struck mines," the IRGC said in a statement, according to state news outlets.

"These two tankers had deactivated all their navigation and identification systems. Supported by the aggressive and terrorist U.S. military, they attempted to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an unauthorized path; however, upon striking mines, they caught fire and were immobilized," the statement said.

On Thursday, Iranian media reported that five oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz in similar incidents.

There has been no confirmation of any of the incidents from maritime officials, and President Trump has accused Iran of making up such attacks to drive up global energy prices.

A U.K. naval agency said earlier this week , however, that despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe, there were at least 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region during October alone, a record high.

Since the war began with joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, Tehran has sought to control traffic through the strait, a key passage through which, before the war, about a fifth of global crude oil supplies would typically pass. In response, the U.S. imposed a blockade on Iranian ports.

The U.S. military has escorted tankers through the strait, which, along with other routes has helped bring shipments from the Gulf back up to or at least near to pre-war levels, but ships continue coming under attack.

CBS/AFP

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei in Moscow Thursday to discuss strengthening ties between the two countries, including with the potential construction of a pipeline for Iran to import Russian gas.

Speaking with journalists after their meeting, Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called it "an extremely important exchange," according to the Iranian embassy in Moscow.

"During the meeting with Mr. Vladimir Putin, discussions were held regarding the construction of gas pipelines from Russia to Iran," Rezaei was quoted as saying by Iranian state TV.

He noted the aim was to enable Iran "to address its own gas shortages while also facilitating the sale of Russian gas to neighboring countries."

Despite being a major producer, Iran has long suffered natural gas shortages, which have been exacerbated by the war with the United States and Israel.

During the most intense phase of the fighting, which lasted nearly 40 days, the U.S. and Israel struck key Iranian infrastructure including natural gas refineries, according to Tehran.

CBS/AFP

President Trump said Thursday that people will soon know his decision on whether to order a new round of U.S. strikes on Iran.

Mr. Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that he believed it would take Iran 25 years to rebuild the country from the damage already inflicted during the war.

The president said he didn't want to bring further destruction to the country, but he may not have a choice.

Mr. Trump kept the possibility of a major new U.S. assault on Iran on the table in the run-up to the midterm elections this week, but hadn't renewed the threat since his Republican Party's dismal performance in the vote, which he acknowledged was, at least in part, a repudiation of the war.

Mr. Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening, as U.S. ballots were counted, that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran.

scraped.author: Leslie Josephs
scraped.h1: Using miles to fly for Thanksgiving? These are the most expensive and cheapest routes
scraped.body_text:
Airline ticket prices have surged this year, especially for travel over the holidays. Don't expect many bargains if you're booking flights with miles, either.

Tickets bought with frequent flyer miles for flights between large U.S. airports over the Thanksgiving travel period will cost 32% more than last year's holiday, according to data from Seats.aero, a miles and points redemption search site. While fares have skyrocketed this year, airline executives last month said demand remains strong.

Airlines have largely gotten rid of static mileage redemption charts in favor of dynamic pricing, making budgeting for an award ticket more difficult. Dynamic pricing means redemption costs change depending on demand, routes and other factors.

Many of the most expensive routes this Thanksgiving are understandably longer, including from Hawaii, but the list also includes a nonstop from New York to Houston.

Here's how mileage redemptions for the holiday are stacking up, based on one-way flights on average as of early November and compared with last year:

Jet fuel prices have surged since the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, which has eaten into airline profits. Carriers have sought to pass costs along to consumers as much as possible.

Even some of the cheapest routes for award tickets are more expensive than last year, including for short routes like Tulsa, Oklahoma, to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

Here are the routes where award trips are cheapest on average and how they compare with the Thanksgiving holiday last year:

scraped.title: The American Dream is no match for climate change
scraped.description: Homeownership is billed as a way to build wealth. For many, it’s turning into a trap.
scraped.author: Kate Yoder
scraped.h1: The American Dream Is No Match for Climate Change
scraped.body_text:
Grist/Getty

This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration. It is part of a series The Dream That Oil Built , which explores the connections between climate change, fossil fuels, and the American Dream.​

To Sierra Isley , the American Dream brings to mind a home ringed by a white picket fence. “The house in the suburbs is just what you’re taught growing up,” the 26-year-old said. “You know, that’s what you see on TV.” What she wanted for her life was a bit different from that picket-fence ideal, but she still saw the prospect of buying her first house two years ago as a chance to live out what she called “that big dream that everybody has as a kid.”

Isley and her girlfriend, Jamie, were moving from Philadelphia to Asheville, North Carolina, and found a home they liked, a three-bedroom brick house with lots of natural light and a big tree out front. With some help from their parents, they put down a deposit and got their offer accepted. But when they went to sign the closing papers, a complication got in the way: The house had a huge lien on it. After consulting with lawyers, they decided to break the contract and hunt for an apartment to rent in Asheville.

It was a blessing in disguise. One month later, while Sierra and Jamie were still unpacking boxes and building furniture, the remnants of Hurricane Helene turned Asheville into a disaster zone. The basement of their apartment flooded, but they were luckier than some of their neighbors, whose homes had been destroyed.

Owning a home has long been seen as a cornerstone of the American Dream—a way to build wealth that you could use one day to pay for your children’s education and fund your retirement. That arrangement was always more precarious than it was made out to be. But as fires and floods damage homes and drive up insurance rates, pouring your life savings into a house has become riskier than ever. In a report called “ Property Prices in Peril ,” the firm First Street projected last year that climate risks could knock nearly $1.5 trillion off the value of American homes by 2055. For some people, the sociologist Rebecca Elliott wrote , “the American dream of homeownership may become a nightmare.”

Americans are beginning to grasp the threat that climate change poses to their aspirations. According to exclusive polling for Grist from the think tank Data for Progress, 58 percent of likely US voters believe that climate change will hinder their ability to achieve the American Dream over the next 20 years, including 42 percent of Republicans. The survey suggests that people are worried that climate change will increase the cost of living, a concern so widespread that it may have swayed the midterm elections on Tuesday.

“Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable”

The irony is that fossil fuels have long been promoted as necessary ingredients for the American “way of life.” Starting a century ago, oil and gas companies led extensive campaigns to tie their products to comfort and prosperity, a narrative that has been repeatedly deployed by politicians and oil industry executives to thwart climate action. President Donald Trump’s administration has often said that efforts to rein in fossil fuels threaten the American Dream. Earlier this year, when the administration scrapped Biden-era rules to cut emissions from cars, along with the Environmental Protection Agency’s authority to regulate climate change, it touted the effort as “ restoring the American Dream .”

But the fossil-fueled American Dream is in the process of destroying itself. Greenhouse gas emissions from burning coal, oil, and gas have ushered in a new period of precarity, undermining the promise that each generation can expect a better life than the last. Scientific reports warn that climate change “ imperil[s] the quality of life ” for communities in the United States, disrupting livelihoods and cultural traditions.

Either Americans decide to reimagine what makes up the American Dream and abandon that oil-soaked version of prosperity, or climate change will dismantle it for them .

The memories of living through Hurricane Helene are still fresh in Isley’s mind. Hauling water from their flooded basement up to the toilet to flush it when the water ran out. Driving to Jamie’s parents’ house in Atlanta, holed up in a room with both of their cats until they couldn’t take it anymore. Coming back to Asheville and cooking meals in the Crock-Pot with disposable liners because even when the water was running again, it wasn’t safe to wash dishes with.

Two years later, Isley browses Zillow for fun, but she looks at homes through a post-disaster lens. “Now I have that fear in the back of my mind—anywhere near a river, or even a stream, if there’s a little bit of water on the map, I’m like, ‘Oh, no,’” she said. Jamie is trans, and after Trump was elected in 2024, the two of them briefly entertained the idea of moving somewhere with more protective policies, like California. But Isley’s mind immediately went to wildfires. Out of the question.

Isley had fled from hurricanes before, when she lived in Florida during college. She thought she’d be safe from them tucked away in the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville was supposed to be a “ climate haven ,” somewhere that would fare better than the rest of the country as the world warmed. Those promises were shattered when almost 14 inches of rain fell on Asheville over three days in September 2024. The French Broad River overflowed its banks, flooding homes and destroying parts of the town’s River Arts District. In western North Carolina, more than 74,000 homes were damaged, and only about 4 percent had flood insurance, resulting in $9.5 billion in uninsured residential property losses.

Home values in western North Carolina have declined since the storm , especially in the hardest-hit counties. Asheville’s average home price shrunk 5 percent over the past year, while the national average increased 1.2 percent.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace.”

To some degree, housing markets are already pricing in the risk of increased environmental hazards. Homes within FEMA’s high-risk flood zones sell for 2.8 percent less , on average, than what they would otherwise sell for, according to a 2023 study published in the journal Nature Climate Change. The researchers found that homes exposed to flood risk were still overvalued by between $121 billion and $237 billion, though—and they identified Appalachia as a hot spot of overvaluation, one year before Helene hit. The devaluation of homes in high-risk zones is unfolding unevenly and causing “tremendous social harm,” said Elliott, a sociology professor at The London School of Economics and Political Science.

Homes are billed as a way for people to build wealth, but they can turn into a trap. After Superstorm Sandy devastated New York City and the New Jersey coast in 2012, many homeowners couldn’t sell their houses for enough money to buy a new place, leaving them stranded . Even homes that haven’t seen any kind of devastation are at risk of losing value as more people become wary of living in floodplains, coastal places exposed to storms, and wildfire-prone areas. “Those homes could become, in effect, economically worthless even before they are physically uninhabitable,” Elliott wrote in a study about property values and climate change .

Insurance is meant to offer a measure of safety when taking on a huge debt for a mortgage on a house. Douglas Heller, the director of insurance at the Consumer Federation of America, called it “the safety net for the American Dream.” But insurance rates are part of what’s making homeownership unaffordable for so many. Since 2020, property insurance costs have ballooned almost 80 percent , with the average single-family mortgage holder now paying $209 per month. Homeowners in the riskiest areas are paying substantially more , and many in California have been dropped by their insurers . Home insurance rates are rising faster in the Midwest than any other region, driven by the costs of severe storms.

“We are, for a lot of people, on the edge of a dysfunctional insurance marketplace,” Heller said. The more extreme weather we’re seeing is only part of the story: He argues that the insurance industry has become a “climate opportunist,” using climate change as an excuse to justify excessive rate increases.

People relying on Social Security benefits who own condos around Lake Tahoe are particularly vulnerable to rising rates, said Andrew Engler, the founder and CEO of Rock Rose Risk, who helps people in California protect their homes against wildfire and get their insurance premiums down. They’re facing ballooning homeowners association payments, to share the cost of insurance in a risky wildfire area, on a limited paycheck. If they try to move, their properties are worth significantly less because of the huge HOA bills, Engler said. Economists estimate that rising insurance costs linked to disaster risk have reduced the growth of home prices by more than $40,000 in the most hurricane- and wildfire-prone zip codes.

Renting might make you more nimble, but it doesn’t insulate you from these costs. One reason rents are going up is because landlords’ property insurance rates are increasing . “Whether you are a homeowner or a renter, we’re all paying for living under the increased risks of climate change,” said Caroline Nagy, the associate director of housing policy at Americans for Financial Reform. That makes it harder for people to save for a home—if that’s even a good idea anymore.

When Sierra Isley walks around her neighborhood these days, she sees the evidence of Helene all around her—in the form of banners with the slogan “Asheville Strong” and shirts that say “WNC Strong.”

One of the most surprising things about disasters might be the way that people who live through them rise to the occasion and come together . In the aftermath of the Helene, with the power and cell service knocked out, Sierra and Jamie walked all around town, talking to their neighbors to try to learn what had happened. People started congregating at the fire station where there was fresh water.

“It’s hard to put into words what that experience was like, but I’ve never felt more of a community, and really having to lean on my neighbors and feeling like my neighbors were leaning on me,” Isley said.

“I owe it to people like me, in other rural communities, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters”

While the American Dream is usually all about independence and personal freedom, living through a disaster has a way of revealing how people depend on each other. The experience can prompt people to hold tightly to what they have, doubling down on protecting their communities, said Nick Tinoco, a sociology researcher in a doctoral program at the University of California, Los Angeles, who interviewed survivors of the 2018 Woolsey Fire in Los Angeles County. Some of the residents he talked to have taken things into their own hands and organized volunteer fire brigades, and plan to stay behind to defend their neighborhoods during future fires.

As supposedly safe “climate havens” like Asheville experience more disasters, the idea that people can simply move out of harm’s way is losing its grip. “I think we have to just reckon with the fact that we’re going to have to make people secure in the places that they live,” Elliott said.

She thinks it’s time to rethink the bargain of the American Dream—the expectation that so much of a person’s economic future depends on the fate of a single structure. Many young people have begun to define success differently. A poll from Ipsos last year showed that 46 percent of baby boomers associate homeownership with the American Dream, but only 13 percent of Gen Zers do, suggesting that there’s room for its defining features to change.

Sierra and Jamie couldn’t help but wonder what happened to the house they’d almost bought, and they drove over to check it out soon after Hurricane Helene hit. It was still standing, but they couldn’t see if there was any damage hidden inside. “Who knows if it flooded or anything like that, what kind of storm damage it took, and that would have immediately been our problem,” Isley said.

Living through Hurricane Helene didn’t just make Isley relieved she hadn’t bought a house in Asheville. It has shaped what she wants for her life, helping her discover a passion for public health and pushing her to want to work in emergency preparedness. Now she’s applying to schools to pursue a master’s degree in public health.

“I think I owe it to people like me, people in other rural communities who are going to face the same kind of climate change emergencies, to use my skills to help combat climate change and natural disasters,” Isley said. “I just feel such a calling.”

articles.title: El-Sayed: Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
articles.summary: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.
articles.ai_summary: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed states that Democrats are willing to work with Trump if he demonstrates seriousness.

scraped.title: Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
scraped.description: Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed joins "This Week" after his historic victory against Republican Mike Rogers in the midterm election.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Abdul El-Sayed says Democrats will work with Trump if 'he wants to act serious'
scraped.body_text:
The Michigan senator-elect called the president "an unserious fool."

Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed said Sunday that Democrats will work with President Donald Trump to help the American people if "he wants to act serious," but if the president instead chooses "foolishness," the incoming senator said he will not find a willing partner in Congress.

"Let's talk about how he is an unserious fool. Think about this war in Iran that every single president had resisted fighting because, of course, it was a dumb idea," El-Sayed told ABC "This Week" in an exclusive interview. "Let's talk about the foolishness of a tariff war with Canada. ... Let's talk about the foolishness of gutting Medicaid to pass tax cuts for the richest people in America."

"So look, if he wants to act serious, we are happy to work alongside him to actually address these issues," El-Sayed continued. "He is the president of the United States. But if he wants to continue to fool, he will hire people like Stephen Miller to run the White House, and he gets to choose where he goes next."

President Trump on Friday said White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller would assume the role of chief of staff effective Monday, replacing Susie Wiles.

With his victory in Michigan's Senate race last Tuesday, El-Sayed is set to make history as the nation's first Muslim senator. During his campaign, El-Sayed said he focused his message on three issues: "to get money out of politics, put money in your pocket and pass Medicare for all."

But the issue that most defined both the contentious and close primary campaign against fellow Democrat Haley Stevens and the general election campaign against former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers was U.S. support for Israel. El-Sayed has been a staunch critic of the Israeli government and U.S. military aid to Israel.

Asked on "This Week" if he's heard from his Republican opponent, El-Sayed said, "Not that I know of. I think he had a flight to catch to Florida."

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

scraped.h1: Train collision in Egypt kills 4 and injures 88 south of Cairo
scraped.body_text:
At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, authorities said.

The crash occurred in the al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 52 kilometers south of Cairo. A train travelling to the southwestern Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the Transportation Ministry. One of the trains derailed, it said, but did not specify which.

The Health Ministry said at least four people were killed and 88 others were wounded. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.

People gather at the site of the derailed passenger train south of Cairo. (The Associated Press)

President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said in a social media post that he ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.

Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore train services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian Railway Authority said.

Last September, a train driver and his assistant were injured after two freight trains collided in the same district.

scraped.title: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
scraped.description: Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.
scraped.h1: Physicists listened to electrical noise to crack a superconductor mystery
scraped.body_text:
Tuning in to electronic noise can tell us whether electrons have paired up or not.

Superconductors carry electricity without resistance, but most only work a few degrees above absolute zero. In the late 1980s, copper-based materials called cuprates were found to superconduct at higher temperatures—reachable with affordable liquid nitrogen. Yet nearly 40 years later, physicists still don’t agree on why.

In a recent Science study, a team of physicists led by Milan Allan of Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich and Ingmar Swart of Utrecht University in the Netherlands has found some answers by listening to the faint electrical crackle of current flowing into a cuprate.

Central to the mystery of cuprates’ high-temperature superconductivity is a strange state called the pseudogap. “The pseudogap is a phenomenon of missing electrons,” Allan said. Above the temperature at which cuprates become superconducting, some of their electrons seem to vanish—measurements find far fewer of them at the energies where they should be. “Everybody knows that from different probes, you see that there’s these vanishing electrons, but nobody knows why,” Allan said.

Over the decades, physicists have put forward two main competing explanations. The first hypothesizes that the electrons get stuck in some sort of structure. In this view, electrons freeze into patterns, such as charge density waves, and superconductivity develops separately. The alternative explanation tightly links this phenomenon to superconductivity. “Other people think they’re missing because they form pairs,” Allan said. Pairs of electrons, called Cooper pairs, are what carry current in a superconductor. If, as the material cools, these pairs appear before the material becomes superconducting, they would be a precondition of superconductivity, a waiting room of sorts, where pairs exist but can’t yet move together in lockstep.

Settling this proved extremely hard. “Lots of different experimental signatures are kind of lumped inside this,” Allan said. Different instruments all see something, but their readings, Allan said, are never conclusive. “It’s always something kind of incoherent, hard to grasp,” he said. What the researchers needed was a way to see pairs directly, and Allan and his colleagues figured it out.

The team decided to listen to shot noise—tiny fluctuations caused by the arrival of individual charges that form the stream of an electric current. Allan says it resembles rain drumming on the roof. “If you imagine that you have raindrops and then all of a sudden you make the drops twice as heavy, there’ll be more noise,” Allan said. “With the electrons it’s similar. If you have two electrons coming always together, because they’re associated with pairing, then it will be more noise.”

The researchers did this measurement with a scanning tunneling microscope, which passed current between a needle-sharp tip and a cuprate sample, letting them listen to the noise at specific energy levels and different locations on the surface. In conventional superconductors, pairing produces a clean doubling of the noise. In cuprates, the signal is much weaker, because single electrons keep flowing alongside the pairs.

Making the instrument sensitive enough to discern the pairs took years. “What it took is very talented and persistent students who worked for, I don’t know, four years on this to get it working,” Allan said. “There was not a single trick. It was electronics craftsmanship.”

The team examined crystals of a cuprate known as BSCCO, cooled to a few degrees above absolute zero, and compared the noise to the energies at which electrons go missing. By adjusting the voltage between the tip of the needle and the sample, the team could choose the energy of the electrons they were listening to, a bit like turning a radio dial. If the pseudogap came purely from frozen patterns, the team reasoned, the extra noise of pairing should only kick in at energy levels associated with superconductivity. Instead, pairing showed up right at the pseudogap energy.

“The fact that there is more noise indicates that pairing is associated with this large gap,” Allan said. The pseudogap’s energy varies from spot to spot on the surface, but wherever the team listened, the extra noise always started rising at the local pseudogap energy. The same pattern held in samples with different chemical compositions.

Ruling out other sources of noise, such as atoms shifting on the surface, took a lot of effort. “Noise is super hard to interpret, and that was basically the thing that we had the most sleepless nights about,” Allan said. The decisive check involved placing the samples in magnetic fields of up to six tesla, which suppresses pairing while leaving the overall pattern of missing electrons largely intact. As the magnetic field grew, the noise dropped back toward the single-electron level, exactly as expected if pairs were behind it.

The strength of electron pairing can be expressed as the energy required to pull a pair apart. Lowering the temperature helps boost pairing because the warmer a material becomes, the more violently its particles jostle and the more pairs get broken. In conventional superconductors, two ingredients needed for superconductivity—pair formation and phase coherence—occur simultaneously at the critical temperature. (Phase coherence is where the electrons start moving together as a fluid.) In cuprates, Allan and Swart’s study points to a different sequence.

The pairing energy the team measured is well above the temperature at which the material superconducts. “So the picture that emerges is that you first have pre-formed pairs, and then only at lower temperatures, phase coherence sets in,” Swart said. That suggests the superconductivity bottleneck is not getting electrons to pair, but getting the pairs to move together.

“If you have pairing at such high energies, that means that you might be able to push Tc [superconducting temperature] higher,” Allan said. “This is something people hoped for in the very early days of cuprates, and now everybody’s afraid to even mention that. But to me it gives hope.”

An optimistic reading of the results is that cuprate electrons could theoretically pair at room temperature, and we only need to make them coherent to achieve a room-temperature superconductor. The team, though, thinks that’s a bit naive. “I think Ingmar and I both believe that it’s not going to be that simple, because you have all kinds of other effects that are coupled there,” Allan said.

The researchers also stress that their experiment does not fully answer the central question. It rules out the idea that the pseudogap comes from frozen patterns alone, but not that such patterns are intertwined with pairing. “Whatever the detailed explanation of the pseudogap is, pairing should be part of it,” Swart said.

Because the technique used in the study loses sensitivity as temperature rises, the team couldn’t yet listen above the superconducting temperature, where the pseudogap is usually defined. “Hopefully other groups will do that,” Allan said. “What limits Tc, especially if the energy of pairing is high? What happens at Tc? That’s for me the most interesting question.”

Swart wants to make noise maps of the surface with higher resolution and, eventually, an instrument that can detect coherence directly, which he hopes should give us separate markers for the onset of phase coherence and electron pairing. Allan, meanwhile, increasingly thinks the route to better superconductors runs through chemistry, aided by AI, rather than pure physics. “When it comes to trying to make the superconducting material better and increase Tc, I have more hope in direct trial and error,” he said.

articles.title: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time
articles.summary: We're looking at the enforcers, instigators, and heartbreakers who mastered the art of basketball villainy.Read more...
articles.ai_summary: The article examines the most notorious figures in NBA history known for their villainous roles on and off the court.

scraped.title: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time – The Root
scraped.h1: The NBA’s Greatest Villains of All Time
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

We’re looking at the enforcers, instigators, and heartbreakers who mastered the art of basketball villainy.

By

Rashad Grove

Published

SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA – OCTOBER 23: Draymond Green #23 of the Golden State Warriors complains about a call during the first half of their game against the Memphis Grizzlies at Chase Center on October 23, 2026 in San Francisco, California. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and/or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Ezra Shaw/Getty Images)

While the NBA is full of crowd favorites, there’s nothing quite like rooting for a villain. From cold-blooded players who loved nothing more than silencing 20,000 screaming fans to ruthless enforcers who treated the hardwood like a battleground, the league has a long history of players who thrived on boos. Here is a look back at the 20 biggest villains in NBA history—the instigators and enforcers who made playing the bad guy an absolute art form.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

The epitome of the 1970s enforcer, Maurice Lucas was a legit tough guy who would not hesitate to put his hands on you. Standing 6’9 with all muscle, Lucas put up major numbers and made his presence felt with his intense physicality. His legendary toughness was cemented in Game 2 of the 1977 NBA Finals when he fearlessly confronted Darryl Dawkins after the 300-pound center punched a teammate, slapping Dawkins and squaring up with fists raised to alter the physical tone of the series.

Rick Mahorn’s role on the “Bad Boy” Detroit Pistons was to inflict physical pain on opponents, and he did so with pleasure. Dubbed the “Chairman of the Board” by teammate John Salley, Mahorn anchored the Pistons’ frontcourt with pure physicality. What made Mahorn such a great villain was that he never apologized for his brutal style. While his opponents complained, Mahorn went about his business of protecting the lane by any means necessary.

Standing 6’4’ and weighing over 250 pounds, Charles Barkley was a “one of one” and as tough as they come. Along with his Hall of Fame resume, Barkley was never one to shy away from a confrontation. Over the years, Barkley went head-to-head with Charles Oakley, Bill Laimbeer, Patrick Ewing, and, in his classic duel, Shaquille O’Neal, his current co-host of ESPN’s Inside the NBA.

Over his 19-year NBA career, Charles Oakley gained a well-earned reputation as a brother you don’t want to mess with. Standing 6’8″ and built out of solid muscle, Oakley was the gold standard of NBA enforcers—a throwback power forward whose physical presence was felt in every game. Whether insulating Michael Jordan during his early years in Chicago, defining the brutal defense of the 1990s New York Knicks, or taking on security guards at Madison Square Garden, Oakley was not to be messed with.

RELATED: Can’t-Miss NBA Drama: Top 5 Storylines to Watch This Season

No team has embodied the villain character like the Bad Boy Pistons. Led by Isaiah Thomas, the squad featured some of the most physical and dirty players of all time, such as Bill Laimbeer, Joe Dumars, Rick Mahorn, Dennis Rodman, and John Salley. Winning back-to-back championships in 1989 and 1990, the Pistons did it with brutal physicality that hasn’t been seen since in the league.

The 1990s New York Knicks ruled Madison Square Garden with physical intimidation and hard-hitting defense. Led by Patrick Ewing, Charles Oakley, Anthony Mason, and Xavier McDaniel, and coached first by Pat Riley and later by Jeff Van Gundy, the Knicks played bully ball instead of being a finesse squad. When you entered MSG during this era, you had to be ready for some real physical punishment.

Embracing his villainy, Reggie Miller’s sharpshooting and trash-talking more than fit the bill. Miller didn’t just accept road hostility; he courted it. His status as basketball’s ultimate villain was forever forged at MSG when he took on the New York Knicks. Scoring 8 points in 9 seconds during Game 1 of the 1995 Eastern Conference Semifinals, Miller flashed his iconic “choke” gesture at celebrity fan Spike Lee. What an epic villain moment by Miller.

Learning the tricks of the trade from the “Bad Boy” Pistons, Dennis Rodman took villainy to another level. A master of psychological warfare, Rodman was a floor-crashing, instigating force who turned relentless hustle and boundary-pushing mind games into an elite basketball weapon. Known as “The Worm, ” he specialized in baiting opponents into technicals and ejections while maintaining total composure himself.

Rasheed Wallace accumulated an incredible 317 regular-season technical fouls and was ejected 29 times—both all-time NBA records. Wallace was an undeniable talent, but his legacy as an antagonist was defined by his running war with NBA officials. He was the face of Portland’s volatile “Jail Blazers” squad. Whether barking at referees or talking trash to the opposing team’s fans, Wallace was right at home in hostile environments.

Whether he’s going by Metta Sandiford-Artest, Metta World Peace, or Ron Artest, he was always ready for some action. In his 17-year career, Artest was one of the most unpredictable and physically terrifying perimeter defenders in NBA history. His status as a villain came on November 19, 2004, during the infamous “Malice at the Palace” brawl in Detroit. After charging into the stands to confront a fan who threw a drink at him, Artest sparked the most explosive riot in American sports history, resulting in a landmark 86-game suspension.

A modern-day ticking time bomb, Draymond Green is liable to go off at any minute and has the track record to prove it. No one in the game today has more flagrant fouls, technical fouls, and ejections than Green. As enforcer of the Golden State Warriors dynasty, Green uses psychological warfare to bait opponents into technical fouls and plays with an aggressive edge that constantly toes the line of being dirty. He’s something else!

Trae Young has an “ice-cold” aura with his villain status. His villain origin story began during the 2021 Eastern Conference playoffs, cementing his status as the premier visitor enemy at Madison Square Garden. Facing the energized NYC crowd, Young embraced his role as public enemy number one in MSG. After nailing the game-winner in Game 1, he put his finger to his lips to silence the arena and took a theatrical bow on the Knicks’ home floor. A villain was born.

Dillion Brooks is always looking for a problem. A relentless perimeter defensive specialist, he actively seeks out hostility and feeds off arena boos. As petty as they come, Brooks turns every matchup into psychological warfare, routinely poking the NBA’s biggest superstars, such as LeBron James, with brazen trash talk and physical play. Without question, Brooks enjoys being a villain.
