scraped.h1: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
scraped.body_text:
See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives

African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester .

See My World , a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.

The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations .

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.

Sign up to Cotton Capital

Starting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the world

after newsletter promotion

“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”

Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”

See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

scraped.title: Distant polls, spotty mail obstruct Native American voting 6 years after law meant to help them - ICT
scraped.description: California never formed a committee to improve Native American voting, leaving barriers like distant polls unaddressed.
scraped.author: Melanie Henshaw
scraped.h1: Distant polls, spotty mail obstruct Native American voting 6 years after law meant to help them
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Melanie Henshaw ICT + CalMatters

Six years after California passed a law requiring the secretary of state to form an advisory committee to help improve voting access for Native Americans, the committee still has not been formed, the secretary of state’s office confirmed to CalMatters/ICT.

Advocates from the California Native Vote Project said they received some reports of problems at polling sites on Election Day, and say the underlying barriers the committee was meant to address, including distant polling places and unreliable mail service, remain.

A spokesperson for Secretary of State Shirley Weber who declined to provide their name said in an email that the office plans to begin recruiting members “after the November election.”

“It’s really frustrating,” said Calvin Hedrick, director of policy for the project, an advocacy group promoting voting rights for Native American peoples in California. “It’s a bummer to have to fight for something again after it was already promised by statute.”

The law, Assembly Bill 2314 , which called for a Native American Voting Accessibility Advisory Committee, was authored by Assemblymember James Ramos and sponsored by then-Secretary of State Alex Padilla .

“California’s nearly three-quarters of a million Native Americans deserve to have their voices heard in our democracy,” Padilla said in an August 2020 statement released by Ramos’ office.

Anthony Roberts, Chairman of the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, which supports the law, said in 2020 that a lack of polling places and the rejection of certain types of identification remained obstacles. “Until those obstacles are addressed, California’s Native Americans remain at risk of being excluded, with no voice in government, the education of their children and other vital services.”

The law required the committee to set guidelines for reaching Native American voters, recommend public service announcements at least 45 days before elections, suggest ways to improve Native American poll worker recruitment, and advise on language assistance and plain-language materials. But the committee’s recommendations would be nonbinding. The secretary of state was required only to consider them.

The law set no deadline for forming the committee, provided no funding and did not require input from tribal governments or groups.

Members, who are to be chosen by the secretary of state, would have to have experience with voting rights or be county elections officials. The law also set no meeting schedule. By contrast, the state’s separate Language Accessibility Advisory Committee , which is supposed to ensure voters can understand the voting process, must meet at least four times a year.

“Lacking those things, it’s pretty clear it’s just going to end up in the dustbin,” said Allison Neswood, senior staff attorney for the Native American Rights Fund, an advocacy group promoting the interests of Indigenous communities. Neswood is Diné.

Ramos, who is Serrano/Cahuilla and a lifelong resident of the San Manuel Indian Reservation, was not available after multiple requests from CalMatters/ICT. “It’s been difficult finding a time, but still working on it,” wrote a spokeswoman in his office, in October. A Democrat from San Bernardino, he is the first and only Native American from a California tribe elected to the Legislature.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

A spokesperson for Weber acknowledged the committee does not exist, in response to questions from CalMatters/ICT in October. The office said it has been “working closely with Native American advocates to review our committee-related documents” and is planning to recruit members.

The secretary of state’s office did not respond to additional questions about why it had not done anything for six years, who it had contacted for recruitment, whether it had requested any funding and whether it had any documents available for review.

Hedrick said his organization, which promotes voter registration and provides nonpartisan voting information in California Native communities across the state, has been doing its own voter outreach without support from the secretary of state’s office. With only two employees to cover all of Northern California, he said, his team is “stretched really thin.”

Resources from a committee would be an important boost to his group’s efforts, Hedrick said.

“It’s something we need to really be pushing for over the next few years — and we can’t allow them to rest and forget about it,” said Hedrick. “We can’t allow them to promise us it’s something they’re going to do next year, we need to hold their feet to the fire and make sure it gets done.”

In California, the state’s broader responsibilities for ensuring voter access sit mostly with the secretary of state, who is the chief elections officer and must make reasonable efforts to promote voter registration and encourage eligible voters to cast ballots. But when it comes to where people vote, the state points to the counties.

The state sets guidelines for drop boxes, including the minimum number per county. But county election officials decide where they go, whether to add any beyond the minimum and when they’re open. Unlike some states, California, which shares geography with 109 federally recognized tribal nations, does not mandate that there be polling locations on tribal lands.

In Shasta County, a monitor for the Native Vote Project saw a citizen of the Redding Rancheria turned away from the polls on election day. He later reported he was able to vote.

On the Hoopa Valley Indian Reservation, the largest reservation in the state, advocates coordinated a vehicle caravan to transport elders from rural areas of the tribe’s lands to reach the only polling site on the reservation.

The Native American Rights Fund produced reports in 2020 and 2026 that found significant barriers to political participation for Native Americans and Alaska Natives. The 2020 report drew on testimony at nine hearings, including two in California. The 2026 report analyzed federal election data from 2020 to 2024, but did not study any California counties specifically. Hedrick said that he continues to hear complaints from Native Americans, especially those in rural communities, about the time and resource costs of voting.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“For people who live in a city where their ballot box is often a 10-minute drive or less, it’s unfathomable to think someone would have to drive an hour or more to vote — but that’s the reality in many of our communities,” said Hedrick, who is Mountain Maidu. Since 2021, California has mailed a ballot to every active registered voter. Advocates say that doesn’t fully address the gaps, because tribal communities, particularly in rural areas, often lack reliable, timely mail service. Some reservations lack even a single polling place or ballot box, forcing tribal citizens to take time off work and drive miles out of their way to cast their ballots.

A 2024 article in the Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review found that voting by mail in Indian Country was “plagued” by overlapping barriers, including a lack of post offices.

“The inadequate postal infrastructure in Indian Country immediately impacts the ability of voters to receive and cast a ballot via mail,” wrote Torey Dolan, a Choctaw citizen and associate law professor at the University of Wisconsin-Madison.

Native Americans were not granted automatic U.S. citizenship until 1924 and were not able to vote in all states until 1962. According to Ramos, they often live long distances from post offices: About 89 percent of current post offices were established before 1920, research has found.

Registering is also difficult. Many Native people who live on tribal lands in California have no permanent address, which makes it hard to place them in a voting precinct. Tribal communities in California have also historically had less access to internet and broadband services.

At least one California tribe successfully brought voter services closer to its citizens in recent years. In September 2023, the Shingle Springs Band of Miwok Indians accepted a designation from the secretary of state making its tribally run health center a voter registration agency under the National Voter Registration Act. Weber said at the time it was the first such designation of a tribal medical facility in the country.

Hedrick and his colleagues at the California Native Vote Project travel to tribal communities across the state, engaging with voters and educating them about the electoral process. He also meets with people who haven’t registered to vote and works to better understand what’s keeping them from doing so.

If the committee were established it could not require counties to open voting sites. But Hedrick said if the committee existed, it could do similar work and could play an important role in building trust between the state and communities that have long felt ignored.

That trust is thin, Neswood said, in part because Native peoples rarely see themselves reflected in government.

“If Native people consistently see that their voices and their priorities and their people aren’t represented in these institutions, it just reinforces the lack of trust,” Neswood said. “We’re fighting an uphill battle.”

Hedrick said rebuilding that trust starts with showing up in tribal communities.

“We need people out in tribal communities listening to voters and talking to people who aren’t registered — I think that’s something this committee could be doing,” Hedrick said. “It became statute in 2020, we’re talking in 2026, and (the committee) still hasn’t happened yet and it’s not happening now.”

scraped.title: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
scraped.description: Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, who will lead a caretaker government while negotiations take place, said: "I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks".
scraped.h1: No clear winner in New Zealand election, as leaders prepare for weeks of talks
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

New Zealand Prime Minister and National Party leader, Christopher Luxon addresses party faithful in Auckland, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov.7, 2026. Alex Robertson/AP hide caption

WELLINGTON, New Zealand — New Zealanders will wait for weeks to discover who will lead the country after Saturday's election failed to deliver a decisive win for the right or the left, leaving fraught negotiations for a wafer-thin governing majority the only apparent path to victory for either side.

The tightest vote in years delivered a stinging rebuke to the major parties which have long dominated New Zealand politics, Christopher Luxon's center-right National party and center-left Labour led by Chris Hipkins, as voters threw more support behind minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. On Saturday's numbers, minor parties would enter negotiations for a governing deal with leverage to extract deeper policy concessions from a weakened National or Labour.

The near-deadlock was partly produced because voters, apparently weary of New Zealand's economic woes and apathetic about both Luxon and Hipkins, chose to propel a new entrant group to Parliament for the first time in years. Opportunity, led by 38-year-old business consultant and political newcomer Qiulae Wong, is unaligned with either bloc and Wong has said she could work with either side to form a government.

Wong's pledges of evidence-based centrism and an end to partisan bickering had on Saturday's results secured seven seats for Opportunity — enough to frustrate both left and right in a simple path to power. It was a staggering ascension for a party that made three failed attempts at Parliament before Wong became leader less than a year ago.

Other winners were harder to identify and on Sunday, "who won the election 2026" was the top trending Google search in New Zealand. So unclear was the result that parties won't begin negotiations to form a government until final tallies are released on Nov. 27, confirming the exact number of seats they've won.

With 2.8 million ballots counted on election night, the conservative incumbent government led by Luxon's National party appeared close to the slimmest possible return to power — by just one seat. However, Luxon didn't claim victory, instead striking a note of cautious optimism that he could negotiate a second term in power.

Speaking to reporters Sunday, Luxon blamed public dissatisfaction on global shocks which have buffeted New Zealand's trade-based economy, noting that other incumbent governments worldwide have faced voters' rancor over living costs.

Yet his opponent Hipkins, who was turfed from office in 2023 largely over discontent about the same economic issues, didn't appear to benefit on Saturday. The left-wing bloc appeared to fall short of a majority but was still hopeful it could triumph — though that seemed a more remote prospect.

Electoral officials were due on Sunday to begin counting nearly 400,000 so-called special votes, including from New Zealanders who live abroad, a process expected to take three weeks.

Those ballots have historically granted an additional seat or two in Parliament to left-wing parties, which could snatch the current razor-thin majority from the right, although such an outcome would likely leave the left struggling to form a majority too. If a government can't be formed, New Zealand could face a fresh vote.

Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins addresses party faithful in Upper Hutt, New Zealand, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Mark Tantrum/AP hide caption

"I think everyone's over politics so let's all have a bit of a break for the next three weeks," Luxon told reporters on Sunday. He will lead a caretaker government until an outcome is reached.

Luxon suggested that National had a viable path to power and boasted that it had secured more seats in Parliament than any other group. However, Saturday night was bleak for his party.

Several of National's most senior lawmakers would exit politics on results so far, including the ministers of finance and defense, the speaker of parliament, and the attorney general. With the party's traditional governing partners winning increased support, Luxon faces a more strident list of policy demands to secure their backing.

Libertarian ACT won 13 seats and populist New Zealand First won 12. Both are led by canny veteran politicians, and detractors of Luxon, a former business executive who entered politics in 2020, said his dealings with them in the three years since he took office had highlighted his political inexperience.

The Opportunity Party leader Qiulae Wong poses for a portrait outside Parliament in Wellington, New Zealand, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Charlotte Graham-McLay/AP hide caption

New Zealanders don't vote for prime ministers. Instead they cast two votes, one for their preferred party and another for the candidate they want as their local representative.

The country has one house of Parliament and no states, so the central government holds ultimate sway over New Zealand's direction. Governments in the South Pacific nation of 5.6 million people are elected every three years.

National won just 29.21% of the preferred party vote as of Sunday, a collapse of its previous result, and secured its 42 seats entirely by winning local constituency races. Luxon, who unusually faced two separateconfidence votes among his own lawmakers this year, further slumped in popularity as leader close to election day.

However, Labour also won just 29.36% of the party vote, a result that appeared to suggest a second election defeat for career politician Hipkins. Despite winning about the same party vote percentage as National, Labour has secured only 36 seats on numbers so far because they won fewer local races.

Minor parties on the left saw bolstered support. The environmentally-focused Greens won 16 seats and Indigenous rights group Te Pāti Māori secured five.

The total number of seats in New Zealand's Parliament changes due to quirks in how seat allocations are calculated. There would currently be 131 lawmakers elected, with 66 seats required for a majority.

Luxon's conservative bloc would currently hold 67, a razor-thin margin likely to discomfit a leader managing a three-way government with two emboldened minor parties. However, the left bloc held only 57 seats before the historically left-leaning special votes were counted.

Even if the final tally boosted the left bloc's seats slightly, Hipkins would apparently need support from newcomer Wong to govern.

Before the election, Luxon repeatedly ruled out negotiating with Wong. He sidestepped questions on Sunday about whether his vanishingly slim lead had changed his mind.

articles.ai_summary: Pope Leo XIV concludes a successful visit to Uruguay and heads to Argentina as part of his South American tour.

scraped.title: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina
scraped.description: On Sunday, tens of thousands packed the main square in Florida, Uruguay, to watch Pope Leo speak.
scraped.h1: After a successful trip to Uruguay, Pope Leo heads to Argentina
scraped.body_text:
By

The Associated Press

Pope Leo XIV plays with a child as he arrived at the square outside the Cathedral Basilica of Florida, Uruguay, the National Shrine of Our Lady of the Thirty-Three, to preside over Mass on the third day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption

FLORIDA, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV wrapped up his visit to Uruguay on Sunday by praising the women who have passed the Catholic faith onto younger generations, as he highlighted the role the church has played since the founding of Latin America's most secular country.

Leo traveled to the city of Florida, north of Montevideo, to mark an important Catholic feast day before heading to Argentina for the second leg of his South American tour. It's expected to be the most politically delicate stop, given the Catholic Church's sharp criticisms of the austerity program of libertarian President Javier Milei.

For his final event in Uruguay, Leo celebrated the feast of the Virgin of the Thirty-three. According to tradition, 33 independence patriots acquired the Guaraní statue and had it with them when independence was declared from the Brazilian empire in Florida on Aug. 25, 1825.

Leo became the first pope in nearly four decades to visit Uruguay, in hopes of reminding its people that the Catholic Church is part of their very identity as a nation — even if, in subsequent decades, the country went on a deeply secular, and at times anticlerical, route.

In his homily, delivered in front of Florida's cathedral, Leo recalled the presence of the statue at the time of independence in reminding Uruguayans that "the history of peoples, too, cannot be fully understood without reference to God," and especially a mother.

He thanked all the mothers and grandmothers who have passed the faith onto younger generations, and acknowledged their pain when their efforts didn't stick.

"You taught your children to pray, and today they no longer do so. You used to attend Mass together, and it has been years since they entered a church," he said. But he urged them to not despair.

"Mothers and grandmothers: never tire of passing on the faith!"

Tens of thousands of people packed Florida's main square for the Mass under brilliant blue skies, some walking for several kilometers (miles) to reach the site. The city has a population of about 40,000 but the Vatican estimated 50,000 were on hand.

Fiama Pirez, an English professor, traveled from Montevideo for the Mass even though she could have seen Leo in the capital. She said she preferred a family outing to Florida so her mother could fulfill a dream to see a pope.

"I'm religious in my own way, and although I never strayed far from the Catholic faith, I'm rediscovering it today," she said.

Pope Leo XIV is cheered by faithful as he arrives for a prayer vigil at Centenario Stadium in Montevideo, on the second day of his twelve-day apostolic journey to South America, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. Andrew Medichini/AP hide caption

In Buenos Aires, Milei is due to greet Leo at the airport before the two appear together for the traditional welcome ceremony and exchange of speeches. The Catholic Church has criticized Milei's austerity measures that have slashed social spending, and his embrace of artificial intelligence.

Milei has staked his presidency on cutting social spending to overhaul Argentina's troubled economy and deliver a long-elusive budget surplus. He has called social justice "an aberration" that amounts to stealing, and mocked as "huge stupidity" the increasingly common complaint in Argentina that families squeezed by his austerity program can't make it to the end of the month.

Leo, who took his name from the 19th-century pope whose encyclical on labor laid the foundation of Catholic social teaching, has made the poor and vulnerable a focus of his papacy, carrying on the legacy of his Argentine predecessor, Pope Francis.

Posters reading "At last, a Lion who unites" appeared across Buenos Aires this weekend, a jab playing on the pope's name in Spanish — León, or lion — and the lion imagery Milei often uses to portray himself on social media.

"Argentina is a society currently experiencing significant upheaval, deep polarization, and an economic crisis, along with a president who defies conventional protocol — a leader who, at one point, even challenged Pope Francis," said Luis Bahamondes, a professor at the Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Chile.

Since taking office in December 2023, Milei has slashed Argentina's healthcare budget by 48% in real terms. Planned cuts to the public university system, which represents a near-universal point of pride in the crisis-prone country, sent students into the streets.

According to official data, poverty in Argentina reached 32.3% of the population during the first half of 2026, representing about 15 million people.

Much like its allies in the Trump administration, Milei's government has portrayed the cuts as part of a necessary reform process to remake Argentina's troubled economy and eliminate fraud and waste in the federal bureaucracy.

Like Trump, Milei has also courted AI investment and data centers with promises of limited regulation. Leo has warned that the AI race poses threats to humanity and the environment and called for strict, internationally policed safeguards on its development.

Milei's government insists the papal trip is purely religious. "The pope belongs to all Argentines. He doesn't belong to a political party or a political camp," Karina Milei, the president's sister and secretary-general of the presidency, told reporters after a recent planning meeting for Leo's visit with church leaders.

In Argentina, Leo is completing unfinished business left by Francis. The Argentine Jesuit, the former archbishop of Buenos Aires, never returned home during his 12-year pontificate, confounding friends and foes alike.

"There's a lot of disagreement over Francis and his legacy in Argentina," said David Lantigua, a theology professor and faculty fellow at the University of Notre Dame's Kellogg Institute, which focuses especially on Latin American affairs.

Much of the polemics stems from his tenure in Buenos Aires, when the former Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio was a slum priest who advocated for the poorest and most marginalized — the sector of Argentines feeling Milei's social spending cuts the most.

"I think we'll see that kind of tension with Leo — that's the ministry Francis left behind," Lantigua said.

Leo, who spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru ministering to poor people, is very much a pastor in Francis' image and owes his pontificate to the late pope. But unlike Francis, he is returning home to Peru on the last leg of this trip, visiting a country where he spent two decades as a missionary.

Argentina's state intelligence agency said Saturday that a person had been arrested over death threats against Leo ahead of his arrival. A federal court in Campana, some 70 kilometers (45 miles) northwest of Buenos Aires, ordered the arrest less than 24 hours after the agency was tipped off, it said, without elaborating.

scraped.title: The best caregiver support may come with terrible coffee | Blaze Media
scraped.description: At a weekly gathering in Montana, the coffee is ferocious, the cookies disappear, and the tissues get passed around. Nobody has to explain a burden everyone at the table recognizes.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: The best caregiver support may come with terrible coffee
scraped.body_text:
At a weekly gathering in Montana, the coffee is ferocious, the cookies disappear, and the tissues get passed around. Nobody has to explain a burden everyone at the table recognizes.

The election is over. People will spend weeks picking apart the results. Meanwhile, family caregivers are sorting medications, helping someone get dressed, and having late-night conversations with the ceiling fan.

November is National Family Caregivers Month. As the holidays approach, expectations pile up even when a caregiver’s strength is running low.

If you’re a caregiver who’s frazzled, stressed, heartbroken, or weary, you’re in the right place.

You can be surrounded by people who love you and still feel lonely. I often tell pastors that caregivers can feel lonely on a crowded pew.

Family caregivers know what it means to disappear into someone else’s story. People ask how your loved one is doing. You explain the latest procedure or what the doctor said. Somewhere in the conversation, what you’re carrying disappears beneath the details of the person you’re caring for.

When I started this column for Blaze News, I wanted caregivers to find a little respite and something solid to stand on while they caught their breath. Whatever else I write about, I keep coming back to the caregiver who wonders whether anyone understands.

That’s also why I started a caregiver group at our church here in Montana.

Every Thursday morning, we gather around a table. First-timers sometimes arrive nervous, sometimes already teary-eyed. Walking into a room of strangers to talk about caring for someone you love takes courage.

The church has committed to keeping us supplied with tissues.

The pastor or his assistant sometimes has coffee waiting. When neither is there, that responsibility falls to me.

I’m accustomed to making coffee for Gracie. She likes coffee that reaches out and slaps you. Most attendees have learned to politely decline when I’m handling the brewing.

One fellow brought a tin of cookies from Costco. We’ve made a sizable dent in them.

Well, let’s be honest. I’ve made a sizable dent. I keep passing the tin around, but somehow it makes its way back to me. I need to be careful, or I’ll get so big the bears will have to start hiding their food.

RELATED: Would you trust this politician with your wallet?

Sonmez karakurt/Getty Images

We go around the table and check in. Sometimes the circumstances are dire, and the tissues get passed along with the cookies. Sometimes we talk about ordinary things. Even amid the tears, laughter has surprised us at every meeting.

You see, each of us speaks fluent caregiver. Nobody needs a lengthy explanation of why someone is exhausted, frightened, or struggling to make one more decision. We recognize the language because we live it.

This week, one man whose wife lives with dementia told us he can no longer have a rational conversation with her. Around our table, he said, he felt heard for the first time in a long time.

How many more caregivers feel the same way he does?

Sometimes, speaking fluent caregiver sounds like this: “Pull up a chair. Have a cookie. Or three. Sign this waiver before drinking the coffee.”

I can’t offer bad coffee and a tin of cookies to readers. You’ll have to supply your own tissues. If you run out, use toilet paper. We’ve all done it.

But I can bring four decades of caring for someone I love to this page. I can speak honestly about the weariness, the fear, the resentment we’re reluctant to admit, and the laughter that still catches us by surprise.

RELATED: There is a place sin cannot molest

Wwing/Getty Images

I can also remind you of something I regularly need to hear myself: You don’t have to feel better in order to be better.

Making your own doctor’s appointment, accepting help, or sitting with people who understand can be a good decision even when you still feel worn out afterward.

If you’re struggling to find the words to say to a caregiver, try these: “I see you, and I see the magnitude of what you’re carrying, and I hurt with you.”

If tears come, you don’t have to find something profound to say. Stay and listen.

If you’re a caregiver who’s frazzled, stressed, heartbroken, or weary, you’re in the right place. Tell me how you’re doing in the comments. I try to read them all and respond when I can.

If you’re none of those things, you’re still in the right place. Because if you love someone, you’ll most likely become a caregiver.

If you live long enough, you’ll need one.

Friends don’t let friends caregive alone.

Peter Rosenberger

scraped.description: Argentina's president restored the solvency of a bankrupt Treasury and a broken central bank.
scraped.author: Juan Ramón Rallo
scraped.h1: How Milei Defused Argentina's Hyperinflation Bomb
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Inflation

Juan Ramón Rallo | From the December 2026 issue

The December 2026 issue of Reason explores Argentine President Javier Milei's accomplishments and what is yet to be done.

Argentina was approaching monetary detonation. Its Treasury could not finance its deficits voluntarily, its central bank was effectively insolvent, and monthly inflation was accelerating above 12 percent.

That was just three years ago. Today, monthly inflation has fallen below 2 percent, sovereign spreads touched eight-year lows in July, and the central bank's gross reserves reached their highest level since 2019 in September. This is one of the most remarkable disinflations of the modern era to have occurred without dollarization, a currency board, or a new currency. Javier Milei did not merely slow the rate at which prices were rising; he dismantled the fiscal and monetary mechanism that was driving Argentina toward hyperinflation.

But as the events of late 2025 showed, that achievement remains vulnerable. A stabilization can be economically coherent and still be politically mortal. Argentina has restored a substantial degree of public sector solvency, but it has not yet made that solvency independent of the next election.

Deficits themselves do not make Argentina unique. What distinguished Argentina was how those deficits had to be financed. In a country with functioning capital markets and a credible government, the state sells bonds to domestic and foreign savers; it obtains command over present resources, while creditors receive claims on future tax revenues. Public borrowing may be undesirable or objectionable on other grounds, but so long as the government remains solvent in the long run, it is a financial operation that can be sustained over time without debt restructurings or bouts of high inflation.

Argentina had largely exhausted that option. After repeated inflationary crises and serial debt repudiations—nine sovereign defaults, most recently in 2020—investors would lend to the Treasury only at prohibitive rates. Borrowing at those rates would itself make the debt trajectory unsustainable, so creditors expected either another restructuring of dollar-denominated bonds or an inflationary liquidation of peso-denominated liabilities. Those expectations raised borrowing costs further, making the anticipated outcome more likely. The Argentine state had trapped itself in a doom loop.

So the government relied on the one creditor that couldn't refuse it: the central bank. Fiscal deficits were financed, directly or indirectly, by issuing pesos. But that brought it up against a second constraint. The inflationary effect of money creation depends not only on the quantity of money supplied but on the quantity people are willing to hold. And after decades of monetary abuse, Argentines wanted as few pesos as possible.

Every newly issued peso became a hot potato to be exchanged for goods, dollars, or inflation-protected assets. As the demand for real peso balances contracted, the government had to print ever larger quantities to extract the same real resources, which pushed prices up faster, which further reduced the willingness to hold pesos, which required still more issuance. That's the feedback loop of an economy approaching hyperinflation.

Rather than stop the process, the government tried to repress its visible symptoms—a task for which the country has a well-worn tool kit. Its most familiar instrument is the cepo cambiario , a web of capital and exchange controls with which the state prevents its citizens from freely satisfying their demand for dollars and hides the peso's depreciation behind an artificially strong official exchange rate. President Cristina Fernández de Kirchner imposed it in 2011; Mauricio Macri lifted it on taking the presidency, only to reinstate it amid the currency run of 2019; the leaders who followed tightened it further. Under the cepo, exchange rates multiplied. Exporters were forced to surrender their dollars below market value, while politically privileged importers bought them cheaply from the central bank. That arrangement punished exports, subsidized favored imports, invited corruption, and bled reserves.

The second instrument operated through the central bank's own balance sheet: extremely high nominal interest rates paid on short-term liabilities held mainly by commercial banks. These so-called remunerated liabilities were a standing bribe to the financial system to sit on its pesos rather than convert them into dollars or goods. Since those interest payments were themselves financed by creating new money for which there was no demand, they generated what Argentines call the quasi-fiscal deficit—a deficit produced not by the Treasury's spending programs but by the central bank's mounting interest bill. Paying interest to suppress monetary expansion today merely promised greater monetary expansion tomorrow.

By the end of 2023, the numbers had become grotesque. The Treasury's fiscal deficit stood at roughly 5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), while the central bank's quasi-fiscal deficit approached 10 percent. Sovereign spreads hovered near 2,500 basis points—meaning that when an equivalent U.S. Treasury bond yielded 5 percent a year, Argentina would have had to pay around 30 percent to borrow in dollars. Monthly inflation hit 12.8 percent in November and was accelerating. (For perspective: Americans were furious when inflation peaked at 9 percent a year under President Joe Biden.) The gap between the official exchange rate and parallel rates exceeded 100 percent and at times approached 200 percent, strangling foreign trade. And the central bank's net international reserves stood at roughly negative $11 billion, the lowest level in its recorded history.

That was the machine Milei inherited on December 10, 2023: an insolvent Treasury, a central bank buried under remunerated liabilities, a rapidly contracting demand for the national currency, and a regulatory apparatus built to disguise the consequences of all three.

Argentina was not yet in hyperinflation. But it had entered its antechamber.

Milei's strategy was to restore the solvency of the Treasury and the central bank so that the controls concealing their insolvency could safely be removed. The sequencing was important. If he had scrapped every exchange control while the government still ran large deficits, the central bank still printed pesos to cover them, and net reserves were deeply negative, that could have accelerated rather than stopped a speculative run.

The first front was fiscal. Milei cut government spending, and not just in inflation-adjusted terms. Some cuts were explicit: Public works were halted, discretionary transfers to provincial governments were slashed, subsidies were pared back, and government employment contracted. (Such changes struck at many of the mechanisms through which Argentina's political class distributed patronage.) Other cuts operated through inflation itself: The government declined to fully index some nominal expenditures to rising prices, shrinking the real value of public salaries and pensions. This was socially painful, particularly for pensioners, but it allowed the fiscal correction to proceed faster than Congress would otherwise have permitted.

National primary spending fell by roughly a quarter in real terms in Milei's first year—an adjustment with few peacetime precedents—which brought national spending, as a share of the economy, back toward levels last seen in 2007–08. Within weeks of taking office, the government was posting monthly primary surpluses; it closed 2024 with a fiscal surplus and has treated balanced budgets as the nonnegotiable anchor ever since. That change altered the monetary regime before any formal institutional reform. Once the Treasury stopped requiring net financing from the central bank, the primary source of fiscally driven peso creation disappeared.

Milei also devalued the official exchange rate within days of taking office, bringing it closer to the market rate. That produced an immediate price shock, with monthly inflation exceeding 25 percent in December 2023. Critics called the devaluation inflationary, and in an immediate accounting sense, it was. But much of the inflation it unleashed was already latent, repressed behind an official exchange rate that almost nobody could access and nobody believed. By recognizing the accumulated depreciation at once, the government sharply narrowed the gap between official and parallel markets, restored exporters' incentives, and began dismantling expectations of an uncontrolled adjustment. After a transitional period, most exchange restrictions were lifted in April 2025.

Skeptics will note—correctly—that the liberalization co-incided with a new $20 billion loan from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and will be tempted to conclude that it was this that made it possible to lift the cepo: just another bailout in a long history of Argentine bailouts. That reading misses the difference between financing a flow (the deficit) and refinancing a stock (the inherited debt).

Earlier IMF programs had poured external resources into governments that were still generating new fiscal imbalances, so the money flowed in while the pile of public liabilities kept growing—most spectacularly in 2018, when the largest loan in the IMF's history stabilized nothing. This time, the Treasury was already in surplus, and the facility operated on the stock inherited from the past: Argentina's largest external creditor was rolling over its own exposure, thickening the central bank's liquidity buffers, and stretching the horizon over which the old debt would be serviced. That support undoubtedly reinforced the program's healing dynamics and probably brought the lifting of the cepo forward. But it was neither a sufficient condition for success nor, over the medium term, a necessary one. A Treasury running surpluses and a central bank no longer bleeding pesos would eventually have rebuilt reserves and regained market access on their own, though this would have happened more slowly.

The second front was the central bank itself. Once the Treasury stopped demanding monetary financing, the Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) could sharply cut the interest rates paid on its remunerated liabilities. With lower expectations of inflation and depreciation, it was no longer necessary to pay enormous nominal rates to keep pesos from stampeding into goods and dollars.

The relationship ran in both directions. Falling inflation allowed lower nominal rates, lower rates shrank the central bank's interest bill, a smaller interest bill reduced future money creation, and reduced expected money creation further increased the demand for pesos. A virtuous circle began to replace the old doom loop.

The government then dismantled the central bank's stock of remunerated liabilities, shifting the job of absorbing excess pesos—and its cost—onto Treasury instruments. This did not make the debt disappear, but it lengthened maturities and placed the cost where it belonged: on the Treasury's accounts, under public and legislative scrutiny, rather than hidden within the central bank's balance sheet. The distinction matters. The quasi-fiscal deficit had allowed governments to claim more fiscal discipline than actually existed by parking part of the cost of stabilization outside the formal budget. Milei's consolidation made the state's liabilities transparent and stopped the central bank from autonomously compounding them through an escalating interest bill.

As confidence returned, sovereign spreads collapsed from roughly 2,500 basis points when Milei was elected to around 400 in July 2026, their lowest in eight years. That allowed the Treasury to roll over maturing debt at ever longer terms and lower cost. Argentina has not yet fully regained ordinary access to international capital markets; the government still leans on multilateral financing and domestic issuance to meet foreign-currency maturities, and spreads widened again, to above 600 by late September, as long-term U.S. rates rose and investors began to price the 2027 presidential election. But the probability of another restructuring has receded dramatically. The improvement shows on the central bank's balance sheet too: In 2026 alone, the BCRA has bought more than $14 billion in the foreign exchange market, and in early September gross reserves topped $50 billion, their highest level since 2019. Purchases have slowed sharply since the summer, and usable net reserves remain far smaller, but the direction of travel has reversed from the deeply negative position inherited in 2023.

All of this occurred alongside a modest but real reduction in taxes. The Impuesto PAIS, a major surcharge on foreign-currency transactions, was allowed to expire at the end of 2024. Export taxes were abolished for regional economies and thousands of industrial products and were cut for major agricultural exports on a declining schedule; tariffs, internal taxes on selected goods, and the wealth tax were also reduced, pushing the national tax burden to its lowest share of GDP in almost two decades. These cuts were modest relative to Milei's ambitions, but notable because they occurred without sacrificing the surplus. Milei did not balance the budget by raising taxes; he cut spending faster than revenue fell.

The macroeconomic result is hard to dispute. Monthly inflation, 25.5 percent in December 2023, was 1.7 percent in August 2026. Year-over-year inflation has fallen to 33.5 percent from 211 percent in 2023, and it is still declining.

Does all of this mean that Argentina is financially saved and that Milei has completed his task? No. The months before the October 2025 midterms show why.

When the opposition began climbing in the polls, and above all after it crushed the government's candidates in September's Buenos Aires provincial election, markets started pricing a scenario in which Milei lost the political capacity to defend his own agenda. The repricing was brutal. Country risk, which had been trading around 700 basis points in mid-August, doubled to nearly 1,500 by mid-September, and the peso depreciated by more than 20 percent over the episode, even though short-term interest rates soared and the authorities burned billions of scarce dollars trying to stabilize it.

Note what had not happened. The government had not abandoned the surplus, had not returned to monetary financing, and had not rebuilt the remunerated-liability machine. Milei's program had not secretly become insolvent; what triggered the crisis was the rising probability that its enemies might regain the power to make the state insolvent again. Nor was the panic irrational. Asset values depend on expected future policy, not just current policy. Savers who believe a future government will monetize deficits, impose controls, or restructure debt will sell pesos and Argentine bonds before that government takes office, and that means the anticipation of a regime reversal can generate, in advance, the very crisis the reversal would eventually have produced.

And this was not merely a panic among foreign fund managers. Ordinary Argentines know their political class too well and have learned to protect themselves by dollarizing; the threat of a fiscally irresponsible government had them fleeing the peso en masse. The central bank's statistics tell the story. Gross retail purchases of dollars reached some $5 billion in September and almost as much in October—double their previous monthly pace, and the heaviest retail dollarization since the eve of the election in 2019—before collapsing to barely a third of that rhythm the month after the vote.

The panic revealed a real weak point, though. Milei had fixed the flows but not yet the stocks: The state's liquid assets—its international reserves—still fell short of the bills coming due, whether pesos being dumped for dollars or hard-currency bonds maturing in the months ahead. Rebuilding a state's balance sheet takes years. Reserves accumulate purchase by purchase, and maturities lengthen only as fast as creditors' trust returns. Until that slow work is done, any rise in the perceived risk of a political reversal can abruptly close the state's access to refinancing, leaving it with maturing debts it cannot yet cover and a run on the peso it cannot stabilize with its own resources.

That was the gap the U.S. Treasury stepped in to fill. In October 2025, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent set up a $20 billion swap line with Argentina's central bank and—in an operation American taxpayers had every reason to question—bought pesos outright in the days before the vote. Bessent was bridging, for a few weeks, a gap that political panic had blown open. The intervention contained the panic just long enough for the election to remove its immediate political cause. On October 26, Milei's coalition took more than 40 percent of the vote, expanded its bloc in Congress, and locked in enough votes to sustain the president's vetoes. Within days, the peso steadied, spreads resumed their slide, and the central bank was buying dollars again. By year's end, Argentina had repaid the $2.5 billion it had actually drawn on the swap.

Still, the lesson is uncomfortable. A stabilization is consolidated only when an election can no longer plausibly revive expectations of default and monetary collapse. Argentina isn't there yet.

Time, if politics allows, will close the balance sheet gap. Reserves are being rebuilt, and maturities stretch a little further with every successful auction. But some of Milei's central libertarian promises are still, for now, only promises.

Milei inherited a country with no voluntary creditors, almost no demand for its currency, a Treasury hooked on monetary financing, a central bank trapped by its own interest bill, deeply negative net reserves, and capital controls that strangled trade while failing to stop depreciation. In less than three years, his government produced sustained fiscal surpluses, dismantled the quasi-fiscal time bomb, cut monthly inflation from 25 percent to below 2 percent, compressed sovereign spreads to eight-year lows, liberalized the exchange market, rebuilt reserves, and reduced taxes. And it did that without confiscating deposits, without a new default, and without raising the overall tax burden.

Hyperinflation is no natural disaster. It is the political consequence of a state that loses solvency and finances itself through a currency its citizens no longer wish to hold. Milei has stopped that process. Whether he has changed Argentina's institutions enough to prevent its return is a verdict that will arrive only after he leaves office.

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Nithya Raman carried the democratic socialist label without running a socialist campaign. Will she govern like one?

On paper, the second-largest city in the country has its first democratic socialist mayor.

Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman declared victory on Thursday over the embattled incumbent Karen Bass, joining a list of socialist mayors who have risen to power in recent years, including Zohran Mamdani in New York; Seattle’s Katie Wilson; and most recently Janeese Lewis George in Washington, D.C., who won in a landslide this week.

Raman, however, did not campaign unabashedly as a socialist. Though she ran as an endorsed member of the Democratic Socialists of America’s Los Angeles chapter, the national DSA threatened to override the local chapter and rescind the endorsement over concerns around her stances on Israel and Palestine.

Unlike her counterpart in New York, to whom she draws most comparisons , Raman did not make sweeping socialist promises, such as free public transit, universal childcare, or taxing the rich. Instead, she focused on what’s wrong with the city. Riding a wave of resentment for Bass’s alleged mismanagements of the Palisades fire and the Lineage Logistics warehouse fire in Boyle Heights, Raman talked about filling potholes, fixing street lights, and making roads safer for pedestrians and cyclists.

In addition to DSA-LA support, she earned the endorsements of popular anti-corruption City Controller Kenneth Mejia and Unite Here 11, a major local hospitality workers union, whose large membership canvassed for her in the general. But she lacked endorsements from most key labor groups and social justice nonprofits, and the organizing base they provide. Her fellow DSA members on the Los Angeles City Council all pulled for Bass, forcing Raman to battle back the perception that she struggles to build coalitions.

While Mamdani, 10 months into his term, now finds himself under pressure from New York’s left for refusing to fire NYPD’s police commissioner , his massive base of organizer support offers a buffer to criticism. Raman won over the city’s voters, but it’s not clear how much time that will buy her to tackle the city’s most vexing problems once she takes office.

“Folks in New York are willing to cut Mamdani more slack on the movement side, because he was one of them on a bunch of issues,” said David Levitus, executive director of LA Forward, a progressive nonprofit that endorsed Raman in the general election. ”I think Nithya” — who did not come from the ranks of DSA organizing like Mamdani — “has more skepticism from parts of the left because of that.”

Raman will face scrutiny from LA’s progressive left on a host of issues: bloated police department spending amounting to roughly a quarter of the city’s nearly $15 billion budget; fear of collaboration between ICE and law enforcement agencies; the 2028 Olympics prompting an expansion of surveillance ; rising homelessness; and failing infrastructure.

Weeks before the November election, Raman seemed less concerned with movement-based allegiances or ideological labels, saying she is “ a capitalist and I’m also a democratic socialist.” Before the primary in June, she said she was “one of the most independent voices in City Hall” when asked about her membership with DSA. The statements and her votes in city council have prompted intense debate among DSA-LA’s members over whether Raman holds up to democratic socialist ideals.

While most Angelenos do not care about such fine distinctions, Raman’s measured embrace of socialist mantle has created among some activists the perception of a more responsive audience in city hall compared to previous administrations. Yet to others on LA’s progressive left, Raman’s ideological elusiveness reads as political unreliability.

“I don’t think Nithya Raman is accountable to anyone in the movement,” said Kris Rehl, an activist who volunteered for Raman during her 2020 city council run and now runs the mutual aid group LA Street Care. “If you do not subscribe to any ideology, you can’t be held accountable to it.”

Rehl, who advocates for abolishing anti-camping bans that criminalize homeless encampments near schools and daycares, expressed dismay over Raman’s previous votes on expanding the police department despite running on defunding the police in 2020.

Others like Tal Levy, a member of DSA-LA’s electoral politics committee, remain more optimistic about what Raman can deliver as mayor. While DSA-LA is pushing for reallocating funds from the police budget into social services, Levy sees the value of Raman’s pledge to support LA Forward’s initiative of citywide expansion of unarmed crisis response teams, which divert certain 911 calls to teams of social workers and clinicians, rather than police.

“Even if Nithya were a fire-breathing abolitionist, it would still be a long fight to make those changes,” said Levy, who has been organizing with DSA-LA for nearly a decade. “But I believe there is plenty of room for us to make material wins in the short term.”

While there is debate over how much power DSA-LA has within LA’s political landscape, the group provided Raman additional attention and credibility among leftist voters, which was only bolstered by the successes of other DSA-endorsed candidates in New York and in congressional races across the nation.

The DSA’s National Political Committee, however, spurred one of the biggest public rifts during Raman’s campaign. The committee held a vote to un-endorse Raman over her perceived lack of support for the Palestinian-led Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement, which hadn’t been included by the DSA-LA on its endorsement questionnaire. After a week of debate and dueling resolutions, and an email from Raman, in which she wrote, “the best way for working Angelenos to stand in solidarity with Gaza is through non-violent protest, legislative action, and diplomatic pressure, including BDS,” the national committee decided against rescinding its endorsement of Raman by a narrow margin .

Frances Gill, one of three DSA-LA members on the DSA national political committee, voted against rescinding the group’s endorsement. She opposed the idea of alienating the organization’s second largest chapter as “bad organizing and bad leadership,” especially in a high-profile race when the stakes for the regional and national chapters were so closely intertwined.

“The public ties us to one another,” Gill said of the DSA and Raman, “and there’s not a lot of other key players who have also played such a critical role in her being able to win. So I think that gives us an outsized seat at the table.”

She was a part of the faction among national leadership that instead called for a long-term pressure campaign on Raman on the issue of Israel and Palestine. The group is planning to push Raman on what she can do as mayor to halt the transportation of military hardware that makes its way through the Los Angeles International Airport to Israel . Organizers also plan to call for an end to real estate events in LA facilitating the sale of housing illegally built in the occupied West Bank. They will also examine whether the city itself is invested in companies that are profiting off Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid rule of Palestinians.

“I think there is room to push,” Gill said.

Another major public spat between progressives and Raman took place in January before she announced her candidacy for mayor.

Catching housing advocates by surprise, Raman introduced a motion to reform the city’s “mansion tax” to make exemptions for developers. Raman claimed that the tax, known as Measure ULA, was inadvertently preventing construction of new multi-family housing. Organizers opposed the idea, since the tax generates funds for services to support existing affordable housing and keep people housed, and that carveouts for developers would only fuel displacement of low-income renters, possibly pushing more people to the streets.

LA Forward was among those blindsided by the motion, which she eventually withdrew. Before endorsing Raman, Levitus and the group met with the candidate alongside organizers in an activist’s home.

“She talked about, ‘The times when I’ve succeeded, it’s because I built a coalition, the times when I failed, it’s because I didn’t, and I didn’t bring people along,’” Levitus recalled from the July meeting. “She really owned her mistake. I don’t know how much her mind has changed intellectually about the policy, but think clearly she recognizes that she needed to do something different — and that might lead to her pushing for a policy that is different from what she had pushed for before.”

Among Raman’s early tests progressives will be watching for is how she fulfills her pledge to fire LAPD police chief Jim McDonnell. Raman was among the councilmembers who approved his appointment in 2024, despite concerns around his track record of collaborating with ICE as LA County sheriff. She has since said she would fire McDonnell over his response to the ICE raids and his refusal to enforce a state law that banned federal agents from wearing masks .

Yet the pledge to replace McDonnell may present a political quagmire for Raman, given that the mayor in LA cannot unilaterally force out a police chief. The city’s police commission, consisting of five civilians appointed by the mayor, must make that decision. Raman first will need to assemble her own commission, but that process also requires approval from a city council that remains largely supportive of the police department.

William Gude, a vocal police accountability advocate who supported Raman in the election, said he planned to push the mayor to circumvent the process by asking McDonnell to resign. “I’m putting pressure on her from day one,” he said. “There’s some promises that she made, and those promises need to be kept.”

In her first press conference as mayor-elect, Raman sidestepped a question about whether she still planned to fire McDonnell, amid public threats from the police union warning of “Armageddon.” “Public safety is the most important service the city is delivering to its people,” said Raman, noting the chief was one of her first phone calls after winning.

Activist pressure could be a burden for Raman — or a tool she could use to force legislation through a city council she knows well, according to Gude. “Does she want to have activists coming after her, also while battling 15 council members?” said Gude, who goes by @FilmthePoliceLA on social media. “Or would she rather have the activist base going after the council members that are coming after her, to create a buffer, to do a lot of her heavy lifting? It’s a choice she has to make.”

Hamid Khan, who heads the Stop Spying LAPD Coalition, is among those who is closely watching who Raman appoints to her police commission. But he sees Raman’s pledge of firing McDonnell as “a band-aid” for the more glaring structural issues of the department. While crediting Raman’s opposition to automated license plate readers from Flock Safety and Axon, Khan also pointed to Raman’s historic support for expanding the police department.

While in city council, Raman voted to expand LAPD’s budget three times: in 2021, 2022, and 2023 . But she also voted against police raises in 2023, and this year, she opposed a plan by Bass to hire 170 more officers. She has said on the campaign trail she does not wish to expand the police budget, but also said she would not cut into it either.

In the span of her time in city council, the LAPD has expanded its surveillance reach, Khan said. The department is slowly unrolling its Real-Time Crime Centers, which meld automated license plate reader technology, social media monitoring software, and CCTV cameras into a constant surveillance tool. He warned such a technology, while marketed to curb retail theft, will disproportionately harm Black and brown Angelenos.

“We have to situate the people’s expectations in Los Angeles that they’re not based upon the comment, ‘I’m gonna fire Jim McDonald,’” said Khan, who advocates for abolishing the budding police outposts. “What does that do? The fundamentals still remain the same.”

There is a notion among some on the left that Raman is very much a part of the political machine that bred some of LA’s ongoing problems. She has served on city council for five years and was an ally to Bass, having endorsed Bass just weeks before jumping in the race herself. Yet Raman, a Harvard-educated urban planner and former entertainment director of Time’s Up, is in many respects an outsider to the political establishment.

Former City Councilmember Mike Bonin called Raman’s victory a “reordering of the governing class in Los Angeles.” For the past several decades, LA politics has been run by establishment Democrats, such as Bass or her predecessor, Eric Garcetti, son of a former LA County district attorney; the chambers of commerce; lobbyists; longtime city hall staffers; all riding the influence of homeowners.

For Lex Steppling, an organizer with Los Angeles Community Action Network and a critic of Raman’s time in city council, the “political recalibration” with her victory in city hall was a welcome sight.

Steppling grew up in a generation of LA political activists who got their start organizing with Community Coalition, which Bass founded in 1990 and for a long time was the only progressive organization in the city offering paid political work. He watched as his peers grew to leading campaigns on issues such as policing and mass incarceration, then began running for elected office. They brought with them their organizing chops, but also their relationships with the organizations that gave them their start. Steppling described this as a “relational ecosystem,” in which movements would be co-opted into electoral politics — in which scoring political points became more important than addressing the issues.

He blamed the lack of gains on policing and mass incarceration since the 2020 George Floyd uprising on such a relational ecosystem. A victory for Raman could mark a reset to such an establishment, and he hopes activists will capitalize on the opening.

“The right kind of openings to do the right kind of work will reemerge,” said Steppling, who helped lead a successful anti-incarceration measure in 2020. “It’s gonna once again start to be about the demands.”

Raman’s election evoked for Bonin memories of the last time an LA incumbent mayor was ousted. In 2005, then-state Assembly member Antonio Villaraigosa beat James Hahn, becoming the city’s first Latino mayor. Villaraigosa, previously director of Southern California ACLU, was seen as a progressive candidate at the time. That’s not how he governed. An early sign of his establishment politics was hiring a longtime political insider as his chief of staff.

Raman will also signal her governing priorities with the hires for her transition team and cabinet.

Some organizers were encouraged to see progressive figures added to her campaign, such as Faizah Malik, a civil rights attorney and former city council candidate also endorsed by DSA-LA, and Jamie York, an advocate for greater transparency in city politics whose high-profile rejection by the city council as an ethics commission appointee drew public scrutiny . It remains unclear what if any role they would play in city hall.

The LA Times reported that Rick Cole, former deputy mayor, is expected to supervise Raman’s transition team alongside Andrea Conant, Raman’s chief of staff in city council.

“How big is the table,” Bonin said, “and how much of the activist community is at the table?”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

articles.ai_summary: Indonesia is facing potential political turmoil following a wiretapping scandal involving President Prabowo Subianto.

scraped.title: Indonesia Might Be Heading into a Deep Political Crisis - Left Voice
scraped.description: The largest country in Southeast Asia has been rocked by a wiretapping scandal as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s administration.
scraped.author: Samuel Karlin
scraped.body_text:
The largest country in Southeast Asia has been rocked by a wiretapping scandal as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s administration.

Samuel Karlin

Indonesia, which in recent years has risen to the status of a middle power, might soon be rocked by a significant political crisis. Following news of a wiretapping scandal which targeted the country’s president, Prabowo Subianto, the government deployed tens of thousands of military personnel to Jakarta. The government also detained three senior police generals including former national police chief, Listyo Sigit Prabowo (unrelated to president Prabowo).

Despite the massive military deployment, a report by Bloomberg suggests that on the ground in Jakarta, things appear to be functioning as usual, and the military presence isn’t noticeable. But the same report also explains that behind these developments is a larger conflict between President Prabowo and the former president Joko Widodo who had appointed Listyo as national police chief. The conflict between the current president and former president embodies a deeper conflict between the country’s military, of which Prabowo was a top general, and the country’s police, an institution which remains close to Widodo.

The conflict at the level of the regime comes as Indonesians are souring on Prabowo’s presidency. In recent weeks students and civil society groups have been protesting in Jakarta against the government’s handling of ongoing forest fires in the country. Protesters have denounced that these fires were caused by the clearing out of sensitive lands for palm oil plantations.

Hundreds of Indonesian students and civil society groups protested in the capital, Jakarta, and other cities against President Prabowo Subianto's policies, including the handling of ongoing forest fires and government spending priorities. pic.twitter.com/E5BrXBQDtf

Additionally, mineworkers have begun a sit-in at the largest nickel-mine in the world to demand a fair contract. A pillar of Indonesia’s geopolitical significance is that it is home to the largest nickel reserves in the world. Along with nickel being used in many everyday goods, it is a key component to rechargeable batteries, giving Indonesia strategic leverage in the EV industry. This also makes Indonesian miners a strategic sector of Asia’s working class, and it will be important that workers of the world show solidarity with their struggle.

Mineworkers at the largest nickel-mining site in the world (100k+ workers) in Indonesia are staging protests and now a sit-in demanding a fair contract. Workers say at least one worker a month dies due to the lack of safety equipment and the wages are unlivable. pic.twitter.com/3hRBimgyQS

Most protests in Indonesia have remained modest in size, especially compared to student-led demonstrations which have spread across Europe and even emerged in countries in Asia and Latin America. But they speak to larger disapproval of Prabowo. After two years in power, Prabowo’s approval rating currently sits at a low of 44.5 percent, the lowest any president has received in the time that Indonesia has conducted polling. This comes as the country’s economy is stagnating, and its stock market is at risk of being downgraded, which could result in a currency crisis.

Indonesians have also turned on Prabowo due to the failure of his multi-billion dollar meals program, a flagship policy which had been meant to address malnutrition. The program, which was popular as a campaign point, has been roiled by allegations of corruption and thousands of cases of young people being poisoned or being served rice with glass and maggots. The administration has also received backlash for strengthening the role of the military in the government and restricting civil liberties.

In his time as a general, Prabowo led the violent persecution of pro-democracy activists under the country’s brutal military dictatorship which ended in 1998. However, Prabowo successfully branded himself as a cuddly, grandpa-like figure during his 2024 presidential campaign.

Another key to his electoral victory was the support he received from Widodo. The former president left office as one of Indonesia’s most popular leaders, having played a key role in elevating Indonesia to middle power prestige. While the country’s constitution barred him from running for another term, he made a deal to back Prabowo in exchange for cabinet positions for his political allies. This agreement is now falling apart amid the wiretapping scandal, spelling deeper crisis for Prabowo’s regime.

However the different factions in Indonesia’s government choose to maneuver, neither political block represents Indonesia’s students and workers who are beginning to take action against air pollution, exploitation, and attacks on democratic rights, among other issues. What role the workers and popular sectors in the country play in the event of greater political instability is to be seen.

Originally published on Novemer 6 in CRP News .

Protest

Samuel Karlin is a socialist with a background in journalism. He mainly writes for Left Voice about U.S. imperialism and international class struggle.

U.S. Marine Devin Jacob Ballard is suspected of robbing and killing a 39-year-old woman in Okinawa. This is another episode in a long history of the U.S. military presence in Okinawa fueling violence against Okinawa residents.

Samuel Karlin

The latest Trump-Xi summit produced no major breakthrough, instead establishing a fragile “managed stability” amid continuing tensions over trade, technology, Taiwan, and China’s global influence.

André Barbieri

The Lee Jae-Myung government is pushing for the deployment of South Korean troops to the Strait of Hormuz. Korean workers must oppose the deployment and the expansion of the war industry.

March to Socialism

HD Hyundai workers are demanding the end of unfair contracts, wage cuts, and discriminatory treatment. Their voices echoed far and wide across Seoul at the 2nd National Joint Action Rally of Migrant Workers.

Bae Ye-ju

Out now in English from 34 Press and Left Voice --- "Socialist Strategy and Military Art" by Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello draws on Clausewitz, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gramsci, rethinking revolutionary strategy and working-class hegemony for the 21st century.

Adrien Masson

November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo
