scraped.title: An 11-Day-Old Baby Couldn’t Stop Bleeding. For Hours, the ER Didn’t Provide a Critical Vitamin Shot.
scraped.description: As more parents reject a long-standard shot for babies, hospitals are seeing cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding — once considered virtually eliminated. Doctors don’t always recognize or know how to treat the life-threatening condition.
scraped.author: Duaa Eldeib
scraped.h1: An 11-Day-Old Baby Couldn’t Stop Bleeding. For Hours, the ER Didn’t Provide a Critical Vitamin Shot.
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

A Simple Shot

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.

The emergency room was a mile from their Texas home. Stephanie and Eric Biesenbach took comfort in that when their newborn daughter, Gwen, wouldn’t stop bleeding from her belly button. They buckled Gwen into her car seat and made the drive over.

Medical records from that warm August evening in 2023 described her condition as a “generic problem” of a bleeding umbilical cord stump. The doctor on duty, Nicole Malouf, had treated plenty of those as an emergency room specialist. She covered Gwen’s oozing belly button with a special gauze to stanch the flow, and when it appeared to stop, she sent Stephanie, Eric and Gwen on their way.

They made it as far as the parking lot before they noticed Gwen had bled through her footed pajamas. Eric slid his arm under the car seat handle and lifted his 11-day-old daughter out of the car. They walked back toward the glaring lights of the Lonestar 24HR ER, a freestanding emergency department in New Braunfels next to a car wash, a McDonald’s and a deli.

Stephanie told Malouf that Gwen had been bleeding a bit after the scab that replaced her umbilical cord stump fell off. The amount of blood they saw that night worried them. She ticked through Gwen’s history. No fever. No vomiting. Exclusively breastfed. She mentioned that she and Eric had declined a vitamin K shot when Gwen was born and instead had been giving Gwen oral vitamin K drops, which they trusted would protect her.

Malouf tried another type of pretreated gauze. When that didn’t work, medical records show, she turned to silver nitrate, a chemical applied to the tip of a long matchlike stick that cauterizes blood vessels. Malouf rotated one stick after another inside Gwen’s belly button.

Since the 1960s, the vast majority of newborns in the United States have received a vitamin K shot. The injection virtually eliminated vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a rare condition that can cause catastrophic bleeding and even death.

But a shift in recent years has threatened to upend the unwavering protection that many doctors and hospitals had taken for granted. Families — mistrustful of medical interventions, misled by social media and devoted to a birth experience they deem natural — have begun to shun the vitamin K shot.

A pair of studies published last week, both of which involved millions of births, found that babies who didn’t get the vitamin K shot had an increased risk of bleeding. One of the studies found that between 2017 and 2025, the rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding increased a staggering 347%.

Without the single, inexpensive shot — which is not a vaccine — babies are dying . Autopsies reveal how babies’ systems shut down without warning and well-meaning parents who declined the vitamin K shot were left mourning the loss of their children.

Malouf kept trying to stop the bleeding. Over the course of nearly three hours, she used seven methods. At one point, she applied so much pressure to a bandage that, Stephanie said, Gwen threw up. The remedies essentially treated the symptoms and not the cause, like putting a cover on a leaking faucet.

Malouf said she called her husband, who’s also a doctor, as well as a nurse at a local hospital, to see if she was missing something. They, too, were at a loss. The nurse’s only suggestions were the ones that Malouf had already tried.

Malouf decided to transfer Gwen to a small, local hospital, which at least had pediatric specialists and a neonatal intensive care unit. But while she waited for a call back to confirm the hospital would accept Gwen, Stephanie walked out of the room to tell her that Gwen had bled through the latest dressing. Malouf, according to the records, quickly checked to see how long it was taking her blood vessels to refill. It was slower than when she arrived.

Gwen’s condition was growing more dire, and Malouf had reached the limits of what she could do. What followed also wouldn’t be enough.

Stephanie had given birth to Gwen without complications in an inflatable tub in their living room. She was perfect, with doelike eyes and a full head of brown hair that, when the light hit it, hinted at the red of her father’s beard.

Her older brothers and sisters fussed over her like a birthday present. Her aunts from California and Louisiana came in to meet her. When the house quieted, Gwen fell asleep to the calming rhythm of Stephanie’s chest rising and falling.

Stephanie marveled at the way Gwen seemed to study the faces of everyone who carried her. She wasn’t two weeks yet, but the corners of her mouth constantly turned up to form what her parents insisted were smiles. Even when her siblings passed her around, she rarely cried in protest.

Stephanie and Eric met in 2010, when they both worked at Chili’s. Texas natives, they had just returned home after spending time in Florida, where Stephanie spent a semester interning at Walt Disney World Resort.

“I was doing lawn care work and maintenance on restaurants,” Eric said before Stephanie interjected. “He moved there for a girl,” she said as the two erupted in laughter.

He proposed to Stephanie on Christmas Eve. They married at a vineyard on Halloween. The venue capped off the night with fireworks.

Life moved quickly after that. They had a daughter and two sons, then adopted the daughter of a relative who was too young to care for the child herself. Just when they thought their family was complete, Stephanie got pregnant with Gwen.

Overjoyed, they decided to name her after Stephanie’s grandmother, Gwendolyn, who passed down her flowered baby blanket with “Gwen” embroidered in the corner.

There were no signs something could be wrong with Gwen until the day her parents took her to the ER. Stephanie had texted her midwife first.

“So sorry to bother you,” she typed into her phone, writing that Gwen’s belly button had been bleeding most of the day and they couldn’t get it to stop.

“How much blood is too much blood,” she asked.

The midwife told her to send a photo. Stephanie sent two, one of dried blood on Gwen’s stomach and the other of a pile of bloodied tissues. The midwife instructed Stephanie to tape some gauze over Gwen’s belly button. About 90 minutes later, just before going to bed, she checked on Gwen again. She snapped another picture, this one with bright red blood soaking through the gauze and diaper, and texted it to the midwife. “Are you sure this is fine?”

The midwife told her to go to the emergency room.

In many states, all emergency rooms are in hospitals, where patients can be transferred to other units for more care. Not so in Texas, where more than 200 ERs are freestanding, separate and distinct from a hospital. At the ER, Gwen grew increasingly pale. Her heart raced at 177 beats a minute. Around 1:40 a.m., Stephanie and Eric received their first piece of good news: Malouf was transferring Gwen. She had scrapped her plan to send Gwen to the local hospital and would instead transfer her to North Central Baptist, a larger hospital in nearby San Antonio with more specialists. North Central was only about half an hour away, and it was sending a NICU transport team to get Gwen.

Eric’s eyes fixated on the large clock hanging in the room. Ten minutes passed, then 20, then 30, then an hour. He couldn’t understand what was taking so long. He stepped into the hallway and asked if he could just drive Gwen to the hospital.

But, he said, Malouf told him he couldn’t because it would be too dangerous. Malouf, however, said she told him that if he did leave, he would have to sign paperwork acknowledging he was doing so against medical advice. The transport team, she told him, would have blood and IVs. Besides, she said, Gwen was stable. Malouf called to check on the status of the ambulance; she was told they were on their way.

Stephanie and Eric said that was the last time they spoke to Malouf that night.

By the time the ambulance arrived, it had been nearly two hours since Malouf had requested it. One of the team’s first questions was whether Gwen had received a vitamin K shot.

The ER nurse told them they didn’t have the shot on hand.

It was the first time since walking into the ER, Stephanie said, that anyone suggested that vitamin K may be the culprit — and the cure.

At 3:45 a.m., within minutes of the ambulance team’s arrival, they gave Gwen a vitamin K shot in her left thigh. They spent the next two hours at her bedside, hooking her up to an IV, drawing blood for lab tests and giving her antibiotics — all things that, the records show, hadn’t been done yet. Malouf didn’t respond to questions about why not.

Stephanie and Eric observed the ambulance team as they worked, bantering, discussing another call that had come in and, just as they were about to leave, waiting for one of them to go to the bathroom. Between what they viewed as the team’s laidback pace and Malouf’s reassurances that Gwen was stable, Stephanie and Eric were encouraged enough to split up. Eric went home to the kids, who had been with his mom all night, to get them ready for their first day of school. Stephanie stayed and planned to ride with Gwen in the ambulance.

“Grab me a change of clothes and coffee,” Stephanie called to him as he was leaving.

The team transferred Gwen to a temperature-controlled enclosed incubator. As they packed up to leave, Gwen began to whimper. With each breath, Stephanie said, she let out a weak, high-pitched sound. It was unnatural. Stephanie reached through the incubator’s opening and ran her hands back and forth across her daughter’s chest.

The team loaded Gwen onto the ambulance and flipped on the sirens and lights. At 5:55 a.m., they headed down Interstate 35. It had been seven hours since Gwen was first admitted to the ER.

Stephanie appreciated the importance of vitamin K. All of her other children got the vitamin K shot shortly after they were born. But over the years, she and her husband had grown wary of medical intervention. When their youngest son was nearly 2, they fell behind on his vaccines. After getting several vaccines at one appointment, they said, he developed a high fever and suddenly stopped talking for about a year. He was later diagnosed with autism.

“I think that they just gave him too much at once,” Eric said.

Research studies from numerous sources have found that multiple vaccines taken at once do not overwhelm or weaken a child’s immune system. They also do not increase the risk of serious or long-term adverse effects.

Still, seeing their son struggle to speak, Stephanie and Eric were convinced there was a connection. They stopped vaccinating their children after that.

Before Gwen’s birth, Stephanie’s midwife gave her a five-page handout on newborn vitamin K. It covered why babies need vitamin K to help their blood clot and cautioned that babies who don’t have enough of it can start to bleed without warning.

The handout compared the pros and cons of the vitamin K shot with oral vitamin K drops, noting that the drawbacks of the drops are that some babies may not be able to absorb them or may spit them up. They also don’t eliminate the risk of bleeding entirely. Stephanie initially signed the document agreeing to the shot, but as her due date neared, she and Eric changed their minds. If both are effective, they reasoned, why not go for the option that didn’t involve sticking their baby with a needle?

“We did our own research. I don’t remember feeling like there were red flags,” Stephanie said. “I felt like the information we had was sufficient.”

She doesn’t recall exactly what sources she consulted, but she read articles online and spoke to some people who worked in the medical field. No one, she said, warned her against the drops. But she didn’t ask her mother, Lauren Hoel, a longtime family nurse practitioner. Stephanie knew exactly what her mom would say.

Many medical experts consider the drops inferior for several reasons, including those mentioned in the handout. There are also concerns about harried parents of a newborn forgetting a dose and the fact that cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding have been reported even when drops are used.

Only limited data exists about vitamin K drops, and much of it is from Europe, where the drops are more common. In the U.S., the Food and Drug Administration does not provide oversight of the drops. Instead, parents can simply add them to their Amazon carts without any verification of what’s in them, or whether they’re safe or effective.

A single vitamin K shot acts quickly, and then the liver stores the rest of the vitamin K to slowly release into the baby’s system over months.

For decades, the recommendation from doctors, hospitals and medical organizations has been the shot. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the World Health Organization call for giving the shot to all newborns.

“While some countries outside of the U.S. sometimes administer vitamin K orally, it has not been approved by the Food and Drug Administration,” the American Academy of Pediatrics wrote in May , reiterating its longstanding position, “and it is less effective than an intramuscular injection.”

Stephanie and Eric’s choice to opt for the drops reflects a broader trend. Vaccine skepticism grew after the COVID-19 pandemic, and under the direction of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a fierce vaccine critic and champion of the Make America Healthy Again movement, the federal government has fed those doubts. Stephanie and Eric, who voted for President Donald Trump and are ardent supporters of both Kennedy and MAHA, welcomed the change.

In December, the CDC stopped recommending that all newborns get the hepatitis B vaccine. In January, the agency revised its childhood vaccination schedule, reducing the number of routinely recommended shots by six. A federal judge temporarily blocked that move in March, but the CDC’s decisions appear to have caused a ripple effect beyond vaccines.

After the January change to the vaccine schedule, an analysis of more than a million newborns found a rise in the rate of babies not receiving the vitamin K shot so sharp that it resembled a hockey stick. Between January and June of this year, the analysis found, the rate jumped from 5.2% to 8.1%. Despite being asked multiple times at a congressional hearing to assure parents that the vitamin K shot is safe, Kennedy responded by declaring that he has not said anything publicly about the shot. An HHS spokesperson did not answer ProPublica’s questions but said that the CDC recommends that parents give newborns the vitamin K shot within six hours of their birth to prevent vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

In the ambulance, Gwen’s blood pressure dropped.

“Infant looks much more lethargic,” the team wrote in their notes.

They placed a mask on Gwen to increase her oxygen and gave her an infusion of saline in hopes of improving her blood volume.

Gwen’s condition continued to deteriorate. Almost immediately after they arrived at the hospital, her heart stopped. Doctors inserted a breathing tube then began pressing down on her chest with two fingers to manually pump blood through her body. They pushed epinephrine into her IV to stimulate her heart. That appeared to work.

Stephanie couldn’t comprehend what was happening. All night, she said, no one had acted like Gwen’s life was in danger. Suddenly, her daughter was covered in tubes and doctors were performing CPR.

Stephanie said she heard someone yelling into a phone, “Where is the blood?”

She texted her family. “I need you to pray for Gwen like her life depends on it,” she wrote.

She called Eric. “You need to get here now,” she told him.

Eric pressed on the gas pedal of Stephanie’s Honda and sped to the hospital. There, he pushed through a clutch of doctors to find Stephanie crying in the corner of the room. The same wave of shock that had washed over his wife minutes earlier crashed over him. For the first time, he worried he might lose his daughter.

They prayed together, and the chaplain stopped by the room to check on them. He noted, according to records, that they were anxious but hopeful.

Less than two hours after she was admitted, Gwen crashed again. The medical team called a code blue. Doctors performed CPR for the next 34 minutes. They gave her epinephrine four more times. She had lost so much blood. Her heart was barely pumping. Doctors told Stephanie and Eric that they could keep trying to resuscitate Gwen or they could take her off the machines for her parents to hold her.

Stephanie sobbed. Eric collapsed at her knees. She told him she couldn’t make the call. Eric said they wanted to spend the final moments with their daughter. The doctors unhooked Gwen from the beeping machines and handed her to him. Stephanie and Eric told Gwen how much they loved her and how much they were going to miss her.

Shortly after 9 a.m., nearly 11 hours after they’d first brought her to the ER, Gwen took her last breath. The team ushered them to another room where families can mourn in private. They spent hours there. They gave Gwen a bath. Family stopped by. Stephanie’s sister picked up their kids from school so they could say goodbye to their baby sister. Two nurses came in to create molds of Gwen’s hands and feet.

When Eric and Stephanie finally left the hospital, Gwen’s car seat was empty. Their two youngest children slept in their bed that night. At one point, Stephanie jolted awake. She turned to Eric. The look in his eyes told her that it hadn’t been a dream. Without making a sound that could wake their kids, they cried themselves back to sleep.

Eric’s grief soon morphed into anger. His brother-in-law drove him to the Lonestar ER to ask for Gwen’s medical records. He didn’t trust himself to go in, so he asked his brother-in-law to retrieve them.

The file was just 15 pages with the payment and registration forms. They searched for any clue that could explain what happened to their daughter.

“I was constantly assured that it wasn’t that bad,” Eric said. “I can’t tell you how many times they said, ‘Don’t worry, babies are very resilient.’”

They planned Gwen’s funeral. When they couldn’t find a coffin small enough to fit her tiny 8-pound body, Eric’s brother, who makes custom cabinets, built one. They wrapped Gwen in the flowered baby blanket from Stephanie’s grandmother for the viewing.

Stephanie and Eric operated on parallel tracks those next several months: mourning their daughter and trying to understand what led to her death. The family attended a grief camp put on by a local hospice group. They painted a garden pole with things that reminded them of Gwen. When Thanksgiving approached, they escaped to Stephanie’s sister’s house in Colorado to avoid questions about how they were doing.

Eric got Gwen’s handprints tattooed on his chest, the last place he felt them before she died. Stephanie picked Gwen’s footprints, but the tattoo artist had to size them down to fit.

“She had such big feet,” Eric said. “She was gonna be a tall girl.”

“Or clown,” Stephanie said, half laughing, half crying. “One of the two.”

They also reached out to Byron Miller, a medical malpractice attorney, who sought records from Malouf, the ER, the ambulance company and the hospital. Miller investigated whether negligence in Gwen’s care resulted in her death. But the medical expert hired to review the case homed in on Stephanie and Eric’s decision to give Gwen the vitamin K drops instead of the shot. Without an expert’s supporting opinion, which Miller said was a state requirement, his office was unable to continue pursuing a case. Miller recommended that Stephanie and Eric follow up with the Texas Medical Board.

The ER, the ambulance company and the hospital did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The nurse on duty at Lonestar that night also did not respond to requests for comment.

Stephanie had several conversations with her mother, who remembers learning in the 1980s, while in nursing school, that all babies need a vitamin K shot at birth. Hoel didn’t know that Stephanie and Eric didn’t get the vitamin K shot for Gwen.

“It never occurred to me that people would refuse the vitamin K shot,” she said.

Even with that, Hoel couldn’t look past Malouf’s actions that night.

“She should have said, ‘That’s a newborn. Take it to a NICU,’” Hoel said. “And by not doing that, the fate was sealed.”

That next December, Stephanie sat down at the kitchen table and pulled out her laptop. Someone, she said, had to hold Malouf accountable. She found the website for the Texas Medical Board and followed the instructions to file a complaint.

“When Dr Malouf decided to provide medical care to our daughter, despite her lack of training in neonatal emergency care, and lack of appropriate monitoring equipment,” Stephanie wrote to the board, “Gwen was deprived of any potential life saving intervention.”

The seven hours they spent at the ER that night, she continued, could have been used to save Gwen’s life. And she stressed that the ER nurse said the facility didn’t carry the vitamin K injection.

“If Vitamin K was a vital part of the evening,” she wrote, “then we should have been pointed to another location that was fully equipped sooner.”

Malouf became the target of her anger and her anguish. She described how painful it was to drive by the Lonestar billboard with Malouf’s giant photo near her house every day. She wrote that Malouf failed to recognize that her daughter’s life was in danger. “I just don’t understand how it can go from a calm relaxed environment to all of a sudden your child is dead,” she wrote to the board. She recounted feeling intimidated when Eric asked if they could leave when Gwen’s color began to change and Malouf advised against it.

“To this date,” she wrote, “Dr Nicole Malouf does not even know that my daughter died under her care.”

After Gwen died, Malouf said, a doctor from the hospital called. The news, she said, came as a surprise.

Sitting in her home office, her framed degrees hanging on the wall behind her, Malouf spoke to ProPublica for nearly three hours about what happened. Malouf and her husband have three daughters, for whom she is team mom for cheerleading and president of the Fine Arts Boosters. Racks of uniforms filled her home’s entryway in preparation for an upcoming sale.

She said she repeatedly relived the details of that night with her therapist. The first few sessions, she said, were just the two of them crying. She said they discussed what was in her control and what wasn’t. Every life is precious, she said, but it’s one thing to lose a 95-year-old grandmother with a long list of medical problems. It’s another to lose a baby.

“I still have my three daughters,” Malouf said, pushing back her long, dark hair, “and now she has lost hers.”

Malouf said the doctor who called said the hospital would conduct its own review. Malouf said the doctor mentioned that they had already identified some issues, including questions about the transport team.

The hospital wasn’t the only one probing the night’s events. The state Medical Board also launched an investigation. The board subpoenaed records and reviewed the medical documents.

In September 2025, the board held a virtual hearing, which was closed to the public. Stephanie and Eric appeared, as did Malouf and her attorney. The board staff attorney charged that Malouf did not meet the standard of care in her treatment of Gwen and that she failed to halt or limit Gwen’s bleeding. Her lack of timely care, the board’s attorney alleged, ultimately resulted in Gwen’s death. Citing confidentiality, the board would not release a recording or transcript of the hearing.

The next month, the board issued its decision. It found that Malouf failed to recognize that Gwen had a life-threatening vitamin K-dependent bleeding disorder. The ER did not have vitamin K shots on site, and Malouf failed to immediately transfer Gwen to a regional pediatric referral hospital better equipped to handle Gwen’s condition. Finally, the board found that Malouf had failed to quantify the amount of blood lost by Gwen.

The board required her to take 24 hours of continuing medical education; she said she completed her hours in courses on pediatric advanced life support, communicating with patients and vitamin K deficiency bleeding. She also had to inform her employers that she had been disciplined. Malouf neither admitted nor denied the allegations but agreed to abide by the board’s final order.

A board spokesperson would not answer specific questions about Gwen’s case but said the board expects all licensees “to provide appropriate treatment and, if the necessary supplies are not available, to make arrangements for transport to a higher level of care.”

“I felt that I had done everything that I could with the resources I had,” Malouf told ProPublica.

She said she did know that Gwen had vitamin K deficiency bleeding, even though she did not immediately give Gwen a vitamin K shot. Malouf said she thinks the board didn’t believe that she knew because she didn’t act “in a panicked manner.” It remains unclear, even to her, whether the ER carried the vitamin K shot at the time or if it was just in a spot where the nurse couldn’t find it. But she said she asked the nurse for it.

Either way, she believed that giving Gwen vitamin K at that point would just be to make her chart look good.

“It’s really not even going to take effect at that stage,” Malouf said. “As soon as you give vitamin K, the earliest it’s even going to start working is 10 to 12 hours.”

But several doctors told ProPublica that vitamin K should be given immediately if there’s even a suspicion that a baby has vitamin K deficiency bleeding. It’s so vital to stopping the bleeding that they don’t even need to wait for a confirmation. There is no downside, they said, to giving it. Vitamin K, they said, may need to be followed up by blood or blood products, such as fresh frozen plasma, which is rich in the proteins that help the blood clot.

While vitamin K can quickly help to halt the bleeding, it can’t reverse the bleeding that’s already occurred. It also has to be given in time, and some babies need more than one dose of vitamin K to recover. Gwen, as one doctor who reviewed her medical records put it, needed vitamin K, blood and blood products much sooner than she got them.

Malouf said she had learned about vitamin K deficiency bleeding in medical school and during her residency, but she doesn’t recall ever seeing it in practice. Nearly every medical student learns about the coagulation cascade, but not all doctors know or remember how to diagnose and treat an infant who shows up in an ER bleeding, often in the brain and invisible to the eye. Some completed their training at a time when vitamin K deficiency bleeding was still considered a historic condition, much like measles.

The ER staff, Malouf said, has been subsequently trained on the importance of vitamin K, and the ER keeps it in stock. All ERs, she said, should carry vitamin K.

“I still gravely regret that the outcome was still the same,” she said, “even after again assuming that, ‘Hey, I’m putting this baby in y’all’s hands. You guys are the experts. Fix her.’”

Malouf doesn’t understand how the board found that her care that night fell short. She didn’t intentionally harm her patient.

“I can state my whole case and literally one of the board members goes, ‘Well, I just don’t believe you,’” Malouf recalled. “I said, ‘Well, then I don’t know what more to tell you.’”

In addition to working at the ER, she had a part-time job doing telehealth. The telehealth company that employed her, she said, fired her once she disclosed the board’s action. As of August, she was still working some shifts at Lonestar ER; the board’s decision didn’t affect her ability to practice. Following the interview with ProPublica, she declined further comment.

“I feel like the only way to change the outcome is to go back to the beginning, that fork in the road,” Malouf said. “And go, ‘OK, well let’s give vitamin K after birth.”

Stephanie and Eric also have asked themselves what they would have done differently. They wished they had left the ER that night and driven Gwen to a hospital.

“We were just trusting that the person who went to school their whole life for this would know more than us,” Eric said.

In their minds, the role of vitamin K has overshadowed the medical mistakes they believe are most responsible for their daughter’s death. By the time Gwen had arrived at the hospital, her organs were already starting to shut down. The autopsy found that she had tiny spots of bleeding in her kidneys and small intestine and a small scrape on her chest where doctors pushed down for CPR. The medical examiner noted Gwen’s precipitous decline and listed her cause of death as vitamin K deficiency bleeding.

If they could go back, both agreed they would get the vitamin K shot for Gwen.

“I don’t trust a lot of things,” Stephanie said, “but get peace of mind and get the vitamin K shot.”

A few months after Gwen’s death, Stephanie found out she was pregnant with a little girl. They were so ready to love a baby again. She gave birth to her in 2024. This summer, they welcomed another baby girl.

Both got vitamin K shots.

scraped.h1: Trump Orders Justice Department to Investigate Democrats Over Impeachment Threats
scraped.body_text:
President Trump says he has ordered the Justice Department to investigate Democrats who have threatened to impeach Attorney General Todd Blanche and other members of his administration.

Trump made the announcement Saturday afternoon in a post on Truth Social , days after Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate.

“The Democrats are going around threatening a lot of people, including the Attorney General of the United States,” Trump wrote, adding that they were also threatening others with impeachment and “many other forms of punishment.” He said Democrats admit they have “no reason to do so” and described the conduct as criminal.

Since Election Day, at least two House Democrats, Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia and Rep. Deborah Ross of North Carolina, have publicly said they would support impeaching Blanche, according to Fox News.

Trump also said Democrats have threatened Republican donors with prison, though he did not name any donors.

The president’s order sets up battle with the incoming Democratic majority, which has made clear it plans to use its new power to launch investigations and possibly impeachment proceedings against administration officials. Trump’s supporters see the talk of impeachment as political retaliation dressed up as oversight, and the president appears determined to push back before Democrats are even sworn in.

scraped.title: New Migrant Caravan Heads North After Democrats Win Midterms › American Greatness
scraped.description: Between 300 and 500 migrants crossed from Guatemala into Mexico on Friday, bound for the U.S. southern border.
scraped.h1: New Migrant Caravan Heads North After Democrats Win Midterms
scraped.body_text:
A new caravan of as many as 500 migrants has crossed into Mexico and is heading toward the U.S. border, just days after Democrats won control of the House, the Senate and the Texas governor’s office, Breitbart Texas reported.

Between 300 and 500 migrants, most of them from Central America, crossed the Rodolfo Robles International Bridge from Guatemala into Ciudad Hidalgo, Mexico, on Friday, according to reports out of Mexico. The group then began moving north toward the municipality of Suchiate.

Independent journalist Julio Rosas, who shared a report on the crossing from the Mexican newspaper Diario del Sur, linked the timing to the election. “With Dems winning the midterms, migrants will start making their way to the U.S.-Mexico border,” he wrote on X.

Oh look, exactly as I predicted after reporting on a different caravan before the midterms.

With Dems winning the midterms, migrants will start making their way to the U.S.-Mexico border and wait until Trump’s policies go away. Whether that happens after 2028 is up to American voters.

— Julio Rosas (@Julio_Rosas11) November 7, 2026

It is the second caravan in recent weeks. An earlier group left Mexico’s southern border in mid-October under the name “Caravana Sin Fronteras” before renaming itself “Fe y Esperanza #2,” or “Faith and Hope #2.” Rosas reported that members of that caravan said they hoped Democrats would win the midterms. Some were reportedly migrants who had already been deported from the United States.

Illegally reentering the country after deportation is a federal crime, punishable by fines and up to two years in prison for a first offense, or up to 20 years for those with an aggravated felony conviction.

The Department of Homeland Security responded bluntly to the earlier caravan. “There is absolutely ZERO chance this caravan will be allowed into the United States,” the department said.

scraped.title: Rubio Says U.S. in Talks to Establish Military Presence in Venezuela › American Greatness
scraped.description: The secretary of state says Washington wants a “presence agreement” allowing American troops to operate jointly with Venezuela less than a year after Maduro’s…
scraped.h1: Rubio Says U.S. in Talks to Establish Military Presence in Venezuela
scraped.body_text:
The United States is negotiating with Venezuela to establish an American military presence in the country, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.

In an interview with the New York Times , Rubio said the U.S. wants a “presence agreement” that would allow American troops to operate “jointly” with Venezuelan forces. There are currently no U.S. military bases in South America.

The talks come less than a year after the U.S. operation that led to the arrest of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and his wife at the start of the year. Under Maduro, Venezuela hosted military drills with Russia, China and Iran in 2022.

Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signaled the shift weeks ago. Asked by The Center Square in early October about bases in the region, he said the U.S. is expanding its footprint in Central and South America with partners. “We are at war with the drug cartels, with DTOs,” Hegseth said.

President Trump has also pointed to the economic benefits of the new relationship. “We’re taking a lot of oil, and we have a great relationship,” he told The Center Square, adding, “We’re going to start filling up our national strategic reserves with the Venezuelan oil for very little money.”

The administration has targeted narco-terrorists across the Caribbean and South America for more than a year, an approach some have nicknamed the “Donroe Doctrine,” a play on the Monroe Doctrine. Trump-backed candidates have also won elections across South America.

The Venezuela talks are part of a reshuffling of America’s military footprint. The U.S. has reached an agreement to build two bases in Greenland, confirmed a troop drawdown in Germany and floated moving more forces out of Italy and Spain.

Matthew Herper

Matthew Herper covers medical innovation — both its promise and its perils.

The next time someone tells you that artificial intelligence , or any other new technology, is going to cure every disease , point them to the effort to fight heart attacks and strokes, which together are the largest killer in the developed world.

Because again and again, pharmaceutical researchers have learned the same hard lesson: technologies that were supposed to speed new medicines to patients have fallen short. Two studies presented Saturday at the annual meeting of the American Heart Association are a perfect example. A new understanding of genetics was supposed to increase the odds of success – and did anything but.

One study showed that a Novartis drug, pelacarsen , had no effect on the rate of heart attacks and strokes despite lowering a substance in the blood called lp(a), which genetics said should reduce cardiovascular risk. Another large study, from Novo Nordisk, of an anti-inflammatory targeting a protein called IL-6 also showed no benefit .

articles.title: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow
articles.summary: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.
articles.ai_summary: Poland has entered a period of national mourning following a mass shooting in Krakow that left six dead and 15 injured.

scraped.title: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow | CBC News
scraped.description: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.
scraped.h1: Poland in mourning after deadly mass shooting in Krakow
scraped.body_text:
Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday, after authorities say a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into a busy central square in Krakow and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him.

The attack, which Poland’s defence minister described as an "act of terror," happened on Saturday in Main Square in the heart of Krakow’s Old Town. The area is a major tourist hub in the country’s second-largest city.

By evening, mourners had left candles in memory of the victims. The square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as authorities continued their investigation.

Krakow shooting leaves 6 dead, more than a dozen injured

Marie-Ange Collaer wrote on Facebook that she and her family survived the shooting during a trip to Krakow from Brussels.

"We literally ran for our lives and managed to hide from the bullets flying around," she wrote. "Lying on the floor in a shop like in a bad police movie whilst you hear bullets everywhere."

Collaer said her family was "quite in shock" after returning to their hotel but everyone was grateful to be alive.

"We saw a few that did not make it, true horror," she wrote.

Polish police say gunman kills 6 in 'act of terror'; 3 more dead found at suspect's home

St. Mary’s Trumpet Call, a traditional five-note melody played every hour from the highest tower of St. Mary’s Basilica on the Main Square, was paused overnight in tribute to the victims. It is the first time the call has been missed since the Second World War.

Four women and two men were killed in the Main Square shooting. Three of the women and one of the men were Polish, Krzysztof Jan Klęczar, the Malopolska regional governor, said on Sunday. A man from the U.K. and a woman from an unidentified foreign country were also among the dead.

The two police officers who stopped the attacker remain in hospital. One of them is still in a coma while the other woke up from a coma, Klęczar said. Officials launched an appeal for blood donations for the benefit of the most seriously wounded policeman.

Cordoned-off areas at Krakow's Main Market Square following Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

"If it weren’t for the efficient and selfless intervention of these two young men, the number of victims could have been significantly higher," Klęczar said.

Five non-Poles are among the wounded. They come from the U.K., Portugal, Russia, Germany and Austria.

The suspect is also in a critical state, having been operated on multiple times.

There was confusion on Saturday about the shooter’s age, with authorities first saying 24 and later 25. On Sunday they confirmed that he is 24.

The prosecutors said on Sunday they started an investigation for murder and attempted murder of numerous people, including police officers, with the act "constituting a terrorist offence."

Authorities say they also found three dead bodies at the man’s family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, a city about 150 kilometers northeast of Krakow. The police said on Sunday they were the bodies of the attacker’s sister, mother and father.

The family members likely died from gunshot wounds, the police said.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the attacker holds "very radical" and "ultranationalistic" views.

"Everything indicates that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies," Kierwiński said at a news conference.

Videos posted on social media by witnesses show people running away from the square to take cover on small streets nearby, as well as first responders trying to resuscitate victims. In one video, a police officer is seen repeatedly shooting the attacker, who is lying on the street, only to later slowly collapse to the ground himself.

People stand near candles and flowers left near the Main Market Square in tribute for victims after Saturday's mass shooting. (Jakub Porzycki/Reuters)

Klęczar said the attacker’s father owned over 10 guns legally and that the attacker also owned guns. Local officials in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski said they seized seven weapons from the family home, bringing the total number recovered to 11, including four found in the possession of the attacker in Krakow or in his car.

Around 411,000 people hold gun permits in Poland, which has a population of 37 million, and interest in gun ownership has been rising, particularly because of Russia's invasion of Ukraine and fear of instability in the region.

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland. However, in mid-October three attacks at schools in the central province of Mazovia took place within four days, leaving one person dead and many wounded, including children. The young attackers used knives or other sharp objects.

The Krakow attacker’s military gear, guns and overall look were similar to those of other "extreme-right lone actors" committing attacks around Europe, said Kacper Rekawek, a senior researcher at the International Center for Counterterrorism in The Hague.

" We have had attempts before, but now we can say that these kinds of attacks have become successful in Poland."

scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

We’re breaking down who’s playing who in the new Snoop Dogg biopic. Trust us, this list will give you plenty to talk about!

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Snoop Dogg at the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Festival held at T-Mobile Arena on September 19, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Christopher Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)

The forthcoming Snoop Dogg biopic is rounding out its cast. And now, we have a pretty full picture of which stars will help bring the film to life!

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

While the recent news of Cynthia Erivo’s casting may have been met with online disdain this week, some of the other casting choices may inspire a bit more confidence. We’re breaking down who’s playing who so you can get your mind right by the time the film hits screens in August 2027.

Daviss is taking on the lead role of Snoop Dogg in the film. His previous credits include “Outer Banks,” “Do Revenge,” and “Age of Summer.”

Related: Is Snoop Dogg About to Get His Very Own Biopic? For Shizzle, My Nizzle

London will portray Snoop’s mother, Beverly Tate, in the film. Her previous credits include “This Christmas,” “ATL,” and “You People.”

Erivo was cast as Afeni Shakur, mother of the late Tupac Shakur, in the film. Her previous credits include “Wicked,” “Harriet,” and “Widows.”

“Bel-Air” star Sholotan will portray rapper Kurupt in the film, one of Death Row Records’ first signees. His previous credits include “It’s A Sin” and “Run Hide Fight.”

Smith is taking on the role of rapper Warren G in the film. His previous credits include “The Gates,” “The New Edition Story,” and “Young. Wild. Free.”

Bullock will play rapper, producer and entrepreneur Dr. Dre in the film. His previous credits include “BMF,” “White Men Can’t Jump,” and “The Vince Staples Show.”

Booth was cast as rapper The Lady of Rage in the film. Her previous credits include “Rap Sh!t,” “Bad Girls Club: Chicago,” and “Discovering Brooklynn.”

Champagne will portray Snoop’s older cousin, the late Nate Dogg, in the film. His previous credits include “Seven Seconds,” “A Jazzman’s Blues,” and “Brown on Blue.”

Twain, legally Michael Archer Jr. (the son of the late D’Angelo and Angie Stone), is taking on the role of the late rapper The Notorious B.I.G. in the film. Archer, who lost his parents in 2025, will make his acting debut.

Hale plays Suge Knight in the film. His previous credits include “Nemesis,” “Platonic,” and “National Champions.”

Jones was cast as the late Tupac Shakur, one of Death Row Records’ biggest artists, in the film. His previous credits include “Panic,” “The Purge,” and “Shameless.”

Hayes will play Snoop’s wife, Shante Broadus, in the film. Her previous credits include “The Equalizer,” “The Angry Black Girl and Her Monster,” and “Raven’s Home.”

Miller is taking on a massive role – playing his own father, Percy Miller, a.k.a. Master P, in the film. This will mark his acting debut after playing basketball at LSU.

Rogers was cast as Snoop’s mentor, The D.O.C. in the film. His previous credits include “P-Valley,” “My Next Sweet Day,” and “Music and Murder.”

scraped.title: The Most Unforgettable Moments From HBCU Homecoming 2026 – The Root
scraped.h1: The Most Unforgettable Moments From HBCU Homecoming 2026
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From viral Greek strolls and celebrity appearances to historic milestones and unforgettable victories, HBCU homecoming culture delivered moments worth celebrating.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

JACKSON, MISSISSIPPI – OCTOBER 17: Jackson State Tigers fans cheer during the homecoming game against the Florida A&M Rattlers at Mississippi Veterans Memorial Stadium on October 17, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi. (Photo by Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images)

If 2026 proved anything, it’s that nobody does homecoming quite like an HBCU! From celebrity sightings and showstopping marching bands to Divine Nine pride, campus royalty and edge-of-your-seat football finishes, this season delivered plenty of headline-worthy moments. Many historically Black colleges and universities celebrated major milestones, while students and alumni created new memories across their campuses.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

We’ve rounded up the people, places and moments that made HBCU Homecoming 2026 one for the books. The culture was on full display, and the world was watching!

Love was in the air at NCCU! Beloved eagle mascots Eddie and Annie made it official, exchanging vows during the university’s iconic 10:40 Break on Oct. 6, according to HBCU Gameday. Complete with a wedding dress, a tuxedo, and a cheering eagle family, this was one unforgettable homecoming union!

The yard is always serving looks, but Homecoming certainly turned up the heat. From head-turning ensembles to effortlessly fly street style, Howard students and alumni transformed homecoming into a showcase of Black fashion, creativity and individuality. At Howard, the fashion is always the main event.

RELATED : We Found the Freshest Street Style From HBCU Homecoming 2026

Never count the Bulldogs out! Alabama A&M erased an early 14-point deficit against Grambling State before unleashing 44 unanswered points across the second and third quarters. The final score? A commanding 61-31 victory and a homecoming crowd that had plenty to celebrate!

Hampton University’s own Ebony Fire alumni brought the energy, elegance and unmistakable school pride, reminding everyone that the bonds built on campus don’t end at graduation. The years may pass, but the fire of HBCU sisterhood never fades.

One year away from a century of Tiger pride! Texas Southern marked its final homecoming before its centennial with “Mission 99,” celebrating 99 years of legacy, Greek life, royal court traditions and Maroon-and-Gray spirit. The countdown to 100 is officially on!

Grambling State’s World-Famed Tiger Marching Band celebrated 100 years of musical excellence, honoring generations of musicians who helped make its signature performances a cornerstone of HBCU culture.

Gospel icon Kirk Franklin joined North Carolina A&T’s 100th Greatest Homecoming on Earth (GHOE) celebration, bringing generations together through music, faith and the unmistakable spirit of Aggie pride.

We previously told you about Aleem “The Dream,” who is proving that he has talent, discipline and showmanship beyond his years. The 10-year-old drum major captured hearts at Virginia State University’s homecoming football game. He’s reminding HBCU band culture that the next generation is already leading the way!

Purple and gold energy filled the yard! Brothers of Omega Psi Phi Fraternity, Inc. showed up and showed out at North Carolina A&T’s 100th GHOE, turning Greek unity, signature stepping and fraternity pride into a homecoming moment to remember!

Brandy and Kirk Franklin received a special musical welcome from Alabama A&M’s Marching Maroon and White, proving that nothing says homecoming quite like a marching band salute!

HISTORY MADE ✨ Five generations of former Johnson C. Smith University queens came together for homecoming to celebrate the crowning of its 100th Miss Johnson C. Smith University! 🎥: @jcsustudentlife1867/IG pic.twitter.com/IdUr3WV7gt

Johnson C. Smith University celebrated its 100th Miss JCSU, honoring a milestone in campus history and the legacy of queens who have represented the university with grace, leadership and Golden Bull pride.

100 years of Aggie excellence, and the celebration was everything! North Carolina A&T marked the centennial of its legendary Greatest Homecoming on Earth with a milestone weekend honoring a century of tradition, culture, music and unforgettable Aggie pride.

The Morgan State Bears battled back from a 14-point deficit against Robert Morris, securing a dramatic 28–27 victory with a touchdown in the closing seconds. Baltimore had every reason to celebrate!

Members of Alpha Phi Alpha Fraternity, Inc. have been going viral this season while strolling to their take on “Wipe Me Down.” If you haven’t seen it, these men are bringing signature moves, infectious energy and Greek pride to SpelHouse. The moment was a reminder that HBCU culture always sets the tempo!

Top officials from Washington and Beijing held “frank” talks on their countries’ testy trade relationship on Friday, ahead of an Asia-Pacific summit in China this month where their leaders are due to meet.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer held a call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng and discussed economic and trade commitments over the last year, both sides said.

The Americans stressed “the importance of China fully and immediately implementing its commitments” and highlighted “concerns about recent Chinese actions”, according to a statement released by the US Treasury Department.

China’s He, meanwhile, expressed “serious concerns over recent economic and trade restrictive measures imposed by the United States”, according to a state media report shared online by Beijing’s commerce ministry on Saturday.

The report did not specify which measures He was referring to, but added that the talks were “frank, in-depth and constructive”.

Bessent “underscored that continued progress depends on concrete results and that the United States will closely assess China’s implementation of the arrangement”, said the Treasury.

The statement referenced China’s commitments from an October 2025 meeting between presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in Busan, South Korea, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit .

China is hosting this year’s APEC gathering from November 18 to 19 in Shenzhen, which could also see a trilateral meeting with Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Beijing’s foreign ministry said this week it was in contact with Washington and Moscow about the possibility.

The Busan agreement, which reflected calming tensions between the superpowers after they had exchanged tariff escalations earlier in 2025, required China to purchase US soybeans this year and through 2028.

China also agreed to suspend new export controls on rare earths and to issue general licences for exports of the materials.

The accord initially covered one year, but the two sides extended the ceasefire through to January 10, 2027, during Xi’s September visit to the White House.

Both sides agreed during Friday’s call to “properly manage differences” and promote a “stable” US-China trade relationship, according to the Chinese commerce ministry’s readout on Saturday.

In a separate statement, the ministry reiterated China’s “firm” opposition to new US sanctions targeting Cuba, which affected two Chinese companies.

The statement from an unnamed spokesperson added that Washington’s recent sanctions “escalation” against China ran counter to the consensus reached by Trump and Xi.

Trade experts have said one of the main sources of friction is over the level of Chinese rare-earth exports, which are crucial for the production of smartphones, automobiles and military equipment.

scraped.title: How the GOP Can Win Back Latinos
scraped.description: Voters in South Florida shared their frustrations with The American Conservative.
scraped.author: Juan Rojas
scraped.body_text:
Voters in South Florida shared their frustrations with The American Conservative .

It was Election Day in neoconservative South Florida. The torrential rains briefly subsided as I made my way to the local polling station in suburban Fort Lauderdale. A handwritten sign made the following plea to voters: “We didn’t fight terrorists abroad just to come home and watch DEMOCRATS elect them into office.”

The state’s younger generations, however, see matters differently. One 20-something Latino I spoke with described himself as a socialist and said that Republicans had nothing to offer young people. Conversely, a young mother of Peruvian heritage told me she typically voted for Republicans but felt Trump needed a wake-up call over broken promises.

In the end, Republicans avoided a bloodbath in Florida despite voters—and especially Latinos—swinging hard to the Democrats. The Republican gubernatorial and senatorial candidates Byron Donalds and Ashley Moody narrowly prevailed over Democratic challengers Angie Nixon—who was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)—and David Jolly. The Miami neocon trio of GOP Reps. Carlos Gimenez, Maria Elvira Salazar, and Mario Diaz-Balart also appear to have survived, though Salazar and Diaz-Balart’s races were still too close to call at the time of writing.

Elsewhere in the country, Latinos drove historic Democratic victories, including all statewide races in Texas. All told, the group swung 29 points away from Republicans after Trump’s performance in 2024. What lessons, then, should the GOP draw from this Latino backlash?

One thing to note is that there are important differences between Latinos of different backgrounds. Voters of South American and Cuban origin, for example, tend to lean neoconservative when it comes to foreign policy. And second- and third-generation Latinos are often indifferent to political developments south of the border.

In Florida, Moody won Cuban-Americans by seven points, mitigating losses among Hispanics. One Cuban-American millennial, a venue promoter in Wynwood, Miami, told me he split his vote, explaining that he couldn’t vote for Nixon due to her inability to call Cuba a dictatorship. And in the Cuban-American stronghold of Hialeah, the neoconservative faithful held firm in their support for the GOP. “We have to let Trump work”, said Marcos, a middle-aged mechanic, originally from Havana. The president “knows what he’s doing,” he added, referring to both the Iran War and the sanctions-induced crisis in Cuba.

Yet among Venezuelan-Americans in South Florida, MAGA neoconservativism has shown considerable cracks over a range of issues, including the administration’s policy towards Caracas. In the wake of the January kidnapping of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro, concern over Trump’s cozy relationship with the regime successor Delcy Rodríguez was largely confined to media and intellectual circles. Ten months later, many grassroots Venezuelan-Americans continue to give the president the benefit of the doubt. Some, however, have become frustrated with the prospect that the regime in Caracas may ultimately survive Trump’s term.

In suburban Fort Lauderdale, José—a 2024 Trump voter—told me he had been ecstatic following the Maduro raid but since then has soured on the administration. “Things are worse than ever, not just here but also for my relatives that are still in Venezuela,” he said. “They were supposed to arrest the Chavistas , not sign all these deals with them!” José added, referring to Venezuelans who subscribe to the socialist ideology of former President Hugo Chávez.

Then, of course, there’s the elephant in the room of the administration’s approach towards immigration enforcement. At a watch party close to the Trump National Doral hotel for a local Miami-Dade official, some invitees panicked at Florida Republicans’ tight margins on election night. “How could Miami vote for a socialist for senator?” said one Venezuelan-American realtor. “It’s the immigration issue,” another attendee responded. “They’ve gone too far with ICE. A lot of people are just staying home,” he added. Indeed, turnout in majority Hispanic precincts throughout the state fell to 44 percent even as overall turnout stood at 60 percent.

The remarkably accurate pollster Atlas-Intel found that 40 percent of Latinos listed “immigration policy, deportations, and ICE” as one of their top three electoral issues, putting it ahead of “combating corruption” and “economic policy and taxes.”

It’s not hard to see why Hispanics are deeply concerned about immigration enforcement. Around 60 people have died under ICE custody since Trump returned to office. Many of the voters I spoke with told stories of friends and family members—some of whom were U.S. citizens —who suffered abuse under ICE detention. Notably, Salazar has drawn ire from immigration hardliners for criticizing enforcement excesses and championing a pathway to citizenship for certain illegal immigrants.

Nonetheless, it’s foolish to presume that Democrats will dominate among Latinos for the foreseeable future, including when it comes to immigration. In a seeming paradox, Atlas-Intel also found that 45 percent of the demographic still favored mass deportation of illegal immigrants, compared to 40 percent who were opposed. The truth is that Latinos—much like the broader population—remain broadly against illegal immigration even as a slim majority also favor abolishing ICE.

Many of the Latino Trump voters I previously spoke with in 2024 expressed frustration over having migrated legally to the U.S. while millions of illegal immigrants and fraudulent asylum seekers “jumped the line” at the border under President Joe Biden. Progressives are profoundly mistaken if they think that they can avoid renewed border chaos by only deporting criminals, while also allowing anyone to claim persecution and solicit asylum inside the U.S.

If a future Democratic administration reopens the border, it’s quite likely voters—Latinos included—will swing back to the GOP in subsequent elections; as of this writing, voters continue to prefer Republicans by 13 points over Democrats on immigration. If Republicans are truly serious about delivering lasting results on the border while also avoiding endless backlash, there is a conservative but also populist path forward for the party.

In 2008, current Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, made a compelling case against an ICE police state, arguing it would be both less costly and more effective to punish employers of illegal labor under a rigorous, national regime of E-Verify . That program, which verifies the immigration status of employees, has been repeatedly sabotaged at the state and national level by carveouts and selective enforcement, due mainly to employer lobbying.

Much to his credit, Vice President J.D. Vance stated in his post-election autopsy that he was open to changing enforcement “by focusing more on businesses that hire illegal labor.” At present, worksite investigations and prosecutions of employers of illegal labor sit at or near record lows. Actually deterring illegal immigration by cracking down on employers ultimately depends on achieving sufficient scale and consistency of enforcement. In Canada, hiring illegal workers is nearly impossible due to a rigorously enforced equivalent of E-Verify.

In 2023, Gov. Ron DeSantis passed a law mandating that private firms subject employees to E-Verify. The mandate, however, features a carveout for companies with fewer than 25 employees and has been poorly enforced. And even that has been too much for some: The Wall Street Journal , for example, decried the piecemeal mandate in February, claiming that it was “ killing growth ” (the paper also expressed panic at Republican efforts to broaden the mandate).

Given sufficient political will, Kobach estimated his proposal could be implemented at a cost of around $600 million over five years, a trivial expense (compare this to the $85 billion currently devoted to ICE). Illegal immigration by economic migrants—as in Canada—would collapse, and large numbers of recent arrivals would self-deport for lack of employment options. It remains to be seen whether the Trump administration—or Democrats for that matter—will eventually embrace such a proposal.

Foreign policy will be another tricky issue for the administration with Latinos moving forward. So long as the Iran War continues to fuel higher prices at the pump and grocery store checkout, voters of all stripes are likely to deliver another gut punch to the GOP in 2028. Latino neoconservatives—in Miami or elsewhere—will probably continue to prefer Republicans, but some may opt to stay home if they perceive limited progress on regime change in Cuba or Venezuela before Trump leaves office.

There are, however, areas where Republicans will continue to reap dividends with Latinos in the long term. Hispanics are overwhelmingly Catholic or evangelical and generally conservative on issues like crime, family, and energy abundance. In addition to backing mass deportation, Latinos approved of federal recognition of two biological genders and increased fossil fuel production under Trump by margins of 10 and 20 points, respectively; they likewise back Republicans over Democrats on crime by nearly 12 points.

For the GOP, winning back Latinos who defected to the Democratic Party or who sat out this election will remain crucial for the foreseeable future. Republicans can start by embracing the vice president’s four-point plan for reestablishing trust with voters: 1) end the war; 2) focus on cost of living/inflation; 3) put America First; and 4) change our relationship to Israel.

Juan David Rojas is a columnist at UnHerd covering Latin America and the Iberian Peninsula.

scraped.title: The Midterms Prove Left-Populism Is Rising
scraped.description: To save the GOP, the Trump admin should end wars, purge corruption, and deliver wins for working people.
scraped.author: The American Conservative
scraped.body_text:
To save the GOP, the Trump admin should end wars, purge corruption, and deliver wins for working people.

The midterms were a bloodbath. Democrats took both chambers of the U.S. Congress and red-state governorships. The hardest part for Republicans to swallow is how familiar the winning pitch sounded: In 2016, Donald Trump addressed Americans’ concerns regarding the cost of living, Middle East wars, and government corruption. The painful truth is that this year, Democrats addressed those concerns better.

The exit polls tell an interesting story. When asked about their top issues, 39 percent of voters said the economy (46 percent for Republicans and 52 percent for Democrats), 33 percent said the state of democracy (20 percent for Republicans and 79 percent for Democrats), and only 14 percent said immigration (89 percent for Republicans and 10 percent for Democrats). Other questions reveal that the cost of living, the Iran War, and corruption were all critical factors in motivating voters to support the Democrats.

To be clear, President Donald Trump has done excellent work on immigration, anti-white discrimination, and censorship—arguably the three main issues for the online or “dissident right.” But by launching the Iran War, going overboard with tariffs (which much of the online right in principle supports), and allowing widespread corruption throughout the administration, Trump dropped the ball on issues everyday Americans care about. Not the wisest move.

Just look at Gina Hinojosa, a relative nobody who unseated the longtime Texas Governor Greg Abbot on Tuesday. Her campaign was defined by the conscious decision to set aside traditional liberal concerns over identity issues to embrace economic populism. “There is just no winning the culture war,” Hinojosa told the New Yorker . “My agenda is not a Democratic agenda. It’s a populist agenda.”

On the campaign trail, Hinojosa railed against billionaires, corporations, and AI data centers. She called for more school funding, a one-time $1,500 check to every Texas household, and better healthcare access. She framed the incumbent Abbot as a corrupt politician who sold out Texas to wealthy elites. Evidently, Texans loved what they heard, winning her 5.2 million votes (53 percent) to Abbot’s 4.5 million (46 percent).

The Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who easily brushed off Mike Collins’s attempt to unseat him, is another Democrat who embodies this rising tide of left-wing populism. Osoff has lambasted the Trump administration for failing to deliver for the working class. He has decried this administration as “a government of, by, and for the ultra-rich.” Like many elected Democrats, he hasn’t shied away from indulging some of the dumber populist tendencies by invoking “the Epstein class” to bash Trump and his friends.

Many believe Ossoff has a shot at securing the 2028 Democratic nomination. It’s anyone’s guess. But whoever does cinch the nomination will probably sound a lot like him. If midterms proved one thing, it’s that left-wing populism, like it or not, is popular.

The new populist formula appears to eschew some of the more radical economic policies favored by the likes of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. Those policies appeal to many working-class voters but can alienate white-collar professionals who don’t have to worry much about their own health insurance. But the populism of Hinojosa and Ossoff demands little sacrifice from the professional managerial class. After all, who could say no to lower prices, fewer wars, and less corruption?

That, sadly, was pretty close to Trump’s winning formula in 2016 and 2024. Of course, Trump hit on other issues like immigration and left-wing cultural insanity, which Democrats most certainly will not adopt. But they don’t need to. While mass immigration and race preferences remain unpopular, the midterms reveal that enough Americans are willing to support Democrats so long as they are promising to deliver on basic everyday concerns.

But will they deliver? It should be self-evident that the Democrats, once in power, will resume their real agenda: crushing their political enemies, discriminating against whites, censoring your conservative grandma on Facebook, and reopening the immigration spigot. Sure, they might implement some pro-working-class policies, but I doubt most Americans’ lives will dramatically improve.

The Democrats’ control of Congress will cause endless headaches and stymie Trump’s agenda for the next two years. Fortunately, their ability to fully enact vengeance and resume the destruction of our country will be limited at least until 2029, when a new president, possibly a Democrat, enters the White House. The Oversight Committee can issue subpoenas and haul people into televised hearings, but given that Trump’s personal lawyer is running the DOJ, criminal referrals will go nowhere—at least for now.

So although Trump has delivered on issues the online right cares about—not entirely, of course, but the wins are there—he neglected the median voter, who, however capricious and uninformed, must be placated. Any Republican running for office in 2028 will face an uphill battle, especially those who served in this administration.

What matters most now is that the remaining two years are spent delivering wins to Americans and repairing the shattered coalition: ramp up deportations and debank illegals (Dems rarely hit on immigration in their midterm ads for a reason); get us out of Iran; do whatever necessary to get costs down; publicly purge the administration of corrupt officials.

Failure to do so will doom Republicans in 2028. But that’s not all. Such a failure would solidify the GOP’s brand as the party of rich and corrupt old people with horrible Botox jobs who care more about waging distant wars than tending to the needs of their American compatriots. That was the legacy of the George W. Bush era, which in turn gave us Barack Obama. Should Trump fail, expect whatever comes after to be far worse.

Patrick Casey is a writer and editor based in Washington, D.C. He is also the host of the “Restoring Order” podcast.

scraped.title: Eating Ourselves Alive
scraped.description: I have only once been asked to be a witness in a libel trial in which the plaintiff denied that he was a cannibal, contrary to the allegation made in
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
The destructive urge goes beyond politics and even war.

I have only once been asked to be a witness in a libel trial in which the plaintiff denied that he was a cannibal, contrary to the allegation made in print by the defendant, but I suppose that that is infinitely more times than the great majority of people have ever been asked to be such a witness. (I should add that I was to be a witness for the defendant, though my knowledge of the plaintiff’s cannibalism was distinctly limited.)

The plaintiff was Charles Taylor, the president of Liberia at the time. He dropped the case against Stephen Ellis, the author of the brilliant and definitive book about the Liberian Civil War. Taylor did so, he said, because of the cost involved, though no one believed this, as he was by then a very rich man. He would have had to testify in London, and in a libel trial all manner of evidence is allowed; it would not have been too difficult to prove that he had no reputation to lose, which is to say, good reputation. What was hardly beyond dispute was that he had used drugged-up children to fight in his guerrilla army in his determination to become president.

Memories of Liberia returned to me when I read recently an article in the Spectator about Miatta Fahnbulleh, daughter of a Liberian refugee to Britain, Henry Boima Fahnbulleh. She is now secretary of energy security and net zero in the current British government, and as such, as her very title suggests, almost certainly destined to assist and be partly responsible for the further impoverishment of the country. According to the article , not yet and perhaps never to be the subject of an action for defamation, her father:

was indeed foreign minister in Liberia in the 1980s, and latterly a national security adviser to President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf. But he is also a Marxist radical who dedicated himself over a long career to the violent overthrow of those who got in his way.

Unsurprisingly, this took me back to the time during a short lull in the civil war back in 1991 when I visited Monrovia, the capital of Liberia. You could reach the city at that time only by sea, for it was besieged by Charles Taylor’s forces. I travelled on the Steel Trader under Captain Monty Jones, an estimable Welsh sea captain and entrepreneur who was almost solely (and heroically) responsible for the revictualling of the city under siege. He died, alas, in 2019, having been a staunch opponent of the pirates who operated in his West African theater of operations. I had the highest admiration for him and found an article about piracy in the area in which he was quoted:

“They [pirates] spray the wheelhouse with machine gun fire before trying to board. It is a normal military tactic: intimidate your enemy,” said sea captain Jones, who has been hijacked several times.

Many pirates are armed with handguns and long guns, he said, and are often high on drugs. ‘There is no way to reason with them.”

The pirates had evidently turned on, tuned in and dropped out, à la Timothy Leary.

The destruction of Monrovia was complete and very thorough. This destruction was not merely the consequence of war or bombardment. That could not have explained why the medical records of the Maternity Hospital had been used as lavatory paper, why the books of the library of the University of Liberia had been pulled from the shelves on to the ground and trampled upon, or why the castor wheels had been carefully sawn off every single piece of hospital furniture of the now deserted, dark, and echoing John F. Kennedy Hospital (where open-heart surgery had once been performed), all at a considerable expense of effort.

In the Centennial Hall, where national events such as the inauguration of presidents took place, the body of what was possibly the only Steinway grand piano in the country rested on the floor, its legs sawn off, surrounded by a necklace of human faeces. Again, this could hardly be interpreted as destruction wrought by war: There was surely something more to it than that. The destruction was symbolic, as iconoclasm always has been symbolic. Iconoclasm speaks to a hatred of whatever is destroyed, in this case a civilization felt to be both alien and probably superior, or at any rate that regarded itself as superior.

This was not what appalled me most, however. It was when I spoke to two young British journalists about what I had seen, recommending that they went to see it for themselves, that I was most shocked.

They could not see any symbolic significance in the destruction of the piano, or for that matter of the hospital. Why was I worried about a few, ultimately replaceable inanimate objects when a quarter of a million people, something like a 12th to an eighth of the population, had been slaughtered in the war? What was the destruction of a mere piano to that?

They could see no connection between the slaughter and the iconoclasm. This astounded and alarmed me. And I now see this obliviousness as a forerunner of what we now see in Europe, that is to say, a widespread iconoclasm masquerading as political purpose.

The love of or respect for civilization is not universal or automatic. Insofar as the achievements of civilization are not equally accessible to all, it is often, and by many, as much hated as it is loved. It confronts people with their own insignificance or nullity, and they seek to take their revenge upon it. Of course, giving vent to their hatred can easily be given a patina of political virtue, such as the desire for equality or social justice, and demagogues are gifted precisely at the provision of this patina to masses of humanity. There are few joys greater than destruction in the name of higher purpose. Man is a destroyer almost as much as he is a creator.

The Russian anarchist, Mikhail Bakunin, an opponent of Karl Marx, said that the destructive urge is also a creative urge. No: This is not the creative destruction of capitalism as described by Schumpeter. This is destruction for the joy of destruction of what is hated.

Theodore Dalrymple is a senior fellow at the Manhattan Institute and a contributing editor of City Journal . He is a retired physician who, most recently, practiced in a British inner-city hospital and prison.
