A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs. […]
scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Tribal Leaders Oppose Senate Permitting Bill Despite Changes in Substitute Amendment
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro says revisions to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 fail to address fundamental concerns about tribal sovereignty and consultation.

A bipartisan group of U.S. senators has released a substitute amendment to legislation intended to streamline federal permitting, lower energy costs and create jobs.

However, the proposed changes have done little to ease concerns among tribal leaders who say the legislation threatens tribal sovereignty and diminishes the role of Tribal Nations in federal decision-making.

U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), ranking member of the Senate Energy and Natural Resources (ENR) Committee; Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), ranking member of the Senate Environment and Public Works (EPW) Committee; Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), chairwoman of the EPW Committee; and Mike Lee (R-Utah), chairman of the ENR Committee, released the substitute amendment to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) on Saturday.

The amendment includes clarifying, conforming and technical changes intended to reflect feedback received since the legislation’s introduction in September. The legislation is designated S. 5653.

The bill’s amendment comes on the heels of a virtual press conference Friday, during which tribal leaders voiced their opposition to the passage of BAAJA.

Despite the revisions, National Congress of American Indians (NCAI) President Mark Macarro told Native News Online that the changes do not adequately address Tribal Nations’ concerns.

Your contribution is appreciated.

Macarro strongly criticized both the substance of the legislation and the process being used to advance it during the lame-duck session of Congress.

“First, the premise that Tribes, Tribal sovereignty, and Tribal decision-making are impediments to federal permitting is a fallacy. Tribal Nations, when at the table early in the planning and design process, are key to successful project outcomes.

“Any amendments to S. 5653 merely puts lipstick on a pig. This bill is rotten from the inside and there is no fixing the rot. Tribal sovereignty continues to be diminished in this bill.

“An amendment of this magnitude demands regular order, which would allow deliberation and meaningful consultation with Tribes. But the process of 5653 in this lame duck session is a rush job and insulting to sovereign Tribal Nations. They are selling out the Tribal Nations for green energy,” Macarro said in an email to Native News Online on Saturday.

Heinrich defended the revised legislation, saying the substitute amendment incorporates feedback from Tribal Nations and New Mexicans while addressing energy affordability.

“I’ve worked hard to incorporate the feedback we’ve heard from Tribes and New Mexicans into this Substitute Amendment, and I’m proud to join my colleagues in releasing it today. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help lower energy costs, strengthen Tribal consultation, and create more good-paying jobs,” Heinrich said.

He added that the legislation would require data centers to pay for the electricity they consume and the grid upgrades needed to support their operations, rather than shifting those expenses to households.

“It also makes sure data centers pay for the energy they use and the grid upgrades they cause, instead of passing those costs on to New Mexico families. Americans can’t afford to wait for lower electricity prices. We need to pass this bill now,” Heinrich said.

Whitehouse also emphasized the bipartisan effort behind the legislation and the feedback received from lawmakers, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves BAAJA and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Whitehouse said.

“Now’s it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs,” he added.

The disagreement highlights a fundamental divide over federal permitting reform: while the legislation’s supporters argue that changes are needed to accelerate energy development, lower costs and expand infrastructure, tribal leaders continue to question whether the proposed approach adequately protects Tribal Nations’ sovereign authority.

For Macarro and NCAI, the issue extends beyond technical changes to permitting requirements. It is about whether Tribal Nations will have a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their lands, resources and communities.

NCAI maintains that Tribal Nations must be engaged early in the planning and development of projects, with their sovereignty and decision-making authority respected throughout the federal permitting process.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

CHICAGO — High blood pressure has earned its reputation as the silent killer. If someone has diabetes or has had a stroke, the risk of serious cardiovascular events posed by hypertension climbs even higher.

Three studies presented Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions reported on recent attempts to lower blood pressure in people with these challenging medical histories, and how medical care should reach across specialties to treat them. One small but diverse trial tested a common diuretic after a stroke, another looked at intensifying treatment to reach lower-than-standard post-stroke blood pressure goals, and the third looked at going lower in people living with type 2 diabetes.

Advertisement

Each of the scientists leading the studies and the experts commenting on them at a media briefing emphasized the role of blood pressure. Adding a widely available drug earlier held promise for controlling blood pressure, but it was a split decision between the effects of lower numbers post-stroke and with diabetes.

“Blood pressure is defined in guidelines as the most important modifiable risk factor for recurrent stroke,” Jordana Cohen of the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania, said. “We know that blood pressure control after stroke is suboptimal.”

Her trial, called REDUCE, took advantage of the common, cheap diuretic spironolactone — sometimes called a water pill. It’s usually given to people late in treatment, after three other medications haven’t worked. But when spironolactone was given to people right after a stroke, they were more likely than those receiving usual post-stroke care to see their blood pressure drop three months later to less than 130/80 mm Hg.

Advertisement

Small changes are important, Cohen said about the trial, whose mission was to measure blood pressure reduction, not cardiovascular outcomes.. When blood pressure goes down by as little as 7 mm, that reduction has been associated with a 38% lower risk of recurrent stroke.

The trial was presented as an abstract and has not yet been published in a medical journal. In his comments, Bruce Ovbiagele of the UCSF Weill Institute for Neurosciences, said it’s well known that one-third of stroke patients don’t meet blood pressure guidelines, and said the study offers hope for a better approach.

“We also know that one year after a stroke has occurred, about one out of five stroke survivors have discontinued their antihypertensive medications,” he said. “This wonderful notion to try and use spironolactone is a great one because it’s a medication that’s cheap. It’s available and recognizable to so many clinicians.”

A much larger blood pressure trial in Brazil tested whether aiming for a top number of 120 mm or lower would be better than the currently recommended 140 mm.

“Almost all patients enter stroke-based antihypertensive therapy. But what we don’t know is how low should we go,” Gisele Sampaio of the Federal University of Sao Paulo in Brazil said about her OPTIMAL-STROKE study, published in the New England Journal of Medicine .

People who took medications to reach this lower systolic blood pressure goal were significantly less likely to die or have cardiovascular events within four years, compared to those who received standard treatment to lower levels below 140 mm Hg, the study found. The nonfatal events in the OPTIMAL-STROKE study included heart attack, stroke, and hospitalization for chest pain or heart failure.

Achieving these lower numbers will require medical supervision, including monitoring kidney function. There was no increase in the risk of end-stage renal disease, in the need for dialysis, or in deaths but some markers of renal function were off, Otavio Berwanger of Imperial College London and chair of the OPTIMAL study steering committee, said about the study. But there were changes in electrolyte levels consistent with using a diuretic or how much water people drink

Advertisement

The related OPTIMAL-DIABETES trial, also published in the New England Journal of Medicine , came to a different conclusion.

Karla Santo of Einstein Hospital Israelita in Sao Paulo reminded her audience that the ideal blood pressure target in patients with type 2 diabetes is still uncertain. Her study sought to evaluate the lower target of less than 120 in these patients.

Its findings were neutral: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, aiming at a systolic blood pressure of less than 120 mm Hg, rather than less than 140 mm Hg, did not reduce the occurrence of major cardiovascular events or deaths.

Shawna Nesbitt of UT Southwestern Medical Center pointed out differences between men and women and between younger and older patients in these two older trials and the newer OPTIMAL-DIABETES trial. She also wondered about longer follow-up.

“I think it very strongly suggests that this trial supports rather than rebukes what we already have seen in other trials treating hypertension more aggressively in patients with diabetes,” she said. “We might begin to think about blood pressure treatment in a more nuanced way. That is to say, perhaps we’ve been lumping patients together in a way that may not necessarily always be advantageous.”

One common challenge that may arise is how to apply these results in the U.S.

“Post-stroke care is very fragmented. Neurologists take care of patients in hospital. Then patients go into primary care,” Ovbiagele said. “So how does a nephrologist and neurologist and a primary care person manage the utilization of the medications?”

Cheryl Bushnell of Wake Forest University said doctors know what to do.

“It’s not the what, but it’s the how,” she said in her comments. “Managing blood pressure in stroke patients is incredibly difficult, I say as somebody who has to own that as a clinician. Is it the neurologist? Is it the nephrologist? Is it the primary care doctor?”

scraped.title: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
scraped.description: The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.
scraped.author: Sharon Lerner
scraped.h1: Trump Admin Giving $1M to Group Studying Crime Against White South Africans
scraped.body_text:
The new award comes after the administration cut human rights funding to nations in crisis.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

After slashing funding for programs that documented atrocities and protected human rights abroad, President Donald Trump’s State Department is now granting one of its first new human rights awards to a controversial South African organization that promotes the disputed notion that white farmers are a violently targeted, persecuted group, according to multiple sources knowledgeable about the funding.

The group expected to receive the nearly $1 million award, AfriForum, is a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of Afrikaners, a subset of South Africa’s white population. The organization says its members, who have a “ God-given calling ,” fight for Afrikaner interests and self-governance. The money will be used to “ document hateful rhetoric and violent acts ” against Afrikaners and other minority populations in the country.

The new award comes from a State Department bureau tasked with promoting democracy and human rights internationally. Until last year, those funds were mainly spent in poor and authoritarian nations — to fight corruption in the Democratic Republic of Congo, for example, or combat child exploitation and sexual abuse in Afghanistan. Since Trump returned to office, his appointees have transformed the bureau, gutting its staff, canceling programs and reorienting some of its funding toward conservative causes in Europe.

Samuel Samson, who was appointed as a deputy assistant secretary to the State Department bureau by Trump, has claimed the U.S. has a “civilizational” connection to Afrikaners, who descend primarily from Dutch migrants and predominantly speak Afrikaans. Samson, who has met with far-right leaders in Europe since joining the administration last year, has framed the U.S. government’s financial support for Afrikaners as grounded in “a common heritage, a common culture, a common way of life, shared history and ultimately a common anthropology.”

There’s a long shared political history between Afrikaner groups and white nationalists in the U.S., said Audie Klotz, a political science professor at Syracuse University who has studied those connections. But, she said, “There’s no heritage connection here. It’s pure scientific racism. In the history of U.S. immigration, there’s no direct connection between South Africa and the United States.”

AfriForum met with the Trump administration in February 2025 to plead for help. The group told officials that Afrikaners are subject to racial discrimination and murders that are more frequent and asked the administration to “act strongly against hate speech that incites violence” against them, according to a statement .

South Africa is plagued by high rates of violence, and some Afrikaners have been tortured and murdered. But independent researchers have found those killings represent a tiny fraction of murders across the country, whose victims are disproportionately people living in poor urban areas, where residents are predominantly Black. Official government statistics , and two formal inquiries into the matter, do not reveal a pattern of targeted violence against Afrikaners.

But Trump subscribes to the idea that white farmers face a “genocide” and has cited disproportionate violence against them as a reason for punishing Africa’s wealthiest nation. In February 2025, he issued an executive order that cut off hundreds of millions of dollars of aid to South Africa and welcomed Afrikaners to the U.S. as refugees. Since then, the administration has opened the doors to more than 16,000 white South Africans while halting virtually all other immigration. Officials recently told Congress they plan to invite as many as 17,500 Afrikaner refugees to the U.S. in 2027.

AfriForum did not respond to specific questions for this story but said that “our understanding is that the allocation has not yet been finalised. Should the allocation indeed be awarded to AfriForum, we will make a public announcement in this regard.”

The new award is the administration’s latest show of support for the Afrikaner cause. The white South African group governed the nation for decades under a brutal system of segregation known as apartheid, which kept the Black majority an impoverished underclass until the system was dismantled in 1994. Now, with Black South Africans governing the country, white people — of which Afrikaners are the majority — remain one of the wealthiest segments of the population.

The support has caused dismay among several former high-level diplomats, who spoke to ProPublica anonymously because they fear retribution from the administration.

Two former senior U.S. officials responsible for Africa policy said that they would never have met with AfriForum, let alone funded the group, because it was considered to be politically extreme and not credible. They described the organization as cherry-picking crime statistics to create a misleading narrative. “We would certainly not have funded what we would see as a racially incendiary initiative,” said one of the officials.

The decision to direct money toward the group comes after the Trump administration halted programs that advocated for the end of violence in African countries such as Sudan, where the Biden administration determined in 2025 that there was a genocide , calling it “the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe.”

“It’s offensive to provide funding solely to this one group after we’ve cut off funding in countries undergoing real documented crises,” said David Jandura, who managed the Africa portfolio for the State Department’s human rights bureau for several years and lost his job during the mass layoffs in 2025.

Congress has also raised questions about how the award was made. A Senate aide to Democrats told ProPublica that despite repeated requests to State Department officials, they had not received a briefing outlining the recipients of funds earmarked for democracy and human rights, which they described as “highly unusual.”

“The Trump Administration proceeded with funding fringe right-wing causes internationally despite objections from Congress,” said Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, a New Hampshire Democrat and ranking member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, who described the lack of transparency as “unacceptable.”

In response to a series of questions about the AfriForum funding, a senior State Department official wrote in an email that the department does not comment on funding deliberations and that they routinely keep Congress informed of their actions, consulting extensively on this year’s programming. “The Administration has been clear about its concern about the abhorrent race-based discrimination and violence in South Africa,” the unnamed official wrote. “Human rights protections do not depend on a person’s income or ethnicity.”

In July, ProPublica revealed that the State Department originally intended to give the $1 million research award to Lex Libertas, a small organization founded last year by a former AfriForum executive named Ernst Roets. Trump officials later expanded the potential awardees to a small pool of handpicked organizations. The plan drew outrage from Congress over the content of the award as well as plans to bypass the typical competitive bidding process. After ProPublica ’s reporting, the State Department released an open call for the funding opportunity , offering $986,500 to a nonprofit organization to “create a comprehensive record of violence affecting Afrikaner and other South African minority populations.” It’s this grant that is now being awarded to AfriForum.

Both AfriForum and Lex Libertas advocate for Afrikaner rights and have developed relationships with the Trump administration. Trump’s ambassador to South Africa, L. Brent Bozell III, visited AfriForum’s headquarters in September, praising the organization for its neighborhood watch programs while criticizing the South African government for not enacting policies requested by the Trump administration. AfriForum has also met with Trump officials in Washington, D.C. , drawing public criticism from South African President Cyril Ramaphosa. And in September, Roets met with administration officials.

AfriForum was founded 20 years ago and, with some 300,000 members, claims to be the biggest civil rights organization in South Africa. It says it aims to “establish self-dependence and growing self-governance” and provides some local civic services, such as garbage collection and systems for reporting pot holes and broken traffic lights . The group has said it distances itself from “white supremacist and extremist groups” and that it disagrees with Trump’s assertion that white South African farmers are experiencing a “white genocide.” But it has also said the South African government is “ targeting the continued existence of Afrikaners ” through racial legislation and the downplaying of farm murders, among other things. Academics and former U.S. diplomats have repudiated some of the ideas the group promotes as racist.

It unsuccessfully challenged a ban on the “gratuitous display” of the national flag flown during apartheid, which a South African court has found to be a form of hate speech. And while the group’s leader, Kallie Kriel, has said apartheid “ was wrong ,” he has also said it did not constitute “ a crime against humanity ” as the U.N. has determined , on the grounds that not enough people were killed during that time.

AfriForum has been focusing on farm attacks since at least 2009. In 2018, during Trump’s first presidency, Kriel and Roets, who was then his deputy, met with government officials in Washington, D.C., about the issue, and Roets spoke about it with Tucker Carlson on Fox News , as the chyron below him announced in all caps, “White farmers brutally murdered every week in SouthAfrica.”

Additional research on crimes against white South Africans is an unnecessary and confusing use of U.S. taxpayer dollars, said Carolyn Holmes, a professor at the University of Tennessee, Knoxville, who studies democracy in southern Africa. Holmes noted that AfriForum already produces annual reports on crimes against farming communities. “These data already exist,” she said. “You don’t need a new study. You don’t even need a far-right study, we have those.”

The U.S. support offers more than a financial boost to the organization. “For some time, AfriForum has been campaigning for recognition of their claim that white people face discrimination and persecution,” said Alex Dyzenhaus, a lecturer in international relations and African politics at the University of St. Andrews. “Before, they were only getting the Tucker Carlsons and the far right of the news ecosystem. Now they have the U.S. government on their side.”

The Trump administration has made the plight of white, rural South Africans a key foreign policy issue. In addition to the early executive order, Trump held a contentious meeting with Ramaphosa in the White House last year where Trump claimed white farmers were being executed. The administration has also considered an ad campaign focused on encouraging more Afrikaners to come to the U.S.

In September, Roets of Lex Libertas met with the White House to discuss what he sees as the crisis facing the Afrikaner community and, along with the New York Young Republican Club, placed 3,000 white crosses on the National Mall to commemorate South African farm murders.

Roets declined to answer specific questions from ProPublica but, in a text message, described the murders of several Afrikaners that he knew personally. He also wrote, “I see the suffering of black people in South Africa, I am deeply moved by it, and I spend every day of my life campaigning to make things better for us all.”

Appearing at a press conference for the Lex Libertas event, Samson, the State Department official, showcased the sharp shift the administration has made in U.S. relations with South Africa. While apartheid has been understood globally as a symbol of racist oppression, Samson described the current South African government as having discriminatory “race-based” policies and a cautionary tale for the rest of the world.

At the end of apartheid, in 1994, South Africa was a “flourishing, prosperous society,” Samson said. Since then, the country has gone to “ruin.” He blamed the fall on a “radical ideological leftist movement that wears human rights, that wears tolerance and inclusivity, as a skin suit to advance their Marxist communist worldview.”

Part of the Trump administration’s solution to this perceived crisis, he said, was to provide the research funding.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

Sharon Lerner covers health and the environment at ProPublica . Previously, as an investigative reporter at The Intercept , she focused on failures of the environmental regulatory process as well as biosafety and pandemic profiteering.

Anna Maria Barry-Jester is a reporter with ProPublica covering global health. She joined ProPublica in 2022 from KFF Health News , where she covered public health. Follow her on X: @annabarryjester .

scraped.title: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
scraped.description: Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.
scraped.author: Aallyah Wright
scraped.h1: Mississippi Ballot Monitors Say They’re Being Shut Out of Vote Counting
scraped.body_text:
Volunteers say they are navigating confusion and obstacles while trying to ensure a transparent counting process.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

This story was originally published by Capital B .

It took Natt Offiah an hour to realize he had arrived at the wrong location to monitor the provisional and absentee ballots in the Mississippi U.S. Senate race. He drove to Madison County Circuit Clerk’s Office on Wednesday, but the building was under construction.

After a phone call, Offiah, director of organizing for the People’s Advocacy Institute, and his colleague finally reached the temporary clerk’s office. They were redirected again, shared Offiah, still unable to locate officials.

At the next building, one woman said, “I haven’t seen them in an hour or so,” before directing the organizers down a hallway.

Offiah said he banged on the door, to no avail. The duo sat outside the room for 45 minutes before heading back to the front desk. A receptionist then told Offiah about two dozen staffers had left 15 minutes before his initial arrival.

No one could provide him any information on when they would return to continue counting votes.

“There is no standardized process for counting. Each county can pick and choose when they want to start counting. So, we’re running into this runaround issue,” Offiah said.

His experience mirrors the dozens of other volunteers who say they didn’t sign up for chaos and confusion, but to protect the democratic process. Some — who reported their concerns in group chats shared with Capital B — say they’ve been denied a seat to observe the process, while others struggle to find information.

With the nation’s close eye on Mississippi, advocates say it’s even more critical to ensure election officials “do the right thing.” Voters have been on edge since Election Day, waiting to see who will become the state’s next U.S. senator.

Despite no early voting or online registration, turnout and absentee ballots have surged. As of Nov. 6, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith by over 2,500 votes.

Yet, there are still thousands of mail-in and affidavit ballots outstanding .

Issues like voter ID laws and inoperable machines have fueled delays, said Lydia Grizzell, policy and advocacy manager of ACLU of Mississippi.

“It is appalling the number of issues that we’ve seen and we had on Election Day, and now we’re seeing the extension of that post-Election Day in a way that is not great,” she said.

The Mississippi secretary of state’s office did not address the monitors’ allegations of being shut out of the vote counting process, but told Capital B the public is entitled to be present for the counting of ballots, the process where election commissioners announce which affidavit ballots are accepted or rejected, according to state statute. This does not include the preliminary work commissioners do to determine a voter’s eligibility.

There is no uniform process on how officials conduct affidavit ballot counting. In some counties, where ACLU dispatched attorneys, election officials had a closed door process, Grizell added.

“The best thing that we can do is have people watching, witnessing, and doing their best to gather as much information as possible as to what is happening,” she said.

Volunteers across the state are being deployed in a widespread effort prompted by several grassroots organizations. The NAACP has also deployed national legal, policy, and field staff to the state to make sure every vote is counted.

Both candidates sent their own groups to monitor the process and assembled a group of lawyers who are prepared to take legal action if necessary. Lawyers for Hyde-Smith sent a letter to election commissioners requesting “immediate separation, secure custody and preservation of all affidavit ballots.” Following Hyde-Smith’s legal team’s response, Colom’s legal counsel sent a letter to all 82 counties, calling the GOP senator’s demand unlawful.

Ahead of the election, thousands of Mississippians were moved to inactive status because the secretary of state’s office paid $50,000 to use unverified data from credit bureau Experian to clean out voter rolls. Secretary of State Michael Watson told Mississippi Today that the rollout of the commercial data was “wildly successful.”

This unprecedented number of inactive voters led to more affidavit ballots, prolonging the count, Tarekegn said. These ballots must be “cured”, meaning to correct issues with voter identification or mail-in ballots, by Nov. 10.

Organizers also pointed out that Mississippi’s outdated voting system exacerbated the counting issues. With no early voting, most ballots come in on Election Day. This overwhelms the system. Still, Tarekegn praised Mississippians for the high turnout.

“Mississippi is one of the hardest, if not the hardest, state to vote in,” she said. “We’re truly talking about probably more than 90% of the people having to show up on Election Day between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. to cast their vote.”

On Election Day, Rachel Madden was the 20th person in line at her precinct in DeSoto County. After an hour’s wait, she was told she had been made inactive and needed to vote by affidavit.

“She just told me that my name wasn’t in the system, and I was like, ‘Well, that doesn’t make any sense,’” Madden said.

She hadn’t changed her address, so she was confused why she had been flagged as inactive. The poll worker assured her, “It’s not a big deal, you’re like the second person this has happened to,” she said.

She said she was instructed by the poll worker to go to the courthouse to “cure” her ballot after being given a form. She made the 25-minute drive to the courthouse, where the employee informed her she had been inactive since May by District 1 Election Commissioner Laura Edler because of Madden’s supposed move to nearby Memphis, Tennessee.

Madden says she never moved anywhere. Her address was corrected in the system and she received a new voter card.

She recalls she then called to ensure her ballot was accepted. She said that an employee told her they would not be taking any more calls about affidavit ballots for the next 10 days, which would put Madden outside the deadline of ballot curing.

“I was like, in 10 days, it’s not gonna matter,” Madden said. “Even in person that day, they were not helpful. If I had not insisted, I don’t think they would have done it. I just don’t think that’s fair or right.”

Edler did not speak to any individual’s standing, but told Capital B that when the commission receives a change of address from the secretary of state’s office, then the voter will be notified and must rectify the issue or remain inactive.

Ballot monitors say it’s also been difficult to do their jobs.

In DeSoto County, Kelly Jacobs, a local organizer, said District 4 Election Commissioner Sissie Ferguson prevented her from watching as election officials presorted ballots and checked names.

The day after the election, Jacobs said she stopped by the election’s commissioner office, but learned they had changed locations. She then traveled to the police department, which directed her to the new location.

After being barred from entry, Jacobs called an attorney, who affirmed her rights, but officials continued to block her from observing, she said, which she captured on video. Commenters on the video state that they were allowed access to observe vote counting in other counties.

On Nov. 5, around noon, the public was able to monitor the process, but by then, the process had already started, she said. Jacobs is not confident officials will follow the law.

“Why did I have to go and complain? If not for my complaint, they would still be all locked up [in the room],” she said. “There’s five election commissioners. Why would none of them know the open meetings law?”

Ferguson did not respond to Capital B ’s request for comment. However, commissioner Edler said no one has been denied access. As of the afternoon of Nov. 6, she said there’s “a room full of people” who were actively watching the process.

In Lee County, about 100 miles away, a monitor reported that an official told them a count wouldn’t happen until “later this week or early next week,” according to a group chat shared with Capital B . Another volunteer was told it would occur on “Thursday morning” with no additional details.

Offiah, although still battling frustration and confusion, said he is looking forward to continuing the good work with the community.

“As a lifelong Mississippian, I am used to us living in a legacy of constantly fighting back, and this is just in alignment with our legacy,” he said. “And people ask folks from Mississippi, why do we live down here? Why do we stay out here with everything that we’re facing?”

He added: “But we’re fighters, and we won’t ever stop fighting.”

scraped.title: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
scraped.description: The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.
scraped.author: Jon Queally
scraped.h1: Flooding in Gaza Destroys 70,000 Tents as Israel Continues to Block Aid
scraped.body_text:
The Palestinian Health Minister warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions” in Gaza.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation .

The suffering of the people of Gaza went from horrific and beyond comprehension to something worse on Saturday after storm waters overnight destroyed tens of thousands of tents and flooded tens of thousands of people into further desperation, all while the US and Israeli governments continue to maintain a cruel blockade on life-saving supplies despite a fast-approaching winter and a military occupation with no end in sight.

“At least 70,000 tents have been flooded & blown away by the torrential downpour and tempestuous wind in Gaza since last night,” reported Palestinian journalist Abubaker Abed, citing statements from health and media officials. “Families are shelterless. Food prices are soaring. Children are starving and shivering with cold. Caravans and mobile homes must enter Gaza now to avert this cataclysm.”

Gaza’s Government Media Office on Saturday, holding Israel wholly responsible for the disaster, said initial losses from flooded and destroyed tents were estimated at $3 million and that dozens of walls of homes had collapsed, resulting in injuries, while the threat of broader building collapse remained a serious risk.

In a statement, Palestinian Health Minister Dr. Majed Abu Ramadan said, “What is happening in Gaza is not a passing winter crisis. I urgently call on the international community, the United Nations , and health, humanitarian, and relief organizations to intervene immediately to save the lives of hundreds of thousands of displaced people in the Gaza Strip, following the flooding of thousands of tents with rainwater and the absence of basic safe shelter conditions.”

Al Jazeera reports :

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

Ramadan further warned of “a catastrophic deterioration in health and environmental conditions, alongside growing risks of the spread of diseases and epidemics” if an emergency response was not rapidly and comprehensively deployed.

This is the worst morning ever. No one in Gaza City slept last night. The rain completely flooded the tents, soaking mattresses and destroying families' belongings. We are underwater. Thousands of families have been trying for hours to save what little they have left, with…

Video footage and eye witness accounts offered a heartbreaking picture of the suffering by those hit by the floods.

“We woke up and found ourselves surrounded by water ,” a man named Mansour al-Sakni, 33, told the Middle East Eye . “The children were crying. I did not know what to do, and I started crying too.”

“We stood inside the tarpaulin shelter waiting for the rain to stop so we could try to push the water out of the room,” he said. “We are poor people in Gaza. We want to live. We do not want to die from the bombing or the cold. Enough. Have mercy on us.”

According to NBC News :

The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added.

At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents.

Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent.

“This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman.

“Two weeks ago when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.”

While the flooding devastated the people and families trapped by the blockade of life-saving aid and shelter, fresh ire was pointed at the US government for refusing to rebuke the Israeli government for its wanton disregard for human life and suffering.

On the ground in Gaza, the anguish of Palestinians, including children, was on display in videos of the devastation and ongoing catastrophe posted to social media :

🚨 CATASTROPHIC SCENES IN GAZA RIGHT NOW. Heavy rainfall is flooding displaced Palestinians’ tents, leaving families exposed to the harsh winter with no alternative shelter. This is their fourth winter since Israel destroyed their homes and continues to block essential… pic.twitter.com/NI7DRgCSMs

“How long are we supposed to live like this?” declares the young boy featured in the video. “I swear I don’t know what to do. Have mercy on us for God’s sake! For the sake of God, have mercy on us!”

Rain is worsening the suffering of Gaza’s children as water pours into homes damaged by Israeli bombardment, soaking bedding and clothes. With no shelter repair materials or tarpaulins available, families are left unable to protect their children from the flooding. pic.twitter.com/OzVMGHzssI

Children are particularly impacted by the rain water and vulnerable to the increasingly dangerous conditions imposed by the floods.

The image of a little girl in Gaza standing in the rain captures a stark, painful contrast: the innocence of childhood set against the harsh reality of life in Gaza. 🍉 The winter rain has transformed the scene into a tableau that blends spontaneous, childlike joy with profound… pic.twitter.com/YkTRt4RWJW

“What remains of Gaza’s homes is collapsing under heavy rain, amid the ongoing genocide and deafening silence,” said Ramy Abdul, chairman of the human rights groups Euro-Med Monitor.

“For the fourth consecutive year,” Abdul added, “Gaza remains under a suffocating Israeli siege that prevents even the recovery of victims’ bodies from beneath the rubble.”

scraped.body_text:

This story was originally published by Source New Mexico.

Matt Mondschein Source New Mexico

New Mexico’s public education system saw a steep decrease in Native language and culture teachers over the past year, according to data presented to state lawmakers on Friday, Oct. 30.

The state’s certification program for Native American language and culture allows experts in those fields to teach in New Mexico public and charter schools without a college degree and, if full-time, earn the annual salary of a Level 1 teacher at $55,000.

Teachers certified in the 520 Native American Language and Culture Certification program play a role in the New Mexico Public Education Department’s action plan to address the landmark Yazzie/Martinez education equity lawsuit by expanding Native language education and increasing the number of students who graduate with proficiency in English and another language , including Native languages.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

KatieAnn Juanico, assistant secretary for PED’s Indian Education division, highlighted the importance of Native-certified teachers to the interim Indian Affairs Committee, saying: “I was raised on the reservation — without our language, we lose a sense of self, a sense of respect.”

But recent PED data she presented shows a decline in the overall number of 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools statewide. In July 2025, PED reported 234 Native language and culture teachers in public and charter schools, new PED data shows there are now 147— a 37 percent decline in just over a year.

Juanico explained that based on feedback she’s received, many 520-certified teachers struggle with the requirements once they enter a public or charter classroom, particularly with classroom loads and developing lesson plans.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

The 520-certified Native teachers realize, according to Juanico, “‘Whoa, what did I sign up for?’ with all these students that I have to watch, manage and build lesson plans for.” She added that, “Oftentimes, our 520 teachers, our tribal community members, don’t come to the classroom knowing all those things.”

Juanico added that PED only tracks 520-certified teachers in public and charter schools and the decrease may also be due to Native teachers with the 520 certification returning to a tribal school after teaching at a public or charter school. Collecting that data “is an opportunity to understand why those teachers are leaving the district and charter schools,” Juanico said.

To support 520-certified Native teachers, Juanico said the Indian Education Division wants to develop classes for Tribes, Pueblos and Nations to boost Native-teacher success after receiving the 520 certificate, and to work with districts and charter schools to recruit and hire more certificate holders.

State Rep. Patricia Royal Caballero (D-Albuquerque) highlighted the need for the PED Indian Education Division to collect more information on 520-certified teachers and how they’re addressing gaps articulated in the Yazzie/Martinez case.

“It is important to have that information because we should be modeling and showcasing our tribes as leading the charge in this,” Roybal Caballero said.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a governing coalition following elections on Oct. 27.

Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leading a bloc of parties seeking to oust Israel’s longest-serving premier.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu won a clear majority in the vote. But in marathon discussions with the president this week, representatives from most of Israel’s main parties recommended Eisenkot be tasked with assembling a new government.

The announcement, which had been expected on Sunday, came shortly after Netanyahu called for a “national unity government” in a video statement and warned against “hastily swearing in a government with terrorist supporters” – an apparent reference to the Arab-led parties.

Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly portrayed the Arab-led parties as a threat to national security, while Eisenkot has indicated a willingness to partner with them under certain conditions, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Eisenkot’s party, Yashar, slammed the prime minister’s video with a statement posted on X and urged members of his party, Likud, to disavow their alliance with “radical parties,” in an apparent reference to the more extreme parties in his religious-nationalist base.

The statement argued that Eisenkot would only include parties and parliament members who support its principles, including recognizing Hamas as a terrorist organization. ___ Associated Press writer Julia Frankel contributed from Jerusalem.

scraped.body_text:
The Navajo Nation isn’t alone. The Seneca Nation of Indians also elected its first woman president this week.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This story was originally published by The 19th .

Crystalyne Curley is set to become the first woman president of the Navajo Nation, the largest reservation by land mass in the country.

Curley, who also held the distinction of being the first woman to serve as the Nation’s council speaker — the head of its legislative branch —when she was voted by council members to fill that role in 2023, has worked on issues related to water rights, uranium contamination and voter rights.

In another first for tribal governments, the Seneca Nation of Indians in New York also elected its first woman president, Tina Abrams. She previously served two terms on the Nation’s council.

While Native women made history for their tribes in this election, it is not uncommon for women to hold top positions in tribal nations. Activist Wilma Mankiller was appointed as principal chief of the Cherokee Nation in 1985, the largest tribe in the country by tribal enrollment numbers. Though there is no official data on women’s representation in tribal governments, the nonprofit RepresentWomen found that in 2020 at least 78 tribal nations had reached or exceeded gender parity in their legislatures.

Curley’s campaign website lays out her vision as president, including prioritizing behavioral health services, affordable housing programs, workforce development and protecting Diné culture and sovereignty, among other initiatives.

Leading up to the election, Curley told Indian Country Today , a nonprofit news outlet, that she brings her perspective as a mom to the position. “I want to make sure that our children have a safe future, a safe home where they feel they’re proud of who they are,” she said.

By Navajo Nation election law, the results are considered unofficial for ten days after November 3rd. With an 1115 vote count difference between them, Curley’s opponent Justin Jones has not conceded and says he’ll launch a legal challenge over the results, according to the Navajo-Hopi Observer.

The Nation, which has the second largest number of enrolled tribal members nationwide, spans northeastern Arizona and parts of New Mexico and Utah.

scraped.h1: The midterms were fantasy politics for Democrats. What now for Trump?
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Long Read

Topic: US Elections

( ABC News: Lindsay Dunbar )

The Trump political juggernaut has hit a wall. But while Democrats are celebrating, the battle for America's political future is only just beginning.

In the year America celebrated its 250th birthday, voters delivered a once-in-a-century election result signalling a break from a president who has dominated US politics for the past 10 years.

Donald Trump, to mark both the US semi-quincentennial and his own 80th birthday in June, put on a cage fight on the South Lawn of the White House. At these midterm elections, he was repeatedly body-slammed by voters. This was a very personal repudiation of a pharaoh-like figure who had tried, implausibly, to convince Americans they were enjoying a "golden age".

It represented the rebuke of a leader with authoritarian leanings who has sought to turn the White House into something akin to a palace, and Washington into a monument to himself.

Needless to say, exit polls showed voters were angry about the spike in fuel, food and, in rural states, fertiliser prices caused by a trade war that Trump framed as a "Liberation Day". The conflict with Iran had turned every gas station in America into a billboard for the Democrats. But alleged government corruption was also prominent in voters' minds, even higher in some exit polls than cost-of-living concerns.

Ahead of the election, a poll by Fox News showed alleged government corruption was actually the number one issue.

The billionaire president and his family have been getting ostentatiously richer while many Americans are suffering personal recessions.

Hard-pressed voters eyed decadence in the gold-bedecked walls of the Oval Office when their own quality of life was deteriorating. When Trump flew into the heartland to campaign, he did so aboard a $400 million Boeing 747-8 luxury airliner gifted by the Qatari royal family.

This wasn't simply an "it's the economy, stupid" election. It was also about the self-enrichment of Trump, his family members and acolytes such as Elon Musk, the world's first trillionaire. American voters were rejecting the excesses of an increasingly imperial presidency. Ending his campaign in front of the renovated Reflecting Pool in Washington seemed to many voters the perfect expression of his narcissism and tone-deafness.

More so than winning this election through the attractiveness of their policies, Democrats became the beneficiaries of the anti-Trump backlash. And theirs was a landslide win. The stuff of fantasy politics.

In regaining control of the US Senate, they took deep red Republican bastions: Texas, Kansas, even South Carolina.

In the House of Representatives, Democrats will enjoy at least a 50-seat advantage. It is the kind of lopsided congressional majority not seen since Barack Obama's victory in 2008 which took a couple of successive waves to achieve. The cumulative vote in all the House seats, which gives the national picture, showed the Democrats had close to a 13-point lead over the Republicans.

To put that in historical perspective, in the famed " Republican revolution" of 1994 the GOP beat the Democrats by 6.8 points.

For the first time in 16 years, the Democrats will control a majority of governorships. These include noteworthy racial firsts. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman ever elected governor of an American state. Texas will now have a Latina governor, Gina Hinojosa. Disquiet and fear amongst Hispanic voters over ICE raids helped her triumph.

Not only the landscape but the face of US politics changed. For the first time in the country's history, the House of Representatives will have a Black speaker, New York congressman Hakeem Jeffries.

Small wonder, the term "bluenami" is being used. But it is also a red meltdown.

This is the first time in the Trump era his Republican Party has been severely punished. This result recalls the post-Watergate midterms in 1974 when Republicans were punished for the transgressions of Richard Nixon. Nixon had been forced to resign the presidency less than three months before Election Day.

That 1974 election brought about a generational shift. The Class of '74 included the so-called "Watergate babies". Remarkably, 87 members of the new Congress were aged under 40.

This election hasn't produced quite such an infusion of young blood. Still, at a time when Capitol Hill has often looked like a gerontocracy, the average age of lawmakers will be significantly lower. James Talarico, the Presbyterian seminarian with choir boy looks who won in Texas, is 37. Incumbent Democrat Jon Ossoff, who comfortably regained his seat in the Republican target state of Georgia, is 39. Abdul El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim US Senator, is 42. Annie Andrews, who took South Carolina, is 46. Melat Kiros, who was endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America in Colorado's first district, became the first Gen Z woman elected to Congress. She is just 29 years old.

What this election does not necessarily signify is a long-lasting political shift, or permanent realignment.

While the Republican Revolution of 1994 seemed to herald a period of conservative domination, just two years later Democrat Bill Clinton won his second term as president.

The 1974 midterm elections foretold that Republicans were set for a prolonged spell in the political wilderness. Yet Ronald Reagan won the presidency in 1980, and Republicans dominated the presidency for the next 12 years.

Democrats, understandably, are joyous about the outcome of the 2026 midterms. Yet their celebrations should come with circumspection.

A poll conducted in the run-up to this election suggested 52 per cent of voters had an unfavourable view of the Democratic Party; only 29 per cent had a favourable view. For months beforehand, the Real Clear Politicspolling average showed the American public looked on the Democrats only marginally more favourably than the Republicans.

Nevertheless, this is a mighty political achievement, which raises an important question: has the curtain come down on the age of Donald Trump?

As always, it is dangerous to write off or underestimate Donald Trump.

Just seven weeks after the storming of the US Capitol on January 6, 2021 as Congress met to certify the 2020 presidential election results, I watched as Trump was greeted like a conquering hero at a conservative conference in Orlando, Florida. The event had the feel of a cargo cult.

Likewise, after Trump-backed Republican candidates failed to make expected breakthroughs in the 2022 congressional midterms, pundits composed obituaries for the MAGA movement which proved wildly premature.

Yet this week's results are certainly a game-changer.

Any ambitions Trump might harbour of illegally defying the 22nd Amendment, which limits presidents to two terms in office, have surely been snuffed out. The notion of Trump 3.0 is even more outlandish now. A Trump dynasty also seems more unlikely. The thought of President Donald Trump Jr taking the oath of office in 2029 or 2033 requires a giant leap of imagination.

Instead, Trump has been badly weakened. His fear factor, within a Republican Party that over the past decade has come to resemble a Trump Party, has been diminished. Signs of his waning power have come already from his Vice President JD Vance who, in a 600-word screed on social media, broke spectacularly with the president.

"The reason we lost is the war," he wrote. "The president himself said so last night."

But the president had not said so last night, and the ambitious vice president, who is eyeing a bid for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, is already trying to distance himself from a damaged brand.

In anointing his political heir, Trump might not be the all-powerful kingmaker after all. Maybe Republican presidential aspirants will not even crave his endorsement. When Texas Republican Senator Ted Cruz published his own 1700-word election post-mortem on X — he described the midterms as "an ass kicking" — it did not include a single word of praise for a president who is used to sycophantic encomiums from his party.

Trump, however, still commands fierce loyalty from millions in his MAGA base. His approval rating among self-described "MAGA Republicans" is 96 per cent. Again, it is worth remembering what happened in the aftermath of January 6. Republicans could have banished Trump into the political wilderness. Instead, his grip on the party tightened. He successfully managed to purge the party of Trump critics, such as former Congresswoman Liz Cheney, and easily saw off the challenge from rivals such as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis in the 2024 Republican primaries.

This election was not only a rejection of Trump but a repudiation of his hyper-aggressive style of politics.

In Michigan, he slandered Democrat Abdul El-Sayed as a "jihadist" and "terrorist", repeatedly called him "Mohammed". But in this bellwether of bellwethers, El-Sayed won comfortably.

The defeat of Trump acolyte, Vivek Ramaswamy, was also emblematic. Ramaswamy aired one of the most vile political attacks in US campaign history, which featured the mother of his Democratic rival, Amy Aston, castigating her daughter as a liar for accusing her ex-husband, who had been criminally charged of rape and then fled from police, of sexually molesting her as a child. Senior Republicans, including the state's outgoing Governor Mike DeWine, called for Ramaswamy to take down the ad. Trump described it as "very powerful".

Voters overwhelmingly rejected that kind of hateful politics.

James Talarico, who Trump labelled "Talafreako", made this yearning for a gentler kind of politics the centrepiece of his victory speech in Texas.

"We are tired of being told to hate each other," said Talarico. "It has been 10 years of this kind of politics, politics as blood sport, politics as trolling and owning, politics as professional wrestling."

Much of the MAGA agenda, however, will survive. Strong borders. Economic nationalism. A rejection of globalisation and frictionless free trade. The insistence that US allies must cough up more money for their own defence.

Democrats will be more wary of pushing what might be called "woke" issues. Even New York congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez remarked in August that " Woke 1.0 was crazy ".

Democrats have already made concessions to Trumpism.

This election they focused on economic issues rather than identity politics. Crucially, however, in the 11 years since Trump came down that golden escalator he has not managed to create a pre-eminent new political order.

For much of the past century, as the historian Gary Gerstle noted in his 2022 landmark study, The Rise and Fall of the Neoliberal Order , US politics was dominated by two political orders.

First, the New Deal created in the 1930s by Franklin Delano Roosevelt, marked by broad consensus between Democrats and Republicans on the role of the state in regulating capitalism and providing a basic welfare safety net for the economically disadvantaged.

Next, from the 1970s to the 2010s, came the neoliberal order, based on a reduced role of government and greater emphasis on the market, which was championed by Reagan and acquiesced in by Clinton, who presented himself as a market-friendly "New Democrat".

Since the Great Recession of 2008, however, no party has managed to impose its ideas on the other, or accrued enough power for long enough in Washington to do so. Instead, we have entered what Gerstle describes as an "interregnum characterised by disorder and instability".

This election offers further proof that we remain in this liminal phase, with neither side establishing lasting dominance.

Trump believed there had been a conservative vibe shift in 2024 after he regained the presidency by winning all seven battleground states. Republicans also controlled both houses of Congress. Two years later, Trump and his party have been hammered.

In a chronically polarised nation, we are witnessing a period of unusual political volatility.

At the presidential level, three consecutive two-term presidencies (Democrat Bill Clinton, Republican George W Bush and Democrat Barack Obama) have been followed three consecutive one-term presidencies (Republican Trump, Democrat Joe Biden, Republican Trump).

Not since the late 19th century, when Grover Cleveland lost the presidency only to win it back four years later, have we seen the presidency switch quadrennially between the parties. Likewise, no party has managed to command Capitol Hill for an extended period. Already this century the House has changed hands five times.

In the entire second half the 21st century, during which Democrats dominated the House of Representatives, that scenario has only occurred three times. In the final 25 years of the 20th century, the Senate changed majority control just three times. In the first 25 years of the 21st century, it has flipped eight times.

Now we will see divisions not only between the parties but within them. Progressive Democrats will point to the success of El-Sayed in Michigan, and the energising effect of Zohran Mamdani's 2025 mayoral victory in New York, as proof that a left-wing version of economic populism can succeed at the national level.

Among the Democratic victors on Tuesday were a record number of candidates backed by, or affiliated with, the Democratic Socialists of America. Centrists will cite the breakthrough in Texas of Talarico, a moderate Christian Democrat, and the mega-church pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas as evidence that the party should occupy the middle ground.

All the party's winning presidential candidates since World War II — Harry Truman, John F Kennedy, Lyndon Johnson, Jimmy Carter, Bill Clinton and Barack Obama — have been pragmatic centrists.

The orthodoxy that only a moderate can win the White House will now be challenged, and contested, ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

On the right of politics, what remains of the more traditionalist wing of the Republican Party might argue the party has to move away from its Trump branding and become more recognisably Reaganesque. Reagan was a free-trade internationalist who backed traditional conservative governance, compared with Trump's populist nationalism that embraces economic protectionism and rejects global alliances and institutional norms.

MAGA diehards will remain faithful to Trump, though some will argue he has not been MAGA enough, especially by launching an unpopular war with Iran. Think-tanks, such as the Heritage Foundation which produced the controversial policy blueprint Project 2025, have lurched a long way to the right. So, too, have media channels such as Fox News and NewsMax, whose "angertainment" business models are based on stoking culture war outrage.

So, it is by no means inevitable that the party will move back towards what is sometimes called the sensible centre.

How could the Republicans remain viable if MAGA voters withdrew their support? Some are now likening the Trump Republican Party to the Trump casino empire. That did not end well.

If, moreover, Texas becomes the new California — the Golden State voted Republican in every presidential election between 1968 and 1988 but Democrat ever since — then it could face a prolonged shut-out from the White House. Try gaining an Electoral College majority without at least one of the country's two most populous states.

Looking to the future, the youth vote does not augur well for the Republicans. Nationally, in House elections, exit polling suggest 66 per cent of voters aged 18-29 voted for a Democrat candidate.

Always, though, we must be wary of over-extrapolating in the aftermath of what look like transformative elections. I have seen too many victorious parties over-reach and then face push-back from voters. Remember the heady talk after Barack Obama's election in 2008 that suggested he would usher in a phase of post-partisanship, and even post-racialism.

As a correspondent in the US at the time, I witnessed how the country's first African-American president was followed into the White House by the untitled leader of the Birther Movement, who placed himself at the head of the anti-Obama white backlash. As Obama himself described the shift after Trump's victory in 2016: "History doesn't move in a straight line. It zigs and zags."

For the past decade, anti-incumbency has so often been the driver of American politics. That, and the negative partisanship that comes with it. Voters often cast their ballots against a party rather than for a party. In these midterms we saw it again. In a 50/50 nation, where for much of this century the results of elections have been far narrower than on Tuesday night, politics has been marked by deadlock not dominance.

What we do know for sure is that the Democrats have just won the authority to scrutinise and investigate. When the new Congress meets on January 3, expect Democratic lawmakers to use those subpoena powers to the full.

Robert Garcia, the top ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, which tends to spearhead congressional investigations, has said already that allegations of Trump family corruption will be his main priority, with the president's eldest son, Donald Trump Jr, and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, coming under closer scrutiny. On election night, he posted two words on social media: "LAWYER UP!"

Garcia also released a statement pledging to take on "the Trump Crime Family, corporate corruption, DHS [Department of Homeland Security] and ICE abuses, and the cover-up of the Epstein files". Hakeem Jeffries has accused the "Trump Cartel" of "massive corruption" and warned: "We are going to hold the crooks accountable."

With a majority in the House, the Democrats could for a third time impeach Donald Trump (previously, only two presidents — Andrew Johnson and Bill Clinton — have faced the charge of committing high crimes and misdemeanours). But winning a conviction in the Senate trial that would ensue requires 67 votes, the kind of super-majority the Democrats are not close to achieving. Besides, attempts to punish Trump have often worked in his favour, by allowing him to claim a political form of martyrdom.

The Democrats could also try to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth for waging military hostilities without congressional authorisation, which is a violation of the 1973 War Powers Resolution. Moves are already afoot in what is now a lame duck Congress, spearheaded by the anti-Trump Republican Thomas Massie, to trigger an impeachment vote against Hegseth as soon as this week.

The newly-elected 120th Congress, whose members will take their seats in the new year, could become known as the Accountability Congress. But House Democrats will also want to make it an Action Congress, by passing bills, on healthcare especially, that meet the concerns of struggling American voters — even though they could be blocked by Republican filibusters in the Senate, which require 60 votes to break, or vetoed by the president.

Ethics reform is an area the Democrats could highlight, such as beefing up financial conflict-of-interest rules in the executive branch and placing limits on presidential pardons. The post-Watergate Congress placed a heavy emphasis on ethics reform, with the creation of the Office of Government Ethics and independent Inspectors General within federal departments.

Among the challenges for the Democrats will be to restore the power of Capitol Hill, which has been the home for the past two years of an incredible shrinking Congress.

Since returning to the White House, Trump has sought to expand the power of the presidency and to govern almost by decree through signing so many executive orders with the flourish of his Sharpie felt tip pen. Already, he has signed 292 executive orders during his second term, well over 100 more than Joe Biden issued during his entire four-year term.

The conservative-dominated Supreme Court, while sometimes checking his power, has helped him create a more maximal presidency. In Trump v Slaughter, the court ruled in June that the president can fire the heads of independent regulatory agencies at his behest, without being required to show "cause".

In its landmark Trump v United States ruling in 2024, brought in connection with the criminal charges he faced over his attempt to overturn the presidential election, it decided presidents possess substantial immunity from criminal prosecution for official acts taken while in office. Among the three branches of government, Congress has felt like the third wheel.

The founding fathers, however, had a very different power ranking in mind. The legislature was supposed to be the most powerful branch of government, which is why Congress was vested with the power of the purse. The presidency was meant to be second. The Supreme Court a distant third.

Democrats on Capitol Hill will attempt to restore parity with the executive branch, especially over trade policy, and to overtake the Supreme Court. Supreme Court Justice John Roberts has been a more influential figure than the departing Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries will attempt to restore the sway of a role traditionally regarded as the second most powerful government position in the country.

After the Republicans' shellacking at the polls, it will be tempting to describe Trump as a "lame duck" president, the usual descriptor for an incumbent whose party loses control of Congress and cannot seek re-election. With Trump, that would be an act of folly. Normal nomenclature does not apply to such an abnormal president.

Trump will not be a lame duck until the final second of the final minute of his presidency. In his last supposed lame-duck phase, from his defeat at the 2020 election to inauguration day in 2021, he propagated the "Big Lie" about Joe Biden stealing the election, amassed his supporters in Washington and did little to restrain them when they first started storming the US Capitol.

Trump still has enormous executive powers at his disposal. He remains the commander-in-chief of the world's most powerful military. He still has control of the FBI and Justice Department, and could use both in an attempt to take vengeance on political opponents. Overcoming a presidential veto requires a two-thirds super-majority in both houses of Congress, which alone the Democrats cannot muster. Trump has issued 12 vetoes over the course of his two terms; congress has only overridden one of them.

By appointing as his new White House chief of staff arch loyalist Stephen Miller, the hardline architect of the ICE immigration crackdown, Trump is signally there will be no retreat from MAGA. Heading the West Wing is a figure who Trump will regard as a wartime consigliere, an aggressively combative figure in upcoming battles with Congress.

Often, if presidents are thwarted on the home front by an obstructionist Congress, they look to make their mark in the foreign realm. Trump could press for a peace deal in the Ukraine war, on terms that would likely be highly favourable towards Vladimir Putin. He could renew the kind of summitry with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un, which became such a feature of his first term diplomacy.

He might agree to carve up the world into spheres of influence as part of a grand bargain with Putin and President Xi Jinping of China, which would require concerns in Taiwan. Trump has made no secret of his desire for regime change in Cuba.

As the dust settles after such an extraordinary electoral event, it is worth noting what did not happen in the 2026 congressional midterms.

For sure, Donald Trump tried to disrupt the polls beforehand, by attempting to limit postal voting and demanding, unsuccessfully, that states surrender their voter registration lists to the Justice Department in Washington.

Yet worries that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, or even federal troops, would be deployed at, or in the close vicinity of, polling stations on Election Day did not eventuate. Nor has Trump tried to interfere with the count. The Republican defeat, of course, was too big to rig. In a closer election, disputed contests could easily have become flashpoints. But it is worth pointing out that, although he has distanced himself from the results, he had not disputed them.

In the year America marked its 250th birthday, the country faced a democratic test, and passed.

Nobody was assassinated during the campaign. Election Day passed without violence. On January 3, when the new Congress is seated we will not see a repeat of the American insurrection that unfolded on January 6, 2021.

That alone, in a country as divided and fractious as America, is cause for celebration.

scraped.description: “The Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” reads the petition.
scraped.author: Jon Queally
scraped.h1: Petition Urging Dems to Reject Jeffries as House Speaker Passes 1M Signatures
scraped.body_text:
“The Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment,” reads the petition.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

An online petition that demanding that Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-NY) not be the next Democratic Speaker of the House has hit one million signatories on Saturday as the clamor for a leadership change within the party explodes after historic midterm wins driven by populist demands.

As of this writing, the Change.org petition — titled “ House Democrats: CHOOSE A NEW SPEAKER ” — has 1,007,831 verified signatories, with the number rapidly rising.

While the final totals are not yet established, Democrats emerged from Tuesday’s elections with at least 254 seats in the next Congress, reclaiming the majority from the Republicans who currently can count on just 162 seats when new members are sworn in come January.

While Jeffries is clearly the presumptive choice for Democrats, and he formally put himself in the running on Wednesday with a letter to all members, outside progressives have voiced serious opposition given his failure to embrace many of the positions — including backing Medicare for All , taking on entrenched corporate power , and restricting military assistance to Israel over its genocide in Gaza — that have animated voters nationwide this election cycle.

According to the petition:

We believe the Speaker should represent the Democratic voters, not just the Democratic establishment.

The Speaker has enormous influence over the direction of the House, including its legislative priorities and agenda. Before casting their votes, representatives should closely examine Jeffries’s public record, policy positions, campaign donor record and leadership … and listen to constituents who do not want him elevated to Speaker.

This is not a foregone conclusion. There is still time for other Democratic members of the House to step forward and seek the nomination for Speaker, someone whose priorities more closely reflect the voters who hope to elect the Democratic majority.

We are calling on every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Hakeem Jeffries for Speaker in January 2027 and choose a different candidate.

Axios reported Friday that members of Congress have been “inundated” with calls urging them not to elect Jeffries and suggested that some of the hesitations are not just among progressives.

The outlet reporting interviewing “nearly a half-dozen incoming House Democrats in deeply red seats Thursday who declined to state a firm position one way or another on voting for him.”

Sign this petition if you want a new speaker of the house. https://t.co/G88VLySjsQ

As Corbin Trent, the former top aide to Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) who now runs a progressive organizing outfit called A Fight Worth Having, wrote in a column published at Common Dreams on Friday, “the Democratic leadership we have today is completely ill-suited for this moment. They do not have the vision for what it’s going to take to rebuild the trust the American people have lost in their government, their institutions, and the Democratic Party itself.”

“Democrats have spoken loudly and clearly that they want new leadership,” Trent said of the election. “Unfortunately, too many of the people in Washington aren’t listening.”

While the large Democratic majority in the House makes it easier for Jeffries to maneuver leading up to the leadership vote, and given that no challenger has stepped forward to take him on directly, the betting money is still safe that Jeffries will be the next Speaker of the House.

But the public push denouncing him as the wrong choice of leadership in a moment where Democratic voters are clearly demanding — and expecting — a much bolder agenda, the pressure may yet have an impact on his calculations.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.
