scraped.h1: Peltola Campaign Sues Alaska Over Rejected Absentee Ballots as Decoy Dan Sullivan Siphons Thousands of Votes
scraped.body_text:
The Peltola campaign sued Alaska over rejected absentee ballots as the decoy Dan Sullivan siphons thousands of votes.

The Associated Press reported that as of Saturday morning with 75% of the vote tallied, Democrat Mary Peltola is ahead of Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan by approximately 625 votes.

Peltola has 102,962 votes at 48.17% and GOP Senator Dan Sullivan has 102,325 votes at 47.88%.

The decoy Dan Sullivan has 3,600 votes at 1.68%.

The Peltola campaign’s scheme to siphon votes away from Senator Dan Sullivan is working.

Mary Peltola’s campaign is now suing Alaska for access to the rejected absentee ballots.

The Hill reported :

Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign is suing the state of Alaska to obtain access to records for absentee ballots that were rejected by the Alaska Division of Elections, a new court filing shows.

Peltola’s campaign said they previously requested records of the rejected ballots on multiple occasions but were denied access.

“Plaintiff cannot ensure that its voters’ lawful votes were properly counted without knowing whose absentee ballots were rejected or questioned, and why,” the lawsuit reads. “Each hour and each day that Defendants deny Plaintiff the requested records to which it is entitled costs Plaintiff the opportunity to help ensure that qualified voters have their ballots counted.”

Peltola currently leads Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in the Alaska U.S. Senate race by just over 600 votes, but with approximately 30 percent of the vote still outstanding, according to The Hill’s partner Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ). No winner has been projected in the race as of Saturday morning.

The Division responded in a release on Friday, saying voters who have had their ballots rejected have not yet had access to the information, therefore, the campaign should not be able to have access yet either.

articles.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride

scraped.title: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn’t expect a smooth ride
scraped.description: Laura Kuenssberg talks to government insiders about the prime minister opening the conversation about the UK rejoining the EU.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride
scraped.body_text:
Andy Burnham wants to get closer to the EU - but he shouldn't expect a smooth ride

Déjà vu? The Eurostar has been booked. Strategic leaks of draft agreements have started.

The EU's former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier is warning the UK it can't have it all and it will not be able to rejoin its single market "à la carte".

Naturally, there is even a row about smoky bacon crisps – an argument between the UK and EU about food labelling has become a classic of the genre. Remember the bendy banana? Or the so-called sausage war between Boris Johnson and Emmanuel Macron?

It's a clash between those arguing it's worth swallowing some new rules to ease trade with the continent, or those whose message to Brussels is, "hands off our snacks" - even though we are not actually in the EU anymore.

Andy Burnham's big moment with the bloc top brass is fast approaching - the second annual EU-UK Summit since the UK's withdrawal from the EU takes place in Brussels on 20 November.

That meeting is not supposed to be about whether the UK might one day go back in. The prime minister has suggested that is his long-term ambition - but is he really ready for what is to come?

First, Burnham inherited the broad deal that's likely to be signed. The UK and EU were originally meant to mint a new and, they hope, improved agreement back in May, then in July, and well, political upheavals mean one thing for getting things done – delay.

But that means the outlines of a new agreement have been clear for many months, an approach based on "closer alignment" as Sir Keir Starmer proclaimed to us at the start of the year.

So if the prime minister hails agreement, spare a thought for those who started the work to get it this far many months ago.

One source familiar with the negotiations told me, "They are 90% there", with agreements designed to make life easier for food producers, a deal on emissions trading which could help manufacturers, and new arrangements for youth visas (although it's understood there is still haggling over putting a cap on the numbers).

An EU source close to the process said: "The bone of contention is a cap – we proposed 150,000, the UK proposed 50,000 – but we would expect to reach a compromise", even though it has been "very tense" on both sides.

A last-minute call from the EU to cut tuition fees for its students is expected to be parked for now with more months of discussion to come. Another fine tradition - agree what you can, but file some tough stuff away for future chat.

There are dilemmas too on the EU's so-called "Made in Europe" plans – draft laws to protect its industries from being hammered by Chinese competition. The purpose is clear – to help the economy grow, with the prime minister quoting figures that suggest closer ties to the EU without going back in could add 0.4 percent to GDP.

But as the tabloid-friendly row over salty snacks illustrates, making it easier to do business with the bloc doesn't come without a cost, and a political awkwardness.

Andy Burnham with Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission

Talking to my colleague, the BBC's Business editor Simon Jack this week, the prime minister admitted the UK would have to follow more EU rules. "That's where we've ended up," Burnham acknowledged.

And whatever your feelings on the matter, that lands us slap-bang back in the middle of the eternal dilemma of the relationship between the UK and the European Union.

How much control is the UK willing to lose in the hope of bigger wins? Even when it comes to a relatively limited number of important issues that are on the table in the current discussions?

The prime minister has scrapped the limits of this troubled conversation, not just suggesting a closer relationship with the relatively dry and technical changes being discussed right now, but dangling the possibility of going back into the bloc one day.

Suggesting freedom of movement again, unlimited immigration for Brits who want to live or work on the continent and vice versa. That's after repeated promises, including from him, that that sometimes toxic debate would not be reopened.

What is he up to? It seems the prime minister's main line of thinking is that with problems like long passport queues and red tape for business it is right and proper to try to sort them out.

That is after all, what Rishi Sunak and then Sir Keir Starmer tried to do.

But his willingness to contemplate going a lot further is based on a belief that the public's attitude has shifted – if you look at polling it does suggest that a majority of voters support going back into the EU , external .

It just so happens his own long-time conviction is to go back into the bloc one day. And that idea chimes not just with many Labour activists and members, but also with the Lib Dems, Greens and SNP – whose voters he'd be only too happy to peel off.

But hang on, don't let Burnham's easy-breezy style mask that just casually mentioning he is open to us going back into the EU in the run up to this summit is a huge and difficult thing. Whatever relationship he truly wants to seek, and even those involved in the conversations aren't quite sure he is even sure, don't expect a smooth ride from the EU.

In an interview you can see tomorrow, the EU's chief negotiator last time, Michel Barnier, told me the UK cannot pick and choose the relationship "à la carte".

If we wanted to go back in, he told me, the UK could forget the famous rebate, and there is no way to be in the huge trading bloc, the single market, without accepting freedom of movement.

One government figure told me, even now dealing with the EU there are "lots of very warm words, but quite a lot of arms folded".

An EU insider told me the mood has certainly changed. "There is big scope getting closer to the EU, but nobody wants it to be toxic… we wonder, does he know what he is doing?"

Last time round, the majority of businesses, with some notable noisy outliers, were keen to stay in the EU. But after several years having to make the relationship work, and spend money on rearranging how they do business, that might not translate into such solid support if the prime minister does choose to pursue a return to the EU.

One prominent business figure explains: "You're a langoustine exporter from Ullapool? Yes, please. You are manufacturing and making that car? Yes, get me back in. You're a drugs manufacturer? Well, sort of, yes and no. You're in financial services? We've spent the money. Do we want to unpick this?"

There are prominent backers of the idea of a return to the EU, if Burnham himself decides to make that case. The former Chancellor Rachel Reeves and the London Mayor Sadiq Khan make the case as well.

We've already talked about the Lib Dems, the Greens, the SNP, and Plaid Cymru being up for it, as are many Labour MPs and ministers.

But the political risks of arguing for a return to the union are, frankly, enormous. Labour is divided, just as the country could be, whatever the current polls suggest.

One former Labour minister told me, "the prime minister wants us to go back in, but it is a very hazardous route", saying of the party's broadly pro-European rank and file: "Nobody wants to criticise Andy, but if it blows open they won't all be in the same place".

One cabinet minister's eyes rolled so violently when I asked if they fancied another referendum they nearly went into the back of their head. And it is a safe bet that if the prime minister really decides to pursue a return that there'd be a ferocious pushback from the other side.

The Conservatives and Reform are already howling with protest about the deal expected to be signed this month.

Kemi Badenoch criticised the prime minister for "unpicking the deal this country signed with the EU a decade after the referendum" adding, "he is not going to get a better deal… it's not just that the EU are tough negotiators, he has already revealed his entire negotiating hand."

Meanwhile Reform UK deputy leader Richard Tice accused Burnham of "trying to sneak us back into Brussels via the back door", and said Reform would "never let this betrayal go unchallenged".

And you can expect similar financial arguments to be made as last time round. Vote Leave was always only too happy to have noisy clashes over the cash the UK paid to be part of the EU – that £350m – the gross contribution, not the net.

But every argument about the amount reminded the public that the UK did spend millions, even if the figure was officially judged as misleading.

While EU leaders might want to be helpful to Burnham, the Czech prime minister's comments on the issue were rather unhelpful. Asked recently if he'd like to see the UK go back his answer was, "Yes, of course – we need more money".

There could be enormous opportunity for the economy, important support for the UK's security, and a boost for the prime minister's backing among some voters if he does indeed end up deciding he will make the case for the UK to rejoin the European Union.

But it would be a heck of a gamble. A decade ago, a relatively popular prime minister named David Cameron with expert communication skills wanted to reset the UK's relationship with the EU. That blew up his leadership, unleashing a series of political disasters that saw him off, and dogged his party for years.

Andy Burnham is a relatively popular prime minister too, also confident in his ability to communicate with you, and serious about improving our ties with the EU. But in his party, there are those preaching caution about opening this conversation.

The successes or failures of the impending summit will give him, and the rest of us, a taste of what might lie ahead.

Topic: Music

Ella Thompson begins touring this month behind her new album, Triumph & Sadness, a showcase of masterful soul music. ( Supplied: Nick McKinlay )

Writing her new album, Ella Thompson fell in love with a quote from French philosopher Simone Weil.

"Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity," Thompson says.

"I'm really interested in how artists and writers have responded to that idea over the centuries. How we give attention to others and ourselves; what we pay attention to and how it can also distort our view of the world."

Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

When art and attention have become increasingly "commodified and distorted, exploited and manipulated" in our current AI-and-algorithm-saturated world, Thompson's new record is its own form of generosity.

Its title, Triumph & Sadness, conveys the bittersweet.

"I'm always drawn to that sweet spot in music, art and writing," Thompson explains, "where you find that balance in between the extremes.

"For this record, every triumph, there is something sad behind it, of seeing the state of the world."

A masterful set of warm, cinematic soul music that would fit snugly into any self-respecting vinyl enthusiast's collection, the album again proves Thompson as one of Australia's underrated masters of the genre's sound and spirit.

Boasting tasteful, timeless arrangements — slinky guitars, keys and airtight rhythm section adorned with lush brass, flutes and harp — the music offers the soulful sweetness while Thompson's thoughtful lyrics provide the bitter.

She interrogates tricky realities with effortless vocal performances ranging from smouldering to show-stopping.

She scales impressive heights on the jubilant Make You Believe and My Weakness, a song inspired by a Caravaggio painting based on the myth of Narcissus and being "absorbed by things that don't really matter much,"

However, Thompson approaches the subject — losing meaningful attention and connection with others to self-obsession — with humour as much as critique.

"I think tragedy can be funny as well. We beat ourselves up about our phone addictions and all these sorts of thing, but it is kind of funny," she says.

"I like dramatic soul music. I don't necessarily like drama in my real life."

Thompson has been embedded in the Melbourne/Naarm music scene for years.

She fronted electronic duo GL, genre-shifting pop group Dorsal Fins, and has lent her imperious pipes to Paul Kelly, The Bamboos and even Mark Ronson .

But Triumph & Sadness, like her previous solo records Ripple On The Wing (2024) and Domino (2023), reaches back full circle to the jazz and soul of Thompson's childhood.

She grew up absorbing the personal and political stories, sounds and studio craft of greats like Billie Holiday, Nina Simone and Curtis Mayfield.

She was later mentored by her idol , trailblazing Australian jazz, blues and soul artist Renée Geyer , who took Thompson on her first tour at age 16.

That advice shaped Thompson's entire approach, acutely aware that the tradition she's working in, soul music, has deep social and spiritual roots.

"I try to be respectful of where this music is from and not just the aesthetic of it."

For Ella Thompson, soul music is about the connection between people, the environment and the world we live in. ( Supplied: Nick McKinlay )

Marvin Gaye and Sam Cooke's progressive protest records; Aretha Franklin and Curtis Mayfield's searing emotional deliveries — Thompson recognises that many "of those great records have a brilliant message and they're made from a particular social context".

"One that isn't too dissimilar from the one that we're living in now… There's definitely parallels. We've come a long way but in a lot of ways, we haven't."

Lesser contemporaries and countless algorithmic playlists get caught up in reproducing the genre's sound, forgetting that soul is essential, not optional.

It's a conversation between artist and listener about what it means to be human, Thompson observes.

Music that emerges from a specific community is something Thompson admires in the records she loves, and an authenticity she commits to.

"I love hearing that sense of place in music. I'm making music here in Naarm, with creatives here."

Like its predecessors, Triumph & Sadness was made alongside Thompson's regular crew: Liam McGorry, trumpet-toting alumni of Dorsal Fins and Saskwatch, and Henry Jenkins, formerly of The Cactus Channel.

Together, with a crack studio band comprising members from instrumental labelmates Surprise Chef and Karate Boogaloo, Thompson shares an intuition forged through years of collaboration.

"There's definitely a shared language [and] shorthand."

Cooking on the same wavelength, they dish up tasty grooves on Parable, the sizzling Dandelion and swooning, harp-assisted Lover's Game.

Everything was recorded in four days at an all-analogue studio in Castlemaine.

"There's no computers in the building and we cut all the band tracks direct to tape," says Thompson.

"Usually the third or fourth take… that's the one [and] there's no editing.

"All of the records from the '60s and '70s that we love so much and have studied were recorded in that way."

The pressure of getting it right is outweighed by the benefit of capturing "that raw feeling in the room. And going back to that bittersweet thing, it's falling in love with those imperfections as well."

Starting a solo career, after years of experience in the local scene, still felt in some ways like "beginning again", says Thompson.

"That can be really humbling.

"Confidence is something that's taken me a long time to build in my artistic direction. But I feel lucky to have arrived at [this] point now.

"There's nothing else I'd rather be doing than making records with my friends," she adds.

"I'm really grateful for the opportunities to be able to do that."

Thompson has just headlined her first international shows in London and Paris, where she undertook an artist residency at Cité internationale des arts, writing "songs for a month thanks to APRA … Always just gathering acorns and see how they grow."

The sense of development and community she finds in the Melbourne music scene is "really inspiring," she says.

"Our music might not reach everybody, but that's OK. It's a craft that people are really dedicated to and have a lot of respect for each other… show up for each other."

The soul of Triumph & Sadness isn't just in its sumptuous sound but its spirit of resilience.

"Where we go through these difficult parts of our lives, we still need music, art, community, friendships to uplift us out of that and feel triumph and to overcome adversity."

Ella Thompson's tour for Triumph & Sadness kicks off on November 13 at The Vanguard in Sydney.

She then plays Melbourne, Adelaide, Healesville and Meredith Music Festival in December .

scraped.body_text:

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Due Process

"It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here ... to warrant the unusual step of ... find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 12:25 PM

From U.S. v. SGO Corp. Ltd. , decided Tuesday by Judge Kathleen Williams (S.D. Fla.):

For a six-year period, the Government investigated SGO executives for their role in a money laundering and bribery scheme related to the May, 2016 Philippine elections. The investigation culminated in a six-count indictment (" First Indictment "), returned on August 8, 2024, which charged [executives of] SGO and Smartmatic … [with] conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (" FCPA ") (Count I); violations of the FCPA (Count II); conspiracy to commit money laundering (Count III); and international laundering of monetary instruments (Counts IV, V, and VI). The FCPA "prohibits officers of a domestic concern from making corrupt payments to a 'foreign official.'"

SGO was not charged. In fact, SGO had been cooperating with the Government since 2021, years before the First Indictment was returned. {Although the Parties may dispute the breadth and quality of SGO's efforts to cooperate, there is no question that SGO and the Government were engaged in discussions and the exchange of documents related to this matter.}

The original trial date was set for October 7, 2024 … [but was eventually reset for 2026]….

As the court notes, the Trump Administration was skeptical of FCPA prosecutions, deprioritized FCPA enforcement generally, and "elected to close FCPA investigations into multiple companies." But despite that, in October 2025, the government added SGO as a defendant in the case. SGO then moved to dismiss the superseding indictment, alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, and sought discovery in support of that motion, "premised on political events that have embroiled Smartmatic in the wake of the 2020 election":

Since that election, multiple high-profile individuals and organizations connected to then-Former President Donald Trump have alleged that Smartmatic, a subsidiary of SGO, interfered in the election…. President Trump has also reposted content blaming Smartmatic for interfering in United States and Venezuelan elections, calling Smartmatic "disgraceful" and expressing that those who "rigged" the 2020 election must pay. In response to the statements by President Trump's confederates, Smartmatic brought various defamation suits, which are largely ongoing. SGO contends that President Trump's personal animus against SGO and assertion of its rights against President Trump's confederates precipitated the filing of the Superseding Indictment….

The court lays out the demanding standard for defendants' attempts to get discovery related to allegations of vindictive or selective prosecution, but concludes that in this case the standard was met. A brief excerpt (for more, including citations to precedents to which the court analogizes this case, see the full opinion ):

First, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by evidence that the Government bucked a trend in enforcement activity in prosecuting the defendant…. [W]hile the Blanche and Bondi Memos and Executive Order 14209 explicitly announced an intention to rein in and limit FCPA enforcement, particularly against corporations, SGO was charged, nonetheless.

Second, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the timing between a defendant's assertion of a right and the allegedly vindictive prosecutorial act…. [Here,] it is telling that the Government chose not to indict SGO originally, that SGO was charged only after President Trump reassumed office and after SGO had been cooperating with the Government for years, and that the Government has presented no evidence adduced between the First and Superseding Indictments warranting SGO's addition as a defendant.

Third, a vindictive prosecution claim may be supported by the Executive, prosecutor, or law enforcement's stated positions, even when they do not explicitly admit that the case was brought against the defendant for an improper purpose…. The Court finds probative not just that President Trump signed an executive order regarding FCPA enforcement but also that President Trump has personally expressed animus towards SGO regarding election interference. Indeed, President Trump's confederates were sued by SGO for making false claims regarding SGO's role in interfering with the 2020 presidential election that President Trump lost….

After evaluating the totality of the circumstances in this case, the Court has concluded that limited discovery regarding SGO's Motion to Dismiss is warranted…. [T]ere is "some evidence" tending to support SGO's Motion to Dismiss: the individual Defendants were charged over a year prior to when the Superseding Indictment against SGO was returned; for years prior to the initiation of this case and up until the Superseding Indictment was returned, SGO was cooperating with the Government; the Government charged SGO amidst a public shift away from charging defendants for similar FCPA violations; SGO brought suit against the President's confederates prior to being charged; and the President has expressed at least some degree of animus towards SGO. "It may well be that no fire will be discovered under all the smoke, but there is enough smoke here … to warrant the unusual step of … find[ing] out how this unusual prosecution came about."

[T]he Government shall provide the Court with the following for ex parte and in camera review under seal:

NEXT: Prosecution Over Threat to American Federation of Teachers President Randi Weingarten Can Go Forward

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast .

Binance’s chief financial officer Kaiser Ng is leaving the cryptocurrency exchange.

According to Bloomberg , co-CEO Yi He said in a statement that Ng’s departure will allow him to “pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance,” and that a transition plan has been “implemented over the last half year.”

The announcement comes barely more than a week after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance users. The company froze withdrawals for several days; after accounts were unfrozen, users withdrew a net $3.6 billion in the first few hours.

Binance and the FBI blamed a North Korean group called TraderTraitor for the hack. The company also said that it would cover all losses, promising, “Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds. These losses will not be passed on to users.”

Ng will be replaced as CFO by Justin Yek.

In October, Amazon announced its refreshed Kindle lineup, its first significant design overhaul in years. The highlights included a new edge-to-edge design that eliminated traditional raised bezels, thinner and lighter Paperwhite and Colorsoft models with better displays, and page-turning accessories like a Bluetooth remote and a magnetic cover with page-turn buttons.

However, given the impact of the global memory-chip shortage driven by the AI boom, the new Kindles also debuted with pricing that had increased by $40 to $50 across the lineup. That makes it more difficult for the average consumer to consider buying one of the more premium devices.

For that reason, the Kindle I most wanted to get my hands on was the 6-inch entry-level device , which starts at $169.99 for the ad-free version. With the price hikes, this is the Kindle that will remain the most affordable to new e-reader buyers.

The question I weighed was whether or not the basic Kindle is even worth buying at this price when there are arguably better Kindles on the market. The answer, after a couple of weeks of testing, is yes — if you can live without the bells and whistles and prefer a smaller, lighter device.

On the 6-inch Kindle, there’s no warm light to reduce eye strain, no color display, no auto-adjusting brightness, no option to use the page-turn cover, and it’s not waterproof. Obviously, because of its size, the screen is smaller, as is the battery. Battery life is 6 weeks compared with the Paperwhite’s 12 weeks or Colorsoft’s 8 weeks.

Still, even this basic Kindle has seen improvements of its own, mostly from a physical design perspective.

The plastic 2026 Kindle is 11% lighter and 14% thinner than the 2024 model, weighing 140g versus 158g and measuring 6.85mm thick versus 8mm. While this seems like a small change, the 18-gram difference is noticeable and particularly welcome for a device you’re likely to carry in your purse or bag. Plus, it makes it easier to hold for hours on end when you’re really binging your way through a book.

(The aluminum version, meanwhile, is slightly heavier at 162g, or 4 grams more than the 2024 Kindle, though it still benefits from the slimmer design.)

And despite being the “starter” Kindle, the 6-inch basic device still received the new flush-front screen update. This makes it more comfortable to hold in your hand, especially for those long reading sessions. Amazon explained that you don’t have to worry about no longer having a bezel to rest your thumb upon, either, as the new Kindles have been updated to detect a dead zone in the capacitive touch that will readjust to account for the fact that your finger is there.

In practice, that doesn’t mean you can just press your thumb down anywhere on the Kindle’s screen as you hold it — doing so would register this as an attempt to highlight or look up a word. Instead, it means you can rest your thumb or fingers on the outer edge of the Kindle’s screen (the colored border) without triggering an unintentional tap, even though some of your finger will be touching part of the Kindle’s capacitive screen.

In terms of the software, the new basic Kindle is a bit snappier than its 2024 predecessor. This is most noticeable when opening books, which Amazon claims to be 30% faster.

If you’re coming from the 2019 Kindle Basic, the 2026 version is an even bigger upgrade, as you gain USB-C, more storage (from 4GB to 8GB to now 16GB or 32GB), the new flush screen, and the screen resolution jumps from 167 ppi to 300 ppi. It’s faster, thinner, and lighter, too, and the battery lasts weeks longer.

Another perk about the basic Kindle beyond its small size (this thing fits in your jeans’ back pocket!), is that you can now pay a little more for an upgraded version with an aluminum backing instead of plastic and more storage. The new $189.99 aluminum option comes in Seagrass and Alpine Sky hues, and ships with 32GB of storage. Meanwhile, the $169.99 plastic model offers 16GB of storage.

However, even if you go for the less expensive option, you can at least now pick a fun color other than black (aka Graphite), as Amazon has introduced a cheery purple option called Ube. (I almost wish I’d gone for this one, just for the whimsy of it, even though I prefer the feel of the aluminum.)

I should point out that you can use the Kindle Click, the new Bluetooth remote for page turning, with the basic Kindle, but I’m not sure why you’d need to, if not for some accessibility-related reason. The 6-inch Kindle was already the smallest, and now it’s lighter and easier to hold, too. (But perhaps I just don’t get the appeal of the remote? I’ve barely used the remote with my Kobo either!)

The big thing to consider here is whether you want to spend this much on a Kindle that lacks a warm light. While this is something of a personal preference, for some readers, no warm light is a dealbreaker. The warm light shifts the color tone of the Kindle’s display from a cooler bluish-white to a softer amber glow, which is meant to help reduce eye strain and improve reading conditions in low light or at night.

Whether you need this feature depends on where you like to read and how long your sessions tend to be. If you read nightly in bed with little light, you might prefer paying extra for a $199.99 16GB Kindle Paperwhite. (That version only comes in Graphite. The 32GB Paperwhite can come in Seaglass, too, but is $249.99).

If you often read by the pool or on vacation, you also might want to upgrade to a waterproof Kindle.

But if you can live without the extra features and want the best purse- or pocket-sized device, the 6-inch Kindle is still a viable option.

scraped.body_text:
WWE legend Glenn Jacobs, better known to millions of wrestling fans as Kane, has reportedly emerged as the favorite to replace Sen. Marsha Blackburn in the U.S. Senate after her election as governor of Tennessee.

Jacobs, who recently completed two terms as mayor of Knox County, is considered the frontrunner for the appointment, according to The Washington Sun , which cited multiple Republican operatives and people familiar with the discussions.

Independent reporting has also identified Jacobs as one of the leading contenders for the seat.

Say hello to your frontrunner to replace Marsha Blackburn in the Senate:

Glenn Jacobs, aka ex-WWE star KANE

w/ @reporterjoe @kadiagoba https://t.co/sqKLQfo87M

— Al Weaver (@alweaver22) November 6, 2026

Blackburn is expected to vacate her Senate seat when she takes office as governor in January.

She has previously indicated that she intends to appoint her own successor, although she has so far declined to publicly discuss whom she will choose.

Jacobs, 59, played a major role in Blackburn’s gubernatorial campaign, serving as her campaign treasurer and campaigning across Tennessee on her behalf.

The WWE Hall of Famer has already confirmed that he would be interested in the job.

“Obviously it’s a huge honor for me, so I would consider it very seriously,” Jacobs said last month when asked about a potential appointment.

Jacobs became one of professional wrestling’s most recognizable stars during his decades-long WWE career.

He performed as the masked “Big Red Machine” Kane and winning multiple world championships before entering Republican politics.

scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Free Speech

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 12:00 PM

From U.S. v. Spitzer (N.D. Ga.), filed by Magistrate Judge John Larkins on Oct. 9, and just affirmed Wednesday by Judge Eleanor Ross:

The indictment alleges that on July 23, 2024, Mr. Spitzer posted the following message on the website for the American Federation of Teachers, a labor union, regarding its president ("Individual #1"):

[Individual #1] is an ignorant incompetent cunt that should be worried for her safety. Fact that she is still alive. Liberal nazi deserves the bullet to head. Resign before she ends like what happened to trump at his speech. They won't miss fat bitch.

The indictment alleges that the post violated 18 U.S.C. § 875(c), which makes it a federal crime to transmit in interstate commerce any communication containing a threat to injure another person.

Mr. Spitzer argues that assuming the allegations in the indictment were true, it fails to state an offense because the posting was not a "true threat," or even a threat at all, and thus is protected by the First Amendment. As he sees it, the posting was simply political speech about a public figure and did not advocate the use of force or violence against Individual #1.

{In an effort to contextualize the posting, Mr. Spitzer points to an internet article in which Mike Pompeo, the former U.S. Secretary of State, described Individual #1 as "the most dangerous person in the world"; examples of "conservative politicians and commentators" criticizing her approach to school closures during the pandemic; and examples of Individual #1's own political statements. But these are not facts that the Court can consider at this juncture because they fall outside the four corners of the indictment.}

The government responds that whether Mr. Spitzer's posting qualified as a true threat is a question for the jury and that a pretrial determination of the sufficiency of the evidence is procedurally improper. The government further asserts that Mr. Spitzer improperly relies on facts not alleged in the indictment to contextualize the posting. The government has the better argument….

Considering the allegations on the face of the indictment—as this Court must—the Court finds that a jury could conclude that Mr. Spitzer's alleged posting constituted a "true threat." There are at least four separate references to harming or killing Individual #1, including: that she should be "worried for her safety"; that she "deserves a bullet to [the] head"; that unless she resigns she risks being shot similar to the attempted assassination of President Donald J. Trump; and that she will not be missed. In addition, the posting makes an oblique reference to her still being alive, which when combined with the other statements, can reasonably be interpreted as evidencing a present intent to intimidate and place Individual #1 in fear of bodily harm or death. The screed's liberal use of epithets further tends to show that the posting was not simply on a matter of public concern, but rather a threat against Individual #1 personally….

In his reply, Mr. Spitzer relies on the Supreme Court's decision in Watts v. United States , to argue that "political hyperbole" is not a "true threat." True enough, but Watts is distinguishable. In that case, the Supreme Court overturned the conviction of Watts, an 18-year-old Black protester who was charged with threatening President Lyndon B. Johnson during a political rally at the Washington Monument during the 1960's. During the protest, Watts said:

They always holler at us to get an education. And now I have already received my draft classification as 1-A and I have got to report for my physical this Monday coming. I am not going. If they ever make me carry a rifle the first man I want to get in my sights is L.B.J. They are not going to make me kill my black brothers.

The Supreme Court held that considering the full context of the statement—including that it was conditional upon Watt's joining the military (which he said he would not do) and that the listeners laughed at his statement—it was "political hyperbole," not a true threat. In contrast, Mr. Spitzer's alleged statement is much more threatening for the reasons explained above. Also, significantly, Watts was decided after trial, based on a developed evidentiary record, which underscores why dismissal at this juncture is not appropriate.

Accordingly, dismissal of the indictment is not warranted. But, of course, Mr. Spitzer is free to renew his challenge to the sufficiency of the evidence at trial….

Brent A. Gray and Eric John White represent the government.

Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast .

scraped.title: "Mercy For The Wolves": California DAs Revolt After Newsom Wipes Out Death Row
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: "Mercy For The Wolves": California DAs Revolt After Newsom Wipes Out Death Row
scraped.body_text:
California's district attorneys are vowing to keep seeking the death penalty in new cases , and some are looking for a way to block Gov. Gavin Newsom's commutation of all 548 death sentences in the state before it takes effect. As we reported , Newsom announced Thursday that he would commute every death sentence in California to life without parole, writing in a letter that "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values."

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer went first. Newsom's commutations are "mercy for the wolves," he said in a statement Thursday, before making the vow: "I, as the elected District Attorney of Orange County, have, and will, continue to pursue the death penalty."

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer Issues Statement on Governor Newsom's Commutation of All Death Sentences in California Click here for full release: https://t.co/x65hY8Hlvx SANTA ANA, Calif. - Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer issued the following... pic.twitter.com/xWsH1Y8eby

— OCDA Todd Spitzer (@OCDAToddSpitzer) November 5, 2026

Newsom's own letter leaves them that opening. The commutations do not repeal the death penalty, so prosecutors can still seek it in new cases, as the Mercury News noted. San Mateo County District Attorney Stephen Wagstaffe, whose office is seeking death against the man accused of killing seven farmworkers at a Half Moon Bay mushroom farm in 2023, told the paper he was "disgusted." "It is contrary to two separate votes of the people of California," he said. "What he's done today is specifically undemocratic and serves his own personal philosophy."

The bigger question is whether the commutations survive at all. The state constitution bars a governor from commuting the sentence of anyone convicted of more than one felony without the California Supreme Court's approval, which covers 382 of the 548 cases , and the governor's office says none of the commutations take effect until those legal steps are done. That is where prosecutors are looking. San Diego County District Attorney Summer Stephan said her office is "researching any lawful remedies" for victims' families, who she said were "deprived of any input."

San Diego County District Attorney @SummerStephan issued the following statement on Governor Gavin Newsom's commutation of all death sentences in California: pic.twitter.com/cAW314gNmZ

— SD District Attorney (@SDDistAtty) November 6, 2026

Victims' rights are the likeliest line of attack. San Bernardino County District Attorney Jason Anderson said Newsom ignored Marsy's Law, the victims' rights guarantees in the state constitution: "I am not aware of any victims' family members receiving notice of these commutations from the Governor." He singled out Kevin Cooper, convicted of murdering Josh Ryen's family and his friend Chris Hughes and leaving Ryen for dead. Cooper maintains his innocence, and Newsom ordered an independent investigation of his case. "Josh has never received a call from Gavin Newsom," Anderson said, calling the commutations "arrogant and political showmanship."

Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho made the voters' case. A blanket commutation stands "in direct conflict with the will of California voters," he said. Californians have twice rejected abolishing the death penalty and in 2016 reaffirmed it through Proposition 66 , the measure meant to speed up executions, Ho noted. It also ignores "the voices of victims who have waited decades for justice," Ho said.

A statement from Sacramento County District Attorney Thien Ho. pic.twitter.com/NuspYtYFci

— Sacramento County DA (@SacCountyDA) November 6, 2026

Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter Polly was kidnapped from her Petaluma home and murdered in 1993 by Richard Allen Davis, fears the commutations are a first step. "We're all looking at the prospect of potentially them getting out someday, because they're one step closer now," he told the Mercury News. Spitzer made the same argument, pointing to state parole regulations that took effect Oct. 1 and, he said, make thousands of inmates serving life without parole eligible for parole. The governor's office says the commutations release no one and make no one eligible for parole, and that the commuted prisoners are excluded from the parole board's new commutation and resentencing rules.

Not every prosecutor objects. Santa Clara County District Attorney Jeff Rosen called the commutations "the right thing to do," and Contra Costa District Attorney Diana Becton said they would "save California taxpayers hundreds of millions of dollars." The state has also set aside $239 million to turn San Quentin, home of the old death row, into a rehab center , as we reported.

Newsom leaves office in January and is weighing a 2028 presidential run. California has not executed anyone since 2006, and his successor, Xavier Becerra, has said he will extend the moratorium on executions Newsom imposed in 2019.

scraped.author: Janeé Bolden
scraped.h1: Idris Elba is set to star in and direct new action-comedy ‘In Laws’
scraped.body_text:
The “Luther” star will play a disgraced secret agent in the upcoming buddy comedy, which is expected to begin filming in 2027.

Idris Elba is preparing to flex his comedic muscles in a new project that will put him both in front of and behind the camera.

The Golden Globe-winning actor is set to star in and direct the upcoming action-comedy “In Laws,” according to an exclusive report from Deadline . The film, which is expected to begin production in Spain in March 2027, will mark Elba’s fourth feature as a director.

Elba will play Carson Hughes, a blacklisted secret agent who gets an unexpected opportunity to redeem himself. But there’s a catch. He’ll have to work alongside a younger, by-the-book rookie agent to stop a deadly plot.

As the unlikely partners race against time, their differences threaten to derail the mission. Adding to the chaos, the two discover they have a wedding neither can afford to miss, assuming they can survive working together long enough to get there.

For Elba, who has spent much of his career playing intense characters in projects ranging from “Luther” to “The Wire,” the film offers an opportunity to explore a different side of his talents. Elba will produce the film alongside Gina Carter through their production company, 22Summers.

“Gina and I are really excited to make movies that make people laugh, and there’s nothing I love more than a great buddy comedy,” Elba said according to Deadline. “It’s a genre I’ve always loved, and one we’re excited to bring our own spin to.”

Jeffrey Greenstein of A Higher Standard and Mark Fasano of Nickel City Pictures are also producing. Greenstein co-wrote the screenplay with brothers Eshom and Ian Nelms, based on an original script by Adrian Speckhert and Cory Hughes. Additional casting is underway.

Although audiences know Elba primarily for his acting, he’s been steadily building his directing résumé. He made his feature directorial debut with the 2018 crime drama “Yardie,” and his upcoming film “Above the Below” is scheduled for release Dec. 4.

A post shared by Lionsgate (@lionsgate)

He’s also attached to direct an untitled Apple Original Films project featuring Wunmi Mosaku and Charlie Cox, expected in 2027.

Meanwhile, Elba and Carter’s 22Summers recently completed production on another installment of the actor’s popular “Luther” franchise for Netflix, titled “Luther: The Day Will Come.”

With “In Laws,” Elba appears ready to combine his action-star credentials with a little more laughter, and this time he’ll be calling the shots

scraped.h1: National Bison Day: Buffalo Restoration Reconnects Tribal Nations to Culture, Food Sovereignty
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

National Bison Day recognizes an animal central to Indigenous culture and survival, as Tribal Nations continue efforts to restore buffalo herds, revitalize traditional food systems and strengthen tribal sovereignty.

Today is National Bison Day in the United States, observed annually on the first Saturday in November. The day honors an animal deeply revered by Tribal Nations — one that has sustained Indigenous peoples for generations, providing nutritious food, clothing, tools and materials for ceremonial and cultural practices.

In 2016, the American bison was designated the national mammal of the United States. Before westward expansion and mass slaughter decimated their populations, an estimated 60 million bison roamed North America, with the largest herds concentrated across what is now the central United States.

For generations, Native Americans throughout the Great Plains and other bison territories depended on the buffalo for virtually every aspect of life. The animal provided sustenance, supported tribal economies and held profound cultural and spiritual significance.

But that relationship was violently disrupted. By 1889, commercial hunting and government-backed eradication efforts had brought bison to the brink of extinction. Their near disappearance devastated Indigenous communities, disrupted traditional ways of life and contributed to the degradation of grassland ecosystems.

Today, Tribal Nations are helping lead the effort to reverse that history. Through conservation, herd restoration and Indigenous food sovereignty programs, tribes are bringing buffalo back to their lands — restoring not only an animal but also cultural connections, traditional food systems and an important part of their sovereignty.

Uplifting stories of Native traditions, language revitalization, and cultural innovation.

“The American bison is inextricably intertwined with Indigenous culture, grassland ecology and American history. While the overall recovery of bison over the last 130 years is a conservation success story, significant work remains to not only ensure that bison will remain a viable species but also to restore grassland ecosystems, strengthen rural economies dependent on grassland health and provide for the return of bison to Tribally owned and ancestral lands,” then-Interior Secretary Deb Haaland said in March 2023.

According to a report from Tribal Business News , the InterTribal Buffalo Council has transported more than 20,000 buffalo to Indian Country since its founding in 1992. As recently as 2024, approximately 25,000 buffalo lived on tribal lands, according to another Tribal Business News report .

Nationally, decades of conservation and restoration efforts have helped increase the number of wild bison in the United States from fewer than 500 to more than 15,000. The Interior Department currently manages approximately 11,000 bison in herds across 4.6 million acres of public lands in 12 states.

For Tribal Nations, however, the return of the buffalo represents far more than a conservation success. It is a restoration of relationships, traditions and food systems that were nearly destroyed. As buffalo return to tribal lands, they also help restore a measure of cultural continuity and Indigenous self-determination.

Levi “Calm Before the Storm” Rickert (Prairie Band Potawatomi Nation) is the founder, publisher, and editor of Native News Online. Rickert was awarded the Best Column Award in the print/online category... More by Levi Rickert

scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Bar Exam

Eugene Volokh | 11.7.2026 11:33 AM

From the Arkansas Supreme Court Thursday :

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The full statement from the court:

An internal review by Robert Brech, Executive Director of the Supreme Court of Arkansas's Office of Professional Conduct and Programs, has uncovered extensive irregularities involving the Court's Office of Professional Programs and the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination. The matter was turned over to state and federal authorities.

As of today, the Prosecuting Attorney's Office for the Sixth Judicial District filed formal criminal charges against Nancie Givens for 65 counts of tampering with a public record under Arkansas Code Annotated section 5-54-121 in connection with the alleged altering of numerous Arkansas Bar Examination scores and the deletion of files purportedly intended to conceal that misconduct. The charges followed a criminal investigation initiated in April 2026 by the Arkansas State Police and the Federal Bureau of Investigation. As always, all defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

Moving forward, we are committed to holding those involved accountable, taking continued corrective oversight of the Arkansas Bar Examination, and determining the appropriate course of action.

* * * * *

In February 2026, Givens, the former Executive Director of this Court's Office of Professional Programs, resigned. At that time, Robert Brech was serving as Executive Director of the Court's Office of Professional Conduct. Following Givens's resignation, the Court directed Brech to supervise the Office of Professional Programs, which oversees the administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination.

Upon his review of the Office of Professional Programs' records and administrative operations, Brech discovered that a large number of files and electronic communications were modified or deleted in early January 2026. Approximately 11,400 files were deleted or rendered unavailable. Most of those files included Arkansas Bar examinee applications, profiles, and examination score sheets that the Office of Professional Programs was required by this Court's rules to retain for twenty-five years.

Brech immediately notified a member of this Court, who directed him to determine the extent of the missing records and identify any other irregularities. On the basis of his review of the remaining files, Brech identified numerous discrepancies involving Arkansas Bar Examination scores across at least eight test administrations between July 2020 and July 2025. At that time, the matter was referred to the appropriate state and federal authorities.

Evidence exists that Givens harvested points from a number of examinees' scores and then added them to other examinees' scores within the same test administration. Thus, she unilaterally elevated some examinees' scores to the minimum passing score of 270 or greater. Brech also identified at least one instance in which score alterations may have reduced an examinee's score-who otherwise would have passed-to a failing score. And in at least one instance, the individual who should have received the top score on the Arkansas Bar Examination had their score reduced thereby naming another examinee as the recipient of the highest score on the exam. If these allegations are true, these actions constitute an unprecedented breach of public trust.

The vast majority of examinees who were previously informed that they had passed the Arkansas Bar Examination by the Office of Professional Programs did, in fact, pass the exam. Those examinees affected will be notified by the Office of Professional Conduct as soon as possible upon definitive confirmation of their status.

The Court is working with state and federal authorities to recover deleted and missing data, analyze all test administrations within that time frame, and determine the full scope of this grave and potentially criminal abuse of power. The people of Arkansas deserve, and the Court is committed to providing, total transparency in this matter. However, further disclosure will be forthcoming in a manner so as to not compromise the ongoing state and federal criminal investigations. Accordingly, additional disclosures will be limited as those efforts remain underway.

As an immediate step, independent of any state or federal criminal investigation or prosecution, Nancie Givens has been referred to the Office of Professional Conduct for investigation of extensive violations of the Arkansas Rules of Professional Conduct. See Ark. R. Prof. Conduct 8.1(a) & 8.4(a)-(e). Furthermore, new testing procedures and security measures were implemented with the February 2026 administration of the Arkansas Bar Examination to ensure systemic accountability and safeguard the integrity of the examination.

* * * * *

We recognize the profound consequences for affected examinees, the Bar, and the public at large. Our paramount concern is safeguarding litigants, the integrity of the legal profession, and public confidence in the administration of justice. While these matters remain under criminal and administrative investigation, we commit to pursue continued corrective measures in an effort to reestablish confidence in our institution.

scraped.description: Heavy rain has flooded temporary shelters used by Palestinians displaced during Israel's war with Hamas.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
scraped.body_text:
Ninety percent of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas

Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help.

Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter.

Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil.

Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation.

Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season.

Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate.

"We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help."

The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical.

Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts.

"We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said.

"But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help."

Israel has said it restricts the entry of items into Gaza that could be used for military purposes.

Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, told AFP news agency: "We no longer know how to protect our children.

"My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer."

Khaled al-Najjar, 41, told AFP: "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents, but also from the cold and the widespread diseases."

Veitch said aid workers were being "stopped on the street" by Gazans "begging us for help".

He continued: "They're absolutely desperate. We saw last year what winter does, and we had deaths from hypothermia last year.

"We can expect the same again unless we have very, very urgent action now."

A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.

Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.

Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.

The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.

Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.

scraped.title: The GOP’s post-midterms scramble is pure “Survivor”
scraped.description: JD Vance’s radical honesty is straight out of the season 51 playbook.
scraped.author: Gabriella Gladney
scraped.h1: The GOP’s Post-Midterms Scramble Is Pure “Survivor”
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Chuck Snyder/CBS/Getty; Robert Voets/CBS/Getty; Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty

The show Survivor is currently airing its 51st season, and you might think that after 25 years of television, every kind of strategizing and maneuvering has already been tried. But this fall, one contestant is making an attempt to manipulate his fellow contestants in a different way: by using honesty.

Conventional Survivor strategy entails keeping your cards close to your vest, lying to people’s faces so that your target doesn’t see the vote coming. But current contestant Devin Way’s strategy is to appear trustworthy so that he can more easily deceive down the line. “My whole thing now is weaponized honesty,” Way said at the start of the second episode, after ending up on the wrong side of the vote.

Another scramble is taking place after a different kind of vote: After the Republican Party suffered historic losses across the country this past Tuesday, many prominent GOP figures are scurrying to mitigate the damage. Texas Senator Ted Cruz went on X to call the results “a blue tsunami” and “a Watergate level repudiation.” House Speaker Mike Johnson, who told CBS in October that if Republicans lost the majority, “my intention is to stay and serve,” told his staff Wednesday morning that he won’t run for minority leader . And President Donald Trump admitted his war in Iran hurt Republicans—though he insisted, “ if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again .”

Vice President JD Vance has taken a page straight out of the Survivor season 51 playbook. On Wednesday, he posted a roughly 600-word diatribe on X that has the veneer of an honest assessment of why so many voters turned on the GOP. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote. “Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.” Donald Trump Jr. reposted it with three 💯 emojis .

But where was all this honesty before election night? In September, as missile strikes on Iran continued, Vance told reporters, “I wouldn’t call it a war right now.” In mid-October, he said at a CBS town hall that in “some ways” the US had “won decisively.” His honesty showed up only once it was useful, which makes it look a lot like a manipulation tactic, especially from a man widely seen as Trump’s potential heir .

At the first tribal council this Survivor season, Devin Way put everything out in the open. (Warning: spoilers ahead.) As everyone around him whispered about last-minute plans, he made it known that he planned to vote for his tribe-mate Jenna, but was blindsided himself when his ally Aaliyah left instead. His strategy, meant to show his tribe-mates exactly where he stood, mostly gave them what they needed to plan around him.

Vance and the Republican party are trying a similar sleight of hand: appearing to show the American people where they stand in hopes of winning them back. But as Tuesday’s outcome made clear, the American people aren’t buying it.

scraped.author: Sharmaine Johnson
scraped.h1: ‘It’s Like a Vacation’: Russell Wilson Sets the Bar High Ahead of Baby No. 5 as Ciara Gushes Over His Delivery Room Routine
scraped.body_text:
Russell Wilson ’s wish for baby number five, affectionately known as “Cinco,” has officially come true!

Three years after expressing his desire to expand their family, the former NFL star and his wife, Ciara, are preparing to welcome another addition.

Many wonder how the singer balances motherhood, marriage, and her thriving career while continuing to expand her family. Ciara has made one thing clear: having five children isn’t just Russell’s dream. It’s hers, too!

The couple announced the pregnancy in September with a social media post showcasing Ciara’s growing baby bump .

The couple announced the news in September with a social media post showing Ciara’s growing baby bump , giving fans a glimpse into the next chapter of their love story.

‘That Ciara Prayer Still Going Strong’: Russell Wilson and Ciara Shut Down the ‘Gram on Their Seven-Year Wedding Anniversary with New Photos

‘Definition Of Love’: Ciara Pulls at Heartstrings with Reaction to Russell Wilson’s Retirement — Proving Why They’re the Internet’s Favorite Couple

Since then, the excitement surrounding the newest addition has continued to build as the family prepares for its latest bundle of joy.

During a Friday appearance on “ Today with Jenna & Sheinelle ,” the “Goodies” singer opened up about her love for motherhood and how having a supportive husband makes the journey even more rewarding.

“I’m an only child, so I want a big family. I love being a mom. It’s my favorite job in the world,” Ciara shared.

The multihypenate also opened up about embracing life at 41. Ciara said she feels more empowered than ever as she prepares to welcome her fifth child.

“I just turned 41 w-o-n, okay, so I feel really good. It was hard for me to say 40, you know that, but now I’m embracing every part of my journey. I feel so empowered. We’re on our fifth baby, 41, and I’m feeling younger than ever. I am really excited,” she said.

And when it comes to welcoming a new baby, Russell knows exactly what his wife needs.

Rather than leaving Ciara with an ordinary delivery experience, he makes it his mission to create a comfortable, relaxed environment where she feels celebrated.

“He makes the process fun for me. It’s like a vacation. He gets into it. He has, like, the twinkle lights in my room that I love. He hooks it up. He has the Apple TV,” she revealed.

She said Russell goes above and beyond to make sure she is calm, cozy, and at peace with each delivery.

The couple are already raising four children: Future Zahir, Ciara’s son from her previous relationship with rapper Future, and their three children together, Sienna Princess, Win Harrison and Amora Princess.

The excitement wasn’t limited to the parents, either. When it came time to share the big news with their children, Ciara and Russell made the announcement a family moment to remember.

They initially set things up as a family photo opportunity for the grandparents.

But instead of an ordinary picture, Ciara had the children count to five in Spanish before revealing her baby bump. The surprise quickly turned into an unforgettable moment filled with excitement and joy from everyone.

Ciara once prayed for a husband, and judging by how things are going, that prayer came with a few extra blessings. But it seems motherhood remains one of her greatest joys.

During a May 10 interview with Angie Martinez, Ciara opened up about the qualities she wanted in a husband.

She said faith, discernment, and wisdom topped her list. She also wanted a man who genuinely loved children, knowing he would need to embrace her son.

Ciara added, “I prayed for a man that was worldly as well. Because I love to explore so someone that was gonna edify my world, that was important to me. I was ready to level up!”

Between a husband who goes above and beyond to make the delivery experience special and children who are just as excited about their newest sibling, it’s clear that baby Cinco is already surrounded by plenty of love.

scraped.title: What happens to the human soul when AI makes work optional? | Blaze Media
scraped.description: Allie Beth Stuckey asks pastor Jonny Ardavanis what Elon Musk’s AI utopia will do to people hardwired by God to work.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: What happens to the human soul when AI makes work optional?
scraped.body_text:
Allie Beth Stuckey asks pastor Jonny Ardavanis what Elon Musk’s AI utopia will do to people hardwired by God to work.

Tech entrepreneur Elon Musk has repeatedly predicted that a day is coming soon when AI and robotics will make traditional work optional in a utopian age of abundance, where humans will rely on universal high income while pursuing personal interests.

Trading the daily grind for a life of comfort and leisure may be compelling, but is it good for the human soul?

That’s the question Allie Beth Stuckey asked Stonebridge Bible Church Pastor Jonny Ardavanis, whose new book, “Get to Work: Seeing Your Daily Grind as God’s Good Gift,” explores why work is a divine gift rather than a burden to escape.

“I just think that’s going to be a horrible, horrible existence,” Ardavanis says of Musk’s AI utopia.

Regardless of one’s belief system, there’s an intrinsic understanding that work is a necessary part of the human experience, he argues, citing the oft-used expression “a job well done.”

“You mow the lawn, you see the stripes in your lawn, and you put your hands on your hips and you go, ‘There’s something Edenic about this,”’ Ardavanis says.

This sense of fulfillment, he says, can be traced back to the Garden of Eden, where Adam and Eve were first charged to cultivate and keep the garden as part of God’s original good design.

“Deep down, God has hardwired Eden into our souls, and we’re pining away to get back there,” he tells Allie, citing Ecclesiastes 3:11’s reminder that God has “set eternity in the human heart.”

But if AI removes the necessity of work, Ardavanis warns that the human heart, with its God-given orientation toward purpose and vocation, will wither.

“When a robot starts mowing your lawn, you know, you’re going to start to be stripped and starved of the opportunities to reflect God in that way. And I think it is going to be soul-crushing,” he says.

Work, he points out, isn’t just about doing; it’s also about thinking. When robots can think in our stead, what happens to the God-created mind?

“What does it mean to be made in the image of God? Well, it means we have a mind. It means that we are to engage that mind,” Ardavanis says. “Almost all of the instruction in the New Testament regarding the Christian life is what we do with our mind.”

“Your mind is God's gift to you, to employ it.”

This longing isn’t limited to believers. Even non-Christians recognize the irreplicable uniqueness of the human experience. Ardavanis points to globally famous actor Tom Cruise, who, in response to a question about AI’s impact on filmmaking, said , “There is nothing like human.”

“Even though Tom Cruise doesn’t know the God of the Bible, the God of the Bible has hardwired something into Tom Cruise’s heart,” he says. “We are to mirror and mimic God. When we do so, it gives us joy, and it gives us a level of purpose and meaning.”

“I’m looking into a world where people are excited about the absence of work, the three-day work week ... and biblically speaking, I think that that’s hard to reconcile with the fact that we’ve been given a mission by God.”

To hear more, watch the episode above.

To enjoy more of Allie’s upbeat and in-depth coverage of culture, news, and theology from a Christian, conservative perspective, subscribe to BlazeTV — the largest multi-platform network of voices who love America, defend the Constitution, and live the American dream.

articles.summary: Authorities in Poland are investigating a shooting that left six people dead and at least a 15 injured in the Main Market Square in Krakow, a cultural center of the historic city, according to officials. Emergency responders gather after a deadly shooting on Nov. 7 in the Main Market Square of Krakow, Poland.

scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

Authorities in Poland are investigating a shooting that left six people dead and at least a 15 injured in the Main Market Square in Krakow, a cultural center of the historic city, according to officials.

The shooter, a Polish national, was shot by police at the scene and taken to the hospital around 3 p.m. local time. The shots were fired from a vehicle moving through the area, Krakow officials said in a series of posts X.

An earlier post from the city’s official municipal government account said that investigators were working to determine the scale of the incident.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the perpetrator was wearing military-style fatigues and he used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

Dramatic video posted on social media shows what appears to be an injured police officer firing at the suspect before dropping to his knees and rolling over onto his back. The officer, who did not appear to have backup nearby, is seen struggling to reload his firearm and appeared to be clutching his right arm.

That officer’s condition was not known. Małopolska Police wrote in an X post that no officer had been killed, citing what they said were incorrect reports.

Other chilling video clips taken from the scene show a black sedan racing through the square. Dozens of people began running in various directions at the sound of gunfire.

Some social media clips depict responders attempting life-saving measures on victims. Lifeless bodies could be seen scattered around the streets after the attack.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also wrote on social media that police were trying to determine the circumstances surrounding the attack.

“We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland,” Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X. “America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow.”

The Main Market Square sits at the heart of Krakow’s medieval Old Town. Laid out in 1257, the sprawling plaza is home to the historic Cloth Hall and St. Mary’s Basilica.

scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Berkshire's Post-Buffett Era Gets Off To Rocky Start As AI Bets Stumble
scraped.body_text:
With Warren Buffett gone for not even a year, Berkshire Hathaway is already facing questions over its investment decisions. Under new CEO Greg Abel, the conglomerate has made a multibillion-dollar push into artificial intelligence, only to see some of its biggest bets stumble as enthusiasm for the technology fades, according to Bloomberg .

In his first year at the helm, Abel has committed $10 billion to Google parent Alphabet and another $930 million to Italian technology group Bending Spoons, marking a shift from Buffett's traditionally cautious approach to technology investments.

But the timing has raised concerns. Alphabet shares have fallen more than 24% since June, slipping below Berkshire's purchase price, while Bending Spoons has also retreated following an initial rally.

CEO Greg Abel

Still, analysts say Abel may be taking a longer-term view, much like Buffett did with his highly profitable Apple investment in 2016. With $365.5 billion in cash at the end of the second quarter, Berkshire has plenty of room to capitalize on lower valuations and expand its AI exposure.

Meanwhile, Berkshire's upcoming third-quarter earnings will offer a broader look at the conglomerate's performance under Abel. Solid US economic growth could support its businesses, although inflation and high fuel prices may weigh on retail operations.

Investors will also be watching Geico, where higher claims costs and advertising spending hurt recent profits, and railroad operator BNSF, which could benefit from stronger freight volumes and fuel surcharges.

Bloomberg notes that another focus will be share buybacks. Berkshire resumed repurchases earlier this year after a lengthy pause, but its stock has since climbed to record highs, potentially discouraging further purchases.

The results will offer an early test of Abel's leadership as he seeks to put Berkshire's enormous cash reserves to work while preserving the investment discipline that defined the Buffett era. He will have to do so in an era where Democrats now control a large majority of AI/data center planned capacity in the US...

Recall, under Buffett, Berkshire spent years building one of the largest cash piles in corporate America, more than doubling its reserves from roughly $150 billion at the end of 2021 to over $370 billion by late 2025.

Buffett largely resisted chasing soaring stock valuations, preferring to sit on the sidelines rather than overpay for investments. Now, less than a year after his departure, Abel is putting billions of those reserves to work in AI, with early results proving less than encouraging.
