scraped.title: AI Companies Are Preying on Under-Resourced Schools, Students Say
scraped.description: Poorer schools are being lured into spending their limited funds on AI tech in the face of chronic understaffing.
scraped.author: Finley Williams
scraped.h1: AI Companies Are Preying on Under-Resourced Schools, Students Say
scraped.body_text:
Poorer schools are being lured into spending their limited funds on AI tech in the face of chronic understaffing.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

When high school librarian Tara Donnelly talks to her classes about how AI has changed online search, she always starts with one question: “What is Google’s main goal?”

Students generally reply, “give you information,” or “tell you the answers to things” — until someone hits the nail on the head and ventures, “Make money.”

Donnelly, a member of the AI working group in the Chicago Teachers Union, says Google is one of many tech companies that are centrally motivated by profit, despite purporting to serve other aims. As AI developers like Microsoft and OpenAI push to integrate their products into U.S. schools and pupils’ lives more broadly, Donnelly said she believes that students are entitled to a clear understanding of the forces shaping their education.

“The ed tech industry is profiting off of running a race with school districts to see who’s going to adopt their chatbot or whatever their tech piece is, and it’s forced on students,” Donelly told Truthout . “Students should have the opportunity to refuse to use AI if they want to. They deserve to have the whole picture and not just to be the money-maker for these ed tech pieces.”

“Students should have the opportunity to refuse to use AI if they want to.”

Indeed, experts, education advocates, and students interviewed by Truthout portrayed a bleak reality in which desperation creates pressure for marginalized students to use AI, and for under-resourced schools to adopt it as a surface-level solution to structural problems like chronic underfunding and understaffing. Many education policy analysts say that in the absence of conclusive evidence that AI improves learning outcomes, companies’ pitch of AI tools as an educational cure-all distracts from more pressing needs: holistic, culturally responsive education that prioritizes human interaction and productive struggle.

Donnelly — an educator at Foreman College and Career Academy, a predominantly Latine school on Chicago’s Northwest Side — said she thinks about these concerns specifically in the context of racially equitable schooling.

“Whenever we’re talking about education, we’re talking about students of color. We always have to be very intentional about, how is this going to affect these students and what do we need to do differently? ” Donnelly said.

Yeisbel Peña, a Latino high school senior in Boston who is interested in computer science, said it’s possible for young students to use AI to advance their thinking. But “raw education — just one-on-one, [the] old type of education — is the most appropriate way a person can actually engage and learn,” he said.

“When you have AI, it just says ‘yes,’ constantly. Any question you ask, it’ll probably just tell you yes,” Peña told Truthout. “It won’t give you complexity. And I believe that that complexity that you get from being in a classroom with a teacher … without it, you’re kind of just limiting yourself.”

Still, he said that in the absence of well-staffed after-school homework help, students at his charter school, which mostly serves students of color, often turn to chatbots instead. Peña described classrooms with only one teacher to assist 10 or 20 students.

“All of them trying to get one-on-one help, it definitely gets very diluted,” Peña said. “So you definitely don’t get the best quality of help.”

In Raleigh, North Carolina, Sacdiya Rashid, 17, said she sometimes chooses to turn to chatbots, which have helped her understand difficult math problems. Though she said that students can harm their learning by becoming over-reliant on the technology, she believes there are commercial influences at play beyond any individual student’s choices.

“I think these AI companies are trying to benefit off of students, like, struggling students,” she told Truthout.

“I don’t think we should really blame students for these AI companies and [the] narratives they’re trying to push. Because I think it just hurts the students,” Rashid said.

Indeed, students at Donnelly’s school in Chicago nominally have access to after-school tutoring, but the primarily immigrant, first-generation and high-poverty student body was hit hard by “Operation Midway Blitz,” President Donald Trump’s anti-immigration raids in the city last year. Because of that, Donnelly said, “There’s not a lot of after-school life within the school.”

“So it’s tough to get extra help,” she said. “In my experience here, it’s more that they’re using [AI] to do the work for them, because they either don’t have time or maybe aren’t understanding it as well as they need to.”

Even as AI chatbots and other AI-enabled ed tech tools spread rapidly in U.S. schools — through both formal and informal avenues — there is extremely limited evidence supporting the conclusion that this technology supports student learning.

Stanford University’s AI Hub for Education within the SCALE Initiative seeks to find and disseminate equitable education practices through research. The organization earlier this year conducted a meta-analysis of K-12 education studies to evaluate the presence of causal evidence indicating AI’s impacts on students’ educations. Lily Fesler, a senior research associate at SCALE, told Truthout that although causal evidence is the only way to concretely judge the technology’s effects, “it’s really hard to conduct randomized control trials, quasi-experimental studies, so there just aren’t a lot of those studies right now.”

Still, senior technologist at the Center for Democracy & Technology’s Equity in Civic Technology Project, Hannah Quay-de la Vallee, told Truthout that poorer school districts may still be coaxed into spending their limited funds on unproven technology. In August, the Center for Democracy & Technology published a report examining how administrative AI use could potentially cause disparate impacts in schools, violating students’ civil rights — for example, AI content filtering on student devices could block material related to immigration or sexual orientation, or AI-enabled predictive analytics designed to identify “at-risk” students could mistakenly flag students of color.

“In a school with more resources, more unrestricted resources, they have more avenues for saying, ‘Well, we want to accomplish X goal, and we could do that with AI, or we could do it by hiring more staff, or we could do it with enrichment programs’ or whatever it may be,” said Quay-de la Vallee. “In other cases, you’re going to have schools that have funding that has to be spent on tech.”

At the start of September, New York City Public Schools banned classroom AI use for K-8 students. Shortly after this, the Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) announced a policy limiting AI use for all of its roughly 370,000 students. In Chicago, advocates have pressured Board of Education candidates to pledge their support for an AI moratorium.

In interviews with Truthout , activists named ChatGPT, Gemini, and Amira Learning (an AI-enabled reading program) among the tools they’ve seen appear in their schools, both formally and informally.

Across the country, parents, teachers, and students have grown apprehensive of modern technology’s potential adverse effects on student learning and well-being, and suspicious of Big Tech’s motives.

Indeed, recent reporting has revealed tech companies’ decades-long concerted effort to embed themselves more deeply into U.S. schools.

Among many examples, journalist Natasha Singer cites Google’s push to “[hook] students early on services like Gmail and Chrome. The real revenue, made from amassing consumers’ data and showing ads based on their online activities, would come later.”

Google’s narrative that one-to-one tech programs would enhance student learning had considerable buy-in; schools have spent tens of billions of dollars on Chromebooks and other ed tech programs and devices since the tech wave began. Schools’ adoption of Google products only accelerated during the pandemic, when Chromebooks seemed essential to distance learning.

“It feels very predatory to be coming to the most under-resourced schools and communities and trying to sell these things.”

The Trump administration, for its part, has encouraged the wholesale adoption of AI throughout the economy, and particularly in U.S. schooling; in 2025, Trump signed an executive order designed to promote AI education and integration for youth and teachers across the country. A new opportunity to create lifelong customers has emerged, and tech companies are vying to become the dominant AI peddler.

Trump-era AI industry lobbyists continue to exert their influence over U.S. politicians, promoting anti-regulatory views and sidelining the counsel of academics and impartial researchers. The goal is to underplay AI’s potential risks and externalities in every aspect of contemporary life.

Silicon Valley, Singer writes, is exercising its power — and “the public education system, hungry for resources to improve opportunities for students, has become an avenue for multitrillion-dollar companies to enact their agendas.”

Parent and educator activists with the Los Angeles chapter of Schools Beyond Screens and New York City’s AI Moratorium Coalition told a similar story, in which cash-strapped public schools feel they have little choice but to invest in technology.

“Everyone is stretched so thin. Education is so deeply devalued and de-professionalized and defunded. We are all so desperate to the point where, when a sales pitch comes in, someone is willing to just shake hands and sign the contract,” Alisha Maynoush Mernick, an organizer with Schools Beyond Screens LAUSD, told Truthout . “It feels very predatory to be coming to the most under-resourced schools and communities and trying to sell these things, and trying to frame it as giving out of their own goodwill.”

AI Moratorium Coalition steering committee member Kaliris Salas-Ramirez described the bind in which schools and educators sometimes find themselves: “If we don’t have the opportunity to invest in that human capital — because it’s going to take too long, because we can’t find the teacher, because we can’t find the interventionist — then [people say], OK, well maybe this could be the next best thing.”

Mernick sees a bigger issue in AI and ed tech adoption.

“This is just one symptom of a much, much larger problem, which is that when we underfund public schools, we are creating an opportunity for companies to swoop in. That’s privatization in a nutshell,” Mernick said. “It really is just funneling public taxpayer money out of public institutions and into corporate pockets.”

For Rashid, the Raleigh senior, AI tools that don’t improve student learning have no place in the classroom.

“It doesn’t really help the student, and it’s only really so that AI companies can kind of line their pockets,” she said.

Truthout is funded almost entirely by readers — that’s why we can speak truth to power and cut against the mainstream narrative. But independent journalists at Truthout face mounting political repression under Trump.

scraped.h1: Canadians choosing pricier destinations over Cuba amid crisis: travel agents
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Δ

2 comments

Maybe we should let canadians go. They will see what a socialist/communist country looks like, which is where we’re heading.

I stopped going to Cuba long ago. I found it garbage and moved over mainly to Mayan Riviera for basically the same price but better quality.

As the winter holiday season approaches, one of the most popular sunny destinations for Canadian travellers remains out of reach.

The United States’ oil blockade against Cuba triggered severe fuel shortages in the country and prompted Canadian airlines to indefinitely suspend flights to the island destination earlier this year.

Travel agents say Canadians looking to escape the cold weather this year will have to pay more than what they’re used to for affordable all-inclusive packages in Cuba.

Ashley Harold, a travel agent at Flight Centre Canada, said Mexico, Dominican Republic and several other Caribbean countries and territories such as Aruba, Barbados and Jamaica seem to be getting most of the diversions.

“There isn’t one new Cuba, if you will. Canadians, they’re really spreading their winter travel across a much wider mix of destinations and trip types,” she said in a recent interview.

“We’re also seeing some travellers consider Caribbean cruises or tours to still-warm places like Costa Rica or Peru.”

Domestic tourism is also gaining traction as some Canadians are choosing to visit “fantastic” winter destinations, from Alberta to the West Coast, she said.

“Folks, now more than ever, are wanting to explore their own backyard and keep their dollar within Canada,” she said.

Even though advance bookings have become a new normal after COVID-19, the lack of Cuban vacations has led Canadians to make reservations in other destinations much earlier for best pricing and choice, Harold said.

Cuba welcomed more than a million Canadians annually before the pandemic but that number has been steadily declining in recent years, with visits dropping to around 700,000 in 2025, according to Statistics Canada. The agency recorded 127,000 Canadian visits to Cuba in the first quarter of this year.

Those numbers dropped significantly after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed the oil blockade on Cuba early this year, and the Canadian government subsequently issued a travel advisory due to the shortage of medicine, food and fuel in the country. It still advises Canadians to avoid all non-essential travel to Cuba.

After airlines suspended flights and major hotel chains pulled out of Cuba, the country’s tourism industry and the local economy that heavily depended on it were further devastated. The country of around 11 million people is facing a humanitarian crisis caused by the latest sanctions and the decades-long U.S. trade embargo.

Cuba’s tourism market was dominated by Canadians who relished its affordable winter vacation options. Now, they need to spend hundreds of dollars more to explore other destinations or cut down the number of trips they are making each year, travel agents say.

John Wood, president of Durham Travel east of Toronto, said Cuba visitors are “value conscious” and want to travel as often as they can within their budgets.

Some of Durham Travel’s clients used to go to Cuba “three, four or five times a year … because they could go for a very reasonable price, get away and enjoy the sun and beautiful beaches,” he said in a recent interview.

“And now they can’t do that anymore.”

Wood said his travel agency’s sales to Cuba dropped from more than $389,000 last year to just $24,000 so far into 2026.

Meanwhile, travel sales for the Dominican Republic increased from about $1 million in 2025 to nearly 1.3 million so far this year, he said.

“The Dominican Republic appears to have absorbed most of the difference from Cuba,” he said, noting travellers’ concerns about crime and large seaweed blooms in Mexico.

At Flight Centre Canada, however, Mexico remains the top destination — even if it’s pricier, Harold said.

A seven-day package at a four-star resort in Varadero, Cuba with a flight from Toronto cost under $1,400 per person around the last holiday season, she said. Comparable trips to Mexico, Dominican Republic and Jamaica cost around $1,800 this year, according to Flight Centre data.

“So, for travellers that are used to Cuba pricing, there may need to be a reset in expectations before they start shopping,” Harold said.

But that means tourists can “get creative” with their vacation plans this holiday season, she said.

“I think this is a great opportunity for Canadians to branch out a little bit more with their travels and experience something new.”

scraped.title: Berkshire Hathaway more than doubles buybacks in third quarter as earnings decline
scraped.description: Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
scraped.author: Fred Imbert
scraped.h1: Berkshire Hathaway more than doubles buybacks in third quarter as earnings decline
scraped.body_text:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.

The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.

The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.

Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.

The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.

Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.

Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .

Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.

— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

scraped.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
scraped.description: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Michel Barnier says there will be 'no cherry-picking' in a deal for the UK to returns to the EU

The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.

The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.

But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.

He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.

Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.

But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.

He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".

"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.

Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime .

Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again

Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.

Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.

Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.

He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.

Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.

The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".

Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."

Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".

The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".

Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".

Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.

Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.

​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".

Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

CHICAGO — Lipoprotein(a), a genetic risk factor for cardiovascular disease carried by 1 in 5 people, is the target of novel therapies trying to cut down heart attacks, strokes, and deaths in those at risk. The growing field of research aimed at the particle took a hit earlier this year when top-line results showed an experimental drug reduced Lp(a) but failed to lower serious outcomes.

More details of the study, funded by Novartis, were revealed Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine .

Advertisement

In the Phase 3 trial, the drug pelacarsen dramatically lowered Lp(a), a mashup of lipids and proteins that at high levels can heighten the risk of severe heart problems. But despite lower Lp(a), the HORIZON trial showed no difference in heart attacks, strokes, urgent coronary revascularization, or deaths in participants followed for almost five years who were randomly selected to take the drug or a placebo.

If only the fun loving houthi terrrr or ists leadership just didn’t hide behind women and children the world would be a better place.

Airstrikes hit homes in a village near Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, on Saturday, killing at least 25 people and wounding 30 others, mostly women and children, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry said.

Speaking to The Associated Press, Anees Alasbahi accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out the strikes on al-Shariya. The AP could not independently verify the claims, and Saudi Arabia’s Information Ministry did not immediately reply to an AP request for comment.

The toll reflected the rapid worsening of Yemen’s civil war, where a yearslong truce fell apart over the summer. Fighting has escalated between the Iranian-backed Houthis — who control Sanaa, the north and the west of the country — and their Saudi-backed opponents based in the south and east.

On Friday, an airstrike in a market in southern Yemen killed at least 30 people, according to Houthi officials. The Houthis and Yemen’s Saudi-backed military each blamed the other for that strike.

Footage from Houthi-run Al-Masirah TV of the aftermath of Saturday’s strikes showed staff carrying limp bodies of multiple young children out of ambulances at a local hospital. One little girl’s head had been cleaved open. Other children lay on stretchers, bloodied and bandaged as staff tended to them.

Footage from the farming village — located in Houthi-ruled territory about 15 kilometers (10 miles) northeast of Sanaa — showed the rubble of destroyed houses and dust filling the air as people hid in nearby agricultural fields.

Alasbahi told Al-Masirah at least 25 people were killed, up from a toll of 22 he gave earlier to the AP. He told the channel that civilians were still buried under the rubble of houses hit in the strikes, and that subsequent strikes targeted emergency workers as they tried to pull survivors out of the wreckage.

Footage showed one wounded man covered in dust and wearing a first responder’s orange vest being helped out of an ambulance.

The renewal of fighting has raised fears that Yemen will be dragged back into the horrors of a civil war that has dragged on for more than a decade and created one of the world’s worst humanitarian disasters.

The war began when the Houthis stormed out of the north in 2014 and seized the capital, driving out the internationally recognized government. Saudi Arabia assembled a coalition backing the government, waging a yearslong campaign of air bombardment that brought it international condemnation over civilian deaths.

The war has killed at least 150,000 people, according to the U.N., along with widespread deaths from hunger and disease outbreaks. The lines of control in the country changed little for years, and a truce was reached in 2022.

The relative quiet, however, collapsed over the summer when the Houthis launched new offensives in response, they said, to Saudi Arabia’s continued blockade of their territory. The rebels made a lightning advance capturing much of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. At the same time, they have stepped up strikes on Saudi Arabia, targeting oil and military infrastructure and shipping in the Red Sea.

Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition has said it has been carrying out airstrikes in Houthi-held territory, targeting the rebels’ military infrastructure. The heaviest ground fighting has centered around Taiz, a strategic, government-held southern city that the Houthis have now encircled, worsening an already dire humanitarian situation among civilians. Residents are struggling to secure drinking water and food supplies as the Houthis restrict movement into the city. ___ Abou AlJoud reported from Beirut.

CHICAGO — Out-of-control inflammation is often called the root of all evil in cardiovascular and metabolic disease. Recent clinical trial results, described in brief in July , showed that while an experimental drug could lower two biomarkers of inflammation, it didn’t limit serious heart events in patients with severe illness.

The Novo Nordisk study, called ZEUS, showed that the monoclonal antibody ziltivekimab reduced levels of the inflammatory cytokine interleukin-6, or IL-6, but that drop did not translate into fewer heart attacks, strokes, or deaths in the treatment group compared to those taking a placebo. Once top-line results were disclosed, Novo halted two other trials of the drug called HERMES and ATHENA after a data monitoring committee found in September they were unlikely to succeed.

Advertisement

The ZEUS results were detailed further on Saturday at the American Heart Association’s scientific sessions and published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine .

scraped.h1: Before AI takes a teacher's job, send it to the district office
scraped.body_text:
A teacher’s hunt for a payroll answer led through unanswered emails, two buildings, and a maze of offices. A chatbot could have saved the trip — and maybe a few salaries.

With shrinking enrollment and ballooning expenses, public school districts across the country are not only facing massive budget deficits but are also quickly losing the goodwill of the public.

Here in Texas, districts like Houston and Austin are seeing huge budget shortfalls. Around the country, school systems are on the path to bankruptcy yet have done little to cut spending.

So many meetings, conferences, and email exchanges could be phased out, leaving more time to actually teach students.

Many district leaders and their respective school boards seem to believe that these enrollment drops are nothing serious or that they can blame someone else for the problem and absolve themselves of responsibility. Consequently, instead of making significant spending cuts, they go on draining rainy-day funds or spending money they don’t have.

Worse still, the bulk of these expenses do not go toward hiring more teachers , but instead go toward administrative staff, extracurricular programs, curriculum and technology specialists, and countless office workers with undefined roles working in office buildings that the district inexplicably owns and maintains.

In the rare instances that cuts are made, it is mostly the teaching staff — that is, the actual people in the classroom working with students — who are affected.

Realistically, can anything be done to prevent these districts from imploding in spectacular fashion? Speaking as a teacher currently in the trenches, this might be a place where AI can reduce costs while boosting instructional quality.

I’m not talking about replacing teachers with AI-enhanced educational software, turning classrooms into computer lounges, and replacing principals with bored babysitters making sure the kids continue vegetating in front of their screens.

According to a recent essay in the New York Times, this is the bold new idea at Alpha private schools: “At Alpha, there are no traditional teachers, few books, and little paper. All of the academic lessons are delivered via apps, and students can earn lavish prizes for completing their work. Adults are present, but only as motivational guides.”

Predictably, this approach to education has mixed results. While the stronger students usually cruise through content and perform well on their standardized tests, the weaker students who need more help will often experience delays in their progress and opt out of the program altogether.

More importantly, it neglects the most important aspects of schooling: socialization and humanization. Education is as much about results as it is about relationships. Teachers do not merely dispense information to compliant drones who mentally download this information through note-taking and worksheets. Teachers are supposed to design their instruction around the needs of their students, govern their classes equitably, and connect the content of their subject to the world outside the classroom.

RELATED: The forgotten colleges that could restore hope to American education

Crisserbug/Getty Images

When this learning is outsourced to a computer and mediated through a screen, everything is reduced and flattened — of course, the superficial people in tech will mistake this for efficiency.

Separated from the outside world, students engage with material through drill-and-kill pedagogy, working through assessments that offer practice on state standards. While this works well enough for math instruction, it becomes far less effective in the sciences or humanities.

With all this said, there still might be a key role for AI in public education. While it can’t replace teachers, it can replace many of the people around them. And if used properly, it can also enhance the work that teachers do.

In terms of cutting down bureaucratic bloat, all districts, even solvent ones, could use a DOGE-style audit to identify useless positions, departments, and redundancies. There are countless individuals in a school district who could permanently disappear without anyone noticing. Many of them are collecting paychecks and later pensions for irrelevant work, but no one notices them because they are usually hidden.

Case in point: Years ago, I had a question about one of my paychecks. I sent out emails to the dozen HR people listed on the district website to see who could answer my question. When no one replied, I took a half-day off and drove over to the administration building to see if I could talk to someone face-to-face. Apparently, I went to the wrong administrative building and had to drive to the other one a mile away.

Once there, the receptionist directed me to a hallway on the fourth floor to look for a person who knew about paychecks. After wandering about for 10 minutes, I finally found someone who directed me to yet another person who finally had the answer to my question.

RELATED: AI doesn’t know you, but a good physician does

Moor Studio/Getty Images

Most public teachers have a story like this. Some random thing prompts them to take a journey through their district’s Kafkaesque bureaucracy, and then they realize just how many useless people are on the payroll. Today, most queries could be answered in a few seconds with a chatbot. Moreover, most duties done by non-teaching staff, like setting up schedules, organizing information, compiling data and documentation, and making presentations, could be done with AI.

Just as importantly, the people who work with students could accomplish far more with AI support. So many meetings, conferences, and email exchanges could be phased out, leaving more time to actually teach students. So many roles requiring specialized training and higher salaries could either be removed entirely or replaced by those with general experience and aptitude.

In such a system — which would resemble something like Singapore’s exceptional educational program — good teachers would be rewarded with more respect, authority, and income while administrators would function as their subordinates. Good teachers are far less replaceable than administrators, so they should be encouraged to stay in the classroom and help more students.

Like any large organization, most school districts have grown into something so unwieldy and chaotic that enacting meaningful reform is next to impossible. Those with the authority to do so are usually too incompetent and complacent to do anything, and those with competence and wherewithal to do something lack the authority. Meanwhile, taxpayers funding public schools tend to focus their ire on the people they can see and ignore the true source of the problem.

It may be difficult to imagine an alternative to the current dysfunction, but it can be done. And if done right, it will be a good thing for everyone involved.

Auguste Meyrat

scraped.body_text:
President Trump appeared to confirm Friday that the U.S. military had carried out limited strikes on targets in Iran. Following reports of explosions on Iran’s Qeshm Island, Hengam Island, and the mainland area of Bandar Abbas, the president told reporters, “We do minor strikes, but they knock out. [Iran] built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five.” These are the first U.S. strikes since the midterm elections.

Also on Friday, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it would offer a reward of up to $20 million for “information about Iran’s nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment, and associated personnel.”

Attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have continued, with the UK Maritime Trade Operations organization reporting at least eleven ships hit during the week ending November 6.

AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline is $4.04 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.21 per gallon.

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

scraped.body_text:

It’s cranberry season in southeastern Massachusetts. At bogs throughout the region, growers are collecting the ruby-red berries destined for holiday cakes, juice bottles, and cans of jellied sauce. At two farms, however, the harvesting process looks a little different: Pickers are navigating equipment around metal poles in the shade of solar panels.

The two bogs are the first in the country — perhaps the world — to grow cranberries beneath an operating solar installation. This fall marks the second season cranberries have been harvested from beneath the panels.

“We are literally proving it can be done,” said Prateek Tare, co-founder and executive vice president of Distributed Energy Infrastructure. His company constructed the two projects — a 4.4-megawatt array paired with a 13.5-megawatt-hour battery in the town of Kingston, and a 1-MW solar array in neighboring Plymouth.

Solar development is a major part of Massachusetts’ plan to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2050. The state has offered solar incentives since 2001, evolving and expanding them over the decades to drive even more development.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

However, the question of where to site solar projects has become a major point of contention in the densely populated and heavily wooded state. Building on rooftops and parking lots in developed areas can increase costs and limit generation capacity. But proposals for arrays on previously undeveloped land often spark protests from locals worried about the character of their community and environmental groups opposed to disrupting ecosystems. Using pre-cleared farmland has potential, but raises concerns about taking agricultural acres out of production. Many of these same dynamics are at play in communities across the U.S.

One of the solutions Massachusetts has been encouraging is agrivoltaics, or dual-use solar, which involves building solar panels above active agricultural operations. This strategy, which is gaining traction nationwide, allows farmland to be used for energy generation even as livestock graze or crops flourish beneath the elevated arrays.

In 2018, Massachusetts became the first state to offer a financial boost to dual-use solar projects like these. The state’s solar incentive program pays participants a set rate for every kilowatt-hour of electricity they generate; an array with a capacity between 1 MW and 5 MW currently gets a base rate of 23.17 cents. Agrivoltaic projects get an extra 9 cents per kilowatt-hour.

That can be enough money to attract developers interested in leasing land for solar arrays or, less commonly, buying property outright with an agreement to keep it in agricultural use. Farmers who agree to lease are also generally paid for their services maintaining the landscape around the panels and poles.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

In Kingston and Plymouth, clean energy developer Greenbacker Renewables bought the land, which had been home to cranberry-growing operations for decades, from farmers who were ready to get out of the business. Greenbacker then worked with Distributed Energy Infrastructure to build the arrays, and hired Iain Ward, a solar consultant and longtime cranberry farmer in the area, to manage the growing operations. Both projects use a community solar model, selling power to customers interested in the lower prices and environmental benefits offered by renewable energy.

Solar can be particularly advantageous for cranberry farmers in Massachusetts, which grows more of the fruit than any state other than Wisconsin. While sheep farms and cornfields can often be sold to housing or commercial developers, cranberry bogs are protected wetlands: Even if they go out of production, they cannot be built on. Not all bogs are well placed to connect to the grid, but for those that are, solar panels can be a financial lifeline.

“This is a farm viability opportunity,” Ward said.

Figuring out how to build a solar array over a cranberry bog was a unique puzzle, Tare said. The first challenge was the foundations. For most solar arrays, the foundation goes 8 to 10 feet into the ground, he said. But in a cranberry bog, you have to go well past that to find ground solid and stable enough to hold the pilings. It took some trial and error to find the right machine to sink piles that deep. Wiring couldn’t be buried in the boggy ground, so it had to be hung overhead.

“You’re trying to figure it out from a farmer’s perspective,” said Tare, who worked closely with Ward on the design of the two projects.

The resulting installations have photovoltaic panels mounted 10 feet off the ground on an axis that allows them to tilt throughout the day to follow the sun. Pilings are spread farther from each other than standard so that harvesting equipment can be moved freely through the bog.

These successes in Kingston and Plymouth have led to more agrivoltaic opportunities for Tare’s company, including arrays in apple orchards, a cattle pasture, and a Christmas tree farm. Preliminary work is also underway at another bog.

Meanwhile, a stalled cranberry solar project in the nearby town of Carver could be resuscitated. Five years ago, a different pair of bogs there were set to become the nation’s first cranberry agrivoltaic operations. The arrays were built, and crops are growing beneath them, but the company behind the developments went bankrupt before they could get up and running. Today, the new bog owner has ​“every intention to finish them,” Ward said.

“They’re not a failure,” Ward said. ​“There is an opportunity for them to be finished.”

Tare expects future cranberry projects to get easier each time, as the company carries forward the lessons it learns. Though momentum has been slow so far, Ward expects development to accelerate soon.

“It is picking up steam, and the lessons learned have been significant, he said. ​“When you change a paradigm, it takes a little time.”

scraped.title: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections
scraped.description: The U.S. and Iran are on a collision course as tensions in the Middle East simmer.
scraped.author: Spencer Kimball
scraped.h1: Risk of Iran war escalation remains high despite Democratic sweep in U.S. midterm elections
scraped.body_text:
In this article

The U.S. and Iran are careening toward renewed war despite growing hopes this week that the Democrats' decisive midterm election victory will bring the conflict to an end, analysts say.

Crude oil prices fell more than 16% over the last five trading days after Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Republicans' stinging loss on the war. Vance's remarks raised questions about whether there is still support within the administration to continue the conflict with Iran.

The Democrats plan to use their comfortable majorities in both chambers of Congress to pass a war powers resolution that demands President Donald Trump end the war. But tensions in the Middle East have not eased since the election, and the Democrats aren't sworn in until January, the analysts say.

"Throughout the week, we were struck by the divergence between deepening escalation concerns in the Gulf and the headline driven off-ramp optimism of market participants thousands of miles away," Helima Croft, head of global commodity strategy at RBC Capital Markets, told investors in a note Friday.

Several oil tankers have come under attack near Oman since the election, killing one seafarer, according to maritime security agencies. Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to fire missiles at neighboring Saudi Arabia.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military buildup continues, with a third carrier strike group en route to the region. The consulting group Rapidan Energy sees an 80% chance that fighting will resume as diplomacy stalls.

President Donald Trump told reporters Thursday that he will make a decision soon on whether to attack Iran again.

"I would rather not destroy the rest of the country if possible but maybe I'll have to," Trump said in the Oval Office. "You'll know soon enough."

"We're locked and loaded," the president said. "If we have to do the rest of the Iran thing, we're very much locked in."

Crude oil prices will vault above $100 a barrel again in response to renewed fighting, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan and a former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. Brent crude, the international benchmark, was trading above $97 on Friday while U.S. crude was around $90.

"President Donald Trump is determined as a legacy item, almost at all costs, to prevent Iran from getting a nuclear weapon, having them give up their nuclear capabilities," McNally told CNBC's " Squawk Box Asia " on Friday.

"The Iranian regime, on the other hand, is not willing to do it," the analyst said. The escalation dynamic remains in place so long as that core difference between the U.S. and Iran persists, he said.

The risk of war is still alive, especially since Trump doesn't face anymore future elections, said Amos Hochstein, a former energy advisor to President Joe Biden. Gasoline, diesel and jet fuel prices would all surge as a consequence, Hochstein told CNBC's " Power Lunch " Friday.

Tehran has been taunting the Trump administration since the election. The social media account of Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei said the "process of the U.S.'s collapse has accelerated" after the midterm results.

And Congress is unlikely to pass a war powers resolution until Democrats take control in January. Trump can veto such a resolution in any case.

The main leverage Congress will have is the power of the purse, Croft said. Government funding expires on Dec. 11 and negotiations for another continuing resolution could drag into 2027, she said. This would give Democrats more leverage when they take power in January, the analyst said.

"Importantly, deferring funding decisions would not immediately constrain Trump's ability to conduct military operations, but could significantly reshape the administration's longer-term funding outlook," Croft told investors.

Trump discussed diplomatic efforts to de-escalate tensions in the region with the emir of Qatar during a Friday phone call, according to Qatar's state news agency .

An unnamed senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran sent a nuclear proposal to the U.S. through Qatar. Tehran will only discuss the proposal after the U.S. meets its demands, the Iranian official told Reuters.

Trump seemed to dismiss the diplomatic efforts Thursday.

"Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," the president said. "They're not doing anything without our approval. It doesn't make any difference what they're looking at," he said of the diplomatic efforts.

articles.title: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
articles.summary: Anthropic is poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market at a time when the public is increasingly leary of the industry.
articles.ai_summary: Anthropic is set to become the first AI company to go public amid growing public skepticism towards the tech industry.

scraped.title: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
scraped.description: Anthropic is poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market at a time when the public is increasingly leary of the industry.
scraped.author: Ashley Capoot
scraped.h1: Anthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centers
scraped.body_text:
Americans were unequivocal at the ballot box this week as they expressed disdain for tech billionaires and mistrust of artificial intelligence. With that backdrop, Anthropic is about to try to go public.

The AI company is gearing up for a potentially historic IPO, likely targeting mid-November for its Nasdaq debut. CNBC reported on Friday that Anthropic investors see the company aiming for a valuation of $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion, down from a target of $2 trillion that had been floated in recent months.

From Wall Street to Main Street, it's becoming a tougher environment for Anthropic. The Nasdaq on Thursday suffered its steepest drop in 19 months, and it's down to start November after October marked its worst month since March 2025. Chipmakers and neoclouds, the companies most closely tied to the AI buildout, are getting hit the hardest.

Voters rebuked AI in Tuesday's midterm elections, while sending Democrats to sweeping congressional victories across the country. Candidates who advocated for more stringent AI regulation won handily in states like Michigan, Ohio, Texas and Georgia, which will all now have Democratic governors, and local communities opposed data center-related ballot measures in 40 out of 41 cases .

More than half of voters said AI data centers were a "crucial" or "major factor" in who they supported for Congress, according to an exit poll from NBC News.

"People don't want a data center going near them if it's just going to house AI that's going to help a big tech company profit," Maura Austin, a behavioral scientist at the University of Virginia, told CNBC. "What Anthropic is doing when they're going public with such a high valuation is they're really leaning into that big tech, billionaire kind of caricature. I expect that's not going to go well with the public."

Anthropic has long tried to position itself as a safety-conscious company that takes AI's potential risks and benefits seriously. CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company alongside a handful of researchers who defected from OpenAI , now its chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.

The company's enterprise focus has helped it avoid becoming the public face of AI, leaving that distinction to OpenAI and CEO Sam Altman . But with Anthropic poised to become the first pure-play AI company to hit the public market, minting a number of new billionaires and many more millionaires in the process, a heightened level of scrutiny is coming.

"Being a public company, just that by itself pushes you in the limelight," Reena Aggarwal, a professor of finance at Georgetown University, said in an interview. "And then AI is such a hot-button issue that Anthropic will be in the limelight even more."

Matt Kennedy, a senior IPO market strategist at Renaissance Capital, said that's not necessarily a bad thing for Anthropic.

Public markets force greater transparency, he said, and the company could attract new users through its debut. And since AI has become such a mainstream conversation topic, several private companies are already household names.

"I would say that a public company does not deserve more criticisms than a comparable private company," Kennedy said. "So Anthropic should not be put in a harsher public spotlight than OpenAI just because it's public."

Anthropic declined to comment.

AI backlash accelerated over the summer after a series of high-profile safety and security incidents rattled the public. As concerns mounted, the debate over data centers intensified, while tech's hyperscalers simultaneously boosted their forecasts for capital expenditures, each reaching into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

Anthropic and OpenAI depend on state-of-the-art data centers to train models and serve customers, and they're trying to build out capacity as quickly as possible to meet demand. Anthropic said in an amended IPO prospectus this week that it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion , "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."

Americans grappling with inflation and stubbornly high gas prices have grown worried that the facilities could exacerbate environmental harms, raise utility bills and contribute to job loss. For many, a proposed data center in their backyard became the physical manifestation of the widespread antipathy toward AI.

In the risk factors section of its prospectus , Anthropic said opposition to data center development has become more organized across jurisdictions, and that the company's public profile could draw particular scrutiny to projects associated with it.

Nicole Greene, an analyst at Gartner, said she expects that Anthropic's executives have long been prepared to contend with AI backlash, especially given the disruptive nature of the technology.

"There's going to be big emotions," Greene told CNBC. "With big emotions and feelings — fear and excitement — comes heightened scrutiny."

Amodei acknowledged the souring sentiment around AI in a post on X in August. He said it's the result of a "crisis of trust," and that people believe companies, the government and the tech industry are always "cooking up some new way to screw them over."

Rebuilding public confidence is going to be an uphill battle as the company begins providing quarterly financial updates.

The University of Southern California published a survey on Monday that found that 71% of respondents don't trust big tech companies to act in society's best interest "at all" around data center development.

"Once you've lost trust, it's hard to gain it back," Wändi Bruine de Bruin, a professor at the University of Southern California's Schaeffer Institute, said in an interview. "The numbers are not good."

articles.title: At least 6 killed, several injured in shooting at Polish market square: Police
articles.summary: Six people were killed and several others injured after shots were fired in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday, according to regional police.
articles.ai_summary: Police confirmed that six people were killed and several others injured in a shooting incident at Krakow's Main Market Square.

scraped.title: At least 6 killed, several injured in shooting at Polish market square: Police
scraped.description: Six people were killed and several others injured after shots were fired in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday, according to regional police.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: At least 6 killed, several injured in shooting at Polish market square: Police
scraped.body_text:
The perpetrator has been shot by police, officials said.

At least six people were killed and 15 others were injured after shots were fired in a market square in Krakow, Poland, on Saturday, according to regional police.

A man drove a car near the historic Main Market Square and began firing shots at random people at around 3 p.m. local time, according to Małopolska Police.

The incident occurred near Slawkowska Street, just off the main square.

"Initial information suggests that the shots were fired from a passing vehicle," according to the local government.

The perpetrator was shot by police and has been transported to a hospital, authorities said.

Katarzyna Cisło, a Krakow police spokesperson, told ABC News the suspect was wearing military-style camouflage clothing, though not an official military uniform, and was reportedly armed with an AR-15-style rifle.

Police also found a variety of different weapons and ammunition in the vehicle he had been driving, according to Cisło.

Małopolska Police said the attacker was a Polish citizen and denied reports that a second suspect was involved.

"The only known perpetrator of the incident is in police custody," police said.

Two police officers are among those wounded, according to Polish Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński.

"One officer was shot, and the other is in very critical condition—3 gunshot wounds. Surgery is underway," Kierwiński said in a post on X.

Emergency services are urging people not to approach areas where police officers and rescue workers are operating, according to the Krakow municipal government.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki expressed his condolences to the victims and all those affected by the attack.

"I remain in contact with the relevant services and expect a full clarification of the circumstances surrounding these dramatic events. The Head of the National Security Bureau is on his way to Kraków," the president said.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he is being kept informed on the shooting, and that police are "investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."

In another post on X, Tusk expressed condolences to all families and loved ones affected in the attack and praised the "heroic police officers who risked their lives."

U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose called the "horrific" shooting "a savage and murderous attack that’s shattered the peace of Poland," in a post on social media.

"What we know so far is that several innocent precious lives were viciously cut down on a Saturday afternoon in Kraków’s historic and iconic central square," Rose said.

"America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow. May the blessed memory of those lost today assuage the grief of those who mourn," Rose said.

This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

scraped.title: Mass shooting in Krakow, Poland market leaves at least 6 dead, 15 injured
scraped.description: Krakow police said a man who had driven onto the square began firing at random people from his car.
scraped.h1: Mass shooting in Krakow, Poland market leaves at least 6 dead, 15 injured
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 7, 2026 / 12:57 PM EST / CBS News

A man drove into an open market in the Polish city of Krakow and opened fire from his car, killing at least six people and injuring at least 15 others, authorities said. The shooter was shot by police and taken into custody.

The shooting happened in the Main Market Square in Krakow around 3 p.m. local time on Saturday. Krakow police said the alleged shooter began firing at random people from his car. Police said the victims were four women and two men.

Police officers are among the wounded. The perpetrator was shot and wounded during a confrontation with police a short distance away from the initial violence, and was taken to a hospital for treatment.

The death toll earlier stood at five, but the Malopolski regional government updated it to six in a post on X .

Marcin Kierwiński, Poland's interior minister, wrote on X that two police officers were wounded by gunfire and one is in serious condition.

"Police officers in Kraków risked their lives to intervene. Immediately. Thanks to their heroic actions, the attacker was quickly apprehended," he wrote.

In a social media post, Krakow police said the gunman is a Polish citizen and that he acted alone.

Katarzyna Cisło, a spokesperson for the Krakow police, told TVN24 that the suspected gunman was wearing military-style fatigues and used a military-type long gun in the attack. Police found many pieces of other weapons, as well as ammunition, in his car.

"I am being kept informed by the Minister of the Interior about the situation in Krakow following the tragic shooting," Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote on social media, adding that "the police are investigating the background and all the circumstances of the attack."

He later headed to Krakow from the capital, Warsaw, a government spokesperson said.

Other details were not immediately available.

"We are just learning details of the horrific mass shooting in Krakow, a savage and murderous attack that's shattered the peace of Poland," Tom Rose, the U.S. ambassador to Poland, wrote on X . "America stands with Poland at this dark hour as Poland stands with her beloved citizens of Krakow."

Mass shootings are uncommon in Poland, a European Union and NATO member of 38 million people.

"I saw a man shooting at people and walking around the square," Annette, a woman in her sixties, told news wire Agence France-Presse. "It's a tragedy for Krakow; we've never seen anything like this before."

Kaja Kallas, the European Union's top diplomat, said in a statement that the EU stands with Poland and offered her condolences.

"The tragic loss of life in the shooting in Kraków is a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland," she wrote on X . "Poland's strength lies in the resilience of its people. In this moment of grief, Poland does not stand alone."

Krakow is the second-largest city in Poland and roughly 155 miles from the capital, Warsaw.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

scraped.title: Built from Scratch: How a rented kitchen and hand-squeezed fruit became a versatile mixer
scraped.description: Johnna Rossbach, Mixly's co-founder, developed a mixer for non-alcoholic drinks, dirty sodas and more through hand-squeezing fruit, funding her own project and a lot of hard work.
scraped.author: Julia Fields
scraped.h1: Built from Scratch: How a rented kitchen and hand-squeezed fruit became a versatile mixer
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Mixly's mixers aren't just for cocktails. The unique flavors are in dirty sodas, marinades and more. (Mixly Beverage Co)

Johnna Rossbach never expected to become an entrepreneur. After spending 15 years in a career that left little room for creativity, she found the motivation to build something of her own after becoming a mother.

"I wanted to show my daughters what it looks like to be empowered, and that if you’re not happy with something, change it," Rossbach said.

Rossbach loved cocktails, but she was disappointed by the mixers on store shelves. They often featured similar flavors, contained ingredients she wanted to avoid and required too much preparation.

CEO SUNDAY: AVELO AIRLINES CEO REVEALS THE HABIT HE CREDITS FOR HIS SUCCESS

That's when she created Mixly .

Rossbach drew on her background in marketing and communications and teamed up with Megan Sather, who brought design expertise to the venture. Together, they created a line of fruit-forward cocktail mixers made with real ingredients.

The team behind Mixly Beverage Co. created a line of fruit-forward cocktail mixers made with real ingredients. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

The very first night the team began working on Mixly, just about everything that could go wrong did. They started at 4 p.m. and didn't finish until 3 a.m.

When their juicer broke, they squeezed limes by hand . Then their labeler stopped working, forcing them to apply every label themselves.

Around midnight, Rossbach remembers looking at Sather and realizing they still had hours of work ahead of them. They had a choice: Call it a night and try again the following week or push through. The answer was clear. They turned up the music and kept working.

BUILT FROM SCRATCH: HOW A FAMILY TURNED CRAFT BEER INTO A HOLIDAY TRADITION

"That was the moment we realized we made the best business partners," Rossbach said. "We had the same determination and the same willingness to roll up our sleeves and figure things out, even when nothing was going according to plan."

That night set the tone for building Mixly — and it's a big reason the co-founders have always handled their own manufacturing.

The team began developing recipes, with help from a mixologist friend to refine the flavors. Then COVID-19 disrupted their plans, forcing the founders to figure out production as they went. In an early interview, Rossbach said they were still making the products themselves in a rented kitchen while exploring ways to scale.

"When you start a business, there is no map," she said. Rossbach described the hardest part as facing the unknown: the constant decisions, self-doubt and possibility of getting things wrong.

The company has been self-funded from the beginning, without outside equity investors. The founders were intentional about building something of their own and maintaining control of the business. But that also means every dollar matters, and the stakes feel deeply personal.

"We've put our own money, time and countless hours of work into Mixly," Rossbach said.

Discover dozens of cocktail and non-alcoholic recipes on the Mixly site. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

Cocktails were the founders’ entry point, but they wanted their mixers to work for people who weren’t drinking, too. Rossbach was pregnant while the company took shape, just as the sober-curious movement began to emerge.

The founders saw an opportunity to create a product that could be enjoyed with or without alcohol, so no one at the gathering had to feel left out.

"Let’s make this versatile. Let’s make this for everyone," Rossbach said, recalling their early thinking.

That’s why Mixly’s alcohol-free positioning isn’t a recent response to a trend. The mixers have always been alcohol-free . What has changed is the surrounding market: More consumers are looking for flavorful drinks without alcohol, and retailers are beginning to recognize the variety of occasions Mixly can serve.

CEO SUNDAY: ATOMIC WINGS CEO SHARES HIS JOURNEY FROM WALL STREET TO THE RESTAURANT BUSINESS

"I think the interest in drinking less extends well beyond January or October," Rossbach said. "People want a good option for an ordinary Tuesday, dinner with friends or a celebration."

The mixers are designed to work whether customers add a spirit or pour them over sparkling water. That calls for more than sweetness. Mixly builds flavor with fruit, acidity, herbs and bitter botanicals. Its Bitter Orange Cherry mixer, for example, uses gentian root to balance sweetness with a more complex bitter note.

"A good alcohol-free drink does not need to apologize for what is missing," Rossbach said. "It doesn’t have to imitate a cocktail to deliver that."

The founders began hearing from customers who were using Mixly in ways they hadn’t initially anticipated. One customer told them she added a mixer to her children's water for extra flavor. Others mentioned using the products in cooking and marinades.

Then Rossbach’s daughters became regulars at a local dirty soda shop. After spending about $20 on two drinks, Rossbach started thinking about how Mixly’s flavors could work in dirty sodas, too. Her daughters now make the drinks at home and have even set up a neighborhood stand.

That discovery opened a new occasion for the brand. A Mixly flavor can go into a dirty soda, a mocktail or a cocktail. The drink changes; the mixer stays the same.

Shop Mixly in store at more than 4,000 retail locations nationwide. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

In June 2026, the company changed its name from Mixly Cocktail Co. to Mixly Beverage Co. The broader name reflects products and occasions beyond the bar cart, including dirty soda and coffee.

The expansion has brought Mixly into major retailers. Five flavored syrups launched at 685 Walmart stores. The company expects its dirty soda products to reach nearly 4,000 stores by the end of November, and two holiday kits launched at 1,300 Target stores and online. Mixly says its products are now available in approximately 4,600 retail locations nationwide.

What you think customers want isn't always what they actually want.

For Rossbach, that growth connects back to the idea the founders had from the beginning: Make something flavorful that people can share, whether they’re drinking alcohol or not. The market is catching up to that versatility, but it took hand-squeezed fruit, a rented kitchen and plenty of decisions without a map to get Mixly here.

When she first launched Mixly, Rossbach had an ultra-premium product line and a very specific idea of what the business would look like. But she quickly learned that what you think customers want isn't always what they actually want. The team listened, made adjustments and became more comfortable pivoting as they learned what was working and what wasn't.

That willingness to change has helped refresh the brand, expand beyond cocktail mixers and grow into opportunities they never would have imagined when they were squeezing limes in a kitchen at 3 a.m.

Inspired by a Hugo spritz, this mixer is bright and fresh, whether you're drinking alcohol or not. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

Add whiskey, vodka or plain soda water to this unique mixer. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

Try three best-selling mixers from the brand in one bundle. (Mixly Beverage Co.)

articles.title: Pope Leo calls for universal healthcare weeks after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV spoke about access to healthcare on his first stop in Uruguay during his 12-day Latin American tour.
articles.ai_summary: Pope Leo XIV, following his lung cancer surgery, advocated for universal healthcare during his visit to Uruguay.

scraped.title: Pope Leo XIV champions universal healthcare during speech in Uruguay weeks after lung cancer surgery
scraped.description: Pope Leo XIV spoke about access to healthcare on his first stop in Uruguay during his 12-day Latin American tour.
scraped.h1: Pope Leo XIV champions universal healthcare during speech in Uruguay weeks after lung cancer surgery
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 7, 2026 / 12:36 PM EST / CBS News

Montevideo - Pope Leo XIV drew on his own recent experience of illness and hospitalization after surgery for lung cancer on Friday to make an impassioned appeal for universal access to healthcare, greater social equality and a society that does not measure people's worth by their productivity or wealth.

"Recently I experienced firsthand the limitations imposed by illness and I received care for which I am grateful," the Pope said in his first speech after arriving in Uruguay, to the country's political and civic leaders.

Pope Leo XIV was released from Rome's Gemelli Hospital four days after removing a cancerous tumor from his right lung . "The experience made me think of the many men and women who lack the means to obtain a timely diagnosis or receive the treatment they need."

"Ensuring that healthcare is accessible to everyone, regardless of their resources, is a duty that confronts every society," he said.

Uruguay is the first stop of a 12-day trip that also includes Argentina and Peru. Leo's doctors said he needed no further treatment after his operation and was cleared to travel. The trip schedule is the longest international journey of his pontificate so far, with 19,000 travel miles, 14 flights, 36 speeches and approximately 50 events.

Vatican officials told reporters ahead of the trip that the Pope would have a medical team travel with him, as is customary on papal trips, but that no special measures were being taken. "We're speaking of a 71-year-old person in good health," the Vatican spokesman said.

The Latin America journey is Leo's first return as Pope to the country and region that has profoundly shaped his vision, and where he spent decades of his life, first as an Augustinian missionary, and then as bishop of Chiclayo, Peru. The pope holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.

Leo's remarks on caring for the sick were part of a broad appeal for a society where the most vulnerable are protected, and where economic development benefits everyone rather than just the elite.

"The creation of wealth and economic initiative…must also translate into goods and opportunities that effectively reach everyone," Leo said.

While praising Uruguay for four decades of uninterrupted democracy, he stressed that a country's success is ultimately measured by how it protects human dignity and cares for the most vulnerable in society.

Leo also spoke in defense of children, including the unborn. Abortion was legalized in Uruguay in 2012, making it one of the first Latin American countries to do so.

"Their absolute dependence on their mother does not diminish the dignity to which they are entitled or the protection they deserve," the pope said.

Children, he said, must have access to quality education and opportunities to enter the workforce and achieve personal independence. Touching on a subject close to his heart, he said that technological advances and artificial intelligence must serve human beings rather than replace workers.

Leo will remain in Uruguay until Sunday when he will continue his travels to Argentina and Peru. The Vatican spokesman said there, Leo would address a range of issues, including the environment, arms tracking and political instability.

The Pope will also hold meetings with survivors of clerical sex abuse, but no further details are available as of now.
