scraped.title: Voting while disabled needs to get easier
scraped.description: Midterm voters faced a cascade of challenges to voting access in both red and blue states.
scraped.author: Julia Métraux
scraped.h1: Voting While Disabled Needs to Get Easier
scraped.body_text:
Mother Jones illustration; Bryan Dozier/NurPhoto/AP

Disabled people faced a myriad of hurdles to voting during the midterm elections, reflecting both apathy in accommodating marginalized people across the country and voter suppression in states that have sought to deliberately throw up physical and bureaucratic challenges to the process.

“Disabled voters are unable to access the right to vote in every state, in many circumstances, in every county, at every polling place,” said Casey Doherty, a policy analyst for the Center for American Progress’ Disability Justice Initiative . Around 40 million disabled Americans are eligible to vote.

That includes attacks on mail-in voting, which Doherty said effectively disenfranchise many disabled people, especially immunocompromised and otherwise Covid-cautious potential voters who may be hesitant to go to a potentially poorly ventilated polling location. But access issues extend to every stage of the voting process, Doherty noted, including in registering to vote and receiving voting materials on time.

Many states attacking mail-in voting have legislated some exemptions for disabled people, who tend to break evenly along party lines. But some disabled voters, including many I spoke to, are surprisingly likely to emphasize voting in person—in part out of concerns that mail ballots, even if sent back on time, won’t be properly counted.

That’s especially true for voters in a state like Georgia, which months after the 2020 presidential election made it a felony for certain people to return a ballot on another voter’s behalf; many disabled voters seek ballot assistance at polling places and by mail. And, especially in the South, people may have to travel further to vote, with ABC News finding that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2013 Shelby County v. Holder decision, which weakened voting protections, around 2,700 polling locations closed over a period of a decade.

A 2024 report by the US Election Assistance Commission and Rutgers University found that 14 percent of voters with disabilities faced issues with voting in the 2022 midterm elections, in comparison to 4 percent of non-disabled people, and that more people faced accessibility issues voting in person than voting by mail.

“The most common reported difficulties among in-person voters with disabilities in 2022 were difficulty waiting in line, reading or seeing the ballot, writing on the ballot, and getting inside the polling place,” the report reads. In the run-up to the 2026 elections, even more voting restrictions were deployed by states that have taken advantage of the Supreme Court’s gutting of the Voting Rights Act—some forcing disabled people to re-register, sometimes in person, and others slashing the window of time in which they can vote.

Voting accessibility has improved overall across the past two decades, the report noted, with more ramps at voting locations and accessible voting machines. “The improved accessibility reflects funding…for accessible voting systems, improvements to polling places, poll worker training, and increased information about voting accessibility for individuals with disabilities,” the report says.

But where problems still exist, the only remedy is often to file individual complaints under federal or state disability laws, a hurdle that has historically limited enforcement of accessibility statutes and makes it more challenging to expand voting accessibility specifically.

As I reported in 2024 , many polling places, particularly in the South, are in churches—but places of worship are exempt from the Americans with Disabilities Act when not acting as a polling location, which leaves few options when they’re inaccessible. And according to a Ballotpedia analysis, the average level of reading expertise needed to correctly parse the average ballot measure in 2026 was that of a graduate student, posing clear challenges to some disabled people, including would-be voters with intellectual disabilities.

Failure to accommodate access needs while voting can vary immensely. One Deaf voter in Georgia told me that she had been repeatedly instructed not to use an electronic device she requires for captioning. In New Mexico, a woman with severe ME/CFS reported that her county clerk’s office said it never received her absentee ballot request, forcing her to obtain a sworn statement from her doctor attesting to her disabilities in order to receive a last-minute one—another obstacle significant numbers of disabled voters wouldn’t be able to clear. A chronically ill Illinois voter asked for a chair while waiting in line, but inadequate staffing at the polling place meant she had to lug it through the line herself as it moved.

Maria Town, president and CEO of the American Association of People with Disabilities, reported not being able to vote privately on Election Day in Maryland’s Prince George’s County, where the only voting table without long lines at her polling place lacked a privacy screen that matched the height of her mobility scooter, “preventing our ballots from being anonymous,” Town said.

“Polling places should be provided with more privacy shields as a temporary accessibility remedy for voters who may need to vote in a different configuration than a typical booth,” Town said.

Justin Salas, who is blind, wanted to access a sample ballot for his area before he went to vote on Election Day, but the ballot on his county’s election website didn’t work with a screen reader. Salas, who lives in Nevada, said he’d been reprimanded intensely for using a magnifying tool on his phone to vote in the 2024 primary elections, and wanted to iron out problems in advance. But the county never got back to him with a resolution.

“I just wanted to be an informed voter,” Salas said, “and I was not an informed voter.”

In Riverside, Missouri, Patrisha Gillette set out to use curbside voting. Gillette lives with lupus and small fiber neuropathy, both of which contribute to mobility issues. But signs at her polling places directed prospective voters to go inside to inquire about curbside voting.

“I’m like, ‘You’re kidding, right? You want me to come inside to then ask you if I can vote outside, and then get back into my car and pull around’” to vote, Gillette said.

That obstacle, Gillette said, could easily deter other disabled and aging people who want to vote in the state. (The Missouri Secretary of State did not reply to a request for comment.)

“I worry about everybody who it’s just too much [for],” Gillette said, who was able to find a phone number for her polling location—though it wasn’t readily available—eventually online. “Then they leave and don’t end up voting.”

“There’s a failure of empathy and lack of understanding on the state and local government level as well as the federal level,” Salas said. “It doesn’t matter if it’s left or right or center; people seem to think that the accessibility issue can be blown off.”

articles.ai_summary: The midterm elections may catalyze a shift towards clean energy in three states, as local governments step up in response to federal climate policies.

scraped.title: Three states where the midterms could unleash a new era for clean energy
scraped.description: Trifectas in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin are a big deal for climate action.
scraped.author: Jake Bittle
scraped.h1: Three States Where the Midterms Could Unleash a New Era for Clean Energy
scraped.body_text:
Supporters of Wisconsin Democratic governor-elect David Crowley watch early election results at the campaign's election night event on November 03, 2026, in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. John Moore/Getty

This story was originally published by Grist and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

When Trump was elected in both 2016 and 2024, promising to make the federal government hostile to climate action, many climate advocates insisted that state and local governments would take up the mantle of pushing for clean energy. That’s the thesis of the “ America Is All In ” coalition, which brings together cities and states that have vowed to uphold America’s “climate commitments…[i]n the absence of federal leadership.” The unspoken caveat in these claims is that the states leading the way on climate policy are concentrated in a few liberal parts of the country, like New England and the West Coast.

The Democratic Party’s historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could change that. Democrats have secured control of both state legislative chambers and the governor’s mansion—also known as a “trifecta”—in Arizona, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, three states that have spent years or decades under Republican or divided control. The three states have also lagged in their support for clean energy. Democrats also restored trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan, and Nevada this week, but those are states where they last had unified control earlier this decade.

“It is impossible to overstate how monumental these results are,” said David Weiskopf, the senior policy director at Climate Cabinet, a nonprofit that works to elect climate-focused candidates and pass state climate policy. He said that the six states where Democrats have secured trifectas would be one of the world’s largest emitters if they made up their own country, rivaling Canada and Saudi Arabia. “This is just a massive opportunity to make progress.”

Here’s how the election could open up the floodgates for new climate policy:

Compared to its neighbors in the Upper Midwest, Wisconsin has been far less ambitious when it comes to ditching fossil fuels in its power sector. While Michigan and Minnesota have both passed laws that mandate that the states get all their power from clean sources by 2040, Wisconsin set a measly 10 percent renewable electricity standard more than two decades ago. It blew past that goal but never set a new target. Unlike most other states, it doesn’t even require utilities to plan for what kinds of power plants they want to build. The state gets a larger share of its electricity from coal than its immediate neighbors.

Renewable energy advocates in the Badger State believe they can make some short-term gains with Democrats’ first trifecta since 2010. Erik Kanter, the policy director for the nonprofit Clean Wisconsin, said he believes that the new Legislature can agree on the “low-hanging fruit” of making utilities plan for the future, which he said will nudge more of them to build renewables rather than extending the lifespans of gas and coal plants. The Wisconsin Legislature failed this year to pass a law that would require data centers to source their power from clean sources, and Kanter expects such a measure to pass once Democrats take control. The Legislature will also likely renew programs like Knowles-Nelson, a longstanding fund for parks and ecosystem preservation, which once enjoyed bipartisan approval but has lost support from Republicans in recent years.

Weiskopf, of Climate Cabinet, believes that even more ambitious moves are in the offing. He expects Wisconsin’s new class of legislators to pursue a 100 percent clean electricity standard, filling what he calls a “Wisconsin-sized hole” in the Upper Midwest. Not only would that help to phase out coal in the state, it would also make it easier for neighboring states to meet their climate goals, since the whole region shares the same interconnected power grid.

The Pennsylvania Senate has long been known to Democrats as the place where climate policy goes to die. Even though the party managed to flip the lower house of the Legislature a few years ago, Republican leaders in the upper chamber often refused to bring climate bills to a vote . The Keystone State’s status as a large producer of both natural gas and coal also made it difficult to secure agreements within the Democratic Party on clean energy proposals.

“You don’t want to let yourself fully imagine what it can be, because you’ve been let down in the past,” said Lindsey Williams, a state senator who represents a swath of the Pittsburgh metro area. “Now we’re in that moment of, wow, there’s so many things that we can accomplish.”

Every year since 2019, Williams has introduced a bill that would establish mandatory energy and water efficiency standards for appliances like ovens and showerheads, a measure she said could save consumers millions of dollars a year. The legislation has never moved forward—but she thinks it will in next year’s session.

She hopes Democrats will use their first trifecta since 1993 to advance a full-scope climate agenda. In addition to passing laws that would allow community solar and warehouse rooftop solar , Democratic lawmakers also want to pass a funding package for struggling mass transit systems like Philadelphia’s. The $1.5 billion infusion would help prevent the transit “death spiral” for those systems and would reduce reliance on gasoline-powered cars.

The state’s reelected centrist governor, Josh Shapiro, appears to be on board with at least some of these proposals. Although he withdrew the state from the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative , a Northeast-wide carbon pricing system , he has promised to create a similar cap-and-trade system for Pennsylvania itself if he can get legislative support. He has also named funding for mass transit as a leading item on his agenda for the new legislative session next year. But Democrats will have to be careful: While they will now control both chambers, they’ll have slim majorities in each, and may have just a narrow two-year window to pass climate policy before one flips back.

“We need to be brave and lead,” said Williams. “Yes, what are the low-hanging fruits, but what are the big ambitious things that we can get done this session?”

The last time Democrats had a trifecta in Arizona, the Grand Canyon State, was in 1966, decades before the general public was even aware of global warming. The state has ample sunshine and wind, so its renewable energy industry has grown quickly over recent years , and its grid is cleaner than in regions like the Midwest. Furthermore, the many newly built suburbs of the Phoenix metroplex tend to be heated with electricity rather than natural gas . Yet Republicans in the state Legislature have all but banned climate and environmental policy, prohibiting the state government from regulating greenhouse gas emissions or energy use, and numerous climate and water bills have failed in recent years.

Lauren Kuby, a longtime Democratic legislator who represents the Phoenix suburb of Tempe, says she and her colleagues have a long wish list that spans several issues. Their first order of business is to reform the Arizona Corporation Commission , the state’s utility regulator, which Kuby says has been slow to embrace new technologies like solar and wind even as developers seek to build more of them. Legislators want to pass a law that would direct the commission to make utilities invest in solar, batteries, and “virtual power plants,” or networks of homes and businesses that coordinate their energy usage. As part of the reform, they might even change the commission’s name, taking out the “corporation” and replacing it with “public utilities.” The two Democrats who appear set to win seats on the commission will make these reforms easier to push through.

The Legislature could also break long-standing logjams on the crucial issue of water—a scarce resource in a desert state where climate change is worsening droughts. Kuby and other senators have been trying for years to pass a bill that would regulate groundwater pumping in the state’s rural areas. These areas are home to massive dairies and alfalfa farms like Riverview and the Saudi-backed Fondomonte , which have been blamed for sinking land and dried-up residential wells. The bill has failed in several legislative sessions , but Kuby believes that some form of regulation can pass in the coming year, bringing an end to the water free-for-all in the desert areas outside Phoenix.

“That has been languishing and has not been heard in the Legislature, even though we have agreement from a lot of Republicans on water and environmental protection,” said Kuby. Of the trifecta, she said, “It’s a game-changer.”

scraped.title: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
scraped.description: Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.
scraped.h1: The Bantu expansion changed Africa. Scientists are still tracing how.
scraped.body_text:
Genes and archaeology are revealing how Bantu speakers spread across much of Africa.

It’s not easy to extract iron from its ore. But the peoples of the ancient city of Great Zimbabwe—the capital of a thriving kingdom in southern Africa between 1000 to 1700 AD—were masters.

At sites near the city’s stone ruins, clusters of iron-smelting furnaces survive today as mounds of rubble. At Mashava, a village 25 miles northwest, fragments bear fingermarks of those who long ago smoothed the structures’ clay interiors.

Some of the furnaces were nearly an adult’s arm span in width, with walls thick and strong to contain the heat of more than 2,100° Fahrenheit needed to smelt iron. Unlike other furnaces that required workers to force air into them with bellows, these were designed to suck air in, then out through a chimney, no human labor required. This would have made it significantly easier to produce the iron, which was fashioned into hoes, axes, and arrowheads.

“The number and size of these furnaces, together with the use of natural-draft technology, indicate intensive and technologically sophisticated iron production,” says archaeometallurgist Ezekiel Mtetwa of Chicago’s Field Museum of Natural History, who has long studied the furnaces .

Scientists are extremely interested in the peoples who created this and other iron-powered societies across eastern and southern Africa. Research points to an adaptable and innovative group from western Africa as the masterminds. Known as Bantu speakers, these communities began gradually expanding across the continent’s southern half, starting from 6,000 to 4,000 years ago. In doing so, they introduced a fundamentally new, sedentary way of life—characterized by farming, raising livestock, pottery-making, and metalworking—to regions previously dominated by hunter-gatherer communities.

This migration transformed not only the region’s history and technology, but also its languages: Today, around 350 million Africans speak one of roughly 500 distinct Bantu tongues, from southern African Zulu to eastern African Swahili. And at least as many Africans—as well as many African Americans and Afro-Latinos—carry Bantu ancestry in their DNA.

Reconstructing this expansion has been a tough puzzle, especially given the region’s sparse written historical records and limited research funding . But a unique blend of scientists—linguists, archaeologists, and geneticists—have teamed up to unearth clues about the deep origins of the Bantu-speaking people, their path across Africa, and their relationships with other cultures. Although much debate and uncertainty remain, little by little the work is uncovering one of history’s largest and longest human migrations.

“It completely reshaped the demography in sub-Saharan Africa, and we are really interested in trying to understand it,” says population geneticist Sandra Beleza of the United Kingdom’s University of Leicester.

The first evidence of the Bantu expansion came from observations of similarities among Bantu languages. They’re so alike, in fact, that when the Portuguese explorer Vasco da Gama sailed around the southern tip of Africa in 1497, a Portuguese crew member who had spent time in west-central Africa could reportedly communicate with locals in southeastern Africa.

Linguists working in the 19th century started referring to the language family as Bantu , the plural of muntu , meaning “human being” in many Bantu tongues. Later linguists reasoned that the languages stemmed from an ancestral people who migrated across the continent from western Africa, which harbors the greatest diversity of Bantu languages (as would be expected for where the languages originated).

Soon, archaeologists found supporting evidence: across eastern and southern Africa, pieces of pottery of similar yet diverse styles, alongside first-time traces of village life, metal-making, domesticated animals, and western African crops—all developed within the last 2,000 years. Northern sites usually dated back to earlier time periods than sites farther south. “You can clearly see a north-to-south progression,” says archaeological scientist Shadreck Chirikure of the University of Oxford.

By the 1990s, however, some scholars began to question the idea that Bantu languages and skills spread through a migration. Couldn’t these cultural habits have spread while people stayed in the same place, with hunter gatherer communities passing along new technologies, languages, and habits to each other?

Genetic techniques that could analyze people’s ancestry helped to resolve that debate. All of us share DNA with our relatives: 50 percent on average with siblings, 12.5 percent with cousins, 3.3 percent with second cousins, and so on. Though these proportions become minute the further back in time a shared common ancestor lived, statistical techniques can tease out patterns.

Sure enough, a 2009 genetic analysis of 2,432 Africans found that Bantu-speaking people from western, central, and southern Africa are much more closely related than one might expect given their geographic distance. And in 2024, a team of scientists analyzed the genomes of 1,763 Africans and found the greatest genetic diversity among Bantu speakers in western Africa. As distance from the region increased, diversity declined. “This is a typical signature of a population expanding from one place to another,” explains coauthor Carina Schlebusch, a geneticist at Uppsala University in Sweden.

But while linguistic and genetic data point to western Africa—particularly the Grassfields region of Cameroon—as the Bantu homeland, conclusive archaeological proof is thin. At the best-studied archaeological site in the Grassfields, a rock shelter called Shum Laka, pottery fragments appear dating from 7,000 to 6,000 years ago and become abundant by 5,000 to 4,000 years ago. Bowls and jars at first decorated simply with incisions and stamps and later bearing the marks of carved or braided tools rolled over wet clay are a possible, yet inconclusive , trace of Bantu ancestors.

South of Cameroon, archaeologists have searched for artifacts in one of the Bantu-speaking people’s first destinations: the Congo rainforest. A handful of times between 2010 and 2023, archaeologist Alexandre Livingstone Smith of Belgium’s Royal Museum for Central Africa traveled via boat along the Congo River as part of a team led by linguist Birgit Ricquier. In a number of villages, Smith found pottery shards of a style consistent with that found farther west, dating back to 2,300 to 2,000 years ago. “That would be the potential first Bantu settlers of the forest,” Smith says.

Many experts interpret the trails of pottery as evidence that ceramics traditions were brought by Bantu-speaking people all the way from their original home. What’s unclear, however, is when and how Bantu-speaking peoples acquired their farming and metalworking skills—and, in particular, whether they invented iron smelting themselves or learned it from neighboring, iron-extracting cultures .

Scientists have been able to deduce the path that Bantu speakers took to eastern and southern Africa. Some scholars have argued that the path split into two before entering the Congo rainforest, with one group heading east while another went south through the forest. But evidence is now mounting that these groups crossed the rainforest together, and only upon reaching its southern fringes roughly 2,500 to 3,500 years ago did they split into east-moving and southward-moving groups.

Some of this evidence comes from linguistic studies. Not unlike the evolution of species, languages diverge and transform over time, creating “trees” that linguists can reconstruct from similarities in grammar and vocabulary. In 2015, a group of researchers did this computationally using data from about 400 Bantu languages . They observed a much larger diversity—and deeper splits—among the Bantu languages spoken in the Congo rainforest, suggesting that Bantu-speaking ancestors spent a long time there, allowing their languages to diversify. Languages spoken farther east and farther south appeared to stem from a less diverse subset of this larger group, explains coauthor Koen Bostoen, a linguist at Belgium’s Ghent University.

Later linguistic studies , as well as genetic analyses, have reached similar conclusions. In 2023, Beleza and her colleagues compared the genomes of Bantu speakers from Angola —south of the Congo rainforest—with those from the eastern African country of Mozambique and ones from Cameroon, the Bantu homeland.

Remarkably, the eastern African samples were more genetically similar to those from Angola, hundreds of miles to the south of Cameroon and south of the rainforest, than to any of the samples from Cameroon. That points to a recent common ancestor in the Angola region—suggesting that the Bantu split into eastern and southern streams only once they reached the rainforest’s southern edge, Beleza explains.

By the time the Bantu people commenced their movement east and south, they had already come into their own as a farming, iron-making, livestock-herding, and pottery-making people, Chirikure says: Many ancient Bantu settlements across eastern and southern Africa contain evidence of this Bantu “package.”

Key to the Bantu’s success in southern and eastern Africa, experts suspect, was their sedentary lifestyle. This—and their iron tools—would have allowed them to produce more food and grow in number, propelling them to occupy new territories. Their lifestyle affected the landscape as forests turned into farmland , and it also affected the hunter-gatherer communities who were already living there. Some groups were likely crowded out and disappeared, experts suspect, while others were probably pushed to marginal regions, including Indigenous groups such as rainforest hunter-gatherers and Khoisan peoples, who continue to live in central and southern Africa, respectively, to this day.

Still, scientists are learning that Bantu peoples had deep relationships with these two groups. In the 2024 genetic analysis, Schlebusch and her colleagues found that some Bantu-speaking groups in central Africa share about an eighth of their DNA with rainforest hunter-gatherers, and some southern African Bantu speakers share a similar amount with Khoisan groups. Clearly, their ancestors once intermixed.

Curiously, in the case of the Khoisan, this mixing tended to arise from pairings of Bantu-speaking men with Khoisan women. One 2021 study of southern African Bantu speakers found that the DNA inside their mitochondria—which people inherit only from their mothers—had greater-than-expected proportions of Khoisan DNA. But the Y chromosomes, which come from fathers, had much higher proportions of DNA with Bantu ancestry. Some experts speculate that this pattern could be the result of Bantu men raiding Khoisan women or preferentially marrying Khoisan women for whom the traditional bride prices would have been cheaper. “Whenever there is a power difference… between two groups, it tends to melt down to this,” says coauthor Ananyo Choudhury, a geneticist at the University of Witwatersrand in South Africa.

This pattern also left marks on the language. The characteristic clicks of Khoisan languages also occur in southern African Bantu languages Zulu and Khosa. Bostoen suspects that the children of Khoisan-Bantu pairings were, at first, bilingual. Eventually, “they lost their mothers’ languages, but they left a substrate of the mothers’ languages in the Bantu language.”

Archaeologists are also studying the relationships between Bantu farmers and their neighbors. While there may have been conflicts over land, the groups also cooperated with and learned from one another, says Décio Muianga, an archaeologist at Eduardo Mondlane University and the research institute Kaleidoscopio in Maputo, Mozambique. He’s been excavating a rock shelter in Mozambique containing thousands of years’ worth of stone tools, wild animal bones, and wild plant remains—telltale signs of hunter-gatherers living at the site. But interestingly, Bantu-style pottery also appears. “My assumption is that the hunter-gatherers were getting these ceramics from the farmers,” Muianga says. “They were interacting, communicating, and exchanging resources.”

There is evidence, too, for cultural exchanges: European anthropologists have reported that some Bantu-speaking groups would solicit San hunter-gatherers to conduct traditional rainmaking ceremonies , for example.

Bantu social networks eventually extended well beyond Africa. By 1100 to 1600 AD, many of the complex state societies that Bantu speakers built developed trade networks across the Indian Ocean. Archaeological data shows they imported Chinese porcelain and glass beads ; in return, they exported gold, ivory, and iron. In fact, a 12th century Muslim cartographer once wrote that iron from parts of southern Africa—likely referring to Great Zimbabwe’s iron-producing hinterlands, Mtetwa suspects—was deemed to be of much higher quality than that from other places like India.

Mtetwa has found evidence that iron smelters near Great Zimbabwe would add bone fragments to the furnaces, perhaps as part of a smelting-blessing ritual, but one with scientific merit: This material contains calcium, which can accelerate the separation of iron from the rest of the ore. That may be a testament to the Great Zimbabweans’ iron-smelting skills: “Some materials introduced within ritual or medicinal practices may simultaneously have had technically beneficial effects on the smelt,” says Mtetwa.

Though they’ve made great progress in reconstructing the Bantu world, scientists are aware of, and trying to address, the limitations of their research so far.

Linguistic studies, for instance, have been a popular tool to reconstruct Bantu history, but Bostoen cautions that very few Bantu languages have been documented thoroughly enough to definitively trace linguistic trees back in time. Linguists may never get a complete dataset, because some old branches of the Bantu language family may have died out .

Another limitation of computational Bantu language-family reconstructions is that they’ve usually assumed that languages have evolved in isolation after different Bantu groups separated. But there may have been extensive cross-pollination among languages as different groups met and interacted.

In fact, when linguists factored in the possibility of contact among Bantu languages in a 2026 study, they couldn’t reconstruct the diversification patterns described by previous linguists, says coauthor Igor Yanovich of the University of Vienna, who wrote about the challenges of Bantu linguistic studies in the 2025 Annual Review of Linguistics . In his view, linguists should first focus on thoroughly documenting Bantu languages before attempting to use them to understand Bantu history.

In hopes of adding new insights, Schlebusch is working to obtain DNA from ancient human remains. By revealing the identity of people who were living in particular places at particular times, this could help to elucidate when and where different Bantu communities moved into, overlapped with, or repopulated areas. “What we see more and more in genetic data is that the movement was probably complex—that it was these ‘spread over spread’ events,” Schlebusch says.

Archaeologists, for their part, hope to fill in the vast gaps in the archaeological record of sub-Saharan Africa—by both conducting new excavations and re-examining existing artifact collections for fresh insights. But all this work requires funding for research and laboratories , especially from African governments, says Chirikure; he, like many of his colleagues, has largely relied on funding from Europe, which is limited. Without more funding, “you are not generating fresh ideas, you are not formulating new hypotheses and testing them using some of the cutting-edge science,” he says.

Scientists from all three disciplines are hopeful that they will eventually tell the complete story of how an innovative people spread and diversified across sub-Saharan Africa, mixing traditions with those of earlier peoples and of others who still live there, to create myriad cultures, each one a unique blend of food, philosophy, language, music, and traditions. “If you travel from West Africa today all the way to East Africa, you have a unique cultural diversity that is very hard to find in many other parts of the world,” Muianga says. Combined with the legacy of other groups, he says, “this is the result of the Bantu migration.”

scraped.h1: Ousted Paraguayan president appears before prosecutors
scraped.body_text:
By

Ava Berger

Paraguay's President Santiago Peña waves after a meeting with Venezuela's interim President Delcy Rodriguez at the Miraflores Presidential Palace in Caracas, on September 19, 2026. Federico Parra/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña was impeached and placed under house arrest Friday after the collapse of a prominent U.S.-owned bank with ties to Paraguay's government. The fallout has left millions across the country without access to their money.

Peña is one of Washington's closest allies in the region and was a shareholder in Ueno Bank, a digital lender that served about 3 million customers — more than half of the country's adult population.

He was known as a pro-market leader focused on making it easier to do business in the country, but legislators said he jeopardized state assets and benefitted himself through his connection to the bank.

Ueno Bank previously said more than a million people opened bank accounts for the first time using its services, which included generous cash back offers on groceries.

A trial has proceeded against Peña, and he appeared before prosecutors Saturday morning . The last president ousted from office was Fernando Lugo in 2012.

Peña has denied any wrongdoing but on Thursday he announced his resignation . Lawmakers refused to accept that resignation, and instead moved forward with the country's impeachment process.

At proceedings inside the country's Senate Friday, legislators unanimously found Peña guilty of malfeasance in office, according to the Senate's website .

Prosecutors then accused him of a breach of trust, among other charges, before placing him under house arrest .

"I want to apologize to the Paraguayan people if I have failed you," Peña said in a speech posted to social media.

Demonstrators burn an image depicting Paraguay's President Santiago Pena, during a protest over the banking crisis and his resignation, at the main square in the surroundings of the National Congress in Asuncion, on November 5, 2026. Daniel Duarte/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Pedro Alliana, the country's vice president, was sworn in as president to serve out the rest of Peña's term until August 2028. In a speech on Friday , he announced he would take action to compensate people whose money was lost in the bank's collapse.

Paraguay's central bank said it seized control of Ueno Bank on Tuesday because its solvency ratio, an assessment of a company's long-term financial viability, no longer met legal standards.

Protests erupted across Asunción , the country's capital city, following the seizure.

NPR's John Otis and Catherine Osborn contributed reporting to this story.

scraped.body_text:
Out now in English from 34 Press and Left Voice — “Socialist Strategy and Military Art” by Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello draws on Clausewitz, Lenin, Trotsky, and Gramsci, rethinking revolutionary strategy and working-class hegemony for the 21st century.

Adrien Masson

First published in 2017, Socialist Strategy and Military Art by Argentinian Marxists Emilio Albamonte and Matías Maiello returns to the vital question of revolutionary strategy, an issue which seemed to lay dormant for decades. Following the work of important figures in the Marxist tradition, Albamonte and Maiello draw lessons from military theory and strategy — or the “art of winning” in Trotsky’s terms — to achieve working-class hegemony. Today we launch the English-language edition of the book, with an original prologue by the authors.

The fight for a socialist future is no longer a debate confined to the margins. It is expressed by a massive youth movement across Europe and general strikes in Italy, France, and Spain that put forward demands against militarism and the rising cost of living. In the United States, a new class consciousness is expressed by the rise of the DSA and the strike against ICE in Minneapolis.

These are trends that have been accelerating quickly since the 2008 financial crisis, which created a global economic downturn and marked the end of the “End of History.” No longer could the myth be sustained that the capitalist system would develop and expand without limit. What we saw instead was a world that has become racked by repeated crises, wars, climate change, campaigns against immigration, rising inequality, and an ascendant Far Right. But this new period has also brought with it renewed waves of class struggle, from Occupy Wall Street, to the Arab Spring, to the Yellow Vest movement in France, to Black Lives Matter, to the worldwide movement for Palestine. It is in this 21st-century context that new debates are emerging around the strategy these movements need to seriously confront not only capitalism’s morbid symptoms but the system itself.

Socialist Strategy and Military Art draws on the strategic thought of revolutionaries in the Marxist tradition across the 20th century, including Vladimir Lenin, Leon Trotsky, Antonio Gramsci, and Rosa Luxemburg, while seeking to apply their analysis in a non-dogmatic way to the conditions facing the workers’ movement today. The book also undertakes a critical examination of others claiming the banner of Marxism who are once again becoming a reference point for many on the Left, such as Karl Kautsy, Che Guevara, or Mao Tse-Tung.

Unlike many other books that have taken up the question of strategy in recent years, Albamonte and Maiello connect socialist strategy and military theory, engaging critically with the work of Prussian general Carl von Clausewitz. Though his relevance is often overlooked today, Clausewitz’s military writings were deeply influential for Marx and Engels and later studied by Lenin and Trotsky — not just in relation to the relationship between war and politics, but as a framework for thinking how the working class can conquer power. The authors investigate ideas like workers’ hegemony, the united front, soviets, and dual power as key elements of revolutionary politics.

As Albamonte and Maiello write in the prologue to the Spanish edition:

The world crisis will continue to increase and sharpen class struggle; the question is whether these opportunities are exploited to open the way to revolution and socialism in the 21st century or whether they will give rise to the triumph of the right and, eventually, fascism. This depends on the work of strategy. As Trotsky noted : “Had the Bolshevik party failed to carry out this work, there couldn’t even be talk of the victory of the proletarian revolution. The Soviets would have been crushed by the counter-revolution and the little sages of all countries would have written articles and books on the keynote that only uprooted visionaries could dream in Russia of the dictatorship of the proletariat, so small numerically and so immature.” This may be one of the main conclusions, 100 years after the Russian Revolution, for the new century that has begun. It is the starting point of the work that you find in your hands.

Although the book examines key lessons and political thought from the 20th century, these ideas are closely related to struggles taking place in our own time. The authors spend a significant portion of the book articulating a vision of working class self-organization, and the fundamental obstacle posed by the bureaucracies that control working-class organizations. They aim for the construction of a genuinely international revolutionary party, capable of preserving these lessons and guiding the working class towards its world-historic mission.

First published by Ediciones IPS and the Party of Socialist Workers ( Partido de los Trabajadores Socialistas ) in Argentina, 34 Press and Left Voice are publishing the English-language edition of this important work. You can order your copy now and we encourage you to share it widely. We offer our pages to debate its contents.

Left Debates

Leon Trotsky

Marxism

Party of Socialist Workers (PTS), Argentina

Strategy

Vladimir Lenin

In this episode, Tatiana Cozzarelli speaks to Andrew Feffer, author of Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism. They discuss the Rapp-Coudert investigation and the anti-communist witch-hunt of the early 1940s — and the parallels to today's repression against the movement for Palestine.

Left Voice

A generation caught in global chaos is rising up in the face of a capitalist system that grows more corrupt by the day.

Julien Anchaing and Enzo Tresso

The war against Iran, differences over Israel, the culture war, and the battle to succeed Trump expose the tensions within a heterogeneous coalition. Behind the slogan America First, different factions compete to define the movement's direction and the strategy for maintaining U.S. hegemony.

Farid Reyes and Ezequiel Silva

In Los Angeles, a DSA-backed challenger leads the mayor favored by business. Statewide, billionaires are spending millions against a wealth tax. But Raman’s silence on Prop 40 and the DSA’s BDS controversy raise bigger questions about the left’s strategy inside the Democratic Party.

Tubman Amaru

November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

All of Mayor Mamdani’s endorsed candidates won landslide victories on Tuesday night, including Governor Hochul.

James Dennis Hoff

scraped.body_text:
ICT

Nika Bartoo-Smith Underscore Native News + ICT

Voters across the country weighed in Tuesday on more than 140 statewide ballot measures. Across 17 states, 31 ballot measures were on the docket that had the potential to impact Native people and communities.

Of the 31 ballot measures, 15 passed.

Major themes of the ballot measures spanned across issues including voting rights, 2SLGBTQIA+ rights, abortion access, cannabis regulation, environment and beyond.

A number of laws aimed at limiting trans rights passed throughout the country, relating to students’ access to play sports, bathroom usage and gender-affirming care.

“I think it’s good to point out that many of these propositions did not come from the voters, did not come from the general population. Many of these were proposed by [the] establishment that was there,” said Jaynie Parrish, Navajo Nation, executive director of Arizona Native Vote.

Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington all passed these anti-trans ballot measures. All states with tribal nations and a high number of Native people.

“We already have some of the highest rates of violence against transgender and Two-Spirit people, and this kind of feeds a bit into that as well as underrepresentation in general for these communities that are under attack,” she said.

Voters in Arizona also voted to pass Proposition 318, a measure that changed private space access and sports eligibility requirements. Parrish said they were hoping it wouldn’t pass.

“But I think a lot of folks just didn’t quite understand what that measure meant, and I think it’s on the cusp of the wave of what we’re seeing across the country, and how there has been rhetoric and actions to really suppress our Two-Spirit, transgender relatives in any capacity,” she said.

Next door in New Mexico, voters passed a ballot measure to pay its state legislators.

“New Mexico was the only state in the country that did not pay its legislators a salary, and this affects who can serve in office, who this actually is accessible to,” said Angel Charley, who is Laguna Pueblo, Zuni Pueblo, and Diné.

Charley, a state senator in New Mexico, was one of four women of color who introduced Constitutional Amendment 4.

“When you think about who can actually serve their communities and serve them well, we need to pay our legislators to be able to do that,” she said. “It also opens up the possibility of running for office for someone who might not have thought about it before, so I’m thinking about young people, students, people right now who are working two or three jobs to make ends meet. Those are the kind of lived experiences that we need in government to change the system so it works for working people.”

It was a toss up between states with voter ID requirements on the ballots: Nevada and North Carolina both voted in favor of ballots requiring photo identification to vote. Arizona, California and Colorado voters voted against such measures, while Massachusetts will move forward with same-day voter registration.

Voters in Arizona voted against Proposition 144 that would require a government-issued ID to vote and that only U.S. citizens can vote in the state.

“With [Proposition] 144, we already know that Arizona already has some of the most restricted laws already when it comes to voter ID,” Parrish said. “So, for us that have been in this work, as organizers and as part of our team, we’re well versed to see what voter suppression looks like in many of these legislative pieces, and so for us, that’s what it amounted to was another measure to try to make it harder for our people to vote.”

This is a developing story and will be updated as ballots are counted.

Below are the results and updates for the 31 ballot measures in 17 states.

Both states with measures on the ballot that would have restricted the authority to legalize and grow marijuana voted against those measures.

scraped.description: Pope Leo XIV has urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Thousands pour into a park in Uruguay for Pope Leo's first Mass in South America
scraped.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV has urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay to build bridges of fraternity and faith

PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay -- PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay (AP) — Pope Leo XIV urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, using his first Mass in South America to deliver an ode to the region's beloved mate tea and raise the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country.

The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, pope, pope!” when Leo's plane landed in Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in Parque París Londres, a sprawling green space on the southern edge of the city.

In his homily, Leo reminded them that the Catholic faith had been "part of the life of the Uruguayan people since their earliest days, and it must be passed on to future generations with creative courage!"

More than 30,000 people — many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil — had registered in advance to attend the service, around 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said Saturday that another 10,000 had attended, despite the morning rain and blustery, gray skies.

Because of its accessible location on the Uruguay River, the city was chosen to host Leo’s first Mass at the start of his three-nation South American tour that was in doubt after he underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13.

“He’s the representative of Christ but he’s human. And we weren’t sure if he could make it, but he pushed through for us,” said Soledad Sánchez, 73, who had driven to Paysandú from northern Uruguay, her eyes filling with tears. “He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now.”

Leo, who arrived in Uruguay on Friday, is urging the people in South America’s most secular country of 3.5 million to turn to the Catholic faith for strength in confronting today’s problems and challenges.

In his homily, Leo asked the faithful to build bridges of fraternity, recalling the nearby bridge over the Uruguay River that connects Uruguay and Argentina and over which many pilgrims crossed to attend the Mass.

He also pointed to the ritual of drinking mate, the bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans and their neighbors carry everywhere, as a poignant symbol of unity and encounter that he suggested should be applied to spreading the faith.

Mate, a cherished national symbol in Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay, is above all a sharing ritual. The leaves are steeped in a hollowed gourd and the drink is sipped through a metal straw called a bombilla, and the gourd passes from hand to hand among friends, family and sometimes strangers, refilled for hours.

Everyone drinks from the same straw, and Uruguayans drink more mate per person than people anyone else, roughly 9 kilograms (about 20 pounds) of the dried leaf a year, according to industry estimates.

“We must reflect on these symbols that we share, which give us identity and a sense of belonging, which speak to us of our origins and point us toward the future,” Leo said.

The message landed.

“I’m not religious. I’d never go to Mass if it weren’t the pope, but he surprised me. He made it appealing, the way he talked about things we all have in common, like mate,” said Jorge Monzón, 64, from Paysandú. “I personally felt a sense of communion.”

Leo was to press the message of the church's commitment to helping Uruguayans later Saturday by touring a Montevideo neighborhood beset by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church is working in the area with municipal authorities to build housing and provide rehab programs for addicts.

His final event Saturday was likely to drive home the call to reject religious indifference and embrace the faith: a prayer vigil in Montevideo's Centenary Stadium.

Located in western Uruguay and just across a bridge from the eastern Argentine city of Colón, Paysandú was easier to reach for many Argentines than any of the stops on Leo’s tour in Argentina, his next stop after Uruguay.

In Argentina, Leo will visit Buenos Aires, Luján and Córdoba before heading to Peru, his second homeland and the final destination of his tour.

“Argentina is a much more religious country than Uruguay, and there’s this desire to be here to witness something historic,” said Luciana Lobato, 20, an Argentine tour agent who organized buses for 180 pilgrims from across the border.

Some young Catholics involved in local church groups hoped the sight of a pope drawing crowds would challenge Uruguay’s image as a country indifferent to religion.

“The reality I see in my town is that there are tons of young people who are really interested in religion, who are trying to find meaning and community in difficult moments,” said Teresa Sabellini, 18, from Paysandú.

“And now look around here. This place is full of people,” she added.

Leo’s mention of bridges in his homily resonated with Laiana Córdoba, who drove 20 hours and crossed the border from Cascavel, in southern Brazil, to hear it. “It’s something we understand, being neighbors means more than just sharing a border. It means finding ways to connect, opening paths to each other,” she said.

Still, Paysandú itself greeted the pope quietly, as though it were an ordinary weekend, with scant decorations and only a few homes seen flying Vatican flags.

Some younger attendees on Saturday said Leo’s humane tone and emphasis on care for the vulnerable resonated beyond the faithful in their secular country as people grapple with a turbulent world.

“I wouldn’t call myself religious, but I like this pope. He has a really good message for humanity,” said Santiago Biglieri, 18, a Colombian who lives in Uruguay. “Even for the nonbelievers, there’s something to take from his ideas.”

___

Winfield reported from Montevideo, Uruguay.

scraped.title: Disability Is Bad. Plus…
scraped.description: In today’s Weekend Press: Suzy Weiss sits down with Dustin Hoffman’s right-hand woman. Spencer Klavan on the Greek comedy that explains Trump’s ruin. Kat Rosenfield on a masterful new movie. And more!
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
Welcome back to The Weekend Press ! Today, Kat Rosenfield reviews “Fjord,” a new movie that examines whether liberal democracies actually tolerate conservative Christian immigrants. Suzy Weiss drinks with the woman inside Dustin Hoffman’s head. Spencer Klavan on the ancient Greek tragedy that Republicans need right now. And more!

But first: Disability isn’t “magic.”

Good intentions can become ugly realities. And nowhere is that clearer than in how we treat the mentally unwell.

America closed an overwhelming number of its psychiatric hospitals, because surely its schizophrenics didn’t deserve to be locked up like they were in prison? And so, many of them ended up on the street.

An anxious mother hears her teenage daughter say she has developed multiple personality disorder, like the other girls on TikTok, and takes her to see a therapist. And so, pediatricians report, they’re overwhelmed with patients more likely to be suffering from social contagion than genuine illness.

Disability activists encourage us to see autism as a “superpower,” to help erode stigma. And so, those with a profoundly life-inhibiting form of the disorder are erased from the awareness-raising conversation.

“The rhetorical alchemy of recasting disability as something not bad, or even as a positive good, might serve the needs of relatively high-functioning people with relatively high-status disabilities,” writes Freddie deBoer in our lead essay. “But this way of thinking utterly abandons those for whom disability is a daily assault on their ability to function.”

His piece is an excerpt from his remarkable new book, All in Your Head : Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered . It’s not a memoir, but it is personal; Freddie has spent a lifetime suffering from bipolar disorder, and, he writes, “stigma has never been one of my hundred biggest problems.”

The same is true of most disabled people. “Talk to someone struggling to live with cystic fibrosis. Talk privately to the caretakers of severely autistic adolescents who are prone to violent outbursts,” writes Freddie. “They don’t need euphemisms. They don’t want saccharine narratives.”

They want society to recognize the painful realities of their lives—and offer material support.

And therein lies a lesson for the newly empowered Democratic Party: A true politics of the left is not about shouting at people on social media, even if that’s more fun. It is about doing the hard, and not very sexy, work of legislating to make life in America fairer for the most vulnerable.

Read his full piece below:

If you want to watch a movie that will make you think, go see “Fjord.” It follows a devoutly Christian family that migrates from conservative Romania to very liberal Norway—only to have the state take their kids away from them because it doesn’t approve of their parenting. “This is the so-called paradox of tolerance,” writes Kat Rosenfield, in her latest essay. “In an age where welcoming immigrants has become a fundamental tenet” on the left, the fact is that “new arrivals often come armed with values, beliefs, and practices that make progressives profoundly uncomfortable.”

Ariel Levy co-wrote Dustin Hoffman’s new memoir, "Look At Me," which is out this week—but before that, she first met the leading man at a museum in the ’80s. “We followed him around and around the Met because I was so into him,” Levy said. Now, 40 years later, he’s grown so famous that Time called him “the fifth Beatle”—and he has hated every second of it. “He was like ‘It was unbearable. I wanted to climb out of my skin,’ ” she said. Over two Manhattans with Suzy, Levy explains how she got inside the mind of Hollywood’s most reluctant star—and what he makes of his legacy.

Where does American politics go from here? While we all debate the future, Spencer Klavan thinks the best answer lies in an ancient Greek comedy, Aristophanes’s “Clouds,” about a clash between a moral relativist and a traditionalist. The latter’s “solid ideals are fatally undermined, because he turns out to be a venal fraud,” Klavan writes in today’s Things Worth Remembering. The play offers the Trump administration an enduring lesson: “When the Right Argument destroys its own case through mismanagement and corruption, the Wrong Argument wins.”

Is foie gras the new paper straw? This week, among all the election headlines, you may have seen that the French delicacy has been banned in Denver and D.C.—but is this anything more than a feel-good nod to animal rights in a nation full of pigs in cages? In the latest episode of Second Thought , Suzy and Dan Ahdoot get into it—as well as last weekend’s most cancel-worthy Halloween costumes, and the Englishman who just got home after spending nearly 30 years walking around the world. “This is such a British celebrity,” says Suzy. “Just someone who plods along in pain for half of their life.” He didn’t even enjoy it!

Click the link below to watch the episode, or listen wherever you get your podcasts.

This week, we published a full slate of election coverage—which you can catch up on here . Also, Larissa Phillips reflected on the ideological whiplash of being a MAHA mom; Arthur Brooks gave advice on how to raise your kid to be a reader; and Evan Gardner reported on bona fide data centers in space!

A new batch of ads from single Free Press ers is live on the site. Click here to meet a fabulous octogenarian in Los Angeles; a Canadian conservative; or a touring musician in Oz. Your special someone could be just one email away! If you’d like to take a chance at Free Press love, write a paragraph that defines you, including your age, where you live, and what you’re looking for, and send it over to Cupid@TheFP.com .

How should you spend the rest of your weekend? We asked our columnist Kat Rosenfield for her recommendations . . .

🚶 Walk . . . the Hudson Highlands for a scenic stroll in the woods at Harriman State Park—or channel your inner mountain goat and scramble up the Butter Hill loop for spectacular vistas at Storm King (where I spent a very enjoyable Tuesday this week not-thinking about politics or elections). The October crowds are gone, but thanks to an exceptionally mild fall, the foliage is still near peak.

🎵 Listen . . . To the best late autumn mood music, by English folk musician Vashti Bunyan, whose 1970 album Just Another Diamond Day was critically underrated in its time but has since acquired a cult following; the songs are the ideal soundtrack for skipping through a golden wood at twilight or chopping root vegetables for a stew.

🎃 Eat . . . As a wise man once said,“ It’s decorative gourd season, motherfuckers ”— but also, more importantly, decorative gourds are also edible gourds. My husband and I love this recipe for acorn squash roasted and stuffed with Moroccan-spiced lamb sausage, rice, and mint, which is beautiful enough for a Thanksgiving side dish but easy enough for anytime. Pair it with a cute salad and a big, fat glass of red wine.

That’s all, folks! Have a great weekend.

“the ideal soundtrack for skipping through a golden wood at twilight or chopping root vegetables for a stew”

Now that is funny, intentionally or not. The gourd season line, too. She is the best writer of the bunch. Maybe the best mass media culture writer anywhere.

I may even actually try the music and the recipe.

"... rhetorical alchemy...."

Almost exclusively the province of the Left.

scraped.h1: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
scraped.body_text:
Soldier told repeatedly to lock down devices before deploying, got sextorted, court-martialed.

An Estonian newspaper recently revealed that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border.

As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him.

Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention.

According to a 21-page British appeals court document shared with Ars Technica by Eesti Ekspress, the Estonian newspaper that first reported on this saga, the story begins in January 2026.

At the time, Barton-Kennedy was a corporal, with over seven years of service, serving in the 1st Battalion of the Duke of Lancaster Regiment of the British Army.

His unit was deployed to participate in “Exercise Eastern Warrior” in Tapa, Estonia, roughly halfway between Tallinn, the capital city, and the Estonia-Russia border.

While in the United Kingdom, on January 7, Barton-Kennedy, along with other members of his unit, were briefed on their orders and given specific instructions to “remove SIM cards and switch off location settings and to use a trusted virtual private network on all personal electronic devices.”

Once the unit arrived in Estonia, days later, they were given further briefings and reminders of this policy. Despite this, Barton-Kennedy ignored the instruction.

On January 19, Barton-Kennedy informed his platoon commander that he had received a message “from an unknown party who had acquired nude photographs of him from the photo section of his mobile phone and had identified him on social media.”

Barton-Kennedy initially acquiesced to paying the attacker 100 British pounds ($133) but balked when he was asked to pay 250 British pounds ($333), and only then informed his platoon commander what had happened.

Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed and pled guilty at a hearing on July 30.

During that process, according to the court filing, Barton-Kennedy understood the orders that were given to him at the time, but asked the court to “consider the personal circumstances” that he faced at the time. Without his phone, he told the court, he could not reach his daughter on her birthday, nor his pregnant partner.

In a written statement, Barton-Kennedy said he was stunned when he received the first blackmail message.

“Despite still being in a state of shock and uncertainty, I recognised that I had a duty to report the compromise without any further delay,” he wrote.

Additionally, he said that he “deeply regrets” the incident and added that serving in the British Army “has been one of the greatest privileges of my life.”

Barton-Kennedy appealed the sentence, which was denied in August 2026.

In response to an inquiry for comment, Lt. Col. EP Mackie, a British Army spokesperson, told Ars in a statement that the security measures imposed are meant to protect the safety of military personnel.

“Any breaches of Army security measures that might compromise personal safeguarding or operational security will be dealt with swiftly, and offending personnel can expect uncompromising disciplinary action,” he wrote.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

scraped.description: Janeese Lewis George is part of a new class of socialist mayors. Unlike her peers, she'll be running a city under federal rule.
scraped.author: Jessica Washington
scraped.h1: How a Socialist Can Govern a City Under the Thumb of the Trump Administration
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Janeese Lewis George is part of a new class of socialist mayors. Unlike her peers, she’ll be running a city under federal rule.

Socialists will soon govern three of the United States’ most influential cities: Los Angeles, New York City, and the District of Columbia.

Janeese Lewis George joins Zohran Mamdani and Nithya Raman as part of a new wave of socialist local executives. But unlike Mamdani and Raman, Lewis George will govern a city under federal rule.

D.C. is a “federal district,” subject to the whims and micromanagement of the president and Congress. If the federal government doesn’t like the city’s legislation, it can override it. This poses additional challenges if Lewis George wants to change how things are done in the nation’s capital.

Lewis George, a current D.C. city councilmember, has promised to usher in sweeping reforms centered around affordability, including stronger tenant protections, investments in affordable childcare, and long-sought-after reforms on the city’s restrictive zoning laws. She rose to political prominence as the first socialist on the city council, winning her seat on a platform of defunding the police in the wake of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor protests in 2020. (She has since called for hiring additional Metropolitan Police officers.)

For Lewis George to fulfill her campaign promises is “going to require Janeese to use her position and her longstanding reputation as an organizer to convince members of Congress that we can exercise Home Rule and that we deserve the dignity of any other collective body, like a state, in this country,” said Kurtis Hagans, chair of Metro DC Democratic Socialists of America, which endorsed Lewis George in the primary.

All local D.C. bills are required to go through a congressional review period of 30 working days for civil legislation and 60 working days for criminal bills. If Congress doesn’t like the bill, it can either decide to let that review period lapse, allowing the legislation to go into effect, or pass a joint disapproval resolution in both the House and the Senate. If they pass a disapproval resolution, it goes to the president’s desk, where they can choose to veto and let the new law stand or sign it and override the legislation.

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins “Dead Man Walking”: Officials Say Hegseth Has to Go Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

Speaking to The Intercept on Election Day, voters said they supported Lewis George because they wanted to elect someone who would fight for everyday Washingtonians.

“I was certainly motivated by wanting really strong leadership for D.C. and people who are going to put D.C. first, in the sense of the residents and the community members and not solely as our role as the capital city,” said Izetta Mobley, a voter in Ward 4, where Lewis George serves as a councilmember.

For Mobley and other voters, that primarily means tackling issues of affordability. “Affordable housing and the rise in unhoused folks, and making sure that unhoused folks have support and city resources …those were very important to me,” said Mobley.

Although Democrats took both houses of Congress on Tuesday, paving a clearer path for the district to flex its autonomy, Lewis George will still have to contend with Democratic leaders like Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries, both moderates, who are likely to lead the Senate and the House next session. Schumer and Jeffries were often critical of Mamdani when he was running for mayor in their home state of New York, though they seized primarily on his stance on Israel .

Hagans pointed out that Lewis George has the longtime support of former at-large councilmember Robert White, who was elected as Washington’s non-voting delegate on Tuesday. But Hagans said the DC Metro DSA is also preparing to organize residents to put pressure on Congress, given ”the relative powerlessness of the district in the face of Congress.”

Governing Washington has other pitfalls. The district is hamstrung by the fact that the D.C. Council is required to pass a balanced budget and is prohibited from carrying it over into the following year. (Congress also gets to approve it.) The city is already struggling to close a $1.1 billion budget deficit for the upcoming fiscal year — caused by Congress.

In order to achieve her agenda, Lewis George has suggested raising taxes on businesses and the city’s wealthiest residents . For that, she’ll need the support of the city council.

Lewis George is aided by the fact that Tuesday also ushered in a record number of socialists on the city council, adding two, Aparna Raj and Oye Owolewa. “A big part of the vision for the district is to have these organizers on the council as well as an organizer-in-chief at the executive level,” said Hagans.

Aside from bold economic policies , many voters who spoke to The Intercept said they want the new administration to prioritize resistance to the federal takeover of Washington, D.C., and ending the scourge of Immigration and Customs Enforcement. “We’ve seen ICE raids in our neighborhood, literally where our kids used to go to school,” said Jason Cherkis, another Ward 4 voter. “That’s one reason we voted for Janeese for mayor because she was out front and speaking about ICE in a way our current mayor never did.”

Despite the restrictions placed on a D.C. mayor, immigrant advocacy and civil rights groups concerned about the incursion of ICE in the district are pushing for Lewis George to take a stand.

“We want to see the next mayor doing everything possible to protect these most vulnerable communities from continued attacks,” said Peggy Ramin, policy counsel at the American Civil Liberties Union of the District of Columbia. “Whether that is legislation or the mayor ensuring that the administration’s agencies are well educated as to what that means in terms of limiting cooperation and even prohibiting cooperation.”

In particular, Ramin said that her organization is calling on the D.C. council and Lewis George to pass legislation that would allow residents to sue any officer — local or federal — who violates constitutional rights.

Ramin is aware of the challenges facing the district to pass this type of legislation without incurring interference from Congress or President Donald Trump — who has personally vowed to oppose Lewis George .

“No matter what Congress ends up doing, whether it disapproves or passes a disapproval resolution or not, I think people here in D.C. are really demanding and asking our council to step up and pass this sort of legislation,” said Ramin.

Aside from federal immigration officials, residents also complained about the National Guard, whose presence was felt even on Election Day. “I have two boys, Black men,” said one voter, Tamika Jackson, “and the harassment is out of control.”

As evidenced by the record number of socialists winning power across the country, Hagans says it’s clear both D.C. and the nation are looking for fighters.

“Democrats have promised a lot for a long time, but they seem unwilling to stand up to Trumpism,” said Hagans. Voters are noticing “this new class of democratic socialists,” he said, concluding, “Maybe I don’t know what that means entirely, but let’s give it a shot.”

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

Alain Stephens

Only in defeat are Republicans eager to distance themselves from the war with Iran they used to champion.

Nick Turse

scraped.title: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
scraped.description: Democrats won back the Texas House for the first time in 24 years. Gov. Greg Abbott’s bullishness on vouchers turned off some Republican voters in rural communities that have historically been strongholds for his party, politicians said.
scraped.author: Lexi Churchill and Jeremy Schwartz
scraped.h1: Texas’ School Voucher Program Could Be “Unrecognizable, If Not Extinct,” Says Democratic Lawmaker
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes
