articles.summary: Candidates made history in the 2026 midterms, breaking barriers and flipping Republican-held seats as Democrats reshaped the nation's political landscape.Read more...
articles.ai_summary: The 2026 midterm elections saw historic victories for Democrats as they flipped several Republican-held seats, significantly altering the political landscape.

scraped.title: Here are The Biggest Flipped Seats of Midterm 2026 – The Root
scraped.h1: Here are The Biggest Flipped Seats of Midterm 2026
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Candidates made history in the 2026 midterms, breaking barriers and flipping Republican-held seats as Democrats reshaped the nation’s political landscape.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

(Photo by Megan Varner/Getty Images), (Photo by RONALDO SCHEMIDT / AFP via Getty Images), (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images)

The 2026 midterm elections produced a sweeping political shake-up, with Democrats emerging in control of both chambers of Congress. Keisha Lance Bottoms, Cyril Jefferson and James Talarico were among those making headlines as historic races turned into victories. But alongside the national party shift came another significant development: Black candidates secured landmark victories across the country.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

Several contests also resulted in Democrats taking seats previously controlled by Republicans. Here are the major flips reported by the Associated Press.

High Point, NC, Mayor Cyril Jefferson defeated Republican incumbent Addison McDowell to flip the district McDowell once carried by more than 38 points in 2024. His election to the U.S. House of Representatives marks a significant change in the district’s congressional representation.

Western Michigan saw a historic change as Democrat Sean McCann defeated eight-term Republican incumbent Bill Huizenga to represent Michigan in the U.S. House. His win puts the district in Democratic hands for the first time in nearly 100 years, adding another longtime Republican seat to the Democratic column.

North Carolina saw a major political shift as Democrat Lakesha Womack unseated Republican incumbent Tim Moore, capturing 51.1% of the vote. After Moore won the district by roughly 16 points in 2024, Womack’s victory turned a previously Republican-held seat in the U.S. House blue and changed the district’s political landscape.

RELATED : New Doc Takes a Look Inside the Texas Colonies Built By Black Americans After Slavery

Indiana’s 5th District delivered one of election night’s surprises. Democrat J.D. Ford defeated Republican incumbent Victoria Spartz, who had won reelection by more than 18 points in 2024. It was a major turnaround in a district Republicans expected to hold.

Georgia just elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as its first Black governor and the first Black woman governor in American history. Her victory ended nearly three decades of Republican control in the statehouse. More than a simple party flip, it marked a historic, barrier-breaking milestone in U.S. politics.

Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Greg Abbott, becoming Texas’ first Latina governor and the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990. In a state Republicans had dominated for decades, this was a generational political shift and a historic breakthrough for Latina representation.

Aaron Ford defeated Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo, becoming Nevada’s first Black governor. His victory added another Black governor to the nation’s political landscape and flipped a Republican-held governorship. The significance extends beyond Nevada: Black political leadership is no longer an exception in gubernatorial politics.

Josh Turek defeated Republican Ashley Hinson, flipping Iowa’s open Senate seat. A former Paralympic basketball player, Turek becomes the first former Paralympian elected to the U.S. Senate. Iowa also elected a Democratic senator for the first time since 2008.

Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley made history as Wisconsin’s first Black governor. His win flipped the Republican-held office and placed a Black executive at the helm of a critical presidential battleground state. Representation and political geography collided in one consequential victory.

Amy Acton defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, becoming Ohio’s first Democratic governor since 2006. Her victory ends two decades of Republican gubernatorial control and gives Democrats another major Midwestern governorship. It’s a significant reversal in a state that has moved toward Republicans in recent presidential elections.

Troy Jackson defeated longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins, ending her decades-long Senate career and flipping a seat Democrats had not won since 1988. The result is particularly significant because Collins had repeatedly survived Democratic challenges in a state that votes Democratic in presidential elections.

Adam Hamilton defeated incumbent Republican Roger Marshall, making history in a state that had not elected a Democratic U.S. senator since 1932. That’s nearly a century of Republican dominance in Kansas’ Senate representation interrupted by one election.

James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, giving Texas Democrats their first Senate victory since 1988. He also became part of a broader Democratic breakthrough in statewide Texas politics, alongside Gina Hinojosa’s gubernatorial victory. Two statewide victories in one election fundamentally changed the state’s political narrative.

Former governor Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley to claim North Carolina’s open Senate seat. Democrats hadn’t won a Senate race in the state since 2008, or an open Senate seat since 1974. That’s a 52-year drought for open-seat victories finally ending.

Dr. Annie Andrews defeated Darline Graham, flipping a South Carolina Senate seat held by Republicans since Strom Thurmond switched parties in 1964. She also becomes the first woman elected to represent South Carolina in the U.S. Senate. A remarkable breakthrough in one of the South’s most reliably Republican states.

Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted, reclaiming an Ohio Senate seat after losing his previous reelection bid in 2024. The former senator’s return flips a Republican-held seat and restores a familiar Democratic figure to Washington. A comeback with real consequences for Senate control.

Penny Brown Reynolds defeated Republican Tim Fleming, becoming Georgia’s first Black secretary of state and the first Democrat to hold the office in nearly 20 years. A former judge and Biden administration official, Reynolds’ victory marks a historic breakthrough for Black women in statewide elected leadership.

articles.ai_summary: Taiwan has closed its representative office in Papua New Guinea, citing Chinese coercion as the reason for the withdrawal.

scraped.title: Taiwan says closes representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
scraped.description: The announcement comes after a months-long dispute following PNG's decision in July to shutter Taiwan's office in the capital Port Moresby, which Taipei rejected.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Taiwan says closes representative office in Papua New Guinea, blames China
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Taiwan said Friday it has decided to close its representative office in Papua New Guinea and withdraw its staff, blaming Chinese coercion of the South Pacific nation for the decision.

“In the future, we will allocate relevant resources to friendly nations and other regions with cooperative potential that warrant continued engagement, in order to further deepen substantive cooperation and expand Taiwan’s international space,” Taiwan’s foreign ministry said in a statement.

The announcement comes after a months-long dispute following PNG’s decision in July to shutter Taiwan’s office in the capital Port Moresby, which Taipei rejected.

China, which claims Taiwan is part of its territory and opposes the self-governed island’s participation in international organisations and exchanges with other countries, previously welcomed PNG’s move.

Like many countries, PNG has formal diplomatic relations with China but had allowed Taiwan to have a representative office in the Port Moresby.

Taiwan’s foreign ministry said on Friday the island democracy was “proactively” closing the office, withdrawing “all posted personnel” and reviewing and adjusting “bilateral cooperative relations”.

Taiwan said “a series of recent actions” by the PNG government had “severely undermined the foundation of mutual trust built through long-term cooperation between the two sides”.

“These actions also reflect China’s continued use of political pressure and economic influence to interfere in the diplomatic decisions of other countries and suppress Taiwan’s international space,” the ministry said.

“The Papua New Guinea government’s decision once again highlights China’s use of political and economic means to interfere with other countries’ autonomous diplomatic decision-making and to undermine international mutual trust and the principles of fairness.”

Taiwan previously announced that it had stopped spot purchases of liquefied natural gas from PNG, but on Friday the ministry said it also would no longer sign new spot purchase contracts with the country.

The foreign ministry said Taiwanese LNG purchases accounted for one-third of PNG’s exports.

The South Pacific Nation accounted for eight percent of Taiwan’s natural gas imports in 2025, compared with Qatar (34 percent), Australia (33 percent) and the United States (10 percent), official figures show.

Taiwan will also end technical cooperation and assistance programmes, “including medical missions, related scholarship and talent development programmes”, the ministry said.

articles.title: Debt, energy, war and the fight for socialism

scraped.title: Debt, energy, war and the fight for socialism
scraped.description: On present trajectories, the world is heading toward roughly $375 trillion in total debt by the end of 2026. For comparison, capitalism—taken globally and using generous arithmetic—generates perhaps $15–25 trillion in profit or surplus each year.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
“They have no ideals to realize, but to set free the elements of the new society with which old collapsing bourgeois society itself is pregnant.”—Karl Marx, The Civil War in France

In the wake of the mass repudiation of Trump’s policies in the US midterm elections, a new stage of political and social conflict is set in the United States and around the world.

Working people seethe at rising costs, the lack of decent work and the rapid deterioration of healthcare, education and other social provisions essential to life. We watch with horror as wars in Gaza, Iran, Ukraine and Russia destroy human lives and whole societies, squandering trillions of dollars in the process. Presiding over it all is a class of billionaires dripping not just with avarice, but with outright contempt for human life.

But that which drives this crisis is not some fleeting mood of the capitalist class or temporary policy failure. As David North stated in a lecture delivered on the eve of the vote:

Whatever the outcome of tomorrow’s vote, policy will be determined in the final analysis by the crisis of the capitalist economy, by the disposition of a technology that is transforming the conditions of labor for the entire human race, by the drive of American imperialism to war and by the response of the international working class.

The direction of the world economy, and with it the politics of the ruling class, is increasingly defined by the intersection of three destructive processes.

First, the pile of debt undergirding global growth has reached astronomical proportions. On present trajectories, the world is heading toward roughly $375 trillion in total debt by the end of 2026. For comparison, capitalism—taken globally and using generous arithmetic—generates perhaps $15–25 trillion in profit or surplus each year.

Debt is a stock of financial claims backed by assets and future income, and much of it is continuously refinanced rather than paid off. But the comparison conveys the extraordinary scale of the claims that have accumulated against future production. Capitalism is mortgaging its future on an unprecedented scale.

And each year, more is added. Nearly $30 trillion in debt was added in 2025 alone. Debt is accumulating on a scale comparable to the annual expansion of the world economy itself. Interest payments on public debt alone have risen to $3.3 trillion. An ever greater stream of social wealth is sucked up and siphoned off to service the claims of banks and other creditors.

Alongside this is a second critical process: the rising cost of basic necessities and of the energy and raw materials on which economic life depends.

Diesel, a fuel essential to trucking, mining, agriculture, construction and manufacturing, has more than doubled in price for many users over the past year. European diesel futures traded between roughly $600 and $700 per tonne before the Iran war began in February. They now trade above $1,400 per tonne. These increases work their way through the economy, raising the cost of producing and transporting almost everything.

Natural gas prices, meanwhile, have tripled in Europe and Asia since the war began, with the United States relatively insulated. Similar pressures have appeared in jet fuel used by planes and the bunker fuel used by ships.

But the pressure extends beyond hydrocarbons.

Copper, a pivotal metal underpinning electronics, electrification, renewable energy and the infrastructure of AI, has also surged in price. Throughout much of the 2010s, it traded between roughly $2 and $4 per pound. It has recently traded above $6.50, reaching record levels.

Global food prices, meanwhile, remain dramatically above their levels of a decade ago. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization’s Food Price Index stood at 136 in September 2026, compared with an annual average of 91.9 in 2016—an increase of nearly 50 percent.

War, climate change, higher energy and transportation costs, and broader inflationary pressures are all to blame. For households already spending much of their income on food—grain, meat, cooking oils—it is a punishing drain.

But accompanying these two damaging processes—debt and inflation—is a third: war.

The war in Ukraine, the war in Iran, the genocide in Gaza, the fighting in Yemen, and beneath them all the mounting confrontation between China and US imperialism—these conflicts are increasingly intertwining and intensifying.

“Are we sleepwalking into World War III?” asked the Financial Times last month. In August, North described the growing conflicts as a “metastatic process” which “progressively transform[s] the world economy and every national state in preparation for the general conflagration toward which it tends.”

These three forces—debt, inflation and war—are increasingly connected expressions of the instability and crisis of the global capitalist economy. Each aggravates the others.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran and the fighting in Yemen have directly affected global energy, transportation and food prices. They have driven up the cost of fuel and agricultural production, spreading the pressure through industry and into household expenses.

By aggravating inflation, fiscal pressures and uncertainty, these wars have also contributed to rising borrowing costs, making it harder to keep the train of debt moving. The yield on the 10-year US Treasury has now reached a quarter-century high, moving past 5 percent and toward 6 percent. Higher interest payments demand still more money to service the debts already accumulated.

Meanwhile, financing the drive towards war requires enormous new expenditures, funded through a combination of borrowing and intensified extraction from the working population.

Global military spending increased by 41 percent in real terms between 2016 and 2025, while 2026 and 2027 are each expected to set new records. The Trump administration is demanding a $1.5 trillion military budget for 2027—an increase of roughly 50 percent.

Europe, meanwhile, is madly rearming for war with Russia. Germany alone plans roughly €1 trillion in military spending over the next five years, with annual expenditure rising to €168 billion by 2029, while the IMF calls for “deep cuts in the European model and the social contract” to accommodate the mounting fiscal burden.

But the connection runs in the other direction as well. Deteriorating economic conditions intensify the desperation among rival capitalist powers to control the energy, resources, markets and supply chains upon which their wealth and power depend. Each seeks to secure its own position at the expense of its competitors, even as the resulting conflicts damage the conditions of production on which they all depend.

The turn to war expresses the increasingly desperate struggle of these ruling classes to preserve their wealth and world position. They look to military power for a way out of the crisis. This is above all the course being pursued by the American and European ruling classes.

In Athens on October 7, Marco Rubio posed the question as “whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline,” calling for control over critical supply chains, economic and technological dominance and military rebuilding.

“We will make the Bundeswehr the strongest conventional army in Europe,” Chancellor Friedrich Merz declared in June 2025, justifying that goal with Germany’s size, economic strength and geographical position. At the Munich Security Conference in February, he explained, “competition policy is security policy and security policy is competition policy.” Germany’s economy is in a dire state, with high energy costs battering its industrial base and fierce competition from Chinese automakers threatening its once-dominant car industry.

And so the attempts to resolve one crisis ricochet to deepen the others.

Debt finances war; war raises the cost of necessities and of borrowing; and mounting economic pressure feeds an increasingly desperate struggle to secure control over the sources of global wealth.

The ruling class increasingly looks to artificial intelligence as a potential escape from this impasse. AI has generated enormous speculative valuations and investment, sustaining the appearance of renewed dynamism in an otherwise stagnating economy. But even as it revolutionizes production, it heightens the social contradictions of capitalism. The very advance hailed as a way out intensifies the crisis. Meanwhile, a new financial bubble has been inflated around it. It is only a matter of time before it bursts.

Who will pay for this astronomical debt? For this warmongering and rampant inflation?

The ruling class has its answer: social programs must be dismantled and hundreds of billions found for war, while private fortunes remain sacrosanct. Everything may be sacrificed to preserve and augment the wealth and power of those at the top.

Nothing remotely comparable is demanded of the immense private fortunes accumulated at the summit of society. Billionaire wealth has risen by more than 80 percent since 2020, reaching record levels even as austerity is imposed on the population. In California, a modest proposal for a one-time 5 percent tax on fortunes above $1 billion has already provoked more than $187 million in opposition spending, including over $102 million from Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone.

It is working people—the employed, unemployed and underemployed, across the world—upon whom the costs of these intersecting crises are being imposed.

They are squeezed harder every week, every month—at the grocery store, in their rent, at the gas pump and when the electricity bill comes due. Inflation means the erosion of life.

In Europe, Latin America, the United States and elsewhere, healthcare, pensions, unemployment benefits, support for families and virtually every other form of social expenditure become targets for cuts. Amid an already profound social crisis, everything afforded to the population is declared unaffordable. The debts accumulated by governments, banks and corporations, meanwhile, must be paid.

The mass youth protests in Europe and the midterm rebuke against Trump in the United States express deep popular opposition to this course. Working people are resisting the attempt to make them pay for the wars of the ruling class and the downward spiral of capitalism.

But these processes will not be halted by this or that ‘progressive’ candidate who remains fundamentally pledged to the continuation of the existing social order.

As the WSWS previously wrote :

In opposition to these forces, the working class must base its struggle on a strategy which is grounded on a complete break with finance capital. Anything less, no matter how “radical” it might sound, means subordination to its dictates.

The financial crisis cannot be resolved by adjustments, tinkering and bookkeeping measures. In the first place, the debt must be repudiated. It has been incurred to meet the interests of the capitalist oligarchy, not the working class.

The crisis of world capitalism offers its ruling classes no progressive way out. They turn instead toward war, even as its prosecution further destabilizes the capitalist economy upon which their own power rests.

In Ukraine and across the Middle East, warfare increasingly takes the form of economic attrition. Energy infrastructure, trade routes and productive capacity become military targets. The destruction of the infrastructure necessary to sustain civilian life becomes a means of exhausting an opponent’s capacity to continue the war.

Ukraine’s campaign against Russian refineries, for example, has driven Russian refinery throughput to its lowest level in more than two decades in 2026, with diesel production estimated by the IEA to have fallen nearly 30 percent. Dozens of warehouses and other commercial sites have also been struck. Russia, meanwhile, has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s power infrastructure. Russian attacks on Tuesday killed dozens and further damaged the grid as the region heads into winter.

This grinding stalemate, in which tens of thousands are sacrificed every month, increasingly turns on each side’s capacity to withstand prolonged economic and social destruction. American, Chinese and European war planners are studying its implications for future conflicts, including the possibility that a war over Taiwan could develop into a similar struggle of attrition.

The same logic is at work in Iran. The Trump administration and the Iranian government confront one another over who can withstand the sustained disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. For Washington and Israel, the failure to secure a decisive outcome creates pressure for further escalation. The United States is actively contemplating the use of its largest non-nuclear weapon on Iran.

In all cases it is working people who bear the cost of war.

Together, these convulsions express the historical exhaustion of capitalism. They emerge from contradictions accumulated over decades and intensified after the financial collapse of 2008. The vast expansion of debt and financial speculation that followed deferred the crisis while deepening the conditions that produced it: social inequality, economic instability and the struggle between the major powers over markets, resources and strategic advantage.

Capitalism as a system of organizing global social life has nothing left to offer the world. Nor can it secure its own future. Its attempts at self-preservation increasingly undermine the economic and social foundations of its continued existence. As Marx wrote, “The real barrier of capitalist production is capital itself.”

All roads here lead in one direction: the intensification of the class struggle.

Strikes and protests driven by soaring living costs, austerity and deteriorating working conditions are spreading across Asia, Latin America, North America and Europe; from truckers and healthcare workers to industrial workers and youth. The world is replete with signs of anger and refusal.

But the growth of opposition does not by itself provide a way out. So long as struggles remain divided along national lines and subordinated to the trade union bureaucracies, Social Democratic parties and their political satellites, they can be isolated and contained while the broader movement toward austerity and war continues.

The international character of the crisis demands an international response. Humanity’s accumulated scientific knowledge, technology and productive resources make possible a secure and dignified life for all, with shorter working hours and greater scope for human development. AI, automation and other developments can have a positive, revolutionary effect on humanity’s future.

But realizing these possibilities requires ending the subordination of production to private profit and the nationalist ambitions of the financial aristocracy. The productive resources of society must be placed under democratic social control and directed toward human need.

The struggle against war is inseparable from the struggle against the impoverishment of the working class. Both demand the independent political mobilization of workers, young people and the unemployed across all national borders. This movement must fight for an irrevocable break with finance capital and the expropriation of the financial aristocracy, whose wealth and power stand in the way of humanity’s further development. That is the revolutionary socialist program, and the only way through this historical impasse.

articles.title: US midterm elections anticipate explosive growth of the class struggle
articles.summary: The midterm elections expressed an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, inequality and the assault on democratic rights that will not be contained within electoral forms and will erupt in the class struggle.
articles.ai_summary: The recent US midterm elections reflect a significant rise in social discontent regarding living costs, war, and inequality, indicating a potential escalation in class struggle.

scraped.title: US midterm elections anticipate explosive growth of the class struggle
scraped.description: The midterm elections expressed an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, inequality and the assault on democratic rights that will not be contained within electoral forms and will erupt in the class struggle.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Behind Tuesday’s midterm elections, which produced the largest defeat of a sitting president’s party in half a century, lies an immense growth of social anger over the cost of living, war, social inequality and the assault on democratic rights. That anger cannot and will not be contained within electoral forms. It will erupt in the form of the class struggle.

Three days after the vote, the process is already visible. At midnight Friday, the citywide contract between New York City and American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees (AFSCME) District Council 37 expired. It covers about 90,000 municipal workers, including clerical staff, caseworkers, school aides, library workers and 911 operators. The deal it replaced, signed in 2023, provided raises of 3 percent a year and an $18 wage floor, $1 above the city minimum.

An $18 hourly wage comes to $37,440 a year for full-time work, before taxes. The median asking rent in New York City reached a record $4,199 a month in May, according to StreetEasy, or more than $50,000 a year. A city worker at the wage floor would have to hand over more than a full year’s gross pay to rent the typical apartment on the market.

These conditions are universal. In exit polls for the election, 90 percent of voters named the cost of living as a major concern, and those who described themselves as struggling financially swung by 60 points against Trump and the Republicans. Nearly 70 percent said the economic system favors the wealthy.

Friday’s jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed average hourly earnings up 3.1 percent over the year, while consumer prices rose 3.7 percent in the 12 months through September, driven by gasoline prices pushed up by the war. That is, real wages are falling. In the New York metropolitan area, prices rose 4.5 percent, and the official figures understate the inflation working people face on gas and food.

Mass layoffs are also on the horizon. Companies have cited artificial intelligence for 121,401 announced job cuts in 2026, about one in five of the total. A survey by the consulting firm Mercer earlier this year found that 99 percent of corporate executives expect AI to drive headcount reductions within two years.

On Wednesday morning, the day after Iowa elected a Democratic senator and governor, Deere announced the closure of its 115-year-old Ottumwa Works and its plant in Clarion. In Detroit, Dakkota Integrated Systems is shutting its instrument panel plant and eliminating 397 jobs.

The coming months will bring these conflicts to a head across every section of the working class. In New York, DC 37 joins the 40,000 subway and bus workers of Transport Workers Union Local 100, who have worked without a contract since May, while the Metropolitan Transportation Authority offers 2 percent raises and demands a doubling of health costs. In Boston, more than 4,000 nurses at Brigham and Women’s Hospital have called an open-ended strike for November 12.

Graduate workers at Harvard have been on strike since October 27, and strike deadlines loom this month at MIT and the California State University. Tens of thousands of steelworkers at US Steel and Cleveland-Cliffs have worked without a contract since September 1. In New Hampshire, 250 grocery warehouse workers are on strike, and UPS is eliminating up to 30,000 jobs.

The Democrats have responded to the overwhelming opposition to Trump with calls for “bipartisanship” and “common ground.” This is motivated above all by the fear, shared by every section of the ruling class, of the growth of the class struggle. Tens of millions voted for higher wages, affordable healthcare, an end to war and an end to oligarchic rule. But the incoming Democratic House and Senate have been given their marching orders by Wall Street: Rescue the markets and fund war.

Whatever their posturing before the vote, the Democrats will be compelled to wage war on the working class. Who is to pay for a national debt approaching $40 trillion? How is the military budget to be raised to $1.5 trillion? The answer of both parties is the same, and a collision is inevitable.

This is already developing in the cities and states the Democrats run, including those governed by their Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) faction.

In California, Governor Gavin Newsom’s refusal to meet the demands of state workers provoked the first strike in the history of Service Employees International Union (SEIU) Local 1000, by 100,000 workers, on October 21. In Chicago, overseen by Democrat Brandon Johnson, an ex-Chicago Teachers Union staffer backed by the DSA, the city and its school district face deficits of more than $1.5 billion. Plans for enormous cuts and “restructuring” are being announced as municipal elections get underway.

In Seattle, Mayor Katie Wilson, a self-described democratic socialist though not a member of the DSA, has proposed nearly $50 million a year in cuts while increasing police funding by $68 million. Firefighters packed the City Council’s budget hearing early last month to protest cuts that the fire chief said would take units out of service.

New York City itself is run by DSA member Zohran Mamdani, who has led the Democrats in forging a political alliance with Trump. Facing a projected budget gap of $7 billion to $9 billion next year, he has ordered two rounds of agency spending cuts and sued to block $10,000 bonuses for paraprofessionals under the Taylor Law, the state statute that bars public employees from striking.

In the developing collision, the trade union apparatus plays a decisive role in attempting to suppress the class struggle. Mamdani has also brought the union apparatus into his administration. Julie Su, who as Biden’s acting labor secretary helped block national rail and port strikes, is his “Deputy Mayor for Economic Justice,” and Jahmila Edwards, a top DC 37 official, runs his intergovernmental affairs office. If the Taylor Law is invoked against city workers, a member of the DSA will enforce it.

The United Auto Workers bureaucracy under Shawn Fain poured its resources into electing Democrats, in what Fain called its “biggest political program” in decades, while suppressing every struggle in the plants. At Bradford White, it isolated a 47-day strike and brought back the company’s terms four times until they were ratified. It has done nothing to fight the closures at Dakkota and Deere.

Teamsters President Sean O’Brien campaigned for Republicans, including Florida Senator Ashley Moody. The United Steelworkers just announced a tentative agreement with Cleveland Cliffs, which includes raises barely above the rate of inflation after keeping thousands of steelworkers on the job under rolling 48-hour extensions. Whether it backs the Democrats or the Republicans, the apparatus ties workers to the corporations and the state and blocks any independent movement of the working class.

Workers need organizations of their own: rank-and-file committees in every workplace, democratically controlled by workers and independent of the bureaucracy and both parties. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) spearheads the fight to build such committees and to link them across workplaces, industries and borders.

The same process is unfolding internationally. In France, public sector workers struck nationally on Thursday. Spain faces a general strike on November 11, Ireland a public sector strike on November 12 and Italy a general strike on November 20, while the unions everywhere confine the struggle to one-day actions. Workers in every country confront the same crisis and the same demand that they pay for war through austerity.

The IWA-RFC advances demands based not on what the corporations and the city budgets claim is affordable but on what workers need: raises that make up for inflation and rise automatically with prices, guaranteed healthcare, no layoffs or closures and control over new technology by those whose labor it is being used to replace. In New York, that means committees in every city agency, prepared to defy the Taylor Law.

All of these struggles raise fundamental political questions. Equality and an end to the domination of society by the oligarchy cannot be won under capitalism. The DSA speaks for privileged sections of the upper middle class, which seek not to end the wealth of the oligarchy but a more favorable distribution of it within the top 10 percent of the population. Genuine socialism means the transfer of power to the working class, the expropriation of the ill-gotten wealth of the oligarchy, and the placing of the banks and giant corporations under the democratic control of the working class.

The decisive question is leadership. The radicalization expressed in the vote will not develop spontaneously into a conscious movement for socialism. That requires bringing this perspective into every struggle: exposing the role of the Democrats, the DSA and the trade union apparatus, building rank-and-file committees, and winning the most advanced workers and young people to socialism. That is the task of the Socialist Equality Party.

scraped.title: Europeans got blue blinders in wake of midterm sweep
scraped.description: Western elites are tying the elections to Ukraine while ignoring the anti-Iran war sentiment that sent the GOP packing
scraped.h1: Europeans got blue blinders in wake of midterm sweep
scraped.body_text:
Western elites are tying the elections to Ukraine while ignoring the anti-Iran war sentiment that sent the GOP packing

The Democratic sweep of the midterm elections has been greeted with a wary relief across Europe . After two years of President Donald Trump's tariffs, threats to annex Greenland and scolding of European NATO allies on defense spending, many European politicians see the Republican defeat as a welcome course correction.

Yet the reactions also expose the contradictions of the European Union’s own foreign policy, particularly toward the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

Rather than examining the causes of Trump’s defeat, EU leaders have chosen to interpret it as a vindication of their own ideological beliefs.

The EU high representative for foreign policy, Kaja Kallas, unsurprisingly, saw in the election a hope that the new Congress will strengthen transatlantic unity and support for Ukraine, presumably reversing Trump’s insufficient devotion to the Ukrainian cause, which she criticized earlier.

In a similar vein, Christel Schaldemose, a vice president of the European Parliament, voiced “cautious optimism” that the results could “benefit Ukraine and the green transition.” Spain’s center-left prime minister, Pedro Sanchez, meanwhile, interpreted the vote as a “rejection of inequality, hatred, sexism and climate denial.”

Yet there is no evidence that the GOP debacle was caused primarily by Trump’s perceived lack of support for Ukraine or that it was a vindication of a progressive social agenda.

Rather, the polls, including Associated Press-NORC , New York Times/Siena , Fox News , and Gallup , consistently showed that, on average, around 75% to 80% said the “cost of living” (gas prices) and Iran war played an important role in how they planned to vote. In exit polls, 74% of voters said the war was a “crucial” or “major” factor in their decision Tuesday. Vice President JD Vance himself rated the Iran war as the top reason for the Republican wipeout.

Those in Europe who quickly seized on the anti-war sentiment were, revealingly, not the centrists opposed to Trump for ideological reasons, but his erstwhile admirers on the nationalist right.

Jordan Bardella, leader of France's National Rally, and Alice Weidel, the leader of Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD), both parties leading the polls in their respective countries, blamed Trump’s defeat on the economic consequences of his war in Iran.

This was an astute political move by the nationalists. They opposed the Iran war from the start, while some of the European leaders who initially welcomed the war are now complaining about its consequences.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz is a particularly revealing example. When Israel attacked Iran in June 2025, he praised it for doing the West's "dirty work." He defended the much larger American-Israeli bombing campaign launched in February 2026, declaring that this was “no time to lecture our allies on international law.”

Now Merz laments that the war has cost Europe more than €100 billion through higher energy prices. The “dirty work” has come with a hefty bill.

The European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who spoke of a “democratic transition” in Tehran as the U.S. and Israeli bombs began falling, now places the war’s price tag at €127 billion ($143 billion) in additional fossil fuels. Neither Merz nor von der Leyen are on the record of connecting publicly the outcome of the elections to the war on Iran, however.

Merz and von der Leyen epitomize a broader European failure. EU governments had little meaningful influence over Washington's decision to go to war. Nevertheless, some, like Germany, supported it. Others, like France, acknowledged that the war violated international law, but put emphasis on Iran’s “destabilizing behaviour” in the region. Still others, like Italy, Portugal, Bulgaria, and Cyprus cooperated by allowing the U.S. to use military bases on their territories to attack Iran. Spain's Pedro Sánchez was a notable exception, fully opposing the war from the outset.

Now, EU leaders find themselves in a bind of their own making, being blamed by the opposition for enabling a war that impoverishes their own citizens. And the cost of that support is no longer measured in inflation and prices alone, but also security. Iran made it clear that, should the U.S. and Israel attack again, it will retaliate against any country that facilitates those attacks. The NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte foolishly boasted that “5000 sorties” of U.S. aircraft were launched from Europe. European countries that cooperated in these actions are becoming legitimate targets, from Tehran’s perspective .

The only way out of this predicament is for EU leaders to follow Sanchez’s lead and refuse to play any role in supporting, in any way, any further U.S. or Israeli attacks against Iran. Instead, they should work to recover their own diplomatic role in the Middle East , including engagement with Iran and working with regional countries , like Turkey, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia , Qatar and Oman, to de-escalate tensions.

Yet Europe’s inability to distance itself from Washington’s war on Iran wasn’t simply a matter of bad judgement. It reflected EU leaders’ belief that submission to Trump was a necessary price to keep him on the side of Europe and Ukraine against Russia .

That was an obvious miscalculation; Trump has consistently shown his preference for cutting a deal with Moscow. European leaders must now understand that hoping Democratic control of Congress will simply mean a restoration of hawkish trans-atlanticism would be no less delusional than appeasing Trump has proved to be.

It is possible that a Democratic Congress could seek to increase military assistance to Kyiv and impose tougher sanctions on Moscow. But there is another possibility: Democrats may well choose to concentrate on domestic affairs and the economic consequences of the Iran war, leaving Trump considerable room to pursue negotiations with Moscow. The elections, after all, had little to do with Trump’s Ukraine policy.

The inherent uncertainty about the U.S. approach is part of the problem. EU elites must finally recognize that their security cannot remain hostage to the shifting fortunes of American domestic politics.

Fortunately, two European countries have recently demonstrated a way forward. On October 27, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke directly with the Russian President Vladimir Putin about the war in Ukraine and prospects for renewed negotiations.

Both Finland and Norway are NATO members, share borders with Russia, and strongly support Ukraine. Yet their leaders recognized that deterrence and diplomacy are not mutually exclusive. Although their initiative did not produce an immediate breakthrough, it showed that Europeans can engage Moscow without abandoning Kyiv or waiting for Washington to act.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine expose two sides of the same European predicament. In the Middle East, Europe has paid an enormous economic price for military decisions it did not control – and failed to oppose. In Ukraine, it has committed substantial resources while hoping for Washington to take the lead in confronting Russia.

Both gambits failed. A Democratic Congress cannot rescue Europe from the need to pursue its own strategic autonomy. That means more than higher defense spending or buying fewer American weapons. It also requires rejecting unnecessary wars, engaging adversaries, and pursuing diplomatic initiatives independently.

Contrary to the claims of many EU elites, the vote in the U.S. appears to be less a sign of a global rollback of national populism than a reflection of a growing backlash in the West against endless wars. The governments in Europe can only ignore that sentiment at their own peril.

scraped.title: Republicans’ Post-Midterms War Denialism Is an Exercise in Special Pleading
scraped.description: Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Just because it wasn’t only the war doesn’t mean it wasn’t mainly the war.

Republicans took a pounding on Tuesday that made past wave elections look like a mild drizzle by comparison. Just whatever you do, don’t blame the Iran war.

In a bizarre crashout in the early morning hours after the GOP’s midterm debacle, the radio commentator Erick Erickson likened blaming the war for the result to pretending the 2020 election was stolen.

That bold truth-teller Sen. Thom Tillis, the North Carolina Republican who slithered away rather than defend his Senate seat in a supposed act of defiance against President Donald Trump, also poured cold water on the idea.

“Do you honestly believe, for example, respectfully, Mr. Vice President, that we saw the departure of Hispanics over the war?” he asked on CNN the day after the seat he declined to defend fell to the Democrats by 20 points. “Give me a break. It’s more complicated than that."

Among the reasons it has taken so long for “standing up to Trump” to go anywhere in the GOP is that until relatively recently, most of the Republicans who do so are worse than he is. But I digress.

Vice President J.D. Vance has taken a lot of heat for stating the obvious about the war. Some like to imagine his Trump-ordered Iran diplomacy is somehow a form of insubordination. They should instead ruminate on the number of Republican congressional seats that could have been salvaged if the memorandum of understanding had held and the war had ended in June. The New York Times has confirmed Vance’s account that the White House received polling to that effect.

The Wall Street Journal ’s Kim Strassel thinks it’s a “hoot” that Vance recognizes the war’s downsides rather than blaming the tariffs exclusively.

“Trump’s first-term success came from largely following that Reagan playbook,” she writes. “The second-term leaned into me-too progressive populism—at the veep’s urging—and it ain’t working.”

Or, hear me out, Trump’s first-term success—which still resulted in a 40-seat loss in the 2018 midterm elections—was because he followed the Reagan playbook of limited military interventions, no new foreign wars, and his more limited tariffs regime was compatible with inflation running consistently below the Federal Reserve’s preferred target of 2 percent.

The second term leaned into me-too progressive neoconservatism dressed up in “How do you do, fellow MAGA?” populist garb against the veep’s advice, and it ain’t working.

That’s not to say the tariffs have helped, especially in the farm states where Republicans took a beating. Anything that cut against affordability was always going to be politically damaging, even if the goal was to reshore jobs. Voters continued to be angry about the economy despite relatively low unemployment under both Trump and former President Joe Biden because of the high cost of living.

Beyond the fact of the tariffs, their implementation has been capricious and haphazard. On this, there is much in common with how Trump has conducted the Iran war: purely unilateral moves, no working with Congress or recognizing its constitutional powers, no clear explanation to the public of what is going on or what the point is, and no empathy for families straining under several years of elevated inflation.

Even many Buchananite economic nationalists have long favored free trade with Canada and comparable economies, the target of Trump’s current trade war. Perhaps we have been at war with Canada , like Iran, for decades.

But the Iran War is the single biggest driver of inflation and the reason it hasn’t continued to come down. The war is the primary reason inflation remains stubbornly above where it would need to be for the Fed to consider lowering interest rates. The spike in gasoline and diesel prices is felt more broadly than the tariffs, and it also makes the tariffs’ bite worse. And for better or worse, Trump never implied he wouldn’t impose tariffs during the 2024 campaign.

There is never just one cause of something like the GOP’s midterms flop. Trump’s foibles are what they are at this point, and they aren’t likely to improve at the age of 80. He has never worn well with his more timorous supporters, and he has now been around for a decade.

Even in 2006, Republicans had other problems besides the Iraq War. But this furious denial of the war’s impact is reminiscent of those who wanted to blame GOP congressional losses 20 years ago on earmarks. Yes, earmarks often were used for wasteful projects. They were part of the culture of corruption and neatly illustrated Republicans’ abandonment of any pretense of fiscal discipline.

But the attempt to pretend they were a bigger driver of the 2006 blue wave than Iraq was always absurd. Hawks are upset today because two decades ago, they would have had a Republican vice president who went along with their ridiculous spin.

The persistence of inflation has also elevated other issues like corruption as Republican problems. This cost the GOP seats. This is downstream of the war, which itself alienated some people who voted for Trump and Republicans just two years ago, and left the party limited to voters and media voices who were always going to go down with the ship when the blue wave came.

Strassel allows that voters are “unhappy about the war, though the numbers might be different if the president had been clear about an exit strategy.” But hawks and Vance-bashers have made clear they don’t want to hear about exit strategies beyond “Just win, baby!”

“I don’t think the war itself was per se a mistake,” Erickson says. “I think half-assing the war was a mistake.” But it is the war itself that led to the Strait of Hormuz quagmire and it is the “half-assing” that is keeping this a more limited, less deadly (to Americans) operation than Iraq.

How many times will Republicans in Congress listen to the same people with the same result? Will the last one let us know before they turn out the lights?

W. James Antle III is executive editor of the Washington Examiner magazine and a contributing editor of The American Conservative .

scraped.title: The ‘Invade the World, Invite the World’ Election
scraped.description: You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
You can’t transform a nation’s demographics without upending its politics.

The Republican Party got smacked in the midterm elections because of voter frustration over the Iran War and its economic consequences, as even many Republicans, including Vice President J.D. Vance, have acknowledged.

But the scale of the Democrats’ sweeping victory was enabled by another factor: America’s racial-demographic transformation over the past several decades, driven largely by mass migration. If only whites had voted, the Republican Party would have strengthened its hold on the Senate, the House of Representatives, and state-level offices. If only nonwhites had voted, well, even the Chinese Communists would envy the Democratic Party its utter dominance.

“Invade the world, invite the world,” as the right-wing social commentator Steve Sailer famously put it, summarizing our inept leadership’s military and immigration policies. That’s the story of this election.

Georgia, once a ruby-red state, has gone from being supermajority white in 1990 to minority white today. So even though white Georgians favored the Republican candidates by wide margins, the Peach State sent Jon Ossoff back to the Senate and elected Keisha Lance Bottoms as governor, both Democrats.

The results in Texas—the most populous state traditionally held by the GOP—were even more shocking. But the data tell the same basic story. Only 37 percent of Texans are white, which is a big reason why Democrats dominated in the Lone Star State. Texas Hispanics, who tend to be fairly conservative, not only shifted blue but turned out in large numbers.

Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina, the list goes on and on, but you get the idea.

To be sure, if the Trump administration had governed more competently during the past two years—and especially if it hadn’t launched the disastrous Iran War—then whites and nonwhites alike wouldn’t have swung as sharply as they did toward the Democrats, and Republicans might have held onto the Senate. But that’s not the whole story. America’s racial diversity sets the context for its elections, and that context is an increasingly difficult one for Republicans to navigate.

I’ve argued in print and online (and online again) that the Democrats are heading toward a permanent majority because of America’s changing demographics. Few people agree with my analysis—and even the authors of the classic text The Emerging Democratic Majority (2002) have disavowed their book’s thesis—but I harbor little doubt.

If you remain skeptical, reflect on these two facts for a while: 1) No Republican presidential candidate since Herbert Hoover has won a majority of votes from any nonwhite racial group, and 2) America will be majority nonwhite by around 2045.

Done reflecting? Here’s another fact: Whites remain more divided than other racial groups between the two parties. A Democratic coalition of white liberals and nonwhites, if it holds, will achieve stable domination years before America’s electorate turns majority-minority.

Several factors have slowed the emergence of a permanent Democratic majority. The voting electorate is whiter than the general population. The Red Team can occasionally win more than 40 percent of Hispanics, America’s largest minority group. Many non-college-educated whites have fled to the GOP, partly in reaction to the Democrats’ boutique cultural fixations like transgenderism. And countermajoritarian institutions—gerrymandering in the House, malapportionment in the Senate, and the electoral college—mostly benefit the Republicans.

Some analysts, after Donald Trump’s dramatic victory in 2024, posited a new “multiracial coalition” that would keep the GOP in the game. It was wishful thinking. Trump made inroads with nonwhites, but he merely brought the GOP back to its George W. Bush numbers, more or less.

The margin of error for Republican presidential candidates is apparently slim. In 2024, Trump mobilized blue-collar whites and did reasonably well among minorities. And yet, facing a disastrous candidate installed at the 11th hour, Trump won the popular vote by a smaller margin than Hillary Clinton in 2016.

What transpired this week was a different matter altogether—an electoral backlash that some thought impossible in our age of polarization—and it will have long-lasting political consequences. The Dems will probably maintain their Senate majority over several election cycles, and if Texas just became solidly blue, Republicans won’t stand a chance at winning the White House in 2028.

Of course, a permanent Democratic majority doesn’t mean an eternal one. Perhaps the Democratic Party will splinter between its moderate and progressive factions, or maybe a viable third party will emerge that, over time, replaces the GOP. On the other hand, in cities and states that long ago became majority nonwhite, the Democrats enjoy one-party rule, and governance generally suffers.

A nation is its people, as right-wingers often say. And you can’t transform a nation without upending its politics.

Andrew Day is the senior editor of The American Conservative . He has a PhD in political science from Northwestern University. You can follow him on X @AKDay89 .

Sequoia this week announced a broad overhaul in a memo posted to X, a move that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program. Observers warn that it would be a mistake to read too much into the London closure, since the British capital has a thriving AI scene. On the other hand, the decision to end scouts says more about where venture investing is headed.

That’s partly because 17 years ago, Sequoia pioneered the scouts model, in which select founders and operators write checks on the firm’s behalf. Amid increased competition for deal flow, many VC firms followed suit . But a consensus now seems to be emerging that the model has reached its limits in its current form.

Not everyone was sold on the model in the first place. “They pioneered the scout program but [to be honest] it never made sense to me!” VC Sheel Mohnot wrote on X this week. “The scouts themselves don’t really care that much about the investments, you can still miss (like they did with Uber), not sure what it gets you. I suspect other firms will shutter theirs too,” he added.

To be clear, Sequoia didn’t make a case against scouts in the memo. Instead, it framed its decision as part of a broader need for more focus. But its goal of “putting more energy behind fewer people and things” is likely to resonate with others who’ve questioned the ‘spray and pray’ approach to scouting.

Rival firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), for instance, rolled out a global scout network aimed at spotting opportunities in the U.S. and also in smaller European hubs. But a16z partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm had revamped its program to double down “on the best people.”

Under this new approach, Vasquez explained, scouts get more resources but are also expected to be more active, such as by co-hosting dinners with the firm. “They get more budget, but we have reduced the number,” he said.

This also seems to indicate that it is VC firms that have been driving an overhaul of the model. For founders, being a scout is attractive: it brings them closer to firms they may want checks from someday, or even a partner role with, and being seen as someone who can write a check can raise their standing among other founders.

Some scouts will undoubtedly mourn the end of Sequoia’s program. Among them is Station F boss Roxanne Varza, who wrote on LinkedIn that she was “sad” to hear that the program was getting cut off, and “hope[d] that other funds [w]on’t follow suit.”

Varza, a former Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, told TechCrunch that she had no information beyond what has been shared publicly, but observed that becoming a scout had often been a stepping stone for aspiring investment managers.

“I cannot name all of the incredible scouts that have gone on to join or build funds, but there are quite a few. And the scout programs may have helped them get there — allowed them to build an investment track record, allowed them to build relationships with various funds directly, and more,” she wrote to TechCrunch.

According to Varza, the program’s impact went beyond the individual level, instead helping the entire ecosystem become more mature. “I believe they have helped to foster the investment culture and early-stage investment landscape that we now see in Europe, for example,” Varza said.

While others may agree with Varza about the role these programs have played, they may still have run their course for two reasons. First, seasoned operators may get more financial upside as angels. When it’s their own money, they get to keep the returns, too. Second, leading VC firms are now big and well-known enough that the best founders tend to come to them, so they worry less about missing deals, except at the very earliest stages or in niches and geographies where they have less reach.

Still, the pull of those early and niche deals is why scouts programs are much more likely to get revamped than to disappear entirely. “While Sequoia may be cutting the program, venture partner-style deals are likely to continue,” said Varza in her email to TechCrunch. “Scouts was just a way to scale the format. I don’t imagine Sequoia would end all forms of venture partners, but they are full of surprises.”

Anna has moderated panels and conducted onstage interviews at industry events of all sizes, including major tech conferences such as TechCrunch Disrupt, 4YFN, South Summit, TNW Conference, VivaTech, and many more.

articles.title: Australia: Police with military weapons start patrolling NSW streets
articles.summary: This historic turn is designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.
articles.ai_summary: In a historic move, police in New South Wales, Australia, have begun patrolling with military-grade weapons, aiming to normalize their presence amid rising social unrest.

scraped.title: Australia: Police with military weapons start patrolling NSW streets
scraped.description: This historic turn is designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Under conditions of rising social discontent in Australia and globally, the state Labor government in New South Wales (NSW) is spearheading an unprecedented turn in policing operations, featuring officers carrying visible military-grade long-arms on daily patrols for the first time in Australian history.

This month, Premier Chris Minns’s government began taking the militarisation of policing to a new level, deploying its newly-established Armed Response Command (ARC) to patrol prominent public places in Sydney, including potential protest locations near the Harbour Bridge and the Opera House.

Officers are also cruising in purpose-built vehicles—BMW X5s and Toyota LandCruisers—fitted with technology to receive intelligence information from the command’s operations centre. Established at an initial cost of $94.3 million, the command is expected to comprise 250 officers by the end of 2027, with 28 civilian staff members.

This historic turn is clearly designed to create a threatening political climate, normalising the presence of heavily-armed police squads on the streets, with their weapons on visible display.

ARC officers are armed with shortened versions of the semi-automatic Australian Combat Assault Rifle, developed primarily for use in wartime battle. Measuring over 70cm long and with a range of more than 500 metres, they can fire 50 rounds per minute, raising the spectre of lethal shootings.

This is part of a wider response, brought forward amid explosive mass struggles by students and workers across Europe against war, re-militarisation, the soaring cost of living and the deteriorating conditions in schools and social services.

Minns has personally boasted of, and identified himself with, the new force. “The security challenges facing our state have changed, and our policing model needs to change with them,” Minns said when unveiling the ARC in early October, claiming it was targeting violent threats.

Last Sunday, NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley made a more revealing statement. She refused to rule out the ARC being deployed at protests. “If they’re required to be there because of the heightened risk, they will be,” she said. Catley claimed that police would make those decisions, but her green light for the use of the ARC at demonstrations itself indicates government pre-approval.

Catley added that the Minns government would “absolutely not” introduce regulation to define when and where ARC officers could be deployed. The government has rejected calls by Amnesty International to publish accessible rules governing when and where the ARC combat assault rifles can be fired.

Alongside the federal Albanese Labor government, the Minns government has a repressive record. It has been in the forefront of ramming through far-reaching anti-democratic measures, such as banning so-called “hate speech,” outlawing protests in declared zones and boosting police powers to issue “move on” orders and carry out searches and arrests.

Like Labor’s other police-state measures, the government and the corporate media have presented the ARC as simply a reaction to last December’s terrorist attack at Sydney’s Bondi Beach, where two alleged Islamic State gunmen killed 15 people at a Jewish community festival. But this cannot explain the large-scale mobilisation of heavily-armed police on the streets.

Moreover, many unanswered questions remain about how the two accused Bondi Beach perpetrators, a father and son, were able to carry out a reactionary atrocity despite being well known to the police and intelligence agencies.

The government’s intent is to intimidate—and potentially use lethal force against—demonstrations or other eruptions of opposition, not individual gunmen. That includes not only the continuing demonstrations against the US-backed Israeli genocide in Gaza and the occupied West Bank of Palestine, but any unrest, as in Europe, or rallies by striking workers.

NSW police commissioner Mal Lanyon last month declared that the ARC would have a dual purpose, that of deterring people who “incite hatred or cause fear,” as well as those “who wish to commit harm.”

This is line with the efforts of the political and media establishment to conflate opposition to the genocide in Palestine to antisemitism and to accuse Gaza demonstrations of causing fear in the Jewish population, even though the protests have been joined by many Jewish people who denounce the Israeli regime.

Over the past three years, the anti-genocide protests in Australia have been among the largest per capita in the world. In August 2025, 300,000 people took part in a march across the Sydney Harbour Bridge despite intensive attempts by Minns and the police to ban it.

After four decades of increasingly militarised policing in all Australian states and territories, primarily involving para-military riot and “tactical response” squads, the ARC represents a sharp further shift in police operations, designed to establish an intimidating presence on the streets.

Rather than acting as a “flying squad” or an on-call SWAT team, the ARC represents Labor’s adoption of US and European-style policing operations where military-grade firepower is a permanent open fixture in civilian areas, often backed by heavily-armed troops.

Already, over the past decade, existing units, such as Victoria’s Critical Incident Response Team (CIRT) and Public Order Response Team (PORT), have had access to military-grade, semi-automatic rifles. They are often deployed to visible positions outside designated major public events, but with their military-style weaponry mostly kept inside their vehicles.

In 2017, the previous Liberal-National government in NSW armed the Public Order and Riot Squad (PORS) with Colt M4 carbines. That was the first time in NSW history that such a squad was equipped with military-grade rifles.

Labor’s establishment of the ARC represents a doubling down by the Minns government on its already violent response to demonstrations.

In June last year, a large contingent of police, including the riot squad, set upon pro-Palestinian protesters in Sydney outside a factory listed as participant in Lockheed Martin’s construction of F-35 fighter jets, which the Israeli military has used to drop bombs on Gaza. Several participants were bashed, with one—former Greens election candidate Hannah Thomas—facing the possible loss of her sight in one eye as a result.

On February 9 this year, the Minns government authorised a violent police operation in Sydney against a peaceful protest opposing a visit to Australia by Israeli president and war criminal Isaac Herzog. A deployment involving hundreds of police culminated in cops indiscriminately pepper-spraying, bashing and charging at the demonstrators.

Widely-viewed footage on social media showed multiple assaults perpetrated by the police. Pre-dawn police raids were then conducted on the homes of alleged protest participants, charging them with offences such as refusing to obey police orders to disperse, affray, and assaulting or hindering police.

Labor Prime Minister Anthony Albanese had invited Herzog despite a United Nations inquiry finding that the Israeli president incited genocide in Gaza. That was a measure of the Labor government’s commitment to the US-Israeli war offensives and US militarism globally.

The introduction of the para-military ARC, alongside the far-reaching laws and measures imposed under the banner of combatting antisemitism, is another warning of the repression to which the Labor governments, as well as their Liberal-National counterparts, will resort, not only to threaten anti-genocide protests but to suppress opposition to war and militarism more broadly.

Over the past two decades, Labor also has backed legislation to enable the military to be called out to combat domestic unrest or alleged threats to designated infrastructure, giving soldiers unprecedented peacetime powers , including to use lethal force, detain civilians, issue directives and search people and premises. That is in line with the deployment of troops against demonstrators internationally, most recently in France and the US.

The strengthening of the police and intelligence apparatuses, alongside the military, will be directed against the working-class discontent and political disaffection that is brewing as the burdens of war are imposed on working people, via the soaring cost of living and cuts to essential disability, health, education and other social programs, while billions of dollars are poured into the military in preparation for war.
