scraped.title: 'I ain’t trying to see her like that': Raamla Mohamed on writing Jax’s lowest moment in 'Reasonable Doubt'
scraped.description: ‘Reasonable Doubt’ creator Raamla Mohamed breaks down the intention behind Jax Stewart’s addiction storyline in season 4.
scraped.author: Haniyah P.
scraped.h1: ‘I ain’t trying to see her like that’: Raamla Mohamed on writing Jax’s lowest moment in ‘Reasonable Doubt’
scraped.body_text:
‘Reasonable Doubt’ creator Raamla Mohamed breaks down the intention behind Jax Stewart’s addiction storyline in season 4.

Creator Raamla Mohamed cringed at the thought of seeing her beloved character Jax Stewart lick the remnants of a pain pill off of a public bathroom sink in “Reasonable Doubt.” But she knew that discomfort was part of the uncomfortable reality of addiction.

“I’m a fan of the show, right? So I was like, I ain’t trying to see her like that sink. Oh my god!” Mohamed said in an exclusive interview with theGrio. “But for me I’m like, it does really get us to understand where she is, and to be honest, if you hadn’t seen something like that before…seeing the behavior it had to feel bad.”

For the “Reasonable Doubt” creator, showrunner, and executive producer, the addiction storyline in this season felt inevitable. In fact, it’s a topic she always knew she wanted to explore through the show. And while in earlier seasons it is blatantly shown through Jax’s father, Eddie (played by Richard Brooks), and her client, Ozzie Edwards (played by Kyle Barry), Mohamed has teased the prominent lawyer’s addictive personality throughout the past three seasons.

“Even in the pilot, Jax asks for some Ambien when she needs to sleep, and we see her smoke cigarettes. She has an addictive personality. So obviously, then with the trauma of being shot, it felt like an inevitable storyline, “ she explained. “It’s not until you really see it through Jax that you see that it can happen to you.”

While some social media users have shared mixed feelings about seeing the show’s leading lady fall into the cycle of addiction, others have applauded the how Jax’s storyline this season exposes one of the realities of being a “high-achieving” Black woman.

“In my mind, an addict is in an alley, smoking crack. And I think that, unfortunately, that is kind of how we think of Black people, if they’re addicts… It’s also what we’ve seen on television,” Mohamed shared. “But the truth of the matter is that now we are also part of a high-functioning community where there are lawyers, doctors, plenty of people who do well and become addicted to [substances].”

“So it’s not about how strong you are or how smart you are,” she added.

And part of the reason Jax’s storyline hits so hard that it is almost hard to watch at times is a result of the work done behind the scenes. Just as Mohamed has been intentional about creating a world that feels unapologetically and authentically Black on and off-set, the “Reasonable Doubt” team has been intentional about spotlighting the realistic escalation of addiction through careful research, bringing in Black addiction consultants like Dr. Candice Washington, and having an on-set mental health coordinator at all times. This is paired with the creative decisions amplifies the layered truths of addiction and how it impacts not only addicts but also their loved ones.

This is especially seen in the show’s explosive episode 7, which Mohamed wrote and Anton Cropper directed. Beyond the dialogue, Mohamed said she wanted it to feel “silent and intense,” which explains the decision to feature very little music in the episode, aside from Beyoncé’s “Save the Hero” closing it out.

While not all viewers can relate to the specifics of Jax’s trauma and addiction, many Black women can relate to the weight that she’s carrying. Like many Black matriarchs, Jax is balancing showing up for everyone professionally and personally and keeping up with an image people have grown to know. Jax is the dependable one, the strong one, the one who can solve any problem and still come out of the trenches looking flawless. But this season, viewers are getting a front-row seat to what happens when you spend so much time running and maintaining everything but your mental health.

“There are two lines in the season so far that I think are the most important,” Mohamed shared. “The first is from episode three, when Jax tells her therapist she’s tired of being sad. [She’s like] I’m over it. I just want to be the baddest bitch in the room. The second is when she says, ‘I’m tired of being strong; it’s exhausting.’ To me, that’s a bit of the arc. It’s like, I want to be strong, and then it’s like, oh gosh, it actually is exhausting.”

Which is why sometimes you need to tell yourself to “sit down,” the same way Lewis told Jax to and the same way our parents did when we were kids. Though this season is uncomfortable, Mohamed hopes it reminds women to that it’s okay to slow down.

“You don’t have to keep chasing more of the things, “she reminds us. “I think as women, it’s hard every day we always feel like we’re failing at something. But look around and see what you have, and [ask yourself] what you really want and what you need.”

As far as Jax, the “Reasonable Doubt” creator, described her future as “aspirational.”

“I know that there were people who were questioning this journey, but I hope that by the end of episode [7], and definitely by the end of the season, that it’ll make sense [to them].

scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

The United States Treasury Department has slapped sanctions on eight Canadian businesses for allegedly helping to evade sanctions on Iran’s government.

The department says it sanctioned money services businesses in British Columbia and Ontario in co-ordination with Fintrac, Canada’s anti-money laundering watchdog.

The U.S. Treasury said several of the entities being sanctioned also worked with Ryan Wedding , the alleged drug kingpin and former Canadian Olympic snowboarder.

The department names several companies based in Ontario and British Columbia, including the Million Exchange, NIA Nations Currency, Farah Exchange, Darvish Exchange and several numbered companies.

The department alleges that Wedding used several of these services to launder millions of dollars in drug money through the transfer of digital assets before he was arrested in January.

“Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions-evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a news release.

“Treasury will pursue and disrupt the Iranian regime’s financial channels anywhere in the world.”

The sanctions are the latest in a series of moves by the United States to clamp down on financial transactions evading sanctions as it continues its war with Iran.

Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January this year and taken to the United States to face drug trafficking, murder and attempted murder charges.

He remains in federal custody awaiting two trials in March and October of next year.

A Mexican judge was arrested this week on allegations that he accepted a $2-million bribe in exchange for granting bail to a man accused of acting as second-in-command to Wedding.

The U.S. Department of Justice said Luis Benitez Alcantara is accused of unlawfully securing the release of Andrew Clark, a Canadian man alleged to have played a key role in a violent international drug trafficking ring.

Wedding is alleged to have ordered the murders of several people, including a witness who could testify against him in a 2024 narcotics case. U.S. authorities have said Wedding had been on the run for years.

Wedding represented Canada in a snowboarding slalom during the 2002 Winter Olympics in Salt Lake City.

Canadian and American law enforcement officials allege that after competing in the Olympics, he became deeply involved in drug trafficking.

He was convicted in the United States of conspiracy to distribute cocaine and was sentenced to prison in 2010. U.S. authorities have alleged that after Wedding’s release from prison, he resumed drug trafficking under the protection of the Sinaloa Cartel in Mexico.

U.S. court documents said Wedding’s drug trafficking enterprise brought cocaine from Colombia into Mexico, then used semi-trailers to distribute the drug in the United States and Canada.

Eight people were also arrested in Canada a year ago as part of the U.S. investigation of Wedding.

— With files from Paola Loriggio in Toronto

scraped.author: Keelan Jacobs
scraped.h1: ‘It’s all fake. It’s all rhetoric:’ MP Billy Morin doesn’t have much good to say about Budget 2026
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Conservative MP Billy Morin during an Interview at APTN news Ottawa Bureau (November 06, 2026). Photo by: Keelan Jacobs/APTN

Conservative MP Billy Morin says Budget 2026 reveals a pattern of performative reconciliation that leaves Métis governments on the sidelines.

Morin, the opposition critic for Indigenous Services and former chief of Enoch Cree Nation in Alberta, went further while holding a copy of the budget.

“It is ironic that it says ‘Masters of Our Destiny,’ he said. “I have crossed out destiny and put the masters of our deficit, debt, and deceit. And when it comes to Indigenous people in particular, the deceit one really, I think, is highlighted.”

In Thursday’s budget, the federal government announced nearly $50 billion in spending over the next ten years, with $32 billion in new investments for First Nations housing and infrastructure.

“The prime minister said he was going to do $32 billion of investments, and he portrays that as new spending. I see very minimal new spending in that… All he did is keep the funding going. They had two options: cut it or keep it going. And they portray it as an investment or new funding. It’s not.”

APTN reached out to Indigenous Services Canada to ask whether the $32 billion announced in the budget was new spending or not. We were told that, at the moment, all questions related to the budget are to be directed to Finance Canada.

According to the department that responded after the story was published, “Budget 2026 newly allots $32 billion worth of new cash into community infrastructure that wasn’t previously there. This includes $1.3 billion of new money going towards First Nations off reserve, Inuit, Métis and modern treaty and self-governing partners to invest in affordable, supportive and transitional housing – which represents 10% of BCH’s [Build Canada Homes] new capital,” said the department. “How that money was derived or pooled is immaterial to the point, what matters is that community money that wasn’t available just yesterday now is – and is already flowing into Indigenous communities across the country.

“This is new money. Suggesting otherwise is patently false.”

Métis reaction

Manitoba Métis Federation president David Chartrand said Friday that his government was “appalled” by being left out of the budget.

“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” Chartrand said in a statement. “However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”

The MMF noted that Métis appear only once in the 532-page document — “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families – a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”

“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” Chartrand said. “The Red River Métis pay billions in taxes in this country, yet we have been forgotten by this government.”

Read More:

Budget 2026 delivers $32B to First Nations, but Métis, Inuit largely left out

Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ they were left out of budget

The MMF said it had met with “numerous Ministers as well as the Prime Minister” ahead of the budget to discuss infrastructure, housing, health, and child and family services.

Morin said he understands the Métis questioning the government.

“How serious is this government about partnering with the Métis when they can’t even put them and acknowledge them in the budget? Morin said. “President Chartrand has every right to be appalled with this budget because every indication from this government is just like it treats First Nations people; it’s all fake. It’s all rhetoric and they don’t really mean it.”

Keelan is Anishinaabe from Walpole Island First Nation (Bkejwanong Territory). He graduated with an Honours B.A. In Political Science from the University of Toronto and follows the stories where power, money and public policy meet. Keelan has a strong interest in economics and finance, and is a lifelong hockey and sports fan.

scraped.title: Doctors pull knife from man's eye that went through his brain—and he's fine now
scraped.description: It's the exact path, not the apparent severity that matters most, doctors say.
scraped.h1: Doctors pull knife from man’s eye that went through his brain—and he’s fine now
scraped.body_text:
It’s the exact path, not the apparent severity that matters most, doctors say.

A man in his 20s showed up to a UK hospital with the hilt of a knife sticking out of his face. The 15 mm-wide blade hidden within went completely through his right eye and through his brain, with the tip of the blade hitting the top of his skull.

Despite the ghastly injury, the man was alive and conscious when he arrived. He could still talk and move all four limbs. His doctors described him as being in a state of agitation. On the Glasgow Coma Scale, he scored a 12 (E3 V4 M5) , indicating a “moderate” brain injury, just one point above “mild.” He could open his left eye when told, but otherwise kept it closed (E3 score); he could talk and answer questions, but was confused (V4); and he intentionally moved away when pressure was applied to his body (M5).

In a report published Friday in BMJ Case Report, his doctors said they were concerned that in his confused, agitated state he may try to pull the knife out on his own. So, they swiftly sedated and intubated him. They put him on prophylactic treatments for bacterial infections, including tetanus. Then they used images to see what was going on in his head.

The blade was entirely through the right eye socket and eyeball. It traversed the left frontal and temporal lobes of his brain, passing through in front of—and without apparently injuring—the corpus callosum, which connects the two sides of the brain and is full of nerve fibers. The blade also missed the left internal capsule, which holds another bundle of nerve fibers.

In terms of damage to major blood vessels, doctors found that the blade was close to the left internal carotid artery, a major blood vessel, but didn’t seem to have damaged it. Doctors did find, however, that a branch of the middle cerebral artery looked to be indented by the knife.

After consulting with various medical specialties, the man’s doctors moved to emergency neurosurgery. They opted to remove part of his skull to directly see into the brain, but used a conservative “ pull-and-see ” method to slide the blade out rather than invasively excavate it. After it was out, the doctors saw no signs of significant hemorrhaging. The brain wound was cleaned and drained before surgeons patched up his skull. His right eye, however, couldn’t be saved. Given its extensive damage, it was removed.

The man then moved to intensive care, where he recovered rapidly. A day after surgery, doctors were able to remove his breathing tube. He developed some minor right-side weakness, but it resolved two days later. Scans of his brain showed steady improvement—a little bleeding and swelling, and there was some air in his brain tissue from where the knife had been. But otherwise, it appeared to be healing. He developed no infections and had no seizures.

Despite the “dramatic intracranial trajectory,” his language function was preserved, and he had no loss of movement or coordination, they reported. He was discharged from the hospital and at follow-up appointments remained “neurologically well,” with ongoing eye and mental health care.

As for how the injury happened, his doctors still don’t know. “The mechanism is unclear,” they wrote. However, they noted he had a history of depression.

The doctors reflected on how lucky the man was to have survived and to have such a full recovery. Such injuries that go through the eye and the brain are rare. When they do occur, they’re usually from “high-velocity mechanisms” such as gunshots or other ballistic injuries. Knives, rods, and nails fit into the rarer “low-velocity mechanisms. “Such “low-velocity penetrating brain injuries carry substantial morbidity and mortality because of hemorrhage, vascular injury, abscess, meningitis, cerebrospinal fluid leak, seizures and neurological deficit,” they wrote.

But such fortunate recoveries aren’t unheard of; they cited reports of other remarkably unexpected recoveries from seemingly devastating brain injuries. That includes the famous case of Phineas Gage , a railroad foreman who survived an 1848 accident that sent a large iron rod directly through his head. The rod entered below his left cheekbone and exited the top of his skull. (Although he survived and recovered, Gage’s personality was said to have changed after the accident. The doctors in the knife-wound case did not mention any such personality changes.)

“Echoing classic and contemporary examples of severe frontal lobe penetration with unexpectedly preserved neurological function, including Phineas Gage and a reported nail-gun injury , this case highlights that outcome may depend less on external severity than on precise trajectory relative to critical vascular, cortical and subcortical structures,” the doctors concluded.

After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

So too in Aristophanes’s ‘Clouds,' writes Spencer Klavan. scraped.title: A 2,400-Year-Old Explanation for the Republican Midterm Disaster
scraped.description: Trump promised to restore the principles that built America. But his execution has veered so far into depravity as to put many young people off the project altogether. So too in Aristophanes’s ‘Clouds,' writes Spencer Klavan.
scraped.author: Spencer Klavan
scraped.body_text:
Depending on your perspective, the Republicans’ recent belly flop in the midterm elections might seem like a tragedy, a farce, or a bit of both. Hysteria and ecstasy have been easy to come by. Wisdom, it must be said, has not.

At moments like this, when panic and fanaticism reign in the present, I find it helpful to take a break from the fracas of the news feed and look for enduring insights from the past. Right now, in particular, I’m getting a lot out of an ancient Greek comedy: Aristophanes’s Clouds .

When Clouds was first produced in the late 5th century BCE, Athens was just beginning to lose its grip on the sprawling naval empire it gained in the wake of a stunning victory against Persia a generation before. A little like America after the World Wars, Athens emerged from the Persian Wars as a freshly minted world leader, flush with cultural and political confidence. Just as America’s postwar energies largely dissipated into partisan infighting and foolhardy military expeditions, Athens found its golden-age glow quickly fading away as chronic overreach brought it into conflict with its rival Sparta in the disastrous Peloponnesian War.

All of this sets up Clouds to be remarkably informative about the question of how the MAGA movement, in just a few short years, ceded its extraordinary momentum to the young Turks of the Democratic Party.

Let’s back up to set the scene. Clouds ’ playwright, Aristophanes, had a long-standing feud with various Athenian political leaders—especially Cleon, a general in the ongoing Peloponnesian War and a blustering populist hawk (not entirely unlike Donald Trump in his later years). But Aristophanes was no revolutionary itching to tear down the system and bring on anarchy. Rather, his plays bitterly savage Athens’s leaders not because they represent law and order, but because, in his view, they mis represent it by thundering about virtue while indulging their own vices.

scraped.description: November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.
scraped.author: Damien Bernard
scraped.body_text:
November 5 brought 1.6 million to the streets in France and high strike rates on the railways and in education, confirming workers are joining the youth movement. While the government seeks to channel discontent through negotiations, we need a plan of action for a general strike.

Damien Bernard

Public discontent was palpable, as the massive protests on October 17, 24, and 31 had already shown. But November 5 marked a leap forward, with nearly 1.6 million protesters, including 350,000 in Paris, according to the CGT labor federation. The mobilization was particularly strong in the major cities: 150,000 protesters in Marseille, 120,000 in Bordeaux, 100,000 in Lille, 80,000 in Toulouse, 55,000 in Lyon, 35,000 in Nantes and Rennes, 30,000 in Rouen, 28,600 in Grenoble, 26,000 in Caen and Strasbourg, 25,000 in Brest, 22,000 in Tours, and 20,000 in Orléans, according to the CGT.

The scale recalls certain days of the 2023 battle over pensions and reflects an outrage that extends far beyond young people and certain sectors of the workforce, sweeping across the entire country.

This widespread participation has led to major strikes across various sectors. At the SNCF (the French national railway company), strike participation was particularly high, ranging from 50 percent to 80 percent depending on the sector, according to management’s own figures.

In the national education system, according to the SNES-FSU union, 52 percent of secondary school staff joined the strike — marking the first majority strike since December 5, 2024 — compared to 38 percent on September 29. Having backed high school students since early October, education staff are thus taking their solidarity with young people a step further.

In the private sector, reports indicate that approximately 50 percent of refinery workers went on strike in Donges, La Mède, and Flandre. The striking workers’ main demands of the striking workers are support for young people and higher wages. Wages are also central for employees at Disneyland Paris, who took action on Thursday to demand raises that keep pace with inflation and lower gas prices.

This day marked a new phase in the convergence of the labor movement and the youth uprising. The latter remained a driving force behind the mobilization, with 1,000 high schools blocked or closed, according to student organizations. At universities, more than 50 campuses were already blockaded as of November 3, roughly half of all campuses, according to the same organizations. And on Thursday, numerous universities saw protests, blockades, and even occupations, such as Jussieu in Paris and Le Mirail in Toulouse.

This convergence was particularly evident in the rallies held across the country and called by interprofessional general assemblies. In Saint-Denis, at Paul-Éluard high school — where 80 percent of the staff were on strike to protest the administrative investigation launched after they opposed the intervention of the BAC (Anti-Crime Brigade) — strikers from the RATP bus depot at Barrage and students from Paris 8 University joined the rally organized by the city’s interprofessional union, before marching toward the Gare du Nord and then on to République.

About a hundred people gathered at 9 a.m. in front of the Châtillon maintenance depot to hear speeches and take part in a joint march organized by the Paris South Interprofessional General Assembly. In eastern Paris, hospital staff and social workers joined high school students and marched, despite police action that led to the arrest of an RP activist. These groups ended up at the head of the Paris demonstration, alongside anti-racist activists, drawing thousands of people around slogans calling for a “general strike” or opposing the Far Right, despite police repression.

The fight against repression has also been a major driver of this solidarity. In Montpellier, SNCF workers, hospital staff, teachers, and university students joined the picket line at Clémenceau high school at the call of the young people. Where police had deployed in large numbers every morning to break up the blockade, they withdrew when the workers and students arrived. In Le Havre, the arrest of four high school students on Tuesday strengthened ties with workers, and several demonstrations — some drawing as many as 1,000 people — were held to demand their release, joined by workers from CIM, Total, Sidel, Stillwater, and Safran. The issue is all the more pressing given that police violently suppressed the protests on Thursday, even charging the inter-union contingent in Toulouse and causing numerous injuries.

More broadly, however, this convergence rests on shared demands. At the Paris demonstration, teachers from Charlemagne high school accompanied their students in a show of support, saying that the students’ demands were also their own: “They want to improve our working conditions.” Wages, the high cost of living, public services, and the future of young people were common causes. In Sens, Lou, a high school student at the protests, summed up this link between generations: “I’m also fighting for my parents, for gas prices, for the cost of living — period.” All these factors could help build a genuine general strike, building on the momentum generated by young people, provided that the right plan of action is developed.

While the mobilization has taken on a new scale and shows a genuine desire to escalate the strike and build momentum, the government is seeking to regain control. On Thursday, Prime Minister Lecornu announced a “social conference” for Monday, responding in particular to a request from the CFDT, the largest labor federation. This initiative aims to steer the mobilization back into the realm of social dialogue, offering some concessions and relying on the union leadership’s willingness to negotiate.

This approach, which relies on the pressure of protests to secure some concessions, is a dead end for winning our demands, as the government’s proposals show, with an initial minimum wage increase of just a few euros. Meanwhile, CFDT General Secretary Marylise Léon is demanding a net increase of €100 in the minimum wage — which does nothing to address the “high cost of living” — and her CGT counterpart, Sophie Binet, is putting the onus on the government instead of calling for an escalation of the strike. What is needed is a battle plan equal to the moment, one that moves toward a general strike by bringing in sectors that have not yet joined the struggle and putting forward demands that inspire people to fight.

Grassroots organizing will be key to advancing this strategy, as Anasse Kazib explained ahead of the protest day. In recent weeks in Toulouse, more than 800 people gathered to prepare for the rolling strike and organize actions at Airbus, among sanitation workers, and at Tisséo (the public transit company); and on Thursday, the interprofessional bloc turned out in force at the demonstration.

In Bordeaux, students called for interprofessional general assemblies to join forces with the labor movement. All these initiatives serve as levers to fight for change and oppose the government’s attempts at negotiation; they should become concrete tools in the struggle, coordinate real sectors of society, help convey the radicalism of the youth to the workers, and combat repression. As a symbol of this potential, in Paris, the rally in front of the SNCF maintenance depot in Châtillon turned into a spontaneous march toward Montparnasse to confront Sophie Binet and fight for a general strike.

The strike rates reported in various sectors and the ties being forged with young people show that there is a foundation for moving this movement forward. Our strength lies in the streets, in workplaces, and in schools: we must use this mobilization to widen the movement. Now more than ever, we must set up interprofessional assemblies everywhere to organize joint actions, send delegations to workplaces, and bring new sectors into the strike.

The government is growing nervous; we must seize this opportunity to take the next step and organize a general strike capable of paralyzing the economy and imposing concrete demands, such as a net minimum wage of €2,000, a €400 raise for everyone, a ban on layoffs, major investment in public services, the repeal of Parcoursup (the French university admissions platform), the release of all detainees, and the government’s resignation.

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

A generation caught in global chaos is rising up in the face of a capitalist system that grows more corrupt by the day.

Julien Anchaing and Enzo Tresso

The mobilization that put Aleksandar Vučić’s government on the ropes reflects a deep political crisis. Vučić has conceded defeat to the Student List, but beating the ruling party at the polls is not enough: we need an independent working-class alternative built on worker-student unity.

In this episode, Tatiana Cozzarelli speaks to Andrew Feffer, author of Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism. They discuss the Rapp-Coudert investigation and the anti-communist witch-hunt of the early 1940s — and the parallels to today's repression against the movement for Palestine.

Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, flipped Texas, and saw DSA send a record five new members to the House. The midterms marked the beginning of a post-Trump moment, but the Democrats have no answer to the crisis that brought them here.

scraped.title: Stephen Miller To Take Over As White House Chief Of Staff
scraped.description: Stephen Miller, perhaps the Trump administration's foremost immigration and deportation hawk, will take over as chief of staff.
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Stephen Miller To Take Over As White House Chief Of Staff
scraped.body_text:
Miller has demonstrated laser focus on mass deportations and how government policy needs to benefit the American people.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, perhaps the Trump administration’s foremost immigration and deportation hawk, will take over as chief of staff after Susie Wiles resigned her position Thursday night.

President Donald Trump announced Miller’s promotion on social media, stating Miller is one of his “most trusted advisors,” adding, “Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!”

The shake-up at the top comes after devastating midterms for Republicans, where many voters were angry with the protracted war in Iran and its resultant high gas prices and a lack of focus on domestic issues like affordability.

Staffing changes after election defeats are fairly common, and more could come. Officials in top positions at the Department of Justice have also started turning in their resignations, including Assistant Attorney General for Civil Rights Harmeet Dhillon and Assistant Attorney General for the National Security Division John Eisenberg .

Some on the right, like Steve Bannon, who served as the White House chief strategist in Trump’s first term, called for Wiles to be removed , stating, “I think that you have to look to people like Susie Wiles, the chief of staff, and the political consultants that are there … because of the results, they should be removed and removed immediately.”

Matthew Peterson, a Claremont Institute fellow and founder of FORUM, a debate platform for the new right, added that Wiles’ ouster “needed to be done a good long while ago, but was necessary this week,” calling Miller’s succession a “game changer.”

“Wiles is obviously an extremely capable operator, good at managing Trump, and deserves credit for the win,” he stated. “But after the first heady 6-9 months of the admin, as time went on, her lack of internalized understanding of the actual MAGA agenda became damning. The amount of stuff that has been blocked, from MAHA to immigration, and the fools who have been suffered — long after proving they can’t do the job — is, well A LOT.”

Miller is well-liked on the right as someone who has demonstrated laser focus on mass deportations and how government policy needs to benefit the American people, economically and culturally.

When speaking of mass deportations, Miller said , “At every turn illegal aliens have always been treated better than Americans.”

“Do you have any idea how many resources will be opened up for Americans when the illegals are gone? No more waiting in line at an emergency room, no more massive traffic in Los Angeles,” he continued. “Your health insurance premiums go down, your public school classroom size will shrink dramatically. They have more time to educate every student. You won’t have to compete for public benefits.”

Miller’s message on why drug traffickers from South and Central America needed to be “treated just as brutally and just as ruthlessly” as ISIS or al-Qaida is because successful domestic family formation is dependent on securing the homeland, adding , “A country cannot pursue economic growth, cultural enrichment, art, architecture, education, science, if it doesn’t have fundamental security first.”

Fraud is another area in which Miller has spoken about an issue fully in terms of Americans’ birthright and how it is being stolen by foreigners who do not belong in the country, stating, “The main thing I want the American people to know is that if you’re a middle-class taxpayer in this country, before President Trump came along, you spent half your working life paying for fraudsters and scammers, many of whom are refugees, illegal aliens, and foreigners who came to this country to loot and plunder us.”

scraped.author: Elyse Wild
scraped.h1: ‘An existential threat to Indian Country’ | Tribal Leaders Warn Bill Would Reduce Tribal Consultation, Destroy Sacred Lands
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

On Monday, Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate will vote on a bill that, if passed, could have far-reaching consequences for tribal preservation, sacred sites, and cultural resources across Indian Country.

The Senate Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) aims to accelerate federal environmental review of project proposals. The bill proposes significant changes to long-standing environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act. The bill was introduced in September, with no congressional oversight, public hearings or tribal consultation.

Advocates and lawmakers opposing BAAJA say that while the bill includes provisions that would advance clean energy initiatives, other provisions would devastate tribal sovereignty and environmental protections by allowing developers access to public lands for uranium mining, oil and gas pipelines, large-scale data centers, and more, without judicial review.

Your contribution is appreciated.

As well, it would narrow which projects receive review under Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, which mandates tribal consultation to determine how projects will affect areas of cultural significance to tribes.

At a virtual press conference held on Friday, Nov. 6, by conservation nonprofit Earthjustice, tribal leaders and advocates outlined their opposition to the bill.

All Pueblo Council of Governors chairman Joey Sanchez said the council is taking direct action and urged lawmakers to vote against the bill.

“APCG is headed to Washington, D.C., to make sure our voices are heard opposing this harmful legislation,” Sanchez said.

National Congress of American Indians President Mark Macarro (Pechanga Band of Indians) said many cultural and religious sites are outside reservation boundaries, making Section 106 crucial to protecting sacred lands.

“This is such an existential threat to Indian Country in the way that we try to protect our religion, our culture, our homelands,” Macarro said. “Having most of our land, having had it be stolen over the years, over the decades, over the centuries, there’s so much off our existing reservations and tribal lands.”

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., said that while permitting reform needs to happen to bring down the cost of energy, the bill would only do so at the expense of tribal sovereignty.

“So many of us want permitting reform, but we’re not going to do it by selling out and throwing under the bus Section 106 tribal consultation and these important environmental bedrocks, and that’s why I’m against this bill,” Leger Fernández said.

Native American Rights Fund staff attorney and Navajo Nation citizen Daniel Cordalis also spoke at the press conference, saying that BAAJA would roll back generations of hard-won tribal rights.

“Rights that we have fought for for generations, the bill, as written, blindly reduces and even stops the ability of tribal governments to participate as sovereign partners in federal decisions that can impact our legally protected rights in land, water and species interests,” Cordalis said.

While its rumored forthcoming amendments could ease the bill’s implications on tribal consultation, Macarro said they would fall short.

“The premise of the product is all wrong, and one of the reasons that it’s wrong is procedurally it is lacking in consultation with tribes,” Macarro said. “As leaders of tribal nations, sovereign leaders of tribal nations, we expect tribal consultation. That hasn’t happened, and a bill of this magnitude should not be the product of a rushed process at the end of a congressional session. It requires order and a deliberate process, where tribes have the opportunity to submit comments, not just on the fly.”

Elyse Wild is Senior Health Editor for Native News Online, where she leads coverage of health equity issues including mental health, environmental health, maternal mortality, and the overdose crisis in... More by Elyse Wild

scraped.title: Germany’s Gen Z Joins the Revolt While Die Linke Forms Coalition with the Center - Left Voice
scraped.description: The Berlin Left Party's state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.
scraped.author: Ari Aalto
scraped.body_text:
The Berlin Left Party’s state convention is likely to approve the coalition talks on Saturday. But the fight against expropriation and solidarity with Palestine must continue.

Ari Aalto

The Berlin Die Linke (Left Party) state convention this Saturday will most likely give a green light for coalition talks with the Social Democrats (SPD) and the Greens. Since these two parties have already approved in principle, coalition talks will probably begin next week. The acceptance of the coalition agreement, which the negotiating teams are expected to submit around the beginning of December, will then be put to a vote by party members.

On the same day, the still somewhat vague youth phenomenon of GenZ regelt (“GenZ’s got this”) will also be mobilizing. Spurred by a massive movement in France, demands for youth protests in numerous German cities are circulating on social media. Because here too, many young people feel that they are growing up in a world that offers them nothing but wars and crises, while schools are crumbling and teachers are overworked. Even if the full impact is still difficult to predict, the strong response proves that there is also a generation in Germany that feels the need to take their future into their own hands and is prepared to take to the streets. This will continue to be necessary. Because the exploratory talks between the red-red-green coalition in Berlin promise only more of the same – social cuts, militarization, and police repression – rather than any real change.

Not all members of the Left Party are happy about the prospect of a red-red-green coalition governing Berlin. Even before the election, but especially since the preliminary and exploratory talks were announced, the Left Party Youth organization [‘solid], state and federal Palestine solidarity movements within the party, portions of the party’s grassroots organizations, and the network “Left within the Left” (LidL) have criticized the coalition’s participation in the government. And rightly so. The joint exploratory statement from the three parties suggests that the future coalition won’t even meet the Left Party’s one central campaign promise : a public referendum on expropriating housing from massive real estate concerns like Deutsche Wohnen & Co., Vonovia, Adler and Heimstaden. Draft legislation will not be presented to the House of Representatives until mid-2028, and it would only apply to housing with at least 10,000 units and would not even be implemented in the next legislative session. This leaves more than enough time for companies to restructure or for the SPD, together with the CDU at the federal level, to simply prohibit the socialization of housing . And as it is, all of the coalition’s projects are subject to strict funding approval.

Disappointing for many was the party leadership’s complete capitulation to a media smear campaign, primarily directed against pro-Palestinian factions within the party. Not only did they swallow the lie that the Left Party has a massive antisemitism problem, they also insisted upon a mechanism in the exploratory agreement that allows the SPD and the Greens to interfere in the Left Party’s internal democracy and demand expulsions if they so choose. And already, Vedi Emde, the Neukölln representative who won her direct mandate with 46 percent of the vote, is being threatened with expulsion from her parliamentary faction because of her stance on Palestine . However, the overwhelmingly strong election results of candidates who campaign on a pro-Palestinian platform demonstrate that, after three years of the Gaza genocide, a large portion of Berliners no longer accept the conflation of criticism of the Israeli state with antisemitism.

All of this shows that those in the Left Party who want to govern within a bourgeois state need to rely on media smear campaigns, other bourgeois parties, and the state apparatus itself (for example, the threat of contacting the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution) to discipline or eliminate opponents within their own party. However Elif Eralp’s recent scandal with Der Spiegel may have come about, the result was that, while she was forced to publicly humiliate herself this allowed her to clearly align herself with the press attacks against a Palestinian activist like Ibrahim Ibrahim—the only person in this entire affair who was actually attacked and threatened. These attacks, which the leadership of the Left Party joins in, are currently directed against anti-imperialist movements, but will soon target even those who oppose rearmament of the German state.

A demonstration against entering coalition negotiations on this basis will take place on Saturday at 11 a.m. in the Dong Xuan Center in East Berlin, prior to the party congress. The demonstration is being organized by, among others, the Internationalist Alliance, in which we as Klasse gegen Klasse (Class Against Class) are also involved, together with left-wing factions within the Left Party. Union members from the Berlin hospital movement are also planning a protest before the party congress, as the exploratory agreement makes no mention of the reintegration of the outsourced subsidiaries of the Berlin hospitals Charité and Vivantes.

The call to action from the Internationalist Alliance for the rally states , among other things:

The German state is militarily, politically, and ideologically complicit in the crimes of the Israeli state. […] Party chair Ines Schwerdtner promised at the ‘Together for Gaza’ demonstration on September 27, 2025, to stand with the Palestinians and to take action against both the genocide and the repression of the Palestinian movement. […] But for the leadership of the Left Party, opportunism and the pursuit of managing capitalism, together with the racist, genocidal parties SPD and Greens, means throwing Palestinian solidarity under the bus. […] This is particularly evident in their dealings with the Left Party in Neukölln, as well as the Federal Working Group (BAG) and State Working Group (LAG) for Palestinian Solidarity. […] They show once again that German militarization and imperialist ambitions in Southwest Asia, along with the maintenance of Israel’s settler colonialism, are a more important concern than the struggle for the political and economic rights of workers. […] To put this into practice, the Left Party now wants to strengthen the Office for the Protection of the Constitution and the police in coalition with the SPD and the Greens, in order to restrict our rights to demonstrate and freedom of expression using state power. Thus the party leadership betrays both voters and its own grassroots members in order to attack solidarity with Palestine supporters together with genocide supporters.

We call on everyone who recognizes the exploratory paper as an attack to join us at the rally: the Palestine solidarity movement; supporters of expropriating Deutsche Wohnen & Co.; students campaigning against arms research and their universities’ own complicity in genocide and apartheid; victims of racist and sexist police violence; and neighbors from Neukölln and Wedding. Let’s make the rally a place for networking and exchanging ideas on how we can fight for real change from the bottom up. Not by lazy compromise with capitalist government, but through mass mobilization, strikes, and blockades like those in France and Spain.

Whether the Left Party forms a coalition with the SPD and the Greens is a fundamental decision about its direction. Governing at any cost or building a militant opposition on the streets? This is a decisive question that separates party members by those who want to support the capitalist regime and those who want to fight it — even if they aren’t yet convinced that a revolutionary party, clearly distinct from reformism, is necessary. That is why we at Klasse gegen Klasse and Waffen der Kritik (Weapons of Critique) have tried, in recent weeks and in various ways, to gather forces for a clear rejection of the Left Party’s participation in government and for building a grassroots movement that can defend Palestine solidarity and actually enforce the expropriation of Deutsche Wohnen and similar companies.

As part of the Neukölln local group, we campaigned at the State General Assembly (LVV) of the Left Youth [‘solid’] at the beginning of October for a clear rejection of participation in government and for the active organization of resistance. [‘solid’] Berlin passed two important resolutions at this assembly: It reaffirmed the Berlin Left Youth’s position against participation in government with Greens and the SPD and emphasized “that renewed participation in government will have no positive effect on building a socialist party of resistance (which is what we need), but rather a negative one.” At the same time, the assembly expressed solidarity with all those affected by the smear campaign launched by the mainstream media together with the SPD and the Greens since the Left Party’s election victory in Berlin.

We promoted this same perspective at a large event organized by the “Left within the Left” network on October 13th, which drew nearly 200 participants , as well as at the plenary session of the “Left within the Left” network (LidL) on October 23rd, in grassroots organizations of the Left Party, and in the State Working Group (LAG) and the Federal Working Group (BAG) for Palestine Solidarity. Partly at our initiative, the BAG resolved at its meeting on October 25th to

call upon the members and delegates of the Berlin State Party Congress to mobilize and vote against the party’s participation in the government. It calls upon all left-wing members of the federal party, all left-wing currents within the party, and all socialist groups outside the party to fight for a joint socialist anti-government campaign.” This is because “the alliance with the SPD and the Greens requires abandoning a program that directly attacks the interests of capital.

Within the “Left within the Left” network, as well as in the LAG Palestine Solidarity, we have also proposed submitting a corresponding motion to the party congress against entering into coalition negotiations with the SPD and the Greens, and instead

advocating for the building of a militant opposition on the streets, in factories, schools, and universities. Only with mass mobilizations, strikes, and blockades like those in France or Spain will it be possible to actually attack the interests of capital instead of making weak compromises, to fully implement the expropriation of large real estate companies, to defend Palestine solidarity, and to repel the governments’ rearmament and austerity plans and the rise of the extreme right.

Unfortunately, many members of LidL and the LAG were concerned that such a clear rejection of participation in government would fail to garner a majority. Instead, the LAG adopted a motion demanding simply better results than those achieved in the exploratory talks as a basis for entering coalition negotiations. This logic inevitably leads to powerlessness, as it avoids clearly stating the cause of the party leadership’s concessions and betrayals—co-management of capitalism and participation in government—out of fear of being temporarily in the minority (which certainly reflects the balance of power within the Left Party, a predominantly reformist party where some sectors are becoming more radical in light of current events, but where considerable confusion still prevails, particularly regarding the question of class independence from capitalist parties).

But only by clearly stating it and disseminating it with the greatest effort will other sectors of the party be able to join this critique. By systematically refusing to speak out loud and clearly, these opposition forces risk becoming mere pawns of the left, serving only to promise that a different, somewhat less subservient, form of government participation might still be possible. We consider this a grave mistake, but we remain committed to the urgent need to unite all sectors within and outside the Left Party that oppose adapting to the SPD and the Greens and the perspective of simply managing the imperialist state. We invite all members of the Left Youth [‘solid], the SDS (the party’s Socialist-Democratic Student Association), and the Left Party itself who share this perspective to fight alongside us and join the “Left within the Left” network (click here for the Telegram channel).

We critically support a motion raised by the Left Youth [‘solid] Berlin for the state party conference, which rejects a coalition with the SPD and the Greens. However, we are critical of the motion’s proposal to elect a minority government comprised of the SPD and the Greens. This would ultimately amount to a “light” version of government participation, as it sacrifices the perspective of class independence just as much and generates the same pressures for integration and loyalty to the state. The only difference is that the left-wing representatives who would vote for a Green and SPD budget might feel they are getting off more lightly, since they are only complicit in the policies of the Greens and the SPD instead of supporting them themselves.

Also worth supporting are the motions by [‘solid] for the reintegration of outsourced subsidiaries, as in the case of the Vivantes hospitals, whose workers have struck for more than 60 days this year for this very purpose and were likewise sacrificed to the alliance with the austerity parties SPD and the Greens — against the sanctioning mechanism and expulsions from the parliamentary group, as well as for a six-week deadline between the conclusion of coalition negotiations and the members’ vote.

Even if the rejection of coalition negotiations by the party congress on Saturday seems unlikely, the fight for an opposition perspective is not over. We must use the time until the membership vote to raise awareness of this perspective. Anger over the media smear campaign and the spineless way the party leadership handled it is shared by many people both inside and outside the Left Party, who voted for the Left as a voice for the expropriation of large real estate companies and for a free Palestine. Many people are also justifiably disillusioned by the results of the exploratory talks, even if some still harbor some hope that at least expropriation might be achievable with a red-red-green coalition. Now it all comes down to engaging in dialogue with all these people and transforming their disappointment and anger into action.

We have to engage with them on why the disastrous outcome of the exploratory talks wasn’t simply an operational mishap that could have been prevented with a better negotiating team. The crisis of the German economic model means that even modest reformist policies have extremely limited room for maneuver. The only force that can compel the bourgeoisie and its state to make genuine concessions is the independent power of youth and workers. With the school strike against military conscription, a certain youth vanguard has emerged in Germany that recognizes that it must mobilize itself for its own defense. But the spark from the European mobilizations is also beginning to ignite even the heavy battalions of the German labor movement, as exemplified by the IG Metall shop stewards at Mercedes-Benz Untertürkheim . We have to strengthen these movements and unite them under a revolutionary program. That alone should be the linchpin of a truly socialist party – not pandering to the Greens and the SPD, not betraying every principle and its own party members just for a few government seats — where at the end of the day they will be forced to help manage the capitalist misery of social cuts and police violence.

There is still enough time before the membership vote to initiate discussions on this issue within all grassroots structures of the Left Party. To this end, the networking of the left wing must be strengthened: all members and branches that are critical of the coalition with the SPD and the Greens must now join the “Left within the Left” network (LidL). But above all, this discussion has to extend beyond party lines in order to truly mobilize all forces that, with the fiasco of the coalition negotiations, are beginning to recognize the limits of reformist government policies. These are the forces we can convince, based on their current experiences, to join us in intervening in the class struggle and to build a force of workers and youth independent of the state and the bosses.

For this reason, we are planning a defense rally with [‘solid] Neukölln in November, to which we want to appeal to everyone who is angry about the media smear campaign and disappointed with the party leadership, and who wants to build a strong opposition on the streets, in schools, universities, and workplaces. We invite all bodies of the Left Youth, the SDS, and the Left Party to do the same.

Because it’s clearer every day: the expropriation of large housing corporations that line the pockets of shareholders with our money and leave us to get sick in moldy apartments; the cutting of ties with institutions that actively promote murder, oppression, and displacement of our class siblings in Gaza and the West Bank; the abolition of military conscription; retirement at age 60; reduction of working hours to 30 per week with full pay; the disarmament of the racist and homophobic police; and the abolition of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution—no government can simply hand this to us; only we can fight for it ourselves. To realize this vision, we must now find as many allies as possible.

Originally Published in Klasse Gegen Klasse on October 30

DIE LINKE

Germany

Klasse Gegen Klasse

Social Democratic Party (SPD), Germany

October 17 opened a pre-revolutionary period in France. The question now is whether the students and their working class allies can expand, organize themselves, and win the political independence required to fight for its own way out of the crisis.

Juan Chingo

A generation caught in global chaos is rising up in the face of a capitalist system that grows more corrupt by the day.

Julien Anchaing and Enzo Tresso

The mobilization that put Aleksandar Vučić’s government on the ropes reflects a deep political crisis. Vučić has conceded defeat to the Student List, but beating the ruling party at the polls is not enough: we need an independent working-class alternative built on worker-student unity.

Óscar Fernández

From India to Chile, with France at the center, youth protests have put class struggle on the international stage. The struggles differ by country, but young people are taking to schools, universities, and streets in response to deep anger. This past weekend, hundreds of thousands marched in France and clashed with police for hours. For now, repression has not stopped the movement, which is also growing in Italy, Albania, Spain, and Portugal.

Diego lung

In this episode, Tatiana Cozzarelli speaks to Andrew Feffer, author of Bad Faith: Teachers, Liberalism, and the Origins of McCarthyism. They discuss the Rapp-Coudert investigation and the anti-communist witch-hunt of the early 1940s — and the parallels to today's repression against the movement for Palestine.

Left Voice

All of Mayor Mamdani’s endorsed candidates won landslide victories on Tuesday night, including Governor Hochul.

James Dennis Hoff

Democrats swept both chambers of Congress, flipped Texas, and saw DSA send a record five new members to the House. The midterms marked the beginning of a post-Trump moment, but the Democrats have no answer to the crisis that brought them here.

Madeleine Freeman

A week after the elections in Brazil and just before the midterm elections in the United States, it is essential to trace international maneuvers and their structural arrangement.

André Barbieri

scraped.title: Hell on earth: Stephen Miller is Trump's new chief of staff
scraped.description: The president makes it clear. The next two years will be war.
scraped.author: Inae Oh
scraped.h1: Hell on Earth: Stephen Miller Is Trump’s New Chief of Staff
scraped.body_text:
Mark Schiefelbein/AP

President Donald Trump is ending a bruising week of electoral humiliation with a clear message: He has no intention of changing tack. In fact, the president appears ready to double down on his worst instincts.

“I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.

That’s the singular message of Friday’s announcement that Trump is tapping Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, marking the alarming further rise of one of the administration’s most publicly reviled figures. The shake-up follows Tuesday’s Democratic sweep across the country, a rout widely viewed as a rejection of Trump and MAGA politics amid a deeply unpopular war and rising costs.

But perhaps most ominously, Miller’s ascension signals that Trump’s immigration crackdown will not slow down over the next two years unless Democrats find a way to break it with their new control of Congress. In selecting Miller, who is known for his aggressive, xenophobic rhetoric , Trump also replaces yet another prominent woman in his administration, following the firings of Kristi Noem, Pam Bondi, and Kimberly Guilfoyle.

“Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I’m so proud to have been a part of what we’ve accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First,” Wiles posted on social media. “While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will.”

articles.summary: Trump revealed the shake-up three days after Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, winning majority control of the House and Senate.

scraped.title: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
scraped.description: Trump revealed the shake-up three days after Democrats' landslide victory in the midterm elections, winning majority control of the House and Senate.
scraped.author: Kevin Breuninger
scraped.h1: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles .

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections , gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump's last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump's controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government's immigration policies.

Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post , praising his longtime aide as "one of my most trusted advisors."

Wiles, "who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation," the president wrote.

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP's huge election losses, "let me make this easy on you - I am going to resign," MS NOW reported.

"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime."

"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.

The official X account for Trump's political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, "It's Miller time."

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Civil Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump's foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump's winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued "retribution" as president and that he had an " alcoholic's personality ."

Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

scraped.description: The massive, still-unfinished Deep Tunnel project was supposed to be the answer. But wastewater dumped in the river now threatens human health and wildlife. Here’s why—and some ideas on what can be done.
scraped.author: By Brett Chase, Chicago Sun-Times
scraped.h1: Billions of Gallons of Raw Sewage Are Pouring Into the Chicago River After Storms
scraped.body_text:
This article originally appeared in the Chicago Sun-Times . It has been republished with permission.

Joe Gamble knows what to expect when he arrives at work at the Bridgeport Art Center after days of heavy rain.

“There was raw sewage floating in the creek,” Gamble says after storms in early October. “The wind carried the smell for at least a block or two.”

The Bridgeport Art Center sits along the south branch of the Chicago River at a spot known as Bubbly Creek, a small body of water that marks the south fork of the river and divides Bridgeport and McKinley Park.

It’s a really disgusting spot after big storms.

Layers of feces, condoms, tampons and other items flushed down toilets float past and get stuck in the low-lying trees along the shoreline. There are so many condoms that they’ve picked up a nickname: “Chicago whitefish.”

More and more people have been drawn to the river in recent years for recreation, many of them taking to the water in canoes and kayaks.

Bubbly Creek appeals particularly to beginner rowers and paddlers because it’s calm and easy to navigate. After storms, though, it often stinks so badly that the smell clings to Gamble’s clothes even after he’s left the area.

“I am sometimes tolerant of smells,” says Gamble, who works at the Chicago Maritime Museum, “but it’s a different level.”

The culprit behind the stench? A sewage pumping station on Racine Avenue south of the Bridgeport Art Center building. The Racine Avenue pumping station has big pumps that help move sewer water—both wastewater and stormwater—to a treatment facility where it’s sanitized, then sent on to the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal, then the Des Plaines and Illinois rivers and ultimately to the Mississippi River down to the Gulf of Mexico.

But sometimes the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District of Greater Chicago, the government body that operates the station, says heavy rains mean it needs to dump untreated sewage directly into the river to prevent flooding of homes.

And it’s a lot of sewage. This year, the Racine station, which is nearly 90 years old, has dumped more than 10 billion gallons of sewage into the river. That’s more than it has since 2019. In Chicago, stormwater and wastewater go into one big sewer.

Like what happens at the Racine station on the South Side, the water reclamation district’s North Branch pumping station—at Lawrence Avenue and the river on the North Side, on the border of Albany Park and Lincoln Square—has spewed nearly 2 billion gallons of untreated sewage this year into the north branch of the Chicago River.

And all of this is happening despite the billions of dollars in taxpayer money that has been spent over 50 years on the Deep Tunnel project, the sprawling system of more than 100 miles of underground tunnels and massive reservoirs designed to capture floodwater in the Chicago area and help protect the river and Lake Michigan from pollution.

The Deep Tunnel is one of the many ways that government officials in Chicago and engineers have tried to adapt a big city that originally was built on a swamp and remains highly prone to flooding to its environment.

But climate change has complicated those efforts. It’s contributing to intensifying weather patterns that bring storms that drop rain faster and harder than ever before. That overwhelms our sewers, streets and homes.

These intense storms can bring us more than 8½ inches of rain in just 24 hours.

But Chicago’s sewer system, designed decades ago, can handle just 2 inches of rain before flooding is likely.

All of that sewage flowing into Bubbly Creek and the north branch of the river isn’t just gross. It also poses a health risk for people with weak immune systems because of the bacteria and other pathogens the water carries. The contaminated water also can wreak havoc with nature, wiping out fish populations for weeks. That’s bad for the larger ecosystem, something that environmental advocates and government officials have been working over the last three decades to restore.

Tara Hoffmann, executive director of Recovery on Water, a group that has a rowing team for breast cancer survivors, says she worries about keeping its members safe in the sometimes nasty water. Some of the women have compromised immune systems following their cancer treatment. And they are out on the water, rowing, much of the time during warm weather months.

Hoffmann recalls a particularly bad day on the creek in June, when the women were paddling through excrement.

“One of the first things you notice,” she says, “is fish up at the surface, gasping for air. They’re just desperate to breathe.”

District officials say the more intense storms we’re seeing mean that Chicago needs more flood prevention measures in addition to the Deep Tunnel, like creating green spaces and tapping other strategies in an effort to capture water before it reaches the sewers. The district has designed nearly 300 flood mitigation projects, many of them still in the planning stages.

Raw sewage is a clear threat to the river’s water quality, says Phil Nicodemus, who’s the research director for the organization Urban Rivers, which works to turn urban waterways in Chicago into wildlife sanctuaries.

“It dumps a bunch of nutrients into the water at the same time,” Nicodemus says of the sewage. “That causes a massive oxygen drop, which causes a huge die-off. If that happens enough times throughout the year, you might be talking about a whole summer without much oxygen at all. That creates an enormous problem for wildlife.”

On a late summer day, Nicodemus traveled in a pontoon boat with a team surveying the floating ecosystems near River Park on the North Side, not far from the North Branch pumping station. He steered the boat. Urban River team members jumped into the water and collected bug samples. These will be studied to help provide insights on water quality.

Other experts also are examining the problem of these raw sewage dumps in the river.

Bubbly Creek, formerly a dumping area for discarded animal carcasses from the old Union Stockyards, was studied after a large sewage spill in 2023. What research biologist Austin Happel from the Shedd Aquarium found was disturbing.

The Chicago River provides a home to hundreds of animal species, and the sewage is having a dramatic impact on them, according to Happel. He has found that oxygen levels dropped while nitrogen levels rose significantly. Fish swam off and didn’t return until weeks later.

“There’s a stark shift in the food chain,” Happel says.

Oxygen in the water gets depleted. That makes it impossible for fish and other water life to exist. For weeks on end, the fish will disappear from the water, which flows into the south branch of the Chicago River.

The Deep Tunnel system includes more than 100 miles of massive tunnels hundreds of feet underground. The tunnels—basically giant pipes—range in diameter from under 10 feet to 35 feet. They help stormwater flow to two former rock quarries in the south and southwest suburbs that can hold billions of gallons of water.

Cleaner water was one of the main reasons it was decided in the 1970s to build the Deep Tunnel, formally known as the Tunnel and Reservoir Plan. The Deep Tunnel also is supposed to ease flooding in and around Chicago. The costly flood control measure has worked to a degree, but not entirely. This is why the Chicago area still sees chronic flooding and the Chicago River continues to be tainted by sewage.

The intensity of the rains we now see is too much for the tunnel and reservoir system to handle as envisioned. It’s being overwhelmed.

This summer, the biggest of the two quarries—the Thornton reservoir in South Holland—became filled with stormwater for the first time since it was opened in 2015. That mean it contained nearly 8 billion gallons of sewage. And it still hasn’t completely drained.

To the west of Chicago, the McCook reservoir in Bedford Park has filled up 10 times this year. Since it was opened in December 2017 through last year, that 3.5 billion gallon reservoir had filled to capacity only five times.

McCook is now undergoing an expansion. Eventually, it’s expected to hold 10 billion gallons of sewage water when it’s completed in 2032. The water reclamation district previously told the EPA the expansion would be finished three years sooner, in 2029.

In the race against time and nature, “The efforts aren’t keeping up,” Nicodemus says.

Margaret Frisbie, executive director of the environmental advocacy group Friends of the River, agrees. As more people turn to the river for recreation, Frisbie says, the problems are being more widely noticed.

The answer, she says, will rely on a mix of many new and innovative smaller projects, including moves to create more green space across Chicago and to create structures that capture rainwater before it gets into the sewers, where it ultimately can overwhelm the current system.

This year has been a whopper for rain, with more than 37 inches already recorded at O’Hare Airport and more rain forecast this weekend.

That’s a big hurdle, according to Frisbie.

“I don’t think you can engineer your way out of that,” she says.

articles.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
articles.summary: The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October, the highest outside of the pandemic period in a decade.
articles.ai_summary: The average duration of unemployment has exceeded 27 weeks, indicating a troubling trend in the job market.

scraped.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
scraped.description: The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October, the highest outside of the pandemic period in a decade.
scraped.author: Alex Harring
scraped.h1: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers
scraped.body_text:
Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.

The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.

About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed " and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.

"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."

It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.

Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.

What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year .

"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.

Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.

"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."

While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.

Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.

Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.

The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs , the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.

"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."
