scraped.description: President Donald Trump issued a ‘big warning’ to a top military planner fired by Defense Chief Pete Hegseth, except there’s one big problem. Trump seems
scraped.author: Shelby Erdman
scraped.h1: Trump Goes on the Attack Against a Decorated War Hero He Can’t Even Identify, and One Word Gives It All Away
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump issued a ‘big warning’ to a top military planner fired by Defense Chief Pete Hegseth, except there’s one big problem.

Trump seems to have no idea who Army Lt. General Brett Sylvia is.

Hegseth fired the director for strategy, plans and policy on the Joint Staff on Oct. 29, without giving a reason, according to USA Today .

Hegseth accused Sylvia of misconduct related to allegations that he leaked classified information on the Iran war and Russia’s war in Ukraine, CBS News reported .

The former lieutenant general failed three polygraph tests over whether he shared classified intel with the press, CBS reported, citing anonymous sources. Those sources also confirmed the firing was related to the polygraph tests but maintained the allegations against Sylvia are false.

‘You’re Going to Jail!’: Mother Gets Swarmed by Cops at California Pumpkin Patch After Sitting at Table Woman Was Saving for Relatives

More of Sade Robinson’s Remains Wash Ashore Two Years After the Black Teen Was Killed and Dismembered After First Date

The Pentagon also confirmed it has turned the Sylvia case over to the Department of Justice for a criminal investigation.

A day later, a reporter asked Trump about the situation with “Gen. Sylvia,” as the reporter put it.

Trump’s response shows how little he seems to know about what’s happening under Hegseth.

“She’s got problems. She’s going to have big problems. She did,” Trump barked.

“We’re very much looking for leakers, and uh, she’s going to have big problems, long-term problems,” he threatened.

Social media exploded in glee over Trump’s ignorance about his own military as some commenters pointed out the seriousness of being so clueless.

“It’s a good thing that question wasn’t on the cognitive test,” an X user joked.

“The commander in chief threatening a three-star general while not knowing who he is sums up the whole operation. maximum menace, minimum command,” another chimed in.

This observer is tired of it all. “Just 25th amendment him already.”

This X user pointed out the obvious: “He is seriously clueless.”

Hegseth has presided over turmoil at the Pentagon since taking control in early 2025. He’s fired or pushed aside more than two dozen military leaders .

The departures include former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. CQ Brown Jr.; Adm. Lisa Franchetti, the Navy’s former top officer; and former Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy George.

Gen. David Allvin, the former Air Force chief of staff, left before completing his term. Gen. James Mingus, the former Army vice chief of staff, retired early.

Another General, Gen. Christopher Donahue, also retired after Hegseth reportedly blocked efforts to extend his career leading Army forces in Europe and Africa.

Army Secretary Dan Driscoll resigned over the summer following months of reported clashes with Hegseth.

Driscoll repeatedly clashed with Hegseth over removing longtime, qualified leaders, including George’s abrupt removal in April.

The Army has operated without a permanent chief of staff since George’s ouster. Gen. Christopher LaNeve currently holds the position in an acting capacity, but his path to Senate confirmation remains uncertain.

Against that backdrop, his purge of veteran military officials continues amid his crackdown on leaks.

Sylvia has a long, distinguished 32-year service record, including serving as commander of the 101st Airborne Division and deploying to Iraq and Afghanistan, CBS reported. He also earned a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart after sustaining wounds while fighting the Taliban.

"She's got problems" — Trump gets asked about Lt. Gen. Sylvia (Brett Sylvia, a guy!) leaking classified information, and he's so clueless that he thinks the reporter is talking about a woman with the first name Sylvia pic.twitter.com/3iAxkauzTG

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.

articles.summary: After Weeks Of Riots, France's Thursday General Strike Forces Macron's PM To Blink France's nationwide strike put 575,000 people in the streets on Thursday by the Interior Ministry's count, topping the 550,000 it counted on Oct. 17, when protests in several cities turned into riots and looting. France's major labor union, the CGT, claimed close to 1.6 million, France 24 reports. After the marches, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called unions and employers to Matignon on Monday for talks on ...
articles.ai_summary: France's nationwide general strike saw 575,000 participants, prompting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to initiate talks with unions and employers.

scraped.title: After Weeks Of Riots, France's Thursday General Strike Forces Macron's PM To Blink
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: After Weeks Of Riots, France's Thursday General Strike Forces Macron's PM To Blink
scraped.body_text:
France's nationwide strike put 575,000 people in the streets on Thursday by the Interior Ministry's count, topping the 550,000 it counted on Oct. 17, when protests in several cities turned into riots and looting . France's major labor union, the CGT, claimed close to 1.6 million, France 24 reports . After the marches, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu called unions and employers to Matignon on Monday for talks on wages and the cost of living.

The CFDT, CGT, FO, UNSA and FSU called the strike over wages, pensions and the 2027 budget, and Sortiraparis reported that every other union federation had said it would take part, with the CFTC backing it.

Grève du 5 novembre: la CGT prévoit 244 lieux de rassemblement à travers la France pic.twitter.com/G8EohjyrBP

— BFM Première (@BFMPremiere) November 4, 2026

The Interior Ministry said the declared marches "generally went well" (translated) and reported 448 arrests, according to franceinfo , against 1,314 after the Oct. 24 protests.

Riot police fired teargas at the end of the marches in Lyon and Bordeaux, while officers in Lyon also used water cannon as fires were set in the streets.

Manifestation du 5 novembre: quelques tensions éclatent à Lyon au sein d'une manifestation pacifique pic.twitter.com/OpfSfiyKMu

Police were pelted with pétanque balls in Rennes and projectiles in Pau and Orléans , and in Toulouse, fireworks fired at a school started a blaze that burned its student services office. In eastern Paris, police used teargas to keep students from reaching the Hélène Boucher high school after stopping students from building barricades out of wheeled bins outside of schools in the early morning.

The unions called the strike after leaders met Lecornu on Oct. 21 and left "unanimously disappointed," according to Euronews. CGT leader Sophie Binet said Lecornu announced no measures and showed "no consideration of our demands," and that she wants strikes to take over from street protests so the movement can "generalise the strike." The CFTC's Cyril Chabanier was more upbeat, saying the government "opened the door" to talks on the minimum wage.

The strike follows weeks of unrest. According to the Interior Ministry, the Oct. 17 protests at about 550,000 people and the Oct. 24 protests at 410,000, the Rio Times reports, with unions claiming higher figures. The Oct. 24 protests brought 1,314 arrests and 53 injured police and gendarmes. In response, Paris imposed a curfew from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. around Place de la République and Les Halles, and Lyon renewed its own. Euronews says Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin put the number of people taken into police custody nationwide at 2,500, with 917 sent for immediate trial, and that the government blames "the ultra-left" for much of the violence. President Emmanuel Macron, speaking from Qatar, called for "firmness" against those responsible.

High school and university students have been protesting for weeks as well, demanding more funding for education, repairs to school buildings and the scrapping of the Parcoursup admissions platform - which the government says will be replaced for the 2028 admissions round.

Rail was the most exposed sector to the strike, since the four representative SNCF unions called the strike. About one in ten TGVs was expected to be canceled, and Intercités, TER, RER and Transilien services disrupted, with only one train in three running on RER D. SUD-Rail secretary Fabien Villedieu called it "a big strike over pay, jobs and working conditions." Paris metro, bus and tram services were forecast to run normally, though CGT-RATP's open-ended strike notice let staff walk out individually. Airport ground-staff unions also called a strike, but France's civil aviation authority had not asked airlines to cancel flights at Roissy or Orly. The Eiffel Tower closed for the day.

In schools, the Education Ministry estimated 17.54% of public primary teachers were on strike , while the FSU-SNUipp union said nearly 80 Paris schools were closed and up to 75% of teachers were out in parts of Seine-Saint-Denis. The government said 81 high schools were disrupted on Thursday, against 1,000 by the student unions' count, and that a third of higher education sites were affected, the Guardian reports.

Monday's talks at Matignon will hopefully be more productive than the Oct. 21 meeting , where, by the unions' account, Lecornu offered nothing. Labor Minister Jean-Pierre Farandou told TF1 that "the government wants to act fast on the Smic," France's minimum wage, with a boost he said "is exceptional in nature" (translated). Echos Plus reports the government is weighing a 0.6% increase , against the extra 100 euros a month net the CFDT wants.

That said, the 2027 budget the unions are striking over has already hit a wall . On Wednesday, the day before the walkout, the National Assembly unanimously rejected the revenue half of the bill, as we noted , which sinks the whole bill in the lower house and sends the government's original text to the Senate, LCP reports .

Whether Thursday becomes the start of something longer is still an open question. Binet, who had urged workers to extend the strike beyond one day, called it "a very serious time, with a very dangerous authoritarian drift from the government" (translated), according to the Guardian. The eight unions in the coalition said "the only thing that will stop the mobilization is an answer to our demands" (translated), and they meet again Monday, after the Matignon talks, to decide what comes next.

The Yellow Vests coordination, which called Thursday a "People's November 5," called for the strike to "continue and spread" with blockades and local actions across France on Friday, Sortiraparis reported . For Saturday, Paris police approved a union march from République to Nation on Thursday's route but banned the Yellow Vests' "Act IV" rally at Place de la Concorde, both called for 2 p.m., it reported Friday . The movement says it will turn out anyway and "disobey massively" (translated); joining a banned demonstration carries a 135-euro fine.

scraped.title: Congress has a chance to fix the Endangered Species Act
scraped.description: Next week, Congress will vote on a bill to modernize the regulation that hurts property owners and conservation efforts.
scraped.author: Megan Jenkins, John Nagle
scraped.h1: Congress Has a Chance To Fix the Endangered Species Act
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Energy & Environment

Megan Jenkins and John Nagle | 11.6.2026 2:35 PM

Next week, the Senate will consider a new permitting deal that promises to make it easier to build in America. From mines and pipelines to transmission lines and renewable energy projects, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) would prune our regulatory thicket that delays development and increases costs for commonsense projects.

While the bill's proposed reforms to the National Environmental Policy Act have attracted much of the attention, its changes to the Endangered Species Act (ESA) are especially promising in helping the law achieve its goals while reducing unnecessary obstacles to infrastructure, energy production, and economic growth.

More than five decades after its enactment, the ESA has struggled to achieve its ultimate objective: recovering endangered species so they no longer need federal protection. Meanwhile, its regulatory requirements can discourage conservation and create costly uncertainty for landowners and businesses.

According to a 2023 analysis by the Property and Environment Research Center , just 3 percent of species listed under the ESA were delisted due to recovery. That's 57 of 1,732 species over the law's first 50 years. Meanwhile, the ESA's costs are huge . Federal agencies spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually administering the law, but those expenditures capture only a fraction of its potential economic burden. The costs of delayed projects, restrictions on private property, and regulatory compliance remain largely unmeasured.

One major problem with the ESA is the uncertainty surrounding its application. The law requires federal agencies to rely on the "best scientific and commercial data available" when deciding on species protections. But Congress never clearly defined that standard, leaving agencies substantial discretion in determining what evidence is sufficient, and courts often defer to those judgments.

Consider the Delta Smelt, a fish, typically no longer than three inches, native to California's Sacramento–San Joaquin River Delta. This small fish created big problems for California farmers. In a 2008 biological opinion , the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (FWS) concluded that two major water projects that deliver water from the Delta to California's agriculture-rich Central Valley needed to reduce operations substantially to protect the endangered fish.

In practical terms, federal protections for the Delta Smelt meant restricting water deliveries to farmers in one of the nation's most productive agricultural regions.

However, the scientific basis for that decision raised serious questions. The FWS' biological opinion imposed onerous water-pumping restrictions when smelt caught in the pumps reached a certain threshold, without accounting for the overall smelt population. This departed from standard industry practice, as raw numbers provide little context for assessing threats to a species without population data. When challenged in court, the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals found that FWS had departed from standard scientific methodology. Nevertheless, it upheld the agency's approach, deferring to its determination of the "best scientific data available."

The Delta Smelt controversy illustrates a major flaw in the ESA: When Congress leaves a key scientific standard undefined, agencies can, and often will, exercise broad discretion over decisions that affect water supplies, private property, and economic livelihoods.

BAAJA would address this problem by establishing clearer scientific standards for such decisions. The bill defines best available science as "all relevant and objective scientific and commercial information available at the time of the agency action."

It would also establish criteria for evaluating scientific evidence, including whether models account for potential errors and use accepted professional methods. These requirements would make ESA-related decisions more transparent and easier to evaluate, and would prevent agencies from putting a thumb on the scale when evaluating scientific evidence.

The bill would also give states a stronger role. State wildlife agencies frequently possess extensive population data and local expertise, yet federal decision making does not always adequately incorporate their findings. BAAJA would require federal agencies to consider specified scientific information submitted by states and create pathways for qualified states to conduct certain ESA consultations.

Perhaps most importantly for project developers, BAAJA would shorten the standard timeline for formal ESA consultations from 90 days to 60 days.

These consultations are required when federal projects may adversely affect protected species or their critical habitat. They can affect everything from mining operations to roads and energy infrastructure.

A 2015 study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found that approximately 20 percent of formal ESA consultations exceeded the applicable 135-day regulatory timeline. Some dragged on for years.

Shorter deadlines won't eliminate every permitting delay. But they could help prevent prolonged reviews from creating unnecessary uncertainty and expense for businesses seeking to invest in American infrastructure.

Taken together, the proposed reforms would make ESA administration more transparent, predictable, and efficient while preserving its conservation responsibilities.

After more than 50 years, Congress has an opportunity to reform the ESA to ensure it is serving both wildlife and the people whose cooperation is essential to conservation. Protecting endangered species and allowing Americans to build, invest, and develop natural resources should not be mutually exclusive goals. BAAJA offers Congress an opportunity to move toward a system that better achieves both.

President Donald Trump said Friday that Deputy White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to Chief of Staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Announcing the move on Truth Social, Trump wrote that Miller would start in the position on Monday, and that Wiles—who the president praised as having done “an outstanding job”—would move to another role in the “Trump Political Operation.”

Miller has played a major role in driving the White House’s domestic policy agenda, particularly when it comes to immigration. He has worked for the president since the 2016 campaign, and is widely viewed as a hard-liner within the administration. The shake-up comes just three days after Republicans suffered devastating losses in the midterm elections.

scraped.body_text:
A statement from the organizer specifically says 'Zionist' businesses should leave the city.

Local leaders in Pennsylvania are condemning a demonstration targeting Jewish businesses on the eve of the 88th anniversary of the infamous Kristallnacht attacks in Nazi Germany.

The self-described "Anti-fascist" group Philly Bike on Your Left has promoted the ride, and a flyer that the group posted on social media specifically cites Jewish-owned businesses and crosses them out.

'As the political ideology of Zionism dies a long deserved death these businesses will die with it. Free Palestine.'

"NO BUSINESS FOR ZIONISTS!" read the text on the flyer. "THESE ZIONIST ESTABLISHMENTS MUST GO! NOT IN OUR CITY!"

The ride is scheduled for Sunday at noon.

The flyer did not mention Kristallnacht, but the boycott will be held just one day from the 88th anniversary of the violent attacks on Jewish people and businesses.

The groups behind the boycott said in a statement online they want to show solidarity with the Palestinian cause. They also called the action an "anti-fascist" operation and insisted that "conflating Zionism with Judaism" is "disingenuous."

"As the political ideology of Zionism dies a long deserved death these businesses will die with it. Free Palestine," the statement concluded.

Philadelphia Democrat Mayor Cherelle Parker was among those who condemned the ride.

"As Mayor, I serve every Philadelphian under the explicit premise that freedom of speech and freedom from fear are not competing values," she wrote in a lengthy statement. "No one should be targeted, threatened, or made to feel unwelcome because of their faith, identity, or background. Every person deserves to feel safe and respected in the city they call home."

She went on to say singling out businesses because the owners are Jewish is "unacceptable" and has no place in Philadelphia.

"Let me be clear: safety is non-negotiable," she continued.

"Anyone who engages in threats, intimidation, or unlawful conduct will beheld accountable. One Philly, A United City will always mean that every Philadelphian can feel safe, respected, and welcome, with no place for threats, intimidation, or harassment."

RELATED: Videos capture Palestinian activists screaming at Mamdani: 'Opportunist piece of s**t!'

Parker said local law enforcement would coordinate to maintain safety and order during the demonstration.

Democrat Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania called on "every Democrat of conscience" to "condemn this sick parade of rank antisemitism."

Commissioner Jeffrey Nash characterized the boycott as an "appalling act of hatred, bigotry, and intimidation towards the Jewish community."

Some of the businesses targeted will remain open to defy the intimidation from the groups.

Topic: Endangered and Protected Species

An alpine spiny crayfish prepares to be released back into the wild. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

An endangered crayfish species was rescued after bushfires in January tore through Victoria's High Country.

Some are now returning home after months in captivity.

Conservationists expect more species will need rescuing after bushfires amid climate change.

In a rugged corner of Victoria's High Country, two scientists are making their way slowly through fire-scarred bushland that is slowly returning to life.

They are travelling with precious cargo: a group of endangered alpine spiny crayfish that are heading back to their home waterway near Lucyvale.

Tree canopy is recovering at Lucyvale after 2026 bushfires. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

The scientists were here in the immediate aftermath of the January bushfires that tore through the region, and they salvaged 11 endangered crayfish that were at risk of suffocating in the stream from debris and sediment.

The alpine spiny crayfish are restricted in their movement and found in small, isolated pockets that make it tricky for scientists to find, adding to the pressure of rescue efforts as water quality declines after a fire.

"If they aren't rescued they can disappear from these areas," Arthur Rylah Institute senior scientist Will Sowersby said.

Scientists prepare to capture alpine spiny crayfish. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

The alpine spiny crayfish were taken to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery, which is run by the Victorian Fisheries Authority near Eildon, where they were cared for until water quality improved post-bushfires.

It is the first time the endangered species has been taken into captivity, and it proved a learning curve for staff.

"It's a new process for us," Snobs Creek's senior conservation hatchery officer Dylan White said.

"They are a bit feisty so we have had to separate them, and we have kept them separate this whole time because they will attack each other."

Spiny crayfish being weighed at Snobs Creek hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

As the Victorian High Country starts to spring back to life from the Walwa-River Road bushfire that burnt around 121,000 hectares, scientists are continuing to monitor the alpine spiny crayfish's habitat and ponder their future.

Conservationists hope the endangered crayfish can be included in a future captive breeding program at the Snobs Creek hatchery to help bolster numbers and geographical diversity.

But with another summer on the horizon, Mr Sowersby predicts their work is far from over.

"We know that bushfires are increasing in their frequency and their intensity, so we suspect it's going to be more and more important that we rescue species post-bushfire and that we also establish new populations to (prevent) the risk of an extinction event due to a catastrophic fire," he said.

Topic: Environmental Impacts

Topic: Environmental Impacts

Topic: Crop Harvesting

Topic: Missing Person

Topic: Police

It has been a busy year for Snobs Creek hatchery staff who carry out important conservation work with vulnerable species, especially after natural disasters.

Dylan White is surrounded by rare species at the hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangelsdorf )

"Most of these species we have here are so critically endangered they have never been kept in captivity before, so it's really new for everyone," Mr White said.

"The important thing is we are experienced and we are putting that knowledge and skill set towards caring for them and learning more about them."

Some of the species at the facility are found nowhere else in the world.

That includes a special type of galaxias fish that only exists in a sole tributary of the La Trobe River after experiencing a major population collapse in the past decade, and the critically endangered blackfish that were rescued after bushfires tore through the Grampians region.

A blackfish at Snobs Creek hatchery. ( ABC News: Andrew Mangesldorf )

Some species rescued after Victoria's summer bushfires have already been re-released, including more than 100 Macquarie perch and trout cod taken from Seven Creek after the Longwood bushfire.

"It was quite challenging to look after a large number of trout cod at the same time due to their aggressive nature …took up a lot of space," Snobs Creek head of fish production Chris Mullins said.

The species' stay at the facility can be hard work for staff, who have to manage unique diets, water temperature, lighting, and behavioural issues.

Scientists comb an alpine stream for endangered species. ( ABC News: Erin Somerville )

With Australia predicted to face more natural disaster as climate change progresses, staff value the significance of the hatchery.

"Every year (natural disasters) seems to be getting more and more, so we have got to have a facility here that we can take some of these species as quickly as we can," Mr White said.

"If we weren't doing it no one would be."

scraped.body_text:
Miller with Trump in August

US President Donald Trump announced on Friday that Stephen Miller, his deputy chief of staff, would replace Susie Wiles as chief of staff.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said Wiles did an "outstanding job" and would be moved to the "Trump Political Operation".

The news comes after Republicans suffered a series of major defeats in the 2026 midterm elections, including losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Miller, considered the architect of Trump's hard-line immigration policy, has been a loyal ally of the president and served as a senior adviser to Trump during his first administration. Trump said he would take on the new role on Monday.

This video can not be played

'Hopefully things get done': Americans react to historic political shift

Wiles gave her resignation to Trump on Thursday night, a US official told CBS News, the BBC's media partner.

Her resignation was related to Republican midterms defeats, three sources told CBS.

It was unclear if her deputies would remain at the White House.

In a statement, she said being on Trump's team was "the honor of a lifetime".

"I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First," she said. "While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will."

Wiles, 69, is seen as among the most powerful figures in the Trump administration and someone particularly close to the US president.

Asked last month whether Wiles could be replaced soon, Trump said there was "zero chance".

"Susie is here and she's gonna be here for a long time," he said.

Wiles recently battled cancer, announcing in September, six months after her diagnosis, that she was in remission.

During Trump's first and second term, Miller has been the architect of some of his most controversial immigration and deportation policies, which have sparked a backlash from Democrats.

One of Trump's closest aides, Miller stuck by the president following his 2020 election defeat, and followed Trump back into power last year.

Wiles is not the only high-profile Trump official to leave this week following the midterm elections, which have prompted a reckoning among Republicans about how to address voters' rebuke of Trump's agenda.

Several justice department officials have also resigned, including John Eisenberg, the head of the department's National Security Division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who was known for enforcing conspiracy probes into officials investigating Trump's handling of classified documents.

The old provision dated back to 1868, and read, "The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for their common defense." The new , which passed 71%-29%, will read :

(a) The citizens of this State shall have the right to keep and bear arms, for: (1) Their common defense; (2) Lawful hunting and recreational use; and (3) Any other lawful purpose. (b) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section includes without limitation the possession and use of: (1) Ammunition; (2) Firearm accessories; and (3) Firearm components. (c) The right to keep and bear arms under subsection (a) of this section is a natural, fundamental, and individual right that shall not be infringed.

scraped.title: Manitoba Métis Federation 'appalled' they were left out of budget
scraped.description: The president of the Manitoba Métis Federation says he's 'appalled' that Métis were not included in the federal budget.
scraped.author: Mark Blackburn
scraped.h1: Manitoba Métis Federation ‘appalled’ by being left out of budget
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

MMF President David Chartrand, seen here at a news conference in Ottawa in 2025, says it's not acceptable for the government to leave Métis out of the budget. Photo: APTN.

The Manitoba Métis Federation (MMF) says it’s “appalled” that it was left out of the federal budget.

“In recent years, Canada has finally started to address the long-overlooked needs of the Red River Métis in areas such as housing, early learning and childcare, and post-secondary education,” said David Chartrand, president of the MMF, in a statement released Friday.

“However, a significant gap still exists between our Nation and the general population. There’s no doubt our people will be angered that their needs have been dismissed by this Budget.”

On Thursday, the federal government tabled a budget with $50 billion worth of promises, mainly for First Nations housing and infrastructure. For Inuit, the budget renewed the Inuit Child First Initiative / Piratsiagutiit at $575 million over five years, and the government is also putting $610 million over four years for the Nutrition North subsidy.

Métis are only found once in the 532 page budget document, “as part of the title for a piece of legislation, An Act Respecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis children, youth and families – a piece of legislation that Canada has claimed they do not have a mechanism to fund us for.”

“The hugely successful distinctions-based approach has vanished, and government is reverting to phrases like ‘Indigenous’ when, in reality, they mean First Nations and Inuit,” said Chartrand. “The Red River Métis pay billions in taxes in this country, yet we have been forgotten by this government.”

Read More:

Budget 2026 commits $32B to First Nations housing, infrastructure while leaving most Métis, Inuit budget asks unaddressed

In its pre-budget submissions, a document that lists its needs for the government to consider, the MMF said it met with “numerous Ministers as well as the Prime Minister” to talk about its financial needs including infrastructure, housing, health, child and family services.

“We are disheartened that none of these priorities found their way into this Budget,” Chartrand said.

“We are never looking for a hand-out – rather, we are looking for our tax dollars to be reinvested in the Red River Métis so we can put a shovel in our hands and continue addressing the critical needs of our Nation, and strengthen Canada.

“We hope that the commitments made in these meetings become a reality so we can continue the historic progress we’ve made in recent years.”

APTN News reached out to the MMF to see if there were any meetings planned with Prime Minister Mark Carney, who was in Winnipeg Friday to discuss his homelessness plan, but did not hear back before this story was published.

Before moving to become the APTN News social media producer, Mark was the executive producer for the news in eastern Canada. Before starting with APTN in 2009, Mark worked at CBC Radio and Television in Newfoundland and Labrador and Ottawa.

scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

Topic: Courts

British actor and comedian Russell Brand is behind bars this weekend after being convicted of rape and sexual assault. ( Reuters: Toby Shepheard )

If Russell Brand was at all worried about being found guilty in his four-week rape and sexual assault trial, he was not showing it.

I was standing a few people behind the British actor and comedian in the queue for security checks outside London's Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, when he broke briefly into song.

"Sweet Caroline," he sang to a woman beside him in the line, quoting the famous Neil Diamond hit.

The woman had introduced herself to the star as Caroline, and the pair chatted jovially while waiting to move forward.

Inside court, just minutes later, the jury began its second day of deliberations.

On other mornings, as Brand was greeted at court by a flurry of camera flashes, journalists asked how he was feeling.

"Blessed," was always the reply.

Throughout the trial, the comedian-turned-born-again Christian influencer continued to make social media videos with his wife, Laura, for their millions of followers.

As the court heard harrowing, graphic and often tearful accounts from Brand's six accusers, he did not flinch.

When he gave evidence himself, he did so standing up unnaturally straight.

Russell Brand giving evidence during his trial. ( Reuters: Julia Quenzler )

At crunch time — when the guilty verdicts were read out on Thursday — the comedian stood to attention like a soldier on parade and showed no emotion.

When his lawyer applied for bail ahead of sentencing on Monday, he said his client wanted time to say goodbye to his wife and three children over the weekend.

Outside court and in, this was a defendant who did not seem to think he would go to jail.

British newspapers cover the opening of Russell Brand's sexual assault trial. ( ABC News: Alex Parsons )

Brand has been on trial since mid-October for seven historical sex offences relating to six women spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009.

After eight and a half hours of deliberations, the jury of four women and eight men found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

He was acquitted of a further two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

British actor and comedian Russell Brand arrived at court with his wife Laura on Thursday before he was remanded in custody. ( Reuters: Maja Smiejkowska )

On the steps of Southwark Crown Court afterwards, police praised the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination" of the women, while pulling no punches about Brand.

"Russell Brand used his influence, status, and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement," Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said.

Russell Brand was found guilty of raping a woman at his house in 2009. ( Supplied: Metropolitan Police )

During the trial, journalists could only report what was said and done in front of the jury, but with verdicts returned and restrictions lifted, we can now give more detail from one of the most high-profile criminal trials in recent British history.

Brand is no longer a mainstream comedian and actor, and instead styles himself as a Christian influencer, broadcasting online prayer videos and sermons to millions.

His faith was on full public display from day one of the trial. When he was first shown into the dock before jury selection, he went down on one knee and appeared to pray.

British actor and comedian Russell Brand arriving at Southwark Crown Court during the third week of his trial. ( Reuters: Hannah McKay )

During the trial he wore crucifixes of different sizes, he sometimes carried a bible with sticky notes marking pages, and at least one day he was handling what looked like prayer beads.

Unusually for a defendant in a criminal trial, he posted repeatedly on social media — not about the evidence but about his feelings, his faith, and his disdain for the mainstream media.

It can now be reported that Brand's legal team tried to have the case thrown out, before the trial had even begun because of negative press about him.

Russell Brand told the court he did not commit the crimes and believed sexual consent was "fundamental, essential, necessary" and "more important than sex itself".

Barrister Ian Winter KC argued his client could not receive a fair trial because of 2023 media reports with allegations about Brand — allegations that prompted the women who would ultimately be the complainants in this trial to come forward.

Mr Winter's application was denied, but he would go on to say during the trial that the 2023 reporting had "poisoned the well".

The 2023 allegations in the media were not part of the trial.

In an extraordinary moment in the corridor at the end of proceedings, Mr Winter launched a tirade at Sunday Times Chief News Correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who worked on the 2023 investigation.

“I hope you are pleased with yourself,” Mr Winter said.

Ms Urwin responded that she was “pleased justice has been done".

Mr Winter replied, “well, it wasn’t. You f***** it. Congratulations".

On Friday the top silk reported himself to the Bar Standards Board over the exchange.

Photographers greeted British actor and comedian Russell Brand and his wife Laura at court every day of the trial. ( Reuters: Toby Melville )

There were other moments of courtroom drama during the trial.

On day one, lawyers for People Magazine in the US were hauled before Judge Joel Bennathan to explain why the magazine had reported the attempt to have the case thrown out, when a court order had been made to keep that out of the public domain.

Judge Bennathan then put journalists in court and beyond on notice that he would not be lenient if there were further contempt of court risks.

Another day, police arrested a blogger who had identified one of Brand's accusers, all of whom are granted lifelong anonymity by the court.

The man, who had been sitting in the spillover court watching proceedings on a large video screen, was detained for 12 hours, cautioned, and forced to amend his blog posts.

There are more allegations about Brand that we can now report too.

Metropolitan Police Commissioner Mark Rowley said more accusors were likely to come forward. ( Reuters: Chris J. Ratcliffe )

The Metropolitan Police revealed its detectives are currently investigating allegations of rape from two more women in the UK, while there are two civil claims afoot against Brand relating to his time in the US.

The head of Scotland Yard Sir Mark Rowley has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations. He has appealed for them to do so.

Brand, meanwhile, is spending his first weekend behind bars.

Judge Bennathan denied his bail application saying that while he regrets the impact on the 51-year-old's children, their father had the resources to be a flight risk.

The verdict marks a massive fall from grace for the entertainer; once a swaggering exhibitionist performing to huge crowds, now a convicted rapist in a prison cell.

Russell Brand during one of his police interviews. ( Supplied: Metropolitan Police )

For the rape and three sexual assaults he was found guilty of this week, Brand will be sentenced on Monday.

The judge has already flagged the rape conviction alone will mean a "significant custodial sentence".

scraped.title: The Republicans Who Love to Lose
scraped.description: When you blame an election on the inexorable march of demographic change, you erase the poor policy choices that caused voters to swing wildly against the GOP in just two years.
scraped.author: Charles Fain Lehman
scraped.body_text:
Bo French was just one among the many losers in Tuesday’s statewide Democratic sweep in Texas. French, who was running for a seat on the powerful Texas Railroad Commission (which regulates the state’s oil and gas industry), had attracted public outrage for an X post of a photo of Indian students at a University of Texas at Austin football game. “I heard UT graduation this year looked like this,” French wrote. “I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined.”

It’s unclear whether French’s remarks were what cost him his election. Governor Greg Abbott lost by roughly the same margin, and Senate nominee Ken Paxton by nearly twice as much. But all three performed worse than other statewide Republicans. And French measurably underperformed in South Asian areas, specifically.

For some, though, the obvious cause of Republicans’ comprehensive defeat was the demographic change that had alarmed French in the first place. “Demographics is destiny,” wrote commentator Benny Johnson, noting that Texas is 50 percentage points less white than it was in 1970. Gregory Bovino, the former Border Patrol commander who led the crackdown in Minneapolis, blamed Abbott’s loss on votes from H-1B nonimmigrants from India, of whom “70 to 80 percent vote Democrat.” Other pundits piled on with the same message: Democrats won, in Texas and elsewhere, because non-white immigrants voted for them overwhelmingly.

The trouble with this argument is not just that it is wrong on the facts, although it is. Nor is the problem that these influencers are speaking some forbidden truth. The trouble, rather, is that their theory absolves Republicans of responsibility for their historic loss. When you blame an election on the inexorable march of demographic change, you erase the poor policy choices that caused the electorate to swing wildly against the GOP in just two years.

scraped.title: Houston voters approve restrictions on marijuana arrests and a ban on no-knock police raids
scraped.description: The first provision might curtail local pot busts, but the second one is unlikely to have a meaningful impact.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: Houston Voters Approve Restrictions on Marijuana Arrests and a Ban on No-Knock Police Raids
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

War on Drugs

Jacob Sullum | 11.6.2026 2:20 PM

This week Houston voters overwhelmingly approved a ballot initiative that instructs local police to make marijuana misdemeanors their "lowest possible enforcement priority" and prohibits them from seeking or executing no-knock search warrants. The first provision might significantly reduce low-level marijuana arrests in Houston, which have risen dramatically in recent years. But the second one, although well-intentioned, is unlikely to make much difference in practice.

More than 70 percent of voters said yes to Proposition A , which requires the Houston Police Department (HPD) to deprioritize marijuana arrests involving possession of two ounces or less, a Class B misdemeanor punishable by a maximum $2,000 fine and up to six months in jail, or two to four ounces, a Class A misdemeanor punishable by a maximum $4,000 fine and up to a year in jail. The initiative, which amends the city charter, says "the City shall update its annual budget, police department manual, and relevant policies and procedures to ensure that public safety resources are not wasted on misdemeanor marijuana enforcement."

Although the HPD arrested just 10 people for marijuana misdemeanors in 2022, Houston Public Media reports , that number shot up in subsequent years, peaking at 538 in 2024 before falling to 426 in 2025. As of September, the number for this year was 232. From 2021 through 2025, 74 percent of marijuana arrests involved black people, who account for less than a quarter of Houston's population.

Proposition A requires the city to conduct an audit of arrests and citations during that period, including "demographic information for each person charged with an offense." The audit is also supposed to estimate the time and money spent on those cases.

Voters in Austin and Dallas have approved similar measures. But for a couple of reasons, they had little measurable impact.

By the time Austin voters passed their initiative in 2022, the city council had already restricted low-level marijuana arrests. In 2020, the Austin Police Department reported that possession arrests involving two ounces or less had fallen from 319 in 2017 to 54 in 2019 and dropped further in 2020, when police reported just three such arrests in the first quarter.

In Dallas, low-level marijuana arrests likewise declined before the ballot initiative passed in 2024. The Dallas Police Department implemented the measure in January 2025 by instructing officers to stop arresting people for simple possession of four ounces or less. But that July, the city agreed to stop enforcing the policy after a state appeals court ruled , in response to a lawsuit by Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, that Austin's initiative was preempted by state law. Paxton had sued Dallas on the same grounds.

Assuming the Houston initiative does not suffer a similar fate, it should accelerate the downward trend in low-level marijuana arrests that began last year. But the ban on no-knock raids seems less promising.

The controversy over no-knock search warrants in Houston was driven largely by the January 2019 drug raid that killed a middle-aged couple, Dennis Tuttle and Rhogena Nicholas, whom veteran narcotics officer Gerald Goines had falsely implicated in drug dealing by describing a heroin purchase that never happened. That fiasco prompted a new HPD policy requiring officers to obtain high-level approval for no-knock warrant applications. And since then, the Houston Chronicle reports , no such warrants have been issued.

The details of the operation that killed Tuttle and Nicholas provide further reason to doubt that Proposition A's knock-and-announce rule will have a meaningful impact. After breaking through the front door around 5 p.m. without warning, police immediately shot the couple's dog. At that point, Nicholas was sitting on a couch in the living room, where she had been watching TV. Tuttle, who had been napping in a bedroom, responded to the tumult and gunfire by grabbing a revolver and firing at the intruders. By the time the shooting stopped, Tuttle and Nicholas were dead, and four officers, including Goines, were grievously wounded, mostly by friendly fire .

After Goines' lies were revealed, he was convicted of felony murder and sentenced to 60 years in state prison. During his trial, the prosecution argued that Tuttle did not realize the intruders were cops and reacted as "any normal person" would to a violent home invasion. But it is not clear that the outcome would have been any different if the cops had knocked, announced themselves, and waited "at least 15 seconds" before entering, as Proposition A requires.

Perhaps Nicholas would have heard the cops, digested what was happening, restrained the dog, and managed to open the door within 15 seconds. But if not, the cops still would have broken in and opened fire, and Tuttle still would have responded the same way.

Something similar happened when Louisville police officers killed Breonna Taylor during an early-morning drug raid in March 2020. In that case, which likewise involved dubious drug-trafficking allegations, the cops also had a no-knock warrant. They nevertheless banged on the door for at least 30 seconds, and they claimed that they also identified themselves as police officers.

All but one of Taylor's neighbors said they heard no such announcement. Taylor's boyfriend, who was in bed with her at the time, likewise said he did not know that the men who broke into the apartment were police officers. Like Tuttle, he grabbed a gun, which he fired once, prompting the hail of bullets that killed Taylor, who was unarmed and standing near him in a dark hallway.

The 15-second requirement imposed by Proposition A clearly would not have saved Taylor. Nor would it make a difference in other cases where police enter homes in the middle of the night, a practice that invites potentially deadly confusion . Since a knock-and-announce rule works only when people can reasonably be expected to hear, comprehend, and promptly respond, it is unlikely to have an impact without restrictions on the timing of police raids and a presumption against the "dynamic entry" tactics that cops tend to use when they execute drug warrants.

Whatever such reforms might accomplish, they do not address the fundamental problem , which stems from the decision to criminalize peaceful transactions between consenting adults. When politicians authorize police to invade people's homes in the hope of discovering arbitrarily prohibited intoxicants, they should not be surprised by the ensuing violence.

scraped.title: New Report Reveals the Moment Trump Realized Stephen Miller’s Immigration Agenda Went Too Far — and It Wasn’t After Two Americans Were Killed By Feds
scraped.description: President Donald Trump has picked Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, elevating the architect of his immigration
scraped.author: Mary Spiller
scraped.h1: New Report Reveals the Moment Trump Realized Stephen Miller’s Immigration Agenda Went Too Far — and It Wasn’t After Two Americans Were Killed By Feds
scraped.body_text:
President Donald Trump has picked Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, elevating the architect of his immigration crackdown just days after Republicans lost control of Congress.

Miller takes over Monday, while Wiles moves to Trump’s political operation.

The promotion comes despite Trump reportedly telling aides that Miller had pushed his immigration agenda too far.

Trump entered his second term believing voters had given him a mandate to crack down on illegal immigration. But the aggressive enforcement campaign sparked private complaints from Republican officials in Texas and Florida, according to The Wall Street Journal’s examination of the party’s midterm losses .

Still, according to the report, it wasn’t the fatal shootings of two Americans by federal agents in Minnesota that prompted Trump to reconsider the approach. The concerns that got through to him came from inside his own home.

First Lady Melania Trump complained that people she knew were being deported. Only then, the Journal reported, did Trump begin privately questioning the direction of the crackdown.

Family Tried Everything to Get 10-Year-Old Out of Foster Care, Now Foster Mom Faces Murder Charges for Her Death

‘You’re Going to Jail!’: Mother Gets Swarmed by Cops at California Pumpkin Patch After Sitting at Table Woman Was Saving for Relatives

The political consequences became increasingly difficult to ignore after federal agents fatally shot two Minnesota residents during separate confrontations in January.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents killed Renee Good, 37, on Jan. 7 while she sat in her car during an encounter in Minneapolis. Weeks later, on Jan. 24, Border Patrol agents fatally shot Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, while he recorded officers attempting to arrest someone.

Videos of Pretti’s death circulated widely, drawing further scrutiny of the administration’s immigration operations. According to the report, Trump grew concerned about footage showing the shooting and instructed Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt to distance him from statements made by members of his administration. He also directed immigration czar Tom Homan to travel to Minneapolis and “fix it.”

The administration’s initial response had been markedly different. Miller and then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem defended the officers involved in Pretti’s shooting and described the nurse as a “domestic terrorist.”

WSJ said Trump’s advisers recognized the political damage surrounding the shootings, with the president eventually replacing Noem and directing her successor to keep immigration enforcement out of the headlines.

The administration’s enforcement strategy had initially delivered a result Trump could point to as evidence that he was fulfilling a campaign promise to decrease illegal border crossings.

But the crackdown increasingly reached beyond the southern border. Federal operations targeted Home Depot parking lots, construction sites and other workplaces, rounding up people described as nonviolent offenders in reports.

Those operations brought immigration enforcement into communities where the administration had expected its policies to remain popular. The backlash also showed up at the ballot box. In Tuesday’s elections, counties where Hispanic residents made up at least 80 percent of the population favored Democrats by 40 percentage points.

The immigration controversy was not the only issue weighing on Republicans. Trump’s decision to launch the war against Iran also contributed to the party’s losses, with the conflict costing taxpayers more than $47 billion, claiming the lives of more than 20 U.S. service members and driving up expenses across several industries, including freight and fertilizer.

Advisers had warned Trump during the spring that the war could hurt Republicans in the midterms, but he reportedly told them there was still plenty of time to address the political fallout.

Conservative commentator Matt Walsh called the conflict “the greatest political blunder in the last two decades,” arguing that Trump had abandoned the America First movement.

“We’re going to have to find a new leader because Trump abandoned it,” Walsh said in an interview.

The findings suggest that immigration enforcement, once a central part of Trump’s political appeal, had become another source of frustration for voters already concerned about the economy and the administration’s decision to enter a prolonged foreign conflict.

The Minneapolis shootings was an early turning point for the administration, with the first signs of internal strain emerging months before the Iran war began. By the time voters headed to the polls, the immigration crackdown had become a political burden rather than the advantage Trump expected it to be.

The report has also sparked criticism across social media, with commenters questioning whether Trump is now trying to distance himself from an immigration crackdown he once championed. One user dismissed the reported shift as too little, too late, writing , “Sounds like backpedal to me. Too late.”

Another argued that Trump should not be allowed to shift responsibility onto Miller, pointing out that the president had the authority to rein in his adviser or remove him from the administration at any time.

“Sorry, but Trump can’t place all the blame at Stephen Miller’s feet. Miller serves at the pleasure of the president, and Trump could have reined him in at any time or even fired him. Don’t let Trump pass the buck on this,” the commenter wrote .

Others took aim at Miller personally, with one user asking , “What did he expect a racist, Nazi wannabe, sociopath was going to do?”

Another commenter responded with little sympathy, writing , “Good that her friends were deported I’m shocked though. Imagine how others feel.”

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

scraped.title: Neocon Marc Thiessen Denies Reality And Lies About J.D. Vance
scraped.description: Marc Thiessen said there would be 'no ... downside to striking' Iran. Of course he's mad at J.D. Vance for noticing the obvious downsides.
scraped.author: Eddie Scarry
scraped.h1: Neocon Marc Thiessen Denies Reality And Lies About J.D. Vance
scraped.body_text:
That Washington Post content creator Marc Thiessen is out here lying wouldn’t be worth commenting on if not for his reportedly being one of the main people who advised President Trump that striking Iran would be a good time for all. So he needs to be corrected.

In a piece of content this week for the Post, Thiessen accused Vice President J.D. Vance — a favorite target of the thoroughly discredited neocons — of a “stunning act of disloyalty,” citing Vance’s post-midterms tweet about the election results. “Vance is publicly distancing himself from the person who plucked him from political obscurity, rescued his failing Senate campaign and then elevated him to the vice presidency,” Thiessen wrote , probably while enduring a nasty bout of meat sweats. “It’s an extraordinary act of disloyalty.”

What Vance did in that now-famous tweet was state the obvious . Citing internal GOP campaign data, he said the Republican electoral wipe-out was the result of the unpopular Iran war: “The reason we lost is the war.” He said the president himself had said so, which is true. And when Trump was asked to react to Vance’s tweet, he said it was “largely true.”

It’s a wonder then that Thiessen claimed in his piece of content that Vance was “publicly disagreeing” with the president. He hadn’t. He simply acknowledged reality. The war is unpopular, and voters were predictably, understandably responding to its fallout, especially surging gas prices, which have in turn continued to raise the price of everything else.

Thiessen, who once had a grand total of four different country flags on his X.com profile, is doing what neocons always do . When critics acknowledge the reality of neoconism and say it’s bad, neocons accuse them of lying and bigotry. When supporters acknowledge the same reality of neoconism and say it’s good, neocons thank them for being honest patriots. If Vance had said the war did hurt Republicans, but that it was worth the cost, Thiessen would have had no problem. But because Vance is well known to be ambivalent toward the war, Thiessen is in a rage.

He even imagined what he would have liked Vance to say. “President Trump did the right thing, and I support him 100 percent,” Thiessen said, conjuring up a J.D. Vance who doesn’t exist. “Iran has been at war with us for 47 years, and Trump is the first president to fight back. It was the most courageous decision any president has made in my lifetime.”

And I thought Pam Bondi was a clownish brown-noser.

This is the man who wrote before the war that there would be “no … downside to striking” Iran. Of course he’s mad at anyone who would see the downsides, like Republicans losing control of the House, the Senate, several governorships, and state legislatures. Or, as Marc Thiessen might call that, small potatoes.

Like Vance said in his tweet, an honest person can insist the war is worth whatever price Trump or Republicans have to pay in electoral defeat. They surely believe it. But we’re not talking about an honest person. We’re talking about Washington Post neocon and content creator Marc Thiessen.

scraped.title: Muslim, Jewish Groups Warn “Right to Worship” Bill Could Undermine Free Speech
scraped.description: “Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights,” the groups explained.
scraped.author: Chris Walker
scraped.h1: Muslim, Jewish Groups Warn “Right to Worship” Bill Could Undermine Free Speech
scraped.body_text:
“Protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights,” the groups explained.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation .

Two religious organizations — one Jewish and one Muslim — are urging lawmakers to reject a bill that ostensibly aims to protect houses of worship but that would actually quell free speech rights.

“The Right to Worship Act,” sponsored by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and cosponsored by Republicans and Democrats alike, seeks to “protect” religious buildings and people inside them by limiting the First Amendment right to protest in nearby areas.

The bill prohibits activities within 100 feet of a house of worship that include actions that are “knowingly disrupting the scheduled religious service” or “impeding people from participating at [a] scheduled religious service.”

While the legislation limits protections to the period of time “beginning 1 hour before the start of and ending 1 hour after the conclusion of a scheduled religious service,” the ambiguous language of the bill could feasibly allow houses of worship to define almost any event as being “protected” from demonstrations happening nearby — for example, a church bake sale could be considered a “scheduled religious service” by some, as could a political event featuring a controversial speaker discussing religious topics.

“Offenders” could be fined $2,500 by the federal government for their first instance of violating the rules laid out in the bill, and up to $10,000 for subsequent violations. The bill also grants private individuals who feel that their religious rights have been violated the ability to sue for “damages” of up to $5,000 per violation.

While most sponsors of the bill are Republican, it does have bipartisan support. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan) has signed on as a cosponsor , and 13 Democrats are cosponsors of the House version of the bill .

The Muslim Public Affairs Council (MPAC) and Bend the Arc: Jewish Action issued a joint statement urging lawmakers to reject the legislation , arguing that it sacrifices protections for one fundamental liberty to provide unnecessary protections for another.

“As Muslim and Jewish organizations, we understand the urgent need to protect houses of worship from threats, violence, intimidation, and physical obstruction,” the statement from the two groups explained. “Every person deserves to practice their faith freely and safely. However, protecting religious freedom must not come at the expense of other constitutional rights.”

The organizations argued that the broad language of the bill risks “chilling lawful speech, peaceful assembly, and political protest, including on public sidewalks and streets.”

“The legislation fails to adequately distinguish between genuine threats to religious exercise and constitutionally protected expression,” they said, adding :

Our communities know firsthand the consequences of religious hatred and discrimination. We reject the notion that protecting Muslim and Jewish Americans requires weakening the constitutional freedoms that safeguard us all.

The groups are calling on other members of Congress to reject the bill, and in the future, for lawmakers to only “pursue narrowly tailored protections that safeguard religious communities without restricting lawful expression.”

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has also condemned the bill , warning that it could limit speech protections for protests outside religious venues that are hosting Israeli settlement land sales, further promoting dispossession of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

In an explainer on the legislation published in September, CAIR labeled the bill as essentially an “Illegal Israeli Settlements Protection Act” that, if enacted into law, could be used to “discourage lawful demonstrations against events promoting Palestinian dispossession.”

“Existing federal law already prohibits force, threats of force, and physical obstruction directed at religious worship,” the organization said in a statement . “CAIR therefore questions the need for a new civil-liability regime that could be used to burden constitutionally protected advocacy and dissent.”

“Hosting a political or commercial event in a religious building should not shield that activity from public accountability,” CAIR added.

scraped.title: Microsoft Pulls The Plug On Oracle AI Rental As Post-Election Data Center Fallout Spreads
scraped.description: ZeroHedge - On a long enough timeline, the survival rate for everyone drops to zero
scraped.author: Tyler Durden
scraped.h1: Microsoft Pulls The Plug On Oracle AI Rental As Post-Election Data Center Fallout Spreads
scraped.body_text:
More bad news for Oracle.

About an hour after we checked in with Oracle's PR team on how that whole " force majeure is commonplace" thing was working out...

Hey guys, any updates here? https://t.co/GCPReT2mE1

... we got our answer, just not from Oracle :

Guess not: *MICROSOFT IS WINDING DOWN ORACLE DEAL TO RENT AI CLOUD CAPACITY https://t.co/2MizsjS9yq

According to Bloomberg , Microsoft has spent recent months switching off the computing capacity it rented from Oracle after declining to renew the contract. The reason is about as unflattering as it gets for a company that has staked its balance sheet on AI infrastructure: the Oracle hardware ran on older-generation Nvidia chips and, over time, "no longer fit the company's specifications."

ORCL promptly slid 4%, which put it, in our words, below the $116 equity offering price it sold $10 billion in stock at just four days ago. Recall that the stock hit $248.15 on June 1. Investors who bought the "de-risked" story this week are already underwater on a deal that is barely four days old , and the stock has lost more than half its value in five months.

But the Microsoft headline is just the latest entry on a list that has grown every single day since Tuesday night, when voters handed governors' mansions in the states holding roughly 45% of planned US data center capacity to candidates who promised to pause them. Put the two together and Oracle has a problem at both ends of its pipeline: its old capacity is too old to rent , and its new capacity may be too blue to build .

Some history first. The Oracle-Microsoft deal was announced in 2023 to power the AI version of Bing, and at the time, Bloomberg notes, the idea of Microsoft renting servers from a direct rival was taken as early proof of just how short the world was of compute. (The full size of the deal was never disclosed.)

Three years later, the same arrangement is proof of something else: GPUs age, and the biggest buyer of rented compute in the world is no longer willing to pay for the old ones.

Oracle, naturally, disagrees. A spokesperson told Bloomberg demand for its AI infrastructure "remains strong, including for earlier-generation" GPUs, and reminded everyone that in September it said it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original price. That 20% premium has been a staple of the bull case: just this Wednesday, Wells Fargo's Jerry Revich, in " Texas Policy Reset Adds Timing Risk to 20-30% of the Data Center Power Pipeline " ( available to pro subs ), cited Oracle's 97.9% AI infrastructure utilization and "20% average renewal/resale premium" as evidence that "token economics remain attractive."

Well, one renewal just came in at a 100% discount.

Microsoft's retreat also fits a pattern we have been tracking for weeks. Microsoft committed more than $80 billion to rent capacity from neoclouds like CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius, and per Bloomberg, key leaders there have grown frustrated over high costs and delays, tightened oversight of data center projects and debated whether to sign any new neocloud deals at all. In October, Microsoft walked from Nscale's UK deal ; on Thursday came the report that it won't expand its Texas deal with Nscale either , along with the disclosure that it spent $5 billion less on Q3 capex than projected due to delays at third-party capacity, including IREN's.

Translation: Microsoft wants new chips, on time, in its own specifications, and it is increasingly unwilling to pay landlords who can't deliver all three. Which is a problem for every landlord whose collateral is a rack of chips that gets one generation older every year the power doesn't show up.

And the power is now even less likely to show up on time.

Cleanview counts nine states where the governor or governor-elect has promised or already imposed a pause on new data centers. Together they hold 158.6 GW of planned capacity, or 41% of the entire US pipeline :

Now look at who is most exposed. Every single gigawatt of OpenAI's planned capacity sits in a state whose new governor backed a pause on the campaign trail , as does 45% of Microsoft's:

Why does that matter for Oracle? Because OpenAI is Oracle. The $300 billion compute contract that sent ORCL soaring in September 2025 is being built across Texas (Abilene, Shackelford County), New Mexico, Wisconsin and Michigan, which is why OpenAI shows up at 100% above. Two of those states, Texas and New Mexico, delivered the most hostile results of the night.

Take New Mexico, home of Project Jupiter, the 2.45 GW Oracle-OpenAI Stargate campus that regular readers know all too well. Back on Sept 24 Oracle sent a force majeure notice to the Blue Owl unit developing the site, then insisted the notice was "commonplace" and meant nothing. We had a different reading at the time:

Hey guys, you are right: the force majeure by itself does not change delivery expectations. You just have to pay the rent until the delivery actually takes place. Contractually. https://t.co/GCPReT1OOt pic.twitter.com/rj721cRTu9

The more important detail came that night, when the FT reported that Oracle remains on the contractual hook regardless: if Jupiter isn't ready, Oracle still owes a "carry cost" in lieu of rent for up to three years, enough to cover the interest on the debt in full plus a set equity return for Blue Owl's funds. As one person familiar with the contract put it, "The power delivery risk sits with Oracle, not the investors." Here is the structure we mapped out at the time. Note who sits at the bottom of every arrow:

And for the record, here is what we wrote in that same Sept 24 post , six weeks before the vote: the construction delays "will only get worse if Democrats win back the house at the midterm elections." They won back a lot more than the House, so we'll allow ourselves a modest victory lap.

Two weeks later, Oracle was trucking compressed natural gas to its data centers because the Jupiter pipeline was running late, and the $18 billion of construction loans behind the campus were already quoted at 89-91 cents on the dollar (per the FT).

On Tuesday, New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, and the morning after, she told reporters her plan for day one : "a moratorium for large-scale data centers with the legislature passing a set of guardrails." As for Jupiter's gas plants specifically, Cleanview notes Haaland has written that under her watch they would "not exist." The fuel-cell air permit is still pending, with a Nov 23 decision deadline. Hey guys, any updates?

Texas is no better. As we laid out in " What's Next For Data Centers After The Blue Tsunami ", governor-elect Gina Hinojosa turns Abbott's audit-based freeze into one tied to legislation, which means at least through the May 31, 2027 session end. And the Goldman TMT desk noted this morning that part of today's bounce came from "benign comments from Texas governor-elect on datacenters." When "benign" is the bull catalyst, you know where the bar is.

Goldman's research department spent Friday pushing back on the panic, and in fairness, it has the numbers. In his " End of Week Market Intelligence: dc downside ?" ( available to pro subs ), Chris Hussey frames this week's debate as follows:

"At the core of market concerns this week is a debate around whether all of the compute power that has been ordered (semiconductors, servers, fiber optic cables) will have a place to be installed when it is delivered in the years ahead ."

Goldman's answer is mostly yes, at least through 2027. Hardware analyst Mike Ng " US Data Center Capacity update: Framing risks to our data center forecasts ", also available to pro subs) says capacity already under construction implies 22/24 GW-IT of net additions in 2027/28, matching his 20/24 GW forecasts, and calls the key risk "timing rather than cancellations." The catch is Texas, which accounts for 20% of 2027 and 27% of 2028 under-construction additions:

E&C analyst Adam Bubes went a step further and actually raised his US data center construction spending forecasts to $80 billion/$100 billion for 2026/27 (from $67 billion/$87 billion), introducing $125 billion for 2028. His reasoning: every project in Goldman's 2027 forecast has already broken ground. 2028 is another story, though: only about half of the 2028 projects on Goldman's watch list have broken ground , and beyond that it's almost all PowerPoint:

Note the light blue. That is the "announced" capacity, and it is exactly what a governor's moratorium hits first. Bubes concedes as much, arguing moratoria "would primarily impact projects that have not yet started" and would smooth the cycle into 2029/30 "rather than impacting the TAM."

Maybe. But today's Microsoft story shows why "timing" is not as harmless as it sounds. A project that slips two years gets delivered into a world where the chips ordered for it are two years older. For a hyperscaler, a delay is a timing issue. For whoever owns the GPUs, it's a depreciation issue. Microsoft just told Oracle which one it is.

And somebody is going to have to fund the wait. Goldman credit strategist Amanda Lynam estimates hyperscalers are financing 36% of this year's capex with credit (and 35% next year), while only 43% of the $687 billion of AI-related financing so far this year came from hyperscalers. Oracle has already done its share: as we noted on Monday, it blew through its entire four-year $20 billion "hard cap" in a single morning, five days after promising it. Which, as regular readers know, is why we have been calling AI a debt bubble since last October.

The Oracle news landed at the end of a week that saw the Nasdaq suffer its worst day since March 2020 on Thursday (-6.4%), while Goldman's AI data center-levered basket fell 12% in a single session. The headlines since then haven't helped much:

Here is the updated ZH Casualty List , with Oracle as the newest entry:

Jefferies' Julien Dumoulin-Smith summed up the sellside consensus on the election in one line " The Blue Morning After: State-by-State Election Scorecard "): "Demand moves right, not away." Goldman says the same thing with more charts.

Perhaps they're right about demand. But capacity that moves right ages , financing that moves right costs more , and a landlord that moves right keeps paying for the slip (just ask Oracle's lenders on Jupiter). Today's Microsoft story is the first clear sign of what happens at the other end: the tenant with the deepest pockets in AI is choosing newer chips over older contracts , and that probably makes Oracle's 20% renewal premium look a lot more like an exception.

Which leaves Oracle squeezed on both sides: the older chips it already owns are losing their best renter, while the new campuses meant to replace them sit in exactly the states that just voted for a pause. Goldman hosted Oracle management today, of all days; we'd love to know what was said in the room. Until then, we'll keep asking the obvious question:

If Oracle has cash flow visibility all the way to 2029 maybe they can answer something far simpler: when will the force majeure on their massive NM data center be lifted? What’s that, they have no idea?

Much more in the full Goldman " End of Week Market Intelligence: dc downside ?", and " US Data Center Capacity update " both available to pro subs .
