scraped.title: The Cybertruck is dead
scraped.description: Ugly, broken, and ultimately rejected, Tesla’s Cybertruck keeps tracing the MAGA trajectory.
scraped.author: Inae Oh
scraped.h1: The Cybertruck Is Dead
scraped.body_text:
Kotaro Numata/AP

After years of lagging sales and multiple high-profile recalls, Elon Musk announced on Friday that Tesla will start closing out production of the Cybertruck in 2027. The announcement marks the end of the road for a vehicle that became synonymous with the politics and aesthetics of MAGA: brutal, aggressive, and in-your-face .

“Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production,” Musk posted on X.

The announcement concludes a humiliating week for Musk , after spending $445 million backing Republicans ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections only for Democrats to seize control of Congress in dozens of history-making elections around the country. The blue wave was especially felt in Texas , where, in recent years, Musk moved significant portions of his business in order to avoid regulation and oversight by Democrats in California. It was during this relocation that the Cybertruck, which debuted in 2023, quickly became linked to Musk’s politics, and later, his singular role in destroying much of the federal government.

But the Cybertruck was plagued with serious problems that went well beyond its association with Musk’s MAGA embrace. Its obnoxious, hulking steel design—which included bulletproof windows that many saw as emblematic of the right’s crime panic—was roundly mocked; multiple recalls were announced; and sales repeatedly struggled.

In other words, ugly, broken, and ultimately rejected. Even in the end, the Cybertruck traces a familiar MAGA trajectory.

scraped.title: NO LEAGUE OF THEIR OWN? Trans athletes force women to fight for what they've already won. | Blaze Media
scraped.description: More than 50 years after Title IX, girls are fighting to keep biological males out of their sports.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/140738092630206
scraped.h1: NO LEAGUE OF THEIR OWN? Trans athletes force women to fight for what they've already won.
scraped.body_text:
More than 50 years after Title IX, girls are fighting to keep biological males out of their sports.

Do you ever notice ... how something women spent decades fighting for now requires an election to keep?

A league of their own.

A national organization cannot be the only voice your daughter hears defending her. Moms and dads need to stand up in their own communities.

Not a guaranteed championship. Not a participation trophy.

A fair chance to compete against other females. Apparently, we need to count the ballots on that.

Girls shouldn’t need an election to have their own sports. But here we are.

On November 3, voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska, and Washington considered measures addressing sex-based athletic eligibility.

Different proposals, different provisions, but a common question: Will we preserve female sports categories for females?

Voters in Nebraska, Arizona, and Washington approved ballot measures prohibiting boys from participating in girls’ sports. Proposition 134, a similar measure in Colorado, was also leading as votes continued to be counted.

My wife and I attended an election-night watch party with supporters of Protect Kids Colorado , the grassroots organization behind Proposition 134 and two other ballot measures.

Chaired by XX-XY Athletics founder Jennifer Sey, Protect Kids Colorado helped organize the effort behind Proposition 134 alongside local moms Erin Lee, Lori Gimelshteyn, and other concerned parents.

The room was filled with volunteers and supporters, hopeful and energized as the results trickled in.

These folks had worked hard.

More than 3,300 petition circulators helped qualify the organization's three measures for the ballot, with 170,000 Coloradans signing its petitions.

They knocked on doors, visited churches, and talked with their neighbors.

And catch this: October campaign finance reports showed roughly $4.4 million raised by opponents, compared with about $216,000 supporting the effort.

About 20 to 1.

Apparently, concerned parents didn’t get the memo that they were supposed to be overwhelmed.

And guess what?

As of Wednesday morning, Proposition 134 was leading with roughly 52% of the vote, although the outcome remained uncalled.

But this story started long before anyone ordered campaign signs.

Women fought for years to get their daughters onto playing fields, into gymnasiums, and onto college rosters.

They fought for equipment, practice time, coaching, and scholarships.

Representatives Patsy Mink and Edith Green and Senator Birch Bayh helped carry that fight into Congress .

President Richard Nixon signed Title IX on June 23, 1972.

Its prohibition against sex discrimination extended across federally funded education, with athletics becoming one of its most consequential applications.

Implementation required years of additional pressure and litigation.

Before Title IX, girls accounted for roughly 294,000 high school sports participation entries. In 2025-2026, that figure exceeded 3.65 million .

Pause on that for a moment.

That is an extraordinary achievement.

Yet, now we’re arguing over whether the category that helped make that progress possible should remain female.

We finally opened the gym doors for girls.

Then some adults apparently forgot why there were separate teams inside.

Biological sex matters in sports.

Boys are male. Girls are female. Period.

Identifying differently does not change that.

Hormones and surgery can alter physical characteristics. But they do not change a male into a biological female.

The American College of Sports Medicine identifies biological sex as a major determinant of athletic performance.

Its consensus statement explains how male puberty produces substantial differences in muscle mass, strength, power, oxygen-carrying capacity, and other physical characteristics relevant to competition.

Before puberty, performance differences are much smaller. That doesn’t mean every boy beats every girl.

It explains why we have girls’ teams.

We understand competitive categories when weight classes are involved.

Nobody tells a lightweight boxer that objecting to a heavyweight opponent demonstrates a disappointing lack of inclusion.

Yet girls are expected to accept a comparable dismissal of the physical differences their category exists to recognize.

These are actual girls with actual consequences.

We know Riley Gaines , who became a national advocate after tying Lia Thomas at the NCAA championships.

We remember Italian Olympic boxer Angela Carini abandoning her Paris bout after just 46 seconds, overwhelmed by powerful punches from Imane Khelif.

The fight intensified the controversy over why the IOC permitted him to compete after a previous disqualification over sex eligibility.

We saw fencer Stephanie Turner take a knee rather than compete against an opponent identifying as female, receiving a disqualification for refusing the bout.

In Connecticut, runners Selina Soule, Chelsea Mitchell, Alanna Smith, and Ashley Nicoletti challenged a policy allowing male athletes who identify as female to compete in girls’ track.

Their attorneys report that two such competitors collected 15 girls’ state titles between 2017 and 2020.

Their lawsuit concerns lost honors and competitive opportunities, not an abstract disagreement over terminology.

Then there is Payton McNabb , the North Carolina volleyball player struck in the face by a ball spiked by a transgender opponent in 2022.

McNabb has described sustaining a concussion and lasting problems, including impaired vision and partial paralysis.

Sports involve injuries. Everybody knows that.

The question is why adults should require girls to accept additional concerns about physical mismatches while treating their objections as the real problem.

And girls should not have to sustain a serious injury before somebody decides their concerns deserve a hearing.

The issue follows them into the privacy of a locker room.

Former University of Pennsylvania swimmer Paula Scanlan testified that administrators told the women that Lia Thomas’ participation and presence in their locker room were nonnegotiable.

When the women objected, they were offered psychological services to become comfortable undressing in front of a male.

Scanlan summed up the university’s response this way: “We, the women, were the problem, not the victims.”

Let that settle in.

The women raised concerns about their own privacy.

The university decided that it was the women who needed adjusting. Apparently, the boundaries that needed moving were theirs.

In 2025, Penn entered a federal Title IX resolution agreement that included policy changes and personalized apologies to affected female swimmers.

An apology matters.

So would having listened to them in the first place.

But many more girls have names we don’t know.

The girl who missed qualifying for state.

The girl who lost a college scholarship.

The girl changing in a bathroom stall.

The girl wondering whether speaking up will cost her teammates, friends, or a place on the roster. More of them are finding their voices.

A championship race happens once.

And for many, that is once in a lifetime after years of dedicated training. You cannot give a teenager those starting blocks back at age 30.

They shouldn’t need a national following before the adults in their own community listen.

Here in Colorado, the dispute is still unfolding.

Parents at Dakota Ridge High School have objected after a male student who identifies as female made the girls’ junior varsity volleyball roster while female students were cut.

Their account raises a straightforward question about whose opportunities a girls’ roster is supposed to provide.

Jefferson County Public Schools says its gender-identity policies comply with Colorado law. The federal government says those policies violate Title IX.

In March, the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights found violations involving female sports, bathrooms, locker rooms, and overnight accommodations.

In June, it issued another warning over the district’s refusal to change course.

President Trump’s February 2025 executive order directed federal agencies to protect female athletic opportunities and locker rooms through Title IX enforcement.

Jefferson County Public Schools continues to resist that enforcement position.

The Supreme Court, meanwhile, upheld Idaho’s and West Virginia’s sex-based sports restrictions in June 2026.

To be precise, it ruled that states may maintain those restrictions; it did not order every state to adopt them.

Which helps explain why Coloradans had Proposition 134 on their ballots.

Jeffco Kids First has helped bring local parents’ concerns into public view. Jeffco’s school board opposed Proposition 134.

Parents shouldn’t need a working knowledge of federal litigation to ask who can try out for their daughter’s volleyball team.

Even the International Olympic Committee has changed course.

Its new female-category policy, beginning with the 2028 Los Angeles Games, limits eligibility to biological females , using a one-time SRY gene screening.

Yet defending female sports can still make you a target at a women’s basketball game.

Ask Jennifer Sey.

Her company, XX-XY Athletics, sells shirts with a simple message: “Refuse to Pretend.”

Sey has been outspoken in support of the Camas cross-country girls who walked away from a race rather than accept their male teammate’s participation in the girls’ category.

That runner has since qualified for the girls’ state championships, finishing seventh at the regional qualifier. That is a place in the girls’ state competition that is now occupied by a male.

When somebody says this affects only a small number of athletes, ask them which girls are supposed to consider their opportunity expendable.

Your daughter?

Or is it OK if it’s somebody else’s child?

RELATED: The WNBA has a tolerance problem — and it’s not coming from the women in XX-XY shirts

Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images

Earlier this WNBA season, security told fans to cover their XX-XY shirts .

At the Finals, Sey recorded the harassment directed at her and her friends, including people telling them to kill themselves.

Security escorted them from their seats for a “conversation,” then allowed them to return.

You would think supporting female sports would be an ordinary position at a women’s basketball game.

Apparently, the shirt needed its own league approval review.

Meanwhile, the WNBA’s collective bargaining agreement says “only players who are women are eligible,” without defining “women” or spelling out transgender eligibility rules.

That leaves the boundary of its female category unresolved.

The league can tell you when a foot crosses the three-point line. You would think it can explain who qualifies for the women’s league.

Moms for Liberty has helped bring these concerns into public view.

Alliance Defending Freedom has represented female athletes, including the Connecticut runners, in their fight for fair competition.

Those efforts make a difference, but a national organization cannot be the only voice your daughter hears defending her. Moms and dads need to stand up in their own communities.

At the school board meeting. In the athletic director’s office.

When policies are written and when their daughters say something is wrong.

A dad can spot a missed holding penalty from the upper deck through somebody’s nachos. Surely he can find his voice when his daughter’s opportunity is on the line.

Show up.

Ask direct questions. Insist on answers.

Support her when she speaks, especially when speaking carries a cost.

We tell our children to stand up for what is right. They ought to see us doing it.

Scott Smith’s daughter was sexually assaulted by a male student in a Loudoun County school bathroom.

The attacker later assaulted another girl after being transferred to a different school. Investigations did not establish that he claimed a female identity to gain entry.

What they did establish was serious institutional failure.

Protecting private spaces also requires acknowledging that access rules can be exploited. Girls should not have to determine whether someone entering their private space is sincere.

And a father demanding accountability should not have to fight an institution more concerned with managing the controversy than answering for what happened.

Nebraska and Arizona have decided.

They are still counting votes in Colorado and Washington. But whatever the final tally, the girls deserve an answer.

Their mothers and grandmothers fought to get them onto the field.

Their daughters should not have to spend their athletic careers in court explaining why that field exists.

Refuse to pretend.

Girls should not have to surrender what women fought so hard to win.

Jonathan Flora

scraped.title: CAIR Ends Operations in Florida as “Domestic Terrorist” Designation Takes Effect
scraped.description: Gov. Ron DeSantis has been attempting to put the Muslim civil rights organization out of business for nearly a year.
scraped.author: Mitch Perry
scraped.h1: CAIR Ends Operations in Florida as “Domestic Terrorist” Designation Takes Effect
scraped.body_text:
Gov. Ron DeSantis has been attempting to put the Muslim civil rights organization out of business for nearly a year.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

The Council on American Islamic Relations (CAIR) has suspended operations in Florida, the organization has announced .

It did so after a federal judge rejected an emergency request Wednesday by the Muslim civil rights organization to stop the state from designating the group and its state chapter as domestic terrorist organizations, allowing the designation to take effect while its legal challenge, litigated by the ACLU and the Southern Poverty Law Center, continues.

Federal Judge Allen C. Winsor of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida denied CAIR and CAIR Florida’s request to reverse the designation. In a ruling released Wednesday night, Windsor said the plaintiffs were unlikely to succeed at this stage on their claims that the designations under a new law ( HB 1471 ) violates their due process and First Amendment rights.

The judge did issue a narrow form of preliminary relief, stating that Florida prosecutors cannot enforce the law against CAIR and CAIR Florida, their employees, or third parties with respect to provision of legal services to the groups.

That designation took effect Thursday. As a result, both groups say they have been forced to shut down their advocacy and operations in Florida.

“Today’s ruling is deeply disappointing and we are appealing it,” said Ashley Gorski, senior counsel with the ACLU’s National Security Project.

“Today’s decision upholds state officials’ sweeping power to punish American organizations they brand as ‘terrorist,’ without due process and in violation of the First Amendment. Florida officials have been relentless in seeking to silence our clients’ civil rights work and advocacy, damaging not only them but also their community. We cannot allow this dangerous and sweeping censorship regime to stand.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis and Attorney General James Uthmeier hailed the ruling Thursday. “Great win by our Solicitor General’s office and for the people of Florida!” Uthmeier wrote on X.

DeSantis and other members of the Florida Cabinet voted to designate CAIR and CAIR Florida as domestic terrorist organizations on Sept. 29. They contend the group operates as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood.

Attorneys for CAIR have vehemently denied the allegation, contending its mission, “rooted in faith, is to enhance the public’s understanding of Islam, protect civil rights, promote justice and empower American Muslims.”

The designation in late September came months after DeSantis signed legislation approved by the Legislature earlier this year that gave five Florida executive officials — the head of domestic security (the commissioner of the Florida Department of Law Enforcement), the governor, and the three members of the state Cabinet — power to designate and eliminate groups operating in the United States without filing any legal charges or submitting their case to a jury.

The legislation prohibits any state agency, political subdivision, or public school district from expending or accepting state funds to support groups thus designated. It bans public schools or school districts from spending state or federal funds or maintaining programs on campus that “promote” a designated group.

The law also says any college or university must report information relating to the status of a student attending that school on a student visa if the student “promotes” a terrorist-designated organization. Students found to have promoted the group can be expelled.

The ACLU, the ACLU of Florida, and two other legal groups representing CAIR and CAIR Florida filed a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the legislation in July in the Northern District.

“As Florida chief of domestic security, I know there are imminent dangers to public health, safety, and welfare due to increasing risks from foreign and domestic terrorist groups,” then-FDLE Commissioner Mark Glass said on Sept. 11. Glass has since been replaced by Larry Keefe.

DeSantis has been attempting to put CAIR out of business for nearly a year. He issued an executive order in December designating CAIR and CAIR-Florida as terrorist organizations, directing state and local agencies to block them and their supporters from public contracts, funding, and benefits. After the groups sued, a federal judge issued a temporary injunction blocking the order in March.

Shortly afterwards, the Legislature passed and DeSantis signed HB 1471.

CAIR and CAIR-Florida say the impact on the communities they serve will be “immense.” They say they provide a range of pro bono legal services to Florida residents, including those who suffer government and workplace discrimination in violation of their civil rights, as well as those navigating the immigration system.

“CAIR-Florida categorically rejects Florida officials’ baseless designation of us,” said Hiba Rahim, executive director of CAIR-Florida, in a written statement. “Nevertheless, we are heartbroken that we have no choice but to close our doors to protect our staff and people of all faiths who support our work.”

Truthout is funded almost entirely by readers — that’s why we can speak truth to power and cut against the mainstream narrative. But independent journalists at Truthout face mounting political repression under Trump.

We rely on your support to survive McCarthyist censorship. Please make a tax-deductible one-time or monthly donation.

Mitch Perry has covered politics and government in Florida for more than two decades. Most recently he is the former politics reporter for Bay News 9 . He has also worked at Florida Politics , Creative Loafing and WMNF Radio in Tampa. He was also part of the original staff when the Florida Phoenix was created in 2018.

scraped.title: Democrats take control of Georgia’s powerful utility regulator
scraped.description: Swept in on the blue wave, new commissioners plan to tackle power bills, clean energy, and data center accountability.
scraped.author: Emily Jones
scraped.h1: Democrats take control of Georgia’s powerful utility regulator
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Beginning in January, three of the five officials on the Georgia Public Service Commission will be Democrats. It will be the first time the party has controlled the powerful energy regulation board in 30 years. The commission, which regulates utilities including the state’s largest electric provider, Georgia Power, has come under more scrutiny in recent years due to rising power bills and the high energy demands of data centers.

Now, Democrats plan to focus on affordability, clean energy, and closer scrutiny of Georgia Power.

“There’s a long laundry list of things that need to be looked into,” said Democratic commissioner Peter Hubbard, who won his reelection bid this week. “And so we’ll have to triage, in fact, and decide how best to move forward.”

One of his first priorities will be launching an affordability docket, he said — a series of hearings that would delve into the reasons for high power bills and ways to save customers money. Hubbard said he and his fellow Democrats also plan to bring close scrutiny to upcoming Georgia Power requests around making more energy and adjusting customer rates. Shelia Edwards and Alicia Johnson are the other two Democrats on the PSC.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

But any changes, especially to power bills, will likely take time.

“We may not be able to expect immediate effects on our wallets,” said Emory University associate professor Kristin Phillips, who studies energy burden and the PSC. “But I think we can expect immediate change in the types of decisions that are made.”

Affordability and high energy bills were driving issues in the campaigns both this year and last year, the two elections that together resulted in the new Democratic majority on the commission.

“We knew that we had to connect the dots between energy and affordability,” said Brionté McCorkle of Georgia Conservation Voters, a group that campaigned for the Democratic candidates and worked to draw attention to the PSC elections. “It’s not just this obscure regulatory body like it used to be treated. Its decisions directly affect household budgets, communities, health, and our energy future.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Chris Womack, the CEO of Southern Company, Georgia Power’s parent company, also acknowledged the central importance of affordability during the company’s third-quarter earnings call on Thursday. But Womack said he’s confident the utility can address those concerns with the new commissioners.

“If you look at what we have been doing with rate freezes, with benefits, with how we are providing benefits from growth to customers — existing customers — as well as to the communities, we think that’s a strong platform to stand on,” he said.

Since the data center boom in Georgia began, Georgia Power has maintained that the increased revenue would more than pay for the new infrastructure to serve them, which the utility argues would keep rates lower for residential and small business customers. The utility calls this “downward pressure.” It doesn’t mean rates will go down, but rather that any increases would be offset by the influx of revenue from data centers.

The utility recently doubled down on that promise as part of its deal to serve a massive new OpenAI data center. The deal, Georgia Power said, would bring $15 of not savings but downward pressure per month for what Georgia Power calls the “typical” residential customer.

Separately, Georgia Power also credited the increased revenue from data centers for the temporary rate freeze approved last year. But the rate freeze received criticism from some advocacy groups. Instead of first holding a PSC hearing to give advocates a chance to verify the utility’s financial claims, Georgia Power announced the temporary rate freeze. Advocates feel that the backward process left them unable to confirm whether the company was delivering on its promises and fully shielding ordinary customers from data center costs.

It’s part of a broader criticism often leveled at the PSC and Georgia Power: lack of transparency. The OpenAI contract was entirely redacted, and only a summary provided to the public after it was approved. Specific details involved in service contracts, deals to buy energy, and construction costs are often redacted from the utility’s public filings under the auspices of trade secrecy.

“I absolutely think transparency is potentially one of the biggest impacts here,” said Phillips of the election results. “It has been often on advocates to push on the way that the PSC communicates about the decisions that it’s making, and I’m hoping that there will be more clarity and transparency.”

The Democrats on the commission have promised to bring increased scrutiny to the next rate-setting process, due in 2028, along with Georgia Power’s long-term plans to make and deliver energy, its forecasts about rising demand, and other issues. Hubbard has also proposed conducting a rate case for the state’s natural gas utilities, which he said hasn’t been done in over a decade. And he said they’ll push for other changes going forward.

“We’ll continue with an agenda next year and the year after that to take advantage of this four-year period when we have the majority and can push for long-lasting reforms and shifting the direction of the state in terms of energy,” Hubbard said.

articles.title: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
articles.summary: Data centers are a crucial part of President Donald Trump's push to win the global artificial intelligence race, which he continues despite the midterm results.
articles.ai_summary: Despite midterm election results, the Trump administration plans to continue expanding data centers for AI development.

scraped.title: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
scraped.description: Data centers are a crucial part of President Donald Trump's push to win the global artificial intelligence race, which he continues despite the midterm results.
scraped.author: Kevin Breuninger
scraped.h1: Data center double-down: Hassett says blue wave won't stop AI build-out
scraped.body_text:
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday he expects data center growth to continue as projected, despite the blue-wave election that saw voters overwhelmingly favor limiting the tech infrastructure buildout.

Hassett, on CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ," acknowledged the dozens of measures on states' midterm ballots seeking to constrain data centers, a crucial part of President Donald Trump 's push to win the global artificial intelligence race.

In at least 46 of the roughly 50 such initiatives on ballots in 2026, majorities voted to restrict development of the facilities, according to Ballotpedia's tally.

"We respect the localities that decide that's what they want to do," Hassett said. "But America is a big place, and right now, the data centers scheduled over the next couple of years aren't affected by these ballot initiatives."

"And the stuff after that, you know, there's plenty of room in the U.S. for data center growth to continue, as it was projected ahead of the election," he said.

Hassett said he expects data centers will continue to expand in states with more welcoming governors, and he suggested that even hostile states will eventually come around.

"That's exactly what's going to happen," he said. "That, or what'll happen will be that the benefits of the data centers will be so obvious that people decide to change their minds about the way they regulate them."

Hassett also blamed Thursday's tech-driven market plunge on "uncertainty about what the political change is going to mean for data centers going forward."

"We've now got a ... new majority that maybe is going to go in there and muddle around in there, and I think that markets are anxious about that," he said.

"But I think that the economic strength that we see everywhere else is so strong, and of course, in the end, you could take something that's growing as fast as the data centers and make it grow a little bit slower, and you still have a blockbuster economy."

"And so, I think we're still very, very optimistic about what's going to happen going forward," he said.

The CNBC Voter Poll found 56% of midterm voters identified data centers as either a crucial or major issue — and of those who considered it crucial, 62% favored the generic Democratic candidate.

Trump has strongly embraced AI and data centers and has even tried to reverse their seeming unpopularity by rebranding the tech as "super intelligence," or SI.

In a Truth Social post Friday, Trump made clear that despite the midterm losses, his support for the nascent industry has not faltered.

"As President, I am 100% in favor of Super Intelligence (SI), and will work with the many States in the U.S. that want to become RICH by having them," Trump wrote. "They are GOLD, and only foolish leadership will say 'NO' to the riches they bring!"

scraped.title: AIPAC Has Lost Over 30 of Its Midterm Races So Far, In Sign of Major Shift
scraped.description: Roughly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable lobbying group this cycle went toward races they lost.
scraped.author: Sharon Zhang
scraped.h1: AIPAC Has Lost Over 30 of Its Midterm Races So Far, In Sign of Major Shift
scraped.body_text:
Roughly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable lobbying group this cycle went toward races they lost.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has lost dozens of races in which it backed a candidate in this year’s midterm elections, accounting for nearly two-thirds of the spending by the once insuperable political lobbying group, in a sign of its waning influence.

Politico found in a report on Thursday that more than 30 of the group’s candidates lost their elections this week. This marks “defeat for AIPAC in over three-fourths of the competitive races that have been called so far where it backed an incumbent,” Politico reported.

This includes candidates like Republican Representatives Mike Lawler (New York), Brian Fitzpatrick (Pennsylvania), and Max Miller (Ohio), as well as Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), who fell to progressive Israel critic Troy Jackson, and Mike Rogers in Michigan.

Collins has been a staunch defender of Israel in the Senate, and AIPAC was her biggest outside donor by a massive margin during the race. AIPAC gave $2.8 million supporting her race against Jackson, as data from OpenSecrets showed ; the next-largest outside donor, investment firm KKR & Co., gave just a fraction of that, at $160,000.

AIPAC dumped even more money into the race against Michigan candidate Abdul El-Sayed, whose opposition to the U.S.-Israel relationship has been a hallmark of his campaign. AIPAC and its super PAC, United Democracy Project (UDP), reportedly dropped up to $9 million supporting Rogers in the last weeks of the election. This came after AIPAC spent a whopping $30 million opposing El-Sayed and backing Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Michigan) in the primary.

The next largest target after El-Sayed was Daniel Biss, who won his election to the U.S. House in Illinois after UDP dumped $6.3 million against him. Biss explicitly ran on a platform opposing AIPAC and its influence.

These losses are staggering for a political group whose name was once synonymous with power in D.C. In fact, these results indicate that being affiliated with the group is becoming politically toxic, due in large part to the work of pro-Palestine advocates who spoke out against the group amid Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

AIPAC, perhaps concerned about losing donors, defended its record on X, arguing that it backed 245 candidates who won their races. But the contributions to these races represented only about a third of their spending in this cycle.

According to Responsible Statecraft , almost two-thirds of the money that AIPAC and UDP spent this cycle went toward losing candidates. Via UDP, AIPAC spent $84.1 million on elections — $55.3 million of which went toward races where their preferred candidate lost. This stands in sharp contrast to prior election cycles. In the 2022 midterm election, Responsible Statecraft found, 69 percent of UDP spending went toward races their candidate won. In 2024, their winning ratio was 87 percent.

AIPAC can still wield enormous power over Congress. In its first post-election post on social media on Wednesday, the lobbying group congratulated Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) and Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-New York) for the “resounding victories for their caucuses.” The lawmakers are currently poised to lead the House and Senate when the new Congress begins in January, and are two of Israel’s staunchest defenders in Congress and major allies of AIPAC.

But the sands are quickly shifting under their feet. Opposing Israel and AIPAC have become increasingly normalized positions for politicians as the public overwhelmingly rejects the U.S.-Israel relationship, with even candidates in deep red states running against the lobbying group.

NEW poll: A supermajority of Jewish Americans believe Israeli & AIPAC actions increase antisemitism. 80% say Israel’s actions in Gaza & the West Bank increase antisemitism in the US. 66% say AIPAC’s campaign spending against candidates critical of Israel increases antisemitism. pic.twitter.com/oIS1wUYSRi

In Mississippi, for instance, Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom pledged to never take AIPAC money. He is currently holding on to a narrow lead over Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Mississippi) in their election, and, if he wins, will be the first Democratic senator elected from the state since 1989.

“I will never take a penny from AIPAC or Super PACs that don’t put Mississippi and America first,” Colom said in a post on social media last month. “This Senate seat belongs to the people of Mississippi. That’s who I’ll answer to.”

Security researchers have discovered hundreds of copies of a Chinese-made AI hacking tool publicly exposed to the internet for anyone to access, potentially allowing outsiders to launch cyberattacks against unsuspecting targets.

The hacking software, called Artex, is an open source autonomous penetration testing tool, meaning software that automatically probes computer systems for weaknesses, and it’s been linked to several cyberattacks since its public release in July. As open source software, it’s free for anyone to download and run on their own servers, making it a popular tool for those who cannot access Anthropic or OpenAI’s most advanced cybersecurity AI models for discovering security vulnerabilities. Microsoft has previously described Artex as a system of AI agents that can conduct cyberattacks “from reconnaissance through data exfiltration with little needed human interaction.”

In a blog post , cybersecurity firm Censys, which scans the internet for exposed or vulnerable systems, said that it identified more than 800 distinct deployments of Artex that were accessible from the web without needing a password to log in.

Silas Cutler, principal security researcher at Censys who wrote the blog post, said that not every instance of Artex is operated maliciously and many are used for authorized testers. But it’s unclear why hundreds of these Artex systems are exposed to the web, as the software does not require them to be accessible from the internet.

The findings underscore how even powerful hacking tools can be misconfigured to be publicly accessible by anyone, increasing the chance that someone will find and misuse them. The publicly accessible systems also expose attack tools, such as implants (hidden malicious software) used to compromise and maintain persistent access to a victim’s network.

Security companies have linked the use of Artex to several broad-scale cyberattacks, including against the Korean finance industry in September . Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike attributed the attacks to a Chinese-speaking hacker who used an Artex instance in the attacks, in part because the hacker had left an “open directory” hosting the system. Censys said that its data showed the Artex instance in question had been publicly exposed for months, and appeared to contain more attack data that extended “well beyond South Korean banks,” including payment and gaming companies.

Artex was also used in an attack on IT support giant ConnectWise earlier in October , which allowed Chinese-linked hackers to spy on thousands of organizations whose data and files are hosted in Microsoft’s cloud. Microsoft, which has visibility into the attack, said in a blog post that the hackers used Artex to break into customers’ cloud environments and steal their data at such speed that defenders had “little time to detect and respond.”

Many of the attacks linked to Artex involved exploiting simple vulnerabilities, such as guessing weak or known passwords, and a lack of multi-factor authentication.

The findings show that simple vulnerabilities, including misconfigurations, can expose both the attacker and their targets.

Artex has since announced it would go closed-source, effectively limiting further releases for paid customers. There are still dozens of copies of Artex’s code available on code-sharing sites that can still be used in active attacks.

Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

articles.title: Turkish parliament approves Mecca defense pact amid Middle East war
articles.summary: Türkiye’s parliament has ratified the Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a step tied to the Yemen war and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
articles.ai_summary: Turkey's parliament has ratified a defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan amid ongoing conflicts in the Middle East.

scraped.title: Turkish parliament approves Mecca defense pact amid Middle East war
scraped.description: Türkiye’s parliament has ratified the Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, a step tied to the Yemen war and the US-Israeli war on Iran.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The Turkish parliament on Thursday evening ratified the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement signed by Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan on August 7.

Of the 279 votes in favour, 222 came from President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s Islamist Justice and Development Party (AKP), 24 from its fascist ally the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), and 25 from the Kemalist Republican People’s Party (CHP) led by Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu.

Of the 119 votes against, 60 came from the New Party, a split from the CHP, 22 from the Kurdish nationalist Peoples’ Equality and Democracy Party (DEM Party), 15 from Islamist New Path and 13 from the far-right Good Party. The Workers Party of Turkey (TİP) and the Labor Party (EMEP) each cast one vote against.

Two TİP deputies and one EMEP deputy did not take part. According to reports, 34 of the DEM Party’s 56 deputies, 30 of the New Party’s 90 and 19 of the CHP’s 44 were absent from the vote.

Speaking for the AKP, former Defense Minister Hulusi Akar said, “This agreement is in no way an alternative to NATO or anything of the sort.” According to the Associated Press (AP), Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Fuat Oktay said that Türkiye would “not be drawn into an uncontrolled process against its will.” Declaring his party’s support, the MHP’s Kamil Aydın said, “Türkiye’s place in world politics is the center.”

Speaking to the daily Milliyet , Kılıçdaroğlu said he had spoken with the foreign minister of Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, adding, “I told them as well: We want to go there not to fight but, on the contrary, to bring peace and tranquillity to the region.” He went on: “We are not supporting the [Erdoğan] government. We are supporting the state of the Republic of Türkiye.”

Murat Emir, Deputy Parliamentary Group Chair of the New Party, a split from the CHP, told parliament, “They brought this agreement to send Turkish soldiers to the deserts of Yemen,” while his party colleague Yunus Emre said, with this agreement “We will shoulder America’s burden.” The DEM Party’s Gülcan Kaçmaz Sayyiğit said of the alliance, “It is not clear whether its target is Iran, Israel or Pakistan’s rival India.”

The New Party’s objection is directed not at the alliance itself but at its timing and procedure. New Party deputy Utku Çakırözer, who asked in the parliamentary committee, “What business do we have in the deserts of Yemen?” had, in September 2025, while then a member of the CHP, presented a report to the NATO Parliamentary Assembly. This advocated a “maximum pressure” strategy against Tehran, repeated imperialist propaganda by declaring Iran the source of regional instability and proposed that NATO consider expanding toward the Middle East.

A pamphlet by Keith Jones

The Sosyalist Eşitlik Partisi – Dördüncü Enternasyonal (Socialist Equality Party – Fourth International), the Turkish section of the International Committee of the Fourth International, declared its unconditional rejection of the agreement in a video statement before the vote.

The statement explained that what the agreement would “defend” is the Saudi regime, which has opened its bases to the US war on Iran and is slaughtering the people of Yemen through bombardment and starvation, along with the reactionary geopolitical interests that the Turkish bourgeoisie seeks to advance in collaboration with US imperialism. As military spending rises and the cost of war is imposed on workers through falling wages and social cuts, it is accompanied by growing political repression in Türkiye.

The Mecca Agreement is a product of the global imperialist war bound up with the genocide in Gaza, the US-Israeli war against Iran, the Saudi monarchy’s war against the Houthi Ansar Allah movement in Yemen, NATO’s war against Russia over Ukraine and US preparations for war against China. The pact ties workers to a chain of conflicts stretching from the Eastern Mediterranean to South Asia. Under the agreement, which is modelled on NATO’s Article 5, an armed attack against one party is considered an attack on all three, and the parties may withdraw only after 10 years. Although the text contains no provision on nuclear weapons, Pakistan’s nuclear umbrella is effectively being extended over its allies.

The parties’ own statements refute claims that the pact represents an alternative to alliance with the US and NATO or a step toward independence from them. US President Donald Trump hailed the agreement as a “big, bold, and important first step,” and Turkish Deputy Foreign Minister Levent Gümrükçü described it as “complementary” to NATO. The real issue driving Washington’s three allies into such an alliance is the regional powers’ pursuit of their own reactionary interests amid the violent US-led restructuring of the oil-rich and strategically vital Middle East.

Reuters reported that the ratification in the Turkish parliament was “clearing the way for Ankara to send military support to Riyadh.” Al-Monitor , for its part, described it as a “boost to Saudi Arabia” and claimed that “any Turkish deployment is likely to be limited to training, advisory services and supplying military equipment.”

According to an AKP deputy who spoke to Reuters in October, “the mandate would be sent to parliament once a bill ratifying the accord has been approved.” Although Defense Minister Yaşar Güler said, “We absolutely do not foresee entering into any conflict with the Houthis,” the mandate will now be voted based on a collective defense commitment.

The agreement’s target is not only the Houthis but also their principal ally, Iran, against which the US and Israel launched war on February 28. In March, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Riyadh declaration, which did not condemn the US war of aggression but rather Iran’s retaliation.

On October 17, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told Al Jazeera regarding the alliance, “This is a step forward. Muslims should unite. We are ready to participate in this process.” This move by Tehran represents an attempt to ward off, from within, an alliance directed against it.

On October 26, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman, Pakistani Army Chief Asim Munir and National Intelligence Organization (MİT) head İbrahim Kalın travelled to Tehran. According to AP, the aim was “to try to avert renewed fighting in the Iran war”—that is, to prevent an escalation of the war and protect themselves by persuading Iran to submit to the demands of the US and Israel.

The bases in Saudi Arabia used in the US war on Iran became targets of Iranian retaliation in legitimate self-defence. The other Gulf regimes, too, do not want the conflict to escalate again, both because they have been targeted for collaborating with the US and Israel and because the war’s devastating economic consequences are further intensifying social anger.

The expansion of the Mecca alliance is also on the agenda. Asaad al-Shaibani, foreign minister of Syria’s new Al Qaeda-rooted regime, said in Manama on October 31, “Discussions are currently under way to evaluate Syria’s entry into the Mecca alliance,” adding, “Gulf security is an ‘integral part of Syrian regional security.’”

According to Al Jazeera , Shaibani said they support Yemen’s Saudi-backed government. Reuters reported that Damascus was considering assisting in the war against the Houthis. According to the Jerusalem Post , the Saudi and Syrian defense ministries signed a military cooperation agreement, the contents of which have not been disclosed, during a visit to Riyadh by Syria’s new “president,” Ahmed al-Sharaa, the day before the vote in Türkiye.

The agreement is sharpening the rivalry between two US allies, Türkiye and Israel. Three days after the signing in August, a senior Israeli official told Ynet , “This alliance is aimed against Israel,” adding: “The Shiite axis has weakened, and for a long time we have seen the Sunni axis getting stronger. … Israel needs to build alternative alliances, especially with the Hellenic axis, Greece and Cyprus, together with India and the United Arab Emirates.”

On August 18, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase, 70 kilometers from the Turkish border; Netanyahu’s office claimed that by permitting a Turkish military deployment at the base, Damascus was threatening Israel’s security. If Syria joins the Mecca alliance, every Israeli attack on the country could be considered an attack on all parties, bringing NATO member Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan into direct confrontation with Israel. This underscores that the Mecca Agreement, for all its “defensive” claims, is a preparation for broader wars.

The war policy confronts overwhelming popular opposition in Türkiye: In an Areda Survey poll in March, 93.2 percent of respondents said they opposed the US and Israeli attack on Iran. The political establishment and the trade union confederations, however, are doing nothing to mobilize this opposition. Their real role is to keep this social opposition, which is merging with anger over the cost of living and growing political repression, under control.

The vote in parliament has confirmed that the struggle against war cannot be waged through the political establishment. The SEP advances a socialist programme based on mobilizing the working class in Türkiye and internationally as an independent social force against imperialist war and for a Socialist Federation of the Middle East.

We call on workers and young people to build independent rank-and-file committees in workplaces and schools and to demand the cancellation of the Mecca Agreement, Türkiye’s withdrawal from NATO, the closure of US-NATO bases and a halt to oil shipments to Israel through Türkiye.

Fill out this form and we’ll contact you soon.

scraped.title: The folks behind John Wick are back with Karōshi trailer
scraped.description: Stuntman/director Chad Stahelski and 87Eleven bring us an action-packed dystopian, futuristic thriller.
scraped.h1: The folks behind John Wick are back with Karōshi trailer
scraped.body_text:
Stuntman/director Chad Stahelski and 87Eleven bring us an action-packed dystopian, futuristic thriller.

Those of us missing the John Wick universe can take heart, because Chad Stahelski—who created that franchise—is coming back early next year with a new dystopian action film. It’s called Karōshi (a Japanese term that means “death overwork”), and Lionsgate released a killer trailer that puts this film at the top of my list of “must see” movies of 2027.

Dying from working too hard is a very real phenomenon, not just in Japan and much of Asia, but also in Sweden, where some 700 workers die each year from overwork. The physical cause is usually stress-related heart attacks or strokes, as well as suicide ( karōjisatsu in Japan). Writer/director Takashi Doscher has transported that concept to a grim, futuristic corporate Manhattan, specifically a company called Ikigai Technologies. Per the official premise:

Karōshi is an action-thriller set in a near-future Manhattan, where corporate loyalty and cultural tradition have reshaped everyday life. When a mysterious outsider infiltrates a powerful company after a worker’s death, he exposes the violent system hidden beneath its polished surface.

Teo Yoo ( Past Lives ) stars as the aptly named Hiro, who is clearly out for vengeance against the offending corporation. The cast also includes Takehiro Hira, so memorable in the 2024 miniseries Shōgun , as well as Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Bill Camp, Richard Harmon, Isabel May, and Show Kasamatsu.

The trailer opens with Hira’s character lauding the contribution of Ikigai Technologies in helping shape “modern life for millions,” adding praise for employees’ “daily commitment and sacrifice.” Then we see one distraught worker deliberately falling backward to his death from the top of the company’s skyscraper. Enter our protagonist, Hiro, who suspects something more sinister is going on behind the company’s embrace of the samurai path, marked by “integrity” and “honor”—and also violence.

It’s not long before Hiro is battling all kinds of opponents in fine Wickian fashion, including using a paper umbrella to shield himself from the blood spurting from the neck of an opponent he’s just killed—a clever flourish. John Wick would be proud.

scraped.h1: Will midterm losses clear the way for MAGA’s next generation?
scraped.body_text:
Jonathan Keeperman and Jeremy Carl see a chance to rebuild with a stronger bench after the midterm losses.

After Republicans absorbed a broad midterm defeat that erased their Senate firewall and handed Democrats a large House majority, BlazeTV host Jonathan Keeperman is determined to "make lemonade out of the lemons."

The original MAGA in the 2010s and early 2020s, he says, was hugely successful because it was run by the kind of “outsiders and weirdos and misfits” necessary to “[disrupt] the political stasis.” He suggests that lasting success will require a “suite of experience” and “management skills” the early disruptors largely lacked.

Keeperman hopes the midterms, as brutal as they were, will force a hard discussion about what it will take to make the movement “sustainable” and actually “execute on these promises over the long term.”

“Can we construct an environment where, despite everything that's gone on here, we can bring on really good people, convince them to stay and build something that's durable?” he asks political data analyst Jeremy Carl.

Carl is also positive about the future of MAGA.

“I've been talking a lot with my second oldest son who's looking to maybe try to work in Washington, and what I've sort of told him is actually right now is the best time because all the time servers, all the political hacks, all those guys are going to be running for the hills,” he says.

People often forget, he says, that “the Trump movement is only a decade old in terms of its reshaping of the GOP,” and in that span of time, it’s already “cleared out so much of the dead wood.”

“Now look, in a brush fire like we just had, everything gets cleared out — the dead trees and maybe some healthier green ones,” Carl acknowledges.

Many of those dead trees, he notes, were in favor of the Dignity Act, which would have granted legal status to millions of illegal immigrants.

“I'm not trying to sugarcoat what was really, really bad, but it disproportionately hit some of the bad guys in our party, cleared them out,” says Carl.

“I had a sort of viral tweet on this, where I said, ‘Look if you're a young guy and are interested, politically motivated, there have never in my lifetime ... been as many GOP-leaning congressional seats or state House seats or whatever that are going to be out there for the taking than in this next election cycle coming up,'” he continues.

“That’s the really positive end of the vision.”

To hear more of the conversation, watch the episode above.

scraped.description: Part five of a 10-part series on British historian Hakim Adi’s book on the Communist International and Africa examines how it erases Leon Trotsky’s role in founding the International and his theory of Permanent Revolution.

scraped.body_text:
[ Part One ] [ Part Two ] [ Part Three ] [ Part Four ] [ Part Five ]

This is the fifth part of a 10-part series responding to British-based historian Hakim Adi’s recently republished book, Pan-Africanism and Communism: The Communist International, Africa, and the Diaspora, 1919–1939.

Between its Fourth Congress in 1922 and its Sixth Congress in 1928, the Communist International, founded by Lenin and Trotsky, underwent a profound political transformation. The internationalist programme on which it was founded was repudiated in favour of the nationalist doctrine of “socialism in one country”, while the emerging Soviet bureaucracy consolidated its control over the Communist parties. Adi passes over the immense political struggles through which this transformation occurred.

Indeed, Stalin enters Adi’s narrative as Lenin’s “successor” to present the Stalinised Comintern’s policies as a further development of those formulated by Lenin. [ 1 ] The description is deeply misleading. Lenin appointed no political heir, and when illness removed him from active political life, Trotsky, not Stalin, was widely regarded in the Soviet Union and internationally as the figure most likely to inherit Lenin’s leading role. Lenin’s final Letter to the Congress described Trotsky as the “most capable” member of the Central Committee, while warning that Stalin had concentrated “unlimited authority” in his hands, and proposed removing him as General Secretary. [ 2 ]

What took place was not a smooth transition between Lenin and Stalin, but a bitter struggle between the Soviet bureaucracy led by Stalin against the revolutionary internationalism defended by Trotsky and the Left Opposition from 1923 onwards, on which the Comintern had been founded.

The material foundations of the Stalinist bureaucracy lay in the isolation of the first workers’ state. The Bolsheviks took power in an economically backward country devastated by the First World War. They understood that the ultimate fate of the revolution depended upon its extension internationally, above all into the advanced capitalist centres of Europe. Instead, Soviet Russia suffered imperialist intervention, civil war, famine and enormous economic destruction. Large sections of the revolutionary working class that had made October were killed, dispersed from the great industrial centres or absorbed into the expanding state and party apparatus. The defeats of the revolutionary upsurge that swept Europe between 1918 and 1923, culminating in the German catastrophe, left the Soviet Union isolated and the working class exhausted. A growing administrative bureaucracy acquired increasing weight within the state and party. Its outlook was conservative and nationalist, reflecting its role as administrator of an impoverished state and its material interest in preserving its stability and privileges.

The theory of “socialism in one country,” advanced by Stalin and Nikolai Bukharin, gave this emerging bureaucratic layer its political programme. The enforced isolation of the Soviet Union, which the Bolshevik leadership had regarded as a grave danger to be overcome through the victory of the international socialist revolution, the Stalinists transformed into a program for constructing socialism within the borders of the USSR. This nationalist conception fundamentally repudiated the internationalist foundations of October. The struggle for world socialist revolution ceased to provide the strategic orientation for Soviet policy, and the international communist movement was increasingly subordinated to the national requirements of the Soviet bureaucracy.

Trotsky and the Left Opposition fought against this nationalist turn, insisting on the inseparable connection between the fate of the Soviet Union and the victory of the international socialist revolution. The Stalinist apparatus responded with systematic repression: supporters of the Left Opposition were removed from leading positions, denied access to the party press, subjected to administrative reprisals, and eventually expelled. Trotsky was expelled from the Communist Party in November 1927 and deported to Alma-Ata in January 1928.

The suppression of the Left Opposition was the necessary condition for the bureaucratic transformation of the Comintern. The emerging Soviet bureaucracy could not establish “socialism in one country” as the governing doctrine of the Soviet party and the International while permitting an organised Marxist opposition which fought for the programme of world socialist revolution.

Leon Trotsky (1879-1940), was the co-leader of the 1917 Russian Revolution, socialist opponent of Joseph Stalin, founder of the Fourth International, and strategist of world socialist revolution.

For the colonial and semi-colonial countries, the nationalist transformation in the Comintern had fatal consequences. Trotsky’s theory of Permanent Revolution rejected the conception that the democratic and national tasks of the revolution required the proletariat to submit to bourgeois leadership: in countries of belated capitalist development, the struggle against imperialism, landlordism and national oppression could be carried through only under the independent leadership of the working class, drawing the peasantry behind it and extending the revolution internationally. The Stalinist doctrine assigned to the national bourgeoisie in oppressed countries a potentially revolutionary role, in a separate democratic stage, opening the way for the political subordination of Communist parties to bourgeois nationalist organisations.

In China, this programme was put to a decisive test, an experience that Adi’s book excludes.

The Chinese Revolution of 1925–27 developed amid an immense mobilisation of workers and peasants against imperialist domination, warlordism and capitalist exploitation. In May 1925, after British-commanded police opened fire on workers and students in Shanghai, killing demonstrators and wounding dozens, a strike wave swept the country. Approximately 400,000 workers participated in some 125 strikes, accompanied by mass protests and the Canton–Hong Kong general strike, in which around 100,000 workers left Hong Kong and organised a boycott of British goods.

By 1927, the revolutionary movement had reached enormous proportions. In Shanghai, hundreds of thousands of workers joined a general strike and armed insurrection, defeated the warlord forces and seized control of much of the city. Across Hunan, Hubei and other provinces, millions of peasants entered associations, challenged landlord power and began establishing organs of local authority.

The democratic tasks of national unification, liberation from imperialist domination and agrarian transformation were becoming bound up directly with questions of class power. The central issue was whether the working class would establish its own leadership over the revolutionary movement or remain politically subordinated to the bourgeois Kuomintang.

The Comintern leadership under Stalin and Bukharin insisted that the Chinese Communist Party be subordinated to the Kuomintang. The latter was presented as the political expression of a revolutionary “bloc of four classes”—workers, peasants, the petty bourgeoisie and the national bourgeoisie—united in a common anti-imperialist struggle.

Trotsky and the Left Opposition opposed this policy. They warned that the Chinese bourgeoisie feared the revolutionary movement of the workers and peasants more than it opposed imperialism, and that the independence of the Communist Party was indispensable to the victory of the revolution.

These warnings were confirmed catastrophically in April 1927, when Chiang Kai-shek turned against the Shanghai working class and carried out the mass repression of Communists and militant workers. The Stalinist leadership then transferred its political orientation to the supposedly left-wing Kuomintang government in Wuhan, which likewise turned against the Communist Party and the revolutionary workers’ and peasants’ movement.

The Chinese Revolution was the most important practical test of Comintern policy towards bourgeois nationalism in a colonial and semi-colonial country. Its defeat occurred barely a year before the Sixth Congress of 1928. But Adi excludes this experience from his discussion of the Congress and its colonial programme.

The omission becomes more glaring because the Kuomintang does appear in Adi’s account. In his discussion of the International Congress against Colonial Oppression, held in Brussels in February 1927—barely two months before Chiang Kai-shek’s massacre of the Shanghai working class—Adi presents it as an important achievement because it brought together an extraordinarily heterogeneous collection of political forces. These included communists, the Indian National Congress, representatives of the British Labour and Independent Labour parties, nationalist movements from Africa and Asia, and the Kuomintang. Among them were Jawaharlal Nehru of the Indian National Congress, later the first prime minister of independent India; Messali Hadj, who would become a central founder of modern Algerian nationalism; and J. T. Gumede of the African National Congress, the party that has ruled South Africa since 1994.

Adi writes:

The great significance of the Brussels Congress was that it brought together those who were struggling for national independence in Asia and Africa, those in Latin America and elsewhere who were determined to safeguard their sovereignty, as well as representatives of organisations in the imperialist countries that had a critical attitude towards colonialism or were opposed to it. Both the Indian National Congress and the Guomintang [Kuomintang] government in China were represented, as were the British Labour Party and Independent Labour Party. Representatives from China, India and Britain, including British Communists, even signed a joint resolution against “suppression and intervention in the colonial countries.” [ 3 ]

Thus, in February 1927, Kuomintang representatives joined Communists in declarations against imperialism. Barely two months later, in April, Chiang Kai-shek’s forces massacred the revolutionary workers of Shanghai. This was a brutal demonstration of the Stalinised Comintern’s role in providing revolutionary credentials to bourgeois nationalist tendencies that would turn savagely on the working class.

The principal outcome of the Brussels Congress was the establishment of the League Against Imperialism (LAI) which Trotsky would later denounce as a “second-line Kuomintang on the international scale”. [ 4 ] Yet Adi moves from the broad anti-imperialist alliances of Brussels and the LAI to the Sixth Congress without confronting any of the practical consequences of this disastrous political line.

It was Trotsky, and the Trotskyist movement that would extract the central lesson from the Chinese catastrophe: the national bourgeoisie could come into conflict with imperialism while remaining violently hostile to the independent mobilisation of the working class. As Trotsky explained:

The question of the nature and the policy of the bourgeoisie is settled by the entire internal class structure of a nation waging the revolutionary struggle; by the historical epoch in which that struggle develops; by the degree of economic, political, and military dependence of the national bourgeoisie upon world imperialism as a whole or a particular section of it; finally, and this is most important, by the degree of class activity of the native proletariat, and by the state of its connections with the international revolutionary movement.” [ 5 ]

Trotsky’s conclusion from the Chinese experience was categorical: “For fear of the masses the bourgeoisie subsequently deserts the revolution.” [ 6 ]

To be continued

Op. cit., p. 7.

Leon Trotsky, “The Krestintern and the Anti-Imperialist League” (1930). Available at: https://wikirouge.net/texts/en/The_Krestintern_and_the_Anti-Imperialist_League

Ibid., p. 208.

Ibid., p. 213.
