scraped.title: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
scraped.description: Ian Winter allegedly confronted a reporter outside court who had investigated the comedian.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Brand's barrister refers himself to regulator after report he confronted journalist
scraped.body_text:
Ian Winter, left in this court sketch, reportedly verbally clashed with a reporter who had previously investigated his client

Russell Brand's defence barrister has referred himself to the regulator after reports that he confronted a Sunday Times journalist who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023.

In a Times and Sunday Times podcast on Thursday, Rosamund Urwin said she introduced herself to Ian Winter KC outside court after verdicts were delivered.

She claimed he responded with a "snarl" and said "I hope you're pleased with yourself".

"Apparently I said, but I can't actually remember this but I've read it in reporting, 'I am pleased that justice has been done'", Urwin said.

She said that Winter replied "it wasn't" and suggested she was to blame using a profanity.

In a statement, Winter said the "ways matters have been characterised" in the media meant they should be "subject to proper scrutiny".

On Friday, Winter said he considered his professional duty required him to self-report the allegations to the Bar Standards Board.

The Bar Standards Board regulates barristers in England and Wales in the public interest.

In a statement, Winter said: "Having seen the ways matters have been characterised in today's press I consider my professional duty requires me to self-report those allegations to the Bar Standards Board, so the matter can be subject to proper scrutiny. I have made such a report."

Four women variously accused Brand of rape, sexual assaults and emotional abuse in a joint investigation by Channel 4 Dispatches and the Times and Sunday Times in September 2023.

The actor and comedian denied the allegations.

Ian Winter, pictured here in 2014, reported himself to the regulator

On Thursday, he was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week trial.

None of the women who featured in the media investigation were the complainants from Brand's criminal trial.

During a pre-trial hearing in October, Brand tried unsuccessfully to have his criminal case thrown out.

His lawyers argued that the actor and entertainer could not receive a fair trial because of the publicity following the Channel 4 Dispatches, Sunday Times and Times programme.

Prosecutors opposed Brand's application to have his case stopped.

Brand is also being investigated over two more rape allegations made by two other women.

Court documents from a hearing at London's Southwark Crown Court, held before Brand's criminal trial, suggest one of the women was 16 at the time of the alleged offence and appeared in a Channel 4 documentary. Brand has denied the allegations.

This video can not be played

Brand faced further questioning from officers in July 2025

On Friday, Metropolitan Police Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations against Brand.

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark praised the "bravery" of the women who reported their allegations to police and gave evidence during the trial.

He said police would "do everything we can to bring to justice the powerful people who are responsible for probably the most ghastly moment in your life" when sexual assault allegations are made to them.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been asked about Labour's past association with Brand .

Some party figures sought his support more than a decade ago, before police began investigating him.

At the time, Brand had gained a following for his left-wing political punditry.

Then Labour leader Ed Miliband was interviewed by Brand shortly before the 2015 election, and in 2014 Burnham publicly backed Brand during a row over claims about the comedian's housing arrangements.

At the time he said it was "depressing to see media mission to discredit someone who stops playing their game" and urged Brand to "keep going".

Speaking on Friday, Burham said: "It's not always the case that people know everything about people in public life."

He described Brand's crimes as "horrific" and said he had been rightly held to account, adding: "I had no idea of the full extent of what he was doing."

Brand is being held in custody ahead of his sentencing on Monday.

After the jury returned its verdicts, Mr Justice Bennathan told him to expect a "significant custodial term".

scraped.body_text:

A project of Common Dreams

Next week, the U.S. Senate is set to debate and vote on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) ( S. 5653 ), a compromise permitting reform deal. Ahead of the planned vote, David Arkush, director of Public Citizen’s Climate Program, issued the following statement:

“We appreciate the effort and care Senators Whitehouse and Heinrich put into reaching a compromise to facilitate the buildout of desperately needed clean energy and protect ratepayers from Big Tech’s voracious data center binge. The bill’s provisions on transmission and ratepayer protections are strong and sorely needed, and they ought to be enacted. Unfortunately, the bill’s drawbacks are greater, more immediate, and more certain.

“The bill seriously weakens the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act and guts the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act. It fast-tracks the permitting of all manner of projects, then makes it virtually impossible to regulate or arguably even enforce existing rules against them, without an act of Congress. Among other effects, the bill will open the door to a vast increase in exports of liquefied natural gas and facilitate a hasty and reckless buildout of data centers powered by fossil gas. And the bill would make it significantly more difficult to moderate, regulate, or alter these actions later, regardless of what public health , climate destruction, or public sentiment demand. The bill also includes massive giveaways to the mining industry.

“There is also the question of President Trump’s implementation. We do not trust that he will abide by the letter or intent of the law. Regardless of what the law says, we expect him to spend two more years on his reckless and costly fossil-fuel building spree while working to block clean energy. Under BAAJA, his actions will form most of the baseline by which courts assess whether future administrations are discriminating against a given form of energy.

“In the November 3 elections, voters across the country resoundingly rejected data centers. This is not the time to pass a bill that enables Big Tech to charge forward with them, powered by fossil fuels , over the objection of local communities.

“No less important, the makeup of Congress will change substantially in January. It is likely a much better deal can be reached then—one that enacts the laudable and important provisions in this bill, and more, without so many sacrifices.”

Public Citizen is a nonprofit consumer advocacy organization that champions the public interest in the halls of power. We defend democracy, resist corporate power and work to ensure that government works for the people - not for big corporations. Founded in 1971, we now have 500,000 members and supporters throughout the country.

scraped.h1: Meghan Markle’s father Thomas Markle arrested by FBI in Florida
scraped.body_text:

Meghan Markle’s father was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material .

Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades, according to the FBI .

Markle Sr. is charged with one count of possession of child pornography and expected to make his initial appearance Friday in United States District Court in the Middle District of Florida in Tampa.

“Mr. Markle is accused of possessing child sexual abuse material, including photographs depicting himself with minor girls,” said First Assistant United States Attorney Bill Essayli. “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

FBI Director Kash Patel said that an investigation revealed that Markle Sr. was “in possession of child sexual abuse material.”

“Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida. This FBI will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids – any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country or anywhere they try to hide,” Patel added.

“This case highlights the importance of the involvement of the public, even if it’s a family member or close friend, to be vigilant and speak up if they have information on individuals they suspect may be preying on and exploiting our children,” said Patrick Grandy, the Assistant Director in Charge of the FBI’s Los Angeles Field Office.

FBI special agents searched two storage units registered to Markle Sr., who has rented the units in Los Angeles since 2008, with his most recent payments on both made last month by auto-pay, according to the FBI.

Inside the units, agents seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books that contained suspected child sexual abuse material.

If convicted, Markle Sr. would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison, according to the FBI.

Markle Sr.’s arrest comes after The Sun , a British tabloid newspaper, reported that Meghan’s half-brother allegedly found images while cleaning out the home of their father in the Philippines.

Meghan’s father denied the allegations against him in a statement to the Daily Mail , saying, “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me.”

“I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of,” he added.

The Duchess of Sussex said she was “deeply distressed” by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her estranged father’s former home.

“I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed,” Meghan said in a statement to The Associated Press.

She also addressed a letter sent to the Metropolitan Police Service’s Royal and Specialist Protection unit.

“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan Police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated,” she continued.

Meghan went on to say that she has not had a relationship with her father to protect her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5.

“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them,” Meghan said. “I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.”

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children,” her statement concluded.

Thomas Markle Sr., 82, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had his left leg amputated. That forced him to return to the U.S., The Associated Press reports.

The Sun alleged that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., had recently found “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sex abuse images in boxes at his father’s home in the Philippine city of Cebu when he was clearing out the property.

He told the newspaper that he reported the alleged images to police in the Philippines.

Markle Jr., 60, told the outlet that he contacted FBI investigators in the U.S. who are reportedly set to launch their own probe.

“The FBI is aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of U.S. law,” an FBI spokesperson told Global News in October.

Last week, British police said they would refer allegations about Meghan’s father to overseas law enforcement agencies, after a review ‌found the claims had not been passed to other authorities when they were first received in 2019.

London’s Metropolitan Police said it had received a letter in January 2019 in ​which the author said they “were writing to raise concerns relating to the security of the Duchess of Sussex.”

“While the letter did not actually contain any information specifically related to security matters, it did contain a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom,” the Metropolitan police said in a news release .

“The letter was assessed and subsequently passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness. The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies,” said Metropolitan Police’s Protection Commander Adam Slonecki.

Slonecki said that an internal review had led to the matter being referred to the police watchdog and that the force was now sharing the allegations with overseas authorities.

“In recent days, the Met’s Directorate of Professional Standards has carried out an initial review into our actions following receipt of the letter in 2019,” Slonecki said.

“Following that review, a voluntary referral has been made to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in respect of the decision not to inform other law enforcement agencies and the decision to pass the letter to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex,” he said.

“In addition, it is our intention to make a number of referrals to relevant overseas law enforcement agencies in relation to the allegations contained within the letter. That process is underway and will be completed in the coming days,” Slonecki added.

scraped.title: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as Trump's civil rights chief after Democrats sweep Congress
scraped.description: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as DOJ Civil Rights Division chief after Democrats' midterm victories, following a controversial tenure.
scraped.author: Peter Kerich
scraped.h1: Harmeet Dhillon resigns as Trump’s civil rights chief after Democrats sweep Congress
scraped.body_text:
The DOJ official stepped down just two days after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate, setting the stage for increased scrutiny of Trump's administration.

Harmeet Dhillon , the head of the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division, submitted her resignation Thursday, November 5, following the Republican Party’s losses in the 2026 midterm elections.

Attorney General Todd Blanche confirmed that he had accepted her resignation in a statement on X, praising Dhillon for what he described as her commitment to defending civil liberties and enforcing the law. Dhillon also reflected on her tenure, calling the position the “honor of a lifetime.” In her farewell statement, she highlighted efforts to challenge diversity, equity and inclusion programs and oppose transgender participation in women’s and girls’ sports.

Her departure comes just two days after Democrats secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, setting the stage for increased congressional scrutiny of the Trump administration. During her leadership, the Civil Rights Division underwent a significant restructuring, with its enforcement priorities shifting toward issues central to the Trump administration’s agenda.

The division pursued legal action against universities over alleged discrimination, filed lawsuits seeking access to voter registration records in 30 states and Washington, D.C. It also brought a criminal case against former CNN journalist Don Lemon and protesters following a demonstration at a Minnesota church. Federal judges dismissed 27 of the lawsuits seeking state voter registration records, according to NBC News.

Dhillon’s departure prompted criticism from civil rights advocates and former Justice Department officials. Kristen Clarke, the NAACP’s general counsel and former head of the Civil Rights Division under President Joe Biden, accused Dhillon of abandoning federal civil rights enforcement responsibilities. Clarke said Dhillon had “abandoned cases, purged the work force and weaponized the Division to target institutions to achieve illegitimate, partisan goals.” Stacey Young, executive director of Justice Connection, also criticized Dhillon’s leadership

The resignation comes at a significant political moment as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress. Dhillon, a longtime Republican election lawyer, had also maintained a visible presence in conservative media while promoting the administration’s civil rights agenda.

scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

I am headed back West this morning (I am at a remarkable conference on community and data centers. More about that next week.)

To read more articles by Mark Trahant, go to: Marktrahant.substack.com .

A bit of news: Mary Peltola, Yup’ik, is on track to win the Alaska Senate seat. She has a small lead now and the uncounted ballots that remain favor her (significantly). The count still may go to Ranked Choice Voting but she should win on a second tally.

From Alaska Survey Research:

“AK SENATE UPDATE: There are still 70,000 votes yet to be counted. The vast majority are absentees and early votes. Peltola will win these VERY easily. The biggest vote count will happen 11/10. The outcome will become clear then.

“Peltola will likely win in Round 2, when Daniel J Sullivan is eliminated.”

Peltola will give the Democrats at least 55 seats and Mississippi remains contested so the number could climb again to 56 seats. And that’s before jockeying. (For example: What if Lisa Murkowski left the Republican Party, and shifted at least to an independent? That would give her — and Alaska — more of a say in the next Congress.)

Your contribution is appreciated.

We should expect legal challenges from Republicans in both Alaska and Mississippi. (Mississippi has no provisions for a recount, so that could be interesting.) But the whole narrative about “will Peltola be seated?” was buried election night.

Another election watch: Former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez in one of the last undecided races in the House. He and Rep. Eli Crane, the Republican incumbent, continue to go back and forth as votes come in from different regions in the district.

From the Navajo Times:

“Republican incumbent Eli Crane led former Navajo Nation President Jonathan Nez by 966 votes Wednesday afternoon in Arizona’s 2nd Congressional District race, a margin narrow enough to trigger an automatic recount if it holds through the official canvass.

“Unofficial results posted by the Arizona Secretary of State’s Office at 3:15 p.m. showed Crane with 138,582 votes, or 49.28%, and Nez, a Democrat, with 137,616, or 48.94%. Libertarian Curtis Goodwin had 4,848 votes, or 1.72%.

“The lead changed during election night and early Wednesday. An earlier state update showed Nez ahead by 86 votes, 136,344 to 136,258.

“Between the two updates, Crane gained 2,324 votes and Nez gained 1,272. Most of those gains came from Yavapai County, where Crane’s total rose from 63,132 in its 4:31 a.m. report to 65,453 at 3:15 p.m. Nez’s total increased from 38,582 to 39,826.

“State law requires an automatic recount when the margin between the top two candidates is one-half of 1% or less of the votes cast for both. Based on Wednesday afternoon’s totals, that threshold was about 1,381 votes. Crane’s lead was about 0.35%.”

scraped.author: Levi Rickert
scraped.h1: Native Voters Challenge Unequal Voting Districts in Blaine County, Montana
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

Three Blaine County voters have filed a federal lawsuit challenging the county’s commissioner district map, alleging that population disparities violate the constitutional principle of one person, one vote and dilute the voting power of Native American residents.

Three Blaine County voters have filed a federal lawsuit challenging the county’s commissioner district map, alleging that unequal population distribution across the three districts violates the Fourteenth Amendment’s Equal Protection Clause and diminishes the voting power of Native American residents.

Represented by the UCLA Voting Rights Project (VRP) and Helena-based Upper Seven Law, the plaintiffs are seeking a new district map that ensures equal representation among Blaine County voters.

The lawsuit centers on the constitutional principle of “one person, one vote,” which requires electoral districts to have roughly equal populations so that each resident’s vote carries comparable weight. According to the complaint, Blaine County’s current map creates significant population disparities, leaving its most populous district with substantially less voting power per resident than its least populous district.

Your contribution is appreciated.

District 1, which is 94.9% American Indian, is reportedly overpopulated by 16% and contains nearly 700 more residents than District 2, the county’s smallest and predominantly white district. District 2 is underpopulated by 12%, according to county figures cited in the complaint.

As a result, the plaintiffs allege that approximately 1.32 votes in District 1 carry the same electoral weight as one vote in District 2, creating an unequal distribution of political representation.

“The weight of a person’s vote should not depend on which side of a district line they live on,” said Sonni Waknin, senior voting rights counsel at the VRP. “Blaine County’s map goes against the principles of our representative government. We are asking the Court to enforce the Constitution and require districts that give voters an equal voice in their county government.”

Longtime Blackfeet voting rights activist Tom Rodgers (One Who Rides His Horse East) draws parallels between the loss of Native American voting rights and the historical injustices inflicted on Indigenous peoples.

“Their ancestors took our land, they took our children, they destroyed our spiritual sustenance, the bison. They have always stolen our vote and thus now is the time for a moral and legal reckoning,” Rodgers told Native News Online.

Blaine County adopted its district-based commissioner system in 2002 after a federal court determined that the county’s previous at-large election system diluted American Indian voting strength. However, county officials have since interpreted that earlier ruling as requiring the preservation of the districts’ racial composition.

The plaintiffs argue that this interpretation is incorrect and that the county’s 2024 redistricting plan retained boundaries established in 2013 despite population changes. According to the complaint, those decisions have perpetuated and worsened population disparities between districts.

Molly Danahy, litigation director at Upper Seven Law, emphasized the importance of equal representation in local government.

“The right to vote is the starting premise of our free society–it ensures that we, the people, can hold our government accountable to the rule of law,” Danahy said. “Districts that violate the basic principle that every vote should count the same are unconstitutional. Blaine County’s Commissioner map must distribute power equally among its voters.”

The plaintiffs are asking the federal court to declare the current district map unconstitutional, prohibit its use in the 2028 elections and any subsequent elections, and require the county to adopt a new plan that equalizes district populations.

The defendants include Blaine County, its county commissioners and county election officials.

Read the filing here.

scraped.title: Why Is Healthiness Right-Wing Now? Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, Larissa Phillips on being a MAHA mom. Plus: The best of our midterms coverage.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Friday, November 6. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large. Today: How Democrats won red states. Everything you need to read about the midterm elections. And much more.

But first: When did caring about your health become right-wing?

The tribal affiliations of the beliefs you hold dear can switch so fast that it gives you whiplash.

This is something many of today’s politically homeless Americans have learned through experience in the last decade or so. “I’ve heard my fellow refugees from the left say they have the exact same beliefs they’ve always held—about immigration or crime or biological sex—but somehow, these days, expressing them gets us labeled as Republicans or fascists,” writes Larissa Phillips in today’s essay.

And so it was interesting to watch in the run-up to this week’s midterm elections how some Democrats dialed back the rhetoric that so disappointed the nation’s normal lefties. For example, “James Talarico said it was ‘cringey’ that he once said God is ‘nonbinary’—and became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in Texas since 1988,” writes Larissa. Even progressives reached out across the aisle. “Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez privately met with the archetypal MAHA mom, Zen Honeycutt, then started talking about pesticides.”

If this is a sign of good political strategy, it’s also an illustration of how fickle a movement’s orthodoxy can be. In today’s essay, Larissa writes that as a left-wing mom in Brooklyn in the 1990s, it was perfectly acceptable not to give her baby certain vaccines—and to complain to the school about ultra-processed foods. A few years ago, she watched, confused, as these things became the preserve of Trump-voting women.

“I bristled a little—but not because of MAHA,” she writes. She was glad Republicans were objecting to food norms. “But the more the right has claimed this territory, the more the left seems to have let it go.” Once upon a time, the Democrats were the party of holding Big Agriculture and Big Food and Big Pharma to account. Now, it is the tribe that sneers at people who genuinely want to do their own research, because they dare to feel disillusioned with public-health authorities.

With the MAGA-MAHA alliance falling apart, perhaps the left can reclaim good health. For now, Larissa is “missing the spirit of the old left.”

—Freya Sanders

At the end of an enormous news week, we want to take stock of what just happened, and re-up some of our reporting and writing about the day when the American electorate delivered a clear rebuke to Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

On election night in 2024, when Trump defeated Kamala Harris and pulled off the political comeback of the century, Eli Lake delivered the definitive take on “ How Trump Won .” This Tuesday, Eli returned with a follow-up: “How Trump Blew It.” You can tell the story of the last two years in those two pieces. Read Eli’s election night report here:

As the shock waves from Tuesday night spread, we asked Free Press regulars for their first reactions, from Niall Ferguson on why Trump couldn’t escape political gravity to Caitlin Flanagan on the Democrats’ miraculous revival. And Victor Davis Hanson drew five lessons from the wipeout, the biggest of which may be how much we still don’t know.

If one explanation rises above the rest, Michael Brendan Dougherty argued, it’s the war with Iran. Trump ran on ending wars, then launched one. It’s a scenario Michael warned about in our pages over a year ago, and his account of how it unfolded is essential reading.

How did election night go down on the ground? For that, we turn to Olivia Reingold and Noah Bernstein . They were at the victory parties for Democrats in the two most closely watched states this cycle: Michigan and Texas, respectively. Read Olivia’s report from Abdul El-Sayed’s headquarters and Noah’s dispatch from the room celebrating when the Lone Star State turned blue.

Trump may own much of the blame, but Ross Douthat wrote that the new right, the conservative movement that rose after 2016, deserves its share, too. It set out to shape Trump’s second term around border security, American industry, and restraint abroad. Instead, the new right overreached on deportations, delivered data centers instead of factories, and couldn’t stop war in Iran.

As for the winners, Joe Klein said that Democrats should take their governing cues from the “quiet competence” of the moderate candidates along Interstate 35, the highway running from the Texas border up through Kansas, Iowa, and Minnesota, where the party notched some of the most surprising wins of its sweep. What did those candidates get right, and can the rest of the party follow their lead?

That’s just some of what we put out this week. And we’ll be bringing you much more on what the next two years hold in the coming days. But for now, TGIF and have a great weekend.

So hysterical that MAHA, getting medical advice from memes and TikTokers, was considered "Healthiness."

There has never been any such thing as a "progressive principle". The only thing that "progressive" has ever meant is "Saying that what we want is 'progress' and all opposition isn't." That's it.

The original progressives' top cause was opposing democracy. Then they were eugenicists. They have been all over the map.

Well, except for ever loving free markets or America.

scraped.body_text:

Investors fled to the safety of bonds on Friday as stocks extended their slide in both Europe and Asia after worries around the AI boom wiped trillions of dollars off the major U.S. indexes.

Europe’s FTSEurofirst and STOXX 600 benchmarks both fell more than one per cent early on as traders continued to fret that the Democrats’ victory in this week’s US midterm elections will lead to tougher rules around AI data centres.

Wall Street saw a modest bounce early Friday, especially for the Nasdaq later after its trillion-dollar plunge on Thursday, although that did not comfort Asia overnight.

Japan’s Nikkei and South Korea’s KOSPI both slumped about six per cent. For the Nikkei – as for Wall Street – that was the deepest one-day drop since U.S. President Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” trade tariff panic of April 2025.

Taiwan plunged more than eight per cent at one point, before cutting losses as authorities scrambled to stem the selling.

“This has been brutal,” James Athey, a fund manager at investment firm Marlborough in London, said, explaining that retail and hedge fund selling were feeding off each other.

“The question is where we go now? We are still looking at indexes that are near record highs and a sector (AI) where capex is still massive. So I think it is going to be a huge test of market sentiment – and the belief in AI – in the coming days.”

The strain on equities meant government bond markets continued to rally, while the U.S. dollar, Japanese yen and Swiss franc all lured safe haven flows in the currency markets.

The yield on the benchmark U.S. 10-year Treasury note was at 4.84 per cent in Europe, hovering near the lowest level since Sept. 9.

The ten-year Japanese government bond yield dropped as much as nine basis points overnight to 1.795 per cent, the lowest since June 30. Triple A-rated German bunds then saw yields dip to 3.22 per cent, their lowest level since late August.

“Bonds are increasingly behaving like bonds again, with income re-emerging as the primary driver of returns and restoring their traditional diversification benefits,” said Masahiko Loo, chief fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management.

“This looks more like a reassessment of AI policy risk than a reassessment of the AI cycle.”

A near 1.5 per cent rise in Nasdaq futures and a dip in Wall Street’s VIX “fear gauge” pointed to some respite for U.S. markets Friday.

Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosasaid on Thursday that the state – which already has a large share of U.S. data centres – will introduce new laws around them to protect local residents.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq went on to slump 5.5 per cent on Thursday – or US$2.5 trillion. Some $3 trillion was also wiped off S&P 500 firms, with investors worried the brakes will be applied to the AI boom more broadly.

“It’s actually a bit of a disaster,” said Christopher Forbes, head of Asia and Middle East at CMC Markets.

“All night, all day – we had client margin calls, client complaints … because it’s a very emotional thing, right? People are wedded to their positions and views on a stock or outcome and you’re telling them, look, you’ve just lost money.”

The jitters are hitting an AI trade already on shaky ground due to fears that the massive cost of the data centres and other infrastructure will limit future returns – the meltdown has been spurring margin calls and spooking retail investors and hedge funds alike.

Some of Asia’s authorities stepped in overnight to try to soothe nerves.

South Korea temporarily eased rules on retail investors’ leveraged investments and multiple sources told Reuters that Taiwan’s Ministry of Finance called senior executives at state-owned banks, instructing them to support the market.

Taiwan stocks closed down 4.5 per cent, recovering somewhat from their early morning slump. For the week though, the index clocked a 12.2 per cent dive, its biggest since 1991, LSEG data showed.

Korean AI chipmakers also trimmed some of their losses although still closed sharply lower. In Japan, tech investor SoftBank slid 11 per cent, with the cost of insuring its debt against a default jumping to its highest in four years.

“After damage like the sort we’ve been facing, it is difficult to think that we simply can bounce from here,” said Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers.

“We may be oversold in the short term, but the underlying questions and causes can’t simply be wiped away.”

scraped.title: Iran War Day 252: Trump Promises Decision on New Strikes ‘Very Soon’ as Iran Hits More Tankers
scraped.description: State of the Union: The president also called Qatar’s Emir to discuss ending the war.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
On Thursday, President Trump told reporters he was close to a decision on whether to restart strikes against Iran. “I would prefer not to destroy what is left of the country, if possible,” the president said, “but I may have to do so. You will know very soon.” This is the first time Trump has touted the possibility of new strikes since the GOP’s stunning midterm losses earlier this week, which many read as a referendum on the war and its economic consequences.

Three tankers attempting to transit the Strait of Hormuz were reported hit Friday morning. Iran’s IRGC said two of the tankers had struck mines while attempting to use “unauthorized” routes to cross the Strait. Iran also claimed to have shot down a U.S. drone over Qeshm Island on Friday.

Also on Friday, President Trump held a phone call with Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, during which the two leaders reportedly discussed the potential for a diplomatic resolution of the conflict.

Oil prices continued to ease Friday, with Brent crude opening just under $99 per barrel. AAA reports that the average price of regular gasoline in the United States is $4.07 per gallon, and the average price of diesel is $6.23 per gallon.

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/carlos-mureithi
scraped.h1: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
scraped.body_text:
Paul Mackenzie convicted over deaths of children and one adult after followers were ordered to starve themselves and their families

The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.

His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.

In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.

Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.

The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.

In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.

Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.

Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.

Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism , which he has denied.

Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

Reuters contributed reporting

scraped.title: Trump installs Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
scraped.description: President Trump announced Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as his chief of staff, the most significant shakeup of his team since the midterms.
scraped.h1: Trump installs Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 6, 2026 / 2:52 PM EST / CBS News

Washington — President Trump announced Friday that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, the most significant shakeup of his team since Republicans' losses in the midterm elections .

"I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026," the president wrote on Truth Social . "Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff — She has done a great job!"

Wiles submitted her resignation to the president on Thursday night, a U.S. official and a senior White House adviser told CBS News. Wiles' resignation was tied to Republican midterms defeats, according to three sources familiar with the matter. It was unclear if her deputies would remain at the White House.

Miller has been one of Mr. Trump's closest and most loyal aides for years. He has a broad portfolio in the White House, including as the architect of the president's immigration enforcement and deportation program. Wiles ran Mr. Trump's 2024 presidential campaign and has been his chief of staff since his first day back in the White House.

"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles posted on X. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together from securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First. More than anything, I'm grateful for the extraordinary people I've had the privilege of working alongside. While my role may be changing, my commitment to the president and the mission never will."

Mr. Trump's decision to install Miller as chief of staff represents a doubling down on his approach to governing, despite voters' widespread rejection of his and congressional Republicans' agenda on Tuesday.

Miller is loathed by Democrats on Capitol Hill who see him as the driving force behind some of the president's most hardline policies. The president has said in recent days that he thinks he can work with the incoming Democratic leadership, but Miller's elevation in the White House could lay the groundwork for a much more confrontational relationship.

Top Democrats quickly denounced the move and vowed to ramp up the pressure on Miller once they take control of Congress in January.

"Donald Trump learned nothing from his historic defeat," Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said on X . "Stephen Miller is the architect of the most barbaric, inhumane policies of this administration. Trump couldn't have made a worse choice. Our Democratic majorities will fight him every step of the way."

Rep. Robert Garcia, who is in line to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Miller "should lawyer up."

"Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct, and we will fight against his hateful policies in Congress and the courts," Garcia said in a statement.

In mid-October, before the elections, the president dismissed the idea that he was interested in making a change with his chief of staff.

"It's fake news," Mr. Trump said. "I could not be more happy with Susie."

scraped.title: Top Ukrainian official expresses "restrained optimism" about eventual Putin-Zelenskyy meeting ahead of trilateral talks
scraped.description: Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February.
scraped.h1: Top Ukrainian official expresses "restrained optimism" about eventual Putin-Zelenskyy meeting ahead of trilateral talks
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

November 6, 2026 / 2:52 PM EST / CBS News

KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week

Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down . In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.

"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."

"These negotiations are not the last," he said.

Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.

"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.

The meeting follows several weeks of strain in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship. In October, President Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to supply diesel to the United States for the first time since 2022. Elon Musk's SpaceX also imposed limits on Ukraine's Starshield satellite networks, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and some air-defense systems, before reinstating access weeks later.

Despite these developments, Budanov said he is optimistic about Ukraine's relationship with the United States heading into the trilateral meeting next week.

"Look, it's bad. It shouldn't be like that," Budanov said of the Starshield failures. "But along with that, we can remind you that this situation is resolved in one way or another. This gives optimism for the future."

The trilateral meeting comes as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Strikes this week hit energy facilities in 10 regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and cut water to much of Kyiv for more than 16 hours.

Budanov, speaking from his office in the capital, said Russia was using the strikes to create political pressure on Kyiv.

Russia's goal is "to cause the maximum damage to our critical infrastructure," he said. "What they hope to do is to create a foundation for social dissatisfaction, for street protests, and to stifle the national interests. But this will not happen."

articles.summary: The razor-thin margin between GOP Sen. scraped.title: No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
scraped.description: The razor-thin margin between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the U.S.
scraped.h1: No one knows how many ballots are outstanding in Mississippi's Senate race
scraped.body_text:
Miles Parks

Two Madison County election commissioners inspect an affidavit ballot envelope on Thursday in Canton, Miss. The state's razor-thin U.S. Senate race is shining a spotlight on Mississippi's election processes. Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images hide caption

In Mississippi's too-close-to-call U.S. Senate race, every ballot matters.

But no one can say for sure how many ballots there are left to count.

The razor-thin margin between incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democratic challenger Scott Colom is shining a light on an election process in Mississippi that is among the slowest and most decentralized in the country.

"Mississippi is not a model of election administration," said Michael Morse, a law professor at the University of Pennsylvania who studies voting.

As of midday Friday, fewer than 2,000 votes separated the two Senate candidates. But information about exactly how many ballots were outstanding was hard to come by.

Loading...

The Colom campaign said late Tuesday it was aware of more than 15,000 provisional ballots , which require verification before they're counted. And the chair of the state Republican Party said Thursday he thought there were 20,000 outstanding ballots, including potential absentee votes that can legally be received by officials until Nov. 10 if they were postmarked by Election Day.

Mississippi's top voting official, Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson, said counties run their own elections, and even his office didn't know how many provisionals were left to count. He said Thursday nearly 7,000 of them had been processed, with "roughly 80% of them being accepted."

"Until we have the certified results, the individual counties will be the best source of the latest and most up-to-date information," Watson said in a statement. There are 82 counties in Mississippi, and they are not required to transmit election results to the state until next week.

Morse said he was shocked by the lack of good information available for such a high-profile race.

"Right now I would love to know a lot of things about the process and I am struggling to figure out what is unfolding here," Morse said. "I cannot tell you basic things."

What is becoming clear is that the rate of provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi, may end up being among the highest in the country this election cycle. Those ballots are cast by people whose eligibility is questionable, according to local officials, so those votes are segregated and officials decide on a case-by-case basis whether they will be counted.

If the Colom campaign's estimate of 15,000 affidavit ballots holds true, that would represent roughly 1.5% of the total ballots cast in the Senate race, according to unofficial results.

In the last midterm year, 2022, just four states had a provisional ballot rate higher than that, according to federal data . And Mississippi looks to have a provisional rate close to double of that in North Carolina this year, based on the preliminary data in both states.

One potential reason is an in-the-weeds detail on how Mississippi does voter registration.

In most states, when voters don't cast ballots over a certain number of election cycles, or local officials come across data that indicates a voter has moved or is ineligible for some other reason, they move that voter to what's known as "inactive" status . But the voter is still able to vote normally for a period of a few years, mandated by federal law, before they either confirm their eligibility or are eventually removed.

Mississippi is one of the few states that makes those "inactive" voters have to vote provisionally. That means those voters need to fill out another form and their information needs to be reviewed after the fact by local officials before their votes are counted.

It's unclear at this point why so many voters had questionable eligibility when they showed up to vote, although the local outlet Mississippi Today has reported extensively on the state's experimental use of credit data to cull voter lists.

Morse said that list maintenance technique is garnering attention, but it's not the whole story.

"It's pairing the experiment with credit data, which could introduce some unreliability, with an undermining of the typical procedural process [in many other states], where a voter [marked "inactive"] could cast a regular ballot for at least the next two federal general elections," Morse said.

Watson, the Republican secretary of state, has already come out in defense of the state's registration process.

"The extra few minutes it may take to vote via affidavit ballot are well worth the election integrity added by having cleaner voter rolls!" Watson wrote Tuesday in a post on X .

But Kathy Boockvar, the former Democratic secretary of state of Pennsylvania, told NPR that while many people who have to vote with a provisional ballot are likely to be ultimately deemed eligible, the process doesn't breed trust from those who have to interact with it.

"It feels like you have to go talk to the teacher or something in the back room," Boockvar said. "It's a little bit of a suspicious-seeming thing because somebody who's going through it generally thinks that they're eligible to vote and feels like they're being asked to do something other than that."

Boockvar added that the fact that information has been so hard to come by is a sign Mississippi hasn't been in the limelight like traditional battleground states before.

"We all have to be prepared whether we expect it or not," Boockvar said. "Transparency and good data is one of the best solutions we have to combating all the suspicion and distrust."

articles.summary: Capitol Hill leadership elections pit Hakeem Jeffries against progressive dissent while Steve Scalise and Jim Jordan battle for GOP minority leader. And the changes are going to be seismic.But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what ma...

scraped.title: Reporter's Notebook: A user’s manual to upcoming leadership elections in the House and Senate
scraped.description: House and Senate leadership elections loom as Hakeem Jeffries, Steve Scalise, Jim Jordan, Chuck Schumer and John Thune face caucus and conference votes.
scraped.author: Chad Pergram
scraped.h1: Reporter's Notebook: A user’s manual to upcoming leadership elections in the House and Senate
scraped.body_text:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset . Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions . Legal Statement . Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG .

Several newly-elected Democratic senators suggest they are not committed to supporting Sen. Chuck Schumer as Senate Majority Leader. Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Democratic Party’s priorities and leadership plans as Congress prepares to return to session.

Internal party House and Senate leadership elections are some of the most fascinating exercises which unfold on Capitol Hill. Both House and Senate Democrats and House and Senate Republicans will choose their leaders in the coming days. And the changes are going to be seismic.

But not everyone is on board with heir apparent leaders. That’s what makes this process so intriguing.

However, there are only two rules in leadership elections: You can’t beat someone with no one. And, perhaps more importantly, it’s about the math.

PROGRESSIVES FUME AT HAKEEM JEFFRIES FOR SAYING DEMOCRATS WON'T 'GET EVEN' WITH TRUMP

A voter casts their ballots at a polling location inside the Lincoln Depot Museum, in Peekskill, New York, US, on Saturday, Oct. 24, 2026. The 17th Congressional district is one of the few that was carried by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 but is represented by a Republican in the House, making it a prime target for Democrats seeking to pick up a seat and potentially flip control of the House. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

There are some progressives and DSA-affiliated Democrats who will be House Members next year who want someone other than House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y. Who? Well, no one has said. Again, you can’t beat someone with no one. And frankly, it’s hard to believe that Democrats would not elect the first Black Speaker of the House.

But drill down on the math.

For the sake of argument, let’s say Democrats have 260 House seats in the new Congress. First, Democrats must tap a nominee for Speaker in their Caucus. That needs a simple majority. So surely Jeffries will score at least 131 votes in a private ballot for Speaker.

The Speaker of the House is the constitutional officer for the legislative branch of government – much like the president is for the executive branch and the chief justice of the United States for the judicial branch. Thus, the ENTIRE House votes for Speaker when it convenes the new Congress at noon on Jan. 3.

There are 435 Members. If all Members cast ballots, Jeffries simply needs 218. Jeffries could lose 40 votes or so and still prevail. So that is not going to happen. It might not even lose more than a couple votes, frankly.

Now let’s look at the GOP and their case for Minority Leader. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , R-La., is running against Rep. Jim Jordan , R-Ohio. If Democrats have 260 seats, Republicans would have 175. All INCOMING House Republicans (including non-voting delegates from U.S. territories) are allowed to vote in CONFERENCE. The selection of Minority Leader does NOT go before the entire House like Speaker. So, the winning candidate only needs a simple majority. That would be 88.

The same for the race between House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, R-Minn., and Rep. August Pfluger, R-Texas, for Minority Whip.

MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS

House Majority Whip Tom Emmer, a Republican from Minnesota, during a television interview at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Sept. 30, 2025. Emmer has introduced a bill that would denaturalize convicted fraudsters of their U.S. citizenship. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The Senate Democratic Caucus and Republican Conference works much the same way as the House. A simple majority wins for Majority Leader in the Democratic Caucus and Minority Leader in the Republican Conference. However, the selection of Senate Majority Leader is not a vote which plays out on the floor. The concept of "Senate Majority Leader" has only been around since the early 20th Century and is not mentioned in the Constitution. Remember what we said about the House Speaker being the head of this branch of government.

It would be hard to envision a scenario where Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., would not become Majority Leader after Democrats flipped the Senate in a beat down.

First, who else is running? Well, Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, is very popular among Senate Democrats. But he’s running for Majority Whip to succeed retiring Senate Minority Whip Dick Durbin, D-Ill. One could see Democrats defaulting to Schatz is something happens with Schumer.

Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed , D-Mich., has said he wants to look at his options and as endorsed Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., for Majority Leader. But Van Hollen isn’t running. Sen.-elect Annie Andrews, D-S.C., told colleague Bret Baier she wants a "generational change" in leadership. Sen.-elect Troy Jackson, D-Maine, and Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton, D-Kan., both said they would oppose Schumer.

FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR, FIRST BLACK FEMALE GOVERNOR: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS MAKE HISTORY

Maine Democrats picked progressive former state lawmaker Troy Jackson as their new US Senate nominee, giving them another shot at the crucial race after previous pick Graham Platner dropped out. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

But again, you can’t beat someone with no one.

Here’s the math: Let’s say Democrats do win Mississippi and Alaska, giving them 56 senators who caucus with the Democrats. All Schumer needs is 29 Democrats to support him in Caucus and he’s the next Majority Leader.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There has not been as much rumbling about the future of Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D . Heretofore, President Trump has not called for new leadership in the Senate. But Senate Republicans would choose Thune or anyone else on a secret ballot in the Senate GOP Conference. A simple majority would win. If Republicans are down to 44 seats, the winner would just need 23 votes.

Chad Pergram currently serves as Chief Congressional Correspondent for FOX News Channel (FNC). He joined the network in September 2007 and is based out of Washington, D.C.

scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Things have officially gone from bad to worse for Meghan Markle’s dad in connection with his child sex abuse material investigation. Here’s the latest updates.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

Photo by MEGA/GC Images; Aaron Chown/PA Images via Getty Images

Things are continuing to go downhill for Meghan Markle’s father, Thomas Markle Sr. , in the aftermath of his child sex abuse material investigation. Now, more details about his new arrest and what the FBI has found have been released.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told the AP that federal agents searched two Los Angeles-area storage units that Markle had been renting since 2008. Once inside, they “seized approximately 78 items, including slides, film negatives, and books” that had child sexual abuse images.

Per an official FBI affidavit, the feds were tipped off about the U.S. storage units after learning about other images and videos depicting child sexual abuse on Markle Sr.’s electronic devices that were reportedly found at his former home in the Philippines and the national police investigation that followed.

Related: New Developments in Child Sex Abuse Material Allegations Against Meghan Markle’s Father

As a result of those findings and this new search, Markle Sr. was arrested outside of Tampa, Florida, and charged with “one count of possession of child pornography,” per NBC 6 Miami. He’s expected to appear in court at some point on Friday. If convicted, he faces 20 years in federal prison.

In response to the arrest, Essayli said in a statement: “These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law.”

FBI Director Kash Patel also commented on the arrest: “Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions. The agency will use every single resource at our disposal to protect innocent kids— any predator who targets children will have zero safe haven in this country, or anywhere they try to hide.”

As we previously told you, the Duchess spoke out about the allegations against her father when her half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr., contacted authorities in the Philippines after allegedly discovering images and videos depicting child sexual abuse on their father’s electronic devices at his former home. In her statement, she said she was “deeply distressed” by the news and expressed hope that justice would be served. Markle Sr. has denied the allegations, calling them lies and “bullsh*t.”

scraped.title: Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
scraped.description: Pope Leo begins his first South American tour since lung cancer surgery. The 12-day journey takes him to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, where he spent two decades.
scraped.h1: Pope Leo begins a 12-day, 3-country South America tour after his cancer surgery
scraped.body_text:
Carrie Kahn

A mototaxi pass drives past a banner of Pope Leo XIV at Pimentel beach in Chiclayo, Peru, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, ahead of his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from Nov. 6 to 17. Martin Mejia/AP hide caption

MONTEVIDEO, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV has arrived in South America for a 12-day, three-country journey that will be his longest and most far-reaching trip yet, and his first major overseas visit since undergoing lung cancer surgery.

Along the way Leo will take 12 flights, including two helicopter rides, give 36 speeches and visit 10 cities including Cusco, Peru, which sits more than 11,000 feet above sea level. Even the heartiest of travellers can experience altitude sickness there and may require supplemental oxygen.

Last month, Leo underwent surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Vatican officials say he has completed his two-week recovery period and requires no further treatment.

The Vatican's new communications chief Maria Montserrat Alvar said the pontiff was eager to begin his journey. "His doctors are very confident and he'll have plenty of medical care on board should something happen," she said.

It's a puzzling choice for the first leg of the pope's anticipated return to South America, where he spent two decades in Peru, first as a missionary then as Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo. Uruguay, a small nation of around 3.5 million people, where adoring crowds will be small, is famously Latin America's most secular nation.

When asked why go to Uruguay at all, given the high rate of atheists and strict separation of church and state, Communications Chief Alvarado answered simply, "Why Not?" Adding, "the Gospel is meant to go everywhere."

Few welcome banners are seen throughout the capital Montevideo, except for large posters of a waving Pope Leo adorning city churches. A huge banner drapes down the facade of the Blessed Sacrament Church, in Montevideo's upscale Pocitos neighborhood, where 70-year old retiree Ana Maria Saprissa was heading for quiet prayer.

We are thankful, agradecida , she says that the pontiff is coming to visit. "His visit gives us such joy because …he remembered us all here in this tiny country that has so many needs," she said.

Uruguay's tradition of separating religion from government and public life dates back more than a century. Christmas has long been officially referred to as Family Day, while Easter week is given the vacation-friendly name Tourism Week.

Only about a third of Uruguayans identify as Catholics and even less say they practice the religion, according to political analyst Mariana Pomiés , director of the public polling firm CIFRA.

But as a practicing Catholic, Pomies says sometimes Uruguayan and especially officials misinterpret what secularism is. "Secularism is not anti-religion, it's the neutrality of the state in religious matters. But here the neutrality se convirtió en un absoluto… it became an absolute."

A vendor sells scarves featuring Pope Leo XIV's image ahead of his arrival in Montevideo, Uruguay, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Matilde Campodonico/AP hide caption

Dozens of volunteers cleaned streets, mowed lawns and erected a simple stage outside the tiny brick Our Lady of Guadalupe Church. It's the focal spot for many in the Casavalle neighborhood, a working-class city about a half hour north of Montevideo, where the pope is scheduled to visit on Saturday.

"I am very happy, very glad, very grateful … that eyes have been set here," where many are forgotten and stigmatized, said Father Pablo Coimbra who's served as the community's pastoral leader for the past six years

"For the first time many people live their lives always on the margins, on the margins of opportunities, of possibilities, of the future, on the margins of a loving gaze... well, today they are in the heart, in the center," he said.

A proposed papal address to the parliament triggered a swift rebuke from the public and politicos alike and was quickly scrapped. However, Uruguay's left-wing President Yamandú Orsi will oversee a welcome ceremony outside Montevideo's main cathedral, where Leo will later celebrate evening prayers, vespers with church leaders and laypeople.

Sunday mass will take place in Florida, about an hour outside the capital, a town replete with Catholic and national pride. Every Nov. 8, church goers commemorate the Virgin of the Thirty-five, a symbol of Uruguay's independence movement from the Brazilian empire in 1825.

By Sunday, Pope Leo will be in neighboring Argentina, fulfilling a wish of his predecessor, Pope Francis, who had hoped to return to his homeland but never made the trip.

Before his death, Francis had said he didn't want a papal visit to become entangled in Argentina's intensely polarized politics.

Pope Leo's visit to Argentina offers an early test of how he will address the Catholic Church's differences with right-wing populist leaders gaining ground across Latin America. Those tensions have also surfaced in the U.S., where Leo has clashed with President Donald Trump over immigration and the treatment of migrants.

Far-right President Javier Milei's sweeping austerity measures, which have pushed millions of Argentines into poverty, could put him at odds with Leo, who has long championed the poor.

Milei has also embraced data centers and a largely unfettered approach to artificial intelligence regulation, while Pope Leo's inaugural encyclical called for ethical caution and safeguards to protect human dignity in the age of AI.

The upper section of a statue of Pope Leo XIV is transported to 'El Niño' park in Callao, Lima, Peru, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, where it will be installed ahead of his planned trip to Uruguay, Argentina, and Peru from Nov. 6 to17. Guadalupe Pardo/AP hide caption

The final leg of the trip will take Leo back to Peru in what has been billed as a homecoming.

As a missionary priest and later appointed Bishop of the coastal city of Chiclayo, Pope Leo spent two decades in the country. He became a naturalized Peruvian in 2015, and has said the country shaped his life more than anything else.

He will visit several cities and towns where he lived and will meet with President Keiko Fujimori, the daughter of former Peruvian dictator Alberto Fujimori.

As a priest during the Fujimori dictatorship, Leo was openly critical of military violence and human rights abuses and supported efforts leading to Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission following the return to democracy.

But for many Uruguayans Pope Leo is not very well known. Walking past the huge stage set up for Leo's welcoming ceremony, Juan Martin Guerreiro said he wasn't sure he would attend the pope's speeches.

"He doesn't feel as influential to me … as Pope Francis," said Guerreiro. But he said he's willing to give the new pope a chance because he is South American.

When reminded that Pope Leo was born in Chicago, Guerreiro said he wouldn't hold that against him.

scraped.title: Essential Books to Read for Hip Hop History Month
scraped.h1: 15 Essential Books to Read for Hip-Hop History Month
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Hip Hop has come a long way, from its birth in the Bronx to one of the most influential cultures worldwide. For this Hip Hop History Month, we have recommendations for the best books to learn about the origins of this cultural force.

By

Mahalia Otshudy

Published

American rapper, songwriter, record producer, and actor LL Cool J, performs on stage in Boston, Massachusetts in December 1985. (Photo by John Nordell/Getty Images)

November is Hip-Hop History Month, and we are celebrating the culture born in the Bronx that has become one of the world’s most recognized musical and artistic movements. From masters of lyricism to breakdancing and street style, hip-hop remains one of the most influential forces across the globe. What better way to explore its legacy than by diving into books filled with vivid memories and facts about how the genre grew to become such a powerful cultural force?

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

We’ve rounded up some essential reads to add to your collection this Hip-Hop History Month.

J Dilla was one of the most iconic hip-hop producers, and “Dilla Time” by Dan Charnas is a biography that delves into his rise from an underground mastermind to a revered name in the culture with his innovative beats that helped define a new, unique sound.

Many of our favorite head-banging hip-hop tracks incorporate samples drawn from songs ranging from legendary hits to rare finds. In “Bring That Beat Back,” Nate Patrin traces the origins of sampling and explores how it became a defining art form within rap music.

Related: Why The No Limit Records Reunion Means Everything to Hip Hop Culture

Let Grandmaster Flash take you on a musical journey in “Birth of a Culture,” where he narrates the beginnings of hip-hop—a movement he helped pioneer through his DJing innovations and creative vision—culminating in the genre’s landmark anthem, “The Message.”

When discussing hip-hop history, conversations often default to legendary male artists. But we can’t forget the trailblazing women who worked just as hard to move the culture. In “The Motherlode,” Clover Hope highlights these revolutionary women and illustrates why they deserve equal acclaim.

The backstory behind every iconic moment, song, and album in the genre—from its genesis to the present day—is explored in Chuck D’s deep dive into hip-hop history. If you are looking for a comprehensive schooling on how rap became so revolutionary, sit down with this book and prepare to learn.

Queen Latifah paved the way for women rappers to dominate the mainstream, evolving into a powerhouse mogul—a monumental feat for a young woman from Newark, New Jersey. In her autobiography, Queen Latifah shares the unfiltered story of her rise from neighborhood royalty to a true monarch of hip-hop.

Hip-hop and fashion have always gone hand in hand. “Fresh Fly Fabulous” chronicles the vibrant, head-turning style pioneered by rap icons such as Slick Rick, LL Cool J, and many more across multiple decades.

“Sweat the Technique” is the definitive guide every burgeoning lyricist needs to elevate their pen game. Rakim breaks down the creative framework he uses to craft sharp rhymes that stick with folks long after the beat fades. From his five pillars of creativity to behind-the-scenes stories, this book offers actionable insights to hone your songwriting.

In “Hip Hop is History,” six-time Grammy Award-winning artist Questlove delivers a sweeping breakdown of the musical phenomenon. He examines the legendary and overlooked moments that shaped the culture into a global force.

Tricia Rose provides an academic analysis of the politics, origins, and themes driving rap music in “Black Noise.” She illustrates how the genre empowered Black folks to voice critiques of contemporary society set to a compelling rhythm that people could not ignore.

In “The Tao of Wu,” Wu-Tang Clan co-founder RZA shares the philosophical wisdom gained from an extraordinary life—from forming one of the world’s most famous hip-hop groups to becoming one of the industry’s most influential leaders.

For a firsthand account of how breakdancing became a core pillar of hip-hop, look no further than Richard “Crazy Legs” Colón. As a pioneer of the dance form, Crazy Legs shares fascinating stories and rare archival imagery that place readers directly into hip-hop’s earliest days.

As a writer on Netflix’s hit series “The Get Down,” Nelson George brings incredible historical insight to his work. In “Hip Hop America,” George chronicles how hip-hop evolved from a vibrant underground culture into a globally celebrated art form.

If you watched and loved the 2016 biopic “Straight Outta Compton,” add “Parental Discretion Is Advised” to your reading list. Functioning as a literary time machine, Gerrick D. Kennedy digs into the deepest archives to deliver the definitive story of how N.W.A came to be and birthed gangsta rap.

Rounding out the list is “The Come Up” by Jonathan Abrams. The New York Times bestselling author compiled hundreds of interviews conducted over three years with hip-hop’s key figures. To understand how the culture was built from the ground up, there is no better way to learn than directly from the pioneers themselves.
