scraped.title: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
scraped.description: Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/rachel-savage
scraped.h1: ANC faces bruising defeat in South African local elections with 80% of ballots counted
scraped.body_text:
Former liberation movement’s share of national vote almost 14 percentage points below 2021 result

The African National Congress is on course to suffer a bruising defeat in South Africa’s local elections, with the once dominant party of Nelson Mandela falling to under a third of the vote nationally with more than 80% of ballots counted.

Wednesday’s fragmented vote marks another stage in the decline of the ANC, which has led national governments since the end of white minority apartheid rule in 1994. High unemployment, crime, corruption and poor local service delivery have all contributed to voters turning away from the party .

The former liberation movement is projected to lose its status as the biggest party in the two most populous provinces, Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal, as parties began coalition negotiations behind closed doors. The final results are expected to be announced on Sunday.

The ANC was on 31.8% of the vote nationally, almost 14 percentage points below its 2021 local election result. The centre-right, white-led Democratic Alliance (DA) had 24.1% of the vote, while the uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) party of the former ANC president Jacob Zuma was on 9.3%.

Turnout also rose in Wednesday’s poll. The election commission estimated that 54.5% of registered voters cast their ballot, up from 46% five years ago.

The final shape of coalitions in some of the country’s biggest cities remained unclear with the final votes still being counted. Senior figures in key parties said they would talk with almost anyone, while keeping negotiating strategies under wraps.

In Johannesburg, South Africa’s commercial capital and biggest city, with 4.8 million people, voters have had to contend with regular water and power cuts , uncollected rubbish and potholes. The municipality, which has seen 10 changes of mayor in the last decade amid unstable coalitions, has admitted to a 220bn rand (£9.9bn) infrastructure spending backlog.

With just over half of votes counted in Johannesburg, the DA was leading with 40%, having run an energetic campaign under Helen Zille, a 75-year-old former Cape Town mayor. The ANC, which leads the current coalition, was in second place on 17.5%. ActionSA, a rightwing party led by Herman Mashaba, was on 15.5%. Mashaba has pledged never to work with Zille, whom he calls “racist”, something she vehemently denies.

Many of the ANC’s township strongholds have yet to report full results. The Council for Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR), a respected thinktank, has projected the DA will finish with 34%, the ANC 20% and ActionSA 16.8%.

Coalitions in Gauteng’s three city municipalities are often negotiated together. The DA is leading in all three.

Sign up to The Long Wave

Nesrine Malik, Micha Frazer-Carroll and the team guide you through the biggest Black stories from around the world

after newsletter promotion

The MK party, led by 84-year-old Zuma as he continues to weather and deny numerous corruption allegations, is expected to displace the ANC as the largest party in KwaZulu-Natal. Founded in 2023, it mixes socially conservative Zulu nationalism with pledges to redistribute land and wealth from white to black South Africans.

With half of votes counted in eThekwini municipality, which contains Durban, the MK had 41%, meaning other parties could form a coalition to keep it out of power. Meanwhile, the DA is projected to maintain its majority in Cape Town, despite growing middle-class anger over rising housing costs .

Voters choose a local councillor and a party, with seats allocated via proportional representation. Councillors will then have two weeks to elect mayors and form municipal governments.

scraped.title: Wiz Khalifa Avoids Prison Time in Romania Case...For Now
scraped.h1: Wiz Khalifa Avoids Prison Time in Romania, Here’s Why He’s Still Not In the Clear
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Wiz Khalifa finally gets his happy ending in his legal case in Romania. But the good news may not last for too long thanks to a new twist.

By

Shanelle Genai

Published

US rapper and singer Wiz Khalifa attends the premiere of Amazon MGM Studios’ “Madden” at the Culver Theatre in Culver City, California, on November 4, 2026. (Photo by Lisa O’CONNOR / AFP via Getty Images)

There’s finally some good news related to Wiz Khalifa ‘s legal drama in Romania. Unfortunately for him, though, his good deal may not last as long as he’d like. Let’s break it down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

On Thursday, it was announced that the “See You Again” rapper would not have to serve his nine-month prison sentence related to his December 2025 conviction on charges of illegal possession of a risk drug after he brought weed into the country and was subsequently investigated for allegedly smoking it while onstage during a performance at the Beach Please festival in July 2024, per Vice News. In May 2026, Khalifa was added to Romania’s most wanted list, making international travel and touring complicated.

Related: You Won’t Believe The Ironic Reason Wiz Khalifa Was Arrested in Romania…Or Maybe You Will

However, nearly a year later, a judge in the case decided to annul the decision, overturn the conviction, and strike the occurrence from the record. But in a twist the rapper didn’t see coming, Romania’s DIICOT (Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism) has decided to appeal the ruling and has opted to go through the process of trying Khalifa again in court, according to VICE.

This means that while the “Black and Yellow” rapper may be a free man now, he may end up behind bars once DIICOT returns to court in early November 2026. The investigation is still open, and it doesn’t mean that Khalifa’s been acquitted. But it does mean that he has a little room to breathe easy before things heat back up again.

As we previously told you, video footage of Khalifa smoking a joint onstage and getting arrested at the festival went viral at the time, with fans voicing their concerns about how things were going to play out. In the immediate aftermath, he did sound remorseful about the incident, writing in a post on social media then : “Last night’s show was amazing. I didn’t mean any disrespect to the country of Romania by lighting up on stage. They were very respectful and let me go. I’ll be back soon. But without a big ass joint next time.”

Here’s hoping that statement will help him avoid prison for a second time.

articles.title: Neocons Are Desperate To Blame The GOP Midterm Wipeout On Everything But Iran
articles.summary: They blame tariffs, corruption, immigration enforcement–anything but the one obvious thing: the Iran war and its associated costs.
articles.ai_summary: Neoconservatives are accused of attributing the GOP's midterm losses to various factors while avoiding responsibility for the Iran war's impact.

scraped.title: Neocons Blame Midterm Wipeout On Everything But Iran
scraped.description: They blame tariffs, corruption, immigration enforcement — anything but the one obvious thing: the Iran war and its associated costs.
scraped.author: John Daniel Davidson
scraped.h1: Neocons Are Desperate To Blame The GOP Midterm Wipeout On Everything But Iran
scraped.body_text:
They blame tariffs, corruption, immigration enforcement–anything but the one obvious thing: the Iran war and its associated costs.

Neocons sprang into action this week amid the fallout from Tuesday’s historic Republican defeat in the midterms, pushing a theory of the election that’s completely divorced from reality. Their basic argument is that it wasn’t the costly and unpopular Iran War that turned voters against President Trump and the GOP, it was tariffs, corruption, candidate quality, ICE raids — nearly anything you can think of besides the war, which they are still defending amid the smoldering wreckage of the Republican Party.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board, a champion of the war from the beginning, went after Vice President J.D. Vance this week for a lengthy X post on Wednesday in which Vance rightly cited the war as the primary cause of the Republican midterm disaster.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance wrote. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

The WSJ editors are not interested in an honest conversation. They criticized Vance for not mentioning corruption and tariffs as major reasons for Republican losses. Tariffs in particular is a familiar refrain among all those who pushed for the Iran war. The problem is, public opinion on tariffs doesn’t show what the neocons say it shows. After Trump’s “liberation day” tariffs were enacted on April 2 of last year, Trump’s approval rating dropped from 47 percent down to about where it was during the best times of his first term, about 40 percent, which is Trump’s baseline on economic management.

The entire tariffs talking point is just a tactic to distract from the Iran War and its costs and shift the conversation to something else. Dana Loesch went even further than the WSJ and claimed that Iran and Israel weren’t even a top four concern for voters , that instead it was the economy, cost of living, and tariffs. But that’s not what exit polling shows. Loesch in particular was widely mocked on X for her inability to correctly read exit polls that showed three out of four voters said the Iran war was a “crucial or major factor” in their vote for Congress.

There’s also a dim-witted sleight-of-hand being employed here. Loesch and other neocons keep citing “cost of living” as a major reason for voter discontent with the GOP. But of course the number one cost of living indicator is gas prices (because people are reminded of gas price hikes every time they fill up). Ordinary people are not going to respond to a poll question about their major concerns by saying “the Strait of Hormuz is closed.” But the closure of the strait, a direct result of the war, is of course the cause of the cost of living increase that they do cite.

This entire debate is deeply dishonest. The war was never popular, was never sold to the American people, and nothing about it was ever going to be easy or clean. Neocons like Mark Levin and Marc Thiessen went out and argued that the regime in Tehran would collapse and that there would be no downsides to attacking Iran.

What happened was what anyone could have predicted: gas prices spiked, the regime didn’t fall, and the American public soured on the whole thing. Instead of acknowledging those realities, the neocons spent most of this last year arguing that we only need two more weeks of bombing Iran to win the war, like some sick parody of Anthony Fauci’s “two-weeks-to-stop-the-spread” during Covid.

Were there other factors that contributed to voter discontent with Trump and the GOP? Yes, of course. But the overwhelming factor, the thing that caused the president’s approval to crater going into these midterms, wasn’t tariffs or corruption or immigration enforcement. It was the war and the costs that the war imposed on the American people. They were especially angered by higher gas and grocery prices because no one in the Trump administration even tried to make a case for the war before they started dropping bombs on Iran. Moreover, they felt betrayed by a president who ran, in part, on a promise not to start new Mideast wars.

Now that communist Democrats have flipped a bunch of states blue and taken control of Congress, it would be nice if we could have an honest conversation about what went wrong. But the people most responsible for this catastrophe insist on gaslighting the American people and blaming the loss on things that are, at best, secondary factors.

As Vance said, if they think the war was worth an historic GOP midterm defeat, that it was worth losing control of the Senate for the next six years at least, then just come out and say that. Make a case for it. But they won’t — just like they never really made a serious case for going to war against Iran in the first place.

articles.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
articles.summary: The behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution also helped elevate him, writes the BBC's media editor Katie Razzall.
articles.ai_summary: The behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution also helped elevate him, writes the BBC's media editor Katie Razzall.

scraped.title: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
scraped.description: The behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution also helped elevate him, writes the BBC's media editor Katie Razzall.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: How 2000s lad culture helped Russell Brand to hide in plain sight
scraped.body_text:
Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault

Warning: This article contains graphic descriptions of sexual acts

No British celebrity navigated the cultural changes of the early 21st Century better than Russell Brand.

His life has been one long personal rebrand.

He morphed from provocative stand-up comic to TV star and Hollywood actor. He became a YouTuber and political activist, taking up left-wing causes around issues of inequality in the 2010s, then Covid conspiracies and in 2024 supporting Donald Trump for president. That same year he was baptised as a Christian in London's River Thames.

Now he has a new persona to try on: convicted rapist.

On Thursday, the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault at Southwark Crown Court , following a three-week trial.

As he faces jail, it's clear that the behaviour that formed the backdrop to Brand's prosecution is the same behaviour that helped elevate him in the first place.

Brand performing at the MTV Video Music Awards a year after his memoir was published

Brand shot to fame as a sexually outrageous libertine whose risque humour thrilled audiences.

He cultivated the image of an insatiable, shameless womaniser. Sex, drugs and excess were central to his comic material.

Over the decade of his offending, Brand sold out stand-up comedy venues and theatres, broadcasters - including MTV, Channel 4 and the BBC - started to throw money at him.

With his backcombed hair and drainpipe black jeans, Brand regaled audiences at his stand-up comedy gigs with the graphic details of his sexual exploits: anal sex, prostitutes and orgies.

He simulated masturbation and sex on stage. He said he liked oral sex with women "where it goes in their neck a little bit" and their "mascara runs a little bit," acting it out on stage.

Even Brand's own barrister called the humour "a product of its time," reminding the jury in the trial that this graphic sexualised comedy was viewed as "radical and different" back then.

Barely a generation later, many will view it as deeply rooted misogyny dressed up as humour. But these were different times.

Back then lads' magazines ruled - with their covers and double page spreads full of topless glamour models and half-naked female celebrities

The late nineties and early noughties in Britain were an era that celebrated casual sexism and often elevated celebrities who espoused it.

In 1999, FHM projected a naked photo of the Scottish TV presenter Gail Porter on to the Houses of Parliament. She only found out when she saw it on the news, and spoke later about how it deeply affected her mental health.

What might now be termed toxic masculinity was often deemed funny, seen by some as good old-fashioned male humour. By others it was viewed as palatable because they believed it was being done with an apparently ironic eyebrow raise.

"There is no question he was a very talented stand-up," says Sarah Ditum, author of Toxic: Women, Fame and the Noughties. "There was an appetite for taboo breaking.

"I think it looks very old hat if you look back on that stuff. It's dated horribly and I don't think many people are going to be keen to defend Brand's act now knowing that it reflected his real world behaviour rather than an ironic performance."

My Booky Wook topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007

But there were clues at the time that his outrageous stage act did not stop when the show ended - most publicly in his 2007 bestselling memoir, My Booky Wook.

"I'm a bloke from Grays with a good job and a terrific haircut who's been given a Wonka ticket to a lovely sex factory 'cos of ol' fame."

Of course, many of his sexual partners consented. As his defence barrister told the jury "he devoted himself for many years to a highly promiscuous life", reminding them that "having lots of sex is completely lawful".

My Booky Wook, which topped the Sunday Times bestseller chart for seven weeks in 2007 and sold 600,000 copies in hardback in the UK, opens with him checking into a clinic for sex addiction. He writes about going to lap dancing clubs and having "a lot" of oral sex in toilets and many threesomes.

"The rules change when you're famous. In that case two is often better than either none or one."

He writes about how an MTV PR "reminded me that I put lap dances and prostitutes on her gold card and got the hotel to give me cash on her account without her prior knowledge".

The Observer called it "a scandalous, libidinous memoir that is better written and more entertaining than any number of celebrity autobiographies that clog the shelves".

Heat said: "You come away from the book feeling like you really know - and like - the real Russell."

You can't imagine a celebrity these days writing a memoir in which he claims that at stage school a primetime actress, whom he names, "kissed me once in a corridor" and for years afterwards he'd tell people "'I had sex with her… And by sex, I mean bumming'".

But it's all told in a jokey, revelatory way, by "a bloke from Essex who likes birds with big bottoms and big boobs…. Lovely dolly-birds".

Meeting crowds backstage in Sydney in 2010

In light of his offending, writing that was celebrated for being frank, honest - and very funny - now looks anything but.

People "are willing to mistake irony and self-awareness for truth telling and trustworthiness," says Ditum. "The idea that he made these jokes about being this kind of sexual monster was supposed to convince you that he wasn't actually a sexual monster in real life."

Did normalising his behaviour allow him to hide in plain sight? Were the media companies who embraced him, the comedy venues who promoted him, the audiences who laughed at his humour, in some way complicit?

A former TV boss who didn't want to be named explained the thinking of his peers like this: "You've got this charismatic presenter who appears to be very, very good and you don't want to lose that.

"The women who were being persecuted didn't feel empowered to speak up and the few who did feel empowered might have been classed as troublemakers but certainly weren't really listened to because you didn't want to lose the star. That was the process."

Indeed, in Brand's trial, one of the complainants told the court she didn't report what had happened to her because she didn't think she would be believed in "those laddish culture times".

"It was my word against his," she said in her evidence.

Jo Caulfield, a contemporary of Brand's on the early noughties stand-up circuit, says she initially found him "utterly charming" but she sees that he was "enabled and nobody will say anything against it".

"People have people around them, promoters, assistants in TV. It's in the hierarchy of TV. If a runner [an entry-level production assistant] goes to his dressing room and he gets his knob out, it's like, 'oh, come on, don't make a fuss.'"

And while safeguarding standards have been heavily tightened in some parts of the entertainment world, she says it "still goes on".

"Nobody wants to upset the star. This person is making them money so everybody down the food chain better not say anything if they behave badly," says Caulfield.

At the end of My Booky Wook, Brand writes "I have done some terrible things over the course of this booky wook… I mean, over my life."

We now understand quite how terrible.

scraped.title: US attorney tasked with leading 'grand conspiracy' probe into Trump's foes resigns from DOJ
scraped.description: Jason Reding Quinones, the U.S. attorney tasked with leading a sweeping and controversial conspiracy probe targeting President Trump’s foes, has resigned from the DOJ.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: US attorney tasked with leading 'grand conspiracy' probe into Trump's foes resigns from DOJ
scraped.body_text:
Jason Reding Quinone has stepped down, along with the DOJ's John Eisenberg.

Jason Reding Quinones, the South Florida-based U.S. attorney tasked with leading a sweeping and controversial conspiracy probe targeting President Donald Trump's foes, has resigned from the Justice Department, Attorney General Todd Blanche announced Friday.

Blanche also announced that John Eisenberg, the top official overseeing the Justice Department's National Security Division, had resigned from the department.

Reding Quinones and Eisenberg are the second and third high-level DOJ official to depart the Trump administration following Democrats' historic midterm wins, following Thursday's resignation by Trump ally Harmeet Dhillon from the department's Civil Rights Division.

Reding Quiñones is also the latest among several Trump-allied attorneys to step away from the so-called " grand conspiracy " probe launched by the DOJ to examine whether intelligence officials and other government actors organized in a criminal effort to violate President Trump's civil rights dating back to his 2016 campaign.

While the probe has ensnared numerous targets of President Trump in behind-the-scenes legal wrangling over subpoenas and grand jury testimony, it has thus far led to no criminal indictments in what sources have said is a source of frustration for President Trump and other top DOJ officials.

Reding Quinones' departure was seen as a foregone conclusion in recent weeks, according to sources, after DOJ leadership admonished him in private meetings for his lack of progress in the grand conspiracy investigation and his frequent trips to Washington, D.C.

"We are grateful for Jason's leadership in combatting violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime," Blanche said in a social media post announcing Reding Quinones' departure.

Eisenberg was previously one of the central figures in the Ukraine scandal that led to President Trump's impeachment during his first term in office. His office saw a significant reassigning of personnel directed away from cases and probes involving terrorism, espionage and foreign interference, and toward the Trump administration's immigration enforcement priorities.

The National Security Division was also involved in leading the classified documents prosecution of former national securioty adviser John Bolton for which Bolton pleaded guilty earlier this year -- as well as some of leak investigations that led to the subpoena of several journalists.

articles.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
articles.summary: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations.
articles.ai_summary: A series of bomb threats across Europe has disrupted airports and newsrooms, leading to flight diversions and emergency evacuations.

scraped.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms | CBC News
scraped.description: A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations.
scraped.h1: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
scraped.body_text:
A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations to conduct security sweeps.

No explosives have been found, and the threats have so far proved unfounded. But the spate of hoaxes that affected a number of flights, airports and, as of Friday, news broadcasters has raised concern over the widening impact if the threats continue to spread.

It's not yet clear if the incidents are linked, but the bomb threat hoaxes come on the heels of other European disruptions, including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions .

Here is what we know about the hoaxes targeting airlines and broadcasters in Europe.

What appeared to be a co-ordinated wave of bomb threats targeting European air traffic began on Tuesday.

At least seven flights and a cruise ship received hoax bomb threats , triggering emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and temporary airport closures in countries including Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain.

A second wave was reported on Thursday, with at least 27 flights affected .

Bomb threats force multiple flights in Europe to make emergency landings

On Friday, Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain.

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov" claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.

The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

Garda members work outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE on Friday after staff were evacuated from the site following a bomb threat. The broadcaster has claimed the bomb threat is from the same group that has been behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

Bomb threats against planes are often communicated to airlines, airports or authorities through anonymous emails or phone calls claiming that an explosive device is on board. Authorities do not always disclose how threats are delivered, because doing so could encourage copycats and compromise investigations.

A Prague airport representative told CNN on Thursday that they had received a threat from an anonymous email addressed to the airport, and Czech police said similar emails went to other European airports.

Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, told Reuters that an airline's security department first runs the report through a checklist. It then alerts the authorities, who may scramble fighter jets or divert the plane to a designated airport for a full sweep.

The vast majority of bomb threats turn out to be false alarms, though all must be treated as real until investigated, which means authorities are forced to scramble to rule out any danger.

No explosive device has been found on the planes affected this week, but every airline must decide whether a threat is credible and act accordingly.

A spokesperson for the British government called this week's incidents "malicious hoax threats" and said it has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world."

String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe

Bomb threats affect at least 27 flights, leading to emergency landings at several European airports

Airlines are not new to bomb threats, but aviation security experts say the apparent co-ordination and timing of the current incidents is unusual.

All planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.

Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government.

The incidents come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response.

Countries affected by the disruptions, including Denmark, Poland and ​Romania, have previously accused Moscow. Russia denies any involvement.

An EasyJet aircraft takes off at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State," a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia.

Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.

Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said bomb threats can stem from a wide range of motives, including political grievances, activist campaigns, criminal activity, online groups or state-linked hybrid operations.

European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen says that since 2022, Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference.

“We are under attack all the time,” she told Reuters. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilize our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.”

“It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations. Quite often, it is Russia.”

Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority.

Even a false alarm can disrupt airlines' operations, with plane diversions and thorough security inspections causing delays for passengers. Carriers typically bear additional costs including fuel, passenger rebooking, crew disruption and aircraft diversions.

Schouten said a sweep means unloading passengers and baggage, searching the aircraft and reloading. That can push crews past duty limits and lead to missed connections and cancellations.

People gather outside the offices of Irish national broadcaster RTE as officials conduct a security sweep after a reported bomb threat on Friday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

Air France-KLM chief executive Ben Smith said on Thursday he had never previously seen threats reported in such a co-ordinated fashion.

"We're quite confident that we have in place what we need to ensure that it has minimal or no impact on our operation," Smith told reporters. "So we have no ask today of our governments to change the way they manage these types of situations."

Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice-president of the European Cockpit Association.

Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.

Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."

Senior Writer

Sara Jabakhanji is a Toronto-based senior writer assigned to cover news developments in the Middle East. She has worked in CBC bureaus in Ottawa, London and Toronto. You can reach her at sara.jabakhanji@cbc.ca.

articles.title: The midterms show that Latinos could be a powerhouse force on climate
articles.summary: Latino voters are concerned about climate change – and among the most confident in their ability to create political change.
articles.ai_summary: The midterm elections highlighted the potential influence of Latino voters on climate change policies.

scraped.title: The midterms show that Latinos could be a powerhouse force on climate » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Latino voters are concerned about climate change – and among the most confident in their ability to create political change.
scraped.author: Pearl Marvell
scraped.h1: The midterms show that Latinos could be a powerhouse force on climate
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

As the dust settles after the midterm elections, one thing is glaringly obvious: Latinos are furious with Trump.

The New York Times estimates that Democrats won 69% of the Hispanic vote – a 29-point shift from 2024. That’s likely in response to the ICE raids that have deported and even killed loved ones and the rising costs of everyday living. But many Latinos also live in areas disproportionately affected by climate impacts like extreme heat and flooding – places known as frontline communities.

We can’t do this work without you! About 83% of every dollar you donate goes directly to paying our team of reporters, editors, meteorologists, and radio producers. The other 17% pays for this website, laptops, a payroll system, and similar expenses necessary for our work.

For insight on the midterms, Yale Climate Connections sat down with Jennifer Carman, director of survey strategy at the Yale Program on Climate Change Communication and lead author of a recent peer-reviewed study of climate attitudes in frontline communities . (YPCCC is the publisher of Yale Climate Connections.)

This interview has been edited and condensed.

Yale Climate Connections: How are you feeling about what we just witnessed?

Jennifer Carman: A lot of the places in America that have the frontline communities are also the most worried about climate change: Latinos and people in the Southwest and people in border areas. When you dig more deeply into those communities, you find that they experience a lot of swings in how they vote.

I consider them to be a group that’s very electorally up for grabs. But what we’re seeing is just how incredibly powerful and effective they can be as a voting bloc. We saw that in 2024 as well because they experienced some of the largest swings toward Trump in 2024, and that was the big story then.

What we see this year is that they’ve really snapped back. And in some places, especially if you look at the Texas border counties, some of those swings toward Democrats are even larger than the swings that happened in 2024.

My warning to the Democrats is that they shouldn’t consider this to be a permanent realignment, either. I think that depending on what Democrats do with the power that they have, that will be what makes or breaks whether they continue to have support from Latinos in the border areas in the next election cycle.

YCC: What do we know about what Latinos think about climate change?

Carman: Latinos care about climate change more than other racial and ethnic groups in the United States.

They are also affected by climate change in unique ways. Latino communities face a lot of climate impacts based on where they live; many Latinos work outdoors and work in hotter parts of the country. That’s why so many of our frontline communities are disproportionately Latino.

The important thing to keep in mind from my perspective is engaging frontline communities and engaging Latino communities, not just this election cycle but every election cycle. But I think that this cycle is a proof of concept that if this engagement happens, it is possible to win and to win in surprisingly large numbers – to swing even in states that Democrats didn’t think that they could win.

YCC: Do communicators of climate change need to do more to highlight that intersection between these topics and climate change?

Carman: I think that we need to have more conversations about climate change as a really practical issue, as something that affects people in their lives and affects the kinds of issues that we are already talking about: the fact that people are experiencing more harm from heat and higher bills. We know that if you’re experiencing higher temperatures, you have to run the air conditioner more often, and that’s expensive, or if you don’t have air conditioning, then you suffer. There are parts of the country that get extremely hot where people cannot afford air conditioning or cannot afford to run air conditioning.

YCC: Or don’t have the right to install one if they’re renting.

Carman: Yeah, exactly. There are studies that have found that apartments [without air conditioning] can get to be more than 100 degrees in the summer, and that has economic effects and health effects. A lot of these cost-of-living problems are exacerbated by climate change.

When it comes to talking about climate change, it is really important to talk about it not just as this sort of broad, esoteric issue that affects us all, but also as something that affects us personally. It also affects us all individually. For example, in my office today, it is 80 degrees in November.

There can be an aspect of talking about climate change that can be really intimidating. I think that’s part of why there’s this climate hushing that happens. It sounds so big, and you don’t want to have a conversation about giant systems and ocean currents and all of these various interconnected things. Climate change does have those effects, but it also has very personal and direct effects. And there are things that people can do about that. For example, voting.

Putting a name to what people are experiencing is really powerful. It’s getting hotter, and the fact that it’s getting so much hotter is dangerous. And the fact that there’s more flooding, that we’re getting these freak rainstorms in the Southwest and in Florida and wildfires in Hawaii and heat waves in Alaska – it’s really important to put a name to that, and we have a name for that. That name is climate change.

YCC: Where does climate hushing come from?

Carman: I think it comes from a bunch of things. One of them is which voices get amplified. The Dismissive [about climate change] demographic is about 11% [of the U.S. public] and Alarmed are about 25% of the population. So there are two and a half times as many Alarmed as there are Dismissive, but it always surprises people when you tell them that because the Dismissives are so loud and so highly platformed. There are whole news channels that primarily use the time and platform that they have for amplifying the voices of the Dismissive, like our president.

Read: Global warming’s six Americas

When those are the voices you hear, that’s what you think everybody thinks. It can also be intimidating to push back against.

Politicians have a lot more permission to talk about climate change than they think. Going into this next Congress, what I’m really hoping will happen is that members of Congress will be able to see that. A lot of policies to reduce the impacts of climate change and to protect people from climate impacts are really popular.

Ninety-two percent of registered voters support protecting workers from dangerous levels of heat, and it’s one of those policies that feels like a no-brainer. And yet Florida and Texas have banned heat protection laws.

Frontline communities are really central to coalition-building because they play an important role in not just connecting climate but all of these other issues. All these affordability things – frontline communities have been experiencing this for decades.

YCC: And Latinos are the demographic with the highest belief in their ability to collectively effect change at a government level.

Carman: I think that it’s important to recognize that frontline communities are not helpless. Because of the historical neglect, people have had to take a lot on themselves, but the potential for political action is really high.

There’s a lot that they’re already doing to protect themselves. There’s a lot of capacity-building and community power in frontline communities, and I think people within those communities know it. They can serve as powerful examples and powerful leadership and potential for political power. I think that is important for the climate movement and for politicians in general to keep in mind, especially as the new Congress goes forward.

scraped.title: The Standing Rock protests launched one man’s renewable energy transformation » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: Ten years after the protest, Cody Two Bears reflects on how it led him to create energy alternatives for tribal communities.
scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: The Standing Rock protests launched one man’s renewable energy transformation
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

This year is the 10th anniversary of historic protests in North Dakota, when members of the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe and thousands of supporters stood together to oppose the construction of an oil pipeline near tribal land.

Protesters argued that the Dakota Access pipeline would endanger water supplies, desecrate sacred sites, and increase reliance on fossil fuels.

The pipeline was built anyway. But for Cody Two Bears, who served on the Standing Rock Tribal Council at the time, the protests were still transformative.

Two Bears: “I’ve always seen on the news about how extraction affects communities around the world and … never really thought that would come to my backyard.”

The experience motivated him to learn more about the impacts of fossil fuels and to help tribes develop alternatives.

Two Bears: “I decided to get out of the leadership role from my tribe and start a nonprofit called Indigenized Energy.”

Indigenized Energy helped develop North Dakota’s largest solar farm right on the Standing Rock Reservation.

And it leads the Tribal Renewable Energy Coalition, a network of tribes working to install solar on tribal land.

So for Two Bears, the Standing Rock protests ignited a passion for clean energy that continues to drive him today.

scraped.body_text:
Welcome back, one and all. This week, a new world was born. Pronouns are going back into bios, and everyone who has an odd-numbered birthday needs to report for their gender reassignment on Monday. Evens are the week after. Asymmetrical haircuts are back, and so are MFAs in creative nonfiction. Pick up your kale or risk immediate hanging. Jews are, I’m so sorry to report, out. But at least it’s a return to form.

→ Blue tsunami: The final iteration of Trumpism has been roundly rejected. MAGA bye-bye. People took a good, hard look at Trump 2024–2026 and said: No, thanks. They didn’t like the tariffs. They didn’t like random deportations of longtime, law-abiding workers. They didn’t like the family grift. And, though it pains me to say it, people associate Trump now with Israel and Jewishness, and they don’t much like either of those things at the moment either. Republicans lost the House and the Senate. Trump is now a real-deal lame duck. Dems are about to get the largest majority in the House in 36 years. People are flipping Dem so hard that even a woman who was literally served with a felony warrant for auto theft at a campaign event defeated the local Republican incumbent . A democratic socialist just won the Los Angeles mayor’s race, unseating the progressive incumbent who I previously thought was pretty radical. Just look at those arrows (link for 2024 presidential votes and for 2026 Senate ones):

Here is a national exit poll asking about the importance of issues to someone’s vote:

GOVERNMENT CORRUPTION

Crucial/Major — 90%

Minor/No factor — 10%

COST OF LIVING

Crucial/Major — 89%

Minor/No factor — 11%

IRAN WAR

Crucial/Major — 74%

Minor/No factor — 26%

IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT

Crucial/Major — 73%

Minor/No factor — 27%

AI & DATA CENTERS

Crucial/Major — 56%

Minor/No factor — 44%

The presumptive next leader of the Republican Party, J.D. Vance, looks at all this and sees one word: Israel . Oh yeah, baby, here’s our story. It’s all happening. He wrote a eulogy for MAGA on X, saying that the loss is not about immigration enforcement or tariffs or corruption. No, no. Per J.D. Vance: “The reason we lost is the war.” His prescription for winning: “1) End the war, 2) Focus on cost of living/inflation, 3) Put America First, 4) Change our relationship to Israel.” So to translate 1. Israel, 2. Economy, 3. Israel, 4. Israel. Maybe he’s right! Maybe he’s wrong. But what’s clear is that this is what he’s going to build his political future on. It’s not crazy. You can certainly win elections on that. Me, when it comes to this election, I think there were some other factors swaying people too. Such as, perhaps, tariffs ?

scraped.title: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry
scraped.description: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who is heavily invested in the AI industry, is leading the charge to allow tech companies to build data centers on the public lands he oversees.
scraped.author: Mark Olalde
scraped.h1: Trump Official Who Wants Data Centers on Public Lands Has Tens of Millions Invested in AI Industry
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

The Trump administration has likened the need to build out the nation’s artificial intelligence infrastructure to the Manhattan Project, the World War II effort that produced the world’s first atomic bomb.

The White House’s point person on the effort, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, has spoken of the “AI arms race” with China as an existential issue for the nation. “AI is manufacturing intelligence, and, if we don’t manufacture more intelligence than our adversaries, it affects every job, every company and every industry,” he said during his Senate confirmation hearing in January 2025.

But advancing the administration’s AI objectives also could benefit Burgum’s own finances.

Much of his wealth is held in Arthur Ventures, an investment firm he co-founded, according to his 2026 financial disclosure form , which has not been previously reported. Between $18.1 million and $64.4 million of those investments are in AI companies, according to an analysis of the companies’ marketing materials shared with ProPublica by public lands advocacy group Save Our Parks. (Government financial disclosure forms allow filers to report wide ranges instead of the specific value of their investments.)

Burgum made his fortune 25 years ago when he sold a software company to Microsoft and has remained heavily invested in technology. In the year before joining the administration, when he was North Dakota’s governor, he made between $2.1 million and $11 million in capital gains from AI-related investments, Save Our Parks’ analysis showed. In 2025, he sold millions of dollars of stocks and equity in AI companies, bringing in capital gains worth between $2.5 million and $15.1 million.

In the ethics agreement Burgum signed as part of his Senate confirmation, he agreed to resign from his positions at Arthur but not give up his financial interests there.

“Secretary Burgum has met his federal ethics and financial disclosure obligations,” a U.S. Department of the Interior spokesperson told ProPublica in a statement. “Any suggestion that his office decisions are driven by personal investments are false and completely unsupported.”

Officials across the Trump administration also stand to profit from the White House’s support for AI and data centers. For example, 380 of President Donald Trump’s political appointees or their spouses hold stocks or have other financial connections to Nvidia , which has become the world’s most valuable company thanks to the data center boom. More than 320 have ties to Alphabet , Google’s parent company, which plans to spend at least $195 billion this year building data centers and AI-related technology. And more than 240 are invested in or otherwise have financial ties to Meta Platforms , which is developing a “fleet” of data centers. This is according to an analysis of records added last week to the Trump Team Financials database developed by ProPublica to make accessible the financial disclosures of administration officials.

Federal officials’ activities are governed by a criminal statute that sets a high burden of proof for potential wrongdoing — for example, approving permits for a company in which they are substantially invested, multiple ethics professors and lawyers told ProPublica. They said that Burgum’s investments appear to be acceptable under this law.

But ethics rules that do not carry criminal penalties also apply, explained Cynthia Brown, senior ethics counsel with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. These rules, she said, “instruct officials not to work on anything that would create the appearance of a conflict of interest.” She said this would include Burgum’s support for data centers on federal land while holding investments in AI.

Richard Painter, a law professor at the University of Minnesota and President George W. Bush’s chief ethics lawyer, agreed that Burgum should avoid making decisions benefiting an industry in which he is heavily invested. “I, as the ethics lawyer, would insist he stay away from it,” Painter said. “In the Bush administration, the answer would’ve been ‘he has to recuse,’ I can guarantee you that.”

A review of recent Interior Department secretaries’ financial holdings suggests it’s common to have some potential conflicts, but Trump’s appointees are more heavily invested in the industries they oversee than their predecessors. Deb Haaland, President Joe Biden’s appointee, held no direct financial investments in companies the department regulated. President Barack Obama’s first appointee, Ken Salazar, listed ownership of his family’s ranch but few other investments. Obama’s second appointee, Sally Jewell, held stocks in oil and gas , which she agreed to divest as a condition of her confirmation.

Ryan Zinke and David Bernhardt served as Interior Department secretaries during Trump’s first term. The former was found by the agency’s Office of Inspector General to have improperly assisted a development in his hometown, while the latter had so many potential conflicts that he reportedly carried a card listing them . (Zinke said the OIG investigation was a political attack, while Bernhardt recused himself from several decisions in which there would have been clear conflicts.)

More recently, as the effort to build data centers has run headlong into broad public opposition, the current administration has offered federally managed public lands to them. Unlike local or state processes, where concerns about water use, power consumption and the lack of transparency around permitting have slowed or halted projects, the public has less ability to stop them on federal property. The Interior Department oversees most of this land .

A little-noticed U.S. Geological Survey report released earlier this year found at least 91.3 million acres of public lands managed by the Interior Department — an area comparable to Montana — could potentially host data centers.

The department’s mandate includes overseeing tribal affairs, managing national parks, regulating extractive industries like coal and operating dams across the West. Burgum, though, is spending significant time on other things. This includes meeting with representatives of companies such as Amazon, Microsoft and Alphabet more than 20 times from January through November 2025, according to a compilation of his schedules shared with ProPublica by public interest watchdog group Public Citizen.

In response, several Democratic senators sent a letter to Burgum in October saying, “We demand that you immediately cease all efforts to hijack public lands for the development of data centers, and urge you to provide full transparency on your role in the DOI’s efforts to site data centers.”

Some of Burgum’s meetings have been previously unreported, including a June 2025 dinner with a high-ranking United Arab Emirates delegation in the wine room of the upscale Italian restaurant Cafe Milano in Washington’s Georgetown neighborhood. The small guest list included the United Arab Emirates’ AI lead, Sultan Ahmed Al Jaber, as well as Amos Hochstein, a prominent American proponent of AI data centers via his investment firm TWG Global.

Several months later, Burgum signed a memorandum of understanding with the Emirati delegation, pledging to work together to deploy AI.

Neither the Emirati Embassy nor TWG Global responded to requests for comment.

The Interior Department spokesperson said that Burgum “is responsible for helping unleash American energy production and ensuring our nation has the resources and infrastructure necessary to lead the future. That mission requires engagement with industry leaders, stakeholders, and international partners.”

In an August Fox News appearance to promote the administration’s AI efforts, Burgum was asked about the network’s poll showing 70% of voters opposed data centers. He countered by alleging that “foreign influence” and “misinformation” had played a large role in fueling public opposition.

Jayson O’Neill, a spokesperson for Save Our Parks, said Burgum and others in the administration are out of touch with public concerns. “His almost myopic focus on artificial intelligence and the data center build-out at the expense of our public lands serves not only the globalist tech titans behind and within the Trump administration, but also him and the tens of millions of dollars of his own personal wealth invested in the industry.”

Across the administration, political appointees whose offices have AI business before them hold significant investments in the industry.

Steve Pearce is director of the Bureau of Land Management, the Interior Department agency that administers more land than any other entity in the country. The former New Mexico representative was confirmed over Democrats’ concerns that he favors selling public lands and that his career in oil and gas presents a conflict of interest involving an industry the agency regulates.

But public lands advocates say his AI investments now worry them. Pearce owned stock in Nvidia, Meta Platforms, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet and other AI-focused companies, according to his most recent publicly available financial disclosure, signed in October 2025. He also is invested in Titan Development, a real estate company that has managed several land acquisitions for data centers in the Southwest. (He pledged to divest many of his AI investments, but not Titan.)

An agency spokesperson pushed back on the concerns. “Director Pearce complies with all applicable federal ethics requirements and financial disclosure obligations,” the spokesperson said in a statement, adding that “conflating lawful disclosure of financial holdings with an actual conflict of interest ignores the federal ethics framework designed to identify and address precisely these questions.”

The BLM is reviewing permit applications for about 15 data centers and 17 associated infrastructure projects, including nuclear power plants and transmission wires, in Arizona, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Wyoming and Idaho. This is according to an agency spokesperson and its Mineral & Land Records System.

The project that was to be the first data center on BLM land, near Boulder City in southern Nevada, had earned a permit to build a solar plant, before changing its plans. The BLM approved the change in June without studying the potential environmental implications. (An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the project, sending it back to the agency for further review.)

Meanwhile, it remains unclear how much the public will benefit from data centers on BLM land. The foundational federal land management law was passed in 1976, so it does not envision data centers. Even so, the department said it is relying on this statute to permit data centers.

Businesses pay the government to use public land. Oil and gas drillers pay a royalty on each barrel they produce. Solar power plants pay a per-megawatt fee.

For data centers, the main charge appears set to be an “annual fair-market-value rent,” an Interior Department spokesperson said. But such rental fees can be quite low, so the economic benefit to the public won’t be known until the data centers are permitted.

Another key official with a land management agency who’s heavily invested in AI is Michael Boren . He first served as acting assistant secretary of the Interior Department before transitioning to U.S. Department of Agriculture undersecretary, where he oversees the Forest Service, second only to the BLM in the land area it stewards.

Among his many investments in AI companies, Boren reported between about $1.5 million and $6.1 million worth of financial interests in Elon Musk’s xAI, which has since been acquired by SpaceX. Additionally, he has up to $500,000 invested in Valar Atomics, which is pushing to build a data center complex called Project Beehive on thousands of acres of BLM land in Utah, complete with more than 450 small nuclear plants to power it.

“Undersecretary Boren has fully complied with all federal ethics laws and requirements and will continue to follow the advice of USDA’s excellent ethics attorneys,” an Agriculture Department spokesperson said in a statement.

Lee Zeldin , whom Trump appointed to head the Environmental Protection Agency, has also emerged as a major AI booster. He too has dabbled in AI investments. Zeldin’s financial disclosure forms reveal that in May 2025 he bought and sold up to $15,000 worth of shares of Datavault AI, a company selling AI-, data- and blockchain-based products.

“Administrator Zeldin followed every ethical rule to a tee in his disclosure without exception,” an EPA spokesperson said in a statement. The agency added that he was cleared by its ethics officials and that he has no obligation to explain such transactions.

The EPA under Zeldin has taken steps to minimize oversight of data centers and power plants built nearby to keep them running. This includes a rule the agency proposed in July to end a requirement that states gather public feedback as they consider air permits for certain facilities, including data centers .

In October, a group of Democratic senators sent a letter to Zeldin asking the EPA to withdraw the proposed rule. “The federal government should encourage transparency and public engagement around these projects, not make it easier to shroud their construction in secrecy,” they wrote.

Brandon Roberts contributed reporting.

I cover the environment, natural resources and public health around the Southwest.

Have you been affected by oil field wastewater, known as “produced water,” or otherwise have information to share? I want to hear from you.

scraped.title: Defeating Zionism to Free Palestine
scraped.description: Palestinian liberation is the key to fighting racism, imperialism, and genocide around the globe.
scraped.author: Noura Erakat, John Reynolds
scraped.h1: Defeating Zionism to Free Palestine
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Palestinian liberation is the key to fighting racism, imperialism, and genocide around the globe.

Earlier this week, Abdul El-Sayed defeated Mike Rogers in the U.S. Senate race in Michigan after months of Islamophobic abuse, most notably from President Donald Trump, who referred to El-Sayed as “Mohammed.”

“Mohammed goes back to the days of the Jihad. He is a RADICAL Extremist, Terrorist Sympathizer,” Trump wrote on Truth Social last month. “Mohammed’s Values are not exactly those of Michiganders, or those of our Great United States of America!” The people of Michigan thought otherwise.

El-Sayed will be the first-ever Muslim U.S. senator. “He rose to victory,” my Intercept colleagues Matt Sledge and Jonah Valdez wrote , “with a campaign animated by his opposition to U.S. support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, making him a key figure for a left critical of entrenched foreign policy interests and a target for a political establishment intent on preserving the U.S. relationship with the Israeli government.”

In an Election Day equivalent of a Hail Mary, as El-Sayed and Democrats from coast to coast were in the midst of a rout of the GOP, Trump went on Fox News to announce the U.S. would stop providing $4 billion in annual aid to Israel , specifically blaming El-Sayed for making it a hot-button issue. “The left uses the $4 billion payment — that everybody knows about, it’s no secret — as a signal of unfairness,” said Trump.

There is no reason to believe the aid will stop. Trump is an inveterate liar, and structural issues with U.S. assistance make it unlikely. And even if it did end, Israel’s genocide will continue . Almost 75,000 Gazans have been killed since October 2023, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health in Gaza. A recent U.N. report said, “Israeli authorities and forces continue to commit genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinians in Gaza.”

Ending the genocide will mean decolonizing Gaza and offering Palestinians a path to justice. That, Noura Erakat and John Reynolds write in their new book, means “confronting the problem of Zionism” and everything fundamental to it: racism, conquest, settler colonialism, and apartheid laws. Today, Erakat and Reynolds offer an essay adapted from “ Confronting Zionism ,” exploring how the Zionist project can be dismantled and Israeli colonialism can be demolished, leading to Palestinian liberation and a future built on redistribution, reparations, and refugee return.

—Nick Turse, editor and TomDispatch

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here.

Three years on from the onset of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, we are at a crucial hinge point. The world today, when it comes to Palestine, stands at the crossroads: meaningful support for liberation and decolonization, or the normalization of colonial expansion and erasure.

Since the 2021 “ Manifesto of Dignity and Hope ” and the unified call of Palestinians to confront Zionism, the Israeli political sphere has only continued to sustain and entrench its fascist trajectory and its racist laws . After 2023, Israeli settler colonialism and domination escalated into all-out destruction and elimination. Palestinians who had been enduring suffocating apartheid and siege for far too long were now subjected to genocidal assault. Though the context on the ground shifted, the urgent need for a better understanding and challenge to Zionism on political, legal, structural, and ideological grounds remained.

It was a new generation of Palestinian activists who produced the Manifesto of Dignity and Hope, but their text was shaped by the legacy and spirit of Palestinian revolutionaries and anti-colonial thinkers from earlier periods. Common language echoes through the generations. A quarter-century ago, Palestinian intellectual Edward Said wrote the core of the issue of Palestine “is intellectual truth and the need to combat any sort of apartheid. We should concentrate our resistance on … fully confronting the apartheid provisions inherent in Zionism.” And as diplomat Fayez Sayegh captured it in 1965: Racism is not an acquired or incidental or passing feature of the Israeli state; it is “inherent in the very ideology of Zionism.” Today, we can draw inspiration from these intergenerational reverberations across Palestinian theory and activism, in their consonant commitments to confronting Zionism.

Part of our own task as anti-colonial legal scholars is to expand our analysis of the limitations of narrow liberal legal readings of apartheid and inequality, and to highlight how a radical critique of Israeli apartheid is essential to dismantling Israel’s apartheid regime. This requires scrutiny not only of Zionism and Israeli settler colonialism, but also of the concept of apartheid itself. Apartheid was previously understood in the context of the African anti-apartheid struggle, in a formulation originally coined by the South African Communist Party, as “colonialism of a special type.” By the late 1990s, however, apartheid had been stripped in mainstream understandings of its global character and colonial essence, and effectively reframed as “ racial discrimination of a special type .”

Most Read Haley Stevens Destroyed Her Political Career for Absolutely Nothing Eoin Higgins Trump Scrambles to Halt Military Aid to Israel to Deprive El-Sayed of a Talking Point Nick Turse Abdul El-Sayed Wins Senate Seat With Pro-Palestine Campaign Matt Sledge, Jonah Valdez

One factor in this analytical shift was the domestication of racism in international law, which has obscured its relationship to global capitalism and transformed racism into a problem for individual countries to resolve through juridical reform or diversity, equity, and inclusion programs. Racism is not merely abhorrent because people’s feelings are hurt or one feels unseen, however, but because it is entangled with power and economic structures, and because materially, the continuum of racist violence culminates in genocide, which is squarely understood as a global phenomenon. Martin Luther King Jr. pointed to this in 1967 when he said: “In the final analysis, racism is evil because its ultimate logic is genocide. … If one says that I am not good enough to eat at a lunch counter, or to have a good, decent job, or to go to school with him merely because of my race, he is saying consciously or unconsciously that I do not deserve to exist.”

International law attempts to capture this continuum. Three of the specific acts conducted to maintain apartheid are identical to the acts conducted to commit genocide under their respective legal definitions. In the former, they are done with the intent to dominate; in the latter, with the intent to destroy. These are not mutually exclusive, but rather interact with each other: Colonialism, apartheid, and genocide combine under the Zionist project in Palestine to produce a system of oppression based on conquest, structural racism, dispossession, and elimination.

Palestinian opposition to Zionism and the imperatives of decolonization — for political emancipation, material survival, and cultural flourishing — are the central thrust of our work. The colonial origins and early legal mechanics of Zionist settler colonialism and Israel’s apartheid regime reveal how Zionism functioned both as a colonial initiative and a racializing project. This manifested in colonial institutions even before the state was established in 1948, after which they were enshrined in racist legal regimes. A broad structural analysis of the institutional and economic processes of land and capital accumulation that have occurred under settler colonialism in Palestine is necessary to understand the machinery of conquest and dispossession — and the role that racism has played in driving it forward. Drawing on the anti-colonial Palestinian intellectual tradition, we can see that an antiracist analysis has been organic to the Palestinian liberation struggle and is precisely what shaped U.N. initiatives in the 1960s and 1970s that condemned Zionism as a form of racism and racial discrimination alongside apartheid and colonialism.

Read our complete coverage

Despite all the analysis of Israeli state racism and colonial violence since 1948 and all of the mass popular mobilizations and legal advocacy against Israeli apartheid, nothing substantive was done at an international, political, or institutional level to address or redress it. This inaction and the impunity afforded to Israel inevitably culminated in the situation that the world found itself in after October 2023: unsanctioned apartheid accelerating into unadulterated genocide — and given the green light by those who had the power to stop it. There was a decade of increasingly flagged warning signs leading up to this. But Palestinian scholars and international lawyers who had warned of a “prelude to genocide” or “ slow-motion ” genocide over the years were largely ignored, and in some cases castigated. The consequences have been catastrophic. The United States actively funded , armed , and cheer-led the butchery in Gaza. European Union leaders chose to “stand with Israel” as it announced its starvation policy and war of annihilation.

We would not have ended up in this present moment if the critiques of Zionism as colonialism and racism and the reality of Israel as an apartheid regime had been taken seriously. In 1975, the U.N., led by a Third World majority, declared “international co-operation and peace require the achievement of national liberation and independence, the elimination of colonialism and neocolonialism, foreign occupation, zionism, apartheid and racial discrimination in all its forms, as well as the recognition of the dignity of peoples and their right to self-determination.” Against this, the Western world, led by the United States, has worked to normalize Israeli apartheid.

We see part of our task now as one of continuing to build on the recent “mainstreaming” of condemnations of Israeli apartheid and genocide, but in a way that decisively resists the drift toward narrower, liberal articulations and insists on the importance of radical, anti-colonial, and anti-imperial analysis and praxis. In our work as critical legal scholars, we situate apartheid and the shape it has taken as a category in international law, and we explore the limits and potential of legal tactics, arguments, and institutions to dismantle Israeli apartheid and end the genocide in Gaza. We argue that while legal actions should be pursued in the service of political and social movements, legal logic is insufficient in itself — and can risk narrowing or distorting the horizon of Palestinian liberation. In our view, the proliferating condemnations of Israel by major human rights organizations and mainstream figures in recent years have belatedly reflected the popular consensus and a political reality that Palestinian activism had made undeniable. They also fit, to varying degrees, within a wider pattern of containment.

As one example, take the case of European officials and states finally beginning to acknowledge the heinousness of Israel’s obliteration of Gaza in mid-2025, but doing so primarily in the form of calling for a Palestinian state . They did so only after almost two full years of enabling untold destruction, and refusing to impose any serious sanctions to stem the genocide. Their moves to recognize Palestinian statehood were not about any genuine support for Palestinian self-determination, but rather a way to stabilize the apartheid status quo and try to slow down the Israeli–U.S. drive to continue the erasure of Gaza and full annexation of the West Bank.

With all of that in mind, it is important to situate the political moment we are in — the increasing focus on Israeli apartheid in recent years and subsequently on the genocide in Gaza — alongside the urgency of thinking about Palestine’s future and our collective responsibilities. In doing so, we have several core aims: to offer a deeper understanding of the nature and extent of Israel’s colonial rule over Palestinian lands and lives; to think through the relationship between the practices of Israeli settler colonialism, apartheid, and genocide on the one hand, and the institutions and ideology of Zionism on the other; to situate Palestinian liberation and its global solidarity alliances as an antiracist struggle and an anti-colonial movement; and to insist on the need for systemic anti-imperial understandings and critiques of Zionism. To properly confront Zionism and avoid the pitfalls of neo-apartheid, we must be attentive to the necessities and practicalities of decolonization.

The decolonization of Palestine today continues a legacy of other liberation struggles — against European colonization globally, against domestic regimes of fascism, against apartheid in southern Africa, and against white supremacy in the United States and elsewhere. These are political orders that Third World, antiracist, partisan, and socialist movements have fought against throughout the past century and more. We must continue that tradition in the service of decolonization by fleshing out the political, legal, historical, and moral reasoning of anti-colonial and anti-Zionist thinking and movements. In our own writing, we feel we are merely providing footnotes to the political education and organizing that has fanned out from Palestine around the world, and that has shaped what millions of activists and people of conscience have viscerally felt: that Zionist colonial rule should and can be dismantled, and that Palestinians must be supported in their struggle to do so.
