The stakes of confronting Zionist settler colonialism are high for the entire world: first and foremost for Palestinians’ own liberation, but also because their struggle is at the epicenter of wider global struggles against structures of domination and exploitation. Zionism is a colonial project in Palestine, but also a vehicle of imperialism in the region — agitating for U.S. war and intervention, acting as an antagonist of imperial aggression against Lebanon, Syria, Iran, Yemen and beyond, and actively collaborating with reactionary geopolitical forces globally. Zionism has been further mobilized by ethnonationalists and imperial projects as a proposition on how to organize a society on a basis of racial hierarchy that leaves its excluded groups to perish. Palestinian revolutionary intellectual Ghassan Kanafani always insisted on the importance of understanding the Palestinian struggle in the context of “the alliance between Zionism and imperialism.” And in positioning Kanafani’s analysis in the context of global movements against imperialism today, educator and organizer Layan Sima Fuleihan reiterates the Palestinian cause is “a banner for all of humanity.”

Naji al-Ali, the Palestinian political cartoonist famous for his iconic Hanzala (or “Handala”) character who symbolizes Palestinian resolve and future return, was himself displaced from northern Palestine as a boy during the Nakba and grew up in refugee camps in Lebanon. Kanafani came across Al-Ali and his artwork in Ein al-Hilweh camp and began to publish his drawings in the early 1960s. Al-Ali went on to produce tens of thousands of cartoons over the next 25 years, and through his art was renowned as a voice of Palestinian and Arab political consciousness. In 1984, just a couple of years before he would be assassinated , Al-Ali reflected on what Hanzala and Palestine represented:

I feel that I can recall and sense every bush, every stone, every house and every tree I passed when I was a child in Palestine. The character of Hanzala was a sort of icon that protected my soul from falling whenever I felt sluggish or I was ignoring my duty. That child was like a splash of fresh water on my forehead, bringing me to attention and keeping me from error and loss. He was the arrow of the compass, pointing steadily towards Palestine. Not just Palestine in geographical terms, but Palestine in its humanitarian sense — the symbol of a just cause, whether it is located in Egypt, Vietnam or South Africa.

In the decades since then, the idea of Palestine as the compass has resonated in struggles for justice around the world. Most recently, in 2025, the Palestinian Youth Movement and a coalition of solidarity groups brought thousands of activists together for the People’s Conference for Palestine, under the banner “Gaza is the compass.”

A wide array of voices, from community activists to trade union organizers to political representatives, emphasized how central Palestine is to all of the social struggles they are engaged in.

Palestinian doctor Mohammad Mustafa articulated the perspective of the many involved in movements for justice across the globe: “Gaza is the measure of our humanity. It is the litmus test that reveals who we are; as individuals, as a nation, as a world. … The compass points in one direction no matter who you are or where you are. In this way it provides a mandate and direction towards freedom for everyone.”

Lawyer and organizer Huwaida Arraf echoed these ideas: “Gaza is our compass because it points us to the truth. … When we’re fighting for Gaza, we’re fighting for a world where no people live in cages or under siege, under the boot of militarism or of fascism.”

Monadel Herzallah from Gaza, who lost five family members in the genocide, insisted the same: “To fight for a free Palestine is to fight for a free Haiti, a free Congo, a free Sudan — a free and just world which will be molded by all of us.”

Palestine is the compass because of what it represents as a banner for all humanity, and because of the horizons it opens up everywhere in imagining and building a new world.

Excerpt adapted from “Confronting Zionism: Decolonizing Palestine and Building the World Anew,” coming from Haymarket Books on November 10, 2026.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.title: Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material | CBC News
scraped.description: Thomas Markle, the father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, said the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.
scraped.h1: Meghan Markle's father arrested and charged with possessing child sexual abuse material
scraped.body_text:
WARNING: This article contains details of abuse.

The father of Prince Harry's wife, Meghan, was arrested Friday morning by U.S. federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material.

Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, of Lakeland, Fla., is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to the U.S. Attorney's Office for Central District of California.

In a statement, it said Markle was arrested on a federal criminal complaint alleging he kept child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with prepubescent girls, in two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented for nearly two decades.

It says agents seized approximately 78 items, including two images that depict an adult man — whom a witness identified as Markle — with a nude prepubescent girl.

"Mr. Markle allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions," said FBI Director Kash Patel in a statement, indicating the FBI is still investigating this matter.

Patel also thanked FBI partners in Mexico, Manila and the Marshall Islands law enforcement attachés, who aided the investigation.

This image taken on Sunday shows the entrance to a storage facility where Mexican authorities seized a storage unit with belongings of Thomas Markle during a search for alleged child sexual abuse material, on the outskirts of Tijuana, Mexico. (Guillermo Arias/AFP/Getty Images)

The statement from the U.S. Attorney's Office appears to confirm reports by the Sun, a British tabloid, that Meghan's half-brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out their father's home in the Philippines.

"According to an affidavit filed with the complaint, in October 2026, law enforcement learned that an individual signed an affidavit regarding their discovery of suspected [child sexual abuse material] among Markle's possessions in the Philippines," the statement said. "Information from the first individual later led agents to a second unit."

Philippine Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla told reporters on Friday that Thomas Markle Jr. is also being investigated.

"We have a witness saying that underage girls were being brought to his house and we're following it up. We are looking into whether the 60-year-old son, Thomas Markle Jr., was involved in the crime," said Remulla. "To accuse the father is only half the police work."

Thomas Markle Sr. was not at his daughter Meghan's wedding to Prince Harry in 2018. (Phil Noble/Reuters)

There was no immediate comment from Meghan's representatives on Friday.

Meghan Markle recently said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter.

"I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."

Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama Suits , married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.

Thomas Markle is expected to appear in a Tampa court on Friday.

If convicted, he would face a statutory maximum sentence of 20 years in federal prison.

scraped.title: Joshua Wong sentencing: Hong Kong and int'l reactions
scraped.description: Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after pleading guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces. HKFP rounds up reactions.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: Joshua Wong sentencing: Local gov’t, police, officials hail 10-year jail term amid condemnation from foreign gov’t’s, NGOs
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy activist Joshua Wong was sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after pleading guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces, his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

See also: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals

HKFP rounds up local and international reactions.

Chief Executive John Lee

Wong was “among the primary culprits responsible for undermining Hong Kong’s prosperity and stability… Wong Chi-fung has repeatedly broken the law, including organising, taking part in, and inciting others to take part in unauthorised assemblies, unlawful assemblies, and contempt of court, demonstrating his utter disregard for the law.”

Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun

“The central government of China firmly supports the Hong Kong SAR in safeguarding national security and punishing in accordance with the law acts that endanger national security.”

Spokesperson for the Hong Kong Legislative Council

“The sentence fully demonstrates the rule of law and justice, reflecting that under the Hong Kong National Security Law, anyone attempting to endanger national security will inevitably be severely punished in accordance with the law… [T]he evidence against Wong Chi-fung was conclusive and he chose to plead guilty…”

Chief Superintendent of Police National Security Department Steve Li

“I sincerely hope that for the rest of his time in prison, apart from reflecting on the wrongdoings he has done to the country and to the Hong Kong SAR, he must seize the opportunity to learn how to respect the law and properly understand his own country.”

Secretary for Security Chris Tang

“Those launching attacks against us are exactly the same external forces that Wong and Law attempted to collude… They must be strongly condemned, and Hong Kong citizens must recognise and acknowledge that clearly.”

European Union External Action Press Team:

“The EU urges Chinese and the Hong Kong authorities to respect international legal commitments under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration and maintain space for political pluralism in line with the ‘one country, two systems’ principle.”

Spokesperson for the UK Foreign Office

“We call for an immediate end to all unjust prosecutions of individuals charged under the National Security Law and urge the authorities in China and Hong Kong to honour the rights and freedoms guaranteed to the people of Hong Kong under the Sino-British joint declaration (1984).”

Spokesperson for the US Consulate

“Wong has been unjustly imprisoned since December 2020, demonstrating that Beijing will go to extraordinary lengths to silence those who advocate for fundamental freedoms in Hong Kong.”

Taiwan Presidential Office Spokesperson Karen Kuo

“Seeking democracy should not be a crime, and young people should not have to sacrifice their freedom for their ideals.”

Asia Director at Human Rights Watch Elaine Pearson

“The harsh sentence on baseless charges against Joshua Wong is cruel and unjust. Young people promoting social change are an asset for any vibrant society, but the Hong Kong government puts them behind bars.”

Deputy Regional Director for Amnesty International Sarah Brooks

“Today’s sentence is another grim reminder of how Hong Kong’s National Security Law has become a tool to punish dissent rather than to genuinely protect national security… [it] cruelly – and perhaps deliberately – comes mere months before he would have been eligible for release under his previous conviction.”

scraped.description: A biweekly column from ICT with the latest news from the arts and entertainment world
scraped.author: Sandra Hale Schulman
scraped.h1: INDIGENOUS A&E: LA Film Fests, an ‘Old School Indian’ story, Winter Market
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Sandra Hale Schulman ICT

The latest: Film premieres and awards, ‘avatar’ fiction, Santa Fe art market

FILM FESTIVALS: Los Angeles hosts two Indigenous film fests

Two big Indigenous film festivals are taking over Los Angeles for Native American Heritage Month, featuring screenings with the directors and actors in attendance, some major premieres, and awards shows.

Red Nation Celebration Institute (RNCI) is running the 31st Red Nation International Film Festival Nov. 8-15 with screenings at the Grove AMC theater. There are 96 official selections, including six features, 28 documentaries, one animated feature, 38 documentary shorts, 14 narrative shorts, and nine animation shorts.

The competition offers audiences a first look at new voices from Native and Indigenous perspectives in independent film.

The opening night feature is “Timber Lands,” from Director Baylee Toney, starring Wes Studi, Irene Bedard, Robert Clohessy, Tanaya Beatty, Owen Crowshoe, and Myles Clohessy. In the remote Oregon timber country, the sudden death of a celebrated bronc rider exposes a violent rift between two powerful families who will stop at nothing to protect their sovereign land.

Another screening is “Nine Little Indians,” Shannon Kring’s wrenching documentary about nine Charbonneau sisters, members of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians, and their decades-long fight for acknowledgement, justice, and healing after the abuses they suffered in the American Indian boarding school system. Executive producers are Leonardo DiCaprio and Tony Robbins.

Acclaimed actor Lou Diamond Phillips, Filipino/Cherokee, will receive the RNCI Lifetime Achievement Award on Nov. 14 after a screening of “Gangland .’ The RNCI Red Nation Award show with several Native actor presenters takes place at the Beverly Hilton on Nov. 15.

The LA Skins Fest runs Nov. 18-22 at TCL Chinese Theater in Hollywood, California, launching the 20th year with a special screening of the acclaimed series, “North of North.” presented by Netflix. The series shows winter is settling over Ice Cove, and young Inuk mother Siaja, played by Anna Lambe, is still determined to make life better — for herself and everyone around her.

Feature films include, “ What The Crows Saw ,” on Nov. 20. The film features a determined Pueblo woman who must confront the mysterious inhabitants of a strange tavern as she searches for her missing sister.

Indian Country's top stories from Native journalists. Free, every Thursday.

Excellence in Indigenous storytelling will be celebrated at the 15th Annual Native American Media Awards, hosted by Kiowa Gordon, of “Dark Winds,” at the Hard Rock Hollywood on Sunday, Nov. 22 starting at 7 p.m. The awards recognize the talent, creativity, and contributions of Native American artists and filmmakers.

In addition to the film festivals, “People of the West” will be streaming on FNX.org all of November with a marathon of all 10 episodes on Thanksgiving Day of the hard-hitting series that frames California’s complicated history through Native voices.

Creator/executive producer Brad Munoa, Payómkawichum, uses oral storytelling, cinematic dramatization, archival material, and expert testimony to trace five centuries of how California tribes were affected by colonizers who came by sea and by land. Its wealth of natural resources — gold, fish, crops, minerals, and water — made it a last frontier in the push for western expansion.

BOOKS: ‘Old School Indian’ gets schooled

A new book, “ Old School Indian ,” by Aaron John Curtis, Ahkwesáhsne, tells an irreverent coming-of-middle-age story about an Indigenous man’s search for intimacy, healing, and a second chance.

The book’s main character, Abe Jacobs is Ahkwesáhsne, from the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe. At 18, Abe left the reservation where he was raised. He met the love of his life, started writing poetry, and chose to open his marriage — building a life far from the Rez.

Now he’s 43, facing a relationship collapse and a rare yet fatal diagnosis. When he returns to the Rez to undergo a healing from his Great Uncle Budge — a wry, recovered alcoholic — Abe is forced to reckon with who he’s been, and who he might still be.

Curtis jumps the barrier and addresses the reader directly in this unusual format, to explain Indigenous words and customs.

“I did a lot of direct address,” Curtis, who worked as a buyer at Miami’s top tome seller Books & Books for 20 years, told ICT. “A lot of that came from my writers group. Although at some points I was assuming some negative thoughts that the readers weren’t having. So I did have to play around that a little bit.”

Abe is Curtis’s avatar; Curtis did have serious health issues and went home to heal them.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“I had an autoimmune disorder as described in the book,” he said. “I’ve been in remission since about 2021. It started off as a short story and I was venting all this frustration of everything I was going through and fear, and my writers group was really excited by it. So I fleshed it out, and it’s me, but it’s fiction, not a memoir.”

The tone is humorous and serious, sarcastic and direct. It took him 10 years from start to publication.

“The original manuscript was twice as long as it is now,” Curtis said. “I cut out a lot of Miami backstory and may publish that down the road.”

The artsy cover art of a Native in shades and open crown hat,is by artist Alex Jacobs, a former writer for Indian Country Today, and Curtis’s real life uncle.

“That’s my Uncle Alex Jacobs,” Curtis said. “I had that image of his art on my computer for 20 years. Alex had sold the original, so they got Emily Mahome, a digital illustrator, to recreate it digitally for the cover.”

Reviews have been stellar and Curtis embarks on a book tour through the fall.

ART: SWAIA Winter Market

The Southwestern Association for Indian Arts (SWAIA) hosts its 21st Annual Winter Indian Market on Saturday and Sunday, Nov. 28-29, at the Santa Fe Community Convention Center.

The indoor holiday market gathers 160 juried Indigenous artists displaying jewelry, pottery, paintings, textiles, and holiday ornaments.

Smaller and more intimate than the summer Indian Market, Winter Indian Market offers a chance to slow down, linger at the booths, and have genuine conversations with the artists themselves. One can hear firsthand about the techniques, traditions, and inspirations behind each piece, from finely crafted jewelry and hand-coiled pottery to paintings, sculpture and more.

A silent auction adds another way to take home a remarkable work. Winter Indian Market is a meaningful way to celebrate the season and support Native artists directly.

“Winter Indian Market is built for connection,” said Jamie R. Schulze, Northern Cheyenne/Sisseton Wahpeton Oyate, SWAIA executive director. “In a more intimate setting, visitors can spend real time with an artist: hearing the story behind a piece, learning the process and traditions that shaped it, and getting to know the person making contemporary Native art today. That conversation changes what a purchase means. You’re not just taking home something beautiful. You’re investing directly in an artist and carrying their story with you.”

Sales go directly to the artists and their home studios, generating economic support for Native entrepreneurs across New Mexico and North America.

scraped.h1: Election Shakeup Threatens Bipartisan Deal to Speed Energy Projects
scraped.body_text:
Democrats’ electoral sweep has shaken the ground beneath a permitting reform bill in Congress, raising doubts about whether the measure has enough support to advance in an initial Senate vote scheduled for Monday.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) said on Thursday in a statement to POLITICO that he opposed the bipartisan bill in its current form, joining some fellow Democrats and environmental groups in raising concerns that the legislation would revise federal laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act.

Even before Jeffries’ statement, mounting evidence showed support for the bill was wavering.

The legislation, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act , or BAAJA, has support from business groups tied to renewable energy and fossil fuels. They tout its potential to reduce consumer energy costs by bringing new supplies online. The measure would ease regulatory barriers to build energy projects of just about every type—clean and dirty—and it would weaken the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.

And a new report by Kevin Kircher, a mechanical engineering professor at Purdue University, attempts to quantify the proposal’s broader emissions consequences, identifying potential harms that previous analyses may have missed by examining only parts of the bill.

The Senate is scheduled to vote Monday on whether to begin debate on the bill. Its co-sponsors are Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.V.), Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Mike Lee (R-Utah) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.)

Chris Moyer, founder of Echo Communications Advisors, said Democrats’ overwhelming wins in the midterm elections have changed the landscape for the bill. He previously hoped Congress would pass it in the lame-duck session, which begins next week, but has since changed his mind.

“The numbers we’re looking at in the House and Senate are just massive and Democrats will have a ton of leverage,” Moyer said in an interview. He previously worked on Capitol Hill as an aide to the late Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid.

Republicans will control the House and Senate in the lame-duck session, but Democrats will have comfortable majorities when the 120th Congress begins in January. Democrats will soon have more clout to address crucial clean energy roadblocks, like long queues for interconnection to the electric grid, without the trade-offs currently in the legislation that could speed the building of fossil fuel infrastructure in sensitive areas, Moyer said.

“If there’s a way to address some of the concerns that are being raised from the environmental and public lands standpoint and from the Tribal standpoint, and also preserve a lot of the good things that have been negotiated already, that’s something it seems there should be interest in this Congress in working on,” Moyer said. “It can be part of the affordability agenda that the incoming majorities are going to focus on.”

Scott Segal, a longtime environmental policy expert with the Washington, D.C., law and lobbying firm Bracewell, which represents both fossil fuel and renewable energy interests, sees little chance that the legislation will pass by the end of the year.

“In a situation where one side has won a tremendous landslide, they are usually not set to do a lot of lame-duck production,” he said in a post-election webinar. “With something like permitting reform, the Democrats might rightly say that they’d like to negotiate their own version of it.”

Although it might be difficult to imagine Democrats finding common ground with Trump on the issues, Segal noted that some of the most significant U.S. environmental and energy laws have been enacted during periods of divided government in Washington: for example, the National Environmental Policy Act and the original Clean Air Act in 1970, the big Clean Air Act amendments in 1990, and the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007.

“When there’s a distribution of leverage, you can create the conditions for advancing legislation, provided that people on both sides of the aisle don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good,” Segal said. “Almost every major environmental statute occurred under exactly these circumstances, with Dems controlling both houses of Congress and a strong Republican in the White House.”

Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) said Wednesday that he is waiting to see an amendment drafted by the bill’s Senate co-sponsors before deciding whether he supports the legislation. The amendment, whose text has not been disclosed, responds to some of the objections, including that the bill may tie the hands of a future president’s ability to oppose projects.

“There were some pretty significant structural problems with the first version that came out,” Casten said in a conference call that primarily focused on election results.

Kircher, the Purdue mechanical engineering professor, published his report on the bill this week, aiming to provide a more comprehensive assessment than previous analyses, which focused largely on the power sector provisions and overlooked other parts of the legislation with potential emissions implications.

Kircher built a model that calculates the bill’s potential effects, comparing a baseline of 2025 data with a hypothetical 2025 in which the measure was law. He found the bill would increase revenue and jobs in both fossil fuel and clean energy industries, with larger increases for fossil fuels. The bill also would likely increase energy-related greenhouse gas emissions and deaths attributable to air pollution from fossil fuels.

He weighed the trade-offs between negative effects, such as air pollution deaths, and positive ones, such as accelerating renewable energy construction. For example, he found that clean electricity revenue would increase by $2.1 million per life lost due to additional pollution from fossil fuels. This is much less than the roughly $12 million per-life cost standard that the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency has used to evaluate environmental policies, he said.

“I am for making reasonable compromises to get the good things we want out of our energy system, such as accelerating renewable energy development,” Kircher said in an interview. “That said, I don’t think the compromises in this version of BAAJA are reasonable, and I have a hard time seeing that changing without a major overhaul of the bill.”

Other analyses have found a net emissions benefit, with lower emissions under the bill than a baseline scenario. Much of the benefit comes from provisions that make it easier to build transmission lines and connect more renewable energy projects to the grid. But by focusing solely on power-sector benefits, the analyses miss some of the bill’s most concerning parts, Kircher said.

Opposition to the permitting bill has grown as environmental advocates have scrutinized it. One concern is the bill’s “ permit certainty ” provision, designed to protect renewable projects from the kind of moves the Trump administration has made to stall already approved projects. But environmentalists warn the provisions also could make it tougher to challenge fossil fuel projects, even when new evidence emerges of harm to water or land resources.

Environmental groups praised Jeffries’ criticism of the bill.

“We’re grateful that Leader Jeffries made a very wise move that sends a good faith signal that he’s accounting for the full range of interests in the Democratic caucus and is rightly cautious about sparking a bloody factional fight days after a historic political victory,” said Erik Schlenker-Goodrich, executive director of the Western Environmental Law Center.

Meanwhile, clean energy business groups have not wavered in their support for the bill, even as criticism has intensified. They are highlighting the potential to reduce consumer prices after an election in which affordability was a top issue.

“BAAJA is the best opportunity Congress has to lower prices right now, and they should not delay action on that,” said Dylan Reed, managing director of federal and political affairs for Advanced Energy United, a trade group, in a Thursday conference call. “We support passage of that bill and getting it done before the end of this Congress.”

scraped.title: As Data Centers Move In, Iowa Residents Fight Plans for a New Gas Plant - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: Months of community opposition and a rejected rezoning request have cast doubt on the future of a proposed peaker plant in the state’s second-largest county.
scraped.author: By Anika Jane Beamer
scraped.h1: As Data Centers Move In, Iowa Residents Fight Plans for a New Gas Plant
scraped.body_text:
FAIRFAX, Iowa—Nearly 50 people gathered at the American Legion Post on a July evening to learn about a proposed natural gas plant less than three miles from town. Seated in folding chairs, they pulled out their phones and typed responses to a simple question: How are you feeling?

The words “angry,” “disgusted” and “scared” flashed across a TV screen at the front of the room.

For many, the meeting drudged up a familiar feeling of frustration.

Nine months earlier, Interstate Power and Light, an Iowa-based subsidiary of Alliant Energy, had abandoned plans to build a natural gas-fired power plant in Fairfax after fierce opposition from residents and leaders at the nearby Eastern Iowa Airport.

But the reprieve was short-lived. In March, Alliant announced plans to instead purchase land just outside of town for a new plant.

The proposed 160-acre site is in unincorporated Linn County territory, right over the border from neighboring Benton County. The cities of Fairfax, Atkins and Cedar Rapids, home to a combined 140,000 residents, all fall within three miles of the proposed plant. The facilities’ 150-foot-tall exhaust towers would emit carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, particulate matter and volatile organic compounds.

From the podium at the American Legion, Jon Lee, a spokesperson for the grassroots group Save Morgan Valley, urged his neighbors to remain engaged with plans for the plant. “Big decisions like this deserve real answers,” Lee said. “Stay informed, and keep showing up.”

All summer long, the group mobilized opposition. Members invited neighbors to town halls, filed testimony with the Iowa Utilities Commission and presented a united front in matching orange shirts at county zoning commission and board of supervisor meetings.

Their persistence is paying off.

In October, the three-person Linn County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to reject Alliant’s rezoning request for the proposed site, after nearly four hours of comments from residents and Alliant representatives.

Concerns raised by residents at the hearing spanned land use, water use and utility rates. But comments repeatedly returned to the projected emissions of the proposed plant.

“We’re living in an era of extraordinary technological advancement, and yet when it comes to powering that advancement we’re being told that building another fossil fuel power plant is the answer,” Jenny Kellison, of Fairfax, told the supervisors. “I find that incredibly disappointing.”

Supervisor Sami Scheetz voted against the rezoning request, arguing that Alliant’s proposal failed to meet county requirements for water and wastewater infrastructure. Still, he told Inside Climate News, the board’s decision reflected “overwhelming,” bipartisan community opposition to the plant being built.

“What was really important for me was a constituent just asking me, ‘Do you think this is good for the community?’ And I really didn’t feel comfortable saying yes to that,” Scheetz said.

According to Alliant’s filings with the Iowa Utilities Commission, the Morgan Valley Energy Center would consist of three single-cycle combustion turbines, designed to start up quickly during periods of high load demand. The application notes possible plans to expand to a combined-cycle facility in the future.

“We are disappointed with the Linn County Board of Supervisors’ decision not to approve the Morgan Valley Energy Center application,” Alliant wrote in a statement to Inside Climate News.

“We’re living in an era of extraordinary technological advancement, and yet when it comes to powering that advancement we’re being told that building another fossil fuel power plant is the answer.”

The proposed power plant “is critical to meeting growing energy demand and supporting the reliable electric service that customers and communities depend on,” the utility added. “Alliant Energy has decades of experience safely operating energy infrastructure under rigorous regulatory and environmental oversight.”

Single-cycle gas “peaker” plants are significantly less fuel-efficient than combined-cycle plants, resulting in higher carbon dioxide emissions per unit of power generated. The Morgan Valley Energy Center would produce roughly one and a half million tons of carbon dioxide equivalents each year, according to Alliant’s air construction permit application with the state Department of Natural Resources.

While Alliant has not directly linked the additional generation to multiple hyper-scale data centers under development in and around Cedar Rapids, several company representatives acknowledged during the October hearing that the data centers have driven load growth across their service area.

“Alliant Energy does not build generation to serve a single customer or industry,” said Ben Rogers, a senior community and public affairs specialist for Alliant and a former Linn County supervisor. “Data centers are an important source of new demand, but they are not the only reason the electric system must continue to evolve.”

Google and QTS are currently building side-by-side data center campuses on a 1,000-acre industrial lot in Cedar Rapids. When completed, the two campuses will use a combined 1.6 gigawatts of electricity.

This summer, the Linn County Board of Supervisors approved an 18-month moratorium on rezoning applications for large-scale data centers in unincorporated county territory. But the pause doesn’t apply to data centers in incorporated cities, including those in Cedar Rapids.

Google also moved to annex unincorporated Linn County land for a second hyper-scale data center campus into the small city of Palo this year, effectively freeing the project from county jurisdiction. That campus will purchase energy generated by the restarted Duane Arnold Energy Center , Iowa’s only nuclear facility.

The electricity demand spurred by data centers being built in Linn County cannot be overstated, said John Zakrasek, director of the nonprofit organization Linn Clean Energy District and board member of the Clean Energy Districts of Iowa.

If all three hyperscale campuses are built to full capacity, they will increase Linn County’s projected electricity demand nearly fivefold. “How are we going to meet that electricity demand? If we’re going to do it with fossil fuel plants, gas plants, and so on, we’re going to go ahead and push emissions way up,” Zakrasek said.

In 2019, Linn County adopted a climate resolution setting a goal of net-zero carbon dioxide emissions by 2050.

The proposed Morgan Valley Energy Center would run anywhere from 1,230 to 3,950 hours a year, according to filings with the Iowa Utilities Commission. At the high end, the facility would more than double Linn County’s current annual natural gas consumption, Zakrasek calculates.

The project fits into a nationwide trend of utilities turning to natural gas power plants to meet load growth from data centers. In states like Iowa with significant renewable energy infrastructure, gas peaker plants are proposed as easily dispatchable generation sources that can supplement the grid when demand spikes or wind and solar generation wane.

The Iowa Utilities Commission approved Alliant’s application for a 720-megawatt natural gas peaker plant in Marshalltown, Iowa in December.

Next month, roughly a year later, the Commission will hear arguments for and against the Morgan Valley power plant. The three-person utilities commission can overrule Linn County’s zoning decision, but the move would be unprecedented, Lee said.

Lee is one of more than 50 official intervenors in the docket, including Benton County, the Linn County Board of Supervisors and Iowa’s Office of the Consumer Advocate. In his testimony, he asked the commission to mandate a human health impact study for the proposed facility before approving the application.

“There is no reason for us to build power plants or data centers or anything if we’re harming the future generation, if we’re harming our environment,” he said.

scraped.title: Glaciers around the world are endangered — but no two are alike
scraped.description: Globally, glaciers are often lumped into one narrative of loss. These three stories show how they can still surprise us.
scraped.author: M Jackson
scraped.h1: Glaciers around the world are endangered — but no two are alike
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Δ

Globally, glaciers are often lumped into one narrative of loss. These three stories show how they can still surprise us.

Part of my work as a geographer and glacier scientist involves traveling around the world. Literally. Several times a year, I join expeditions, traversing continents and oceans, sometimes half the planet, in mere days. I’ve visited glaciers in some startling places — like Uganda’s Stanley Glacier, where ice retreat influences human health and malaria outbreaks. Or Iceland’s Breiðamerkurjökull, where glacier change is exacerbating the ice-breaking pressures of global tourism . Or South Georgia’s Heaney Glacier, where ice retreat has provided expansive real estate for one of the largest King penguin colonies on Earth.

My job is to translate the landscape: how oceans move nutrients pole to pole; why one mountain might support snow but another does not; how glaciers shape societies.

I’ll own it’s a peculiar way to experience the world.

From 30,000 feet, borders fall away. Trees become forests become systems become a living planet. I see connections everywhere. But that view from 30,000 feet, while striking, can miss much of what’s unfolding below at the individual level — the people, the lives, the histories.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Glaciers, I think, suffer from this same problem of perspective. We tend to see them from a great distance, as a single global story.

They’re tallied together: Some 275,000 individual glaciers remain worldwide . They’re measured together: how quickly they are shrinking, how much they impact sea level change, how long before they are gone. How many of them already are.

But glaciers have never lived identical lives. My work has shown over and over that every glacier has a distinct life history, shaped by and shaping the communities, landscapes, and systems around it. As glaciers change, we aren’t witnessing a single global glacier story from 30,000 feet. We are witnessing hundreds of thousands of individual stories of transformation.

One of the most surprising is unfolding right in my own backyard.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

My most recent expedition took me to nine countries. But I started the trip in Portland, Oregon — just north of my home in Eugene — land of the exhilaratingly perfect medium roast coffee and the Cascade volcano chain I used to orient myself for most of my childhood. The first morning, I ran up to the hotel’s top floor to see if the weather was clear enough to peer 50 miles northeast toward Mount St. Helens, across the border in Washington state. From downtown, it is easy to distinguish her whaleback summit, notably slumped in comparison to the sharper profiles of Mount Hood and Mount Adams.

What isn’t visible from this distance is the secret Mount St. Helens is hiding within.

The volcano erupted in May of 1980, two years before I was born. I grew up hearing stories of how ash coated our family farm, how the afternoon sky turned murky, how one terrified horse kicked through her box stall door. What I didn’t learn until much, much later was that, prior to the eruption, Mount St. Helens supported 11 named glaciers and two small unnamed ones. The nine-hour Plinian eruption destroyed 70 percent of the mountain’s ice, including the Loowit and Leschi glaciers, while the summit and entire north flank collapsed, leaving behind a horseshoe-shaped crater roughly two miles wide.

If you’ve ever received a climbing permit from the U.S. Forest Service, hiked to the crater rim, and gazed into that windy bowl of pumice and dark basalts, I can almost guarantee the very last word on your mind is “nursery.” Trust me. I rocked my baby in a softly-lit Scandinavian-paletted room designed for every possible infant need. But Mount St. Helens, apparently a fan of free-range parenting, took another approach. And it worked. Inside that raw volcanic maw, a baby glacier is growing inside.

The eruption that destroyed most of Mount St. Helens’ glaciers also created the perfect conditions to grow a new one.

Winter after winter, snow fell on the volcano’s steep headwall, and then it avalanched, repeatedly, into the crater floor below. By September 1996, scientists observed that the 16-year-old body of snow and ice had begun to move, flow. This fact is existential — glaciers are defined as moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year. When glaciers stop moving, they are “dead” — it’s not just loss of volume that threatens their identity as glaciers. The Okjökull glacier in Iceland was declared dead in 2014 when it stopped flowing; in 2019, the nation held a funeral for it .

But here, the opposite has happened.

Welcome to the world, Crater Glacier.

There is something equally wonderful and strange about being almost exactly the same age as a glacier. We’re both children of the 80s, who grew up under the same Cascade volcanoes. I became a glaciologist; she became a glacier.

And we’ve both had setbacks. Me: paying my bills, becoming a mother, and learning, repeatedly, that adulthood rarely follows the topography you planned.

Crater Glacier: Mount St. Helens, in 2004, erupted again. Magma began pushing up beneath her. A lava dome swelled through the crater floor and into the glacier itself — the first time scientists observed the emplacement of a lava dome through glacier ice .

It split her in two.

As the dome grew, the now separate arms of the glacier deformed, then thickened and sped up, flowing 1 to 2 feet (30 to 60 centimeters) per day . Within four years, those arms stretched all the way around the lava dome and rejoined. And the glacier kept going. Between 2009 and 2019, she gained some 13.8 million cubic meters of ice and advanced more than a thousand feet.

My colleagues have noted that her advance is slowing. Eventually, warming Pacific Northwest summers may overwhelm the unique climate zone inside Mount St. Helens’ crater. Or, the volcano might erupt again.

And that matters to the people living below.

Crater Glacier’s body wraps around an active vent and lava dome. A future eruption could melt ice, mix with ash, pumice, and rock and become a lahar, a fast-moving slurry of water, mud, trees, and whatever else it picks up as it races downslope. Lahars from the 1980 eruption destroyed homes, bridges, and roads. Growing up, I remember how we were taught drills for lahars alongside earthquakes and fires.

It isn’t lost on me how radically the landscape I grew up with has changed, or how much more it will change in the years to come. But, as I follow Crater Glacier’s development, I’m reminded that it isn’t all bad. This one glacier, among hundreds of thousands, is writing a story I could never have imagined.

I arrive in Baku, Azerbaijan, in July. It is sweltering.

This country has glaciers, but I won’t see them on this trip. The last time I saw ice in the Caucasus, I was on a Fulbright in Turkey, living on the Black Sea and exploring these mountains from the west. The ice I saw then would be unrecognizable today.

Between 2000 and 2020, Azerbaijan lost 77 percent of the country’s total glacier area.

To me, that’s baffling to think about: 77 percent. Over 20 years. Half my life.

And yet, almost no one I meet in Azerbaijan seems particularly interested in talking about glaciers. I risk distracting my driver, Kamran, a delightful 20-something local man who weaves through Baku’s insane, seven-lanes-of-madness traffic like it’s nothing. The Caspian Sea twinkles peacefully to our left, oil derricks lazily chugging. To our right, the city’s iconic blue-gleaming high-rises overlap with mosques and war memorials.

“We don’t bother with them,” Kamran tells me, speaking of the glaciers. He pivots quickly to Gobustan, a district south of Baku that is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Had I seen the mud volcanoes? “Tourists come all the time now to see the methane volcanoes.”

I keep encountering this indifference. My colleague, Suleyman, also doesn’t want to talk about glaciers and spends the bulk of our coffee telling me about the pending F1 race in Baku. He doesn’t even bother glancing at the map I’ve brought. Azerbaijan’s glaciers are remote, tiny, and high in the Eastern Caucasus. By 2025, 14 fragmented glaciers remain, covering together about 124 acres — roughly one-tenth of the ice that covered these mountains in the 1890s.

But glaciers here, like glaciers everywhere, are critical components of regional water cycles. Glaciers hold water — for years, decades, centuries. They are reservoirs that do not need to be constructed. And in Azerbaijan, water and water storage matter. Agriculture relies on a complex system of reservoirs, canals, and irrigation. Groundwater withdrawals have increased some fourfold since 2000, largely fueled by farms growing wheat, fruit, and vegetables.

In 2025, researchers climbed Azerbaijan’s Tufandag Glacier and reported retreat, accelerated melting, and expanding crevasses. Below it, the Mahmuddara River had increased water levels and discharge rates.

This is how a glacier can disappear in plain sight: by transforming into liquid. As a glacier melts, it releases more water downstream. And for that reason, the current precipitous decline of Azerbaijan’s glaciers is almost a boon. Glacier becomes meltwater, river, irrigation, drinking water, wheat, lettuce, peaches. Farmers rejoice.

But, eventually, too much ice dissolves and the runoff peaks, then decreases. In glaciology, we call this “peak water,” when a disappearing glacier gives us the most water it ever will. The cycle of savings and withdrawals that has defined this landscape for centuries will ultimately end like this, when the bank is forced to close.

Has Tufandag Glacier, or any of Azerbaijan’s 13 other glaciers, crossed that threshold? I don’t know. The increased flow of the Mahmuddara is only one measurement, from one glacier, that cannot fully answer that question.

But I can think back to the ice I saw in these same mountains years ago, then look at the Caucasus today, and I understand that it has transformed. Water that was ice, storage, cold is now warm liquid moving downstream.

Azerbaijan’s remaining glaciers may not survive this century. People in the coming years are going to have to do what glaciers once did — come up with more ways to store more water. Catch it when it arrives and hold it until it’s needed.

I keep thinking about the apparent indifference many Azerbaijanis show towards glaciers. Maybe Kamran’s response is more revealing than I initially thought.

Perhaps the first step of a glacier disappearing from a landscape is it disappearing from conversation.

If you ever get a chance, wander through the Tateyama Museum in Toyama Prefecture, Japan. The exquisite open-air museum explores the nearby Mount Tateyama as both landscape and sacred place: a perennially snow-covered mountain, a dwelling place of spirits and the dead, a realm containing hell and heaven.

There is a poem there by the eighth-century poet Ōtomo no Yakamochi about Tateyama’s summer snow and its association with the divine. It stops me. Some 1,300 years ago, people were already writing — marveling — about the snow that refused to disappear.

Japan’s Sea-of-Japan side is one of the snowiest places on Earth, a skier’s powder paradise. And yet, for years, my colleagues and I thought no glaciers existed east of Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula. The landscape was too warm, the mountains too low, to support glaciers under today’s conditions.

For glaciers — moving bodies of land ice that persist year after year — the base variables are critical: snow, time, and temperature. But those variables do interact with intensely local conditions such as wind, topography, shade — even human activity. It matters where snow falls, where it blows, and where a landscape and people allow it to accumulate.

Japan is technically not cold enough long enough to support glaciers. But it is extraordinarily snowy.

When I flew over Tateyama in June, most of the three-peaked massif was gray — alpine bare, with significant snow melt. But I did see a few Dalmatian-like white pockets in shaded nooks and north-facing crannies. If I hadn’t known better, I would have just labeled them as snow patches. Remember: Definitionally, a glacier must flow under its own weight. More movement is a sign of a healthy glacier.

Snow patches, regardless of how long they’ve existed or if they contain ice, do not move.

Everyone in the bustling world of cryospheric research knew Japan had snow patches. More than 100 had been identified in the northern Japanese Alps alone.

In the 1970s, researchers began observing holes in Kuranosuke — one such snow patch, roughly 6 acres in area — that looked and behaved like glacial features called moulins. In 1979, a Japanese researcher investigated one of the moulins by using the time-honored glaciological technique of climbing directly into it. He discovered layers of ancient ice, an observation supported later by radiocarbon analysis of embedded wood and leaf debris that were dated to approximately 1,700 years old.

Old, yes. But old does not make a glacier. Movement does.

And so Kuranosuke remained, scientifically speaking, for decades and decades, a snow patch.

But then, starting in 2009, researchers Kotaro Fukui and Hajime Iida of the Tateyama Caldera Sabo Museum used state-of-the-art geodetic measurements and ground-penetrating radar to take a closer look at several well-known perennial snow patches in the Japanese Alps. They showed that the Gozenzawa, Sannomado, and Komado snow patches were, in fact, flowing. They were glaciers .

Take that in. I have spent my entire life watching ice disappear faster than we can understand it. Yet here are glaciers we never knew existed. It makes me immediately wonder — what other ones might be out there, if only we had time, resources, and the will to look?

The researchers turned to Kuranosuke next. They found that the snow patch was flowing roughly 3 centimeters a year — the equivalent width of one of the LEGO bricks my son always leaves on our stairs. An almost absurdly small measurement, but 3 centimeters is still flow. Movement. This transformed Kuranosuke from a snow patch into a glacier.

Still, identities are never quite so fixed. Recently, Kukui, Iida, and Tomoyoshi Kosaka have argued that Kuranosuke is in the midst of another slow transformation. As Japan warms, its glaciers and snow patches are losing crucial ice mass. They say that Kuranosuke is declining. It exists now in a nebulous no-scientist’s-land between glacier and snow patch, blurring the very boundaries of glacierhood.

One could easily look at that as a poignant story of loss: This glacier is dying, and we’ve barely had a chance to really know her. But when I look at Kuranosuke, I see a story of persistence. For at least 1,700 years, some form of ice and snow has held here, through centuries of summers, through blurring with the divine, through recognition as perennial snow patch and then glacier.

And now, glacier-in-transformation.

I don’t think the disappearance of Kuranosuke will diminish local people’s reverence for Tateyama. If anything, as the mountain’s once-perennial snow and ice disappear, Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem may take on even greater meaning. For 1,300 years, these words and this snow have persisted. We may be the last generation to witness them together.

For all these glaciers, and countless others, their stories are neither simple nor predictable. These are not merely stories of inches lost. If anything, they prove that we are far from certain about what the future holds. Kuranosuke and her neighbors defied decades of settled science by asserting their existence as glaciers. Tufandag is bringing abundance to the river and farms below it — though for how much longer, we don’t know. And Crater Glacier is still growing, thriving as so many others dissolve. I find something profoundly moving in that.

And me? I’m still circling the planet, collecting glacier stories. Maybe, like Ōtomo no Yakamochi’s poem, we’ll need them someday.

To remember.

Good Friday morning.

Here is what’s on President Trump’s agenda today: 8:00 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in Executive Time 10:30 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Pre-Tape Interview 11:30 AM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting 12:30 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Policy Meeting 1:30 PM THE PRESIDENT participates in a Diwali Celebration 6:00 PM THE PRESIDENT delivers Remarks

Two minutes of hate:

The Democrats’ campaign promises of kitchen table issues and affordability is materializing. The judicial system has been largely captured by progressive lunatics and the left has been plotting to colonize the Supreme Court with crazed partisans to transform our established system of laws and fairness for a long time. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said Thursday that the incoming Democratic majority would refuse to confirm a conservative Supreme Court nominee selected by Trump. Schumer also indicated that Democrats would scrutinize nominees for lower federal courts and executive positions, arguing that the election gave his party a mandate to challenge the administration. He declined to say whether Democrats would leave a Supreme Court vacancy unfilled until after the 2028 presidential election.

A good example of the way the left intends the judicial branch to be another vehicle for political activism, is the unprecedented leak of the Supreme Court’s decision on the Dobbs case. The Justice Department has intensified its investigation into the unauthorized disclosure of the Supreme Court’s draft opinion overturning Roe v. Wade in 2022. According to reporting originally published by the New York Times , federal prosecutors have issued grand jury subpoenas seeking testimony and information from individuals who worked at the Supreme Court when the draft opinion was leaked. U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro is overseeing the investigation, with assistance from senior prosecutors and career Justice Department attorneys. The original leak occurred approximately two months before the Court formally issued its decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization , which overturned the constitutional abortion-rights framework established by Roe .

More good news for California residents. Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he would commute the sentences of all 548 prisoners on California’s death row, replacing their death sentences with life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. Newsom described capital punishment as inconsistent with California’s values and argued that the state should no longer maintain a death-row population. The decision represents the largest mass commutation of death sentences in American history. California has not carried out an execution in approximately two decades, and Newsom previously imposed a moratorium on executions. His latest action goes further by replacing the sentences themselves.

scraped.title: Plastic pollution is putting an old legal doctrine to a new test
scraped.description: Public nuisance lawsuits are testing whether companies can be held responsible for pollution after their products are sold.
scraped.author: Joseph Winters
scraped.h1: Plastic pollution is putting an old legal doctrine to a new test
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

Plastic pollution blights the streets, beaches, parks, and lawns of Baltimore. A significant amount of that litter bears the circular red-and-blue Pepsi logo or the flowing white script of Coca-Cola’s branding.

But, legally speaking, none of that rubbish is Pepsi’s fault. Or Coke’s.

That’s what a Baltimore city circuit court judge ruled this summer following a legal battle in which the city and county of Baltimore sought money from PepsiCo, Coca-Cola , and others to clean up plastic pollution. Companies “conducting lawful activities,” wrote Judge Audrey J.S. Carrión, referring to the sale of single-use plastics, “should not be held liable under public nuisance claims because others are misusing the products in an unlawful manner.”

In other words, plastic pollution is a problem of consumer behavior, not corporate irresponsibility. As far as the state’s public nuisance law is concerned, a company’s liability ends at the point of sale.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Similar reasoning scuttled a public nuisance lawsuit the state of New York filed against PepsiCo and Frito-Lay and has arisen in similar litigation from Missouri to California . As environmental advocates and governments continue to develop this legal theory, those setbacks raise a fundamental question: When does a company’s responsibility for its products end? And can public nuisance laws succeed in making polluters pay?

The notion of public nuisance dates to 13th-century English common law and traditionally applied to violations of rights shared by the public, such as access to clean air. Since the 1970s, plaintiffs have increasingly tried to apply that idea to manufacturers whose products allegedly jeopardize public health, safety, and access to a clean environment.

These lawsuits, however, have “a mixed record of success,” said Timothy Lytton, a professor at the Georgia State University College of Law. Cases against opioid manufacturers , e-cigarette companies , and even the landmark litigation against Big Tobacco have sometimes succeeded — but mostly by securing favorable settlements, not because judges ruled in favor of the public-nuisance arguments.

Cases that have been heard, meanwhile, have struggled to convince judges of “causation,” or the idea that corporate defendants are substantially responsible for violating a public right. Judges are wary of extending corporations’ liability past the lawful sale of their products, particularly when those products aren’t used as intended . If a doctor or patient diverts opioids to the black market, for example, are the manufacturers responsible for the resulting harm?

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

This is essentially what Carrión said in the Baltimore case. It also echoes questioning from Justice Stephen Lindley last month as he heard arguments in the appeal of New York’s Pepsi lawsuit. “If [Pepsi] has to pay for the cleanup when somebody else is littering, … it’s not going to be sustainable,” he told the plaintiff’s lawyers. He appeared sympathetic to PepsiCo attorney Andrew Tulumello’s argument that the state had a “honking causation problem”: Pepsi, Tulumello said, “is not encouraging people to throw stuff in the litter.”

According to Albert Lin, co-director of the California Environmental Law and Policy Center at the University of California, Davis, there are three basic elements of a successful public-nuisance lawsuit. The first is demonstrating “substantial interference with a public right.” The second is causation — linking a defendant to that interference. The third, he said, is negligence, intent, or other “ tortious conduct ” in the defendant’s activities.

Environmental groups and governments are trying to get around the point-of-sale argument by linking causation and conduct: Plastics companies, they argue, are responsible for the pollution and knew their actions would harm public rights . Courts will therefore pay close attention to “foreseeability” — whether it was foreseeable that plastic would end up as litter, Lin said. As Lytton put it, manufacturers allegedly acted “in a way that foreseeably increases the risk of misuse.” The word “foreseeable” appears 22 times in Baltimore’s complaint.

Plaintiffs have evidence they can point to in arguing that plastic pollution was foreseeable. At least some manufacturers have known for decades that mass production of single-use plastics would contribute to environmental pollution , and that recycling would be unable to manage the problem . The lawsuits also cite microplastics contamination as part of the alleged nuisance, and an investigation published last week by the Los Angeles Times found that industry scientists have known since at least the 1970s that microplastics could lodge in humans’ bodies.

That history informs the framing offered by Scott Hochberg, general counsel and litigation director for the nonprofit Earth Island Institute. “Companies induced consumers to purchase these products while knowing the likelihood that they would end up as trash,” he said. “And that’s exactly what happened.”

Whether this framing succeeds may depend, in part, on the jurisdiction. In addition to the causation requirement for public-nuisance lawsuits, Lin said some states have a higher standard for demonstrating that defendants had “control” over their products at the time the nuisance occurred. New York and Maryland are two such states. California, on the other hand, is not, and courts there have so far proven more receptive to plastics public nuisance suits.

Judge Richard Seeborg of the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, who is overseeing two lawsuits against Exxon Mobil Corp., allowed one — from the Sierra Club — to proceed to trial . (He has not yet ruled on the other one, brought by the state’s attorney general .)

But even in California, surviving an early challenge is no guarantee of success. A judge there allowed Earth Island Institute’s public-nuisance claim — which rested in part on allegedly misleading recycling labels — against 10 food and beverage companies, but it was ultimately rejected earlier this year in a summary judgment. Earth Island plans to appeal.

Pepsi, Coca-Cola, and Exxon Mobil did not respond to Grist’s requests for comment.

Lin said it’s still “early days” for this legal theory, and the rejections do not necessarily signal a losing strategy. He noted, however, that the courts have shown significant skepticism for public nuisance in ongoing climate litigation, and a case the Supreme Court is hearing this term could make it more difficult for cities and states to bring such claims in the future.

Lin added that in climate lawsuits, plaintiffs have leaned more heavily on fossil fuel companies’ allegedly deceptive conduct, invoking consumer protection and false advertising claims that can be easier to substantiate than those based on public nuisance. Plastics plaintiffs could pursue a similar strategy, he said, potentially winning damages — though likely not orders requiring companies to clean up the pollution their products create.

Public nuisance laws could face new constraints at the state level, too. Last year, Montana enacted a first-of-its-kind law preempting state and local public-nuisance lawsuits based on “lawful activities,” while Kansas and Utah have since enacted their own restrictions. All three states’ laws are connected to model legislation drafted by the American Legislative Exchange Council, a conservative policy organization that brings together state lawmakers and private-sector members to develop model legislation.

Whatever their ultimate outcome in court, Lytton said plastics lawsuits can “win” in other ways — by unearthing new documents, for example, and putting the plastics issue higher on the public-policy agenda. They also provide an opportunity for plaintiffs to refute the plastics industry’s consumer-responsibility narrative.

“When you file a lawsuit, what you’re doing is you’re telling a story” — often about some sort of structural or corporate wrongdoing, Lytton said. “When you talk about tobacco, it’s not just about smokers. Or opioids, it’s not just about users. It’s about the companies and their design and marketing decisions. And so the framing that goes on in these [lawsuits] is moving the discussion of plastics away from ‘litterbugs’ and toward corporate responsibility.”

scraped.title: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.
scraped.author: Cecilia Keating
scraped.h1: ‘Simply staggering’: Rapidly developing ‘super El Niño’ on track to peak in December
scraped.body_text:
The ongoing “super El Niño” is likely to peak at the end of 2026 and push average global temperatures to record levels next year.

That is according to Carbon Brief’s latest “ state of the climate ” update, which analyses El Niño forecasts from more than a dozen climate models, as well as six global temperature datasets. Dr Zeke Hausfather , Carbon Brief’s climate science contributor, described this year’s El Niño as “simply staggering” when answering questions from CB+ members during a CB Connect “ ask me anything ” session.

El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern in the tropical Pacific that releases heat from the ocean into the atmosphere and temporarily boosts global temperatures.

This year’s El Niño event – which has been underway since June – has already broken a number of records and reshaped the world’s weather, fuelling fires in Indonesia and “super typhoons” in the west Pacific.

The strength of an El Niño is tracked using the “Niño3.4 anomaly”, which is a measure of how much warmer sea surface temperatures are than average in a section of the central Pacific.

Analysis of more than 600 forecasts from 14 different climate models by Hausfather for Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” update shows how models project this year’s El Niño will peak with an anomaly of around 4C. This would be more than a degree above the previous record in 2015-16.

Writing on CB Connect on 5 November, Hausfather wrote:

“This El Niño event is developing so quickly and is reaching sea surface temperatures so warm that it’s simply staggering. We haven’t seen anything like this in the historical record and it may end up being the strongest El Niño event in the past millennium.”

This year’s El Niño has already chalked up a number of milestones.

On 18 September, the daily anomaly in the Niño3.4 region broke the satellite-era record set in 2015 when it reached 3.11C.

Meanwhile, September as a whole recorded the highest monthly Niño3.4 region temperature anomaly – 2.84C – since sea surface temperature records began in the mid-1800s.

Membership

Hausfather wrote on CB Connect that this year’s El Niño had been “running well above any prior El Niño event since June, at times by a full degree [Celsius]”.

Carbon Brief’s “state of the climate” analysis indicates that El Niño is set to continue to intensify into December, with 10 out of 14 models expecting temperatures in the Niño3.4 region to peak in the final month of this year. The remainder anticipate a November peak.

While human emissions of greenhouse gases are responsible for almost all of long-term global warming, temperatures in specific years are strongly influenced by El Niño events .

The “state of the climate” analysis explains that this year’s El Niño event will have its largest effect on global temperatures in 2027. This is because global temperatures typically lag warming in the tropical Pacific by around three months.

Carbon Brief projects that the 2027 average global temperature will reach around 1.74C above pre-industrial levels. It calculates a 96% chance that next year will be the warmest on record.

This projection is based on the historical relationship between year-on-year temperature changes and El Niño conditions the preceding autumn. It also factors in uncertainty around how global temperatures will develop across the remainder of 2026.

scraped.description: Committees in both chambers are posting jobs for oversight lawyers as party leaders promise subpoenas, probes and possibly impeachment.
scraped.h1: Democrats Start Hiring Investigators to Target Trump Administration Before Taking Power
scraped.body_text:
Democrats have wasted no time gearing up to investigate the Trump administration, posting jobs for oversight lawyers just a day after winning control of Congress, Politico reported.

House Judiciary Committee Democrats are seeking counsels and staff for “policy, oversight, investigative, and legislative work” in the new Congress that begins in January. Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the panel’s top Democrat, is expected to become chairman and gain subpoena power.

In the Senate, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, who is set to chair the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, posted openings for an anti-corruption counsel and for investigators and oversight counsel.

Democrats are not hiding their targets. Hassan challenged former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem on X: “Want to say that under oath?” Rep. Delia Ramirez of Illinois wrote, “Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what’s up? Clear your schedule.”

House Homeland Security Committee Democrats posted, “If you broke the law to enrich yourself or your cronies at DHS at taxpayers’ expense, we will find you and hold you accountable. That is a promise.” The committee also sent Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin a letter demanding that DHS preserve documents ahead of investigations.

Raskin has accused the president of “profound corruption” and said in September that the administration has “basically converted the president’s pardon power into a for-profit industry.” Some Democrats have openly discussed impeachment, including Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, who said he now supports impeaching Trump.
