scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Tuesday was a historic night for progressive Democrats and, in particular, candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Six new DSA -endorsed candidates were elected to the House, and democratic socialists won mayoral races in Los Angeles, Washington, D.C., and Providence.

“The Democratic Socialists of America had a phenomenal night, and this movement is only going to continue to grow,” says prominent leftist political commentator Hasan Piker. “Now, here’s the problem: Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are two of the least popular politicians in the country right now, and there are demands to change the leadership in the Democratic Party to reflect the desires of this new coalition that was developed on November 3.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

Tuesday night wasn’t just a blue tsunami, or “bluenami.” It was a historic night for progressive Democrats, in particular candidates backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, DSA . Six new DSA -backed candidates were elected to the House: Angela Gonzales-Torres in California, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier here in New York, Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Donavan McKinney in Michigan and Melat Kiros in Colorado, representing Denver. Currently, just two sitting lawmakers, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Rashida Tlaib, are DSA members. And in Los Angeles, democratic socialist City Councilmember Nithya Raman, an immigrant from India, defeated the incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, who conceded Thursday.

For more on the record victory by democratic socialists and progressives, like Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, we’re joined now from Los Angeles by the popular left political commentator Hasan Piker, one of the most prominent online influencers, with millions of followers. His live stream on Twitch was the second most watched individual broadcast on election night, after only NBC News’ live stream. That’s according to Reuters. Hasan Piker joins us now from West Hollywood, California.

Hasan, welcome back to Democracy Now! Your views on what has taken place in this country? How would you characterize it? And what are you expecting from these candidates who have now won?

HASAN PIKER : I think what happened on Tuesday was the final chapter of MAGA closing, after a decade of death and destruction and destabilization. I’ve thought quite a bit about this. I feel like even 2020, given that Joe Biden’s margin of victory did not feel the same way, given that 2020 happened in the backdrop of COVID , did not completely destroy the Trump movement in the same way that November 3rd did. Very exciting.

I think there’s a lot of hunger. This is — a lot of hunger for change. This is something that I observed early on in the oligarchy — “Stop the Oligarchy” rallies that Bernie and AOC were conducting all around the country. It’s something that I saw at the ICE protests. And it’s also something that I saw at the No Kings rallies that were taking place. So, I would say the Democratic Party, and the anti-Trump coalition broadly, got sick and tired of the corruption. They got sick and tired of the impacts on the economy. And they came out, and they voted against the Republicans. They voted for Democrats.

But I also want to talk about what kind of Democrats they voted for. In many blue districts, very clearly, especially in these contentious primaries, a lot of Democrats, lifelong Democrats, came out and voted for figures that in the past would have been billed as radical by mainstream media, corporate media, and also certainly the party bosses. It seems to me like people wanted to place the interests of the working class over the interests of corporations for once. And the Democratic Socialists of America had a phenomenal night, and this movement is only going to continue to grow.

But also, what I heard in terms of rhetoric, from the likes of James Talarico, or even Jon Ossoff, or Annie Andrews in South Carolina, or even Colom in Mississippi, is the left populist rage that they were able to tap into. If you were to look back at some of these candidates who are now being billed as moderates by party bosses who want to regain the narrative over what took place on Tuesday, if you were to listen to what they had to say, if you were to simply read out their comments on the rallies, their acceptance speeches, you would hear Bernie Sanders’s voice being echoed through many of these campaigns all across the country. I believe that this is a testament to where the party’s at, and I believe this is a testament to where the voters are at, the fact that they were able to — the fact that they rewarded people like Talarico, who very clearly designed his campaign around the simple principle that this was, as a matter of fact, class warfare that was taking place, that the billionaire class was actually engaging in class warfare and winning, that it wasn’t about a distinction between left versus right, but more so up versus down. And that is, in my opinion, the true, fascinating story of November 3rd.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Hasan, in a recent piece for the Black Agenda Report , Ajamu Baraka wrote that this election was, quote, “a setback for Donald Trump and the Republican Party. But they should not be confused with a defeat of the political forces driving the consolidation of fascism in the United States and globally.” What do you think are the next steps for voters and progressives who want to see this blue wave actually turn into real, material change?

HASAN PIKER : Great question. So, what people are demanding right now — and I see this personally on the streets, and I also certainly see this on the internet — is real, tangible changes. We want files and trials. We want, to use an expletive, belt to ass, is what the attitude is that many Democrats are demanding, and not just socialists or progressives, not just people that would otherwise be considered radicals, but straightforward, lifelong Democrats, people that self-identify as liberals. They want accountability. They want law and order. And they want to put an end to the corruption, the lawlessness and disorder that’s come from the White House, where Trump has only enriched himself and his immediate family members, and also members of the Epstein class.

Now, here’s the problem: Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer are two of the least popular politicians in the country right now. And there are demands to change the leadership in the Democratic Party to reflect the desires of this new coalition that was developed on November 3rd. Will the Democrats actually follow through on this?

Well, things that I’ve seen from the oversight Dems, including the demand to lawyer up, or the threat, rather, to lawyer up, show me that there is some positive changes taking place. But what needs to happen going forward in order to ensure that this defeat of MAGA is permanent, to ensure that there are real consequences for those in positions of power, and to make sure that this truly becomes an anti-fascist coalition, the Democrats have to do the unthinkable: They have to listen to the demands of their voters. They have to follow through on their just and righteous desires.

We have to, of course, scale back on endless militarism all around the world, another demand that voters have made. Very clearly, a big part of the reason why this election was such a wipeout of Republicans across the board was not just because of the gas prices, but also because of the Iran war. So, I will make sure that we continue marshaling the forces necessary to not only hold the Republicans accountable, but to hold the Democrats to account, as well, if they don’t follow through on these promises that they’ve made.

AMY GOODMAN : Hasan, we just have a minute. Number one, do you think Bernie Sanders should run for the Democratic majority leader in the Senate?

HASAN PIKER : Bernie Sanders can run for anything he wants to, and I would support him. But yes, I think — I think Bernie Sanders is far more reflective of the wishes of the Democratic base of support. So —

AMY GOODMAN : And I —

HASAN PIKER : Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : I wanted to also ask you about your own lawsuit now against Scott Jennings, a major CNN commentator, was being considered apparently to be the press secretary for President Trump now. You have launched a more than $70 million lawsuit against him for mischaracterizing what you’ve said. We only have 30 seconds. Your comment?

HASAN PIKER : I think Republicans need to realize that their days are numbered. They can no longer lie with impunity. If they won’t retract their statements, if they won’t stop the lies, then we’ll make them stop.

AMY GOODMAN : Hasan Piker, we want to thank you for being with us, prominent left political commentator and live-streamer on Twitch, had one of the most popular broadcasts on election night, vying with, larger than most of the corporate networks.

We want to wish a happy birthday to Emily Andersen and John Hamilton!

Oh, Steal This Story, Please! , the documentary about Democracy Now! , is now available on many streaming platforms, from Amazon Prime to YouTube to Apple TV and Google Play, in Canada and the United States. Go to StealThisStory.org to see where you can watch it. And Steal This Story, Please! will be screening at the IFC in New York on November 11th at 4:30. Check our website at democracynow.org. I’ll be speaking afterwards with the directors, Tia Lessin and Carl Deal. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González, for another edition of Democracy Now!

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: National Politics Will Never Be the Same: Juan González on How Latino Voters Remade the Political Map
scraped.description: The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago voted for Democrats in large numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate. Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in an historic victory, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Democratic Latino governors.
scraped.h1: You turn to us for voices you won't hear anywhere else.
scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latinos vote for Democrats. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago voted for Democrats in large numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate. Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in an historic victory, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Democratic Latino governors.

“Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state,” says Democracy Now! co-host Juan Gonzalez. “Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman, with Juan González.

The midterms saw a landslide of Latino voters towards Democrats in state after state. In Texas, California, Kansas and Colorado, Latinos who had voted for Republicans just two years ago swung to Democrats in huge numbers, helping secure Democratic control of both the House and the Senate.

Latino lawmakers will make up about a fifth of the Democratic majority in the House. And in historic victories, the two most populous states in the country, California and Texas, will soon be led by Latinx Democratic governors. On Tuesday night, Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa defeated the incumbent Republican Governor Greg Abbott with a margin of over 700,000 votes. This is a clip from her speech.

GOV .- ELECT GINA HINOJOSA : I am a daughter of the Rio Grande Valley, where the people embody the work ethic and values of our great state, where no one would have imagined that one day a little girl from the RGV would stand before you here as the next governor of the greatest state, Texas.

AMY GOODMAN : That was Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa speaking in Austin, Texas, right after she was declared the winner.

And this is California Governor-elect Xavier Becerra addressing supporters Tuesday night in Sacramento after he easily defeated Republican challenger Steve Hilton.

GOV .- ELECT XAVIER BECERRA : Ladies and gentlemen, you have now entered the Becerra era. Tonight, I have a message for all those who have been made to feel afraid. There’s a new sheriff in town, and he’s got a law degree and a union card. If anyone wants to come after California or any one Californian, they better be ready for a fight.

AMY GOODMAN : For more on the significance of these victories, we turn to Juan González, yes, co-host of Democracy Now! , author of, among other books, Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America .

Juan, can you talk about this massive Latino victory across the country? What was expected? What wasn’t expected?

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: Yeah, well, Amy, it’s been quite a week in U.S. politics, and I’ve been poring over the voting returns and the exit polls the past two days to glean a clearer sense of the trends and outcomes that maybe the major media may have missed, and not just about Latinos.

Let’s begin with the turnout, which I believe is always key. It tells you how motivated and mobilized people were. Well, nationally, the turnout was 63% of registered voters. Now, that’s high by historic standards for a midterm, because, remember, it’s always less voting in the midterms. But it’s still a lower rate than either the Biden midterm election of 2022 or the first Trump midterm elections of 2018. So, while some areas of the country may have had a historic turnout, across the country this was not the highest turnout of any midterm in recent years.

And the most notable shift occurred among white voters. They made up 73% of all ballots cast. That’s the same percentage that they made in 2022. But while they voted 58% for Republicans four years ago — and I’m comparing it midterm to midterm, not midterm to the presidential election — this time they split almost evenly between Republicans and Democrats. So you’re talking a huge shift among white voters away from the Republican Party and to the Democratic Party.

What about people of color, who represented 23% of the electorate? The turnout rate for Blacks and Latinos nationwide stayed about even, or even possibly dropped a little bit, compared to 2022. And both groups, though, shifted much more to Democrats than previously. Black voters nationwide went from about 86% to 90% this year, and Latinos moved from 60% Democratic to — it depends on who you look at. The national exit poll said it went to 64%. The New York Times voter trend says it went to 69%. But both groups shifted nationwide significantly toward Democrats.

But here’s the biggest surprise that no one has paid any attention to, is that what happened among Asian Americans. They not only doubled their share of the electorate — they went from 2% in 2022 to 4% in this year — but 71% of Asian Americans voted for Democrats. That’s a 13-point shift from what Asian Americans did in 2022. And I have to think that the wars in Gaza and Iran, the Trump administration’s banning of travel from many Asian and Middle Eastern countries, its constant belittling of that region’s countries and cultures, the deportation even of refugees from Afghanistan, all have dramatically transformed how Asian Americans view the two major political parties.

Now, there’s been a lot of attention to the Latino vote, and which I’ve been studying for decades, obviously, as you mentioned Harvest of Empire . But we have to begin with what I’ve always called the Brown Belt. That’s a vast area of six Western and Southwestern states where Latinos make up as much as 30% or more of the total population — talking about Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and California. And, of course, as you mentioned, in Texas and California, the first elected Latino governors in both of those states. But the most startling trends came at the congressional level.

Take northern Nevada, for example. Democrat and former social worker Teresa Benitez-Thompson defeated a Republican incumbent to become the first Democrat ever to win that state’s 2nd Congressional seat, a district that Trump won by 14 points in 2024. With her victory, all four of Nevada’s congressional districts are held — will be held by Democrats.

In southern Arizona, JoAnna Mendoza, a 20-year Navy and Marine Corps veteran, flipped another Republican seat. And meanwhile, an emergency room doctor, Dr. Amish Shah, a former state legislator, won the 1st Congressional District in another Republican seat with a large — a district with a large Latino population.

In Colorado, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a Latino attorney and former state legislator, defeated a Republican incumbent in a district in Denver’s northern suburbs with the highest percentage of Latino voters in the state.

Of course, Texas has been the biggest and most important red state in the country for decades, and I’ve been predicting for years that it is the key link for achieving a realignment of national politics. Remember those five [seats] that Trump ordered redrawn to elect more Republicans? Well, the voters didn’t cooperate. Democrats held on to four of those five seats. Henry Cuellar of Laredo and Vicente Gonzalez of McAllen, two moderate congressmen, prevailed in their reelections. Democrat Leticia Gutierrez rode a wave of anti-mass deportation and anti- ICE sentiment to defeat her Republican opponent in the redrawn 9th District outside of Houston. That’s the seat that Al Green, the longtime congressman, used to hold. And in the San Antonio area, former Deputy Sheriff Johnny Garcia won in the newly created 35th District. And at the same time, Republicans lost two other seats in Texas to Latino Democrats. In West Texas, former educator Katy Padilla Stout won a congressional district that had been in Republican hands for the past six elections. That’s followed the resignation of Representative Tony Gonzales in the wake of sexual misconduct and the ethics scandal. And in the lone Rio Grande Valley seat held by Republicans, the famed Grammy-winning Tejano singer Bobby Pulido, who describes himself as a conservative Democrat but favors immigration reform, he defeated Republican Monica De La Cruz, who was thought to be a rising Republican star.

Now, here’s another surprise that no one’s paid attention to, maybe the biggest Texas bright spot that has escaped notice. I’m talking about the remarkable performance by Greg Casar, the chairman of the House Progressive Caucus. He’s also a democratic socialist and someone we have interviewed on Democracy Now! numerous times. He ran for reelection, but to a seat formerly held by Congressman Lloyd Doggett, after Republicans moved Casar’s hometown of Austin out of his district and into this reconfigured district, and Doggett agreed to retire. Well, Casar won that race as expected, but he did so in a super landslide. He amassed over 254,000 votes. That’s 70,000 more votes than any other congressional candidate got in Texas this year — for a socialist in Texas. By my calculations, Casar received the fifth-highest vote in the U.S. out of all of the candidates for the 435 House seats.

The bottom line is that Texas has been suddenly transformed into a battleground state. Republicans not only lost the governor’s seat, a U.S. Senate seat, other statewide races, several state House and Senate seats, but instead of winning five new congressional seats, they ended up with a net loss of one. If Democrats are able to consolidate some of those Texas gains in the coming years, national politics will never be the same. That’s why progressive organizers and fundraisers should be looking at Texas, like the civil rights movement of the 1950s regarded Mississippi and Georgia, as the place to send resources and train new leaders for the upcoming 2028 election.

Meanwhile, over in California, all five Republican districts that Democrats redrew ended up flipping to Democrats. Two of those five went to Latinos. Randy Villegas, a progressive community college professor, won a seat in the Central Valley in the 6th District, and Linda Sánchez prevailed in Orange County’s redrawn district.

And it’s not just the Brown Belt where Latinos had an impact. In Pennsylvania, where Democrats flipped four Republican seats, 73% of the state’s Latinos voted for Democrats, according to The New York Times . That’s a 26-point shift from the 2024 election. And it almost certainly fueled Democratic victories in two of those districts, where Latinos make up 15 to 25% of the population. That’s the 8th District, around Scranton, where the city’s Democratic Mayor Paige Cognetti won, and the 7th District, around Allentown, Bethlehem, where retired firefighter Bob Brooks ousted the Republican incumbent.

So, Democrats controlling Congress, however, does not offer any certainty that a new era of progressive government is dawning in Washington. We shouldn’t forget, for example, that South Texas Democrats have historically been more conservative than those in other parts of the country. So it remains to be seen how those Texas victories will ultimately affect legislation in the new Congress.

In addition, the country’s billionaire class will doubtless ramp up its torrent of cash donations directed at the new Democratic majority, hoping to buy off enough of them or foment sufficient infighting among them to kill or stall any substantive efforts at truly progressive legislation.

So much damage has already been perpetrated on American society by the lawlessness and corruption of the Trump era that it will take who knows how long to repair. To do so, progressives will need to contend not only with their — with the billionaire class and the corporate Democrats, who never tire of conspiring to control things, with Trump for the next two years and his MAGA faithful; they must also contend with their own ultra-left activists, who will increasingly demand no compromise by the new Democratic majority, as if this week’s election was some kind of revolutionary sea change, and not just a much welcome shift in the seesaw world of late-stage neoliberal capitalism, which is what I think it is.

AMY GOODMAN : Juan González, thanks so much for that analysis. Juan, of course, co-host on Democracy Now! and author of a number of books, including Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America .

Coming up, we’ll be joined by Hasan Piker, the popular political left commentator and live-streamer, who had one of the biggest streaming broadcasts on election night, number two just after NBC , beating out the networks. He campaigned heavily in the last months with many progressives and DSA candidates. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Copper Kettle” by Stephanie Coleman and Nora Brown, performing at the Brooklyn Folk Festival. This year’s festival is this weekend, and Democracy Now! will be there.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.body_text:
Sign up for Democracy Now!'s Daily Digest to get our latest headlines and stories delivered to your inbox every day.

Mississippi’s race for the U.S. Senate remains too close to call: Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith by nearly 2,000 votes with 96% of votes counted as of Friday morning. Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 points in 2024. If elected, Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during the Reconstruction era. Colom, the former district attorney for northeast Mississippi, made the issue of affordability central to his campaign. He has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign early on.

“The entire country shifted left. But when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana,” says Cliff Albright, executive director of Black Voters Matter. That “wave of energy” was “largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place. It clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.”

“Without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, [the] wave would have been even bigger,” adds Chris Kromm, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies. “There’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.”

AMY GOODMAN : We begin today’s show in the Deep South, where Mississippi’s Senate race remains too close to call. Democrat Scott Colom is narrowly leading Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by more than 1,800 votes as election officials process provisional ballots and late-arriving mail ballots. Just two years ago, Donald Trump carried Mississippi by 23 points. If elected, Scott Colom would be the first Democrat to win the state in 40 years and the first African American since 1875, during Reconstruction.

Colom made the issue of affordability central to his campaign, and in an ad that went viral, he blasted Senator Hyde-Smith for saying Mississippians should, quote, “pick another protein,” unquote, if they’re upset over high beef prices. The ad features Mississippians saying they’d rather pick another senator.

HUGH KEETON : The price of beef continuing to go up.

SEN . CINDY HYDE - SMITH : You know, you have so many proteins to choose from.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 1: Pick another protein? [bleep], I’d rather pick another senator instead.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 2: Pick another protein? She done lost her damn mind. I’d rather pick another senator.

MISSISSIPPI VOTER 3: Pick another protein? What the [bleep]?

SCOTT COLOM : Pick another senator instead.

AMY GOODMAN : Scott Colom is a former district attorney for northeast Mississippi. In 2022, President Biden nominated him to the federal bench, a nomination blocked by Colom’s opponent in this race, incumbent Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith.

Colom has sharply criticized national Democrats for writing off Mississippi and failing to invest in his campaign. Early on, he told reporters, quote, “Mississippi was never a lost cause. We were a betrayed cause.” This is Colom speaking to NBC News.

SCOTT COLOM : The reality is our country does not do well when it ignores places like Mississippi. … You can’t lead with doubt. You have to believe. You have to lead with belief, and that’s where the power is. When you believe things, you can actually achieve it. And there’s some people in the party that they are just treading water. Right? “What’s the path to least resistance to get to 51? Oh my gosh, we did it.” That’s not the right way to think. In this particular moment, you have to think about how can we win everywhere, because we need to represent working people in a way where we actually deliver.

AMY GOODMAN : The potential electoral upset in Mississippi is part of a much broader political shift across the South, where Democrats have scored major victories in states long considered Republican strongholds.

For the latest on Mississippi and more on the sea change in the South, we’re joined by two guests. In Durham, North Carolina, we’re joined by Chris Kromm, the executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies, publisher of its online magazine Facing South . And we’re joined by Cliff Albright, co-founder of Black Voters Matter. He’s been in Jackson, Mississippi, for much of this week, including election night, but is now back in Atlanta, Georgia, where we’ve spoken to him many times before.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! Cliff Albright, let’s begin with you. To say the least, Colom feels betrayed by the Democratic Party for not backing him sooner, and yet he has shocked the nation in being ahead in this — very narrowly, in this race, where he may be, though it’s not finalized yet, unseating the incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith. Tell us what happened in Mississippi.

CLIFF ALBRIGHT : Yeah. Good morning, Amy. and good morning to my good friend Chris.

Yeah, you know, you all may not be able to claim it, but we’re claiming it. He’s claiming it. He’s ahead. He’s been ahead since election night. His lead continues to grow as they continue to count absentee ballots. We’re continuing, many organizations — it’s an incredible coalition of organizations down there in Mississippi that are fighting right now to make sure that every vote gets counted, people that were forced to do affidavit ballots, or provisional ballots, in some states it’s known as, trying to get organized to make sure that all of those ballots get counted, that people that didn’t have ID get their ballots fixed, get the ballots cured, to get all those votes counted. So we believe that he’s winning and, at the end of the day, that he’s going to be the winner.

But what happened is, in spite of the rest of the country really ignoring Mississippi — and I got to say that in addition to Mississippi, the points that he made about that state, the same could be said about Louisiana, which got even less support than his race got, and still came within a razor-thin margin. The same can be said about Florida — right? — Alabama. All of these states have been ignored, have been underresourced, underinvested. There are amazing groups doing work on a shoestring budget. But because of the tide of Black voter enthusiasm, largely fed by the Supreme Court’s Callais decision, which gutted the Voting Rights Act, ever since that decision, we’ve seen a wave of organizing, a wave of momentum. Of all the shifts that took place in the country — and to be clear, the entire country shifted left — but when you look at it regionally, the biggest shifts took place in the South — Texas, Mississippi, South Carolina, Louisiana. All those points had shifts between 20 and 24 points. And so, the wave of energy, largely led by Black voters who were most under attack with the mid-decade racial gerrymandering that was taking place — it clearly backfired, and all it did was to wake up a sleeping giant.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris Kromm, I wanted to ask you your reaction to the results in Mississippi. And if you could talk a little bit about the history of the two candidates?

CHRIS KROMM : No, absolutely. In an incredible year for Democrats in the South, the story of Scott Colom in Mississippi is one of the most remarkable. I mean, here you have a longtime leader in the Black community in Mississippi up against a longtime Republican. And the history that you brought out was incredibly important to the backdrop to this race, where he was put forward as a federal district nominee from the Biden administration in the fall of 2022, and almost every politician in Mississippi backed him, including the Republican Senator Roger Wicker, but the one person who blocked his nomination is the current senator from Mississippi, [Cindy] Hyde-Smith. And what you see there is — so, there’s a personal history there. And she really seemed determined. You know, she thought she had this race. She was kind of phoning it in. And, you know, to their credit, the Democrats, I think, late in the game kind of realized that this is a race that could be won.

And what you’re seeing now, I think, is really interesting, where armies of lawyers have come to Mississippi. The Republican lawyers are saying that they want to segregate those ballots, pull them aside, that came in, the affidavit ballots, or called provisional ballots elsewhere in the country, and pull those aside. Democratic lawyers and civil rights lawyers are saying that that’s not something you can do in Mississippi. And so this is really turning out to be an important legal battle. But as Cliff said, the trend lines are all going in the direction of Colom. And given that personal history, but also the long political history in Mississippi, it would be truly historic if he can come out on top.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris, in other states, the victories by Democrats at the top of the ticket have had an impact on the — on other races, less high-profile races. What’s happened there in Mississippi?

CHRIS KROMM : Yeah, well, I think that’s something really important to understand, is that these Senate races — so, if Scott Colom wins, which I think is very likely, that’ll be six Democrats who have won statewide U.S. Senate races. And those races really drove a lot of turnout that benefited, played a role in U.S. congressional races and statewide races. And so, you see that playing down the ballot, where this overall shift — as Cliff noted, that there was a 20-point shift overall in the South, when you look at the '24 presidential vote to what happened in the Senate races, a 20-point shift in the Democratic vote margin from ’24 to ’26. And that played out all down the ballot and even in races where — as Cliff notes, the places where Democrats came up short. What it really showed was the possibility of what's possible in Southern states. And I think that’s going to change forever people’s ideas about what the political map looks like nationally and the importance of the South in driving the national political agenda.

AMY GOODMAN : Cliff Albright, I know you have to leave in a second. You’re back in Atlanta, Georgia, where Keisha Lance Bottoms is now the first African American woman governor in the country. And you’ve just been in Mississippi. One of the most remarkable shifts in this country is the massive voter turnout. In many countries, many more people vote, percentage-wise, than in the United States, but it is growing here. If you can talk about also what this lack of Democratic establishment support has meant for Colom, but also Angie Nixon, who came so close to defeating the incumbent in Florida without that support? As Colom has pointed out, if only she had had that from the beginning. Your final comments on what you’re taking away from this election, as you say in Mississippi they’ve accepted that Colom has won, even if the rest of the country doesn’t, and if you think it could be stopped? I mean, here you have Cindy Hyde-Smith, who prevented Colom — she might be sorry now — from being appointed to the federal bench. She blocked Biden’s nomination.

CLIFF ALBRIGHT : Yeah, you know, I think that — so, a couple of things. On the Georgia thing, in addition to Keisha becoming governor, all the way down the ballot — to the point that Chris was just making, all the way down the ballot, it’s almost every state office in the state of Georgia is now going to be led by a Black woman — labor commissioner, agriculture, education — all the way down, except for lieutenant governor, where Josh won that one. But so, it’s absolutely remarkable, and it’s a sign of what could happen all across the South with the proper investment. What’s been happening in Georgia, you know, in 2020, in 2022, with Warnock winning again, this year, this has been from years of investment, the kind of investment that Mississippi, Louisiana, Florida has not seen.

Florida is insane, the way that people have turned their backs on the state of Florida and declared that it was hopeless, even after Andrew Gillum came close in 2018, and then just people just wrote it off. And for Angie to do what she did — and shoutout to her — on almost little, very little investment, really says what the potential is in the South. We’re hoping that the narrative or the question, the debate around what strategy makes sense in the South — do you invest in Black and Brown voters and mobilize that base? Right? Or do you continue to look for these unicorn Trump voters that swing back and forth? This year should really put that debate to an end, but I have a feeling it’s going to continue.

The last thing I’m going to say, Amy, is — and this is very important — with all these victories, there’s a risk that people lose sight of the structural barriers that still exist, the voter suppression that is still taking place. I know the Mississippi coalition is very insistent that people hear that story about things that still went wrong in this election. And this goes for across the South. And a lot of times what happens is, when we win, against all odds, that people say, “Oh, the voter suppression wasn’t that bad.” They said this about Warnock in '22. They said, “Oh, I guess that voter suppression bill wasn't that bad.” No, we were able to overcome the suppression, but that doesn’t mean that it’s not a structural barrier. The racial gerrymandering that took place has still given Republicans a structural edge, that’s been covered in a wave year, but it’s still something that’s got to be corrected. The Supreme Court’s decision has still got to be fixed. We still need voting rights legislation. And that, with investment, means there’s nothing that we can’t achieve all across the South.

JUAN GONZÁLEZ: And, Chris Kromm, I wanted to ask you if you could talk a little bit about what’s happened in North Carolina in this election.

CHRIS KROMM : Remarkable. Not only did you have at the top of the ticket, it looks like Roy Cooper is going to win by 19 to 20 points when all is said and done in terms of counting the ballots, but again, you go down the list. Four of the biggest upsets in U.S. congressional races were in North Carolina. It looks like at this point that we’re going to go from a delegation that, despite extreme gerrymandering, was a 10-4 in favor — delegation in favor of Republicans, will flip to a delegation that’s 10-4 in favor of Democrats.

Incredible stories like the longtime speaker of the House, Tim Moore, who created his own district through redistricting so he could win, was upset by a Black woman in District 14. In the mountains of North Carolina, where Hurricane Helene had devastated the region, you had a farmer, Ager, who’s going to — who’s won that race in District 11.

Just down the ballot, upset after upset, and it really showed that it was a combination of the political environment, how at the top of the ballot, the excitement and the investment that happened, but also some solid grassroots organizing, historic Black and Latino voter turnout. It really was the perfect storm, and it showed what’s possible. And again, I think this is a story — a lot of other Southern states could look like a North Carolina with the right investment, with the right attention. And so, the story of North Carolina, I think, is one that people should be paying attention to across the country, and also about what’s possible in the South.

AMY GOODMAN : And, Chris Kromm, we recently spoke to Justin Pearson, Justin Pearson who ran for Congress from Memphis. He really took on the data center there, as did his brother. He did lose, but he lost by just 2,000 votes in his gerrymandered district. So, even in that case, can you talk about the significance of this in Tennessee?

CHRIS KROMM : Well, this is what’s so important to understand, is that for all of the wins, and there were — you know, Democrats held on to 40 congressional seats, House seats. They are going to flip about 10 to 14 seats. I think that number is growing every day as new results come in, but it’s going to be about another 14 seats. If you think about how much bigger that wave would have been without the extreme gerrymandering, without the extreme voter restrictions that have been seen throughout the South, that wave would have been even bigger. And it really points to the importance of voting rights.

And Pearson is a great example of this. There’s over 30 data centers in the Memphis area. He is an out — a leader in that fight and talking about what the implications are for the community. And so, he didn’t make it to the finish line, but there are so many candidates like that in places where they were able to really move the needle, when you saw this incredible uptick in the electorate of Black and Latino voters, a real shift. And even if they didn’t get to the finish line, I hope the overall story people see is that the South is increasingly competitive and that there’s a real opportunity for engaging more voters and really pushing the region in a more progressive direction.

AMY GOODMAN : Chris Kromm, we want to thank you for being with us, executive director of the Institute for Southern Studies, speaking to us from North Carolina, and Cliff Albright, co-founder and executive director of the Black Voters Matter Fund. He spent the week in Jackson, Mississippi, just back at his home in Atlanta, Georgia.

Coming up, we look at some of the historic elections for Latinos with our own Juan González, author of Harvest of Empire: A History of Latinos in America . And then Hasan Piker will join us from Los Angeles to comment on the elections overall. He had one of the largest broadcasts in the United States on election night. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “When First Unto This Country,” rendition by Down Hill Strugglers, performing at the Brooklyn Folk Festival last year. This year’s festival is this weekend, and we’ll bring you more of those musicians.

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

scraped.title: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals
scraped.description: Jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has said in a mitigation letter submitted to court before his sentencing on Thursday that his six years in prison reshaped his outlook on life, asking for the utmost leniency so he could walk free in his thirties.
scraped.author: Hong Kong Free Press
scraped.h1: ‘6 years in jail has reshaped my view of life’: Joshua Wong sought leniency to be freed in his 30s, mitigation letter reveals
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong has said in a mitigation letter submitted to court before his sentencing on Thursday that his six years in prison reshaped his outlook on life, asking for the utmost leniency so he could walk free in his thirties.

High Court judge William Tam sentenced the activist to 10 years’ imprisonment on Thursday after Wong pleaded guilty to conspiring to collude with foreign forces, his second conviction under a Beijing-imposed national security law.

The 30-year-old has been behind bars since late 2020, when he was 24. He was due to be released in early 2027 after completing a four-year, eight-month jail term for conspiracy to subvert state power in the landmark “Hong Kong 47” case, but was charged with foreign collusion in June last year.

In a Chinese-language mitigation letter obtained by HKFP, Wong said he had missed his university graduation ceremony and lost more than 2,000 days with his family.

“Unlike my peers born in the 1990s, I was unable to start a family of my own or enter the workforce. Instead, I could only watch the years pass inside a stark cell,” the letter reads.

Wong said that while in prison, he exercised regularly, read books, and learned new skills every day. He added that he was learning the guitar, preparing for the International English Language Testing System (IELTS), and taking multiple legal and business courses organised by local universities.

“I pledge to Your Honour that I will not allow myself to be defined by who I was before the age of 24… When the day comes that I step out of this cell, I pray that I will have washed away the naivety of 24, moving forward with a mature mind, enriched knowledge, and a healthy body,” Wong said in the letter.

The activist also said he hoped to care for his elderly parents and give back to society upon his release.

“My experience of imprisonment under the National Security Law has not made me resistant to gaining a deeper understanding of China. On the contrary, it drove me to read extensively, draw wisdom from the past to reflect on the present… I hope to apply my professional skills to contribute to the socio-economic development of our society in full compliance with the law.”

Wong was accused of conspiring with self-exiled activist Nathan Law and other unnamed individuals after the Beijing-imposed national security law came into effect in June 2020 to request that foreign countries impose sanctions and blockades, or engage in other hostile activities, directed against the governments of Hong Kong and mainland China.

During the 2019 protests and unrest, many protesters campaigned internationally to gather support from Western countries and pressure Hong Kong and Beijing authorities to meet their demands.

Wong said in his mitigation letter that once the national security law came into effect, he realised that calling for foreign sanctions was unlawful and he “promptly ceased all such statements and conduct.”

“However, as the law suddenly came into force, the situation was overwhelming. I attempted to adjust my words and actions amid confusion, yet my legal judgment was not thorough and I was not in a clear mind, leaving me unable to properly determine the legal boundaries for every single act,” Wong said.

“At the time, I believed that reposting publications by others, or urging foreign enterprises on commercial grounds to halt cooperation with police, differed from directly calling for sanctions,” he said, adding: “With respect to all statements I made and posts I published, I admit them in their entirety and accept full responsibility.”

Protests erupted in June 2019 over a since-axed extradition bill . They escalated into sometimes violent displays of dissent against police behaviour, amid calls for democracy and anger over Beijing’s encroachment. Demonstrators demanded an independent probe into police conduct, amnesty for those arrested and a halt to the characterisation of protests as “riots.”

articles.summary: If foreign-policy restrainers of both parties are looking for a model the new Congress can follow once it takes office in January, they could do worse than to refer back to the 1974 midterm election that brought to Washington a tidal wave of young Democrats who quickly passed legislation placing unprecedented constraints on the power of the “Imperial Presidency,” which had reached its zenith under former President Richard Nixon.In many respects, the parallels between the 1974 midterms and the...
articles.ai_summary: The article draws parallels between the 1974 midterm elections and current calls for foreign policy restraint.

scraped.title: When the 'Watergate Babies' rode their own wave of anger
scraped.description: Swept into office in 1974, this cohort of Democrats led efforts to gut a rogue CIA, secret wars, and other abuses of executive power under Nixon
scraped.h1: When the 'Watergate Babies' rode their own wave of anger
scraped.body_text:
Swept into office in 1974, this cohort of Democrats led efforts to gut a rogue CIA, secret wars, and other abuses of executive power under Nixon

If foreign-policy restrainers of both parties are looking for a model the new Congress can follow once it takes office in January, they could do worse than to refer back to the 1974 midterm election that brought to Washington a tidal wave of young Democrats who quickly passed legislation placing unprecedented constraints on the power of the “Imperial Presidency,” which had reached its zenith under former President Richard Nixon.

In many respects, the parallels between the 1974 midterms and the results of Tuesday’s election are eerie. Though Nixon, whose own imperial pretensions were more sartorial than architectural , had resigned from office three months before the vote, his abuses of executive powers loomed large over the election. Those abuses were, after all, hard to ignore: from Watergate and the impoundment of Congressional appropriations at home, to the secret bombing of Cambodia and Laos and the covert CIA campaign to overthrow the democratically-elected government of Chile abroad.

The popular rejection of Nixon’s secrecy and executive overreach was coupled with an economic recession made much worse by the 1973-74 Arab oil embargo , which, in an echo of the current U.S.-Israeli war against Iran , was prompted by Washington’s military support for Israel during the October 1973 war .

It was in this context that Democrats, while still a somewhat fractious majority in both houses of Congress on the eve of the 1974 midterms, made a net gain of four Senate seats and a whopping 49 House seats, beefing up their position and bringing to Washington no fewer than 76 new members. Many of these so-called “Watergate babies” shared associations with the antiwar and human rights movements.

Even before the new Congress was seated in January 1975, the lame-duck Congress felt the vote had given it a mandate curb executive powers that had enabled Nixon and his powerful national security adviser and secretary of state, Henry Kissinger, to involve the United States in unpopular conflicts abroad and support highly repressive foreign regimes. That same Congress had passed the War Powers Act two years before by a bipartisan supermajority over Nixon’s veto.

In its December 1974 session, the outgoing Congress approved a foreign aid bill that, among other provisions, imposed strict limits on the U.S. military presence in South Vietnam and on U.S. military and security assistance and arms transfers to the military junta in Chile, as well as South Korea and Turkey, setting the precedent for conditioning future U.S. aid and other support to countries on their respect for human rights.

Included in the same bill was the so-called Hughes-Ryan Amendment , which banned the CIA and the Defense Department from carrying out covert actions without an official “presidential finding” and “timely notification” to as many as eight congressional committees.

Once seated, the new Congress acted quickly to build on those measures. In January, the Senate voted 82-4 to establish what became known as the Church Committee (after its chairman, Idaho Sen. Frank Church), which investigated intelligence abuses by the CIA, the FBI, and other U.S. intelligence agencies. The following month, the House voted 286-120 to carry out its own investigation, known as the Pike Committee after its chairman, New York Congressman Otis Pike.

Among other things, the committees’ work and the abuses they uncovered resulted in the passage of the Clark Amendment . Part of the Arms Export Control Act of 1976, the amendment banned all direct or indirect U.S. military or paramilitary assistance to any faction in the civil war in Angola in which the CIA, at Kissinger’s direction, had secretly intervened alongside South Africa and its proxies in trying to overthrow the regime in Luanda after independence from Portugal.

Passed by a bipartisan coalition in both houses, the Arms Export Control Act also aimed to rein in the transfer of major U.S. weapons systems to various authoritarian regimes, a policy that Kissinger, in particular, favored as a way to enhance bilateral ties with those countries. It required the Pentagon to provide details of all such transfers in advance, gave Congress the power to veto them, and banned transfers to governments with a "consistent pattern of gross violations of human rights,” in what became the precursor to the “Leahy Laws.”

That same year, Congress also passed the National Emergencies Act of 1976 , which, among other provisions, gives Congress the power to terminate any presidential declaration of emergency.

In the 60 years that have since passed, some of these laws have been watered down, effectively ignored, or even repealed — mostly, but by no means exclusively, by Republican administrations and their congressional supporters. And an “imperial presidency”has returned —particularly in Trump’s second term, during which he has issued an avalanche of Executive Orders, many of them to pursue a militaristic domestic and foreign policy by designating people and groups terrorists here and abroad.But Tuesday’s Democratic blowout across the country may have created an opportunity for the reassertion of congressional power on the order of what took place 62 years ago.

It is true that the Democrats will not enjoy the near-veto-proof majorities in Congress they won in 1974. They may claim as many as 56 seats in the Senate, still four fewer than back then. And, despite tremendous gains in the House, they’ll fall well short of 291 seats.

On the other hand, it’s worth noting that much of the 1970s legislation was bipartisan, and Trump’s new “lame duck” status could empower Republicans who have shown signs of discomfort with the presidency policies, particularly on the war..

Despite the hyper-partisanship of recent politics, is it too far-fetched to imagine bipartisan agreement on legislation to constrain the executive, particularly on foreign policy?

A number of Republican lawmakers , for example, have demanded greater oversight over the administration’s lethal policy of bombing boats suspected of carrying drugs in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, noted Peter Kornbluh, a senior analyst at the National Security Archive.

“This new Congress has both the opportunity and the ability to stand up to Trump’s imperial impulses, his wannabe emperor syndrome, which is likely to become more pronounced now that he has so dramatically lost his domestic support,” Kornbluh told RS. “The 1975-76 Congress created a model for curtailing the executive’s interventionist impulses abroad.”

In this regard, one only has to cite Vice President JD Vance’s assessment on X Wednesday morning, in which he blamed the Republican wipeout on the war in Iran. “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,” he wrote in what probably reflects a serious split within the party and even within the administration itself.

Indeed, four Republican members in both the House and Senate voted alongside virtually every Democrat for an Iran war powers resolution in June. Could those numbers increase in the wake of Tuesday’s election and a weaker White House?

Of course, Democrats in the incoming Congress will not have enough votes by themselves to overcome a veto, and Trump has already promised to wield that power against any legislation he doesn’t like. “With the filibuster in place and no veto-proof majority… and a president who is a norm-buster, I just see more paralysis,” Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told RS, “I think the impact (of the election) on foreign policy will be negligible.”

As in 1974, much will depend on how the Republican survivors of Tuesday’s “bluenami” assess the election’s meaning for their own political futures.

scraped.title: Trump must end the war today and fire all top officials connected to it
scraped.description: The president has to replace his inner circle with new appointees who can out maneuver the blob and give the people what they voted for
scraped.h1: Trump must end the war today and fire all top officials connected to it
scraped.body_text:
The president has to replace his inner circle with new appointees who can out maneuver the blob and give the people what they voted for

For the last eight months, the Iran war has been a topic of fierce debate: is the war in our national interest? Was Iran an imminent threat? Should we stay the course or escalate?

This debate raged through the historic MAGA coalition that brought Donald Trump and JD Vance to the White House. My position on it was clear: the war was the catalyst for my resignation from the Trump administration — and likely for many others who left without making their disagreement public.

This debate burned hot and loudly in right wing circles online, on podcasts and occasionally even on right-wing mainstream platforms like Fox News. Then suddenly, on Tuesday night, after months of deafening argument, all of that debate was suddenly silenced, like a father coming home from work telling bickering siblings to knock off the racket. The American people loudly rejected the war by voting against President Trump’s Republican party and handing the Democrats a historic landslide, granting them solid control of the House and Senate.

The American people settled the debate. It's time to end the war in Iran. This is irrefutable, as Vice President Vance has admitted. Over 70% of voters blamed the Iran war and our off balanced relationship with Israel for the out of control inflation that affects their daily lives and have zero tolerance for more wars of choice.

With this clear message from the American people, Trump must immediately end the war – today. No good will come from prolonging the conflict; the American people have made this painfully very clear.

President Trump must end the war by making it clear to his national security team that the war is over. To ensure that he is not thwarted by the neocon national security “blob” as he was in his first administration, he needs to fire and replace the secretary of defense (Pete Hegseth), the CIA director (John Ratcliffe), the secretary of state (Marco Rubio) and his chief of staff (Susie Wiles).

President Trump must bring in new appointees who understand that we must end the war and who know how these institutions will likely attempt to keep us at war. Above all, these new leaders must have the courage and management skills to ensure these organizations do exactly as the president instructs.

We end the war by withdrawing our troops from the Persian Gulf and lifting our blockade. This is not as dramatic as it sounds. Iran has already destroyed most of our bases in the Gulf and proven once and for all that these bases are a strategic liability and not a strategic asset. They are already past their expiration date; leaving them behind once and for all is in our interest, not a defeat.

Removing the naval blockade serves two key functions: first it removes a valuable target that Iran could hit, which would drag us back into the war on Iran’s terms, not ours. Second, removing the blockade throws the diplomatic ball back in Iran’s court. We have reached an impasse diplomatically, with the Iranians refusing to give concessions while they are under blockade and the threat of being attacked.

The Iranians use the blockade to justify their aggression in the Persian Gulf. If we remove the blockade, the Iranians won’t have any more justification for acting aggressively in the Strait of Hormuz and will likely opt for quiet diplomacy with their Gulf neighbors to come up with a workable arrangement for getting tankers through the strait. We can also offer gradual relief of sanctions on Iranian oil and natural gas so that Iran is incentivized to keep the waterway open.

As we remove our troops from the region, we must also meaningfully restrain the Israelis to ensure that they don’t thwart our efforts to end the war, as they have in previous cease fire talks. Restraining Israel means more than just rhetoric: we must remove significant components of the air defense assets like the American missile defense batteries that we give to the Israelis so they are forced to use their resources for defense and not offense.

The president must also demand that the lame-duck Republican Congress remove section 219 from the National Defense Authorization Act and section 662 from the intelligence authorization act. These provisions will give Israel invaluable access to the most sensitive capabilities of our defense and intelligence apparatus and are an affront to our sovereignty.

Finally, to ensure Israel is restrained, the president must recall and fire Amb. Mike Huckabee and all of his team members. Huckabee and his team have blatantly shown more allegiance to Israel than our nation. This can’t be allowed to continue.

The American people have spoken loud and clear and rejected this war. President Trump just has to have the courage to end the war, restrain Israel and put America first.

scraped.title: DeSantis’s Unconvincing Iran Flip-Flop
scraped.description: The Florida governor’s criticism is undercut by a long paper trail of Iran hawkery.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
The Florida governor’s criticism is undercut by a long paper trail of Iran hawkery.

Republicans were eviscerated in an election President Donald Trump and his opponents saw as a referendum on his second term. The outcome bodes ill for the GOP, which now faces strong Democratic majorities in Congress and the prospect of endless investigations and legislative stonewalling.

One prominent Republican with an eye for 2028 decided to attack the president’s record just before the midterms. In an interview with Stephen A. Smith , Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis lambasted the Iran War and other failures of the administration. “We just got to be honest. Gas is higher. It hurts people, working-class people, and it’s higher because of this conflict. That’s just a fact,” DeSantis said.

He continued his criticism of the White House in a press conference after the Tuesday massacre, chastising the president and the GOP for poor messaging and not delivering on their promises.

It’s a clear sign DeSantis plans to run in 2028 and wants to pitch himself, once again, as a Trump critic from the right.

Central to that pitch will be the Iran War. Unlike anyone in the administration, DeSantis bears no responsibility for it. He can present himself as a critic, without the awkwardness of having been in the meetings at which Operation Epic Fury was planned. It’s a smart move—but it also contrasts with his past hawkery on the issue.

DeSantis knows he needs to change his tune to be a viable candidate for ’28. Republicans lost big because of the disastrous war, and many within the GOP base want someone who can deliver the truth. But the governor’s past stances may undermine this pitch. He’s not exactly a consistent non-interventionist.

In his previous presidential bid, DeSantis sought to distinguish himself as a stronger hawk than Trump on the Islamic Republic. This was a central theme of a speech he delivered to Christians United for Israel in 2023, for example, and it featured consistently in his foreign policy messaging. His campaign website promised to “turn the screws on Iran beginning on Day 1—abandoning the naïve, disastrous Obama-Biden foreign policies.”

The Florida governor even attacked Trump for offering mild criticism of Benjamin Netanyahu in the fall of 2023, saying it was “absurd that anyone, much less someone running for President, would choose now to attack our friend and ally, Israel.” DeSantis made this rift a major part of his campaign and kept hammering Trump about it. It didn’t work, with one Republican operative saying it made him “look like members of the Lincoln Project to the base right now.”

DeSantis’s ’24 bid earned the support of many influencers and commentators who still defend the Iran War. That included none other than THE Iran War supporter, Mark Levin . Levin’s stepson worked on pro-Israel outreach for DeSantis’s gubernatorial and presidential campaigns. Unsurprisingly, Levin hosted DeSantis on his show several times throughout the primary to discuss the governor’s strong support for Israel.

Much of DeSantis’s online network that was devoted to his presidential campaign is now devoted to supporting the Iran War.

DeSantis praised Operation Epic Fury when it first began, arguing that it was delivering justice for Americans killed during the Iraq War. “As somebody who was over in Iraq at that time, that saw the casualties, that saw that it was the Iranians behind it. They never really faced justice,” he said in March. “Now... all the ayatollahs are dropping like flies.”

He also backed bombing Iran last year, saying Trump showed “decisiveness.” He claimed military action against the Islamic Republic was necessary because of the state’s “apocalyptic, radical ideology.” The only way to deter the regime was through bombings.

DeSantis’s pitch as a Iran War critic will also be hampered by his rabid support for Israel. He famously signed bills to target “antisemitism,” in Jerusalem, twice . He sent weapons to Israel during its war in Gaza. He has even claimed America wouldn’t exist without Israel being the cradle of Western civilization. These opinions are supported by his pro-Israel donors , a number of whom want America to back the Jewish state’s annexation of Gaza and the West Bank.

It’s also worth recalling that the Florida governor initially sought to position himself as a staunch non-interventionist in the ’24 primary, at least when it came to regions outside the Middle East. He told Tucker Carlson in early 2023 that defending Ukraine was not a key security interest for America. But after receiving backlash from donors, he walked back those comments .

There’s a chance he could reverse himself again in the ’28 primary.

DeSantis is a smart politician. One doesn’t become the most successful Republican governor in the country without some brains. He knows which way the wind is blowing, and he understands that the Iran War offers an opportunity to align himself with the majority of Americans. It sets him apart from potential rivals currently serving in the admin, who can’t easily shed their association with the conflict. It also differentiates him from Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who is loud and proud about his support for the war. DeSantis has the freedom to openly criticize the war and other admin failures, creating the distance between himself and Trump that may be necessary for any Republican to win in 2028.

But he will still face the challenge of convincing the public that he’s a genuine critic of the war and foreign interventionism more broadly. It’s easy to say the war hurt Republicans. Even Vice President J.D. Vance and Trump say that. It’s hard to prove DeSantis will avoid similar catastrophes as president when he’s on record championing military action against Iran.

That DeSantis can recognize reality and understand the GOP’s predicament are positive signs. The base may be ready for a clean break from Trump in the primary, and someone who vows to keep the good things about the admin and ditch the bad would be a strong contender.

To do so, a candidate will have to convince the public that he will learn from Trump’s mistakes and avoid harebrained foreign interventions. After the midterms, it’s clear voters want a different direction. That’s something even an Iran hawk can recognize.

Scott Greer is an award-winning journalist, host of Highly Respected, and author of No Campus for White Men .

articles.title: Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
articles.summary: Several Republicans sought to distance themselves from Donald Trump's trade war during the midterms, in some cases asking for specific tariffs to be rolled back. Even so, Republicans lost. Democrats, who were traditionally the party of protectionism, appear to have been pushed into a more pro-free trade stance, and appear ready to try to reach a deal with Republicans.
articles.ai_summary: Several Republicans distanced themselves from Trump's trade policies during the midterms, but the party still faced losses as Democrats adopted a more pro-free trade stance.

scraped.title: ANALYSIS | Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough | CBC News
scraped.description: Several Republicans sought to distance themselves from Donald Trump's trade war during the midterms, in some cases asking for specific tariffs to be rolled back. Even so, Republicans lost. Democrats, who were traditionally the party of protectionism, appear to have been pushed into a more pro-free trade stance, and appear ready to try to reach a deal with Republicans.
scraped.h1: Republicans ran away from Trump's Canadian tariffs, but not far enough
scraped.body_text:
When wildfires were burning across Canada in July, and the smoke was blowing into the United States, Michigan's Mike Rogers was among those demanding punishment.

The now defeated Republican candidate for Senate, echoing U.S. President Donald Trump, said Canada should pay more, on top of the current tariffs, to cover the cost of that pollution.

"Canada must be held accountable for endangering Americans, and I will work with your administration to ensure they are!," he wrote on X , in a reply to Trump.

Rogers had, separately, enthused about the tariffs — telling Fox News they were "really positive" for the U.S. and that it was "absolutely unacceptable" for Canada to be selling cars into his border state.

Fast forward three months and Rogers — struggling in the race for Senate — tried to cast himself as a friend of Canada.

While drinking a Labatt Blue and alluding to hockey, he called for an end to the tariffs in an ad posted four weeks ago.

"Here in Michigan, we know that Canada is not our enemy," he said.

A man votes in the primary election at Northwestern High School in Detroit, on Aug. 4. (Nic Antaya/The Associated Press)

It was one of many examples of Republicans trying to distance themselves from Trump's trade war and anti-Canadian rhetoric.

Now, according to reporting from the Wall Street Journal, the Democrats are hoping to use Republican discomfort with the cross-border trade war to end tariffs on Canada.

"There is overwhelming support for repealing the tariffs on products from Canada," Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden, ranking member of the Senate Finance Committee, told the WSJ on Wednesday.

Wyden and other Democrats believed they might be able to flip enough Republicans against Trump on the issue to override a veto, the Journal reported. That would likely require persuading about 30 to 35 Republican House members, and 11 to 13 Republican senators, the precise number depending on votes yet to be tallied from Tuesday's elections.

The new House and Senate will be seated on Jan. 3, just two days after punishing 50 per cent tariffs on all Canadian cars, trucks, automotive parts, and steel are scheduled to take effect.

Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rogers in Michigan, told the MS Now morning show on Thursday he was keen to work to lift the "stupid tariffs on Canada," and later told CNN that ending Trump's "vanity trade war" was a legislative priority for him in Washington.

"There is no economic reason why we are having a tariff war with our biggest trading partner. This has to end."

That seems to be one of the lessons American politicians will take from the 2026 midterm elections, perhaps with lasting and positive effects for Canada.

From the early days of Trump's second term, Americans have shown very little interest in picking fights with Canada. Although Trump's verbal attacks on Canada were a staple at rallies throughout October, the issue again failed to catch fire within the MAGA coalition.

Exit polls on Tuesday, according to CNN, found that two-thirds of American voters believed tariffs had hurt both the national and their local economies.

What the historic Democrat midterm surge means for Canada

The tariffs were widely seen as having combined with the Iran war to create a double price shock.

Rural America has been hit especially hard by the spike in diesel, which contributed to higher costs for fertilizer. All of the eight main fertilizers used by U.S. farmers cost more than they did a year ago, according to one industry analysis.

Those numbers were key to the massive hemorrhaging of Republican votes in red states such as Kansas.

In two critical Senate races in Maine and Kansas, Republican candidates appealed directly to Trump to cancel or reconsider specific trade actions against Canada in order to avoid harming voters in their states (and therefore their campaigns).

In Maine, Susan Collins first asked him to drop tariffs on road salt, warning that they would dramatically increase costs for small municipalities, which might then have to raise property taxes. Trump complied.

Later, Trump lifted tariffs on about $5.1 billion US worth of goods to help her. (He replaced them with new tariffs on other goods , although for only about half the monetary value.)

Trump's reversals weren't enough to save Collins. Her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson gave his victory speech wearing a button that said "We can't eat road salt!"

Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas speaks at a campaign event for Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Grosse Pointe Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28. (Paul Sancya/The Associated Press)

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall asked Trump not to proceed with actions against Montreal-based Bombardier, which makes jets in Wichita. Again, Trump complied , but Marshall lost anyway.

Several Republicans mentioned tariffs in post-mortems of the midterm rout.

"Tragically, we alienated rural America," said Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas , who was not up for re-election but saw his junior counterpart lose to Democrat James Talarico. The state's governor also lost to a Democrat.

"Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long."

Cruz blamed the rout, in order, on the high cost of living, corruption, the cost of the war, sub-par candidates and the trade war with Canada.

The tariffs were, meanwhile, a topic of victory speeches in some of the biggest races.

"I will fight to end these chaotic tariffs," said senator-elect Josh Turek after his upset victory in Iowa.

Midterms ‘bluenami’: The exact moment Trump lost control of Congress | About That

Ohio senator-elect Sherrod Brown, famous for opposing NAFTA, said the same.

The success of the affordability message seemed to position Democrats as hard-core free-traders in a way they might not have otherwise been.

"The tariffs are ruining everything," became a kind of slogan for Talarico, who made a video at the Texas State Fair in which he blamed the price of fried Oreos and funnel cake on tariffs.

Tariffs were even an issue down in Mississippi, where underdog Scott Colom accused incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith of going along with them. (That race still hasn't been called.)

Canada is Mississippi's biggest export market , and Colom's region is home to the state's furniture industry, which normally ships about $34 million US worth of kitchen cabinets, bedding and other furniture to Canada annually.

Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to his supporters during his election watch party on Tuesday, in Jackson, Miss. (Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today/The Associated Press)

Not only has the cost of framing a sofa or recliner increased because of tariffs on Canadian lumber, but the furniture now also faces a 50 per cent counter-tariff.

And while Mississippi has its own forestry industry, it depends on specialized logging machinery, much of it imported from Canada and also subject to tariffs.

Colom vowed to local media, if elected, that his first job would be to "get the tariff policy back to Congress."

The tariffs "are not working," he repeated in his election-night speech.

Canada's softwood lumber industry might see some irony in the fact that its old nemesis, Wyden, is likely to lead the charge for free trade with Canada. (He's expected to chair the Senate finance committee.)

Wyden is a lumber hardliner who has butted heads with Canada for years, but more recently his positions have reflected a trend seen across the party. The success of the affordability message, linking high costs directly to tariffs and war, has strengthened a previously lukewarm commitment to free trade.

What the Republican midterm defeat means for Trump, the U.S. and Canada

Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028

Elon Musk gets little bang for his buck in U.S. midterms, with possible Democratic investigations to come

Wyden has opposed all of Trump's tariffs on Canada, calling them a "shakedown" and a "reckless abuse."

He says his fellow Democrats plan to "reassert congressional authority" over U.S. trade policy and roll back tariffs Trump instituted under various emergency authorities — good news for Canada.

But perhaps the best news for Canada from the midterms is that politicians in both parties appear to have concluded that tariffs on Canada cost votes, and that opposing them is good politics.

Senior Reporter

Evan Dyer has been a journalist with CBC for 25 years, after an early career as a freelancer in Argentina. He works in the Parliamentary Bureau and can be reached at evan.dyer@cbc.ca.
