scraped.title: Mike Salisbury, wildlife filmmaker who made plants behave like characters, has died, aged 84
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Rhett Butler
scraped.h1: Mike Salisbury, wildlife filmmaker who made plants behave like characters, has died, aged 84
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

To Mike Salisbury, patience was not a virtue so much as a working method. Lions did not hunt on cue. Plants did not move at a human pace. Polar bears did not respect production schedules, or much else. The task was to wait, improvise, and find a way to show television audiences that the natural world was stranger, livelier and more intricate than they had thought.

Salisbury, who died on May 13th aged 84 , spent more than four decades turning that patience into television.

His route into that work was suitably unpolished, according to an obituary in The Guardian . He did not go to university. He worked as a mechanic with Voluntary Service Overseas in Africa, where he developed his interest in photography. Back in Britain, he pressed the BBC for a chance until Horizon gave him a brief research opening. He worked first on Parkinson , then on science documentaries, before moving to Bristol and the BBC’s Natural History Unit. There he found the place where persistence, practicality, and curiosity could become a career.

His breakthrough came with Life on Earth , David Attenborough ’s 1979 account of evolution. Salisbury helped produce some of its most memorable sequences, including a lion hunt that had defeated him once before. He went back and got it. That became part of his reputation: not bluster, but refusal to be beaten by weather, animals, equipment or logistics.

In 1985 he made Kingdom of the Ice Bear , filmed in Arctic conditions that tested both people and kit. Later came Lost Worlds, Vanished Lives , The Private Life of Plants , The Life of Birds , The Life of Mammals and Life in the Undergrowth . His partnership with Attenborough became one of the longest and most productive in natural-history television. It worked because Salisbury understood both spectacle and explanation. A scene had to astonish, but it also had to teach.

Plants may have been his most unlikely triumph. They were rooted, silent and too slow for ordinary television. Salisbury helped solve that problem with time-lapse techniques that made their lives visible: shoots searching, tendrils grasping, flowers opening, and stems competing for light. The result was not merely pretty footage. It changed the status of plants on screen. They became actors in their own right, organisms with strategies, dramas, and appetites.

He was not, by most accounts, a grand figure. Colleagues remembered warmth, humor, kindness, and generosity as much as determination. He mentored younger filmmakers in Bristol’s natural-history community, many of whom went on to shape the field themselves. At Wildscreen in 2006, when Attenborough began describing the winner of the Outstanding Achievement award, Salisbury reportedly listened with interest , not realizing that the subject was himself.

That modesty sat alongside a performer’s instinct. He loved acting, singing, rugby, and travel. Even in retirement, he remained hard to imagine as still. He continued consulting on wildlife films and, on his 80th birthday, was still skiing black runs.

Television natural history is often associated with the voice in front of the camera. Salisbury belonged to the craft behind it: the planning, waiting, technical experiment and judgment that made wonder look effortless. He helped teach viewers to look longer at the living world. For a filmmaker, there are few better legacies.

Banner image: Mike Salisbury in Tanzania in the 1970s making Life on Earth. Photo credit: BBC

Doug Allan, wildlife cameraman who filmed animals in extreme environments

scraped.title: West Asia conflict brings Norwegian marine research vessel back to Sri Lanka
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.author: Dilrukshi Handunnetti
scraped.h1: West Asia conflict brings Norwegian marine research vessel back to Sri Lanka
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

COLOMBO – Sri Lanka’s marine research efforts have benefited in a rare instance where geopolitical unrest owing to the ongoing conflict in West Asia created an unexpected scientific opportunity.

A United Nations-flagged Norwegian research vessel Fridtjof Nansen was redirected to Sri Lankan waters after security concerns forced the cancellation of a planned survey in Oman, giving the country a second chance to conduct a long-awaited study of its marine ecosystems and fishery resources.

The Norwegian research vessel was originally scheduled to carry out a marine survey in the Sri Lankan waters last year as part of its planned scientific program. However, delays in granting national approvals meant the expedition could not proceed as intended. The vessel canceled the Sri Lanka leg of the voyage scheduled for 2025, an important opportunity lost in marine research efforts.

The Nansen Program is a long-running international marine research initiative led by the Food and Agriculture Organization FAO ) of the United Nations in partnership with Norway. Established in 1975, it operates through the research vessel Dr Fridtjof Nansen , named after Norwegian explorer, scientist and humanitarian Fridtjof Nansen who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for his extraordinary humanitarian work during the First World War.

The Nansen missions survey marine ecosystems in developing countries to support sustainable fisheries management combining oceanographic research, fisheries stock assessment, and ecosystem monitoring while building scientific capacity in the participating countries through training and collaboration.

Scientists from the National Aquatic Resources Research and Development Agency NARA led the scientific work in the recent survey in close collaboration with Sri Lankan institutions, and supported by experts and crew from the Bergen-based Norway’s Institute of Marine Research ( IMR ) that operates the vessel and is responsible for the scientific activities and training aboard.

Surveying island’s changing seas

The recent Nansen research mission marks the fifth scientific survey conducted in the Sri Lankan waters, building on previous expeditions conducted between 1978 and 1980 and most recently in 2018. The survey followed many of the same standardized scientific methods used during earlier Nansen expeditions in Sri Lankan waters in 1978, 1980 and 2018, says Prabath Jayasinghe , a scientist at NARA who served as the co-cruise leader heading the scientific team aboard the research vessel.

Jayasinghe, who was also the leader of the 2018 expedition, said the continuity of missions allows scientists to directly compare decades of data and identify long-term changes in fish stocks and marine ecosystems. The vessel spent 32 days surveying Sri Lanka’s Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), gathering crucial information on fish stocks, biodiversity, pollution, and oceanographic conditions, Jayasinghe added.

Through the Nansen vessel, scientists also conduct hydro-acoustic surveys to estimate the abundance and distribution of pelagic and demersal fish stocks while also studying biodiversity, pollution, and oceanographic conditions.

Methods such as scientific trawling, using nets to sample marine organisms from the seafloor, midwater, and the open ocean at different depths, and the use of plankton nets to collect smaller organisms have been used in the surveys. The expedition captured over 800 different species while surveying different parts of Sri Lankan waters, highlighting that Sri Lanka’s oceans have high biodiversity, Jayasinghe told Mongabay.

The collected species still require further analysis, but according to Jayasinghe, at least 125 of the species recorded during the survey are likely first-time records in the Sri Lankan waters. He added the findings are even more significant because an estimated 5-10 species could be completely new to science. The scientist added that these results highlight how little is still known about the country’s deeper marine biodiversity, highlighting the need for more research.

Previous analyses from the 2018 survey revealed some worrying trends. A comprehensive study based on the 2018 expedition documented 620 marine species from Sri Lanka’s continental shelf but also highlighted regional variations and signs of pressure on fish stocks. This time too, different variations have been found, Jayasinghe added.

Building local scientific capacity

Beyond the scientific surveys, the voyage served as a floating classroom for Sri Lankan researchers. A total of 16 scientists working on different areas had the opportunity to participate in the voyage, getting to work directly onboard, operating equipment, collecting samples, and participating in real-time analysis of fish stocks, ocean conditions, and marine biodiversity.

During the 2018 survey, 20 local scientists had the same opportunity. This time, scientists also got hands-on experience in hydro-acoustic surveys, trawling methods, oceanographic sampling, and data interpretation, skills that are difficult to build without access to a research ship of this scale, Jayasinghe told Mongabay.

Sri Lanka’s fisheries sector supports hundreds of thousands of livelihoods and contributes significantly to national food security. Yet many commercially important fish stocks remain poorly assessed. Climate change adds further uncertainty. Ocean warming, changing currents, deoxygenation, and shifting species distributions are already affecting fisheries across the Indian Ocean.

In this backdrop, updated data from expeditions like this support evidence-based fisheries management, marine conservation planning, and Sri Lanka’s international reporting obligations related to marine biodiversity and sustainable seafood exports contributes to greater understanding, says Susantha Kahawatta, director general of the Department of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources in Sri Lanka ( DFAR ).

Elasmobranch in Nansen survey

Presenting findings from the 2018 Nansen ecosystem survey in Sri Lankan waters, Thejani Balawardana , also a scientist with NARA, said the study has documented 40 elasmobranch taxa (a subclass of cartilaginous fish) including sharks and rays from 88 trawl samples collected across the continental shelf and slope.

The research showed a highly uneven species distribution, with deep water catsharks dominating catches by number, accounting for nearly 60% of total abundance. However, larger ray species such as whiprays ( Maculabatis gerrardi ) and stingrays ( Pastinachus species ) contributed to the highest biomass. Although only a few species were abundant, most of these organisms were rare and infrequently encountered, underlining the ecological significance of deep-water habitats, Balawardana said.

The study also found that elasmobranch diversity in Sri Lankan waters increased with depth, with the richest communities occurring below 300 meters (985 feet).

According to the analysis, depth and environmental conditions were the primary factors shaping species composition rather than geographic region, highlighting the importance of continued monitoring and protection of vulnerable deep-sea ecosystems in the Sri Lankan waters.

While 2026 survey results are yet to be fully analyzed, it appears to be more interesting, Balawardhana told Mongabay. These types of independent ecosystems surveys are important to study different marine habitats and depth ranges to identify ecologically important cartilaginous fish species and to support evidence-based fisheries management and conservation measures in Sri Lanka, she added.

As Sri Lanka grapples with balancing economic recovery and environmental sustainability, the knowledge gathered by the Fridtjof Nansen could shape marine policy for years to come, Jayasinghe told Mongabay. “In an era where wars more often bring destruction than opportunity, the vessel’s unexpected arrival stands as a reminder that even global crises can occasionally produce an unlikely scientific silver lining for a small island nation like ours,” he added.

Banner Image: Limited knowledge exists on the ocean’s mesopelagic zone, often called the “twilight zone.” Among species sampled from the depths of the ocean were scarlet shrimps (Acanthephyridae), lanternfish (Lampanyctus indicus), slender hatchetfish (Argyropelecus affinis), viperfish (Chauliodus pammelas), and leptocephali — the larval stage of eels and related fish species. Image courtesy of Cruising with Dr. Fridtjof Nansen Facebook page.

The Indian Ocean hosts one of the world’s largest tuna fisheries, supplying global seafood markets and sustaining livelihoods across dozens of coastal nations. But scientists warn some stocks are under mounting pressure as foreign-owned industrial fleets continue to overfish tuna and coastal countries expand their fisheries — intensifying disputes over how the resource is managed. articles.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
articles.summary: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
articles.ai_summary: The African National Congress recorded its worst-ever performance in South Africa's municipal elections amid public dissatisfaction.

scraped.title: South Africa elections: ANC marks its worst-ever performance
scraped.description: The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.
scraped.h1: South Africa's ANC hit by worst-ever performance in local elections
scraped.body_text:
The African National Congress, the party of late Nobel Prize winner Nelson Mandela, slumped to its worst-ever result in South Africa's municipal election. The voters blame the ANC for water and electricity shortages.

South Africa's African National Congress (ANC) turned in a historically poor election performance , with the the final tally published on Sunday giving them less than 31% of the vote in Wednesday's municipal polls .

Their closes rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), won just under 25% of the vote.

The ANC also lost its majority in six of the eight metropolitan regions, South Africa 's Electoral Commission said on Saturday. With no outright winner declared in several major cities, politicians are expected enter tough coalition talks to form municipal governments.

While the ANC remains the most popular party in the country, they have been struggling with growing backlash from voters. In 2026, many South Africans are frustrated by water and electricity shortages, with the ANC taking the blame for the poor state of municipalities. High unemployment, crime, and widespread corruption are high on the public agenda.

ANC leader, and South African president, Cyril Ramaphosa , has not yet addressed his party's poor performance. In his weekly presidential letter, however, he admitted that "municipal failures have contributed to declining public trust and confidence in democratic governance."

On Saturday, ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula told reporters that the ANC needs to work on winning back public confidence.

"We cannot ask the people to trust us merely because of our history," Mbalula said.

"This has been a very catastrophic outcome for the ANC ... as much as we are the largest party, it has been catastrophic for the movement," he added.

The ANC had governed with an absolute majority for most of its history up until the general election in 2024 saw it lose an outright parliamentary majority for the first time in South Africa's democratic era.

"This is the most severe result that the ANC would have feared," political analyst Daniel Silke told the AFP news agency.

"It's the ANC's worst result in history," Silke said, adding that the result will undermine the ANC's ability to exert authority on the local and national level. The results could also provide a bellwether of voter sentiment ahead of the 2029 general elections.

Once led by Nelson Mandela , the ANC was instrumental in ending apartheid, and took and power in 1994 after South Africa became a democracy.

But over the past decade, it has steadily performed worse in one election after another. In 2024, the ANC secured just over 40% in the 2024 national polls and 46% at the previous municipal elections in 2021.

After losing the absolute majority in 2024, the ANC formed a cross-party national unity government with all the parties represented in parliament, which is still in power.

The ANC's decline comes amid disillusionment over corruption, mismanagement and high unemployment. Smaller parties have also emerged across South Africa's political landscape, cutting into the ANC's voter base.

The pro-business, center-right DA is set to keep control of Cape Town after winning an absolute majority. It also performed well in the capital, Pretoria, and economic hub of Johannesburg, and is expected to form coalitions that exclude the ANC.

"All of the cut and thrust that comes with the election is now over, and it is time now... to put together governments that can actually fix these towns and cities," DA leader Geordin Hill-Lewis told reporters.

"We have already reached out to many parties over the last 24 hours and will continue to do so today," he said.

articles.title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, many injured
articles.summary: A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying scores of passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.
articles.ai_summary: A train collision south of Cairo resulted in several deaths and numerous injuries, prompting a large emergency response.

scraped.title: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, many injured
scraped.description: A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying scores of passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.
scraped.h1: Egypt train crash leaves several dead, many injured
scraped.body_text:
A train derailed after colliding with another train south of Cairo, with authorities confirming several deaths and saying scores of passengers were injured. Over 50 ambulances were deployed to the scene.

At least seven people were killed in the train collision in Egypt on Sunday, with authorities also confirming over 100 people were injured.

The collision involved one train hitting the rear end of another while traveling through the Giza province on the line between Cairo and the southern Nile city of Aswan. One of the trains then derailed and several cars flipped, according to the Egyptian authorities.

Officials said 52 ambulances were deployed to the scene some 52 kilometers (32 miles) south of Cairo. Emergency crews and cranes were also working to clear the line and restore railway traffic through Giza's al-Ayyat district.

The cause of the accident was not immediately clear.

In a social media post, Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said he ordered an investigation. He also urged the state agencies to "hold accountable anyone found to have been negligent."

The crash tool place in the same area as the worst train disaster in Egypt's history, which saw over 370 people were killed in a train fire in 2002. Several crashes also claimed dozens of lives in the same region in 2009.

In recent years, Egypt has invested billions of dollars into new highways and high-speed rail lines , but is still facing safety issues and repeated crashes while attempting to revamp its aging rail network .

articles.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
articles.summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.
articles.ai_summary: Israeli President Isaac Herzog has tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the responsibility of forming a new government.

scraped.title: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
scraped.description: Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.
scraped.h1: Israel: Eisenkot officially tasked with forming a government
scraped.body_text:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog tasked Gadi Eisenkot with the right of trying to form a government. The opposition leader's way to replacing Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister is full of political challenges.

Israel President Isaac Herzog has officially tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming a government.

Eisenkot, the head of the centrist Yashar party, will have 28 days to secure a coalition to replace current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu 's religious-nationalist government, with Herzog having the authority to prolong Eisenkot's mandate by 14 days.

"The conversations with the different parties were open and transparent, while also resurfacing the many voices in Israeli society. They reminded us the fact that all Israeli citizens have an equal voice, from all parts of society," Herzog said.

He stressed that Eisenkot received the clearest support from the majority of Knesset members when it comes to the question of forming the next government.

"The challenges we face are giant. Iran is not waiting a second in its threats. We have to start building a future in the region and proceed with Trump's 20-point plan in Gaza, as well as negotiating the future with Lebanon and other neighbors," the Israeli president said, adding that "Israel needs a stable government that faces these challenges."

Herzog said that he expected Eisenkot to do his best to form a government that would serve all parts of the Israeli people.

In turn, Eisenkot stressed that he is committed to establishing a national emergency government.

"We do not have the privilege of endless rounds of elections. I will send an official approach to all of the Knesset's members, as parties and individuals, for talks," he added.

Eisenkot also addressed Knesset members. "The public looks up to us... We are in the most complicated political situation since Israel's establishment," he said.

Yashar was Israel's second biggest party in Israel's October elections with 21 parliament seats, behind Netanyahu's Likud with 27. However, more members of the Knesset, the Israeli parliament, recommended Eisenkot as the man who should be given the first right to try and secure a government.

In comparison to Eisenkot's 67 recommendations, Netanyahu received the backing of 46 members, with the ultraorthodox Ashkenazi party United Torah Judaism (UTJ) deciding not to make any recommendations despite having joined Netanyahu's governments of the past 17 years.

Should Eisenkot fail to form a coalition, President Isaac Herzog will have the authority to pass the task on to a different Knesset member, with the second person in line expected to be Netanyahu.

If the Likud leader, too, will not manage to form a government, and if no other parliament member will claim to have enough support to head a government, Israel will likely head to another round of elections.

Dividing Israel's Zionist parties into blocs results in Netanyahu's religious-nationalist allies receiving 53 seats, with the Eisenkot-led anti-Netanyahu bloc having 48 seats.

Israel's two Arab parties, which with 19 seats received historic support due to the high turnout in Arab and Palestinian communities, already voiced their willingness to support the Zionist opposition in ousting Netanyahu and his government. Mostly the religious Muslim party Ra'am, led by Mansour Abbas, said it is willing to join a coalition once again in a bid to improve Israel's Arab and Palestinian communities' lives.

In 2021, Ra'am made history in becoming the first-ever Arab party to join an Israeli coalition, signing an agreement with right-wing candidate Naftali Bennet and liberal politician Yair Lapid.

The other Arab party, the Joint List, is a union of several smaller parties. While its members have never joined an Israeli coalition, its politicians did provide political support for an Israeli government from the opposition during Yitzhak Rabin's second term as prime minister as his government pushed through the Oslo Accords with the Palestinians, a term which was cut short by Rabin's murder in November 1995.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Both sides of Israel's Zionist political divide promised not to rely on votes by Arab parties to form a coalition, meaning Eisenkot's bloc will have to track back on one of its election promises to form a government with them.

However, a poll by the Accord Center of the Hebrew University in Jerusalem carried out two days after the elections found that 59 percent of Israel's Zionist opposition voters would rather have a government with Ra'am, and with the Joint List's abstention, than any other alternative.

Another option touted by Israeli media in the past week was the country's two ultraorthodox parties potentially joining an Eisenkot-led coalition. UTJ and Sepharadi party Shas have seven seats each, but a coalition with any of them would require Eisenkot to backtrack on another campaign promise: to pass through a legislation to secure the army conscription of young ultraorthodox men, which the two parties strictly object, citing fears over the future of religious studies in Israel.

Moreover, Shas supporters are known to hold right-wing views favorable to Netanyahu, with party head Arye Deri being considered as one of the politicians closest to Israel's longest-serving prime minister.

The government formed is bound to have wide-ranging implications on the lives of Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank and the Gaza Strip.

The Netanyahu-led current coalition also includes far-right parties Otzma Yehudit and Religious Zionism, which received 13 seats in the October election. The two parties support annexing the West Bank — a territory illegally occupied by Israel — as well as re-establishing Israeli settlements in the Gaza Strip and carrying out the so-called "wilful migration," the plan to move Gaza's 2.1 million Palestinians to other countries. Large parts of Netanyahu's Likud, too, support the plan.

The two parties often provide political backing to the violent settlers carrying out attacks against Palestinians in the Occupied West Bank.

Eisenkot himself promised to secure a Gaza Strip without Hamas rule within 18 months of becoming prime minister. This stands in contrast to the Netanyahu government's current policy of allowing Hamas to control certain parts of the enclave, despite the US-brokered ceasefire agreement saying a board of technocrats should take over Gaza from Hamas.

While Gadi Eisenkot's bloc includes several right-wing parties, their positions differ from those of Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition. Naftali Bennet , the head of the opposition's second biggest party Beyachad, labels himself as a right-winger and a supporter of settlements.

However, he has repeatedly used strong terms to condemn settler attacks on Palestinians. Eisenkot himself, too, condemned settler violence towards Palestinians, saying they are the result of the Netanyahu government's policies.

scraped.title: Portland’s Socialists Have Built a Political Machine
scraped.description: While New York City gets much of the media attention, the Democratic Socialists of America chapter in Portland, Oregon, has quietly built a local political powerhouse over the last few years.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

While New York City gets much of the media attention, the Democratic Socialists of America chapter in Portland, Oregon, has quietly built a local political powerhouse over the last few years.

Portland DSA’s labor solidarity work helped grow its membership and build its electoral campaigns. It now holds a third of the seats on the Portland City Council. (Mitch for Portland)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

O ver the last two years, the Portland, Oregon, chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) has developed a reputation for punching far above its city’s weight.

The chapter sits just behind the New York, Los Angeles, and Washington, DC, chapters in terms of size, and roughly one in two hundred Portlanders is a member (compared to about one in 530 New Yorkers). Today one-third of Portland’s city council actively participates in the group’s Socialists in Office Committee (SIOC); this election cycle, the chapter ran candidates for state and county office. Yet for most of the chapter’s history, elections weren’t a focus, and candidates for office were often kept at arm’s length.

“For a significant period where I was involved, a number of people just believed that candidates couldn’t do anything for you,” said Dave Coburn, the chapter’s former Electoral Working Group cochair. “People really only wanted to do things via ballot measure.”

That would start to change with the fallout of Portland’s long-lasting George Floyd protests. The protests supercharged existing frustrations with the city’s political status quo — and created an opening for outsiders to achieve significant electoral victories.

F ew American cities experienced 2020 like Portland. For almost a year, the city’s downtown saw sustained demonstrations and an intense response from local and federal law enforcement. The protests and ensuing criticism of the aggressive actions taken by local police hobbled the tenure of moderate Democratic Mayor Ted Wheeler and energized popular calls to reform the city’s commission, its governing body at the time.

In 2022, voters approved Measure 26-228, changing Portland’s legislative structure from four at-large commissioners to a twelve-member city council drawn from four multimember districts elected with ranked-choice voting. Combined with a small donor public financing scheme enacted in 2016, this system significantly lowered the bar for political participation in the 2024 election.

In many ways, the new electoral format catered well to DSA’s strengths. Smaller-district and multimember elections benefited candidates who could mobilize large field operations while also being able to hold a clear lane within a crowded field — unlike in previous elections, candidates would only need 25 percent +1 to win. Similarly, ranked-choice voting allowed candidates to pick up votes from coalition allies, benefiting those with platforms that spoke to a wide range of voters, while the matching funds program helped campaigns critical of the city’s traditional donor class to compete.

These reforms came right as Portland DSA was trying to revitalize itself. The pandemic had seen a sharp downturn in the chapter’s membership, and organizers began looking for opportunities to rebuild their capacity.

One came as part of a push to establish universal pre-K that the chapter had initiated in mid-2019 with the goal of getting a measure on the November 2020 ballot. A month after the Universal Pre-School Now! (UP Now!) coalition submitted the proposed language for the measure, pandemic restrictions were enacted in Oregon, hampering signature collection. Simultaneously, UP Now! faced competition from a more moderate universal pre-K project at the county level called Pre-School 4 All (P4A).

That summer, the chapter threw itself into building support for the campaign and managed to collect more than 32,000 signatures. Its success facilitated a merger with an updated P4A in order to avoid both proposals appearing on the ballot and potentially failing due to voter confusion. The unified measure passed overwhelmingly and marked one of Portland DSA’s first real electoral wins. Both of the chapter’s future 2024 city council candidates, Mitch Green and Tiffany Koyama Lane, were involved in the effort.

“It was an interesting test of our organizing ability,” said Green. “We were able to pass that, and that built the foundations for our city council races.”

The chapter also saw large success during the 2021 Nabisco strike and the 2023 Portland teachers’ strike, when its members organized fundraisers, held rallies supporting strikers, and walked picket lines. Both periods brought in new members and reactivated existing ones. The work also surprisingly helped convince the chapter to take another look at running candidates, according to Coburn.

“Having some elected officials weigh in on the side of the strikers proved to be more impactful to the strikers than many of us thought it would be and also ended up sometimes being more impactful on negotiations than many of us thought it would be,” he said.

B y the time candidates began announcing their campaigns in 2024 under the new system, Portland DSA was well positioned to run. It had proven it could manage a strong ground game, had built a name for itself among the city’s progressive ecosystem, and, importantly, felt that it could recruit strong candidates.

Still, worried about potentially overextending itself, the chapter only endorsed two candidates, Green and Koyama Lane. However, when the dust settled, not only had both won, but so had two more DSA-aligned candidates who hadn’t received the chapter’s endorsement.

“I think we were concerned about endorsing other folks who were progressive but were not close with DSA,” said Carolyn Roderique, the current cochair of Portland DSA. “But the election showed that we had so much more of a lane than we expected.”

Within a single cycle, DSA had gone from no representation in city politics to holding a third of the council. Two additional progressives were also elected, forming a larger progressive bloc nicknamed “Peacock.”

“It’s short for progressive caucus (P-Cauc),” explained Green. “And then, also, peacocks are an ostentatious bird.”

Following the election, Portland DSA created a Socialists in Office Committee in order to coordinate with councilors and facilitate an ongoing dialogue.

“There have been a ton of benefits [to having the SIOC],” said Koyama Lane, who was up for reelection this year. “Just having that time where we can share what’s upcoming, give a heads-up . . . and then also for them to bring back questions to us too.”

The SIOC has also helped the chapter’s candidates cement their status as a bloc, which has helped amplify their power within city council and during elections. In addition to Koyama Lane, Green, and Angelita Morillo — one of the DSA-aligned candidates who did not receive the chapter’s endorsement in 2024 — also faced reelection this year. All three won.

“[Being part of the SIOC] made it so like me, Angelita, and Mitch — people [could] just donate to all three of us at the same time through DSA,” said Koyama Lane.

A s members of the city’s legislative branch, DSA’s city councilors have focused on oversight and accountability.

“We’ve got councilors grilling the city administrator on why [they] didn’t disclose a bunch of housing money and why [they are] spending that on sweeps instead of rental assistance and that sort of thing,” said Green. “We’ve been fighting very publicly and racking up wins.”

Those victories — including banning AI price-fixing and fining the landlord behind the South Portland US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility — appear to be feeding Portland DSA’s popularity.

According to reporting by The Oregonian , recent polling has found that the DSA has a 61 percent approval rating among Oregon Democrats, with 44 percent of Portland voters saying that the group’s endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate.

For Portland DSA members, these numbers reinforce the validity of the lessons they say they’ve taken from their recent victories. These have included using elections as opportunities to build capacity, consistently reactivating members through regular engagement, and publicly identifying opponents.

“I think one of the things that has been exposed through all of the successes that the DSA has had is actually bringing out the bad guys,” said Colleen Carroll, a chapter member working on the campaign of Nathan Ong Norris, who ran this year as a Portland DSA–endorsed candidate for Multnomah County commissioner. “Naming the villains who are harming our communities and keeping us from having the things we want, I think, has been a huge part of the project.”

Roman Broszkowski is a freelance writer covering American and Eastern European politics.

articles.ai_summary: China's leadership has shifted its focus from a revolutionary past to a vision of future rejuvenation, establishing a new social contract that prioritizes stability and economic growth.

scraped.title: Xi Jinping’s Chinese Dream Has Replaced the Maoist Credo
scraped.description: China’s leaders now appeal to the vision of a rejuvenated future rather than a revolutionary past. The new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

China’s leaders now appeal to the vision of a rejuvenated future rather than a revolutionary past. The new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth.

Xi Jinping has promoted the idea of the “Chinese dream,” which is not merely a Chinese version of its American counterpart. While the American dream focuses on the individual, the Chinese dream is one of national rejuvenation. (Greg Baker / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

S ince 1978, China has undergone a series of seismic changes in its economic order that have radically altered its citizens’ relationship to both labor and land. They have unmade the socialist working class and are in the process of expropriating the peasantry, transforming both into a propertyless proletariat.

At the same time, China’s political structure has not undergone a similar revolution. Accordingly, the contradiction between its systems of economic and political organization is increasingly acute.

T he disjunctive fates of rural and urban China have been part of a single story ever since the establishment of the People’s Republic. It is the impoverished hinterland that subsidized the rise of the urban industry under state socialism.

Unlike in England during its industrial revolution, this development did not require the expropriation of rural land and a concomitant displacement of the peasantry. There, the enclosure movement provided both the capital and the labor for industrial development. In China, in contrast, there was no shortage of labor, and the state preferred to keep the peasants precisely where they were rather than allowing them to flow into cities and coalesce into a potentially explosive proletariat of the kind that had become common in much of the developing world.

To obtain industrial capital, the state simply extracted the economic surplus produced by the peasants while keeping the peasants themselves in place. This was the essence of primitive socialist accumulation. After China’s transition to state capitalism, the countryside has continued to subsidize urban development, supporting not only state capital but also private Chinese capital and global capital.

Urban industry no longer extracts just the product of rural labor but the peasants themselves, albeit on a rotational and provisional basis. This has taken the form of a “floating population” made up of hundreds of millions of semi-proletarianized migrant workers who continue to rely in part on collectively owned, nontransferable rural land cultivated by villagers left behind.

With the enclosure of rural land, China is in the process of converting its migrant labor force into permanent city dwellers, transforming an existing reserve army of workers into a reserve army of consumers as well — making them fully proletarianized. Moreover, it is not only the former migrant workers who are proletarianized as their displacement becomes permanent: the arrival of agrarian capitalism proletarianizes even those who remain in the countryside.

T he exploitation of the countryside for industrial development is emphatically not unique to China. Indeed, when viewed from a longer historical perspective, the birth of the new Chinese working class seems rather unexceptional: we have come to take it for granted that people work for wages. However, the sociologist Charles Tilly observes that as recently as 1700, only about 10 percent of the global workforce made their living by selling their labor power — “by selling themselves,” in Karl Marx’s phrase — whereas today, most of us do so.

What is distinctive about the fate of the Chinese working class is the specific way in which state socialism and state capitalism have become conjoined in China, with the former providing the foundation for the latter, as well as the temporal and spatial dimensions of this evolution. Processes of commodification of land and labor that took place over centuries in England have been compressed into just a few decades.

What is more, the People’s Republic of China claims an imperial footprint more encompassing than any other twentieth-century revolutionary state. Because of both the staggering speed of its transformation and its equally staggering size, China plays an oversize role in the development of global capitalism. Accordingly, the incorporation of rural and urban land, as well as rural and urban labor, into a single regime of state capitalism has both local and global implications.

The massive post-1978 reorganization of land, labor, and capital has left China with a series of internal contradictions. Perhaps the most outstanding one is the disjunction between its economic and political orders. The philosopher Jiwei Ci describes it as a contradiction between a radically new organization of desire and a largely unchanged political and ideological structure.

As the state has disavowed its material responsibilities to workers, economic relations have been reconfigured as those of freedom — essentially the freedom of being left alone to fend for oneself. Ci call this “de facto freedom,” a kind of freedom by default. While it is negative in origin, signifying the retreat of the state rather than a result of a social struggle, it has opened the way for seeking the satisfaction of private desires.

To the extent that the state wants China to become a nation of consumers, cultivating this desiring subject has become an economic imperative: while needs are limited, desires are boundless, and only desire can fuel consumption without limits. Ci contrasts this de facto economic freedom with freedom as a positive moral or political value.

I n the absence of a liberal ideology valorizing it, freedom by default is not capable of giving meaning to material prosperity, even if one is fortunate (or well connected) enough to have prospered in the new regime of economic inequality. It is notable, however, that the dominant language of public critique today is overwhelmingly concerned with “social justice” — associated with labor and land protests as well anti-corruption agitation more generally — rather than “democracy” or political freedom more generally.

This reflects at least in part the fact that the discourse of social justice allows people to appeal to the state in terms of its own professed commitment to socialism. In some ways, this makes it potentially an even more damaging critique than a direct challenge to the political order: the gaping, and growing, economic inequality is a threat not only to social stability but to the very legitimacy of the regime.

At the same time, the turn to the idiom of social justice rather than Maoism is a sign of the diminished nature of Chinese socialism. As a result of four decades of “reform,” there exists today, for the first time in China’s history, a vast industrial proletariat of both urban and rural origin. But despite its unquestionable existence in a socioeconomic sense, it has not yet emerged as a political subject with a collective identity. In addition to material obstacles to labor organization, workers do not have access to an adequate public language in which to articulate their grievances.

Responding to these political and economic contradictions, Xi Jinping’s ascendancy has coincided with the rise of neo-Maoist rhetoric. One of the most notable forms worker protest has taken is dagong shige , a form of subaltern writing by migrant workers, often translated as “battler poetry.” However, its political efficacy remains circumscribed: it is subject to state sanction when too critical, and to state co-optation when less so.

After Deng Xiaoping’s singular emphasis on economic development and the need to allow some people “to get rich first,” Xi Jinping is mindful of the need to balance growth with escalating demands for social justice and environmental protection, stressing the need for “common prosperity” ( gongtong fuyu ) and the construction of “an ecological civilization” ( shengtai wenming ).

The invocations of ecological civilization began under Hu Jintao but are now associated with Xi, who wrote the term into China’s constitution in 2018, in symbolic recognition of the damage wrought by rural industry in particular: land and water contamination, soil erosion, environmental disease, declining food safety, the depletion of fisheries, and so on. In the same vein, Xi has made the eradication of rural poverty one of his signature initiatives. In 2021, he declared that China had achieved a “total elimination of absolute poverty,” with every village in China above the official poverty line.

Yet even this victory — partly semantic, given the arbitrariness of any official definition of poverty — relied on neoliberal means, such as teaching electronic marketing to peasants and making entire villages switch to cash crops in order to raise their incomes by the announced deadline. As Ryan Martinez Mitchell observes, what might have been a radical redistributive project turned instead into a campaign “to embed entrepreneurialism as a character trait into society at large,” including rural China.

H owever, the state’s reliance on neoliberal solutions is far from unqualified. Chinese neoliberalism is similar to the North Atlantic variant to the extent that it makes individuals responsible for themselves in economic circumstances that are beyond their control. However, it does not represent a full subsumption of the state by the logic of capital. It is a selective, strategic, and ultimately political deployment of market institutions in the service of the party state.

China’s future is therefore not determined by the dictates of capital alone, nor is the outcome of the rural enclosure preordained. If it so desires, the Chinese leadership can recalibrate its strategies of industrial development and rethink its current trajectory. In fact, because of its centralized structures of political authority, it is able to act more decisively than a liberal capitalist regime. Nonetheless, and despite the push and pull of policy, the long-term trend has been to continue enclosing rural land and commercializing the Chinese lifeworld.

At the same time, it is important to recognize that this trend has improved peasants’ lives in significant ways. Most villages now have running water, electricity, paved roads, and internet, for example. The arrival of capital has helped diversify the rural economy. While there is great regional variation, there are villages that bear a resemblance to middle-class suburbs.

On the other hand, even the households that manage to hold on to their land in defiance of “dragonhead enterprises” and other new commercial actors become fully reliant on buying inputs from the market and cultivating crops for the market. The less fortunate landless peasants who are unable to find rural employment are in turn compelled to join the urban proletariat, even if material conditions improve for at least a subset of those who make it in the commercialized countryside.

Heeding calls by the agronomist Wen Tiejun and others to find a “Third Way,” some villages have sought to return to collective farming. It is indeed the case that, at least in principle, the commodification of rural land need not result in a complete predominance of private actors. If a village chooses collectively not to sell the rights to the use of its land, it can replace cultivation by individual households with a scaled-up agricultural cooperative — one in which each household exchanges its land allotment for shares in a village-based enterprise.

The resulting shareholding cooperative is in some ways an agricultural version of the industrial collectives of rural China that marked the beginning of economic reforms in the 1980s, engaging in commercial farming rather than industrial production. As a form of self-development by the village, establishing such cooperatives is undoubtedly preferable to allowing outside commercial actors take over, yet by no means do they herald a return to the socialist collectives of the Maoist era. Even collectively owned farming enterprises are essentially commercial actors, subsumed by agrarian capitalism and relying on markets both for buying their inputs — including labor — and for selling their output.

I n recognition of increasing economic stratification throughout society, the state has sought to build at least a minimal safety net. In this respect, the evolution of Chinese welfare institutions has been broadly similar to the development of poor laws in England, initially enacted in response to the enclosure of the commons and the rising numbers of paupers without any means of subsistence.

At the same time, although the Elizabethan Poor Laws were motivated by an anxiety about the state of the realm as a whole, they continued to maintain a medieval commitment to territorially based charity, funded by local ratepayers and available only to paupers settled within a parish. Under the so-called settlement laws, it became as difficult for a pauper to change his official place of settlement as for a Chinese peasant under Maoism to change his hukou registration.

By obstructing mobility, both institutions thwarted the development of a national labor market even as land was increasingly transformed into private property. In the wake of revolutionary upheaval in France, the poor laws were further fortified in 1795 by indexing welfare to the price of bread — a reform that Prime Minister George Canning credited with having “saved England from a revolution” of its own.

In 1834, the New Poor Law finally abolished the centuries-old parish-based regime and replaced it with a centralized system that limited welfare strictly to the disabled and the ill. The able-bodied poor were left with no other option than the workhouse, so stigmatized and so horrific that only the truly desperate would enter it. Finally, a nationwide labor market emerged, leading to the proliferation of slums in England’s industrial cities.

In general outline, Xi’s urbanization policies and his restricted program of social welfare envision a similar transition — except for the state’s determination to prevent the emergence of slums. Even while calling for a more robust welfare system, Xi has consistently held back on public funding, preferring social security programs financed through employers and individual contributions, to prevent a fall into “the idleness-breeding trap of welfarism.” Welfare as such is for orphans, the disabled, and the very old, whereas the able-bodied indigent must find work, or else rely on family for support.

I n England, however, the abolition of the old poor laws coincided with major political agitation. It was preceded by the Reform Act of 1832, which expanded the franchise to the middle class and opened the way to the eventual inclusion of the working class. China, in contrast, has offered no democratic reforms, nor have they been at the top of protesters’ demands.

On the contrary, even as the state is making its citizens turn to the market for their economic needs, it continues to appeal to the political subject of Maoism, one that is expected to sacrifice for the collective good. At the same time, and somewhat improbably, the state has begun to cultivate neo-Confucian rhetoric as well. In lieu of waging class struggle, the people are called on to build a “harmonious society” ( hexie shehui ) — the less protest, the better.

In this vein, Xi has promoted the “Chinese dream” ( Zhongguo meng ) as the most urgent political desideratum of the millennium. This dream is not merely a Chinese rendering of its American counterpart. The American dream belongs to the individual, hearkening to the myth of Horatio Alger, whereas the Chinese dream is that of the nation.

Sublating socialism into nationalism and fed by an intensive cultivation of memories of the so-called century of humiliation that followed China’s defeat in the Opium Wars, it seeks to “rejuvenate” the nation and return it to its rightful place at the heart of a Sinocentric world. The realization of China’s long overdue dream — one that was once a reality and now must be restored — may entail personal sacrifice, including temporary economic inequality, but everyone must play his part. This is a deferral of equality now for the sake of a future dream.

The intensifying personality cult around Xi may be interpreted as an attempt to forge unity in the absence of a political consensus, much as Mao Zedong relied on charismatic leadership to overcome social and political fragmentation. The public promotion of “Xi Jinping Thought” — it has been enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution, along with Marxism-Leninism, Mao Zedong Thought, and Deng Xiaoping Theory — has a similar aim, although its ideological vitality remains questionable.

The anthropologist John Osburg characterizes China as “a post-belief” society. The People’s Republic of China officially remains, and must remain, a socialist state, but its credibility in claiming that label is eroding by the day. At the same time, the party is losing its ability to draw on its historical legitimacy. Mao Zedong and his comrades rightfully claimed credit for having unified the nation and secured its international autonomy. In contrast, the current generation of princelings in charge fought no revolutionary battles but rely on inherited credentials instead.

This is indeed why they appeal to a “rejuvenated” future rather than a revolutionary past. Ultimately the new social contract between the people and the party state is a pragmatic one: social stability in return for continued economic growth, a bargain that political scientists characterize as “performance legitimacy.”

This is an extract from The Unmaking of the Chinese Working Class: How Communism Built a Capitalist Superpower , now available from Verso Books.

Teemu Ruskola is a professor of law and East Asian languages and civilizations at the University of Pennsylvania. He is the author of The Unmaking of the Chinese Working Class and Legal Orientalism .

scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
