In recent decades, the basis of US hegemony has shifted from domestic industrial strength to its ability to enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. Today this imperial role is now increasingly under strain.

Donald Trump wants to restore domestic industry while also defending multinationals’ privileges. Understanding why these two goals can’t be reconciled is key to grasping the weaknesses of US capitalism today. (Annabelle Gordon / The Washington Post / Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

I mperialism is again at the forefront of world politics. Large-scale war has become a permanent feature of the present era, from Ukraine to Gaza. Donald Trump’s second term has added a tariff war, threats to annex Greenland, the abduction of Venezuela’s president, and, together with Israel, an unprovoked war on Iran. This is not the whim of one man, for the confrontation with China began under Trump’s first term and deepened under Joe Biden.

At the same time, politics across the mature capitalist countries is in deep turmoil. In the United States, the Left has become a force in mass politics, with a democratic socialist as mayor of New York and widespread opposition to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), Israel’s genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran. In France, governments have fallen one after the other, and social unrest is spreading. But the far right is also rising powerfully, from France’s Rassemblement National and Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland to Reform UK and Austria’s Freiheitliche Partei Österreichs, alongside the Trump White House.

Left and Right draw on the same realities of stagnant wages, industrial decline, and degraded public services. If the Left is to offer a credible political program to the working class and the poor, it must grasp what links resurgent imperialism to the decay of capitalist accumulation in the historic core of the world economy. With millions of people now looking for answers, this means offering a politics of class rupture.

T he starting point is the paradox at the heart of US capitalism, which is also the central paradox of contemporary imperialism. In 1945, the United States produced about half of world manufacturing output; today it produces roughly one-sixth . Productivity growth has been feeble since the great financial crisis of 2007–9, investment has remained weak, and real wages have stagnated for over a generation. Yet the dollar’s share of official reserves has slipped only slightly below 60 percent. US productive preeminence has declined, but the monetary hierarchy has hardened.

The United States alone settles its international obligations in its own liabilities. Everyone else must acquire dollars, manage dollar exposures, and adjust to the policy of the Federal Reserve. Foreign investors hold around $9 trillion of US Treasury bonds , about a third of the marketable stock, and central banks across the world are stuffed with US public paper.

The material basis of US hegemony has thus shifted from domestic industrial strength to the capacity to set and enforce the rules that organize global production, finance, and money. This is also where its imperial power truly lies.

US corporations have flourished within this structure. Among the largest globally active enterprises, US corporations take around 44 percent of profits and hold 34 percent of intellectual property, compared to 11 and 14 percent for their Chinese counterparts. US multinationals led the globalization of production from the 1980s onward, exporting productive capital and building the global chains that shifted industrial capacity abroad, while relying on the dollar to run them.

This was a triumph for private US capital, but it hollowed out industry within the United States and created the social wreckage that became Trump’s political raw material. Global monetary, financial, and corporate dominance has gone together with domestic deterioration.

This is why neither of the two main US parties has been able to reverse industrial decline. Trump’s 2018 tariffs brought little reshoring, since many corporations simply moved their supply chains to Vietnam and Mexico. Biden kept the tariffs and added the subsidies of the Inflation Reduction Act and the CHIPS Act but left US capital’s global strategy untouched.

Trump now wants to restore domestic industry while at the same time defending the privileges of multinationals. One of his first acts on returning to office was to withdraw from the Base Erosion and Profit Shifting framework of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which more than 130 countries had signed, including the Biden-era United States. It would have allowed states to tax a share of the profits generated by multinationals within their borders and to impose a minimum tax of 15 percent, curbing the transfer of profits to tax havens through intellectual property held offshore.

But Trump’s aims cannot be reconciled. To see why, we must look at how production and finance are organized around the world today.

V ladimir Lenin insisted in 1916 that imperialism must be grasped through the dominant mechanisms of accumulation of its time. Drawing primarily on Rudolf Hilferding , he identified these as the fusion of banking and industrial capital into finance capital, the export of capital, and the territorial division of the world among rival powers. His method remains indispensable, but the concrete forms of imperialism have changed profoundly.

Applied to contemporary capitalism, Lenin’s method reveals two structural foundations of imperialism: first, the pairing of globalized productive capital with internationalized financial capital; second, the dollar as world money, which turns that pairing into a hierarchy enforced ultimately by US military power. World money is a crucial element of imperialism today but a consideration that classical Marxist theory never developed.

Contemporary production is organized through global chains coordinated by multinationals — mostly US, European, and Japanese — that control design, intellectual property, logistics, and access to markets. Finance has become global alongside production, but the two have not fused as in Hilferding’s time. They form a pairing in which neither side simply commands the other. Productive capital generates value and surplus value; financial capital supplies the credit, liquidity, and means of payment without which global production could not run. US capital has led on both sides of the pairing: its multinationals built the chains, and its banks and asset managers globalized finance.

The pairing of capitals operates in a world market that has no world state, no world central bank, and no world court of justice. What holds it together is world money, which must serve across separate jurisdictions as unit of account, means of payment, and reserve of value, especially in a crisis. Only the dollar performs these functions.

A manufacturing supplier in Vietnam or Mexico ships components today and waits sixty or ninety days to be paid, but wages and inputs must be paid now. The gap has to be financed, and because the lead firm in the chain invoices in dollars, it is financed in dollars at rates priced off dollar benchmarks. This is not an economic choice but the price of admission to the chain. Between 1999 and 2019, about three-quarters of exports in the Asia-Pacific and virtually all exports in the Americas were invoiced in dollars. Through these chains, the monetary policy of the Federal Reserve reaches directly into workshops on the other side of the world.

The state that issues the necessary dollars is not just another power pursuing its interests abroad. It is the authority that ultimately guarantees settlement, liquidity, and enforceability for globally mobile capital, deciding whose liabilities count as money and whose balance sheets must adjust. Production remains the foundation, but the hegemon’s command over world money is the hinge of imperial power, the point at which the pairing of capitals is disciplined across the world.

The hierarchy becomes fully visible in a crisis. In 2008 and again in 2020, the Fed opened dollar swap lines to a select circle of fourteen central banks. Those inside stabilized their financial systems in days. Those outside, including India, Indonesia, and South Africa, faced currency depreciation, loss of reserves, and austerity. Sanctions and exclusion from payment systems complete the apparatus of coercion, as the freezing of approximately $300 billion of Russian central bank assets in 2022 showed. The fourteen account for roughly 55 percent of US imports and 60 percent of US exports. They also host more than 90 percent of US military personnel stationed abroad. The map of monetary privilege and the map of US military power largely coincide.

The dollar and the F-35 are two moments of a single structure of domination, and US air and naval power guards the choke points through which world trade moves. This is imperialism running through the balance sheets of firms, banks, and states, backed by military power. It does not need to plant a flag over a territory or to establish an expensive colonial administration.

C rucially, the financial side of the pairing has itself been transformed since the great financial crisis of 2007–9. Before the crash there was Financialization Mark I, centered on globally active commercial banks, which turned workers’ homes into a prime terrain of extraction through mortgages and consumer debt. At its peak, bank profits in the United States approached 40 percent of all corporate profits. The crash ended that regime.

It was replaced by Financialization Mark II, resting on shadow banks — above all, asset managers such as BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. Research that I and colleagues have recently done on 426 major asset managers shows that the equity they manage rose from $13 trillion in 2013 to $46 trillion by mid-2025. That is roughly 40 percent of the equity of all billion-dollar listed companies in the world. In every region outside North America, US asset managers are the largest group of foreign investors. They represent imperial power exercised through balance sheets rather than territory.

Unlike commercial banks that draw their profits mostly from the spread between the lending and the borrowing rates of interest, asset managers depend on the gap between the rate of profit and the rate of interest — what Hilferding called founder’s profit. Such profits are realized primarily through rising asset prices. Stock market inflation has thus become a leading channel of financial accumulation.

The entire edifice of Mark II rests on the state. US gross public debt rose from just over 60 percent of GDP in 2007 to more than 120 percent by 2025. At the same time, the Federal Reserve absorbed public debt securities on a historic scale, created vast amounts of new dollars on its balance sheet, and became dealer of last resort for the shadow banks and others in the money markets. Whatever the neoliberal rhetoric of free markets might say, contemporary capitalism survives through state hyperinterventionism, but on behalf of finance, not to rebuild production.

Investment and productivity outside a narrow set of sectors have consequently stayed weak. The vast AI boom does not alter this picture; it confirms it. Spending on data centers and chips is concentrated in a handful of giant corporations, financed from their enormous cash holdings and increasingly by vast debt, while asset managers pour capital into the same few stocks. The promised productivity gains remain largely a matter of expectation, already priced into shares long before they appear in production. This is still primarily accumulation through asset price inflation, not yet a true transformation of production.

The historic core of the world economy thus continues to drift in an interregnum. The old order has lost its dynamism, but no new one has emerged.

S till, the reach of the Fed extends far beyond the borders of the United States, since the dollars it creates are world money. The dollar dependence created by global production chains accumulates into national pressures: dollar debts that must be serviced, profits that must be repatriated, technology payments that must flow abroad. The burden falls heaviest on the Global South, and the result is subordinate financialization. This is not an immature version of the financialization of the United States or Britain but a distinct form produced by subordination in both production and finance.

A peripheral central bank cannot expand its balance sheet at will or ignore the exchange rate when it forms monetary policy, since it operates in the highly precarious environment of loanable capital flowing in and out of the country. Much of that capital is managed by the same US asset managers that dominate Mark II.

In October 2025, the average policy interest rate in Brazil, India, Indonesia, Mexico, and South Africa stood 4 percentage points above the Fed’s. This is a liquidity tribute, levied by the monetary hierarchy itself. High rates choke domestic investment, attract speculative inflows, push up the exchange rate, and undermine domestic manufacturing. Peripheral states are forced to stockpile dollars as self-insurance and park them in US Treasuries, while their own governments and firms borrow at far higher rates. Resources that could build factories, railways, and hospitals are, in effect, lent to Washington.

Tribute on this scale needs local beneficiaries. Large firms in peripheral countries borrow cheaply in dollars and invest in domestic financial assets at high yields; banks profit from the public debt issued to absorb the inflows; and sections of the middle class enjoy cheap imports. In a peripheral country, the exchange rate is a class weapon as much as an economic variable. And the United States does not need a viceroy to collect the tribute, for it flows through the ordinary workings of the world market.

C hina presents the opposite picture to the United States. It accounts for close to 30 percent of world manufacturing value added and around 15 percent of world merchandise exports. State-owned enterprises dominate its strategic sectors, and it has built institutions that partly bypass the US-led order, such as the Belt and Road Initiative and the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank.

Yet China is not attempting to construct a separate imperial bloc or to acquire territory. It seeks a determining voice in the rules that govern trade, technology, and investment, and, in the longer term, new arrangements for world money.

That is where it is at its weakest. The renminbi accounts for less than 3 percent of global reserves and international payments, and less than 5 percent of world trade is invoiced in it, against roughly half in dollars. Chinese public debt does not serve as global collateral, the People’s Bank of China offers no liquidity backstop to the world market, and China’s own payment system processes little more than 12 percent of the dollar volume handled by the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication.

The barrier is structural, not a matter of will. World money requires deep markets in safe public liabilities, legal protection for foreign creditors, and an open capital account. The capital controls and public command over finance that protected China’s industrialization are precisely what prevent the renminbi from becoming world money. China is a productive superpower obliged to settle its obligations in a currency it does not issue and to hold its reserves in its rival’s debt.

Nor is Chinese domestic accumulation free of contradictions. Since 2007–9, growth and profitability have fallen to a “ new normal .” China still invests roughly double the US share of GDP, but the returns on that investment have declined sharply. The rational course would be to lower investment and systematically raise the incomes and consumption of Chinese workers, but the economic, social, and political risks of doing so are enormous.

The result is an impasse. The hegemon cannot recover its productive foundations, and the challenger cannot issue world money. Neither can impose a resolution, and neither will accept permanent subordination. There is no orderly path of succession within a monetary hierarchy that is singular, coercive, and increasingly contested, and therein lies the danger for the world.

The United States has stopped acting as the hegemon, that is, as the power that presents its own interests as the general interest. It acts instead as the biggest and most aggressive contestant in an increasingly open field, treating even its allies as subordinates. When Washington demanded sanctions on Russian energy after 2022, Germany accepted them at severe cost to its own industrial base. Yet US military predominance is no longer uncontested, and the war on Iran has shown that even weaker opponents cannot simply be made to submit. The situation echoes the rivalries before 1914. World war is not inevitable, but proxy wars, reserve seizures, payment exclusion, and technology embargoes have become an embedded feature of world politics.

Should the Left, then, cheer for de-dollarization and the BRICS? Weakening the monopoly of the dollar would loosen a crucial mechanism of domination. But the putative challengers are neither a socialist bloc nor a new anti-colonial movement. They are states competing in the world market and seeking ways around the dollar, not a fairer world money. Multipolarity is not a class category. The Left should oppose sanctions, the liquidity tribute, and the forced accumulation of reserves without enlisting in anyone’s camp.

O ne of the most encouraging political developments in this gloomy conjuncture is the US left seriously debating how to win and use governing power. Max Elbaum has rightly argued here that it cannot limit its positive platform to domestic issues while saying only what it opposes in foreign policy.

The analysis above shows why. The domestic and the imperial are two sides of the same structure, and a left government would confront that structure from day one. Success is not possible without overturning the prevailing capitalist mechanisms of social, economic, and political power. This is precisely the politics of class rupture that the Left should be offering to the millions seeking change.

I saw what this means at close quarters in Greece in 2015. Syriza’s election win had little significance in itself — it was at best only the beginning. A left-wing government that truly sought to save Greece from the disaster of the bailouts had to break the established mechanisms of power. That could only be done by using the machinery of the state in conjunction with the mass movement. To deliver results, a left-wing government would be obliged to transform the state.

The challenge crystallized on one issue — as it typically does in times of a radical upheaval. That was, to stay in the European Monetary Union (EMU), or to exit? Breaking with the euro would have required capital controls, public command over the banks and money, and a far-reaching reorganization of the economy that could have shifted power toward workers and the poor. Inevitably, there would have been a profound rupture with the entrenched class and imperial interests stifling Greece, both of which threw their weight behind the policy of remaining with the EMU. The mere thought was enough to send shivers down the spine of the timid Syriza leadership. Abject surrender followed.

There is a lesson here for the US left — and beyond it — despite the vast difference between the preeminent imperial power and a small European power. If it seeks to offer a politics of rupture that tilts the balance decisively in favor of workers and the poor, it must use and transform the machinery of the state while drawing on the strength of the mass movement. It should also be clear that there will be fierce and violent opposition on all levels. Success will not come without decisively overturning the domestic and the imperial configuration of class power in the United States. Of that there can be no doubt. It is almost redundant to say that the task is of world-historic importance.

T here is, however, plenty of historical experience on which the US left can draw as it seeks a class politics that could bring success. The first step involves developing a program of reversing domestic US productive decline, with the working class in the lead, as has already been argued for other developed capitalist countries.

That means public investment on a scale not seen in generations, public banks directing credit to production, and a central bank brought within a democratic economic plan instead of serving as dealer of last resort for BlackRock. It also means restoring capital controls as a normal instrument of policy and extending public ownership in energy, infrastructure, and housing, where social need and private profit sharply diverge. And it further means democratic, worker-based control of corporations, since a bureaucratic state corporation run on the priorities of capital changes nothing essential.

Such a program would reverse the global accumulation strategy of US capital, subordinating multinational and financial capital to democratically determined priorities. In short, it would aim to deglobalize and definancialize the US economy. This is neither isolationism nor autarky. The aim is an open economy that continues to trade, invest, and cooperate across borders but on terms set democratically rather than by multinationals and footloose financial capital. Openness should serve the reconstruction of production at home and genuine cooperation abroad, not the global strategy of US capital.

A program of this kind ultimately rests on the issue of sovereignty. The problem is that this term has been appropriated by the Right, which uses it to assert the unrestrained power of the US state abroad while defending the interests of capital at home. But for the Left, sovereignty has a different and older content, that of popular sovereignty. If democracy is to have real meaning, workers and the poor ought to have both voice and power at the workplace, the neighborhood, the town, the city, and the country. Popular sovereignty does not mean only electing a government that spends more on social care, housing, and infrastructure while taxing the rich, necessary as that is. It requires building the organized power of working people — channeling the renewed strike militancy of the United Auto Workers and the drives to organize the nonunion factories of the South — alongside the communities and movements that have resisted ICE, the genocide in Palestine, and the war on Iran.

Since, moreover, there is no democratic space beyond the borders of the nation-state, a program of class rupture would also rest on national sovereignty. This is an even thornier issue for the Left to grasp. In a subordinate country, such as Greece in 2015, national sovereignty means breaking out of imperialist domination. But the United States sits at the top of the imperialist hierarchy, and the sovereignty of the US state is a lever through which other nations are subordinated.

For the United States, therefore, national sovereignty raises directly the question of what the nation is and which class constitutes it. For the Right, the nation is the imperial state and the capital it serves. For the Left, national sovereignty is anti-imperialist at its core and means fighting against the oppression of others. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels put it plainly , after stating that workers have no country: the proletariat must “rise to be the leading class of the nation, must constitute itself the nation,” and is in that sense “itself national, though not in the bourgeois sense of the word.”

This is the opposite of nationalism, which asks workers to line up behind their own ruling class. The task is then clear. The US working class can constitute itself as the nation only by taking command of the instruments of imperial power — the Fed, the sanctions machinery of the Treasury, the military budget — and ending their use to subordinate other nations. US workers gain nothing durable from the dollar order. The more Washington pursues imperial primacy, the more it hollows out the domestic economy.

Antiwar politics and anti-capitalist politics are one struggle. Opposition to war that leaves domestic property relations untouched is incomplete, and transformation at home that ignores the imperial order will be crushed by it. The system that extracts value from the periphery is the same system that hollows out the core. That is what gives working-class internationalism a material content, instead of leaving it a liberal slogan compatible with the free movement of capital. It is the ground on which a genuinely internationalist socialist politics can be built.

This article draws on a contribution to the internal programmatic discussions of the Communist Party of Austria (KPÖ).

Costas Lapavitsas is a professor of economics at SOAS, currently at the New School for Social Research, and former member of the Greek Parliament.

Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits . A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.

In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.

Later in the complaint , the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”

Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”

This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG , Isbell, Reservoir Media , and more.

scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Seven-Year-Old Taken Into Custody Over Shorinji Racing
scraped.body_text:
OSAKA - Police across Japan are struggling to contain a rapidly spreading social media trend known as "Shorinji Racing," in which children and teenagers shout "Shorinji" outside police stations and police boxes before running away, with Osaka police recording approximately 280 related incidents and taking around 50 minors aged between 7 and 16 into protective custody or questioning them.

The bizarre activity, which has spread through videos posted on social media, involves young people deliberately provoking police officers, sometimes by approaching police facilities under false pretenses or making nuisance calls before fleeing. The youngest child taken into protective custody in Osaka was a 7-year-old first-grade elementary school student. The trend has gained momentum in recent weeks, with videos showing participants approaching police boxes, shouting the phrase and running away while companions record their actions. Some children have pretended to report lost property before suddenly shouting "Shorinji," while others have used public telephones to dial 110, Japan's emergency police number, as part of the prank. The origins of the expression remain unclear. Although Shorinji is associated with the famous Shaolin Temple in China, known for its martial arts tradition, investigators have not established any connection between the temple and the activity, nor have they identified who first started the trend. Osaka Prefectural Police said incidents involving children approaching police boxes and shouting the phrase have increased sharply since late September. Authorities have identified at least 280 related cases and dealt with approximately 50 boys aged between 7 and 16, some of whom have also been arrested. Hyogo Prefectural Police have also taken action against 25 young people, including elementary school students, as the phenomenon has spread across prefectural boundaries. The situation escalated on November 2 when Osaka police arrested an 18-year-old suspected of obstructing police operations by using a social media account associated with Shorinji Racing to encourage reckless driving and other disruptive behavior. The account reportedly described itself as the original Shorinji Racing account and falsely suggested that its activities had official approval from Osaka Prefectural Police. Despite the arrest, the incidents have continued. In one case near Kansai Television's offices in Osaka, four boys, including junior high school students, approached a police box at around 7:20 p.m. while an officer was taking a break. The boys repeatedly opened and closed a sliding door, shouted "Shorinji Racing" and fled. Footage captured by a vehicle's dashboard camera showed several police vehicles and officers gathering at the scene, apparently conducting an investigation. Three of the four boys were subsequently taken into protective custody, while the fourth remained at large at the time of the report. Police said some children involved in the incidents had been influenced directly by videos they had seen online. One boy told investigators that he had participated to impress his school friends. Another said he had watched videos on social media and thought it would be entertaining to surprise or provoke police officers. The spread of the trend among increasingly younger children has raised particular concern among parents and educators. A third-grade elementary school boy living in Osaka Prefecture, who said he had been invited to participate by older students, described how the activity had become popular at his school. According to the boy, fourth-grade students were particularly involved, with many boys visiting police facilities after school. Some reportedly shouted at police officers, recorded the license plate numbers of police motorcycles and ran away. The boy suggested that almost all the boys involved had visited a police station or police box as part of the activity. He said an older student had invited him to join a Shorinji Racing outing, but he refused because he felt frightened. "I didn't really want to go. I was a little scared," he said, explaining that his older sister had warned him against participating. He told the other children that he would not join them that day. His mother expressed concern about how easily children can encounter such videos online and imitate activities without understanding the consequences. She said children frequently encounter provocative content on social media and may regard dangerous or disruptive activities as entertaining, especially when encouraged by a group of friends. She also questioned whether young children fully appreciate the risks involved or recognize that what appears to be a harmless prank could lead to police intervention. The incidents have also drawn mixed reactions from members of the public. Some residents described the behavior as pointless and foolish, while others expressed surprise that elementary school children were participating. Parents raised concerns about how they could prevent their children from copying online trends, particularly as they grow older and gain more independent access to smartphones and social media. Provoking police officers is not a new phenomenon in Japan. In the past, young people have thrown eggs at officers conducting traffic enforcement or deliberately fled from patrol cars on motorcycles in a form of cat-and-mouse pursuit sometimes described as playing tag with police. However, experts say social media has fundamentally changed the scale and appeal of such behavior. Masashi Usui, a professor at Niigata Seiryo University Graduate School who specializes in the psychology of juvenile delinquency, said similar pranks once attracted attention from only a handful of friends who happened to be watching. "Young people have done strange things in front of police officers and then run away before, but in those days, only a few people there would applaud," Usui said. "With social media, far more people can watch, and some children find that attention extremely rewarding." He said the possibility of attracting viewers from around the world could become a powerful incentive for young people to engage in increasingly disruptive behavior. Usui also pointed to peer pressure and the desire to participate in popular trends as important factors behind the rapid spread of Shorinji Racing. "The children probably don't think of themselves as doing something criminal," he said. "They think that if everyone else is doing it, they can do it too. Being at the forefront of something popular can give them a real sense of satisfaction." He warned that stopping such trends becomes particularly difficult when children interpret widespread participation as evidence that the behavior is acceptable. The legal consequences, however, can be serious. Attorney Kyosuke Nishiwaki, a former television announcer, warned that making nuisance calls to police can constitute fraudulent obstruction of business, while interfering with officers performing their duties may amount to obstruction of official duties, an offense punishable by up to three years of imprisonment. More dangerous activities, including throwing firecrackers or explosive devices into police facilities, could lead to substantially more serious criminal charges. Depending on the circumstances, offenses involving explosives can carry severe penalties, including life imprisonment or the death penalty. Nishiwaki said the danger lies partly in how seemingly minor pranks can develop into more serious acts as participants compete for attention online. He stressed that children watching videos of such incidents may gradually lose their sense that the behavior is wrong, particularly when the footage presents police harassment as entertainment. The incidents have renewed debate over children's access to social media, with some parents and commentators questioning whether stronger age restrictions are necessary until young users develop sufficient judgment. Others have emphasized the importance of improving digital literacy and helping children understand the difference between online entertainment and conduct that can cause real-world harm. With the activity continuing despite arrests and police intervention, authorities face the challenge of preventing further copycat incidents while addressing the social media incentives that have helped turn a simple act of shouting and running away into a nationwide problem.

articles.title: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions
articles.summary: Kyoto's Shin-Kyogoku Shopping Street, a bustling 500-meter arcade with more than 150 years of history, is home to some of the city's oldest restaurants, seven Buddhist temples and a Shinto shrine, while a recently rediscovered 90-year-old restaurant manual has revealed unusual dishes and the philosophy of a pioneering Western-style restaurant. (News On Japan)
articles.ai_summary: Kyoto's Shin-Kyogoku Shopping Street, with over 150 years of culinary history, showcases traditional restaurants and cultural heritage.

scraped.title: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions
scraped.description: Kyoto
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Kyoto Shopping Arcade Preserves 150 Years of Culinary Traditions
scraped.body_text:
KYOTO - Kyoto's Shin-Kyogoku Shopping Street, a bustling 500-meter arcade with more than 150 years of history, is home to some of the city's oldest restaurants, seven Buddhist temples and a Shinto shrine, while a recently rediscovered 90-year-old restaurant manual has revealed unusual dishes and the philosophy of a pioneering Western-style restaurant.

Stretching north from Shijo Street to Sanjo Street in central Kyoto, Shin-Kyogoku is one of the city's best-known shopping destinations, attracting both local residents and tourists. Yet behind its modern storefronts lies a history closely connected to Kyoto's transformation during the early Meiji period. One of the street's most unusual features is the presence of seven temples and one shrine nestled among the shops. Their entrances stand alongside retail businesses, creating a distinctive streetscape where religious institutions and commercial establishments share the same narrow thoroughfare. The arrangement reflects the area's origins as temple grounds. Before the Meiji era, much of what is now Shin-Kyogoku formed part of the precincts of Buddhist temples, some with histories stretching back more than 1,000 years. The shopping street emerged following major political and social changes in the early Meiji period. After the emperor relocated to Tokyo in 1869, Kyoto experienced a significant decline in population and economic activity, leaving parts of the former capital struggling to recover. A government ordinance issued in 1871 reorganizing land held by temples and shrines provided an opportunity to redevelop the area. A new commercial street was established through former temple grounds as part of efforts to restore economic vitality to central Kyoto. The name Shin-Kyogoku, meaning "New Kyogoku," was derived from the neighboring Teramachi Street, historically associated with the eastern edge of the old capital. The new thoroughfare was intended to create a lively commercial district that would help revive the city's economy. Among its longest-established businesses is Sarashina Honten, a restaurant founded 152 years ago that specializes in kishimen, the flat wheat noodles more commonly associated with Nagoya. Now operated by the sixth generation of the founding family, Sarashina traces its distinctive menu to its first proprietor, who came from Aichi Prefecture and introduced kishimen to Kyoto at a time when the dish was relatively unfamiliar to local diners. Although the restaurant is one of Shin-Kyogoku's oldest surviving businesses, its operators say that 150 years is still considered relatively young in Kyoto, where some merchants have operated for 300 or 400 years and temples can trace their histories back 600 to 800 years or longer. Sarashina's signature kishimen has evolved considerably from its Nagoya origins. The restaurant developed an exceptionally thin version of the noodles, measuring less than one millimeter in thickness, to complement Kyoto's delicate broth. Achieving that texture required changes to the flour mixture because noodles rolled so thinly are particularly prone to breaking. The restaurant also refined its individual dishes to suit local tastes, gradually establishing a distinctive Kyoto-style kishimen. The noodles are served with ingredients including bonito flakes and fried tofu, which absorbs the broth. The thinner noodles have a greater surface area relative to their thickness, allowing the soup to coat them particularly well. The restaurant's continued success followed years of experimentation. When kishimen was first introduced, Kyoto residents showed little interest in a noodle dish associated with another region, making it difficult to attract customers. Rather than abandon the specialty, successive generations adapted the recipe until it became an established part of the local dining scene. Another landmark of Shin-Kyogoku is Star Shokudo, a Western-style restaurant that celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2025 and has grown into a business operating 17 locations, mainly in Kyoto. Founded by Kotaro, who had traveled to the United States before returning to Japan, the restaurant was established with the ambition of making Western cuisine accessible to ordinary Japanese diners. At the time, Western-style meals were still unfamiliar to many people in Kyoto. Even knives and forks were a novelty for some customers, and the restaurant's early mission was to introduce new dining customs as well as new dishes. Its founder displayed a message promoting the popularization of Western cuisine, reflecting his belief that access to such food was part of Japan's broader modernization and rising prosperity. Over the following century, Star Shokudo became a familiar destination for Kyoto residents seeking Western-style dishes for family outings and special occasions. Its most popular dish today is an omurice gratin with cheese and demi-glace sauce, combining the Japanese interpretation of a Western omelet with baked gratin. The dish is designed to remain relatively light despite its rich appearance, with the seasoning of the rice, cheese and sauce carefully balanced to avoid overwhelming flavors. However, one of the restaurant's most remarkable discoveries came during preparations for its centennial celebrations, when staff researching the company's history uncovered a service manual dating to 1935, just 10 years after the business was founded. The document, preserved for approximately 90 years, provides an unusually detailed account of how restaurant employees were expected to conduct themselves during the early Showa period. Because the original is fragile, the restaurant has scanned its pages and produced printed copies for examination. The manual contains practical instructions covering customer service, personal appearance, language and professional conduct. Employees were told to speak standard Japanese rather than regional dialects and to greet customers properly when they entered the restaurant. It also contains a system of abbreviated names for menu items, providing a glimpse into dishes served at the restaurant during its early years. Among the more surprising entries is rabbit cutlet, abbreviated as "Usa-Ka," indicating that rabbit meat once appeared on the restaurant's menu. Other entries include seasonal ingredients such as matsutake mushrooms, suggesting that the restaurant incorporated both Western culinary influences and traditional Japanese seasonal foods. Perhaps the most puzzling discovery was a menu item described as "newspaper breakfast," alongside references to newspaper-related meals. The exact meaning remains uncertain, but restaurant staff suggested that customers may once have been able to order breakfast accompanied by access to a newspaper. At a time when newspapers were relatively expensive and not necessarily available in every household, the opportunity to read one while eating could have been an attraction in itself. The theory remains speculative, however, and the original purpose of the unusual menu item has not been established. Beyond its descriptions of food and service, the manual contains a series of philosophical statements expressing the founder's views on work, personal development and the meaning of life. One passage declares, "To live is not merely to breathe, but to accomplish something." Another states, "Those who have never eaten bread with tears cannot understand the taste of life." The sayings suggest that the founder viewed restaurant employment as more than simply a means of earning a living. Staff were encouraged to develop their character, take responsibility for their futures and pursue ambitions beyond their immediate duties. The manual also promoted the idea that employees should think of themselves as future leaders rather than permanent subordinates, encouraging them to acquire the knowledge and confidence necessary to become independent. The rediscovered document has impressed current restaurant executives, who say its advice remains relevant despite the enormous changes in Japan's restaurant industry over the past nine decades. What began as a collection of workplace instructions has come to be regarded as a broader guide to personal and professional life, emphasizing courtesy, determination, responsibility and individual achievement. The discovery illustrates how Shin-Kyogoku's long-established businesses have preserved not only recipes and commercial traditions but also the ideals of the entrepreneurs who helped shape modern Kyoto. More than 150 years after the street was created to revive the former capital, its restaurants, temples and family-run businesses continue to reflect the city's ability to adapt while retaining its historical character.

Stretching north from Shijo Street to Sanjo Street in central Kyoto, Shin-Kyogoku is one of the city's best-known shopping destinations, attracting both local residents and tourists. Yet behind its modern storefronts lies a history closely connected to Kyoto's transformation during the early Meiji period.

One of the street's most unusual features is the presence of seven temples and one shrine nestled among the shops. Their entrances stand alongside retail businesses, creating a distinctive streetscape where religious institutions and commercial establishments share the same narrow thoroughfare.

The arrangement reflects the area's origins as temple grounds. Before the Meiji era, much of what is now Shin-Kyogoku formed part of the precincts of Buddhist temples, some with histories stretching back more than 1,000 years.

The shopping street emerged following major political and social changes in the early Meiji period. After the emperor relocated to Tokyo in 1869, Kyoto experienced a significant decline in population and economic activity, leaving parts of the former capital struggling to recover.

A government ordinance issued in 1871 reorganizing land held by temples and shrines provided an opportunity to redevelop the area. A new commercial street was established through former temple grounds as part of efforts to restore economic vitality to central Kyoto.

The name Shin-Kyogoku, meaning "New Kyogoku," was derived from the neighboring Teramachi Street, historically associated with the eastern edge of the old capital. The new thoroughfare was intended to create a lively commercial district that would help revive the city's economy.

Among its longest-established businesses is Sarashina Honten, a restaurant founded 152 years ago that specializes in kishimen, the flat wheat noodles more commonly associated with Nagoya.

Now operated by the sixth generation of the founding family, Sarashina traces its distinctive menu to its first proprietor, who came from Aichi Prefecture and introduced kishimen to Kyoto at a time when the dish was relatively unfamiliar to local diners.

Although the restaurant is one of Shin-Kyogoku's oldest surviving businesses, its operators say that 150 years is still considered relatively young in Kyoto, where some merchants have operated for 300 or 400 years and temples can trace their histories back 600 to 800 years or longer.

Sarashina's signature kishimen has evolved considerably from its Nagoya origins. The restaurant developed an exceptionally thin version of the noodles, measuring less than one millimeter in thickness, to complement Kyoto's delicate broth.

Achieving that texture required changes to the flour mixture because noodles rolled so thinly are particularly prone to breaking. The restaurant also refined its individual dishes to suit local tastes, gradually establishing a distinctive Kyoto-style kishimen.

The noodles are served with ingredients including bonito flakes and fried tofu, which absorbs the broth. The thinner noodles have a greater surface area relative to their thickness, allowing the soup to coat them particularly well.

The restaurant's continued success followed years of experimentation. When kishimen was first introduced, Kyoto residents showed little interest in a noodle dish associated with another region, making it difficult to attract customers.

Rather than abandon the specialty, successive generations adapted the recipe until it became an established part of the local dining scene.

Another landmark of Shin-Kyogoku is Star Shokudo, a Western-style restaurant that celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2025 and has grown into a business operating 17 locations, mainly in Kyoto.

Founded by Kotaro, who had traveled to the United States before returning to Japan, the restaurant was established with the ambition of making Western cuisine accessible to ordinary Japanese diners.

At the time, Western-style meals were still unfamiliar to many people in Kyoto. Even knives and forks were a novelty for some customers, and the restaurant's early mission was to introduce new dining customs as well as new dishes.

Its founder displayed a message promoting the popularization of Western cuisine, reflecting his belief that access to such food was part of Japan's broader modernization and rising prosperity.

Over the following century, Star Shokudo became a familiar destination for Kyoto residents seeking Western-style dishes for family outings and special occasions.

Its most popular dish today is an omurice gratin with cheese and demi-glace sauce, combining the Japanese interpretation of a Western omelet with baked gratin.

The dish is designed to remain relatively light despite its rich appearance, with the seasoning of the rice, cheese and sauce carefully balanced to avoid overwhelming flavors.

However, one of the restaurant's most remarkable discoveries came during preparations for its centennial celebrations, when staff researching the company's history uncovered a service manual dating to 1935, just 10 years after the business was founded.

The document, preserved for approximately 90 years, provides an unusually detailed account of how restaurant employees were expected to conduct themselves during the early Showa period.

Because the original is fragile, the restaurant has scanned its pages and produced printed copies for examination.

The manual contains practical instructions covering customer service, personal appearance, language and professional conduct. Employees were told to speak standard Japanese rather than regional dialects and to greet customers properly when they entered the restaurant.

It also contains a system of abbreviated names for menu items, providing a glimpse into dishes served at the restaurant during its early years.

Other entries include seasonal ingredients such as matsutake mushrooms, suggesting that the restaurant incorporated both Western culinary influences and traditional Japanese seasonal foods.

scraped.title: Typhoon No. 32 Set to Intensify Before Approaching Japan Islands
scraped.description: As of 9 p.m. on November 8, Typhoon No. 32, known internationally as Champaka, was moving west-northwest over waters south of Japan with a central atmospheric pressure of 970 hectopascals and maximum sustained winds of 35 meters per second, with forecasts indicating that it could intensify into a very strong typhoon before approaching the Ogasawara Islands around Wednesday, November 11.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Typhoon No. 32 Set to Intensify Before Approaching Japan Islands
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - As of 9 p.m. on November 8, Typhoon No. 32, known internationally as Champaka, was moving west-northwest over waters south of Japan with a central atmospheric pressure of 970 hectopascals and maximum sustained winds of 35 meters per second, with forecasts indicating that it could intensify into a very strong typhoon before approaching the Ogasawara Islands around Wednesday, November 11.

Satellite imagery showed a well-developed spiral of clouds surrounding the storm's center over waters south of the Ogasawara Islands, with particularly active cloud formations near its core. Additional rain clouds were developing north of the storm along a frontal system, raising concerns that unsettled weather could reach the islands even before the typhoon itself approaches. The typhoon was traveling west-northwest at approximately 20 kilometers per hour on November 8 and was expected to maintain that general direction through the morning of November 9. Its movement was then forecast to slow considerably, with the storm potentially becoming almost stationary by the evening. During this period of slower movement, Typhoon No. 32 was expected to strengthen further, with maximum sustained winds near its center reaching 45 meters per second, equivalent to approximately 162 kilometers per hour, bringing it into the very strong typhoon category. An approaching upper-level trough was expected to alter the prevailing winds and steer the typhoon eastward from November 10. By the evening, the storm was forecast to move across waters southwest of the Ogasawara Islands while maintaining very strong intensity. Current projections suggest the typhoon is most likely to pass south of Chichijima and Hahajima during the morning of November 11, although changes in its track could affect the severity of conditions across the islands. The storm is expected to weaken rapidly after November 11 as it continues eastward, moving away from the Japanese archipelago. By November 12 and November 13, it is forecast to approach waters near the International Date Line while continuing to lose strength. Heavy rain could begin affecting the Ogasawara Islands on November 10 as the frontal system extending north of the typhoon brings rain clouds into the area. Forecasters warned that significant rainfall could develop even while the storm's center remains some distance from the islands. Rain is expected to continue intermittently from the night of November 10 through the morning of November 11, with periods of locally intense rainfall possible. Although the latest projected track suggests that the most developed rain clouds surrounding the typhoon's center are unlikely to pass directly over the islands, residents have been advised to remain alert to sudden increases in rainfall. Strong winds are also expected, particularly from the latter half of November 10 through November 11. While the typhoon is currently forecast to pass far enough south to avoid bringing its most destructive winds directly across the islands, atmospheric conditions could still produce hazardous gusts. As the typhoon moves eastward, a high-pressure system is expected to extend southward from the north, increasing the pressure difference across the region. This could strengthen winds around the Ogasawara Islands independently of the typhoon's immediate circulation. Forecasters said strong winds could develop during this period, with instantaneous gusts potentially exceeding 20 meters per second, or 72 kilometers per hour, in some locations. Marine conditions are also expected to deteriorate as the typhoon approaches. Waves around parts of the Ogasawara Islands could reach heights of 3 to 4 meters around November 11, with elevated seas expected to persist throughout at least that day. The combination of intermittent heavy rain, strong winds and high waves could create hazardous conditions around Chichijima, Hahajima and surrounding coastal waters, particularly between November 10 and November 11. Residents and visitors have been urged to prepare for deteriorating weather, exercise caution near coastlines and monitor updated forecasts, as the typhoon's precise track and intensity will determine the extent of its impact on the islands.

A smartphone caught fire at Narita Airport's Terminal 1 shortly after 7:30 a.m. on November 4th, prompting the dispatch of 10 fire trucks and other emergency vehicles before the blaze was extinguished about 30 minutes later, with no injuries reported.

articles.title: More than 40,000 gather as Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass in Uruguay
articles.summary: Massive crowds have turned out for the pontiff as he celebrates the first Mass of his South America tour. A nighttime prayer vigil in Montevideo is expected to draw more than 60,000 young people.
articles.ai_summary: Over 40,000 people gathered for Pope Leo XIV's first Mass in South America, with a prayer vigil expected to attract more than 60,000 young attendees.

scraped.title: Uruguay: 40,000 gather as Pope Leo celebrates first Mass of South America tour
scraped.description: Massive crowds have turned out for the pontiff as he celebrates the first Mass of his South America tour. A nighttime prayer vigil in Montevideo is expected to draw more than 60,000 young people.
scraped.h1: More than 40,000 gather as Pope Leo XIV celebrates Mass in Uruguay
scraped.body_text:
Massive crowds have turned out for the pontiff as he celebrates the first Mass of his South America tour. A nighttime prayer vigil in Montevideo is expected to draw more than 60,000 young people.

The Vatican and local authorities in western Uruguay say an estimated 40,000 people turned out on Saturday morning to participate in the first Mass of Pope Leo XIV 's 12-day, three-nation tour of South America .

The Vatican said 30,000 people from Uruguay as well as neighboring Argentina and Brazil had registered for the event, adding that another 10,000 had braved the rain to attend the religious service, which took place in Paysandu — a city on the Uruguay River, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) west of the capital Montevideo.

Leo, who underwent surgery for lung cancer on October 13 , was greeted by throngs of cheering fans as he made his way from the local airport to Paysandu's sprawling Paris London Park.

"He's the representative of Christ but he's human," said Soledad Sanchez, who told France's AFP news agency that she had traveled far to be in Paysandu.

"We weren't sure if he could make it but he pushed through for us," said Sanchez as tears welled up in her eyes, "He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 71-year-old US-born pontiff, who holds US , Peruvian and Vatican citizenship, is seeking to raise interest in the Catholic Church in Uruguay, South America's most secular country, as a remedy for helping the nation and its citizens cope with the troubles of the modern world.

Saturday morning's Mass was dedicated to the Blessed Jacinto Vera, who was appointed Uruguay's first bishop by Pope Leo XIII in 1878.

On Friday, the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics spoke of Bishop Vera, noting that he had walked the countryside and helped the poor, adding that those whom he encountered "found something of Christ's goodness" in him.

Leo will underscore the need for that kind of outreach on Saturday afternoon when he visits a Montevideo neighborhood beset by drug violence and in which the Church has invested in public housing and rehabilitation projects for addicts.

At Pope Leo's final event in the country — a prayer vigil in Montevideo's Centenary Stadium that is expected to draw some 60,000 young faithful — the pontiff will call on young people to reject religious indifference and turn to Christ's teachings.

Leo's emphasis on charity and brotherly love has struck a deep chord with young people in Uruguay and elsewhere.

One 18-year-old attendee at Saturday morning's Mass told AFP: "I wouldn't call myself religious, but I like this pope. He has a really good message for humanity. Even for non-believers, there is something to take from his ideas."

On Sunday, Pope Leo will depart for Argentina , where he will meet with President Javier Milei , a libertarian-populist and close ally to US President Donald Trump , who previously lashed out at the leader of the world's largest Christian faith over his calls to end wars and cruel immigration policies .

scraped.title: Enough With the “Public Option” Already
scraped.description: The public option sounds like a step toward universal health care, but it’s really a delay tactic. The latest versions would force public plans to mimic private insurers, while the fight over the arcane details buys the industry another decade or two.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

The public option sounds like a step toward universal health care, but it’s really a delay tactic. The latest versions would force public plans to mimic private insurers, while the fight over the arcane details buys the industry another decade or two.

The concept of the public option is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. (Kevin Dietsch / Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

T he difference between a vampire and a bad health care policy idea is that vampires jump out of their coffins and drink blood at sunset. Undead health care proposals emerge from think tank closets and suck the life out of useful ideas when the sun rises on a national health care debate. As public fury at exploding costs and deadly corporate claims denials boils over into historic Democratic election gains, can someone please find a wooden stake for the public option?

Improved and expanded Medicare for All would give everyone full coverage at much lower cost than the combined private premiums, taxes, and out-of-pocket payments that are eating up family income today. But it violates a cardinal rule of federal politics: never do anything that causes corporations or the ultrawealthy any pain.

Instead, corporate Democrats wanting to be seen “doing something” about the imploding US health care system have long peddled a vague public option notion because it sounds like the marriage of a big noncorporate vision (it’s public!) with competition and freedom of choice (it’s an option!). Liberal nongovernmental organizations (NGOs) and pundits revived its rotting corpse in response to pro–Medicare for All candidates’ primary victories and Tuesday night’s stunning results.

It’s a perfect nonsolution to our three-headed crisis of health care cost, access, and quality. Nobody knows what a “public option” is because there’s no common definition and nothing like it has ever been seen in the wild, so it can be anything weaselly politicians want it to be. It needs to be put out of our misery.

T here’s danger in chasing the content of various “public options.” The concept is designed as a distraction. Wasting years on policy rabbit holes is the point. But killing it requires some analysis, so it’s worth pointing out that every one of its shape-shifting forms withers under cursory scrutiny.

Rising Democratic Senate star Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) says she “wouldn’t say no forever” to a White House run if “there’s not anyone else who’s on the right path.” Slotkin’s favored path leads to one of the sillier public option proposals. In January, Slotkin, Senator Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), and Rep. Jan Schakowsky (D-IL) introduced the Affordable Consumer Health Options and Insurance Competition Enhancement (CHOICE) Act, or the Affordable CHOICE Act (“ACA” — get it?). The CHOICE Act would get the federal government into the business of selling crummy insurance to almost nobody by allowing the feds to market their own versions of “bronze,” “silver,” and “gold” plans on the Obamacare exchanges.

Even at record enrollment, the Affordable Care Act exchanges covered less than 7 percent of Americans. Nearly everyone with insurance has Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance through a job. Three-quarters of US working-age adults are eligible for job-based coverage, nearly all of which is considered legally “affordable” by ACA rules. That means almost all workers are barred from receiving ACA premium subsidies. Presumably they could buy a Slotkinized plan by paying the full premium cost if they really wanted one. Nice option.

Subsidized or not, Slotkinized plans would cover only between 58 and 82 percent of the actual cost of health care after premiums, depending on the “metal” label attached to the plan.

CHOICE Act public option plans would have to play the same failed “cost control” game as private insurers, building their own private provider networks and trading privileged access to their patients for discounts off market price from providers who join those networks. So, Senator Slotkin’s options will come loaded with the copays, coinsurance, and deductibles that private insurance corporations use to coerce patients into accepting in-network doctors and hospitals. It’s a mockery of “affordability” for patients and would offer neither better nor worse provider payments than UnitedHealth, Aetna, or Cigna.

The contrast between Senator Slotkin and the winner of Michigan’s other Senate seat couldn’t be clearer. At his victory celebration, Abdul El-Sayed turned his three-line slogan into a roaring call and response, with Medicare for All as the closer: “Money out of . . . POLITICS! Money in your . . . POCKET! Medicare for . . . ALL!” Corporate Democrats are still trying to paint Medicare for All as too radical and urge progressive winners toward “moderation,” torturing voting data into arguments about electability. The facts: In 2024, Elissa Slotkin defeated Mike Rogers by a 0.3 percent margin. With unlimited American Israel Public Affairs Committee and corporate cash arrayed against him and in the face of nakedly racist opposition, El-Sayed beat Rogers by a full 7 percent.

C riticize one slippery idea and the optionites will just say, “Hey, I didn’t mean that public option.” In two recent posts , economist Paul Krugman hyped a Medicare “buy-in” version to “allow individuals, and possibly more important, employers, to sign up for Medicare benefits, paying actuarially fair premiums to Medicare reflecting the health status of their workers” (emphasis added). Krugman insists that “many people and many employers would surely take it.”

Surely many who need it the most wouldn’t. The US health care system is so broken in part because we’ve asked six million separate employers who don’t know and shouldn’t be expected to know much about health care to buy it for most of us. But even they know that premiums reflecting the health status of workers would immediately price employers who most need an affordable option — those with high-cost employees — out of any “buy-in.”

The Krugmanite option violates a core Medicare precept. Of course, individual Medicare premiums shouldn’t exist at all. Paying taxes should buy your health care. Even so, except for a few high-income people, everyone pays the same Medicare premiums right now. “Actuarially fair premiums” tailored to health risks contradict the basic notions of solidarity at the heart of public benefits and the very idea of insurance, which is supposed to pool risk across groups of people, not segregate it.

Offering existing original Medicare as a standalone option for employers and nondisabled individuals younger than sixty-five to “buy” is an idea only a Nobel-winning trade economist dabbling in health care could love. Original Medicare’s cost-sharing has already driven most eligible people into Medicare Advantage plans run by the very companies that Krugman dismissed as “parasites.”

So, to fully cover their workers, employers would have to — you guessed it — buy supplemental insurance from the private insurance industry. Never underestimate the power of Nancy Pelosi’s Iron Law of Democratic Health Policy: Congress shall make no law respecting expansion of health care access that does not subsidize the private health insurance industry, and all gestures to the contrary shall be performance art.

S ome people may actually take these ideas seriously, but the essence of public optionism is a bully’s taunt.

Virtually every economic analysis of the issue has concluded that a single-payer system would generate large savings to fund both expanding coverage to everyone and dramatically improving existing coverage. Two key sources of those savings are huge, useless administrative costs: the insurance industry’s skim, and the massive bureaucracies that providers have to build just to get paid by thousands of private insurance plans whose terms and members constantly change.

Original Medicare is far more efficient than private insurance, spending 97 to 98 percent of revenue on actual health care, while private plans capture more than 10 percent of our premiums as overhead and profit.

If public insurance is so darned efficient, the argument goes, a public option should outcompete private insurance. That would have the dual benefit of giving people cheaper, better coverage, and proving to a socialism-averse public that something like Medicare for All could work. So prove it, lefties!

The problem, of course, is that operating in existing markets under rules that will force public options to behave like private insurers strips these plans of the permanence and power that make Medicare and truly “public” insurance relatively efficient.

Medicare controls prices because it permanently covers everyone in the largest group of people who use a lot of health care. When you turn sixty-five and enroll, you’re in for life. If hospitals want to treat the group of people most likely to need their services, they have to take Medicare prices.

The CHOICE Act makes a head fake in that direction. The bill instructs the Health and Human Services secretary to create a provider network and set hospital and physician prices “through a negotiated agreement with health care providers,” without naming which providers or how they’ll negotiate. In the absence of successful negotiations, CHOICE Act plans can just pay any claim at existing Medicare prices. That may sound like a little public muscle flexing to hold prices down, but the CHOICE Act also allows hospitals and doctors to opt out of the public options’ networks, turning Medicare prices into a backstop that applies only to out-of-network claims.

Having a guaranteed right to impose low prices on out-of-network care would give public option plans a little pricing leverage. But in the end, the Slotkinized plans would likely wind up creating networks and setting prices in a manner similar to private plans, whose tussles with hospitals are based entirely on market power. Having surrendered the power that allows Medicare to set its own prices and competing as start-ups with private insurance to entice “covered lives” to enroll, the public options would soon find themselves face-to-face with massively powerful regional health systems affiliated with Ivy League schools or the Catholic Church. Have fun.

To persuade the necessary “covered lives” to enroll, CHOICE Act plans will have to ape private plans by constantly marketing themselves and enrolling and disenrolling clients. Alongside the headache of managing networks, that work requires skimming billions in premium dollars off the top, just like private insurers.

Slotkin, Krugman, and their optional pals have also managed the remarkable feat of finding an idea that would add a little more bureaucracy to the already bloated administrative expenses that choke US hospitals. The CHOICE Act doesn’t create an option. It envisions hundreds of local public option plans with premiums set geographically — ACA plans are offered on a county-by-county basis. Viewed from a hospital’s business office, that means at least three separate local plans, one per “metal,” with each becoming just another payer with its own unique prices, networks, utilization review, and patient cost-sharing to follow, track, bill, and sue when payments don’t show up.

Finally, should policymakers and regulators fool themselves into thinking that these options will be efficient because, you know, they’re “public” and offer below-market premiums, the plans face a potential flood of high-risk sign-ups (the “adverse selection” problem). As Jim Kahn and Hank Abrons point out in Health Justice Monitor , even the more-expansive-than-Krugman version offered by The American Prospect is particularly vulnerable on this question. Being stuck with disproportionately high-cost patients wouldn’t be good for plans trying to prove the efficiency of public insurance, but it would be great for politicians seeking to prove that the government really can’t do health care.

We could go on forever about the details, but the content doesn’t really matter. These ideas are little more than lumps of lead over which political alchemists like Slotkin and Krugman chant their two magic words to dazzle us into believing they’re creating gold. Public options aren’t incremental reforms toward universal coverage. They’re increments of nothing that enable the status quo.

This fantasy nonidea endures because fighting for it achieves a critical bipartisan goal: buying time for corporate control of the rest of the health care system. A legislative timeline would likely look like this: two years until the Democrats have a shot at the White House, followed by a year or two of GOP panic about “communism.” Throw in two to three years to write the regulationss, then five or ten years to roll out the plans and watch them fail. Presto! A decade or two of corporate looting passes, with trillions of dollars squandered and another million or two preventable deaths.

There are plenty of meaningful steps on the way to a publicly financed universal health care system that ensures everyone gets the care they need without facing personal bankruptcy or fighting off bloodthirsty private bureaucrats. Politicians who want to improve access or cost control could jump on a few of these sample bandwagons. Don’t expect a rush, though. Most of these ideas take a bite out of the industry’s hide, and letting poor people who make an extra penny keep their health care will give alleged conservatives apoplexy. But here they are:

Set fair hospital prices by regulation for all payers, to stop the gouging of employers and patients and end the episodic waves of terror that engulf communities when big insurance companies and hospitals threaten patients with loss of access during local rate negotiations.

Lower the age at which everyone becomes eligible for Medicare to fifty or fifty-five.

Eliminate the extreme cost-sharing in the original Medicare program.

Abolish the Medicare Advantage privatization scheme that lets private insurance companies overcharge the federal government tens of billions of dollars a year, and use the savings to fund said elimination of original Medicare cost-sharing.

Buck Washington, DC’s current antitrust fad by lifting restrictions on employers who want to join together to bargain for health care and administer benefits. Look, employer control of health care makes no sense. But if corporate politicians fantasize that it’s a route to better benefits and lower costs, let bosses gather the power to control prices and administrative costs, as long as they do it themselves without the insurance industry, and as long as they’re willing to pay the price of offering uniform plans across their cartel — no more tiny tweaks to networks or boutique cost-sharing provisions for each employer.

Dramatically expand the time people can stay on Medicaid. Medicaid’s constant means-testing makes it an unreliable source of coverage. California applied for a waiver to keep kids enrolled through the first five years of their lives instead of making their parents reapply every year. Do more of that and for longer.

The worst thing about public optionism is enduring smug lectures that Medicare for All is a political fantasy that could never happen from people promoting a vague, unworkable idea now enjoying its twenty-third year of politically viable nonexistence. Yet The American Prospect casually assumes that a series of essential Medicare for All elements against which the industry will fight like rabid dogs can easily be grafted onto a public option.

Health care is a public good. Pretending that having government act like a health insurance corporation will do anything useful is absurd. Let’s kill this putrefying political monster right now.

John Canham-Clyne is an independent health care journalist and publisher of the online investigative newsletter Healing and Stealing .

articles.summary: At least six people were killed and fifteen injured after a shooter opened fire from a car in Krakow's main market square.
articles.ai_summary: A shooter in Krakow's main market square killed at least six people and injured fifteen others, according to police reports.

scraped.title: At least 6 killed in shooting in Krakow, Polish police say
scraped.description: At least six people were killed and fifteen injured after a shooter opened fire from a car in Krakow's main market square.
scraped.h1: At least 6 killed in shooting in Polish city of Krakow, police say
scraped.body_text:
At least six people were killed and fifteen injured after a shooter opened fire from a car in Krakow's main market square.

At least six people were killed and fifteen injured in a shooting near the main market square in the southern Polish city of Krakow on Saturday.

The perpetrator, reportedly a Polish citizen who acted alone, was wounded during an exchange of fire with police, authorities said.

He has been taken to a hospital, police said.

According to Krakow police, the gunman aimed at random people as he drove by the city's main square. Among the wounded are police officers.

"At around 3 pm [1400 GMT], a man who had driven into the market square in a car began shooting at random people from inside the vehicle," police said on X.

"The perpetrator was shot by police ‌officers and is currently being ‌transported ​to a hospital," police said.

Initially, authorities urged people in the immediate vicinity to evacuate to a safe place.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted on X that police are investigating the attack and called it a "tragic" incident to have occurred.

Polish President Karol Nawrocki wrote on X that his thoughts were with the victims and wounded, as well as their families.

Krakow is located about 250 kilometers (155 miles) from Warsaw, the capital of Poland.

With a population of over 800,000, Krakow is Poland's second-largest city, as well as a popular tourist destination. Key attractions include the main square, Wawel Castle, and the cathedral on Wawel Hill.

This is a developing story. Please check back for the latest version.

scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
