Skepticism toward moral absolutes has made the modern mind leery of the very idea of evil. Philosopher Susan Neiman makes the case that explaining wrongdoing is not the same as reckoning with its moral significance.

Susan Neiman argues that understanding Donald Trump requires that we take evil seriously. Her latest book asks what happens when we allow cynicism to displace moral judgment. (Nelson Almeida / AFP via Getty Images)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

Review of Call It Evil: Understanding the Trump Era by Susan Neiman (W. W. Norton & Company, 2026)

L eftists have an unusual relationship to the language of good and evil. On the one hand, we have a reputation for being righteous. . . . at times even self-righteous. Our publications are saturated with enough morally strident language to make a preacher blush. Even the most “scientific” of scientific socialists aren’t entirely immune, from tireless invocations of Rev Martin Luther King Jr and constant demands for justice and freedom for all to calls to end subordination and marginalization around the globe . On the other hand, leftists tend to be averse to describing structures, let alone people, as evil. Exploitative? Yes. Domineering? Of course. But evil? At best, that’s language reserved for your Hannah Arendt reading group.

Philosopher Susan Neiman takes umbrage at this reticence. Author of the acclaimed Evil in Modern Thought and the controversial Left is Not Woke , Neiman thinks we ought to call a spade and spade and describe the Trump administration as what it is: evil. The disturbing question that follows is: If what Donald Trump stands for is evil, why have millions of people chosen to get behind him not once but three times? As Neiman herself notes:

Knowing as much as can be known about a public figure whose cruelty and corruption have been on display for a decade, how was it possible that Americans elected him twice? One New York friend pointed out that no one who ever dealt with the man wanted to see him again — except for the American people.

But Neiman is less interested in explaining why Americans voted for Trump than in the larger philosophical question of what constitutes evil. As she writes, “My concern is with the moral ideas that Donald Trump embodies and reinforces, ideas that are destructive enough to warrant the word evil .”

N eiman’s understanding of modern evil is deeply indebted to Hannah Arendt’s pioneering description of it as “banal.” She acknowledges that Arendt’s description of Adolf Eichmann himself as a thoughtless man devoid of hateful antisemitic feelings is untrue. But Arendt’s broader point about modern evil lacking any “Satanic majesty” remains true. Neiman reminds us that the “Holocaust could never have happened without the willing participation of millions of people who were not particularly committed fascists or fascists of any kind. They were simply willing to accept whatever demands made their lives easier.”

This all-too-human tendency to fall not through active malice but selfishness and indifference is one Neiman thinks is very characteristic of modern American history. Neiman notes how since 1945, “it’s hard to find an example of US foreign policy that isn’t principally Schmittian, though they are usually accompanied by the sort of liberal hypocrisy that Schmitt despised.” Carl Schmitt , the German jurist who joined the Nazi party in 1933, understood politics fundamentally as a struggle between friends and enemies and rejected liberal appeals to universal principles as an ideological fiction that masked power. Schmitt would likely be pleased that the second Trump administration has largely dropped even the veneer of liberal hypocrisy. If hypocrisy is the tribute vice pays to virtue, even the Bush administration at least had the decency to labor for months to convince the American people that the Iraq War was justified. When attacking Venezuela and Iran, not to mention saber-rattling at arrogant Greenlanders and Canadians, the Trump administration is typically much more transparent about the unbridled self-interest at play. After deposing Nicolás Maduro, Trump relished America’s access to Venezuelan oil, proclaiming “to the victor belong the spoils.”

Neiman’s core worry is that the transparently evil cynicism on display will become so normalized that we ignore its vulgarity. As the “Schmitt-Trump consensus grows, it’s easy to conclude that no other outlook is possible, and cynicism becomes inevitable.” While I sympathize with this outlook, it does seem to run counter to the longer history of American atrocities Neiman chronicles. If it is true that most American foreign policy since World War II has been basically Schmittian, it would seem that Trump simply constitutes a further moral step downward rather than a new kind of wicked hegemony. Sometimes Neiman gestures in this direction as when she insists this is “not a book about Donald Trump” but about “. . . . the conditions that allowed him rise.” These include the “imperialism the US has practiced for over a century,” which she insists can only be called “evil.” If that’s the case, then what is at stake is really more a general American malaise than some transformative and deepening “‘Schmitt-Trump consensus.”

Neiman often seems to want to pull back from such a pessimistic thesis. For instance, while she disagrees with the thrust of US foreign policy, she nonetheless expresses deep respect for “individual members of the military.” Neiman admires how their training prizes duty, fellowship, service, and sacrifice — all ideals someone like Trump simply doesn’t understand. It was exactly these principles that led Neiman to hope that “soldiers sworn to defend the Constitution would never follow the worst of his orders after seeing how thoroughly their commander in chief disdained the values they upheld.” Those hopes were dashed when Trump 2.0 strode to power and replaced the military administration with his coterie of brownnoses and appointed Pete Hegseth secretary of war. Neiman insists that we relearn the watchwords of Trump 1.0: “Don’t normalize this.” Doing so helps make the evil deeds of administration seem typical, and consequently over time, not morally objectionable.

I think this ambiguity over whether Trumpism constitutes a continuation of, or break with, the past flows from a few sources. As a leftist, Neiman is keen to acknowledge the harm wrought by American foreign and domestic policy. However, I suspect Neiman is reluctant to suggest to her largely American readers that the country has always had a predilection toward Trumpy behavior. More strategically, she may worry that doing so would further legitimate Trumpism by making it seem normal. It would also blunt the force of the immanent critiques often used to mobilize Americans against their government’s abuses: holding up the country’s shining principles as a mirror to its often-brutal practices and saying, “We don’t look like we ought to.”

Whatever the case, I think Neiman would be better off following Arendt herself by situating the emergence of Trumpism in a much more concrete historical narrative. There was tendency, until recently, for many — especially conservative anti-Trumpers — to describe the Trump administration as an aberration in the American right’s history. Contemporary historians are increasingly pushing back on this view. In Taking America Back , David Austin Walsh stresses how the American right has always had plenty of overt racists, conspiracy theorists, Augusto Pinochet apologists, and outright fascists. William F. Buckley, the alleged poster boy for a more intellectual and less extreme conservatism, was happy to recommend segregation and defend Francisco Franco to own the libs.

Under Trumpism, the more extreme factions of the Right have simply moved from the back seat to the driver’s seat. But they have always been a part of American life. Taking a dialectical approach to American history, however, means recognizing that, just because many Americans have done evil things, the country as a whole is not evil. If anything, the inspiring story of America is of progressive movements successfully mobilizing against wicked practices to bring about a more just society. The arc of the moral universe may be long . . .

M uch of Neiman’s book ranges beyond its central concern, taking on topics from the hegemony of neoliberal ideology to war crimes in Gaza to her long-standing critique of wokism. At their best, these chapters read more like essays that collectively present a panoramic view of the world.

The chapter on wokism was especially interesting. Neiman is very critical of wokism for both principled and strategic reasons. She insists that the Left ought to reclaim its defining principle of inclusive universalism. As she puts it, the “idea of universalism once defined the Left; international solidarity was its watchword. This was just what distinguished it from the right, which recognized no deep connections, and few real obligations, to anyone outside its own circle. The Left demanded that the circle encompass the globe.” Neiman is very critical of identity politics, which eschews universalism in order to insist that “you have deep connections and real obligations only to those who belong to your tribe, though others may have limited use as allies.”

I have considerable sympathy for this view. Neiman is no doubt historically correct that trading Enlightenment reason and universalism for postmodern skepticism and what the Marxist David Harvey calls “militant particularism” constituted a shift from the Left’s historical stance. Marxist literary theorist Terry Eagleton made a similar observation in The Illusions of Postmodernism , noting the irony that some leftists had come to endorse philosophical positions typically associated with the Right. While motivated by different political concerns, this skepticism shares the conservative privileging of cultural particularity over reason and universalism.

A Left that embraced universalism would, of course, be more comfortable with the language of “moral idealism” Neiman affirms, and that would, by and large, be beneficial. That said, I think the question of how to recommit to universalism without falling back into exclusionary modes of thinking that imagine a single perspective ought to speak for everyone remains unresolved. Here, I think the best work has been done by philosophers working at the intersection of liberalism, Marxism, and black radical thought, notably Tommie Shelby and the late Charles Mills.

Both Shelby and Mills are comfortable couching demands for racial justice in the universalistic terms of Rawlsian political theory. But they recognize that universalism risks becoming what Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel criticized as an “abstract universalism” if it is insensitive to the particular forms of subordination experienced around the globe. In the United States, securing the basic rights and liberties to which everyone ought to be entitled means renouncing the legacy of systemic racism.

I was slightly more frustrated with the Chapter on “Socialism Reconsidered.” Despite the title, much of it reads like a microcosm of the book itself, weighing in on any number of different issues in quick succession. The most interesting sections of the chapter reintroduce readers to the socialism of Albert Einstein.

Einstein was, of course, a self-described socialist who was outspoken about his desire for humankind to evolve past the predatory capitalist phase of existence. But, as Neiman points out, these political convictions are rarely addressed by American biographers and commentators, who are usually content to footnote Einstein’s nonprofessional interest in “social justice.” Reacquainting readers with Einstein’s convictions is worthwhile, but the chapter would have been far more interesting if it had remained focused on reconstructing and developing his political ideas more systematically.

It’s perhaps inevitable that Neiman’s book sometimes ranges too broadly, given the complexity of the era it attempts to understand and critique. Anyone who wades into American politics these days can feel immediately overwhelmed by the sheer volume of issues demanding attention: wokeness, neoliberalism, identity politics, Trumpism, the rise of fascism, oligarchs’ control of social media, war in the Middle East, and so much more. There is a risk that the crushing weight of all this might lead many to lapse into the apathetic withdrawal Neiman worries about. Or perhaps worse, to reach for simplifying ideologies that offer a retreat from the complexity of the world. It’s to Neiman’s Socratic credit that she offers moral clarity without resorting to the comfort of cheaply bought moral certainties.

Matt McManus is an assistant professor at Spelman College. He is the author of The Political Right and Equality and The Political Theory of Liberal Socialism among other books.

articles.title: Journalism and AI: Who owns the news?
articles.summary: Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?
articles.ai_summary: Publishers are questioning whether AI companies should compensate them for using their journalism to generate responses for users.

scraped.title: AI answers rely on journalism. Who gets paid?
scraped.description: Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?
scraped.h1: Should AI companies pay for the journalism they use?
scraped.body_text:
Publishers say AI chatbots are using their reporting to answer readers' questions while sending back less traffic and less money. Should the companies that build these tools pay for the journalism they rely on?

Millions of people now use AI chatbots as a source of news to find quick answers to questions about current events.

A 2026 survey by the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism, which questioned more than 90,000 people worldwide, found that 10% use AI chatbots for news on a weekly basis, a figure that is significantly higher among younger audiences.

Explaining what is happening in the world, why it matters, and what it means has traditionally been the work of journalism. Media organizations send reporters into the field, commission investigations and conduct research, producing stories that help audiences understand global events. But as more people turn to AI tools for information, the relationship between those producing journalism and those distributing it is changing.

"In the past, search engines like Google indexed our websites and directed users to their articles, generating traffic in return," Julia Becker, publisher of Funke Media Group, told a panel at the Global Media Forum (GMF) in Berlin. "But now that exchange has broken down."

"AI companies draw on our quality reporting to generate answers, yet the reporting itself often remains largely invisible by the end of this process," said DW Director General Barbara Massing in a keynote address at the forum.

Their remarks reflect a worry that is growing across the media industry. Publicly available news is copied and summarized by AI chatbots, while news organizations are becoming less and less able to rely on the money and visibility that used to come from distributing that work.

There has been growing concern about how copyrighted material is collected, used, and reproduced by artificial intelligence , and whether the companies that build those systems should pay the people and organizations that created the material.

Media houses are now pressing "Big Tech" companies to ask permission before using their work and to pay for it.

In October, German broadcasters ARD and RTL, along with the country's Federal Association of Digital Publishers and Newspaper Publishers (BDZV) and the Association of Private Media (VAUNET), called for stronger copyright protections for media companies.

In the US, lawsuits are adding pressure. The New York Times has sued internet company Brave Softwar for allegedly using its content without permission and getting around its paywall.

Meanwhile, legal institutions in the EU, including the European Court of Justice (ECJ) are examining whether AI-generated answers can themselves infringe copyright.

In February, a coalition of media organizations, including the Guardian , the BBC, and the Financial Times , called for rules that would give publishers more control over how AI systems copy and reproduce their content.

The problem goes beyond whether AI companies may use journalism. It also concerns how publishers and journalists can get paid when their work becomes part of the answers AI systems generate.

"AI systems shouldn't just use quality journalism. They should also pay for it," Massing said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Professor Martin Senftleben, who directs the Institute for Information Law at the University of Amsterdam, separates two ways AI companies use journalistic material: Training their models and generating responses to individual user questions.

Payment for training is a more complicated legal question, he said. The more urgent issue is what happens when an AI system uses journalism to answer a question in real time.

He argued that European copyright law may already offer a way to address part of the problem. Under existing EU law, publishers and journalists may be able to claim payment collectively, without waiting for a new legal framework.

"What are we waiting for? Germany is a large member state. This should be introduced in Germany," he told the forum.

One option, Senftleben suggested, is a legally required payment system in which every AI response that draws on journalism triggers a payment. A collecting organization would gather the money and distribute it among publishers and journalists, in the same way that music royalties are collected and distributed.

Once such a system exists, publishers and authors could use its rates as a starting point when negotiating individual licensing deals with AI companies.

Lutz Mache, senior manager of government affairs and public policy at Google, told the GMF panel that Google is willing to negotiate agreements with German media companies and to discuss new AI products with them.

Google has also started testing other ways to pay publishers for their contributions to AI-generated answers. Its "AI Contribution" pilot, which is being tested with selected publishers, aims to reward content that plays a significant role in answers produced by products such as Gemini and AI Overviews. But the program is still an early experiment, not a general payment system open to all publishers.

Microsoft, Anthropic, and OpenAI have recently said they support clearer, standardized signals that let website owners state whether their content may be used to train AI models.

However, not everyone thinks more regulation is the answer.

Jörg Heidrich, a lawyer who specializes in technology law and serves as AI commissioner at the German media company Heise, warned against adding new rules without considering their effects on the wider tech sector.

Europe has already fallen behind in the global AI race, he argued. More regulation, he warned, could make it harder for European companies to compete with major providers based elsewhere.

Heidrich also pointed to smaller players, including startups, independent developers, and research institutions. They depend on access to data to build and train AI systems. He argued that the debate over copyright and payment risks overlooking these groups, and that new restrictions could hurt their work.

articles.title: In Turkey, When Does a Joke Become a Crime?

scraped.title: In Turkey, When Does a Joke Become a Crime?
scraped.description: Comedian Deniz Göktaş spent 88 days in a high-security prison for insulting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. He turned his sentence into a punch line, but the chilling consequences of the case extend far beyond one comedian.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:

Comedian Deniz Göktaş spent 88 days in a high-security prison for insulting Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan. He turned his sentence into a punch line, but the chilling consequences of the case extend far beyond one comedian.

Comedian Deniz Göktaş’s imprisonment over a performance is of a piece with Turkey’s longer history of conflict between political satire and state power. (YouTube)

Our latest issue, “The New Empire,” is out now. Get this issue plus three more for just $20.

H ave you ever made a joke that offended someone? Maybe they took it personally or stopped speaking to you. A joke can put strain on a relationship or leave someone feeling isolated. But what if the consequences for a joke go far beyond social fallout? What if a comedy performance lands you in a high-security prison cell? For Deniz Göktaş, this question is no longer hypothetical.

Until recently, Göktaş performed for relatively small audiences, playing bars in Kadıköy, an Istanbul district known for political satire, and occasionally in university halls elsewhere in Turkey. He was part of a niche comedy scene.

Things changed when he took his show to one of Istanbul’s most prominent stages and uploaded the performance to YouTube, opening it to a much wider audience. He knew the show might attract attention. Not just because of the words he spoke onstage, but also because the title and stage image played on a grisly visual gag. Ölü Deniz (“Dead Sea”) was a dark play on his first name, Deniz (“Sea”), while an enormous, sculpted image of his face lay on its side as if decapitated.

What began as a night of laughter would end with Göktaş spending eighty-eight days behind bars in a high-security prison. His case exposed not only the limits of free expression in Turkey but also the fraught relationship between political satire and political power.

T he thirty-two-year-old comedian was detained at Istanbul airport on July 2, after his ninety-minute special was released on YouTube. Prosecutors cited passages from the performance in bringing charges: insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, inciting public hatred and hostility, and praising crime or criminals.

At his first hearing, on September 28, 2026, Göktaş addressed the court:

“As a comedian, seeing that sentences can have such a powerful impact makes me proud. But as a citizen, I am saddened by my country’s record on freedom of expression.”

He said he worried the case would discourage others from performing and lead them to censor themselves.

The court ordered his release after sentencing. By then, he had spent eighty-eight days in pretrial detention. He told the court he had been held in a cell without sunlight or contact with other prisoners at Çorlu Karatepe High Security Prison, a facility known in Turkey as a well-type prison.

The court acquitted him of praising crime or criminals. It convicted him of insulting the president and, because public hatred and hostility were not established, reclassified the incitement charge as insulting religious values. The sentences were eleven months and twenty days and seven months and fifteen days, respectively.

The case raised a question beyond the sentences themselves: How had a comedy performance been transformed into a criminal prosecution? Göktaş’s defense argued that prosecutors had removed the alleged offenses from their original context onstage, but the heart of the matter was a dispute over how a comedian’s words should be interpreted.

W hile Göktaş was still in prison, I spoke with his friend and fellow stand-up comedian Emre Günsal.

Günsal distinguishes Göktaş’s comedy from much of what passes for “political humor” in Turkey. A comedian can get an easy laugh simply by mentioning a politician, referring to a current scandal, or repeating a political cliché the audience already agrees with. In Turkey, Günsal says, that is the least risky kind of political comedy.

Göktaş’s work is more deliberate. He combines political satire with social observation, using comedy to say something about the political climate, social tensions, and the shrinking space for free expression. The result can be both funny and cathartic for those who feel alienated or frustrated by the society in which they live. Günsal considers Göktaş one of the leading figures of this tradition in Turkey today.

This may help explain Göktaş’s appeal among young people and audiences opposed to the government. Günsal describes Göktaş’s work as a form of emotional release, then trails off: “Seeing someone stand onstage, knowing millions of people will watch, and say the things that others are afraid to say openly because of what might happen to them. . . . ”

Göktaş made a similar point in an interview with The New York Times after his release. He recalled a viewer writing beneath his performance that watching it made them feel as though they lived in a free country. The comment, he said, captured exactly what he had hoped to achieve.

But he was modest about comedy’s political power. Humor, he suggested, can help people feel understood, given them motivation and the courage to speak, and offer psychological support.

P olitical satire and state power has a long and vexed history in Turkey.

In 1946, two of the country’s best-known writers, Sabahattin Ali and Aziz Nesin, founded Markopaşa , a socialist-leaning satirical newspaper that sharply criticized class inequality and the government of the day. The paper faced distribution restrictions, pressure on printing houses, confiscations, closures, and criminal prosecutions. Its writers and cartoonists were arrested or forced into exile. Markopaşa remains one of the most important examples of socialist and oppositional humor in Turkey.

In later decades, political satire found new forms in cabaret theater and humor magazines, including the work of Ferhan Şensoy and the satirical magazines of the 1990s and 2000s. By the time of the 2013 Gezi Park protests, irony and satire had become prominent forms of political expression.

The protests began with opposition to plans to redevelop Gezi Park near Istanbul’s Taksim Square. The government framed the unrest in terms of hooliganism and terrorism. Many protesters, meanwhile, used humor and irony to defy the government’s account of the movement. Researchers have documented how humor and satire became a form of dissent in an environment where traditional media were subject to tight control.

In his courtroom defense, Göktaş placed himself in this tradition, invoking Aziz Nesin, Rıfat Ilgaz , Ferhan Şensoy, and Turkey’s major satirical magazines. Then he reached back to Nasreddin Hodja , the legendary Anatolian folk figure whose stories have circulated for centuries. Traditionally dated to 1208–1284, Hodja occupies a place in Anatolian culture somewhat comparable to the traditions of folk wisdom and social satire in American humor.

Göktaş distilled the connection between that tradition and contemporary Turkey into a single sentence: “If Nasreddin Hodja were doing stand-up today, half his show would be about President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.”

Göktaş argued that calling Erdoğan, who has governed Turkey for more than two decades, a “dictator” was political characterization, not an insult. As the country’s most powerful political figure, Erdoğan should be expected to face satire and harsh criticism, he said. He argued that politicians must be open to ridicule as well as praise.

The language of this debate is not new in Turkey.

A few days ago, I came across a street bookseller on the narrow Kadıköy street where Deniz Göktaş had performed stand-up for years. Among the books on the shelves was Görülmüştür , a collection by journalist and writer İlhan Selçuk, published in the 1980s.

Leafing through it, I found an essay titled “Freedom of Thought and Tolerance.” One sentence stood out: “Where freedom of thought does not exist, tolerance is nothing more than an empty word.”

Selçuk’s point resonates in the Göktaş case. If political or religious satire is tolerated only as long as it offends no one, can that be called freedom of expression?

O ne of the clearest examples of this problem was Göktaş’s joke about “divers.”

Prosecutors treated it as an insult to women who wear modest swimwear because of their religious beliefs. In court, Göktaş said he used the audience’s expectations to set up the joke. He described people emerging from the sea with their hair concealed and their bodies covered in black clothing. The audience, he said, assumed that he was describing women wearing modest Islamic swimwear. Then came the punch line : “f–king divers.”

The case raised a basic question: Can a stand-up performance be judged solely by a written transcript, stripped of its context onstage?

Göktaş invoked American comedian Lenny Bruce, who had faced similar problems. Bruce satirized the courts with the line, “In the Halls of Justice the only justice is in the halls.” He was repeatedly arrested and prosecuted on obscenity charges during the 1960s. In 1964, a New York court sentenced him to four months in a workhouse. He remained free while his appeal was pending and died in 1966 without serving the sentence. Thirty-seven years after his death, in 2003, New York governor George Pataki granted him a posthumous pardon.

Bruce’s trials showed how words spoken by a comedian onstage should not be evaluated independently of their delivery, facial expressions, timing, and relationship with the audience.

Göktaş argued that tone of voice, pauses, physical performance, audience reactions, and the surprise of the punch line all help make up a joke’s meaning. He compared evaluating a stand-up performance by its transcript to understanding a film by listening only to its soundtrack.

T o better understand how Turkish law treats the line between satire and incitement, I spoke with Professor Tolga Şirin. Göktaş was still being held in a high-security prison.

For Şirin, any legal assessment had to begin with context.

“What does it mean within a stand-up performance?” he asked. A legal assessment, he said, must account for irony, exaggeration, satire, and the possibility that a comedian will deliberately lead an audience in one direction before reversing its expectations. Evaluating a few sentences only according to their literal meaning can exclude other reasonable interpretations and privilege the harshest possible criminal reading.

Şirin stressed that this was not merely an aesthetic question: “The fact that a statement offends or disturbs some people is not sufficient in itself.” Context matters particularly to the charge of inciting public hatred and hostility. Under the Turkish Penal Code, the offense requires more than a statement that people find offensive. It also requires the emergence of a clear and imminent danger to public safety.

Prosecutors cited complaints submitted through CİMER, Turkey’s online public petition and complaints system operating under Turkey’s presidency.

In his defense, Göktaş addressed the 185 complaints submitted against him. He argued that the overwhelming majority of complainants had never watched his full performance but had instead reacted to selectively edited clips circulated on social media. He described the backlash as an artificially orchestrated campaign.

For Şirin, the complaint count alone could not establish a legally significant danger. Otherwise, organized groups could make speech they disliked into a punishable offense simply by launching petition campaigns.

“Public peace is not measured by the number of people who are offended,” he said.

Göktaş said he performed Ölü Deniz 198 times over approximately three years, before more than a hundred thousand people in cities across Turkey, without receiving complaints about the statements in question. According to him, the controversy began only after the performance was uploaded to YouTube and short clips started circulating on social media.

“What development has caused a statement made and made accessible months ago to suddenly create a clear and imminent danger today?” Şirin asked.

When I asked whether the prosecution could affect other comedians and artists, Şirin’s answer was unequivocal: “This is absolutely an act of intimidation.”

According to Şirin, Göktaş had pushed against the fear surrounding political figures and sensitive subjects that many people hesitate to joke about. In Şirin’s view, the proceedings could deter other comedians and artists from crossing the same boundaries.

G ünsal’s account shows how the chilling effect described by Şirin can manifest itself on the stand-up stage.

Small comedy venues in Istanbul have long provided spaces where comedians can speak relatively freely. The risk changes when a performance circulates on the internet. Jokes lose their original context and reach a much larger audience.

After Göktaş’s arrest, Günsal saw comedians grow more reluctant to post political sets.

He believes the greater problem is not simply censorship but the inability to tell where the line lies. “There is no clear line telling you, ‘Say this and you go to prison, but you can say that,’” he explained. Even careful comedians cannot know how their words will later be interpreted. The uncertainty can result in performers ruling out jokes before they have even written them.

Günsal knows that risk firsthand. In April 2020, he was arrested after a clip from one of his performances circulated on social media. The case involved comments about Mustafa Kemal Atatürk, the founder of the Turkish Republic, and the historical religious figures Rumi and Shams of Tabriz.

He spent eleven days in prison. In 2021, he was sentenced to three years and five months; the sentence was suspended. Six years later, while Deniz Göktaş was behind bars, Günsal tells me that political comedy had become both more difficult and more necessary.

After his release, Göktaş told The New York Times that he never regretted releasing the performance during his time in prison, not even for a second. As his popularity grew, he said, he had more to lose and began censoring his own material even before his arrest.

Asked about American comedians’ complaints about cancel culture and online backlash, he replied: “I don’t want to brag, but we have cancel culture — and jail.”

T here is another revealing detail in the Göktaş case.

When the investigation began, he was abroad. According to his courtroom defense, he cut his vacation short and returned to Turkey rather than fleeing.

He said that most of his close friends had moved abroad because they no longer saw a future in the country. He had been trying to persuade them to come back.

Günsal described this decision as one of the qualities he most admired in his friend. Günsal believes Göktaş could perform stand-up in English and appear regularly on stages abroad. But Göktaş does not want to build a new home somewhere else. That determination to keep calling Turkey home is something Günsal admires.

Deniz Göktaş is no longer in prison. But the impact of his case cannot be measured solely by his release on September 28. Perhaps the more telling measure will be the jokes not written, the performances never uploaded to the internet, and the comedians who censor themselves before finishing a sentence because they cannot predict where the legal boundaries lie.

The Göktaş case is not merely about whether one comedian crossed the limits of free expression. It is also a struggle over who gets to draw those limits in Turkey.

Dora Mengüç is a journalist who previously served as news manager at Sözcü TV and has worked across major newsrooms for more than two decades. He is currently a correspondent for Deutsche Welle and writes internationally for outlets including Le Parisien Matin .

With temperatures rising to the 90s in Los Angeles, avoiding the heat wasn’t exactly an option while I was at a relative’s outdoor party in August. So I sat beneath a patio umbrella with a powerful fan nearby, figuring I was protected from the sun and heat. Half an hour later, I felt exhausted, dizzy, nauseous, and generally unwell, symptoms consistent with heat exhaustion.

Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem , from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. It turns out UV radiation wasn’t repelled by this patio umbrella, and it’s hard to ever be fully protected because radiation can be reflected or scattered by objects in the environment. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both.

This led to a discovery: One of my medications increases my sensitivity to heat, which helped to explain similar episodes I’d experienced over the years. The Gem didn’t diagnose anything, but it prompted me to investigate something I might otherwise have dismissed. Since then, I’ve been more mindful about limiting time outdoors during hours of peak heat and UV, staying hydrated, and paying closer attention to how I’m feeling outside.

I’ll admit my initial interest in tracking UV was largely vanity-driven. As much as I try to challenge harmful beauty standards, I’m hardly immune to them. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others.

The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. Thankfully, getting these metrics doesn’t come at the cost of wearing a bulky device. The circular pendant comes with a cute, thin necklace I’d happily wear even if it didn’t track anything. Its titanium, gold- or silver-colored chain pairs well with a variety of outfits. Battery life lasted almost exactly a week (the advertised lifespan), and the Gem recharges using an included charging dock. The90 plans to release a hat clip and bag tag early next year, which seem ideal for those who prefer not to wear it around their neck.

The mobile app is central to the experience. It has easy-to-read graphs and jargon-light explanations. I enjoyed using it. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight.

There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. It also provides a personalized sunburn countdown, sunscreen reminders, and a daily Sun Score.

The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. I appreciated the context, but the individual estimated measurements proved more revealing than the Sun Score.

The UV readings in the app responded quickly as I moved between sunlight, shade, and indoors, even registering changes near windows. I couldn’t independently verify the sensor’s accuracy, but the readings behaved as expected as I shifted between environments. However, there were times when I noticed the Gem sometimes failed to register that I had been outside. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking.

My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too.

The vitamin D countdown wasn’t as helpful as I had hoped. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. I noticed similar fluctuations in the app’s estimated time to sunburn. With both countdowns changing so dramatically, I stopped paying much attention to the exact times and focused instead on the broader picture: whether it felt like I was getting too much or too little sun.

That was perhaps the biggest surprise of testing the Gem. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade.

I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary.

At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

Photography by Sheena Vasani / The Verge

Twenty-five years ago, Kevin Lewandowski founded Discogs , arguably the destination online for obsessive vinyl collectors and music nerds of all stripes. It is a marketplace for buying and selling records, obviously, but it’s also become so much more. It’s a shockingly comprehensive database that covers not just albums and singles, but all the various versions and pressings. It’s a really fun rabbit hole to disappear down when you’re trying to figure out what obscure pressing of Ministry’s The Mind is a Terrible Thing to Taste or Psalm 69 you had in high school, because you definitely blasted the cover of “Lay Lady Lay” all the time and 100 percent never owned Filth Pig .

In the years since it debuted, Discogs has grown to be much more than just a site where audiophiles go to trade rare first pressings of Beach Boys records. There are forums, groups, user-created lists, and more. It’s part eBay, part Reddit, and IMDB — just specifically for music.

With more and more people turning their back on the algorithm and rediscovering physical media , now seemed like a perfect time to check in with Lewandowski.

What is your most indispensable tool?

My AeroPress. I use it multiple times a day. In fact, I just made a coffee with it [sips coffee].

How many tabs do you have open right now?

Probably around 30 on my work computer. My personal computer is worse — probably 40 or 50.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

I look at X and Instagram occasionally, but I don’t really post.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

It’s not really a gadget, but I like to tinker. Lately I’ve been playing around with Home Assistant software and built my own setup to control things like the garage door and outdoor lights. So I guess my favorite gadget is one I made myself.

What is one thing you wish you had created?

Probably a game like Rez , which came out around 2000. It’s a rhythm game where you’re almost controlling the music as you play, about as close to DJing as a video game can get. I’ve actually had an idea for my own version with a similar concept. It’s still just an idea, though.

What do you do when you need to focus?

I’ll either clear everything off my desk or change locations completely. Go to a coffee shop or sit outside. Sometimes I just need a different environment.

What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?

Records. I was at Mint Gallery in Portland last week and picked up four. I still really like going into a record store and finding something to bring home. And I also recently picked up three reissues from the Moodsville / Acoustic Sounds series.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

The Secret Weapon.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

I don’t use memes very often, but one I was kind of proud of was putting a Discogs screen into a North Korean war room photo. I was advised that maybe it wasn’t one for the company chat.

While some retailers were offering preorder discounts on the remastered Legend of Zelda: The Ocarina of Time , it’s not too late to save if you missed out. Costco members can currently get $5 off the digital version online, bringing the price down to $54.99. Considering an annual Costco membership runs $65 , that discount almost offsets one month of your plan — a prime example of “gamer math.”

My colleague Andrew Webster recently shared his thoughts on Nintendo’s latest Switch 2 exclusive, noting how impressed he was with how much impact a few modern quality-of-life changes had on what is otherwise a classic experience. The updated graphics are as thoughtful as they are beautiful, pairing realistic scenery with puppet-like characters. Perhaps, more importantly, Link can now jump anytime he likes, rather than being limited to specific ledges.

scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Sapporo's Snow-Clearing Tram Makes Early Winter Debut
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Sapporo deployed its distinctive Sasara snow-clearing tram for the first time this season early on November 7th, the second-earliest deployment in 10 years, after snowfall reached 8 centimeters at 4 a.m., prompting a vehicle to leave its depot to clear snow from the city's streetcar tracks.

According to the Sapporo City Transportation Promotion Corporation, which operates the service, this year's first deployment came earlier than in all but one of the past 10 years. With temperatures below freezing, the tram made its way through central Sapporo, its rotating bamboo brushes, known as "sasara," sweeping snow from the tracks and sending it flying to either side. The distinctive vehicles are a familiar sight during Sapporo's long winters, helping keep the city's streetcar network operating despite heavy snowfall.

articles.title: Middle East could have big role in Democrats' Trump corruption inquiry
articles.summary: After their victory in the US midterm elections, the Democrats have promised to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Critics say the president's Middle East deals is an area they should focus on.
articles.ai_summary: Following their midterm election victory, Democrats are set to investigate potential corruption linked to Trump's Middle East dealings.

scraped.title: How the Middle East could prove fertile ground for Democrats in Trump corruption inquiry
scraped.description: After their victory in the US midterm elections, the Democrats have promised to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Critics say the president's Middle East deals is an area they should focus on.
scraped.h1: Middle East could have big role in Democrats' Trump corruption inquiry
scraped.body_text:
After their victory in the US midterm elections, the Democrats have promised to investigate corruption in the Trump administration. Critics say the president's Middle East deals is an area they should focus on.

Several polls of US voters taken around the recent midterm elections show that an overriding concern about the Trump administration is corruption.

Just days after the midterms, senior figures in the Democratic Party were quick to proclaim that they will be investigating corruption accusations when they take their seats in January.

It's highly likely that many of those investigations will center on the Trump administration's and the Trump family's links to wealthy Middle Eastern countries.

"The incoming Democratic majority in Congress will no doubt aggressively use their powers to investigate the administration's alleged wrongdoings," Amy Hawthorne, a non-resident fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Arab Center, wrote in a commentary after the midterms. "Cases involving the Middle East will be their top targets."

Financial disclosures made by President Trump in the middle of this year showed that during 2025, his businesses made about $2 billion in income. This was triple the income he reported the previous year, observers noted.

"According to the information available … Middle Eastern countries and businesses have directly contributed to the bottom line of Trump's family businesses — more so than any other region of the world," Brian Katulis, a senior fellow and expert in US foreign policy at the Middle East Institute in Washington, wrote in a July text after the presidential disclosure. "Gulf entities paid around $300 million to the president's businesses in 2025."

A lot of the money Trump made in 2025 came from the sale of a stake in a cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, Katulis noted.

The company was founded by the Trump and Witkoff families in 2024 — Steve Witkoff is Trump's special envoy to the Middle East — and in 2025, a large portion of it was sold to an investment firm backed by a senior United Arab Emirates official, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan. The latter serves as the UAE's national security advisor and is also the brother of the UAE's president.

The deal was done in January 2026 behind closed doors, shortly before Trump's inauguration as president. In May 2026, the US agreed to allow the UAE access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, despite objections from some national security advisers.

Trump's critics allege a connection, the Trump administration denies it.

There are also other alleged instances of Trump administration corruption with links to the Middle East.

Various Trump deals with Saudi and Emirati real estate developers are also being questioned because of possible conflicts of interest.

The Gulf real estate developers, which have close ties to their governments and respective royal families, have agreed to build Trump-branded golf resorts, hotels, mansions, skyscrapers and towers in Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar and the Maldives.

In 2025, Trump reported $59.5 million in foreign real estate licensing income, ten times more than he made in 2023, business media outlet CNBC reported in August. Nearly two-thirds of that money came from projects in the Gulf, CNBC said.

Ethics watchdogs argue that, "the deals create conflicts between Trump's political leadership role and private interests" because some of those Gulf states and their developers were also "pursuing major US investments, seeking government permits or pressing for favorable economic and diplomatic relations."

When the Qatari royal family gifted Trump a luxury jet , worth around $400 million, in May 2025, politicians and ethics experts asked about the propriety of taking such a pricey present from a foreign government.

After his presidency ends, Trump was apparently planning to donate the plane to his Florida-based project, the Donald J. Trump Presidential Library Foundation. Currently, it is unclear whether the Qatari plane will end up there and there's been speculation Trump will try to keep it for personal use.

The library is a non-profit and has received tens of millions in funding — an investigation by the CBS network traced over $100 million in donations — from lawsuits and via corporate donors.

Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren has already said the library project would be investigated. "Giant corporations and foreign governments should not be able to buy influence in Washington with donations to the president's library," she told CBS.

Plans for the so-called Board of Peace were created in September 2025 and the body was to facilitate a ceasefire and reconstruction in Gaza.

It was set up to be a kind of multilateral international organization, similar to the United Nations, except that Trump would serve as its chairman indefinitely and member countries donating $1 billion if they want to sit on the board permanently.

The Board of Peace has not achieved much in Gaza, experts say, and there have been several worrying developments.

Four months after its establishment, the World Bank account set up to manage Board of Peace funds was empty, the Financial Times newspaper reported in May . Instead, money had been deposited into a private JP Morgan bank account, over which there was no oversight.

There have apparently been contributions of around $3 million from Morocco and $20 million from the UAE, as well as pledges of $7 billion from board members and $10 billion from Trump.

The board's legal status was also changed to make it into an international non-governmental organization. This change in legal status may aim "to avoid US congressional oversight and keep much of its activity opaque," Zaha Hassan, an attorney and senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, warned in a June commentary . It also "gives Trump ultimate decision-making authority, including over financial matters," she noted.

"The Trump crime family is the top of our investigative priorities," the most senior Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, said after the midterms .

And he has already expressed concerns about the behavior of Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner in the Middle East.

Most of the issues around Kushner involve potential conflicts of interest. Kushner is acting as a volunteer envoy in the Middle East and has been deeply involved in negotiations to end the Gaza conflict and the Iran war.

In early October, CNN published an investigation that detailed links between Kushner's private equity company, Affinity Partners, and investments into leading Israeli military manufacturers.

It's also been reported that while he was travelling in the region, Kushner was trying to raise billions for his equity firm.

In March, Democratic politicians, including Garcia, wrote letters to the president's office, saying they had "serious concerns about whether the White House is letting Mr. Kushner use his influence for personal financial gain."

The potentially most damaging claims against Kushner come from a recent book, "Prince and Thieves," published late October by American investigative journalist Matthew Cole.

Cole alleges, "Kushner worked with the UAE to shape US policy across the Middle East and that, in the course of this work, he was given access to bank accounts containing roughly $2 billion," the New York Times wrote in its review .

Kushner denies the allegations about any such slush fund held by an Israeli bank and has threatened to sue Vanity Fair magazine, which published excerpts from the book.

But, as the New York Times concluded, "Cole's work is sufficiently calm, detailed and forensic to necessitate a large-scale and urgent congressional inquiry."

scraped.body_text:
Trump said he would be replacing Susie Wiles for the top advisory role. Miller is controversial figure, known as a key architect of the administration’s hardline immigration policies.

US President Donald ‌Trump announced on ⁠Friday ⁠that his ​deputy chief of ​staff and architect of his administration's strict immigration policy, Stephen Miller, will become his new chief of staff.

Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who had been in the post since Trump's inauguration. With the nod, Miller becomes the top aide to the president.

Trump announced the move, saying Miller was "one of my most trusted advisors," adding that Wiles has done an outstanding job, and would be "moving over" to the "Trump political operation."

Wiles also commented on her exit from the White House, saying that her work there was "the honor of a lifetime."

She said she was proud of what the administration had accomplished during her tenure, including "securing our border and cutting taxes to strengthening our economy and putting America First."

The move comes after Trump's Republican Party lost control of the House and Senate after a midterm election rout at the hands of Democrats .

scraped.title: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
scraped.description: Pope Leo’s November 2026 trip to Latin America will bring him back to Peru, where he served as a priest and bishop for two decades.
scraped.author: Eben Levey
scraped.h1: Pope Leo’s trip is a homecoming to Peru – where debate over liberation theology roiled the church during his early years as a priest
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Pope Leo XIV travels to Latin America on Nov. 6, 2026, with a packed itinerary that will bring him through Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It is Leo’s first trip to the region since his elevation to the papacy – and a homecoming for a pope who spent two decades in Peru and holds Peruvian citizenship.

As a historian of Catholicism in the late 20th century , I couldn’t help but notice that the pope’s plans walk a fine line during a fraught political moment in Latin America.

Leo plans to meet with the right-wing presidents of Argentina and Peru . He will also visit sites often associated with the progressive wing of the Catholic Church, including Casavalle, one of the poorest neighborhoods in Uruguay’s capital. In Argentina, where President Javier Milei has drastically cut funding for disability services, the pope will go to a Catholic home for disabled people.

And in Chiclayo, Peru, where Leo served as a bishop, he will pray at a chapel dedicated to St. Óscar Romero. A Salvadoran archbishop, Romero was assassinated in 1980 after years of speaking out against the human rights violations committed by the U.S.-supported Salvadoran military . His ministry was influenced by liberation theology , a controversial movement born in Peru that roiled church politics for decades – including during Leo’s years in Peru.

The name itself was coined in a 1968 lecture by Gustavo Gutiérrez , a Peruvian theologian and priest. He expanded on his ideas in a 1971 book, “ A Theology of Liberation .”

Gutiérrez and like-minded theologians argued that Christians have a moral duty to liberate the oppressed . They saw poverty, violence, racism and discrimination as not just problems but collective sins. While building on earlier Catholic social teachings, these “liberationists” envisioned profound change that went beyond the spiritual care and charitable work of traditional Latin American Catholicism.

Catholics inspired by liberation theology created community organizations and work cooperatives, organized labor unions and fostered other initiatives that sought to measurably improve the lives of the poor. In my own research , I’ve documented how priests and nuns in rural Mexico helped organize transportation, corn milling and carpentry cooperatives.

Gutiérrez also argued that Christians should use Marxist ideas about analyzing society and the economy to better understand inequality . In nations like Peru, which possessed rich natural resources , liberationists tailored their economic justice projects to address how international and national companies profited off the low wages of miners and farmers.

During the Cold War, however, these ideas led some politicians and church leaders to accuse liberationists of socialism and communism.

A minority fringe of liberationists did embrace left-ring radicalism. Christians for Socialism , for example, argued that liberation meant rejecting capitalism . Some clergy, although only a handful, even picked up arms to fight alongside clandestine left-wing revolutionary groups.

This presented a dilemma to the Vatican.

In 1891, Pope Leo XIII – the current pope’s namesake – published “Rerum Novarum ,” an encyclical focused on workers’ rights amid the Industrial Revolution. Since then, the Vatican had critiqued the worst excesses of capitalism while also rejecting socialism and communism, which it viewed as godless ideologies.

During the 1960s and ’70s, Pope Paul VI generally supported local initiatives by liberationist Catholics , including some in Chulucanas, Peru , where Leo began his missionary work. Paul appointed and elevated bishops who shared a vision that the church could help empower the poor and alleviate oppression.

But the Vatican shifted when the Polish cardinal Karol Józef Wojtyla became Pope John Paul II in 1978. For most of his adult life, Poland had been part of the Soviet bloc, which imposed restrictions on organized religion. A staunch opponent of communism , he worried about liberation theology’s use of Marxist analysis. So did one of his top Vatican officials, Joseph Ratzinger – the future Pope Benedict XVI.

The Vatican began investigating some liberation theologians for violations of church teachings. In 1985, for example, Brazilian liberationist theologian Leonardo Boff was ordered to observe a year of silence – no publishing, no public speaking – to discipline him for his critique of the church’s hierarchy. Several priests were suspended over their work in Sandinista Nicaragua.

John Paul ordered that the Peruvian bishops begin an investigation of Gutiérrez – above all, over Marxism’s influence on his work . Gutiérrez was ultimately not punished.

One factor in his favor may have been his consistent opposition to armed revolution, even before violence raged in Peru from the 1980s into the ’90s. The Shining Path , a Maoist guerrilla group, was waging a war of terrorism against the Peruvian government, setting off bombs across Peru.

Under President Alberto Fujimori, the government escalated existing counterinsurgency operations, often using indiscriminate violence against citizens in the region where the Shining Path emerged. In 2009, Fujimori was convicted of human rights violations .

Leo has never described himself as a liberationist Catholic. However, his experiences as a priest were indelibly shaped by liberation theology , the Peruvian armed conflict and the church debates that roiled much of Latin America during his years there.

Leo, born Robert Prevost, was raised in Chicago. After ordination, his journey as a priest began in Peru, where he landed for missionary work in 1985. The young friar followed in the footsteps of other U.S. Catholic missionaries who had been serving among Peru’s poor and Indigenous, urban and rural, since the 1940s.

Sent to Chulucanas, in Peru’s coastal northwest, Prevost found himself in a region of pastoral experimentation. Since the 1960s, Augustinian missionaries had been working closely with the community to provide literacy education, discussion groups about poverty and inequality, and workshops to train artisans.

These programs were a far cry from the more radical actions of some Catholics who supported liberation theology. Nevertheless, the programs in Chulucanas aimed to empower the Peruvian poor, chipping away at exploitation and low wages on the region’s sugarcane and cotton estates. Like Gutiérrez, many Peruvian Christians believed that the Shining Path drew support because of pervasive poverty and inequality , and that churches could help transform the nation.

But the Catholic Church in Latin America was in the midst of another transformation. John Paul gradually appointed conservative bishops across the continent. Experimental pastoral programs lost support, and institutions that trained priests to put liberation theology into action, such as the Regional Seminary of the Southeast in Mexico, were shuttered or “reoriented.”

Yet even as the hierarchy shifted conservative, work on the ground among Latin America’s poorest continued apace. From coffee cooperatives in Mexico to human rights activists across the continent, many programs survived.

Leo’s 2026 itinerary includes multiple stops that speak to this history and on-the-ground pastoral work. The most symbolic, perhaps, is the Capilla San Óscar Romero, located in Chiclayo, the pope’s former diocese.

A neighborhood chapel renovated with donations from Leo’s connections in the United States, it is one of many sites throughout the Americas honoring Catholics who fell victim to right-wing, anti-communist violence. The day before Romero’s assassination, he used his weekly radio address to speak directly to El Salvador’s conscripted soldiers, telling them, “ No soldier is obliged to obey an order counter to the law of God .”

Leo XIV’s visit to the chapel is for private prayer, not a homily or a speech. Still, I would argue that the soft-spoken pope’s stop will evoke Romero’s message – especially at a time of strikes against suspected drug traffickers , which human rights groups have criticized as extrajudicial killings . During his final Mass , Romero pleaded, “I beseech you, I beg you, I command you in the name of God: Cease the repression!”

Assistant Professor of History, Rochester Institute of Technology

articles.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
articles.summary: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.
articles.ai_summary: Ilse Aigner is being considered as a strong candidate for the next German president, with support from her party allies in the Christian Democrats.

scraped.title: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
scraped.description: German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.
scraped.h1: Ilse Aigner tipped by party allies as next German president
scraped.body_text:
German media reports suggest that Bavarian politician Ilse Aigner's chances of becoming the next president are on the up. Long favored by her Bavarian CSU, now it seems Christian Democrats nationwide plan to back her.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (the CDU) and their Bavarian sister party, the CSU , want to nominate a joint candidate to be the next president of Germany when the special "Bundesversammlung" committee that elects one votes at the end of January.

It's long been clear that the CSU favor the current speaker of Bavaria 's parliament, Ilse Aigner, for the role.

But on Friday, multiple German news outlets like Spiegel , the Süddeutsche Zeitung and the DPA news agency cited sources in the CDU as saying that party's leadership had also decided on putting Aigner forward.

DPA reported that Merz would officially recommend Aigner as a candidate at a meeting of the CDU's leadership that will convene in Berlin on Sunday and Monday.

On the record, however, party officials would neither confirm nor deny the reports, pointing only to the upcoming meetings on Monday.

If chosen, Aigner would be the 13th person and the first woman to take up the role as post-war Germany's head of state, which is a more ceremonial one with primarily symbolic power, while the bulk of the political and legislative power resides with the chancellor.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Aigner, 61, is currently the speaker of the state parliament in Bavaria.

The youngest of four sisters and the daughter of an electrician, she worked in the family business in her early adult life before going into politics. She's a Roman Catholic, single and has no children.

Aigner began her parliamentary career in the Bavarian legislature in 1994, then moved to the Bundestag federal parliament in 1998, before returning to the Bavarian chamber in 2013.

She spent five years as federal agriculture minister under then-Chancellor Angela Merkel.

She would also be the first CSU politician to hold the office.

Current President Frank-Walter Steinmeier , a heavy hitter for years for the Social Democrats before becoming head of state, is nearing the end of his second five-year term in the role, having assumed the office in March 2017.

The CDU/CSU's junior coalition partners, the Social Democrats ( SPD ), have also made it clear they would back a presidential bid from Aigner.

"If the CDU steering committee does indeed officially assert itself on Monday and put forward Ilse Aigner, then on behalf of the SPD I can only say that we would welcome this and support it," SPD chairman Lars Klingbeil said at an event in Berlin.

A large committee known as the Bundesversammlung chooses the German president. It will vote on January 30, 2027.

It's made up of all 630 Bundestag parliament members, and another 630 people assigned to represent the various German states — weighted according to each state's share of the national population.

Most of these are regional lawmakers, but municipal politicians and people from other walks of public life are also sometimes given a vote.

The CDU/CSU and SPD combined have a majority of roughly 50 seats in the special committee.

Beyond this, Merz is expected to try to rope in support for Aigner from the Greens, a party that has long championed more female representation at the top of politics and that would not seem to have a realistic chance of propelling a candidate of its own into the role.

This suggests that if Aigner's nomination were to materialize and solidify, she should have fairly good chances of succeeding Steinmeier.
