scraped.title: Typhoon No. 32 Forming, Northern Japan Braces for Blizzards
scraped.description: Central Tokyo recorded its first November summer day in three years on November 6, with temperatures climbing to 25.3 degrees Celsius, while northern Japan faced the threat of violent winds and severe snowstorms from the evening and a tropical depression far south of the country threatened to develop into Typhoon No. 32, potentially the first such storm in 32 years.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Typhoon No. 32 Forming, Northern Japan Braces for Blizzards
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Central Tokyo recorded its first November summer day in three years on November 6, with temperatures climbing to 25.3 degrees Celsius, while northern Japan faced the threat of violent winds and severe snowstorms from the evening and a tropical depression far south of the country threatened to develop into Typhoon No. 32, potentially the first such storm in 32 years.

The unusually warm weather came just one day before November 7, which marks Ritto, the traditional beginning of winter in the Japanese calendar, highlighting a sharp contrast between summer-like conditions across parts of the country and the approaching winter weather in the north. Tokyo began November 6 under a blanket of thick fog, which obscured roughly half of Tokyo Skytree. The morning sun could be seen breaking through the mist before skies cleared and temperatures began rising rapidly. By around 2 p.m., central Tokyo had reached 25.3 degrees, a level more typical of September and a dramatic turnaround from the chilly conditions recorded on November 5. It was the first time in three years that the capital had experienced a November day with temperatures reaching at least 25 degrees, the Japan Meteorological Agency's threshold for a "summer day." In Ueno, visitors were seen removing jackets and switching to lighter clothing. One parent said the family had planned to take a child to the zoo wearing a fluffy panda-themed outfit but had to remove it because of the heat. "It was just too hot. We've even turned on a fan," the parent said. Shizuoka City also experienced unseasonably warm conditions, with temperatures exceeding 25 degrees before noon and reaching a daytime high of 25.9 degrees. Residents were seen walking through the streets in short sleeves and shorts. The summer-like temperatures created an unusual atmosphere at Tokyo's Ueno Park, where a Christmas market opened on November 6. Visitors wearing short sleeves and sandals strolled past Santa Claus decorations, while some chose cold drinks rather than traditional hot winter beverages. One visitor explained the choice of apple juice simply by saying, "Because it's hot." At the Togoshi Ginza shopping street in Tokyo, however, the warm weather did little to discourage customers from enjoying oden, a traditional Japanese winter dish of ingredients simmered in hot broth. Diners were seen eating steaming bowls of oden alongside cold beer. "It's warm today, but this is the season for oden," one customer said. While much of central Japan enjoyed unusually high temperatures, weather conditions were deteriorating farther north. Heavy rain struck Niigata City during the afternoon of November 6, while large raindrops battered rooftops in Noboribetsu, Hokkaido, signaling the arrival of increasingly unstable weather. Northern Japan was expected to face potentially dangerous conditions from the evening of November 6, with severe winds and blizzards strong enough to warrant weather warnings. Authorities were concerned that the approaching weather system could bring widespread disruption as rain turned to snow in colder areas. Meanwhile, a tropical depression that had developed over waters far south of Japan was being closely monitored for signs of strengthening. The system, sometimes described as a "typhoon egg," could develop into a tropical storm as early as November 7. If it reaches typhoon strength, it would be designated Typhoon No. 32, marking the first time in 32 years that the western North Pacific has recorded a 32nd named tropical storm within a single year. The potential development would be particularly unusual for November, when Japan is normally transitioning toward winter and tropical cyclone activity affecting the country is generally declining. The dramatic weather contrasts are expected to continue into the following week, when temperatures in Tokyo are forecast to plunge after the brief spell of summer-like warmth. Overnight lows in the capital could fall below 10 degrees Celsius, bringing a sharp return to late-autumn and early-winter conditions after the unusually hot November 6. The rapid temperature changes, combined with the threat of severe winds and heavy snow in northern Japan and the possible formation of another typhoon to the south, underscore the unusually unsettled weather affecting the country as winter approaches.

articles.title: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
articles.summary: Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas. (News On Japan)
articles.ai_summary: Research indicates that bears may be able to identify when astringent persimmons become sweet, suggesting that removing sweet persimmon trees could help keep them away from residential areas.

scraped.title: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
scraped.description: Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas.
scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Bears May Know When Astringent Persimmons Become Sweet
scraped.body_text:
HYOGO - Bears preparing for winter hibernation may be able to determine when astringent persimmons have lost their bitterness and become suitable to eat, according to research by the University of Hyogo, which suggests that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees could help prevent bears from entering residential areas.

As bear activity increases ahead of hibernation, persimmon trees have been identified as one of the factors attracting the animals into populated areas, raising concerns about encounters with humans. A University of Hyogo study found that bears began eating sweet persimmons as early as late July, while they generally avoided astringent varieties until late November or later. The difference in feeding behavior suggests that bears may be sensitive to changes in the fruit's chemical composition, allowing them to recognize when its bitter taste has diminished. Daisuke Fujiki, an associate professor at the University of Hyogo, said the findings indicate that bears use the concentration of astringent compounds in persimmons to determine whether the fruit is suitable for consumption. "We found that whether the concentration of astringent compounds falls below a certain level appears to be a factor in determining whether bears will eat the fruit," Fujiki said. The findings suggest that bears may be capable of identifying the point at which astringent persimmons become palatable, rather than simply consuming whatever fruit is available. Researchers warn that astringent persimmons could increasingly attract bears as their bitterness naturally declines in the coming weeks, particularly during the period leading up to winter hibernation. However, because sweet persimmons attract bears much earlier in the season, researchers believe that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees in areas vulnerable to bear encounters could be an effective preventive measure. The study highlights the importance of managing fruit trees around residential communities, particularly during autumn when bears are actively searching for food before entering hibernation. However, because sweet persimmons attract bears much earlier in the season, researchers believe that prioritizing the removal of sweet persimmon trees in areas vulnerable to bear encounters could be an effective preventive measure.

The study highlights the importance of managing fruit trees around residential communities, particularly during autumn when bears are actively searching for food before entering hibernation.

scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Putin Places Japan Tobacco Under Russian Control
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree placing the Russian operations of Japan Tobacco (JT) under the temporary management of a local company, effectively stripping the Japanese tobacco giant of control over its business in the country and prompting a formal protest from Tokyo demanding that the measure be immediately withdrawn.

The decree covers four companies responsible for the Russian operations of JT International, the overseas subsidiary of Japan Tobacco. The move effectively deprives the Japanese company of management rights over its Russian business, although the arrangement has been described as temporary. According to Russia's state-run TASS news agency, JT International has operated in Russia since 1999 and has grown into the country's largest tobacco manufacturer, making the decision a significant development for one of Japan's major overseas corporate operations. The Russian government has been expanding measures to place assets belonging to companies from countries that have imposed sanctions on Moscow under state-directed management. In September, similar action was taken against companies including Swiss food giant Nestle. Japan Tobacco said it was carefully examining the situation and its available options while prioritizing the interests of employees and other stakeholders. "We are closely assessing the situation and possible future courses of action, placing the highest priority on our employees and other stakeholders," the company said. The move comes as relations between Japan and Russia continue to deteriorate. In August, Putin made his first visit to Etorofu, one of the Russian-controlled islands claimed by Japan as part of its Northern Territories. Tensions escalated further in October when Russia's Federal Security Service detained a journalist from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara announced at a morning press conference on November 6 that Japan had lodged a formal protest with the Russian government and demanded the immediate reversal of the decree. Kihara said senior Japanese officials currently visiting Russia, including a senior official from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and a senior official from the Foreign Ministry's European Affairs Bureau, had joined Japan's ambassador to Russia in delivering the protest directly to Russian authorities. "The senior officials currently visiting Russia, together with our ambassador, have protested to the Russian government and demanded that the measure be withdrawn immediately," Kihara said. He emphasized that the Japanese government would continue monitoring developments closely and take appropriate action in response to the situation. The decision adds to the difficulties facing Japanese companies operating in Russia, where foreign businesses from countries supporting sanctions against Moscow have faced increasing risks of losing control over their local assets.

scraped.title: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El-Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
scraped.description: About 86% of Black Michiganders voted for Abdul El-Sayed for US Senate, according to preliminary data.
scraped.author: Christine Slaughter
scraped.h1: Black Michiganders helped push Abdul El‑Sayed to victory – but the numbers show he was less popular with this key voting block than some other Democratic candidates
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Progressive Abdul El-Sayed’s victory in Michigan’s U.S. Senate race was one of the most-watched contests in the 2026 midterm elections.

As the results for this race came in, I had my eye on one demographic: Black voters. I am a political scientist who studies Black political behavior. My research has been published in numerous journals , as well as in my forthcoming book, “Black Resilience,” which examines Black voters’ political participation.

The support of Black voters for El-Sayed was not a given. In the August primary, 62% of Detroit voters chose U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens over El-Sayed. Many pundits predicted it would be difficult for El-Sayed to gain support in Detroit, which is about 75% Black .

After the primary, El-Sayed made overtures by sharing his plans to improve the lives of Black Americans, which included supporting the growth of minority-owned businesses, creating more affordable housing, eliminating food deserts and expanding the Rx Kids cash assistance program nationwide.

About 91.8% of Detroit voters supported El-Sayed in the general election, according to the city’s unofficial results . Detroit City Clerk Janice Winfrey said 209,924 residents voted in the 2026 midterms , up about 21% from the 2022 midterm elections. For the 2024 presidential election, 247,770 city residents cast a ballot.

In fact, El-Sayed received 70.6% of Wayne County votes , which includes Detroit. In 2024, Kamala Harris received 62.7% of the vote in Wayne County .

In the 2024 presidential election, Michigan’s Democratic vote share fell to 48.3% , from 50.6% in 2020 , as the state went for Donald Trump instead of Democratic nominee Harris.

Despite their ideological differences, Sen. Elissa Slotkin and El-Sayed drew similar support among Black voters. In 2024, Slotkin – a moderate Democrat – won 48.6% of the vote, a small margin over Mike Rogers, who was the Republican candidate in that race. In 2026, El-Sayed defeated Rogers statewide by a substantially wider margin, winning 52% of the vote.

In other words, these early election results do not indicate whether Black voters embraced El-Sayed’s progressive platform or simply voted for the Democratic candidate. Voters may have been rejecting Republican Party politics or expressing anger toward Trump over pocketbook issues.

Researchers from Michigan State University found that precincts with more than 80% of Black voters supported Democratic statewide candidates over Republicans at a rate of 92% to 94% during the 2024 general election, which is only slightly lower than the 94% to 95% levels observed in similar precincts during the 2020 contest between Trump and Joe Biden.

Even while Black voters overwhelmingly support Democrats, small shifts in their support and turnout can influence the outcome of close and competitive races. These shifts may help explain differing outcomes, including El-Sayed’s victory in 2026 and Harris’ defeat there in 2024.

While Black voter support for El-Sayed was high, estimated at around 86% statewide , Gov. Gretchen Whitmer’s support among Black voters was about 94% in the 2022 gubernatorial race, according to an ABC exit poll .

Similarly, preelection polling indicated that Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, polled more favorably among nonwhite voters compared to El-Sayed . NBC exit poll data shows that 86% of Black voters in Michigan supported El-Sayed, while 90% supported Benson , who won the governorship over Republican John James.

Black voters are often strategic voters who support the candidate they believe best aligns with Black interests, which has usually been the Democratic candidate since the Civil Rights Movement.

Generally, Black voters have made their electoral choices based on what’s believed to be best for the group as a whole – a concept described by political scientist Michael C. Dawson as linked fate .

However, recent research shows that Black social networks and institutions, including churches and civic organizations, reinforce expectations of political solidarity . Weaker ties to these networks may lessen the social pressure that encourages Black Americans to participate in politics and support Democratic candidates.

Lower participation by Black Americans could lead to elected officials paying less attention to issues important to Black voters, such as affordability and the cost of living, healthcare, and reducing racial discrimination . If officials assume Black voters will remain loyal to Democrats, they’re under less pressure to win their votes by addressing their concerns.

My research has demonstrated that after the 2024 election, Black women in particular felt frustrated with the Democratic Party, yet they participated in elections despite these frustrations.

El-Sayed was part of a field of notable Democratic candidates in this election cycle. For example, Angie Nixon, a state representative in Florida, championed affordability alongside a moratorium on evictions and a universal jobs program , while James Talarico, a former schoolteacher in Texas, focused on public education.

El-Sayed is a former public health official who had not previously held elected office. This may have turned off some Black voters who often value governing experience . El-Sayed advocated for Medicare For All and lowering the costs of gas prices and groceries.

Although he doesn’t identify as a democratic socialist, El-Sayed campaigned with several progressive elected officials, such as U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez. U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders endorsed El-Sayed on the day he announced his candidacy in 2025. El-Sayed also campaigned with the Black establishment, including U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn of South Carolina. Former President Barack Obama spoke at a rally for El-Sayed in Detroit in October 2026.

Stevens, who lost the Democratic nomination to El-Sayed in the primary, endorsed Republican Mike Rogers after she attended a service with the Republican candidate at a predominantly Black church in Detroit two days before the election . Stevens’ tactic drew severe backlash from Democratic leaders and may have mobilized some Black voters to turn out for El-Sayed on Election Day.

“I felt like she pimped my community,” one Black voter from Detroit told ABC News in response to Stevens’ last-minute endorsement of Rogers.

Assistant Professor of Political Science, Boston University

scraped.h1: Austrian tycoon Rene Benko sentenced to 2 more years for fraud
scraped.body_text:
Austrian businessman Rene Benko, who suffered a major fall from grace after his real estate empire, Signa Holding, went bust, was handed two more years in prison.

Rene Benko, an Austrian businessman whose legacy as a property tycoon collapsed with the fall of his real estate empire Signa Holding three years ago, was sentenced to two more years in prison on Thursday.

The Innsbruck Regional Court found Beko guilty of defrauding €5 million from the private foundation of Austrian industrialist Hans Peter Haselsteiner. The payment from Haselsteiner arrived just weeks before Signa Holding declared insolvency.

It was the third criminal proceeding against Banko, coming after two earlier convictions. He was sentenced in the first case in October 2025 on charges of insolvency-related fraud. In September 2026, he received a 30-month term for harming creditors.

The new sentence against Benko, 49, comes just ‌three weeks ⁠after ⁠he was released to house arrest to serve out a previous conviction.

Benko's lawyer said he would assess whether to appeal the conviction over the weekend.

Benko was acquitted on a second charge that he had hidden a luxury rifle worth €80,000 from creditors.

Benko was once thought to have been a wunderkind for having established himself as a self-made entrepreneur after dropping out of college.

At its peak, Signa Holdings accumulated a portfolio worth more than $30 billion, with stakes in New York's Chrysler Building and Berlin's KaDeWe department store.

In 2023, Signa Holdings declared bankruptcy, dealing a blow to a myriad of European property investors and others.

The fall of Signa was considered the single biggest financial earthquake to have hit the European property market since the global financial crisis of 2008.

Perplexity is taking on OpenAI and Anthropic with its own work-focused AI agents. The startup’s new always-on “Teammates” can take on multiple roles within a workspace, while pulling existing projects, skills, and memory from the Perplexity tools you already use.

Teammates integrate with Perplexity Computer , an AI system that can deploy agents on your device to complete tasks. But Perplexity says Teammates “build on top” of Computer by offering the ability to collaborate and complete “ongoing, large-scale work.” You can assign each Teammate different jobs that they can perform simultaneously — much like OpenAI’s Dots and Claude Duet . Perplexity’s take on the feature is much more expensive, however, as it requires a subscription to its $200 / month Max plan.

Perplexity notes that you can keep tabs on Teammates’ progress through individual threads in the Perplexity app, as well as interact with them in Slack. “Over time, we envision every org having hundreds of teammates working for each person,” Perplexity CEO Aravind Srinivas says on X .

scraped.h1: Couple Arrested for Secretly Filming Women at Bathhouses
scraped.body_text:
Ishikawa - A married couple from Kanazawa, Ishikawa Prefecture, has been arrested on suspicion of secretly filming women changing clothes and bathing at public bathing facilities, with police saying the pair carried out around 100 illicit recordings and earned approximately 5 million yen by selling the footage online.

Kyoto Prefectural Police arrested Daichi Nakatake, a 35-year-old company employee, and his wife Misato Nakatake, 24, on suspicion of violating Japan's law against the nonconsensual recording of sexually intimate images and other offenses. The couple allegedly used small cameras concealed inside bags and other belongings to record women changing clothes and bathing at facilities in Ishikawa Prefecture between May and July 2026. They are also suspected of providing the videos to three men. According to police, Misato entered the bathing facilities and secretly filmed women under instructions from her husband, who subsequently sold the footage over the internet. Investigators believe the couple concealed miniature cameras inside bags and baskets, positioning the lenses to capture images through small gaps without attracting attention. During questioning, both suspects admitted to the allegations and told investigators they had secretly recorded women on approximately 100 occasions, generating sales of around 5 million yen. Police are investigating whether the couple committed numerous additional offenses beyond those covered by the current allegations, including the extent of their online sales and the number of women whose privacy was violated.

scraped.title: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
scraped.description: The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.
scraped.h1: Russia says bus strike kills 5 in border region with Ukraine
scraped.body_text:
The strike comes as Ukraine launched more than hundreds of drones at Moscow after a Russian missile barrage on Kyiv, as President Zelenskyy sought to calm growing tensions over Ukraine’s military leadership.

Russia said Monday that a Ukrainian strike on a bus in the border region of Belgorod killed five civilians, including a minor, and left three others critically injured.

The attack came after a Ukrainian retaliatory strike on Moscow, with city officials reporting that more than 400 drones targeted the Russian capital.

The latest escalation followed Russian ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities over the weekend.

In eastern Ukraine , Russian attacks on Pavlograd and Kramatorsk killed two people in each city, according to local authorities.

Officials also reported one person killed in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia during Russian bombardment.

Both sides have previously denied targeting civilians.

Ukraine targeted the Russian capital with more than 400 drones from Sunday into Monday, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.

He added that most of the drones were intercepted, but Moscow region Gov. Andrei Vorobyov said at least 10 people were wounded by Ukrainian drones.

Several residential buildings and civilian infrastructure facilities were also damaged.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces were targeting Russian logistics facilities and an oil depot in the region.

"We are responding, justly, to every Russian strike against our cities and communities," Zelenskyy said in a post on X.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's military publicly denied rumors that Zelenskyy was firing the chief of Ukraine's armed forces, Oleksandr Syrskyi.

Zelenskyy has faced criticism over the dismissal of Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov last week.

There have been days of protests in Ukraine following Fedorov's removal, as a long-running dispute between the reform-minded minister and Syrskyi spilled into the open.

Zelenskyy appointed Yevhenii Khmara, the acting head of Ukraine's Security Service (SBU), as acting defense minister and asked parliament to approve him for the position.

On Monday, he posted several messages on social media showing him meeting with Ukraine's top military commanders to discuss the latest developments in the war, which has dragged on for more than four years.

Britain’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, says he can connect with the northern working-class voters who were once Labour’s base. Yet after decades of deindustrialization, it’s less clear that the party can rebuild its roots outside the main cities.

Andy Burnham delivers his inaugural speech as the UK’s new prime minister, July 20, 2026. (Dan Kitwood / Getty Images)

Celebrate the mob that made modern politics and subscribe for $7.89

I am no expert in US politics, but seeing flags on front lawns through the windows of a coach from Chicago to Urbana-Champaign in fall 2022 prompted my first inkling that Donald Trump winning a second term was a distinct possibility. Closer to home in England, a night out this spring in the impoverished but picturesque former mining town of Barnsley — twenty-five miles from where I work and live in Leeds — was my first direct encounter with a phenomenon I had till then only read about in the press. For I saw rows and rows of houses and businesses adorned with “patriotic” St George and Union flags as part of the Raise the Colours campaign. A couple of months down the line and Labour lost control of Barnsley city council for the first time in fifty years, with Nigel Farage’s far-right Reform UK taking charge. If the former Labour stronghold, which suffered more under austerity than virtually anywhere else in Britain, provided a damning indictment of Keir Starmer’s failure to connect with large swaths of the population, it also showcased how and why the future of the Labour Party and national politics would be fought far from Westminster.

If God loves a trier, the time is nigh for the self-appointed “King of the North.” Andy Burnham twice ran unsuccessfully for the Labour leadership (losing to Ed Miliband in 2010 and Jeremy Corbyn in 2015) when the party was in opposition, before being elected mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017. As a mayor rather than an MP, Burnham was ineligible to make a leadership challenge against Starmer following Labour’s battering in this May’s local elections. This changed when Labour MP Josh Simons agreed to step aside and trigger a by-election in Makerfield this June 18, thus allowing Burnham to run as the Labour candidate and win the election. Once back in Parliament, Burnham was rapidly anointed as Labour’s next leader, and Starmer has now stepped aside to let him become Britain’s new prime minister.

Burnham running in this specific constituency was a calculated risk. On the one hand, he had popular grassroots appeal in Makerfield, located roughly halfway between Manchester and Liverpool, not far from where he was born. It is also exactly the kind of postindustrial working-class area in which Reform has overtaken Labour (it had won in May’s local elections there). By running, Burnham was not only putting himself in a position to become leader but also pitching his candidacy by showing that he — and perhaps only he — could reclaim for Labour a northern demographic that the party had for too long taken for granted.

Burnham has reiterated that four-plus decades of neoliberal rule by both Labour and Conservative governments has been catastrophic for the North. He also served as mayor of Manchester at a time when the city council of Birmingham — the UK’s second-biggest city and Europe’s largest local authority — was declared bankrupt. A sports-mad music junkie, Burnham intuitively grasps the real significance of emotion and tribal identities.

Attending a gig in Barnsley recently reinformed my conviction that culture and politics rarely exist in isolation. More than that, it highlighted the challenges Burnham faces in safeguarding his own political future, the Labour Party, and northern England outside of booming Manchester alone.

A s an academic discipline, cultural studies are forever associated with the University of Birmingham, where Richard Hoggart and Stuart Hall ran a highly influential research center. The discipline’s foundational text — Hoggart’s The Uses of Literacy — drew on his experiences growing up further north, in Hunslet, a working-class area of Leeds.

In an age of nearly full employment, he noted the importance of belonging to a local working men’s club (national membership was over two million in the late 1950s) and popular entertainment: “Some features of songs and singing among the working classes illustrate better than anything else both their contact with older traditions and their capacity for assimilating and modifying new materials to their established industry.”

A snapshot of this continuity appears in the most famous cinematic depiction of Barnsley: Ken Loach’s Kes , from 1969. Up north to adapt Barry Hines’s 1968 novel A Kestrel for a Knave for the big screen, Loach and screenwriter Tony Garnett were in Barnsley’s Club Ba-Ba when they witnessed the stage act of local lass Lynne Perrie — affectionately known as “Little Miss Dynamite” across the northern club scene where she had shared stages with the Beatles in their early years — and cast the entertainer in her debut role as the protagonist’s mother. Perrie’s character does not perform on stage in the film. But she is seen enjoying a night out singing along to an innuendo-laden music hall routine, alongside drunken men from the pit, flush with cash after getting paid.

Born in Barnsley, Hines escaped pit life by passing the infamous eleven-plus, a preteen standardized examination that long determined young Britons’ future by putting a select few on an academic pathway to middle-class professions by attending non-fee-paying grammar schools, whereas their peers were sent to secondary moderns — institutions that provided rudimentary education and fodder for local factories. Hines and Garnett (who, like me, attended a grammar school in Birmingham) both felt a sense of class betrayal on passing the eleven-plus, and sought to present an elegiac depiction of the beauty and wasted opportunities of working-class lives.

In a rare public appearance by Garnett in London shortly before his death in 2020, the grammar-school-boy-done-good was brought close to tears talking about how Britain continued to consign so much human potential to the dustbin, before working-class individuals had a chance to begin life. Kes , now considered a classic of British social-realist cinema, was no easy sell: London-based production and distribution companies showed little interest in a film about the uncouth northern provinces. Only the influx of US dollars secured a local booking in the neighboring town of Doncaster. In her memoirs, Perrie is disparaging about the premiere taking place in a small Yorkshire town as opposed to, say, London or Los Angeles. Still, she remained grateful to the role for getting her cast as Ivy Tilsley (1971–94) in the world’s longest-running soap opera, the Manchester-based Coronation Street .

With the closing of the pits and the liberalization of all aspects of life, including the nighttime economy, the golden age of working men’s clubs came to an end. Audiences and bands who cut their teeth in such environments were nevertheless easy to spot. Saxon may never have made it is as big as Iron Maiden or Def Leppard, but the Barnsley heavy-metal titans maintain a loyal global following to the present day, for both their musical chops and repartee. I spent childhood summers during the 1980s and 1990s in Barnsley as my grandparents had bought a small farm locally; after retiring from the armed forces, my granddad worked as a secondary-school teacher. Truth be told, he had picked what he rightly identified as an easy option. He was expected to do the bare minimum for local children, who it was assumed would not amount to much.

W ith dwindling career opportunities, the often angry white youth of towns such as Barnsley were prime recruiting grounds for the army and constituted the fanbase for the cult punk rock band the Macc Lads, formed in 1981, whose most iconic album, Beer & Sex & Chips n Gravy appeared in 1985. Their politically incorrect repertoire includes such classics as “Now He’s a Poof” (“He’s got some black bloke sleeping in his bed / AIDS and herpes, he’s got ‘em / The evidence is written all over his bottom”), “Charlotte” (“Said her name was Charlotte and she wanted to suck my dick / Oh, I thought now lad, times are hard, and it’s nearly closing time”), and “Buenos Aires” (“There was a load of bloody fairies in Buenos bloody Aires / You can keep that poof Ardiles, we’re going to have your Malvinas”).

Concerts often descended into mass brawls. The band was, for example, banned from Birmingham’s Hummingbird venue after their fans caused thousands of pounds of damage at a concert in 1989. According to a later retrospective published in the Guardian : “Listen closely and the Macc Lads were always a subversive parody of such macho bigotry.” I’m not so sure. The band may not be as Neanderthal as their song titles, but much of their audience took the songs at face value, and unlike, say, ska punk band Madness, which also attracted far-right fans, they never issued statements to correct or challenge audience prejudices.

After a decade laying waste to Britain and mainland Europe (they had a surprisingly loyal following in Germany), the Macc Lads disbanded after a farewell gig at Nottingham’s Rock City in December 1995. In recent years, the Macc Lads, or to be more precise, the Macc Lad — given only the singer Muttley McLad (real name Tristan O’Neill) remains from the original lineup — have recommenced touring. They rarely play primary markets in big cities now but retain a loyal following in the Reform strongholds of postindustrial Britain.

Following a mediocre meal in a peculiar Indian restaurant adorned with photographs of the owner with 1960s rock’n’roll juvenile Cliff Richard (the septuagenarian had dined here after being released from questioning over child sexual assault allegations), this March I joined five hundred fans to watch the Macc Lads pay a sold-out show at Barnsley’s Birdwell venue . A pogoing audience did the heavy lifting for a band going through the motions. Muttley — whose relatively healthy complexion suggests he hardly lives off beer, gravy, and chips — milked trademark facial gestures and introduced the band’s latest recruit (in real life an Englishman called Shaun) as smelly Pablo González (“He is Mexican. Like gravy, he arrived in a small boat. Pablo has a drum kit and knows only four English words. Fortunately they are: FUCK!, CUNT! WANK! SHIT!”).

Balding leather-wearing middle-aged men predominated, but a surprisingly number of young people and women were in attendance. For a white, heterosexual male such as myself, the Macc Lads concert and surrounding bars were a welcoming environment in which patrons felt relaxed among their own. Old-school thuggery has not altogether disappeared from northern towns (for instance, soccer hooliganism, in much of Britain a relic of the 1980s, is alive and kicking in Doncaster), but the reactionary turn in British politics is all the more insidious because it caters to all the family. A London editorial meeting of Modern Language Review on May 16 coincided with a Unite the Kingdom rally through the city center. My coeditors and I exited onto the streets to encounter not violence but a carnival-like atmosphere, as intergenerational groups enjoyed a family day with some northerners visiting the capital for the first time.

But communities exclude as well as include. Many of my grandparents’ generation dismissed objections to old-school racist comedians such as Bernard Manning and Roy Chubby Brown (whose performances came with the explicit warning, “if easily offended, please stay away”) as the stuff of politically correct killjoys.

The festive atmosphere at a Macc Lads concert may not include all tastes or racial backgrounds. Still, there are far worse investments of time for southern-based politicians and pundits than having a night out in the north. Vestiges of a traditional working-class British culture can still be detected in the architecture of, say, the City Varieties (a former music hall) in central Leeds or the longstanding Duck and Drake pub. Still, such culture is more overt in ungentrified towns such as Barnsley, whose low rents allow country and western theme bars to coexist alongside more traditional community venues such as the Hoyland Common Working Mens Club (now open to nonmembers) and the fish-and-chip shop featured in Kes , a century-old business that just about remains afloat through loyal local customers and a nascent heritage industry.

The people of Barnsley have lost a lot — and have metaphorically raised the barricades to preserve what is left of their community and culture. Matt Goodwin’s recent bestseller, Suicide of a Nation: Immigration, Islam, Identity , has become a hot topic of conversation in working-class homes, pubs and clubs. Reform UK has capitalized on disenchantment with both the Conservative and Labour parties to inspire many people who have either never voted, or not done so for many years. “When was the last time you voted with enthusiasm?” was among the most successful slogans of Spain’s left-wing Podemos party. In Britain, at the opposite end of the political spectrum, the buzz of conversations in some ways reminds me of the atmosphere in Spain’s squares during the 15-M movement. There, truth be told, I heard just as many false premises and non sequiturs (for instance, one peculiar presentation in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol on the need for the masses to incarnate the spirit of Agustina de Aragón, the nineteenth-century heroine, painted by Goya, who defied local political elites to defend the nation against Europe).

The analogy only goes so far; the potential real-life consequences unleashed by the discourse of right-wing commentator Matt Goodwin and his acolytes are dystopian. If the only remedy against the “suicide” of a nation is self-defense against Muslim communities (just 6.5 percent of the British population), it is hard to conceive how this crusade might be waged without recourse to institutional or vigilante violence.

If universities once provided a refuge for failed politicians, recent populist movements have offered a plan B for frustrated academics. Goodwin took voluntary severance from a full professorship at the financially beleaguered University of Kent (whose website still boasts of his 2022 appointment as a Social Mobility Commissioner for the UK government); Pablo Iglesias and many of the leading lights from Podemos only turned to parliamentary politics once attempts to secure tenure at Madrid’s Complutense University turned sour. While an inability to translate their message to nongraduate working-class voters was instrumental to Podemos’s decline, Goodwin and Farage — the opportunistic, privately educated Reform UK leader — have had far more effective communication strategies.

T he populist right’s success has been delivered on a plate by the frequent perception, in many predominantly white working-class communities, that Starmer and Corbyn (who attended a private primary school before passing the eleven-plus) belong to the condescending, out-of-touch metropolitan elite.

Already long before scandals over Starmer’s appointment of Peter Mandelson as Britain’s ambassador to Washington, Mandelson had lost all credibility with his local constituents when he confused mushy peas in a fish-and-chip shop for guacamole. Doncaster North may have retained Ed Miliband as its MP since 2005, but the then opposition leader made a fool of himself in 2012 with his attempt to brand the Conservatives as out of touch for introducing a so-called pastry tax on takeaway food; his plan backfired after viral images circulated of him looking aghast as he bit into a sausage roll .

Burnham’s personal and professional biography has, up to now at least, made him immune to such gaffes. His free run to the Labour leadership is, in no small part, due to the fact that he is Labour’s first major player in recent years able to inspire similar excitement to Reform UK in long-forgotten places like Barnsley. For once, these towns are at the center of political conversations in Britain. If the Labour government under Burnham’s leadership cannot deliver on the promise invested in him, then we will, I fear, be taken another step closer to a Trump-like administration under Farage and his ilk.

Duncan Wheeler holds the chair of Spanish Studies at the University of Leeds. He is author of Following Franco: Spanish Politics and Culture in Transition (Manchester University Press, 2020).

articles.title: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
articles.summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?
articles.ai_summary: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is set to visit Cyprus to revive stalled peace talks.

scraped.title: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
scraped.description: UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?
scraped.h1: Guterres to visit Cyprus as UN seeks to revive peace talks
scraped.body_text:
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres will visit Cyprus next week in what is seen as an effort to kickstart the stalled peace process. Why now? What is known about the plan? And what might be different this time round?

Monday marks the 52nd anniversary of Turkey's 1974 invasion of Cyprus , which led to the division of the island.

Five decades later, the Cyprus issue remains one of the world's longest-running unresolved disputes.

The United Nations announced last week that Antonio Guterres is due to visit Cyprus from July 27 to 29 — the first visit by a UN secretary-general in 16 years — in an effort to breathe new life into the stalled peace process.

His visit marks the culmination of a renewed UN initiative that was launched after an informal enlarged meeting on Cyprus held in Geneva in March.

Since then, the UN secretary-general's personal envoy, Maria Angela Holguin, has held a series of consultations in Cyprus, Greece, Turkey , the United Kingdom and Brussels to assess whether the political conditions exist for meaningful negotiations to resume.

During his stay in Cyprus, Guterres will hold separate meetings with President of the Republic of Cyprus Nikos Christodoulides and Turkish Cypriot leader Tufan Erhurman.

On July 29, the two leaders are expected to meet jointly with the UN chief at the residence of the UN Special Representative in the UN-controlled buffer zone.

The last time a UN secretary-general visited Cyprus was in 2010, when Ban Ki-moon sought to inject political momentum into negotiations between then President of the Republic of Cyprus Demetris Christofias and Turkish Cypriot leader Mehmet Ali Talat.

Both leaders came from left-wing political parties that supported a bizonal, bicommunal federation and were widely seen as having the political will to pursue a comprehensive settlement.

That momentum, however, faded only months later after Talat lost the Turkish Cypriot leadership election to Dervis Eroglu, while major disagreements over the core chapters of the negotiations remained unresolved.

Ban's efforts were preceded by the intensive engagement of Kofi Annan between 2002 and 2004, when the UN undertook its most ambitious effort to broker a comprehensive settlement of the Cyprus issue.

Annan became personally involved in the negotiations, presenting a series of revised versions of what became known as the Annan Plan.

The initiative culminated in simultaneous referendums in April 2004. The proposal was approved by a majority of Turkish Cypriot voters but rejected by 75.8% of Greek Cypriot voters.

Guterres' visit comes amid reports that the UN is exploring a possible new framework for resolving the Cyprus issue.

The discussion gained momentum after Britain's The Independent reported on July 12 that Holguin is working on a revised settlement proposal.

According to the newspaper, the framework would retain the agreed model of a bizonal, bicommunal federation, as set out in relevant UN Security Council resolutions, while granting significantly greater autonomy to the two constituent states and limiting the powers of the federal government.

The report also claims that, in exchange for this broader autonomy, the Turkish Cypriot side would be expected to accept territorial adjustments, including the return of the fenced-off city of Varosha and the town of Morphou.

It also suggests that new security arrangements are being considered that would allow Greek and Turkish troops to remain on the island under NATO command.

According to The Independent , the proposal seeks to bridge the gap between the Greek Cypriot commitment to a federal settlement and Turkey's long-standing support for a two-state solution.

The UN has neither confirmed nor denied the report.

Asked about it, President Christodoulides said that "not everything reported by the newspaper is accurate," adding that he expects further developments in the coming period.

Despite the expectations surrounding Guterres' visit, diplomats say the UN chief's immediate objective is not to discuss a draft settlement plan.

Diplomatic sources who spoke to DW believe the most likely outcome of the meetings next week will be the announcement of a new informal expanded meeting bringing together the leaders of Cyprus' two communities, representatives of Greece, Turkey and the UK — the island's three guarantor powers under the 1960 treaties — and the UN.

According to the same sources, such a meeting could take place in late August or early September. Unlike previous informal gatherings, however, the UN is said to be seeking a more structured process this time, with a clearer sequence of steps and a defined timeframe.

Although Guterres' renewed engagement is inevitably linked to the final months of his second term, which ends in December, diplomatic sources believe the latest initiative is driven by more than his limited remaining time in office.

For the first time in years, they believe conditions for a renewed political dialogue may be emerging.

A key factor has been the election of Tufan Erhurman as Turkish Cypriot leader last October . Unlike his predecessor, Ersin Tatar, who advocated a two-state solution, Erhurman has said he is prepared to resume negotiations on the basis of a bizonal, bicommunal federation.

That change does not represent a shift in Turkey's official policy, nor does it resolve longstanding disagreements over security, guarantees, political equality or the continued presence of Turkish troops on the island.

It has, however, created conditions that allow the UN to test whether a meaningful return to negotiations is now possible.

Cyprus government spokesperson Konstantinos Letymbiotis believes Guterres' visit should also be viewed in the context of a broader increase in international diplomatic activity on Cyprus.

"The secretary-general's initiative, the European Union 's stronger engagement and the appointment of Executive Vice-President Raffaele Fitto as the EU's envoy on Cyprus are creating new momentum," he told DW.

On July 8, European Council President Antonio Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen discussed the UN initiative with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, urging Ankara to make use of the renewed diplomatic momentum on Cyprus.

A few days later, the Commission appointed Raffaele Fitto as its special representative for the Cyprus issue.

The move was widely interpreted as a sign that Brussels intends to play a more substantive role in the process, while underlining that any future settlement must be fully compatible with EU law.

The EU's increased involvement is also closely linked to the broader trajectory of EU-Turkey relations.

From Brussels' perspective, progress on the Cyprus issue could facilitate movement on several key areas of cooperation with Ankara.

Conversely, the absence of progress continues to be one of the main obstacles preventing any meaningful upgrade in relations between the EU and Turkey.

Edited by: Aingeal Flanagan

articles.title: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
articles.summary: A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?
articles.ai_summary: A historic treaty continues to limit NATO's military operations in the Black Sea amid ongoing conflict involving Ukraine and Russia.

scraped.title: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
scraped.description: A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?
scraped.h1: Why a 90-year-old treaty limits NATO in the Black Sea
scraped.body_text:
A 90-year-old treaty still shapes the balance of power in the Black Sea. As Ukraine fights on against Russia, can NATO project power into waters it can't enter freely?

Now more than four years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , the Black Sea has become one of Europe's key security frontiers. And yet, it is currently "quite empty of warships," Thomas de Waal, a senior fellow at Carnegie Europe, told DW. This, he said, "is a bit of a paradox." To understand that paradox, we first need to need to take a closer look at the map.

The Black Sea is bordered by six countries: Turkey , Bulgaria , Romania , Ukraine , Russia , and Georgia . The first three on that list are part of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, or NATO — the other three are not. To make matters more complicated, two of the latter three are at war with each other.

Access to the Black Sea runs through a single, narrow bottleneck. To get there, a ship coming from the Mediterranean Sea would have to pass the Dardanelles Straits and the Bosporus, which crosses through the heart of Turkey's largest metropolis Istanbul .

At its narrowest point, the Bosporus is just 700 meters (0.4 miles) wide. For comparison, another critical passageway currently in the headlines is the Strait of Hormuz , which is approximately 33 kilometers (21 miles) wide at its narrowest point.

It is this geographic bottleneck to the Black Sea that makes it "an economic choke point," said de Waal. "Whoever controls the Turkish Straits also controls, to some extent, trade through the Black Sea and also has an enormous military advantage."

Russia also has a special interest in the Black Sea, according to Daria Isachenko, a visiting fellow at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs. "A strong military position in the Black Sea for Russia is not an end in itself, but also a means to advance its geopolitical ambitions beyond and also strengthen its great power status."

The second part of the equation goes back to a treaty signed exactly 90 years ago.

On July 20, 1936, representatives from just under a dozen countries gathered in the Swiss town of Montreux to settle a long-standing dilemma: How — and by whom — should these vital waterways be governed? They established the Montreux Convention, an agreement that essentially restored Turkey's sovereignty over the Dardanelles Strait and Bosporus. This came after years of international oversight, following the Ottoman Empire's defeat in the First World War .

Negotiations resulted in a document of nearly 30 pages, which set the legal framework that governs the Turkish Straits to this day. The treaty keeps the straits open to passenger and commercial traffic during peacetime — crucial for the important trade route.

When it comes to military ships, Black Sea states are allowed to move their warships through the straits relatively freely. Any navy from outside the region faces restrictions on their fleet size, tonnage, and how long they are allowed to stay in the sea — no longer than 21 days during peacetime.

During times of war, these rules become stricter. When Turkey is not part of the conflict, warships belonging to any nation involved in the fight are not allowed to pass through — a clause that has had profound consequences for the region since February 2022.

This special system of access rights keeps the Turkish government in a very powerful position. "The most privileged Black Sea state is Türkiye itself," Isachenko said.

It also helps explain why NATO doesn't maintain a continuous presence in the Black Sea — unlike in other waters such as the Mediterranean or the North Sea. "For NATO, Montreux is a constraint," Isachenko pointed out. "For Türkiye, it is an instrument to keep the balance in the Black Sea."

When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in late February 2022, the Montreux Convention arguably faced its greatest test in decades. A few days after the military operation began, Turkey invoked Article 19 of the treaty, which applies during wartime and restricts military ships belonging to countries engaged in the fight from passing through the straits.

Essentially, from that point onwards, neither Russia, nor Ukraine, could freely reinforce their naval forces in the Black Sea — with one exception: warships registered to a home port in the Black Sea could return to their base.

"I think the Montreux Convention and Turkey's policy at the beginning of the war was absolutely crucial in allowing Ukraine to survive," Thomas de Waal told DW.

He argued that it prevented Russia from adding more vessels to their Black Sea fleet, saying that "up to 30 Russian ships stayed outside." This, he added, contributed to Ukraine holding "the upper hand in the Black Sea."

Those restrictions may also have highlighted how warfare itself has changed, with Ukraine turning to drones and other modern technology not covered by the 1936 document. "Ukraine didn't build military vessels," according to Iulian Chifu, a Romanian foreign policy analyst. "It just shifted the generation of attack," he said.

The maritime treaty has also restricted the options available to Ukraine's supporters in the West. In 2024, the United Kingdom donated two minesweepers to Ukraine, which were unable to enter the Black Sea, according to the UK Ministry of Defence. That's because Turkey considers them to be "vessels of war," according to de Waal. Instead, the ships have been docked in Portsmouth, in southern England.

For de Waal, this illustrates Turkey's wider approach: "It's a very carefully constructed strategy," he said," in which Turkey basically says to other NATO countries: 'Leave us alone in the Black Sea, we will handle this.'"

Key to the convention's enduring relevance may be its long-standing recognition by states. "Turkey has come up with an arrangement, a regime, which Russia is not especially happy about, but accepts, and that's very important," he noted.

At a time when the international rules-based order has increasingly come under pressure , the Montreux Convention stands out as a rare example of a multilateral diplomatic mechanism that is still observed and respected 90 years after it was signed.

The geography of the Turkish Straits — plus their complex governance structure — have led to NATO rethinking how it can operate in the region. At times, the issue even creates some tension between its alliance members: "In the Black Sea," de Waal explained, "Turkey is very much Turkey first and NATO second."

This security logic, he argued, has shaped Turkey's message to its Western allies: "We don't want to see your permanent presence in the Black Sea, but Romania and Bulgaria have this shared Black Sea ownership, so you can support them."

As a result, greater focus has been placed on these two Eastern European states, which have been NATO members since 2004. However, some experts remain doubtful: "The military capabilities of Bulgaria and Romania," said Chifu, "are barely limited to their capacity of defending their territories."

Nevertheless, he argued that Romania had been "trying to improve our capabilities building ships," as well as purchasing military assets, with the aim of "enforcing our footprint in the Black Sea."

One example is the planned expansion of Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base near the Romanian port city Constanța. Romania's government is expected to spend € 2.5 billion ($ 2.8 billion) on transforming it into the largest NATO military base in Europe — bigger than Ramstein, a US military base in Germany.

Earlier this month, the region was in the spotlight once again, as leaders of NATO's member states met in the Turkish capital Ankara for their annual summit . There, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria announced a trilateral task group for mine-clearing efforts to protect underwater infrastructure.

The Montreux Convention is "quite an archaic document," de Waal told DW, pointing out that it still refers to the League of Nations — the UN 's predecessor, which ceased to exist 80 years ago. "But I think no one wants to touch it," out of concern that it "opens a kind of Pandora's box when all the issues have to be renegotiated with Russia," he added.

"For Türkiye," said Isachenko, Montreux "also belongs to a number of founding treaties of the Turkish Republic." Beyond its role as a maritime access treaty, it reflects Turkey's core interests: "sovereignty, security and status," she added, so challenging Montreux means "dealing, revising and challenging" those core interests.

Security analyst Chifu stressed that he was "not revisionist" and believed the convention should stay in place while the Ukraine war rages on. "But after the war," he said, "we should reconsider very clearly how this is applied to our allies in NATO."

To him, the question of how exactly the treaty's clauses are applied and interpreted by Turkey remains a sore point.

"You have no option but to work with Turkey," is the key message de Waal took away from the recent NATO summit in Ankara. "You can't work without it," he said, referring to what he calls the strongest power in the Black Sea.

For the past nine decades, the Montreux Convention has outlasted wars, leaders, and entire generations. And as long as it lasts, Turkey holds sway over the Black Sea gateway.

Editors: Peter Hille and Don MacCoitir

scraped.title: Amid grinding war, protesting Ukrainians still want their voices and values heard at home
scraped.description: The defense minister’s firing was the catalyst, but polling suggests Ukrainians are rallying around a broader fight for freedoms and against corruption.
scraped.author: Gerard Toal
scraped.h1: Amid grinding war, protesting Ukrainians still want their voices and values heard at home
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Ukraine is experiencing its largest domestic protests since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022. The spark to the unrest was the summary dismissal on July 15, 2026 , of the country’s youthful defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, appointed just six months ago.

Fedorov, seen as charismatic and tech savvy, was already viewed by some as a leading light for change, with a reformist message that chimed with many Ukrainians . So his ouster – the consequence of a clash with Oleksandr Syrskyi , the head of the country’s armed forces and part of the older guard — tapped into a generational clash over how best to defeat Russia.

Frustrations, though, have been building in Ukraine for some time, including over contentious recruiting methods and corruption allegations. Indeed, the latter was the primary reason for demonstrations in Ukraine in the summer of 2025.

Wars are by nature national emergencies, during which politics as normal is often suspended . Before the war and especially after 2014, Ukraine had a lively democracy and public sphere . After the 2022 invasion, Ukraine introduced martial law , placed its television stations under central government control and suspended elections .

For Ukraine, these protests raise important questions about public unity, corruption and the agility of the military-industrial establishment to fight a war now in its fifth year. Our new polling data, gathered by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS), provides important context to the current demonstrations, and insights into the wartime priorities of ordinary Ukrainians. From June 9 to 26, 2026, we surveyed 1,801 people across the country in a computer-aided-telephone survey.

Here are three findings from that survey that provide a broader context to the demonstrations.

Ukraine may be at war but fighting corruption at home and maintaining media freedom still matter a great deal to Ukrainians.

Mindful of last summer’s attempt by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to scrap the independence of two of Ukraine’s anti-corruption agencies, we asked ordinary Ukrainians if they felt these agencies “should be safeguarded” even with Ukraine at war with Russia. We also asked if they felt the same about “freedom of the press and media.”

About half of Ukrainians think that anti-corruption agencies should be safeguarded a lot during the war. An additional 26% of Ukrainians said they should be safeguarded a little. Only a minority (16%) think that anti-corruption agencies should not be safeguarded at all.

Likewise, Ukrainians believe in the vital role of journalism.

Despite war-time media restrictions, Ukraine retains a robust online public sphere and a free press . Indeed, it played a role in mobilizing Ukrainians against the unpopular dismissal of Fedorov.

The protests are in keeping with our poll which finds that a strong majority (62%) of Ukrainians think that freedom of the press and the media needs to be safeguarded a lot. Only about 5% do not think it should be safeguarded at all.

Previous polling by KIIS revealed that the war with Russia and corruption were what Ukrainians considered the most serious problems facing the country. We decided to follow up by asking Ukrainians what they would rank first as the bigger problem: “Russian aggression” or “government corruption, including around mobilization.”

The results were surprising. Although the most common response was Russian aggression (49%), more than a third of respondents ranked government corruption tied to mobilization as the country’s top challenge. Another 14% said Russian aggression and corruption were equal concerns.

Public opinion research elsewhere reveals that many Ukrainians still optimistically view the war against Russia as a fight for a future in which Ukraine is an established democracy within the European Union. In this sense, the values evident in the survey responses may be what makes the war meaningful for many Ukrainians.

Even during an exhausting war which of late has seen increased Russian attacks on civilians , Ukrainians prioritize domestic reforms and democratic accountability like fighting corruption.

Although manpower is seen as essential for Ukraine’s war effort against a larger Russian adversary, the process of getting new military recruits has proved contentious.

Ukrainian military authorities have sometimes used violent methods to enforce military service, and the lowering of the draft from 27 to 25 in April 2024 was unpopular.

We asked whether Ukrainians agreed that it “was time to draft all young Ukrainian men into military service.” A clear majority of respondents disagreed with this sentiment, with more than a fifth objecting “very strongly.” Less that 8% fully agreed.

What this indicates to us is a strong societal consensus that Ukraine should continue to protect its adolescent and young men from military mobilization, despite the persistent recruitment crisis facing its military.

One of the attractions of Fedorov to young people was that his preference for unmanned drones over on-the-ground combat forces offers a promise of Ukrainian victory without large-scale casualties. Syrskyi, by contrast, is associated with Soviet-style attritional warfare. Fairly or not, the latter acquired the nickname “the butcher ” some time ago.

Fedorov’s promise of victory through technological transformation to support drone warfare may be an illusion. But his very public attack on Ukraine’s current military-industrial establishment posed a serious challenge to its legitimacy and public support. A figure with close ties to Silicon Valley and political ambitions, Fedorov is a disrupter in the mold of many contemporary tech figures.

Whether his polices ultimately serve the cause of Ukraine at this consequential moment in its war with Russia is an open question. But the demonstrations that followed his dismissal nonetheless suggest the multitude of ways Ukrainians view democracy and freedom at home and abroad.

Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Colorado Boulder

Professor of Government and International Affairs, Virginia Tech

Professor of Geography, University of Colorado Boulder

scraped.title: Zohran Mamdani’s City Hall Wants to Build Tenant Unions
scraped.description: A new New York City initiative, led by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Office of Mass Engagement, will send volunteer organizers into neglected buildings to help tenants organize, testing the role government can play in building collective working-class power.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

A new New York City initiative, led by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Office of Mass Engagement, will send volunteer organizers into neglected buildings to help tenants organize, testing the role government can play in building collective working-class power.

Zohran Mamdani’s administration says it’s upping enforcement of tenant protection laws. But the mayor also seems to understand that such enforcement is impossible without organizing mass numbers of tenants to demand action themselves. (Michael M. Santiago / Getty Images)

Celebrate the mob that made modern politics and subscribe for $7.89

A t New York’s first “Rental Ripoff” hearing this year, tenants packed a high-school gym in Brooklyn to share horror stories.

“We’ve had our neighbors trapped in elevators. We’ve had people slip and fall. We’ve had windows fall on people. We’ve had the ceiling collapse on people,” Angela Landress, a representative of one Flatbush tenant’s association, told the crowd.

The hearings were more of a listening session than a traditional hearing, with Cea Weaver, the head of the Mayor’s Office to Protect Tenants, speaking one-on-one with tenants to gather their complaints. As Weaver — a longtime tenant organizer profiled by Liza Featherstone earlier this year for Jacobin — told attendees, “Tenants pay rent every month, and we deserve a say in what happens in the decisions that the city makes that impact our lives. I also believe that the most protected tenant is an empowered tenant who knows their rights and can organize with their neighbors.”

The Mamdani administration is now trying to encourage that kind of organizing. The mayor’s office is launching “Talk to Tenants,” a campaign that will send volunteers door-to-door in buildings with chronic housing code violations, connecting renters with organizing resources, neighborhood organizations, and training on tenants’ rights and how to build tenant associations. The effort will be led by the Office of Mass Engagement in partnership with the Office to Protect Tenants. It will begin in East Harlem, Washington Heights and Inwood, and Flatbush, targeting areas with particularly distressed housing.

“The Rental Ripoff hearings showed us something that every tenant already knows: when landlords neglect their buildings, New Yorkers are left with no heat, kitchens overrun with cockroaches, mold, and broken elevators,” Mamdani told Jacobin . “When neighbors organize, they have the power to hold bad landlords accountable and win safe, dignified housing. ‘Talk to Tenants’ is about empowering New Yorkers to build that power one conversation, one building, and one block at a time.”

The city already funds community organizations that organize tenants in distressed rent-regulated buildings through HPD’s Partners in Preservation program. But under the new initiative, city hall, which describes tenant organizing as a cornerstone of its housing plan , will use its own significant reach and infrastructure to make the first contact.

“From a next-door neighbor who is available to bring in your mail when you’re away to widespread collective action to win better repairs and respect from the landlord, the community and solidarity of a tenant association is the very foundation of New York City,” said Weaver. “The most protected tenant is an organized tenant. Through the ‘Talk to Tenants’ campaign, we are calling on New Yorkers to join together with their neighbors and partner with us to secure dignified and affordable housing for all.”

The administration announced the program following its findings from the Rental Ripoff hearings. The Rental Ripoff report , which summarizes testimony from more than 2,400 New Yorkers, found that the most common housing issue reported to the city’s 311 service is a lack of heat and hot water: over the last three years, heat and hot water complaints made up 35 percent of all reported housing maintenance issues. Pests, mold, and leaks were also frequent complaints.

“Many of these complaints come from a small group of properties, suggesting that some tenants repeatedly face hot water outages or unsafe cold conditions, and that there is a persistent set of noncompliant building owners,” the report states.

Announcing the findings and a suite of proposed reforms — including requiring disclosure of the use of artificial intelligence to alter images or videos in rental listings — and strengthening enforcement against negligent landlords at a press conference in the Tenement Museum last week, Mamdani opened with tenant organizing history.

“December 1907 was not a happy time to be a tenant in New York,” the mayor said. “Two out of every three New Yorkers were living in crammed tenement housing, like those brought to life here in the Tenement Museum. It was brutally cold. Nearly one hundred thousand New Yorkers had just lost their jobs in an economic crisis, and in response, many landlords decided to raise the rent.”

The mayor went on to recount how tenants responded: by organizing. More than ten thousand families went on a rent strike, one of the largest rent strikes in New York history. Recounting that history will be part of the city’s door-knocking initiative.

Sumathy Kumar , director of the New York State Tenant Bloc, said the history matters because tenants are often made to feel that whatever is happening in their building is theirs to endure alone. She pointed to Harlem in the early 1960s, where Jesse Gray and other organizers led tenants on rent strike over rats, broken heat, and other slum conditions. At one Manhattan Civil Court hearing, tenants arrived carrying rats they had trapped in their apartments. They placed the evidence of their landlords’ neglect directly before the court.

“Every force in the real estate industry is trying to tell you that as a tenant, you’re not powerful,” said Kumar. “When you learn about the history of tenant organizing and you join with your neighbors and your neighbors across the city, it gives you the power and the will to fight for more.”

The city’s organizing effort will extend beyond door-knocking. Throughout the summer and early fall, the Office of Mass Engagement also plans to host “NYC 101" workshops on tenant organizing, building tenant unions, and the role collective action has played in improving conditions in New York buildings. The first NYC 101 workshop will be held on August 11 in Lower Manhattan, followed by Prospect Heights on August 19, Flatbush on September 16, East Harlem on September 24, and Washington Heights on September 30.

“So much happens at the door,” Kumar told me. “You get to have a conversation about things that are bringing you together. When we start knocking on each other’s doors, talking about our issues in our apartments, all of a sudden you’re creating a group of people who are acting in solidarity and winning together, even if they’re totally different.”

“The tenants need to run the meeting and the organizing effort,” Kumar said of what meetings are most likely to lead to ongoing tenant associations. “The most important thing in this door-knocking is to find the tenants who are ready to build their own union. That’s when it’s going to be a long-standing fighting organization.”

Earlier this year, tenants in more than ninety Pinnacle Group buildings organized across the landlord’s housing portfolio as the company entered bankruptcy. Through the Union of Pinnacle Tenants, they elected representatives and pushed to participate in a bankruptcy proceeding where tenants rarely have a seat. The Mamdani administration later joined their call to delay the sales.

The campaign did not end in total victory. Bankruptcy law still narrowed what tenants — and elected officials — could achieve. But residents had accomplished something important: they had organized themselves into a constituency that could not be ignored, and city hall had joined them; the Union of Pinnacle Tenants remains active.

“We need to be organizing people right now all the time,” said Kumar. “You never know when a foreclosure might happen or when a sale might happen.” The goal, she argued, is to build organizations that are ready when those moments arrive.

That is ultimately what Mamdani’s initiative is trying to do. Instead of waiting for tenants to organize, the city is asking whether it can help those organizations get started without directing them.

Kumar argued that inspections and stronger enforcement cannot substitute for organized tenants. “Those are not going to work unless the city is partnering with organized tenants at the building level,” she said.

The limits of enforcement are one reason tenant organizers have long argued that inspections alone cannot transform neglected buildings. City agencies can issue violations and bring cases, but organized tenants are often the people who keep pressure on landlords after inspectors leave.

“Every New Yorker has heard the stories — or lived them themselves: landlords who refuse to make basic repairs, ignore dangerous conditions, and leave tenants to deal with mold, pests, and other hazards. ‘Talk to Tenants’ is about reminding renters that they have the right to a safe, clean, and well-maintained home — and the right to organize with their neighbors to demand it,” said Commissioner for the Office of Mass Engagement Tascha Van Auken. “Change often begins with a conversation between neighbors. By knocking on doors and connecting tenants with organizing resources, we’re helping New Yorkers build the collective power to hold negligent landlords accountable and fight for the homes they deserve.”

The administration is trying to pair enforcement with organizing. Its Fix the City initiative, scheduled to launch by the end of this year, will assess large housing portfolios with the most egregious and long-standing code violations and seek to transfer ownership of these properties, while Talk to Tenants is intended to help residents build the organizations that can keep pressure on landlords. What happens after those first conversations is up to the tenants themselves.

Alex N. Press is a staff writer at Jacobin who covers labor organizing.
